The Gemara explains that the verse is necessary because one might have thought that since the community for a הוֹרָאָה (erroneous ruling) brings a bull for a burnt-offering and a goat for a sin-offering, the court in idolatry should bring the opposite.
Alternatively, the verse teaches that one who has no remedy (צָרִיךְ וְאֵין לוֹ תַּקָּנָה) is included in the law.

items.text: Levi's challenge about the number of women and the response
items.text_en: Levi's challenge about the number of women and the response
items.desc_en: Levi asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: why did you teach fifteen women? Teach sixteen! Rabbi Yehuda responds that Levi seems to have no brain in his skull. The Gemara explains that Levi was thinking of the case of a mother who was raped by his father, but that is a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, and the Mishnah does not deal with disputes. The Gemara challenges this with other disputes in the Mishnah, and the Gemara responds that we are speaking of the chapter, and that Beit Shammai's opinion is not considered a Mishnah when Beit Hillel disagrees.

sub.desc_en: Levi asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi why the Mishnah lists fifteen women, suggesting it should list sixteen.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rebukes Levi, saying he seems to have no brain in his skull.
The Gemara asks what Levi was thinking, suggesting he considered the case of a mother raped by his father.
The Gemara explains that the case of a mother raped by his father is a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, and the Mishnah does not deal with disputes.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah does include disputes, such as the case of איסור מצוה (a mitzvah prohibition) and איסור קדושה (a sanctity prohibition) where Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis disagree.
The Gemara resolves that the statement refers to the chapter (פרקין) as a whole, not to individual disputes within it.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah includes a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding צרות (co-wives) being permitted to the brothers.
The Gemara resolves that Beit Shammai's opinion is not considered a Mishnah when Beit Hillel disagrees.

items.text: Rabbi Oshaya's claim and its refutation
items.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya's claim and its refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis disagree in the Mishnah, but Rabbi Shimon does not dispute the case of a yavam born after the yevama. Rabbi Oshaya claimed Rabbi Shimon disputed even that first case, but he was refuted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis disagree in the Mishnah, and the Mishnah teaches the case of a yavam born after the yevama.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Shimon does not dispute the case of a yavam born after the yevama.
Rabbi Oshaya claimed that Rabbi Shimon disputed even the first case in the Mishnah.
The Gemara refutes Rabbi Oshaya's claim, stating that he was rebutted.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's tradition about the Tosefta
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's tradition about the Tosefta
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav, and Rabbi Chiya taught similarly, that in all cases of sisters who are yevamot, the rule applies: the one forbidden to this brother is permitted to that brother, and the sister who is a yevama performs chalitza or yibbum.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rav, and Rabbi Chiya's baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav, and Rabbi Chiya's baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda transmits in Rav's name, and Rabbi Chiya teaches similarly, a general rule: among sisters who are yevamot, the sister forbidden to one brother is permitted to the other, and the sister who is a yevama performs חליצה (chalitza) or יבום (yibbum).

items.text: Rav Yehuda's interpretation: only from his mother-in-law onward
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's interpretation: only from his mother-in-law onward
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets the Tosefta as applying only from the case of his mother-in-law onward, but not to the first six cases (the primary forbidden relatives). The reason is that the daughter (in the first case) can be found through rape but not through marriage, and the Tosefta deals with marriage, not rape.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets the Tosefta as applying only from the case of his mother-in-law onward, excluding the first six cases, and the Gemara asks for the reason.
The Gemara explains that the daughter in the first case can be found through rape but not through marriage, and the Tosefta deals with marriage, not rape.

items.text: Abaye's interpretation: includes his daughter from rape
items.text_en: Abaye's interpretation: includes his daughter from rape
items.desc_en: Abaye interprets the Tosefta as including even his daughter from rape, since she can be found either through rape or marriage. However, he excludes the case of a brother's wife who was not contemporaneous (i.e., a brother who died before the yavam was born), because that case only applies according to Rabbi Shimon, not the Rabbis, and the Tosefta does not deal with disputes.

sub.desc_en: Abaye interprets the Tosefta as including even his daughter from rape, since she can be found either through rape or marriage.
Abaye excludes the case of a brother's wife who was not contemporaneous, because that case only applies according to Rabbi Shimon, not the Rabbis, and the Tosefta does not deal with disputes.

items.text: Rav Safra's interpretation: includes even the non-contemporaneous brother's wife
items.text_en: Rav Safra's interpretation: includes even the non-contemporaneous brother's wife
items.desc_en: Rav Safra interprets the Tosefta as including even the case of a brother's wife who was not contemporaneous, and she can be found in the case of six brothers, according to Rabbi Shimon's opinion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra interprets the Tosefta as including even the non-contemporaneous brother's wife, found in the case of six brothers according to Rabbi Shimon's opinion.

items.text: Mnemonic for the cases
items.text_en: Mnemonic for the cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic to recall the three cases: died, was born, and performed yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic (סימן) to recall the three cases: died, was born, and performed yibbum.

items.text: Rav Adda's resolution: Rabbi Hani does have principles
items.text_en: Rav Adda's resolution: Rabbi Hani does have principles
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Kahana says in the name of Rava that Rabbi Hani does have general principles; the apparent contradiction is resolved by noting that one cannot find a case where a woman is both a sister and a yevamah in two different scenarios.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Hani lacks general principles (כללים) altogether.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Kahana in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Kahana in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Kahana reports in Rava's name that Rabbi Hani does have principles; the apparent contradiction is resolved because one cannot find a case where a woman is both a sister and a yevamah in two different scenarios simultaneously.
The Gemara explains the first scenario: if Jacob raped two sisters, one can find a case where a sister is a yevamah, but not a case where a woman forbidden to one brother is permitted to another.

The Gemara explains the second scenario: if Jacob raped two unrelated women, one can find a case where a woman forbidden to one brother is permitted to another, but not a case where a sister is a yevamah.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative: Rabbi Hani has no principles, the Mishnah is Rabbi Yehudah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative: Rabbi Hani has no principles, the Mishnah is Rabbi Yehudah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that Rabbi Hani indeed has no general principles; the dispute is about the interpretation of the Mishnah, which follows Rabbi Yehudah who forbids an anusat aviv, and therefore the Mishnah does not include that case.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asserts that Rabbi Hani indeed has no general principles, and the dispute is about the interpretation of the Mishnah.

Rav Ashi explains that Rabbi Hani's criticism was that the other rabbi failed to deduce that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehudah, who forbids an anusat aviv (one's mother who was raped by one's father).
Rav Ashi cites the Mishnah's list of six more severe forbidden relatives, noting that 'his mother' cannot be the father's wife (already listed), so it must be an anusat aviv (mother raped by father).
Rav Ashi concludes that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehudah, who forbids an anusat aviv, and therefore the Mishnah does not include that case in its list of permitted tzarot.

items.text: Ravina's objection: Even for Rabbi Yehudah, a case exists if he married
items.text_en: Ravina's objection: Even for Rabbi Yehudah, a case exists if he married
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rav Ashi, noting that even according to Rabbi Yehudah, one can find a case if the brother married the woman after the fact.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rav Ashi that even according to Rabbi Yehuda one can find a case if he violated the prohibition and married her, but the Mishnah does not include such a hypothetical case.

items.text: Rav Ashi's response: The Mishnah deals with permitted cases, not forbidden ones
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's response: The Mishnah deals with permitted cases, not forbidden ones
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi responds that the Mishnah only discusses cases of permitted yevamot, not forbidden ones, and Levi's baraita confirms this by showing that the mother sometimes exempts her rival.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's answer to Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer to Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi tells Rav Kahana that even without the 'if he transgressed' scenario, one can find a case where the mother exempts her rival: Jacob raped his daughter-in-law, had a son, and when Reuben died childless, the mother's prohibition extends to her rival.

Rav Kahana objects that the Mishnah only discusses permitted cases (where the yevamah is permitted to the yavam), not forbidden ones (where the yevamah is forbidden), so the mother's prohibition does not apply.

The Gemara notes that Levi examined his Mishnah and found a baraita that confirms the Mishnah only deals with permitted cases: the mother sometimes exempts her rival and sometimes does not, as shown by the case where the mother was married to the father and then married to the brother.

items.text: Levi's baraita: The mother sometimes exempts her rival
items.text_en: Levi's baraita: The mother sometimes exempts her rival
items.desc_en: Levi's baraita teaches that the mother sometimes exempts her rival and sometimes does not, providing an example where she is married to the father's brother.

sub.desc_en: Levi's baraita teaches that 'his mother' sometimes exempts her co-wife and sometimes does not, giving the example of a mother married to the father and then married to the father's brother.

items.text: Opening Mishnah reference
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah reference
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman was her father's anusat (raped daughter) and then married to her father's brother, and he died, she is the mother who exempts her rival (tzarah) from yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman was her father's anusat (raped daughter) and then married to her father's brother, and he died, she is the mother who exempts her rival (tzarah) from yibbum.

items.text: Gemara's question and Reish Lakish's challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Reish Lakish's challenge
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan why the Mishnah did not include a case where a man performed chalitzah with his yevamah and then betrothed her, and died childless, making her rival forbidden. Rabbi Yochanan responds that such a case is not included because it does not involve a rival's rival. The Gemara then explains that Rabbi Yochanan's answer is based on his view that such a woman is subject to a negative commandment (lav), not karet, and he is speaking to Reish Lakish's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that although the Mishnah listed fifteen women, one could add a sixteenth case like this one.

Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan: according to Levi who includes cases with 'or', why not add the case of a man who performed חליצה (chalitzah) with his yevamah, then betrothed her, and died childless, making her rival forbidden?
Rabbi Yochanan answers that this case is not included because it does not involve a rival's rival (צרת צרה).

The Gemara objects: why not simply say that the woman is subject to a negative commandment (חייבי לאוין), and those subject to a negative commandment are eligible for חליצה (chalitzah) and יבום (yibbum)?

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan was speaking to Reish Lakish's position: according to himself, those subject to a negative commandment are eligible, but according to Reish Lakish, they are subject to כרת (karet), so the case is excluded because it is not a rival's rival.

items.text: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on karet
items.text_en: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on karet
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that the man who performed chalitzah and then betrothed the yevamah is not liable for karet for the chalutzah, but the brothers are liable for karet for the chalutzah; both he and the brothers are liable for karet for the rival. Rabbi Yochanan rules that neither is liable for karet for either woman. The Gemara explains Reish Lakish's reasoning from the verse 'asher lo yivneh' (who does not build), and Rabbi Yochanan's objection that since initially any brother could perform chalitzah, now it cannot become a karet prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that the man who performed chalitzah and then betrothed the yevamah is not liable for karet for the chalutzah, but the brothers are liable for karet for the chalutzah; both he and the brothers are liable for karet for the rival.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that neither the man nor the brothers are liable for karet for either the chalutzah or the rival.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Reish Lakish's position.

The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish derives from the verse 'asher lo yivneh' (who does not build) that once the man has not built, he may not build again, so he is under the prohibition, but his brothers remain as they were.
The Gemara further explains that regarding the chalutzah herself, the man is under the prohibition, but the rival woman remains as she was.
Rabbi Yochanan objects: initially any brother could perform chalitzah, so how can it now become a karet prohibition?
The Gemara resolves that the man acts as an agent of the brothers, and the chalutzah acts as an agent of the rival, so the prohibition applies.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a Mishnah that if a man performed chalitzah and then betrothed the yevamah and died, she requires chalitzah from the brothers. This supports his view (lav) but challenges Reish Lakish's view (karet). The Gemara then notes that the end of that Mishnah states that if a brother betrothed her, she has no claim on him, which would be problematic for Rabbi Yochanan's view. Rav Sheshet resolves that the end of the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that betrothal does not take effect with those liable for a negative commandment.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a Mishnah to Reish Lakish: if a man performed חליצה (chalitzah) and then betrothed the יבמה (yevamah) and died, she requires חליצה from the brothers. This supports Rabbi Yochanan's view (that she is a חייבי לאוין (liable for a negative commandment)) but challenges Reish Lakish's view (that she is a חייבי כריתות (liable for karet)).

The Gemara objects: according to your reasoning, the end of the Mishnah states that if a brother betrothed her, she has no claim on him. If she were a חייבי לאוין (liable for a negative commandment), why would she have no claim?
Rav Sheshet resolves that the end of the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that betrothal (קידושין) does not take effect with those liable for a negative commandment (חייבי לאוין).

items.text: Introduction of the two resolutions
items.text_en: Introduction of the two resolutions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a difficulty and states that Rav Ashi holds like Reish Lakish and resolves the difficulty according to Rabbi Shimon, while Ravina holds like Rabbi Yochanan and resolves it according to the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a difficulty and states that Rav Ashi holds like Reish Lakish and resolves it according to Rabbi Shimon, while Ravina holds like Rabbi Yochanan and resolves it according to the Rabbis.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution according to Rabbi Shimon and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution according to Rabbi Shimon and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains the Mishnah: one who performs chalitzah with his yevamah and then betroths her requires chalitzah from the brothers, referring to brothers born later, in accordance with Rabbi Shimon. If one of those born brothers betroths her, she has nothing against him, in accordance with Reish Lakish.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Rav Ashi's position: he holds like Reish Lakish and resolves the Mishnah according to Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Ashi explains the Mishnah's first clause: 'one who performs chalitzah with his yevamah and then betroths her requires chalitzah from the brothers' refers to brothers born later.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's explanation (attribution of first clause)
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation (attribution of first clause)
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi attributes the first clause to Rabbi Shimon's view.
Rav Ashi explains the Mishnah's second clause: 'if one of those born brothers betroths her, she has nothing against him' accords with Reish Lakish's view.

items.text: Ravina's resolution according to Rabbi Yochanan and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution according to Rabbi Yochanan and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Ravina explains the Mishnah: one who performs chalitzah with his yevamah and then betroths her requires chalitzah from the brothers, referring to brothers born later, in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan. If one of those born brothers betroths her, she has nothing against him, in accordance with the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Ravina aligns with Rabbi Yochanan and resolves the Mishnah according to the Rabbis: the first clause refers to brothers born later (in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan), and the second clause refers to a brother who betroths her (in accordance with the Rabbis).

items.text: Dispute about one who cohabits with a yevamah while another cohabits with her rival
items.text_en: Dispute about one who cohabits with a yevamah while another cohabits with her rival
items.desc_en: It was stated: If one cohabits with a yevamah, and another brother cohabits with her rival, Rav Acha and Ravina disagree. One says the second brother is liable for karet, the other says he violates a positive commandment. The one who says karet holds like Reish Lakish, the one who says a positive commandment holds like Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that a dispute was reported between Rav Acha and Ravina regarding one who cohabits with a yevamah (a sister-in-law awaiting levirate marriage) while another brother cohabits with her rival wife (צרה).
The gemara presents the two positions: one says the second brother is liable for כרת (karet, spiritual excision), the other says he violates only a positive commandment (עשה).
The gemara resolves the dispute: the one who says karet follows Reish Lakish's position, and the one who says a positive commandment follows Rabbi Yochanan's position.

items.text: Rav's ruling on the rival of a sotah and the ensuing discussion
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on the rival of a sotah and the ensuing discussion
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: The rival of a sotah is forbidden. The Gemara explains that tum'ah is written regarding her, like forbidden relations. Rav Chisda challenges this from Rabbi Shimon's statement that the yevamah's cohabitation or chalitzah from the first brother's brother exempts her rival. Rav responds that he was speaking of a biblical sotah, while the challenge refers to a rabbinic sotah. Rav Ashi further challenges from a case where a woman entered seclusion with her husband and is forbidden to her husband and to eat terumah, and if he dies she performs chalitzah.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports Rav's ruling that the rival wife of a sotah (suspected adulteress) is forbidden to the yavam.
The Gemara explains that the Torah writes 'טומאה' (ritual impurity) regarding the sotah, equating her to forbidden relations (עריות), thus forbidding her rival.
Rav Chisda challenges Rav's ruling by citing Rabbi Shimon's statement that the yevamah's cohabitation or חליצה (release) from the first brother's brother exempts her rival wife.
Rav responds that he was speaking of a biblical sotah (סוטה דאורייתא), while Rav Chisda's challenge refers to a rabbinic sotah (סוטה דרבנן).
The Gemara explains why the rabbinic sotah is called 'sotah': the Sages enacted it in the pattern of the biblical law (כעין דאורייתא תקן).

Rav Ashi challenges Rav's ruling by citing a case where a woman entered seclusion with her husband and is forbidden to her husband and to eat תרומה (priestly portion), and if he dies she performs חליצה (release), implying her rival is permitted.

items.text: Rav Ashi's challenge from a sotah who entered seclusion
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge from a sotah who entered seclusion
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises a challenge: If a woman entered seclusion with her husband and stayed with him long enough to become impure, she is forbidden to her husband and to eat terumah, and if he dies she performs chalitzah. This challenges Rav's ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises a challenge from the law of a sotah who entered seclusion: she is forbidden to her husband and to eat terumah, and if he dies she performs חליצה (release), contradicting Rav's ruling.

items.text: Gemara's opening objection
items.text_en: Gemara's opening objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's earlier statement that a definite sotah does not undergo yibbum, while a doubtful sotah does. It asks why a doubtful sotah should be different, since impurity is written regarding her as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's distinction between a definite sotah (who does not undergo yibbum) and a doubtful sotah (who does), asking why the doubtful case should differ since impurity is also written regarding her.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar's teaching and the dispute with the Sages
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar's teaching and the dispute with the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar says in the name of Rabbi Elazar that a man who remarries his divorced wife after she has been married to another is forbidden only if she had been married (nissu'in), but permitted if only betrothed (erusin), based on the verse 'after she has been defiled'. The Sages argue that both are forbidden, and the verse comes to include a sotah who was secluded. The Gemara then clarifies the meaning of 'secluded' and why the verse is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a safek sotah (suspected adulteress) also has the word 'tum'ah' (ritual impurity) written in her verse, so why should she be treated differently from a definite sotah?

A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar says in the name of Rabbi Elazar that a man who remarries his divorced wife is forbidden only if she had been married (nissu'in), based on the verse 'after she has been defiled'.
The Sages argue that both cases (marriage and betrothal) are forbidden, and the verse comes to include a sotah who was secluded.
The Gemara asks: what does 'secluded' mean — it means 'was violated'? But if so, the verse explicitly says 'and she was defiled', so why is the word 'secluded' needed?

The Gemara resolves that the verse establishes a negative commandment (לאו) for the sotah, and Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar does not derive a negative commandment from the sotah case, even for a definite adulteress.

items.text: Reason for Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar's view
items.text_en: Reason for Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar derives the prohibition from the concept of 'havayah' (marital bond) and 'ishut' (marriage), not from impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reason: the Torah writes regarding the sotah the terms 'הויה' (becoming) and 'אישות' (marriage), which imply a unique status.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's inquiry about the co-wife
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's inquiry about the co-wife
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda asks Rav Sheshet: If a man remarries his divorced wife after she has married another and then dies, what is the status of her co-wife (tzaratah)? The Gemara analyzes the question according to both Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar and the Sages, considering whether the co-wife is also forbidden or may enter yibbum.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda asks Rav Sheshet: If a man remarries his divorced wife after she married another and then dies, what is the status of her co-wife (tzaratah)?

sub.text: Gemara's analysis regarding Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis regarding Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar, the co-wife is forbidden like the wife herself, since the verse's 'תועבה (abomination)' applies to her as well.
The Gemara raises the question according to the Sages: whether the verse retains its simple meaning (applying to the remarrying wife) or is entirely uprooted (applying only to the sotah).
Some say that according to the Sages, the verse is entirely uprooted, so the question does not arise.

sub.text: Gemara's question regarding Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar
sub.text_en: Gemara's question regarding Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question according to Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar: whether the verse's 'תועבה (abomination)' excludes the co-wife or only excludes her children.

items.text: Proof from a baraita about a fit and unfit woman
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about a fit and unfit woman
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita: If one woman is fit and the other unfit, if he performs chalitzah he does so with the unfit one, and if he performs yibbum he does so with the fit one. The Gemara clarifies that 'fit' and 'unfit' refer to the man's own status, and the case is one who remarries his divorced wife. This proves that the co-wife may enter yibbum.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita: if one woman is fit and the other unfit, he performs חליצה (chalitzah) with the unfit one and יבום (yibbum) with the fit one.
The Gemara asks: what do 'fit' and 'unfit' mean? If they refer to general fitness, since she is fit for him, what difference does it make?

The Gemara proposes: 'fit' means fit for him (i.e., permitted), 'unfit' means unfit for him, and the case is one who remarries his divorced wife, and the baraita rules that he performs יבום (yibbum) with the fit one.
The Gemara rejects this: 'fit' and 'unfit' actually refer to general fitness, and the reason he does not perform יבום (yibbum) with the unfit one is because of Rav Yosef's principle.

Rav Yosef states the principle: one should not pour out his own water (i.e., waste a permitted woman) while others need them (i.e., the unfit woman is forbidden to others, so he should not render her forbidden by performing יבום (yibbum) with her).

items.text: Another baraita: the co-wife performs chalitzah
items.text_en: Another baraita: the co-wife performs chalitzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita: If a man remarries his divorced wife after she has married another, she and her co-wife perform chalitzah. The Gemara corrects the text: either she or her co-wife performs chalitzah, and the co-wife may either perform chalitzah or enter yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that appears to say the divorced woman and her co-wife both perform חליצה (chalitzah).
The Gemara objects that the baraita cannot mean both perform חליצה (chalitzah) together, and suggests it means either one or the other.
The Gemara resolves the baraita: the divorced woman herself performs חליצה (chalitzah), while her co-wife may either perform חליצה (chalitzah) or enter יבום (yibbum).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's inquiry and the kal vachomer debate
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's inquiry and the kal vachomer debate
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports that Rabbi Yochanan inquired about the co-wife's status. Rabbi Ami asks why he doesn't inquire about the woman herself. Rabbi Yochanan explains that a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument would forbid her, but the question is whether the kal vachomer is strong enough to override the co-wife's permissibility. An alternative version reverses the inquiry.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reporting Rabbi Yochanan's inquiry
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reporting Rabbi Yochanan's inquiry
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports that Rabbi Yochanan inquired about the status of the co-wife (צרה) of a man who remarries his divorced wife after she married another.
Rabbi Ami asks why Rabbi Yochanan does not inquire about the woman herself (the remarried divorcee) rather than her co-wife.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that the woman herself is not in question because a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) would forbid her: if a woman permitted to her husband becomes forbidden when he remarries her, then one already forbidden certainly is.
Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that his real question is about the co-wife: whether the קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) is strong enough to override the co-wife's permissibility or not.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative version
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative version
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak presents an alternative version of the tradition, reversing the inquiry: Rabbi Yochanan asked about the woman herself, and Rabbi Ami asked about the co-wife, with the question being whether the קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) is strong enough in the context of a מצוה (commandment of yibbum).

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's terms 'kasherah' and 'pesulah'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's terms 'kasherah' and 'pesulah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'kasherah' and 'pesulah' in a baraita about a yavam who has two widows, one fit and one unfit. It first suggests they refer to general fitness, then proposes they refer to fitness for the yavam himself, specifically a man who remarries his divorcee. The Gemara rejects the first possibility due to Rav Yosef's principle of not wasting resources.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'kasherah' and 'pesulah' mean in the baraita, first suggesting they refer to general fitness, then rejecting that because if the woman is fit for the yavam himself, why would it matter.

The Gemara proposes that 'kasherah' means fit for the yavam himself, specifically a man who remarries his divorcee, and the baraita rules that he must perform יבום (levirate marriage) with the fit one.

The Gemara rejects the first possibility, explaining that even if the woman is generally fit, the concern is Rav Yosef's principle of not wasting resources (one should not pour away his water while others need it).

items.text: Proof from a Mishnah about a man who remarries his divorcee
items.text_en: Proof from a Mishnah about a man who remarries his divorcee
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah about a man who remarries his divorcee after she married another, stating that she or her rival wife must perform chalitzah. The Gemara clarifies the text: the divorcee herself must perform chalitzah, while her rival wife may either perform chalitzah or enter yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah about a man who remarries his divorcee after she married another, and initially misreads it as saying both the divorcee and her rival wife must perform chalitzah, then corrects the text to mean either one.
The Gemara resolves the text: the divorcee herself must perform chalitzah, while her rival wife may either perform chalitzah or enter yibbum.

items.text: Rav Lelei bar Memel's statement on the rival wife of a me'ana'ah
items.text_en: Rav Lelei bar Memel's statement on the rival wife of a me'ana'ah
items.desc_en: Rav Lelei bar Memel quotes Mar Ukva quoting Shmuel that the rival wife of a woman who performed mi'un is forbidden. The Gemara questions to whom she is forbidden, and after considering the brothers, concludes it is forbidden to the yavam himself. The Gemara explains this as a decree due to the rival wife of his daughter who performed mi'un, and supports this with a baraita of Rami bar Yechezkel distinguishing between mi'un with the husband and with the yavam.

sub.text: Rav Lelei bar Memel quoting Mar Ukva quoting Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Lelei bar Memel quoting Mar Ukva quoting Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Lelei bar Memel transmits a ruling in the name of Mar Ukva citing Shmuel that the rival wife (צרה) of a woman who performed מיאון (mi'un, refusal) is forbidden.
The Gemara asks to whom the rival wife is forbidden, and rejects the possibility that she is forbidden to the brothers, since the woman who performed mi'un herself is permitted to them.
The Gemara concludes that the rival wife is forbidden to the yavam himself, and questions why she should be forbidden when the woman who performed mi'un never performed a marital act with the yavam.

The Gemara explains that the prohibition is a decree (גזירה) due to the rival wife of his daughter who performed mi'un, but then objects that the Mishnah explicitly permits the rival wives of women who performed mi'un.
The Gemara asks in which case the daughter performed mi'un, and suggests it must be with the yavam, since mi'un with the husband is simply a divorce.
The Gemara rejects this and argues that even mi'un with the husband is a distinct case, as it retroactively uproots the marriage, just as mi'un with the yavam uproots the initial marriage.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rami bar Yechezkel
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rami bar Yechezkel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Rami bar Yechezkel that distinguishes between mi'un with the husband (permitted to the father) and mi'un with the yavam (forbidden to the father).

The Gemara concludes that from the moment of yibbum (נפילה, falling to the yavam), the woman is considered as the yavam's daughter-in-law, and similarly here the rival wife is considered as the rival wife of his daughter from the moment of falling.

items.text: Rav Asi's statement on the rival wife of an aylonit
items.text_en: Rav Asi's statement on the rival wife of an aylonit
items.desc_en: Rav Asi states that the rival wife of an aylonit is forbidden, based on the verse 'and the firstborn that she shall bear' excluding an aylonit who does not give birth. Rav Sheishet challenges this from a baraita about three brothers married to three non-Jewish women, which Rav Yosef says is a case where the prohibition of the fall caused the stringency. The Gemara concludes that Rav Yosef's statement excludes the rival wife of an aylonit, who is forbidden by rabbinic law and requires chalitzah, while the aylonit herself requires no chalitzah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi declares that the rival wife of an aylonit is forbidden, citing the verse 'וְהָיָה הַבְּכוֹר אֲשֶׁר תֵּלֵד' (and the firstborn that she shall bear) to exclude an aylonit who does not give birth.

Rav Sheishet challenges Rav Asi by citing a baraita about three brothers married to three non-Jewish women, where the second brother's death creates a situation of two yevamim, and the women must perform חליצה (chalitzah) but cannot enter יבום (yibbum).

sub.text: Rav Yosef's statement on the baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's statement on the baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that this baraita describes a case where the prohibition of the fall (איסור נפילה) caused the stringency, and no similar case exists in the entire Torah.
The Gemara asks what Rav Yosef's phrase 'זוֹ הִיא' (this is) excludes, suggesting it might exclude the rival wife of an aylonit, implying she is permitted.

The Gemara rejects the suggestion and explains that Rav Yosef's statement actually excludes the rival wife of an aylonit, who is forbidden by rabbinic law (דרבנן) and requires חליצה (chalitzah), while the aylonit herself requires no חליצה (chalitzah) because her prohibition is biblical (דאורייתא).

items.text: Reconciliation of the Mishnah with Rav Asi's statement
items.text_en: Reconciliation of the Mishnah with Rav Asi's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara reconciles a Mishnah that permits the rival wives of ayloniot with Rav Asi's statement by distinguishing between a case where the husband knew she was an aylonit (the rival wife is permitted) and where he did not know (the rival wife is forbidden). The Gemara supports this from the Mishnah's language 'were found' rather than 'were'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that permits the rival wives of ayloniot, challenging Rav Asi's statement that such rival wives are forbidden.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where the husband knew his wife was an aylonit (rival wife permitted) and where he did not know (rival wife forbidden).
Rava supports the distinction by noting that the Mishnah uses the language 'were found' (נִמְצְאוּ) rather than 'were' (הָיוּ), implying the husband's prior ignorance.

items.text: Halakha on the tzara of an aylonit and Ravin's statement
items.text_en: Halakha on the tzara of an aylonit and Ravin's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakha that the tzara of an aylonit is permitted, even if the husband recognized her as an aylonit. It then cites Ravin's report in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the tzara of a me'ana (a minor who refuses marriage), an aylonit, and a woman who resumes relations with her divorced husband are all permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakha that the tzara (co-wife) of an aylonit (a woman incapable of bearing children) is permitted, even if the husband recognized her as an aylonit, and even the tzara of his daughter who is an aylonit.
The Gemara resolves a textual difficulty by emending the Mishnah's phrase 'שנמצאו' (who were found) to 'שהיו' (who were).

sub.text: Ravin in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Ravin in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the tzara of a me'ana (a minor who refuses marriage), an aylonit, and a woman who resumes relations with her divorced husband are all permitted.

items.text: Baraita of three women who use a mokh
items.text_en: Baraita of three women who use a mokh
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi teaches before Rav Nachman that three women must use a mokh (contraceptive): a minor, a pregnant woman, and a nursing woman. The reasons are given: the minor might become pregnant and die; the pregnant woman might cause her fetus to become a sandal (flattened); the nursing woman might wean her child and it might die. The baraita then defines the age of a minor for this purpose and records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages.

sub.text: Rav Bibi's teaching before Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Bibi's teaching before Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi teaches before Rav Nachman that three women (minor, pregnant, nursing) must use a mokh (contraceptive) due to specific dangers.

sub.text: Baraita defining the minor's age and dispute
sub.text_en: Baraita defining the minor's age and dispute
sub.desc_en: The baraita defines the minor's age range (11–12 years) and records the dispute between Rabbi Meir (who limits the obligation to that range) and the Sages (who say all women proceed naturally and God protects the simple).

items.text: Challenge from the baraita about a minor who might become pregnant and die
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita about a minor who might become pregnant and die
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that there is a minor who can become pregnant without dying, which would mean we have found a case of a mother-in-law who performs mi'un (refusal). This contradicts a mishna that states one cannot say that a mother-in-law or her mother were found to be an aylonit or performed mi'un. The Gemara resolves by reinterpreting the baraita's phrase as 'perhaps she will become pregnant and die'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that there is a minor who can become pregnant without dying, which would mean we have found a case of a mother-in-law who performs מיאון (refusal).
The Gemara objects by citing a mishna that states one cannot say a mother-in-law or her mother were found to be an איילונית (aylonit) or performed מיאון (refusal).
The Gemara resolves by reinterpreting the baraita's phrase as 'perhaps she will become pregnant and die', meaning the minor who becomes pregnant does not survive.

items.text: Rabba bar Livai's boundary for the minor's danger
items.text_en: Rabba bar Livai's boundary for the minor's danger
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Livai explains that there is a boundary (age limit) for the minor: before this time she cannot become pregnant at all; during this time she dies and her fetus dies; after this time she lives and her fetus lives.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Livai resolves the contradiction by defining three age-boundary stages for the minor: before the age she cannot conceive, during it both she and the fetus die, after it both live.

items.text: Objection from Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita
items.text_en: Objection from Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabba bar Shmuel taught that one cannot say a mother-in-law was found to be an aylonit or performed mi'un because they have already given birth. The Gemara concludes that the baraita's phrase must be 'perhaps she will become pregnant and die', but the objection remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita, which states that one cannot say a mother-in-law was found to be an aylonit or performed mi'un because they have already given birth.
The Gemara attempts to resolve the objection by asserting that the baraita's phrase must be 'perhaps she will become pregnant and die', but concludes that the difficulty remains unresolved.

items.text: Rav Safra's resolution: children are like signs
items.text_en: Rav Safra's resolution: children are like signs
items.desc_en: Rav Safra answers that children are like signs (of puberty), and some say children are superior to signs. The practical difference is that even Rabbi Yehuda, who requires a majority of black hair, agrees in the case of children.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra answers that children (the fact that a woman has given birth) are like signs (סימנים, physical signs of puberty) in establishing her status.
An alternative version states that children are superior to signs (סימנים) in their evidentiary force.
The gemara asks what practical difference emerges from this dispute, and answers that even Rabbi Yehuda, who requires a majority of black hair (ריבוי השחור) for signs, agrees in the case of children.

items.text: Rav Zevid's statement on signs of maturity
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's statement on signs of maturity
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid argues that there are no children without signs of puberty. The Gemara questions whether we can check for signs, and explains that we fear they may have fallen off. It then addresses the concern for the pain of childbirth even for those who do not suspect such loss.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid states that there are no children without signs of puberty.
The Gemara asks why we cannot simply check for the signs.
The Gemara answers that we fear the signs may have fallen off.
The Gemara objects that this concern applies only to the opinion that we suspect such loss, but for the opinion that we do not suspect, what can be said?
The Gemara resolves that even for the opinion that does not suspect loss of signs, we still suspect due to the pain of childbirth.

items.text: Source for tzrarot being forbidden
items.text_en: Source for tzrarot being forbidden
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source that co-wives are forbidden. Rav Yehuda derives it from the word 'tzror' in the verse, indicating that the Torah included many co-wives. Rav Ashi offers a logical reasoning: just as a co-wife is forbidden because she stands in place of an ervah, so too the co-wife of a co-wife stands in that place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source that co-wives (צָרוֹת) are forbidden.
Rav Yehuda derives the prohibition from the word 'לִצְרוֹר' (to tzror) in the verse, indicating that the Torah included many co-wives.
Rav Ashi offers a logical reasoning: just as a co-wife is forbidden because she stands in the place of an עֶרְוָה (forbidden relative), so too the co-wife of a co-wife stands in that place.

items.text: Contradiction regarding death and divorce
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding death and divorce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the co-wives die or are divorced, their tzrarot are permitted. The Gemara cites a baraita that seems to contradict this, implying that only if divorce precedes marriage (or death) is it permitted, but not if marriage precedes divorce. This raises a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the co-wives die or are divorced, their tzrarot are permitted, even if the husband married them and later divorced.
The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing a baraita that describes a case where divorce precedes marriage, implying that if marriage precedes divorce, the tzrarot are not permitted.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that only if divorce precedes marriage are the tzrarot permitted, but not if marriage precedes divorce, contradicting the Mishnah.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution: two tannaim
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution: two tannaim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the contradiction by suggesting that the two sources reflect different tannaitic opinions: one holds that death severs the marriage, the other holds that the first marriage severs it. Thus, they are not contradictory but represent different views.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the contradiction by asserting that the two sources reflect different tannaitic opinions: one holds that death severs the marriage, the other holds that the first marriage severs it.

items.text: Rava's resolution: one tanna, inclusive statement
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: one tanna, inclusive statement
items.desc_en: Rava argues that it is the same tanna, and the baraita is stating a case that is all the more so: if divorce then marriage is permitted, certainly marriage then divorce is permitted. Thus, there is no contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by asserting that the same tanna authored both baraitot, and the second baraita states a case that is all the more so (זו ואין צריך לומר זו), so the first baraita's ruling is included.

items.text: Discussion of mi'un for a yevamah
items.text_en: Discussion of mi'un for a yevamah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a woman who can perform mi'un (refusal) and questions why she doesn't do so now to avoid yibbum. It suggests this supports Rabbi Oshaya's view that mi'un works for ma'amar but not for zikah. However, it concludes that the case of a tzara of an ervah is different, citing a baraita that shows a woman who performs mi'un with her husband is permitted to his father, but if with the yavam, she is forbidden, indicating she is considered his daughter-in-law from the moment of falling to yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a woman who can perform מיאון (refusal) does not do so now to avoid יבום (levirate marriage).
The Gemara suggests this supports Rabbi Oshaya's view that מיאון works for מאמר (a formal betrothal-like act) but not for זיקה (the bond of levirate obligation).
The Gemara rejects the support, arguing that the case of a צרת ערוה (a rival wife of a forbidden relative) is different.
Rami bar Yechezkel teaches a ברייתא (baraita): a woman who performs מיאון with her husband is permitted to his father, but if she performs מיאון with the יבם (levir), she is forbidden to his father.

The Gemara concludes that from the moment of falling to יבום (levirate marriage), the woman is considered the יבם's daughter-in-law, and similarly here she is considered the rival wife of his daughter.

items.text: Mishnah: Six more severe arayot and Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Mishnah: Six more severe arayot and Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists six arayot (forbidden relations) that are more severe because they are married to others, and their tzrarot are permitted. It then notes that Beit Shammai permit the tzrarot to the brothers, while Beit Hillel forbid them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing six more severe forbidden relations whose co-wives are permitted.

sub.text: Mishnah's list of the six arayot
sub.text_en: Mishnah's list of the six arayot
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates the six specific forbidden relations: his mother, his father's wife, his father's sister, his sister from his father, his father's brother's wife, and his brother's wife from his father.

sub.text: Mishnah's ruling on Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.text_en: Mishnah's ruling on Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes by stating that Beit Shammai permit the co-wives to the brothers, while Beit Hillel forbid them.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the core dispute: if a woman performed chalitzah, Beit Shammai disqualifies her from marrying a kohen, while Beit Hillel permits her. If she performed yibum, Beit Shammai permits her, and Beit Hillel disqualifies her. Despite their disagreements, they did not refrain from marrying women from each other's houses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the core dispute: after chalitzah, Beit Shammai disqualifies the woman from marrying a kohen, Beit Hillel permits; after yibum, Beit Shammai permits, Beit Hillel disqualifies; yet they did not refrain from intermarriage or sharing purity practices.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural basis for the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural basis for the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi explains Beit Shammai's reasoning from the verse "lo tihyeh eshet hamet hachutza l'ish zar," interpreting "chutza" to imply an inner woman, thus forbidding the yevamah to a stranger. Beit Hillel uses the same verse to teach that betrothal does not take effect on a yevamah. The Gemara further discusses the grammatical rule of the letter heh indicating direction, and concludes that Beit Hillel derives the law from "l'ish zar" and uses "chutza" to include an arusah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi asks for the scriptural basis of Beit Shammai's position, citing the verse 'לֹא תִהְיֶה אֵשֶׁת הַמֵּת הַחוּצָה לְאִישׁ זָר' and interpreting 'חוּצָה' (outside) to imply an inner woman, whom the Torah forbids to a stranger.

sub.text: Beit Hillel's reasoning via Rav Yehuda said Rav
sub.text_en: Beit Hillel's reasoning via Rav Yehuda said Rav
sub.desc_en: Beit Hillel uses the same verse to derive that betrothal (קידושין) does not take effect on a yevamah, as taught by Rav Yehuda citing Rav: 'לֹא תִהְיֶה... לְאִישׁ זָר' means there shall be no marital relationship (הויה) with a stranger.

The Gemara objects that Beit Shammai's interpretation of 'חוּצָה' as implying an inner woman is problematic because the verse does not say 'לַחוּץ' (to the outside); Beit Hillel responds that since 'חוּצָה' is written, it is considered as if 'לַחוּץ' were written, indicating direction.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Nechemya and Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Nechemya and Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Nechemya states that any word requiring a prefix ל (to) has the letter ה (heh) appended at its end, and Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael gives examples like 'אֵלִים' → 'אֵלִימָה' (to the mighty), supporting the rule that 'חוּצָה' functions as 'לַחוּץ'.

The Gemara asks: From where do Beit Shammai derive the law that Rav Yehuda cited (that betrothal does not take effect on a yevamah)? It answers that they derive it from the phrase 'לְאִישׁ זָר' (to a strange man).
The Gemara asks: Could Beit Hillel also derive the law from 'לְאִישׁ זָר'? It answers yes, and explains that the word 'חוּצָה' comes to include an arusah (betrothed woman) in the prohibition.

The Gemara concludes: Beit Shammai derives the inclusion of the arusah from the definite article 'הַחוּצָה' (the outside), while Beit Hillel does not accept that 'חוּצָה' and 'הַחוּצָה' convey different meanings.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation: No prohibition applies to a prohibition
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation: No prohibition applies to a prohibition
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different reasoning for Beit Shammai: the prohibition of a sister-wife does not take effect on top of the prohibition of a brother's wife, because one prohibition cannot apply to another. The Gemara clarifies that this works when the man married the deceased brother first, but if he married the living sister first, the sister-wife prohibition comes first. However, since the prohibition of a brother's wife does not apply to the sister-wife prohibition, the co-wife is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that Beit Shammai's reasoning is that one prohibition does not take effect on top of another prohibition.
The Gemara questions Rava: this works when the man married the deceased brother first and then the living brother, but if he married the living brother first, the sister-wife prohibition comes first.

The Gemara answers: since the prohibition of a brother's wife does not take effect on the sister-wife prohibition, the co-wife is considered a צרת ערוה (rival of a forbidden relative) not in the context of a mitzvah, and is permitted.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's necessity
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's necessity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that Beit Hillel permits after chalitzah, as it seems obvious. It explains that it comes to exclude the opinion of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who said that co-wives should perform chalitzah but not yibum. The Gemara also notes that the case of yibum is mentioned because the Mishnah mentioned chalitzah, so it also mentions yibum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that Beit Hillel permits after chalitzah, as it seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's statement comes to exclude the opinion of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who said co-wives should perform חליצה (chalitzah) but not יבום (yibum).
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah mentions the case of יבום (yibum) only because it mentioned חליצה (chalitzah), so it also mentions יבום (yibum) for symmetry.

items.text: Digression: The prohibition of forming separate groups and the Megillah reading
items.text_en: Digression: The prohibition of forming separate groups and the Megillah reading
items.desc_en: The Gemara transitions to a discussion about the Megillah being read on multiple days, citing a verse "lo titgodedu" (do not form separate groups). Reish Lakish questions Rabbi Yochanan about this, and they debate whether the verse is needed for its simple meaning or for the prohibition of separate groups. The discussion then shifts to the permissibility of work on Passover eve, with Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagreeing, and concludes with a question about Beit Shammai permitting co-wives.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah from Megillah that the Megillah is read on multiple days (11th through 15th of Adar).

sub.text: Reish Lakish's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan whether reading the Megillah on different days violates the prohibition of 'לא תתגודדו' (do not form separate groups).
Reish Lakish objects that the verse 'לא תתגודדו' is needed for its simple meaning — not to make a wound for the dead.
The Gemara answers that the doubled form 'תתגודדו' implies both the prohibition of wounding and the prohibition of separate groups.
Rabbi Yochanan responds by citing a Mishnah about local customs regarding work on Passover eve, implying that differing practices are permitted.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's objection to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's objection to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish objects that the Megillah reading involves a formal prohibition (איסור) established by the Sages, not merely a custom (מנהג).
The Gemara questions whether the Passover eve custom is also a matter of prohibition, citing a Mishnah where Beit Shammai forbid and Beit Hillel permit work.

Rabbi Yochanan answers that in the Passover case, an observer would attribute the lack of work to the individual's personal situation, not to a separate group practice, and then challenges Reish Lakish about Beit Shammai permitting co-wives.

items.text: The dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: The dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rav says Beit Shammai did not act according to their rulings, while Shmuel says they did. Rabbi Yochanan also holds that they did act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute: Rav says Beit Shammai did not act according to their rulings, while Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan say they did.

items.text: Two resolutions for the dispute
items.text_en: Two resolutions for the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute refers to before or after the Bat Kol. It offers two answers: either it was before the Bat Kol, with Beit Hillel being the majority, or after the Bat Kol, following Rabbi Yehoshua who disregards the Bat Kol.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute about whether Beit Shammai acted on their rulings occurred before or after the Bat Kol, and challenges both possibilities.

The Gemara offers the first answer: the dispute was before the Bat Kol; the one who says they did not act follows the majority (Beit Hillel), while the one who says they acted follows the minority because Beit Shammai were sharper.

The Gemara offers the second answer: the dispute was after the Bat Kol; the one who says they did not act follows the Bat Kol, while the one who says they acted follows Rabbi Yehoshua who disregards the Bat Kol.

items.text: The scope of 'Lo Titgodedu'
items.text_en: The scope of 'Lo Titgodedu'
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava debate the application of 'Lo Titgodedu' (not making separate groups). Abaye says it applies to two courts in one city ruling differently, but not to two courts in different cities. Rava argues that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel are like two courts in one city, so the prohibition applies even to different cities.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle of 'לֹא תִתְגּוֹדְדוּ' (do not make separate groups) as a concern for those who hold that Beit Shammai's rulings were enacted.
Abaye limits the prohibition of 'לֹא תִתְגּוֹדְדוּ' to two courts in one city ruling differently, but not to two courts in different cities.

Rava objects that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel are like two courts in one city, so the prohibition applies even to different cities, and redefines the prohibition as applying to a single court split within one city.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Eliezer's place
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Eliezer's place
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: in Rabbi Eliezer's place they cut wood on Shabbat for charcoal, but not in Rabbi Akiva's place. The Gemara initially thinks this challenges the permissibility of divergent practices, but resolves that different places are different, and the baraita teaches that Shabbat stringency does not make them like one place.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: in Rabbi Eliezer's place they cut wood on Shabbat for charcoal, and in Rabbi Yose HaGelili's place they ate chicken with milk.
The Gemara notes that the baraita implies the practice was only in Rabbi Eliezer's place, not Rabbi Akiva's, citing Rabbi Akiva's rule that work possible before Shabbat does not override Shabbat.
The Gemara objects that this is no proof, since different places are different, and questions why the baraita was cited at all.
The Gemara resolves that one might have thought the stringency of Shabbat makes all places like one place, so the baraita teaches that even Shabbat stringency does not unify them.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Avahu's practice
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Avahu's practice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu would move a lamp (on Shabbat) in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's place but not in Rabbi Yochanan's place. The Gemara explains this is due to respect for Rabbi Yochanan, not a contradiction, and he would inform his attendant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a supporting baraita about Rabbi Avahu's inconsistent practice of moving a lamp on Shabbat in different locations.
The Gemara objects that the practice of different places is not a contradiction, but questions why Rabbi Avahu acted differently in each place.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Avahu personally held like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi but refrained from moving the lamp in Rabbi Yochanan's place out of respect, and would inform his attendant to do it instead.

items.text: Proof from intermarriage between schools
items.text_en: Proof from intermarriage between schools
items.desc_en: A baraita states that despite disagreements, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel intermarried. If they acted according to their rulings, this would be problematic. The Gemara resolves that they informed each other and refrained. A supporting inference from the continuation about purity laws is noted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel intermarried despite their disputes, and challenges: if they acted according to their rulings, why would they intermarry?

The Gemara objects: Beit Shammai marrying Beit Hillel women is understandable (they are only liable for a negative commandment), but Beit Hillel marrying Beit Shammai women would produce mamzerim (liable for karet).

The Gemara rejects the possibility that Beit Hillel held that no mamzer comes from karet liabilities, citing Rabbi Elazar's statement that they agree on this, and concludes that the baraita proves they did not act according to their rulings.
The Gemara resolves: they did act according to their rulings, but they informed each other of their status and refrained from marriage.

The Gemara infers support from the continuation of the baraita: just as in purity laws they did not refrain from using each other's pure items (implying they informed each other), so too in marriage they informed each other.

items.text: Gemara's inference that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel informed each other
items.text_en: Gemara's inference that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel informed each other
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not inform each other of their rulings, then Beit Hillel would have refrained from marrying Beit Shammai's women because they would consider them impure, but they did not refrain, proving they informed each other. It then explains the practical relevance of this inference regarding tzarot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not inform each other, Beit Hillel would have refrained from marrying Beit Shammai's women because they would consider them impure, but they did not refrain, proving they informed each other.
The Gemara explains the practical relevance of the inference: one might think a צרה (co-wife) has a public reputation, so the Gemara teaches that even she is included.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's statement on mamzerut and its clarification
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's statement on mamzerut and its clarification
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that despite the dispute about tzarot, both schools agree that a mamzer is only from a union prohibited by an ervah punishable by karet. The Gemara questions who agrees with whom, and explains that the statement is to exclude Rabbi Akiva's view that a mamzer can come from a union prohibited by a lav.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that despite the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding tzarot (co-wives), both schools agree that a mamzer (illegitimate child) comes only from a union prohibited by an ervah (forbidden relative) punishable by karet (extirpation).

The Gemara asks who agrees with whom in Rabbi Elazar's statement, and rejects the possibility that Beit Shammai agrees with Beit Hillel, since children from unions prohibited only by a lav (negative commandment) are already considered fit.

The Gemara considers the alternative that Beit Hillel agrees with Beit Shammai, but objects that Beit Hillel's own children from tzarot are already subject to karet, so the statement would be redundant.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Elazar's statement indeed refers to Beit Shammai agreeing with Beit Hillel, and it comes to exclude the view of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a mamzer can come from a union prohibited by a lav (negative commandment).

items.text: Baraita listing disputes and Rabbi Shimon's opinion
items.text_en: Baraita listing disputes and Rabbi Shimon's opinion
items.desc_en: A baraita lists several disputes between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, including tzarot, and states that they did not refrain from marrying each other, teaching love and friendship. Rabbi Shimon says they refrained from definite cases but not from uncertain ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing disputes between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, including tzarot, and stating that they did not refrain from marrying each other, teaching love and friendship.
Rabbi Shimon states that they refrained from definite cases but not from uncertain ones.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why they would refrain at all if they did not act on their rulings, and explains that even if they did act, Beit Hillel would refrain from Beit Shammai due to karet, but Beit Shammai should not refrain from Beit Hillel since their children are kosher. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the refraining applies only to the tzarah herself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's statement: if they did not act on their rulings, why would they refrain from marrying each other's women at all?
The Gemara explains that even if they did act, Beit Hillel would refrain from Beit Shammai due to karet, but Beit Shammai should not refrain from Beit Hillel since their children are kosher.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the refraining applies only to the tzarah (co-wife) herself, not to other women.

items.text: Clarification of 'safek' and identification of the baraita's author
items.text_en: Clarification of 'safek' and identification of the baraita's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets Rabbi Shimon's 'safek' as 'setam' (default), meaning they informed each other and separated. It then notes that the baraita teaches that the entire passage is according to Rabbi Shimon, not just the last clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between a definite case (וַדַּאי) and a doubtful case (סָפֵק), since both involve prohibition.
The Gemara reinterprets Rabbi Shimon's 'סָפֵק' (doubt) as 'סְתָם' (default), meaning they informed each other and separated, avoiding the prohibition.
The Gemara asks what new teaching the baraita adds, since the principle of love and friendship was already stated earlier.
The Gemara answers that the baraita teaches that the entire passage is according to Rabbi Shimon, not just the last clause.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's proposal to rectify tzarot
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's proposal to rectify tzarot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri laments the confusion caused by the dispute, as following either school leads to a flawed child, and proposes a remedy for tzarot.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri laments that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding צרות (rival wives) leaves no correct path, as following either school produces a flawed child.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri proposes a remedy for the צרות (rival wives) to resolve the halachic deadlock.

items.text: Opening statement: the decree about tzarot
items.text_en: Opening statement: the decree about tzarot
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the decree that tzarot should perform chalitzah and not yibbum, but notes that before the matter was concluded, the time became chaotic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the decree that tzarot should perform חליצה (chalitzah) and not יבום (yibbum), but notes that before the matter was concluded, the time became chaotic.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's question and the Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's question and the Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel asks what should be done for the earlier tzarot. The Gemara questions whether this implies that Beit Shammai actually enacted their ruling or not.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel asks what should be done for the earlier tzarot (co-wives) from now on.
The Gemara questions whether Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's inquiry implies that Beit Shammai actually enacted their ruling or not.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the question was about the tzarot themselves: how should Beit Shammai treat Beit Hillel's tzarot? Chalitzah is problematic because it causes aversion, and marrying them is not an option due to the pleasantness of Torah's ways.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the question was about the tzarot (co-wives) themselves: how should Beit Shammai treat Beit Hillel's tzarot?

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that chalitzah (the release ceremony) is problematic because it causes aversion to the husband, and marrying them is not an option due to the pleasantness of Torah's ways (דרכיה דרכי נועם).

items.text: First proof: Rabbi Tarfon's statement
items.text_en: First proof: Rabbi Tarfon's statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon expresses eagerness to marry a tzarat habat. The Gemara initially thinks this shows the ruling was enacted, but then explains he meant to marry her off, and this was to exclude Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Tarfon's statement that he eagerly awaits the opportunity to marry a צרת הבת (a co-wife of his daughter), as proof that the enactment was actually carried out.
The Gemara reinterprets Rabbi Tarfon's words: he meant 'I will marry her off' (אשיאנה), not 'I will marry her' (אשאנה), so the statement does not prove the enactment was carried out.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Tarfon's language 'תאבני' (I eagerly desire) implies his own personal involvement, not merely arranging a marriage.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Tarfon's eagerness was to exclude the view of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who permitted marrying a צרת הבת (co-wife of a daughter) even לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

items.text: Second proof: Rabban Gamliel's case and the dispute about an aylonit
items.text_en: Second proof: Rabban Gamliel's case and the dispute about an aylonit
items.desc_en: A story about Rabban Gamliel marrying his daughter's tzarah is brought. The Gemara questions whether Rabban Gamliel was a Beit Shammai follower, and resolves that the daughter was an aylonit. The Tanna Kamma and Others disagree about whether she was recognized as such, with three possible distinctions: whether he recognized it, whether he married and divorced, or whether there was a condition in the marital act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story about Rabban Gamliel marrying his daughter's tzarah, and questions whether this implies Rabban Gamliel was a Beit Shammai follower.
The Gemara resolves that the daughter was an aylonit (אַיְלוֹנִית), and notes that the Tanna Kamma and Others disagree about whether she was recognized as such.
The first distinction between Tanna Kamma and Others is whether Rabban Gamliel recognized (הִכִּיר) that his daughter was an aylonit or not.
The second distinction is whether Rabban Gamliel married (כָּנַס) and later divorced (גֵּירַשׁ) the tzarah, or not.
The third distinction is whether there was a condition (תְּנַאי) in the marital act (בְּבִיאָה) that affected the halachic status.

items.text: Third proof: Rabbi Akiva's etrog and the refutation
items.text_en: Third proof: Rabbi Akiva's etrog and the refutation
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya brings a story of Rabbi Akiva treating an etrog with two tithes according to both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, seemingly proving the ruling was enacted. The Gemara refutes that Rabbi Akiva was uncertain which date was correct.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya brings a story of Rabbi Akiva treating an etrog with two tithes according to both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, seemingly proving the ruling was enacted.
The Gemara refutes that Rabbi Akiva was uncertain which date was correct, so his action does not prove the ruling was enacted.

items.text: Fourth proof: Shammai the Elder's sukkah and the refutation
items.text_en: Fourth proof: Shammai the Elder's sukkah and the refutation
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra brings a story of Shammai the Elder reducing the ceiling and roofing over a bed for a child, seemingly showing Beit Shammai's ruling was enacted. The Gemara refutes that an observer would think he was just adding air space.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra brings a story of Shammai the Elder reducing the ceiling and roofing over a bed for a child, arguing that this proves Beit Shammai's ruling was enacted (עָשׂוּ).
The Gemara refutes that an observer would think Shammai was merely adding air space, not enacting a ruling.

items.text: Fifth proof: The Shukat Yehu and the refutation
items.text_en: Fifth proof: The Shukat Yehu and the refutation
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra brings another story about Beit Shammai widening a water channel, seemingly proving enactment. The Gemara begins to refute but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra brings a story about Beit Shammai widening the Shukat Yehu water channel, seemingly proving that they enacted their rulings.
The Gemara begins to refute the proof by citing a Mishnah about the minimum size of a connecting pipe for a mikveh, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Opening observation about the onlooker
items.text_en: Opening observation about the onlooker
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that an onlooker might think the action is merely to increase water, setting up the need for a clearer proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that an onlooker might think the action is merely to increase water, setting up the need for a clearer proof.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok and the olives
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok and the olives
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok recounts an incident with Rabbi Yochanan haChorani involving olives, which leads to a discussion about a barrel of olives and the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. The Gemara concludes that even though the student was a Shammaite, he acted according to Beit Hillel, proving that Beit Hillel's rulings were followed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok recounts that when he studied with Rabbi Yochanan haChorani, he saw him eating dry bread with salt during a famine, and when he brought olives, Rabbi Yochanan refused because they were moist.

Abba explains that the barrel was originally sealed with sediment, and cites the Mishnah where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether a barrel of pressed olives needs to be punctured, agreeing that if punctured and sealed with sediment it is pure.

The Gemara concludes that even though Rabbi Yochanan was a Shammaite student, he acted according to Beit Hillel, proving that Beit Hillel's rulings were followed; otherwise, what greatness would there be in the story?

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's testimony about tzarot
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's testimony about tzarot
items.desc_en: When asked about the status of a tzara (co-wife), Rabbi Yehoshua expresses fear of the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, but testifies about two families in Jerusalem who were children of tzarot and served as High Priests, implying that Beit Hillel's lenient ruling was followed.

sub.desc_en: The questioners ask Rabbi Yehoshua about the halachic status of a tzara (co-wife) of a daughter.
Rabbi Yehoshua first states that the matter is a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, then refuses to rule, expressing fear of the dispute.
Rabbi Yehoshua testifies about two families in Jerusalem whose members were children of tzarot and served as High Priests, implying that Beit Hillel's lenient ruling was followed.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehoshua's fear
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehoshua's fear
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehoshua was afraid if the ruling was followed, and explains that even if the child is not a mamzer, he is still a pagum (blemished) priest, which justifies the fear.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehoshua expressed fear if the ruling was not followed, and even if it was followed, what was he afraid of?
The Gemara explains that although Rabbi Yehoshua holds a child from a צרה (co-wife) is not a mamzer, he is still a pagum (blemished) priest, justifying the fear.

items.text: Kal vachomer from an almanah
items.text_en: Kal vachomer from an almanah
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer argument: if an almanah (widow) to a Kohen Gadol, whose prohibition is not universal, produces a blemished child, then a tzara, whose prohibition is universal, should certainly produce a blemished child.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if an almanah (widow) to a Kohen Gadol, whose prohibition is not universal, produces a blemished child, then a tzara (co-wife of a daughter), whose prohibition is universal, should certainly produce a blemished child.

items.text: Clarifying the question about tzarot and bnei tzarot
items.text_en: Clarifying the question about tzarot and bnei tzarot
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the questioner asked two things: the status of tzarot themselves, and if they are permitted according to Beit Hillel, what is the status of their children according to Beit Shammai? The practical difference is for the case of one who remarries his divorcee.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the questioner asked about tzarot (co-wives) or about bnei tzarot (children of co-wives).

The Gemara explains that the questioner asked two things: the status of tzarot themselves, and if they are permitted according to Beit Hillel, what is the status of their children according to Beit Shammai.
