The Gemara states that the practical difference is for the case of one who remarries his divorcee, to determine the status of her child according to Beit Hillel.

items.text: Refining the kal vachomer and Rabbi Yehoshua's response
items.text_en: Refining the kal vachomer and Rabbi Yehoshua's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara refines the kal vachomer, considering a potential refutation: the almanah herself becomes profaned, unlike the tzara. Rabbi Yehoshua then says he is afraid regarding tzarot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from an almanah (widow of a Kohen Gadol) to a tzarah (co-wife of a forbidden relative) is valid: just as the almanah's child is profaned (פגום) even though her prohibition is not universal, so too the tzarah's child should be profaned since her prohibition is universal.
The Gemara raises a potential refutation: the almanah herself becomes profaned (מתחללת) by the marriage, unlike the tzarah who does not become profaned herself.
Rabbi Yehoshua responds to the questioners that he is afraid regarding tzarot (co-wives), indicating his uncertainty about the halacha (הלכה) in this matter.

items.text: Gemara's proof from the story of Rabbi Dosa
items.text_en: Gemara's proof from the story of Rabbi Dosa
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that in the days of Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas, צרת הבת was permitted for the brothers. This proves that the earlier ruling was enacted, not just a theoretical statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement: 'I testify to you, sons of rival wives.'
The Gemara cites a baraita that in the days of Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas, the rival wife of a daughter was permitted to the brothers, concluding that this proves the earlier ruling was enacted.

items.text: The story of Rabbi Dosa and the sages
items.text_en: The story of Rabbi Dosa and the sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the narrative: Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas permitted צרת הבת, and the sages sent Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, and Rabbi Akiva to inform him. Rabbi Dosa initially honored them, but when they discussed the halakha, he revealed that his brother Yonatan, a student of Shammai, was the source of the ruling. He then cited a tradition from Haggai the prophet that צרת הבת is forbidden, along with other rulings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the story: in the days of Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas, they permitted צרת הבת (a co-wife of a daughter) to the brothers, and the matter was difficult for the sages because he was a great sage whose eyes had dimmed from coming to the study hall.

The sages ask who will go inform Rabbi Dosa; Rabbi Yehoshua volunteers, followed by Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva; they go and stand at his door, his maidservant announces them, and he invites them in.

Rabbi Dosa grabs Rabbi Yehoshua and seats him on a golden bed; Rabbi Yehoshua asks him to invite the next disciple, and Rabbi Dosa asks if Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya indeed has a son to Azarya our colleague.
Rabbi Dosa recites a verse about Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, seats him on a golden bed, and then praises Rabbi Akiva, telling him to sit and that many like him should increase in Israel.

They begin to engage him in halachic discussion until they reach the topic of צרת הבת; they ask what the law is, and he says the law follows Beit Hillel, but they object that a ruling was attributed to him following Beit Shammai.

Rabbi Dosa asks whether they heard 'Dosa' or 'ben Harkinas'; they say they heard a general statement; he reveals that he has a younger brother, Yonatan, a student of Shammai, who is the source of the ruling.
Rabbi Dosa warns them to be careful that Yonatan not outsmart them in halachic arguments, because he has three hundred responses permitting צרת הבת.

Rabbi Dosa testifies by heaven and earth that Haggai the prophet sat on this mortar and said three things: צרת הבת is forbidden, Ammon and Moab give מעשר עני (poor tithe) in the seventh year, and converts are accepted from the Cardoyim and Tarmodim.

items.text: The encounter with Rabbi Akiva after the meeting
items.text_en: The encounter with Rabbi Akiva after the meeting
items.desc_en: A baraita describes that when the sages entered, they entered through one entrance, but when they left, they left through three. Rabbi Dosa encountered Rabbi Akiva and challenged him, saying he had not yet reached the level of shepherds. Rabbi Akiva responded humbly.

sub.desc_en: A baraita (תנא) reports that when the sages entered Rabbi Dosa's house they entered through one entrance, but when they left they left through three separate entrances.
Rabbi Dosa encountered Rabbi Akiva, challenged him, and said that although Rabbi Akiva had achieved a great name, he had not yet reached the level of cattle herders.
Rabbi Akiva humbly responded that he had not even reached the level of sheep herders.

items.text: Explanation of the ruling on Ammon and Moab
items.text_en: Explanation of the ruling on Ammon and Moab
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Ammon and Moab give מעשר עני in the seventh year: because the lands conquered by those who returned from Egypt were not sanctified for the future, so the poor may rely on them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Ammon and Moab give מעשר עני (the poor tithe) in the seventh year.
The Gemara explains that the lands conquered by those who returned from Egypt were not sanctified for the future, so the poor may rely on them in the seventh year.

items.text: Discussion on converts from Kardoyim and Tarmodim
items.text_en: Discussion on converts from Kardoyim and Tarmodim
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the acceptance of converts from Kardoyim, citing a baraita that rejects them. Rav Ashi resolves that the baraita refers to Kartoyim, not Kardoyim, as people say Kartoyim are invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita from the story of Chaggai the prophet that accepts converts from the Kardoyim and Tarmodim.
The Gemara objects: Is that so? But Rami bar Yechezkel taught a baraita that we do not accept converts from the Kardoyim.
Rav Ashi resolves that the baraita of Rami bar Yechezkel actually said 'Kartoyim' (not Kardoyim), as people say Kartoyim are invalid.
An alternative version states that Rami bar Yechezkel explicitly taught that we do not accept converts from the Kartoyim.
The Gemara asks: Doesn't this imply that Kartoyim and Kardoyim are the same people?
Rav Ashi answers: No, Kartoyim are distinct from Kardoyim, as people say Kartoyim are invalid.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on Tarmodim and a contradiction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on Tarmodim and a contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and an elder both say that converts from Tarmodim are not accepted. The Gemara raises a contradiction from a mishna about stains from Rekem, which implies that converts from there are accepted. The discussion is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rabbi Yochanan and an elder (Sava) both rule that converts from Tarmod are not accepted.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's ruling by citing a mishna that stains from Rekem are pure, implying that converts from there are accepted.
The mishna adds that Rabbi Yehuda declares them impure because the converts are mistaken, but stains from among gentiles are pure.
The Gemara notes that the discussion was left unresolved, indicated by the phrase 'we raised a difficulty about it'.

items.text: Opening statement and Rabbi Yochanan's inference
items.text_en: Opening statement and Rabbi Yochanan's inference
items.desc_en: The Tanna teaches that converts are accepted from among the nations, even from Tadmor. Rabbi Yochanan infers from this that converts from Tadmor are accepted.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna teaches that converts are accepted from among the nations, even from Tadmor.
Rabbi Yochanan infers from this that converts from Tadmor are accepted.

items.text: Question on Rabbi Yochanan's consistency
items.text_en: Question on Rabbi Yochanan's consistency
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan's statement is consistent with his own principle that the law follows an anonymous Mishnah. It resolves that there are two different Amoraim speaking in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan's statement that converts are accepted from Tadmor contradicts his own principle that the law follows an anonymous Mishnah.
The Gemara resolves that there are two different Amoraim transmitting in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, so the contradiction is only apparent.

items.text: Two reasons for rejecting Tadmor converts
items.text_en: Two reasons for rejecting Tadmor converts
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Tadmor is excluded from acceptance. It records a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and the Elders: one says it is because of Solomon's servants, the other because of the daughters of Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Tadmor is excluded from acceptance of converts.
Rabbi Yochanan and the Elders dispute the reason: one says it is because of Solomon's servants, the other because of the daughters of Jerusalem.

items.text: Explanation of the two reasons
items.text_en: Explanation of the two reasons
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the first reason: one who holds it is because of Solomon's servants believes that a gentile or slave who cohabits with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer. For the second reason, it cites a dispute between Rav Yosef and the Rabbis in the name of Rabba bar bar Chana about the number of soldiers who assaulted the daughters of Jerusalem during the destruction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the first reason (Solomon's servants), one holds that a gentile or slave who cohabits with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer (ממזר).
The Gemara asks what the second reason (daughters of Jerusalem) entails.

sub.text: Rav Yosef and the Rabbis in the name of Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef and the Rabbis in the name of Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Yosef and the Rabbis, both citing Rabba bar bar Chana, about the number of soldiers who assaulted the daughters of Jerusalem.
One opinion states that 12,000 men and 6,000 archers assaulted the daughters of Jerusalem.

The other opinion states that 12,000 men, of whom 6,000 were archers, assaulted the daughters of Jerusalem, citing the verse 'נָשִׁים בְּצִיּוֹן עִנּוּ בְּתוּלוֹת בְּעָרֵי יְהוּדָה' (women in Zion they ravished, virgins in the cities of Judah).

items.text: Identity of the speaker of a verse
items.text_en: Identity of the speaker of a verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan states that the verse 'I have been young and now am old' was said by the Sar HaOlam (the angelic prince of the world), not by God or David.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan states that the verse 'I have been young and now am old' was said by the Sar HaOlam (the angelic prince of the world), not by God or David.

items.text: Behavior of Ammon and Moab during the destruction
items.text_en: Behavior of Ammon and Moab during the destruction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan interprets a verse about the enemy's hand being spread over all her treasures: Ammon and Moab focused on burning Torah scrolls because they contained the prohibition against their entry into the congregation.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan interprets the verse 'יָדוֹ פָּרַשׂ צָר עַל כׇּל מַחֲמַדֶּיהָ' as referring to Ammon and Moab, who during the destruction of the Temple focused on burning Torah scrolls because they contained the prohibition against their entry into the congregation.

items.text: Rav's example of enemies surrounding Jacob
items.text_en: Rav's example of enemies surrounding Jacob
items.desc_en: Rav interprets the verse 'The Lord has commanded concerning Jacob that his enemies should be round about him' as referring to a place like Humanya near the river.

sub.desc_en: Rav interprets the verse 'The Lord has commanded concerning Jacob that his enemies should be round about him' as referring to a place like Humanya near the river.

items.text: Concern about converts from the Ten Tribes
items.text_en: Concern about converts from the Ten Tribes
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi states that a gentile who betroths a woman nowadays is suspected of being from the Ten Tribes, so we are concerned about the betrothal. The Gemara objects that one who separates from the majority does so from the majority, but resolves that this applies where the Ten Tribes are a fixed population.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi states that a gentile who betroths a woman nowadays is suspected of being from the Ten Tribes, so we are concerned about the betrothal.
The Gemara objects that one who separates from the majority does so from the majority, so most gentiles are not from the Ten Tribes.
The Gemara resolves that this applies where the Ten Tribes are a fixed population, citing Rabbi Abba bar Kahana's identification of their settlement locations.

items.text: Identification of exiled cities
items.text_en: Identification of exiled cities
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the cities mentioned in the verse: Chadyav, Nehar Gozan, and the cities of Madai. Samuel specifies the companions of Chadyav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the exiled cities: Chadyav, Nehar Gozan (Ginzak), and the cities of Madai (Chamdan and its companions, or alternatively Nihar and its companions).
Samuel specifies the companions of Nihar: Krach, Mushkei, Chidkei, and Dumkei.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that all these cities are disqualified (פסול) for lineage purposes.

items.text: The status of a child from a Jewish woman and a non-Jewish man
items.text_en: The status of a child from a Jewish woman and a non-Jewish man
items.desc_en: Samuel states that a child born from a Jewish woman is called your son, but a child from a non-Jewish woman is called her son. Ravina infers that a son from your daughter and a non-Jew is called your son, but the Gemara explains that the daughters of that generation were exceptional.

sub.desc_en: Samuel states that a child born from a Jewish woman is called your son, but a child from a non-Jewish woman is called her son.
Ravina infers from Samuel's statement that a son from your daughter and a non-Jew is called your son.
The Gemara explains that the daughters of that generation were exceptional and required special treatment.

items.text: Alternative version: They became complete gentiles
items.text_en: Alternative version: They became complete gentiles
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Samuel said they did not leave until they became complete gentiles, as the verse says they betrayed God and bore foreign children.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports that Samuel said the Ten Tribes did not leave their place until they became complete gentiles, citing the verse that they betrayed God and bore foreign children.

items.text: Discussion about the destruction of Tadmor
items.text_en: Discussion about the destruction of Tadmor
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports that Israel will make a holiday when Tadmor is destroyed. The Gemara questions this, and Rav Ashi explains that Tadmor and Tamod are the same city, and it was destroyed on one side but settled on the other.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef, sitting behind Rav Kahana, reports that Israel will make a holiday when Tadmor is destroyed.
The Gemara objects that Tadmor is already destroyed, and suggests the city in question is actually Tamod.
Rav Ashi resolves that Tadmor and Tamod are the same city, which was destroyed on one side but settled on the other.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's embarrassment before Ulla
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's embarrassment before Ulla
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna praises Ulla, but Ulla embarrasses him by asking where he gave his poll tax. Rav Hamnuna answers 'at the mouth of the river,' and Ulla deduces he is from there.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna sits before Ulla and praises him excessively.
Ulla embarrasses Rav Hamnuna by asking where he gave his poll tax.
Rav Hamnuna answers that he gave the tax at the mouth of the river.
Ulla deduces that Rav Hamnuna is from the place called 'Mouth of the River' (Pum Nahara).

items.text: Explanation of Harpanya and its lineage
items.text_en: Explanation of Harpanya and its lineage
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains Harpanya as a mountain where everyone turns. A baraita says those who do not know their family go there. Rava says it is deeper than Sheol, as there is no remedy for their disqualification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Harpanya' means.
Rabbi Zeira explains that Harpanya is a mountain where everyone turns (to settle).
A baraita (תנא) teaches that anyone who does not know his family and tribe goes there.
Rava declares that Harpanya is deeper than Sheol, as there is no remedy for their disqualification.

items.text: Chain of disqualification from Meishon to Harpanya
items.text_en: Chain of disqualification from Meishon to Harpanya
items.desc_en: The disqualifications of Harpanya originate from Meishon, which originates from Tadmor, which originates from the servants of Solomon. A folk saying describes the progression of a measure from Sheol to Tadmor to Meishon to Harpanya.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that the disqualifications of Harpanya originate from Meishon, which originate from Tadmor, which originate from the servants of Solomon.
A folk saying illustrates the progression of a measure from Sheol to Tadmor to Meishon to Harpanya.

items.text: Mishnah: The brother who was not yet born
items.text_en: Mishnah: The brother who was not yet born
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents a case of two brothers, one dies, a brother is born, then the second brother performs yibbum and dies. The first wife is exempt due to being the wife of a brother who was not yet born, and the second due to being her rival. If he performed ma'amar and died, the second performs chalitzah.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the case of two brothers, one dies, a brother is born, then the second performs יבום (levirate marriage) and dies, exempting the first wife as the wife of a brother not yet born and the second as her rival.
The mishnah adds that if he performed מאמר (a formal declaration of yibbum) and died, the second wife performs חליצה (removal of the shoe) and is not taken in yibbum.

items.text: Gemara: Clarification of the mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarification of the mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says that one who teaches 'first' is not mistaken, and one who teaches 'second' is not mistaken, referring to the order of the wives in the mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that neither the version teaching 'first' nor the version teaching 'second' is mistaken, referring to the order of the wives in the mishnah.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's terms
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's terms
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the terms 'first' and 'second' in the Mishnah: 'first' refers to the first wife who fell for yibbum, and 'second' refers to the second wife in marriage. It questions whether the case involves yibbum followed by marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'first' and 'second' mean in the Mishnah, clarifying that 'first' refers to the first wife who fell for yibbum and 'second' to the second wife in marriage.
The Gemara questions whether the case involves yibbum followed by marriage, and concludes that 'second' means second in marriage.

items.text: Source for אֵשֶׁת אָחִיו שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בְּעוֹלָמוֹ
items.text_en: Source for אֵשֶׁת אָחִיו שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בְּעוֹלָמוֹ
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav derives from the verse 'כִּי יֵשְׁבוּ אַחִים יַחְדָּו' that the brothers must have had a shared existence in the world, excluding a brother who was not alive at the same time. The word 'יַחְדָּו' indicates they are unique in inheritance, excluding a maternal brother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where in the Torah is the law of a brother's wife who was never contemporaneous with her husband derived?

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav derives from the verse 'כִּי יֵשְׁבוּ אַחִים יַחְדָּו' that the brothers must have had a shared existence in the world, excluding a brother who was not alive at the same time, and the word 'יַחְדָּו' indicates they are unique in inheritance, excluding a maternal brother.

items.text: Rabba's derivation and the principle of גזירה שווה
items.text_en: Rabba's derivation and the principle of גזירה שווה
items.desc_en: Rabba derives the law from the brothers of Jacob, learning 'brotherhood' from 'brotherhood'. The Gemara questions why not learn from forbidden relations, and explains the principle that we learn from a similar case when one exists.

sub.desc_en: Rabba derives that 'brothers' means paternal brothers by learning a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'brotherhood' from the sons of Jacob.
The Gemara objects: why not learn the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from forbidden relations (עריות) instead of from Jacob's sons?

sub.text: Gemara's answer citing Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer citing Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the principle of Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael teaches that when a similar case exists, we learn from it rather than from a dissimilar one.

items.text: Alternative derivation from Lot and the necessity of both verses
items.text_en: Alternative derivation from Lot and the necessity of both verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers learning from Lot, but concludes that the derivation from Jacob's sons is preferable because it is a free exposition. It explains why both 'אַחִים' and 'יַחְדָּו' are necessary: without 'יַחְדָּו' one might learn from Lot, and without 'אַחִים' one might think it requires uniqueness in both father and mother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the derivation of brotherhood for yibbum is not learned from Lot, who called his sons-in-law 'brothers' (אַחִים).

The Gemara answers that the derivation from Jacob's sons is preferable because the term 'אַחִים' there is a free exposition (מַפְנֵי), as the verse could have said 'בני אבינו' but instead wrote 'אַחִים' to teach a halachic principle.

The Gemara explains that both verses are necessary: 'אַחִים' alone would allow learning from Lot (who also uses a free exposition), so 'יַחְדָּו' specifies brothers who are 'united in inheritance' (מְיוּחָדִים בַּנַּחֲלָה), excluding a brother from the mother.

The Gemara further explains that without 'אַחִים', one might think 'יַחְדָּו' requires uniqueness in both father and mother, so both verses are needed to teach that yibbum applies only to paternal brothers.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on a yevamah who died
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on a yevamah who died
items.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rav rules that if a yevamah dies, the yavam is permitted to marry her mother, indicating he holds there is no זִיקָה. The Gemara explains why Rav did not simply state the halakha: to avoid implying limitations regarding multiple brothers or during the yavam's lifetime.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rav rules that if a yevamah dies, the yavam is permitted to marry her mother, indicating Rav holds there is no זִיקָה (bond of connection).
The Gemara asks why Rav did not simply state the halakha (הלכה) in accordance with the one who says there is no זִיקָה.
The Gemara answers that if Rav had stated the halakha (הלכה) generally, one might think it applies only to two brothers, but with one brother there is זִיקָה.
The Gemara asks further why Rav did not state the halakha (הלכה) explicitly even for one brother.

The Gemara answers that if Rav had said that, one might think it applies even during the yavam's lifetime, so Rav specified after death to teach that during his lifetime it is forbidden because one may not nullify the mitzvah (מצוה) of yibbum.

items.text: Support from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Support from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a yevamah dies, the yavam is permitted to marry her sister, implying but not her mother. The Gemara explains that the Mishnah only mentions the sister because the first clause did, but the same leniency applies to the mother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that if a yevamah dies, the yavam is permitted to marry her sister, implying but not her mother.
The Gemara explains that the same leniency applies to the mother, but the Mishnah only mentions the sister because the first clause did.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's opposing view
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's opposing view
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda holds that if a yevamah dies, the yavam is forbidden to marry her mother, indicating he holds there is זִיקָה. The Gemara explains why he did not simply state the halakha: to avoid implying limitations regarding a single brother.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that if a yevamah (שׁוֹמֶרֶת יָבָם) dies, the yavam is forbidden to marry her mother, implying he holds there is זִיקָה (bond of levirate connection).
The Gemara asks why Rav Yehuda did not simply state the halakha (הלכה) as a ruling that follows the opinion that there is זִיקָה (bond of levirate connection).

The Gemara explains that if Rav Yehuda had stated the halakha (הלכה) as a general ruling, one might have thought it applies only to a single brother, but with two brothers there is no זִיקָה (bond of levirate connection).
The Gemara objects that the dispute about זִיקָה (bond of levirate connection) is specifically about two brothers, so the concern about a single brother is irrelevant.

The Gemara resolves that the concern was actually about implying limitations regarding a single brother, but the objection is left incomplete, implying the answer is that Rav Yehuda's specific case avoids that implication.

items.text: Gemara's initial claim and defense of zikah after death
items.text_en: Gemara's initial claim and defense of zikah after death
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially thought that zikah only applies during the yavam's lifetime, but after the yevamah's death it lapses. The baraita teaches that if his yevamah died, he is permitted to marry her sister, implying that he is forbidden to marry her mother, proving that zikah does not lapse even after death. The Gemara defends this by noting that the same language is used in the first clause about his wife, where the prohibition is biblical, so the second clause is just parallel phrasing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially thought that after the yevamah's death, the zikah (bond) lapses, but the baraita implies it does not lapse by permitting her sister but forbidding her mother.

The Gemara defends the baraita by explaining that the second clause merely parallels the first clause's phrasing, where the prohibition against the mother is biblical, so the baraita does not prove zikah persists after death.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Chiyya's objection and Rabba's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chiyya's objection and Rabba's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiyya objects from a mishnah: if a yavam made a ma'amar (declaration of betrothal) with a secondary forbidden relative (shniyah) and then died, she performs chalitzah and not yibbum. This implies that without ma'amar, she would undergo yibbum, contradicting the view that zikah exists (which would make her a tzarah of a sister-in-law who was never in the world). Rabba answers that even without ma'amar, she only does chalitzah, and the mention of ma'amar is to counter Beit Shammai's view that ma'amar is a full acquisition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiyya objects from a baraita: if a yavam performed a maamar (declaration) and died, the second wife (tzarah) must perform chalitzah (removal of the shoe) and cannot enter yibbum (levirate marriage), implying that without maamar she could enter yibbum, contradicting the view that zikah exists.
Rabbah answers that even without maamar, the second wife would still be prohibited from yibbum and only permitted chalitzah; the baraita's mention of maamar is not exclusive.
The Gemara explains that the baraita mentions maamar specifically to reject Beit Shammai's view that maamar effects a full acquisition (קניין גמור).

items.text: Abaye's objection from a baraita about two brothers
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from a baraita about two brothers
items.desc_en: Abaye objects from a baraita: two brothers, one dies childless, the second intends to make ma'amar but before he can, a brother is born and then dies. The first yevamah is exempt as a sister-in-law who was never in the world, and the second either does chalitzah or yibbum. If zikah exists, the second would be a tzarah of a sister-in-law who was never in the world, which is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects from a baraita: two brothers, one dies childless, the second intends to make ma'amar but before he can, a brother is born and then dies; the first yevamah is exempt as a sister-in-law who was never in the world, and the second either does chalitzah or yibbum; if zikah exists, the second would be a tzarah of a sister-in-law who was never in the world, which is prohibited.

items.text: Gemara's answer: the baraita follows Rabbi Meir who holds no zikah
items.text_en: Gemara's answer: the baraita follows Rabbi Meir who holds no zikah
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Meir, who holds there is no zikah. But then it questions whether Rabbi Meir really holds no zikah, citing a mishnah where four brothers married two sisters, and the sisters' husbands die, leaving the sisters to do chalitzah but not yibbum. If there were no zikah, each surviving brother could marry one sister. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir holds it is forbidden to nullify the mitzvah of yibbum, because while one brother performs yibbum, the other might die, nullifying the mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Meir, who holds there is no זיקה (bond of yibbum).

The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir truly holds there is no זיקה, citing a mishnah where four brothers married two sisters and the sisters must perform חליצה (release) but not יבום (levirate marriage).

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Meir indeed holds there is no זיקה, but he forbids nullifying the מצות יבמים (mitzvah of yibbum) because while one brother performs יבום, the other might die, nullifying the mitzvah.

items.text: Comparison with Rabban Gamliel's view on zikah
items.text_en: Comparison with Rabban Gamliel's view on zikah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabban Gamliel holds there is no zikah and permits nullifying the mitzvah of yibbum, as seen in a mishnah where a minor yevamah can wait until she grows up and then leave due to sister-in-law prohibition. The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Meir is concerned even for a doubt, while Rabban Gamliel is not concerned even for a certainty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if there is no זיקה (bond of yibbum), then the mitzvah of yibbum would be nullified, citing Rabban Gamliel who holds there is no זיקה and permits nullifying the mitzvah.
The Gemara cites a mishnah where Rabban Gamliel rules that a minor yevamah may wait until she grows up and then leave due to the sister-in-law prohibition, showing he permits nullifying the mitzvah.
The Gemara resolves that Rabban Gamliel's view is not comparable to Rabbi Meir's: Rabbi Meir is concerned even for a doubt, while Rabban Gamliel is not concerned even for a certainty.

items.text: Abaye's attribution of Rav Yehuda's view to Shmuel
items.text_en: Abaye's attribution of Rav Yehuda's view to Shmuel
items.desc_en: Abaye tells Rav Yosef that Rav Yehuda's statement follows Shmuel's opinion, as cited in a baraita.

sub.desc_en: Abaye tells Rav Yosef that Rav Yehuda's statement follows Shmuel's opinion, as cited in a baraita.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a yavam's brother betrothed the yevamah's sister, the Sages say in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira to wait until the brother acts. Shmuel rules the halakhah follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a yavam's brother betrothed the yevamah's sister, the Sages in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira say to wait until the brother acts.
Shmuel rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rav's position
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rav's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav holds a different view, concluding that since Shmuel's explicit statement is clear, we do not abandon it for an amoraic version attributed to Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If Rav held a different view, what would it be?
The Gemara resolves that since Shmuel's explicit statement is clear, we do not abandon it for an amoraic version attributed to Rav.

items.text: Rav Kahana's tradition and Shmuel's consistency
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's tradition and Shmuel's consistency
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports a tradition before Rav Zevid from Neharde'a, who notes different versions. Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that if a yevamah dies, the yavam is forbidden to her mother, indicating Shmuel holds yesh zikah. The Gemara explains why both statements are necessary.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports that he recited a tradition before Rav Zevid from Neharde'a, who notes that they (the Babylonians) teach it in a different version, while we (the Neharde'ans) teach it explicitly.
Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel: if a yevamah (a woman awaiting yibbum) dies, the yavam is forbidden to her mother, indicating that Shmuel holds יש זיקה (the bond of zikah exists).
The Gemara infers that Shmuel holds יש זיקה (the bond of zikah exists) and that this is consistent with his earlier ruling that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

The Gemara explains why both statements of Shmuel are necessary: the first teaches that zikah applies even with two brothers, and the second teaches that zikah does not lapse after the yevamah's death.

items.text: Mishnah: Two brothers and a posthumous brother
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two brothers and a posthumous brother
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case of two brothers where one dies, the second performs yibbum, then a brother is born and dies. The first wife is forbidden as a brother's wife who was not in the world, and the second as her rival. Rabbi Shimon permits yibbum or halitzah with either.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of two brothers where one dies, the second performs yibbum, then a brother is born and dies; the first wife is forbidden as a brother's wife who was not in the world, and the second as her rival; if the second performed ma'amar and died, the second wife performs halitzah and does not enter yibbum.
Rabbi Shimon permits yibbum or halitzah with either of the two wives.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's dispute extends to the first wife
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's dispute extends to the first wife
items.desc_en: Rav Oshaya states that Rabbi Shimon disputed even the first wife, proven by the redundant Mishnah. The Gemara explains the Mishnah's structure: the first clause shows Rabbi Shimon's leniency, the second the Sages' stringency, and Rabbi Shimon waited to dispute after the Sages finished.

sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya asserts that Rabbi Shimon disputed even the first wife, proven by the redundant Mishnah.
The Gemara asks for whom the first clause of the Mishnah is necessary, concluding it must be for Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara explains that the first clause teaches Rabbi Shimon's leniency, the second the Sages' stringency, and Rabbi Shimon waited to dispute after the Sages finished.

items.text: How Rabbi Shimon finds a case of 'brother's wife not in the world'
items.text_en: How Rabbi Shimon finds a case of 'brother's wife not in the world'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for Rabbi Shimon, the case of a brother's wife who was not in the world applies when there is one brother who died and a brother was born, or two brothers without yibbum or death. In the case of yibbum after birth, Rabbi Shimon holds yesh zikah and zikah is like a marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Shimon can find a case of 'brother's wife who was not in the world' given his lenient position.
The Gemara answers that the case can be found with one brother who died and a brother was born, or two brothers without yibbum or death.
The Gemara explains that in the case of yibbum after birth, the yevama was permitted when encountered.
The Gemara explains that in the case of birth before yibbum, Rabbi Shimon holds יֵשׁ זִיקָה (there is a bond) and זִיקָה (the bond) is like a marriage.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection and the Mishnah of three brothers
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection and the Mishnah of three brothers
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects: if Rabbi Shimon is uncertain about zikah and ma'amar, certainly he should be uncertain about zikah alone. The Gemara cites a Mishnah about three brothers married to three unrelated women, where Rabbi Shimon permits yibbum with one and halitzah with the second, but not both, due to possible zikah creating two yevamot.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects: if Rabbi Shimon is uncertain whether זיקה ומאמר (levirate bond plus formal declaration) is like full marriage, certainly he should be uncertain about זיקה (the bond alone).

The Gemara cites a Mishnah about three brothers married to three unrelated women, where one dies and the second performs מאמר (a formal declaration) and dies, leaving the women to perform חליצה (release) but not יבום (levirate marriage), because a woman may not have a זיקת שני יבמין (bond to two levirs).

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon's position in the Mishnah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's position in the Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon permits יבום (levirate marriage) with whichever woman he chooses and חליצה (release) with the second, but not both, because of the concern that זיקה (the levirate bond) might create two יבמות (levirate brides) from the same man.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's case that Rabbi Shimon is uncertain whether זיקה is like marriage, because if he were certain, he would allow one yavam to marry and the other to be exempt without חליצה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's case that Rabbi Shimon is uncertain whether זיקה (the bond of yibbum) is like marriage, because if he were certain, he would allow one yavam to marry and the other to be exempt without חליצה (release).

items.text: Rejection: The reason is ma'amar
items.text_en: Rejection: The reason is ma'amar
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that Rabbi Shimon's concern is not uncertainty about זיקה but the possibility that the second brother's ma'amar might be valid or invalid, making the woman either his wife or the first brother's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possible alternative explanation: that Rabbi Shimon's concern is a rabbinic decree, not a Torah-level doubt about זיקה.
The Gemara rejects the alternative, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon explicitly states his reason is the uncertainty of the second brother's ma'amar (formal declaration), not a rabbinic decree.

items.text: Abaye's challenge: Distinguish one yavam from two
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge: Distinguish one yavam from two
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges the Gemara's answer, arguing that Rabbi Shimon might hold זיקה is like marriage only for one yavam, not for two yevamim.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges the Gemara's answer, arguing that Rabbi Shimon might hold זיקה is like marriage only for one yavam, not for two yevamim.

items.text: Gemara's objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon does not distinguish, citing a baraita where he rules that a woman whose birth preceded marriage neither חולצת nor מתייבמת, implying the same rule for one yavam. The Gemara deflects by saying the baraita deals with two yevamim, but the objection is pressed that he should have specified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon does not distinguish between one yavam and two, citing a baraita where he rules that a woman whose birth preceded marriage neither חולצת nor מתייבמת.
The Gemara deflects by saying the baraita deals with two yevamim, not one.
The Gemara presses that if the baraita is about two yevamim, Rabbi Shimon should have specified the distinction for one yavam.
The Gemara resolves that the entire baraita deals with two yevamim, and the term 'כלל' (general rule) is used loosely.

items.text: Rav Oshaya's challenge from three brothers
items.text_en: Rav Oshaya's challenge from three brothers
items.desc_en: Rav Oshaya challenges with a Mishnah where three brothers married two sisters, and Rabbi Shimon exempts both from יבום and חליצה. The Gemara attempts to explain that he exempts only the second woman, but is refuted by a baraita that says he exempts both. Rava's explanation about four pairs is also rejected.

sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya challenges with a Mishnah where three brothers married two sisters, and Rabbi Shimon exempts both from יבום and חליצה.
The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Shimon holds that זיקה (the bond of יבום) is like full marriage, he should permit יבום of the first sister and exempt the second.
Rav Amram suggests that Rabbi Shimon exempts only the second woman, but the Gemara refutes this with a baraita that says he exempts both.
Rava explains that Rabbi Shimon exempts the second woman in each of four pairs, but the Gemara rejects this because the Mishnah uses 'אוֹ' (or) and a baraita explicitly says he exempts both.
The baraita cites the verse 'וְאִשָּׁה אֶל אֲחוֹתָהּ לֹא תִקָּח לִצְרוֹר' to prove that when sisters become rivals, no marriage is permitted even with one of them.

items.text: Rav Ashi and Rav Papa's resolutions
items.text_en: Rav Ashi and Rav Papa's resolutions
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains the case involves simultaneous falls, and Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Yose HaGlili who allows צמצום. Rav Papa distinguishes between yibum before birth (where Rabbi Shimon disputes) and birth before yibum (where he agrees). Both explanations are necessary.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves simultaneous falls (נפול בבת אחת), and Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Yose HaGlili who allows צמצום (simultaneous existence of two conflicting statuses).
Rav Papa distinguishes between yibum before birth (where Rabbi Shimon disputes) and birth before yibum (where he agrees with the Sages).
The Gemara notes that both explanations are necessary for the Sages' position, and the baraita employs the style of 'not only this but also that' (לא זו אף זו).

items.text: Baraita supports Rav Papa, refutes Rav Oshaya
items.text_en: Baraita supports Rav Papa, refutes Rav Oshaya
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Papa's distinction: if yibum preceded birth, the second woman חולצת ולא מתייבמת; if birth preceded yibum, she either חולצת or מתייבמת. This refutes Rav Oshaya's challenge.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Papa's distinction: if yibum preceded birth, the second woman חולצת ולא מתייבמת (performs חליצה and does not enter יבום); if birth preceded yibum, she either חולצת or מתייבמת.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon's ruling and the dispute with Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon's ruling and the dispute with Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Shimon's view that the yibum or chalitzah of one co-wife exempts her rival. It then details cases where a brother is born after marriage or ma'amar, and the dispute between Rabbi Meir (both are exempt) and Rabbi Shimon (he may choose either).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Shimon's ruling that the yibum or chalitzah of one co-wife exempts her rival, and presents the case where a brother is born after marriage, exempting both.
The Mishnah states Rabbi Meir's position that in the case of marriage followed by birth of a brother and then death, both women are exempt from chalitzah and yibum.
The Mishnah presents Rabbi Shimon's dissenting view that since the brother found the woman in a permitted state, he may choose to perform yibum or chalitzah with either.

items.text: Gemara's question: To whom does the latter clause refer?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: To whom does the latter clause refer?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the attribution of the latter clause in the Mishnah. It argues that if it is Rabbi Meir, he does not distinguish between the order of yibum and birth, so the cases should be combined. Therefore, it must be Rabbi Shimon, who only disputes when yibum precedes birth, not when birth precedes yibum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks to whom the latter clause of the Mishnah refers, and argues that if it is Rabbi Meir, he does not distinguish between the order of yibum and birth, so the cases should have been combined.
The Gemara concludes that the latter clause must be Rabbi Shimon, who only disputes when yibum precedes birth, not when birth precedes yibum.

items.text: Clarification of 'stood' and 'did not manage' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Clarification of 'stood' and 'did not manage' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the terms 'stood' and 'did not manage' in the Mishnah's case of a second brother who intended ma'amar but a brother was born. It explains that 'stood' means with her consent, and 'did not manage' means against her will, aligning with the dispute between Rabbi and the Sages regarding ma'amar without the woman's consent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of the terms 'stood' and 'did not manage' in the Mishnah, pointing out that if the brother performed ma'amar he did, and if not he didn't.
The Gemara explains that 'stood' means with her consent, and 'did not manage' means against her will, and this aligns with the view of the Sages against Rabbi.
A baraita is cited: one who performs ma'amar in his yevama without her consent — Rabbi says he acquires, and the Sages say he does not acquire.

items.text: Reasoning of Rabbi and the Sages regarding ma'amar without consent
items.text_en: Reasoning of Rabbi and the Sages regarding ma'amar without consent
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasoning: Rabbi derives from yibum itself that ma'amar can be done against her will, while the Sages derive from regular betrothal that it requires her consent. The dispute is about which analogy is appropriate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi's reasoning for allowing ma'amar against her will, and explains that Rabbi derives it from yibum itself, where intercourse is permitted against her will.
The Gemara explains that the Sages derive the requirement for consent from regular betrothal (קידושין דעלמא), where consent is required.
The Gemara resolves the dispute: Rabbi holds that matters of yibum should be derived from yibum itself, while the Sages hold that matters of betrothal should be derived from regular betrothal.

items.text: Mishnah continuation: Case of ma'amar and birth, and Rabbi Shimon's position
items.text_en: Mishnah continuation: Case of ma'amar and birth, and Rabbi Shimon's position
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case where ma'amar was made and then a brother was born, or vice versa, and the brother died. The first woman is exempt as a sister-in-law who was not in the world, and the second does chalitzah. Rabbi Shimon says either's act exempts the rival. The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Shimon's statement applies only to the case where ma'amar preceded birth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case where ma'amar was made and then a brother was born, or vice versa, and the brother died, stating that the first woman is exempt and the second does chalitzah, with Rabbi Shimon saying either's act exempts the rival.
The Gemara asks on which case Rabbi Shimon's statement applies, considering the two scenarios in the Mishnah.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon's statement applies only to the case where ma'amar preceded birth, not where birth preceded ma'amar.

items.text: Reason for the rule: Chalitzah to the ma'amar wife does not exempt the rival
items.text_en: Reason for the rule: Chalitzah to the ma'amar wife does not exempt the rival
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if one performs chalitzah to the woman who received ma'amar, the rival is not exempt because the rival is a definite tzarah while the ma'amar wife is uncertain, and uncertainty cannot remove a definite status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the rule: if one performs chalitzah to the woman who received ma'amar, the rival wife is not exempt.
The Gemara explains the reason: the rival is a definite tzarah while the ma'amar wife is uncertain, and uncertainty cannot remove a definite status.

items.text: Discussion of Rabbi Shimon's and the Rabbis' reasoning
items.text_en: Discussion of Rabbi Shimon's and the Rabbis' reasoning
items.desc_en: Rav Menasheh bar Zevid questions the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon, but the Gemara notes it is already stated. Then it asks for the Rabbis' reasoning, citing a verse that the original yibum obligation remains. It then references a Mishnah that a yevamah who is married is like a wife in all respects, and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching.

sub.desc_en: Rav Menasheh bar Zevid asks Rav Huna what is Rabbi Shimon's reasoning.
The Gemara rejects the question, noting that Rabbi Shimon already stated his reason in the Mishnah.
The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara cites a verse to show that the original yibum obligation remains upon the yevamah even after ma'amar.

sub.text: Supporting Mishnah and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Supporting Mishnah and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: The Gemara references a Mishnah that a yevamah who is married is like a wife in all respects, and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's teaching that this teaches something.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding the earlier case
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding the earlier case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the earlier case (where a woman was divorced and remarried) requires chalitzah, given that the verse says 'and he shall take her' making her like his wife. It resolves by distinguishing between issur that has a heter (permissible alternative) and issur that does not, and addresses Rabbi Shimon's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the earlier case requires חליצה (release), given that the verse says 'וייבמה' (and he shall perform yibbum with her), implying she is still bound by the first yibbum.

The Gemara distinguishes: in the earlier case, the verse 'ולקחה לו לאשה' (and he shall take her as a wife) makes her like his wife for all purposes, but here the verse 'וייבמה' (and he shall perform yibbum) applies.
The Gemara resolves by applying the principle of assigning permissible cases to permissible ones and forbidden cases to forbidden ones.
Rabbi Shimon objects: if the principle is based on finding the woman in a permissible state, then a maternal sister married to a paternal brother who later dies should be permitted for yibbum.
The Gemara rejects Rabbi Shimon's objection by distinguishing between an איסור (prohibition) that has no permissible alternative and one that does.

items.text: Mishnah: General rule for yevamah
items.text_en: Mishnah: General rule for yevamah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: a yevamah who is an ervah (forbidden relative) does not perform chalitzah or yibbum; one with issur mitzvah or issur kedushah performs chalitzah but not yibbum; a sister who is a yevamah performs chalitzah or yibbum. It defines issur mitzvah as secondary prohibitions (derabanan) and issur kedushah as specific forbidden marriages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the general rule: a yevamah who is an ervah (forbidden relative) does not perform chalitzah or yibbum; one with issur mitzvah or issur kedushah performs chalitzah but not yibbum.
The Mishnah adds the case of a sister who is a yevamah: she performs chalitzah or yibbum.
The Mishnah defines issur mitzvah as secondary prohibitions (derabanan) and issur kedushah as specific forbidden marriages.

items.text: Gemara: What does 'כלל' include or exclude?
items.text_en: Gemara: What does 'כלל' include or exclude?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the general term 'כלל' comes to include or exclude. Rafram bar Pappa explains it includes the rival wife of an aylonit (according to Rav Asi), or alternatively excludes her (according to the other version).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the general term 'כלל' in the Mishnah comes to include.
Rafram bar Pappa answers that 'כלל' includes the rival wife of an aylonit, consistent with Rav Asi's view.
An alternative version reverses the interpretation: 'כלל' excludes the rival wife of an aylonit, contrary to Rav Asi's view.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying 'her sister who is her yevamah'
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying 'her sister who is her yevamah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which sister is referred to in the Mishnah's phrase 'her sister who is her yevamah', concluding it refers to the sister of an ervah, not of an issur mitzvah, to avoid conflict with the principle of 'sister of a zekukah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose sister is referred to in the Mishnah's phrase 'her sister who is her yevamah'.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that it refers to the sister of an issur mitzvah, because that would conflict with the principle of the sister of a zekukah.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah refers to the sister of an ervah (a forbidden relative by Torah law).

items.text: Gemara: Why are these called issur mitzvah and issur kedushah?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why are these called issur mitzvah and issur kedushah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the terminology: Abaye says issur mitzvah refers to secondary prohibitions because it is a mitzvah to listen to the Sages. For issur kedushah, the verse says 'they shall be holy'. Rabbi Yehuda reverses the terms. Rava explains that 'kedushah' means sanctifying oneself through what is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the secondary prohibitions (שניות) are called איסור מצוה (a prohibition of a mitzvah).
Abaye explains that it is called איסור מצוה because there is a מצוה (commandment) to listen to the words of the Sages.
The Gemara asks why the prohibitions of a widow to a High Priest, etc., are called איסור קדושה (a prohibition of holiness).
The Gemara answers that it is called איסור קדושה because the verse says 'קדושים יהיו' (they shall be holy) regarding priests.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda reverses the terms, calling the priestly prohibitions איסור מצוה because the verse says 'אלה המצות' (these are the commandments).
The Gemara asks why, according to Rabbi Yehuda, the secondary prohibitions are called איסור קדושה.
Abaye answers that one who fulfills the words of the Sages is called holy (קדוש).
Rava objects: if one who does not fulfill the Sages' words is not called holy, he is also not called wicked — so the term 'holy' is not a fitting antonym.
Rava resolves: the term איסור קדושה means sanctifying oneself through what is permitted (קדש עצמך במותר לך), i.e., refraining even from permitted things as a discipline.

items.text: Gemara: Why does a widow to a High Priest require chalitzah even from erusin?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why does a widow to a High Priest require chalitzah even from erusin?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a widow betrothed to a High Priest requires chalitzah, since it is only a negative commandment (not a positive and negative). Rav Giddel cites a verse 'yevimto' to teach that only those obligated in positive commandments (like lavin) require chalitzah but not yibbum, excluding kareis. The Gemara then questions why lavin are included and not kareis, and resolves with the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: a widow to a High Priest requires chalitzah whether from marriage or betrothal.
The Gemara questions why a widow from betrothal requires chalitzah, since it is only a negative commandment (לא תעשה) and the positive commandment of yibbum should override it.
Rav Giddel in the name of Rav cites the verse 'יְבִמְתּוֹ' to teach that only those obligated in negative commandments (חייבי לאוין) require chalitzah but not yibbum.

The Gemara objects: why not include those liable to kareis (חייבי כריתות) as well? It answers with the verse 'וְאִם לֹא יַחְפּוֹץ' — only those who could potentially undergo yibbum are eligible for chalitzah.

The Gemara resolves: if the rule applies to those who could undergo yibbum, then why are חייבי לאוין (negative commandment violators) included? The verse 'יְבִמְתּוֹ' teaches that they are excluded from yibbum but included in chalitzah, and the logic of the verse supports this distinction.

items.text: Gemara's initial assumption
items.text_en: Gemara's initial assumption
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a logical assumption: those liable for a negative commandment (חייבי לאוין) can effect betrothal, so their yibbum is valid; those liable for karet (חייבי כריתות) cannot, so their yibbum is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a logical assumption: those liable for a negative commandment (חייבי לאוין) can effect betrothal, so their yibbum is valid; those liable for karet (חייבי כריתות) cannot, so their yibbum is invalid.

items.text: Rava's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava challenges the assumption from a Mishnah: a woman forbidden by an issur mitzvah or issur kedushah, if the yavam had relations or performed chalitzah, her rival is exempt. If the yavam were only obligated in chalitzah, why would relations exempt? Rava answers that the Mishnah is split: relations refers to issur mitzvah, chalitzah to issur kedushah.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects from a Mishnah: if a woman forbidden by איסור מצוה (a negative-commandment prohibition) or איסור קדושה (a sanctity prohibition) is entered or receives חליצה, her co-wife is released — but if those liable for negative commandments are exempt from yibbum, why should entering her release the co-wife?

Rava himself resolves the objection: the Mishnah speaks לצדדין (in a split manner) — entering applies to איסור מצוה (where yibbum is valid), while חליצה applies to איסור קדושה (where yibbum is invalid).

items.text: Second challenge from a baraita on a wounded or castrated man
items.text_en: Second challenge from a baraita on a wounded or castrated man
items.desc_en: Rava brings a baraita: a wounded or castrated man (פצוע דכא) may perform chalitzah or yibbum. If he had relations, he acquires her, but may not keep her due to the prohibition. This contradicts Rava's assumption that such a yavam is only obligated in chalitzah, since the baraita says if he had relations he acquires her.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects from a baraita about a פצוע דכא (crushed testicles) who performs yibbum: if he enters the yevama, he acquires her — but if those liable for negative commandments are exempt from yibbum, why should he acquire her?
The Gemara objects: if one thinks that those obligated by a negative commandment are only bound to chalitzah and not yibbum, why does the baraita say that if they had relations they acquire her?

items.text: Rava's first answer: the prohibition is a positive commandment
items.text_en: Rava's first answer: the prohibition is a positive commandment
items.desc_en: Rava reinterprets: the prohibition for a widow from betrothal (אלמנה מן האירוסין) is a positive commandment (עשה) and a negative commandment, based on the verse 'קדושים יהיו'. Similarly, for a mamzeret or netinah, the verse 'והתקדשתם' applies, making it a positive commandment.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the prohibition of an אלמנה מן האירוסין (widow from betrothal) for a Kohen Gadol is a עשה ולא תעשה (positive and negative commandment), citing the verse 'קדושים יהיו לאלהיהם'.
Rava extends the same reasoning to a ממזרת (bastard) and נתינה (Gibeonite): their prohibition is also a עשה ולא תעשה, derived from the verse 'והתקדשתם'.

items.text: Objection and Rava's second answer: a decree
items.text_en: Objection and Rava's second answer: a decree
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if so, all Torah prohibitions are positive commandments? Rava then says it is a decree: a widow from betrothal is decreed due to a widow from marriage, and a mamzeret/netinah is decreed in a place of mitzvah due to a place without mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if so, every prohibition in the Torah would be a עשה ולא תעשה, since the verse 'והתקדשתם' applies to all.
Rava revises his answer: the prohibition of an אלמנה מן האירוסין is a גזירה (decree) lest one confuse it with an אלמנה מן הנישואין (widow from marriage), which is a karet prohibition.
Rava extends the גזירה to a ממזרת and נתינה: the decree applies in a place of מצוה (yibbum) lest one confuse it with a place without מצוה.

items.text: Further objections to the decree approach
items.text_en: Further objections to the decree approach
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that such decrees are unreasonable: e.g., a wife of a brother from the father should not be forbidden due to a wife of a brother from the mother, since the Torah explicitly links yibbum to inheritance. Similarly, other distinctions are known. The Gemara also notes that a mamzeret/netinah is uncommon, so a decree is unnecessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the decree logic were applied, a wife of a brother from the father would not undergo yibbum (ייבום), but this is unreasonable because the Torah explicitly ties yibbum to inheritance, which is well-known.

The Gemara further objects that a woman without children would not undergo yibbum due to a decree for a woman with children, but the Torah explicitly conditions yibbum on having children, which is well-known.

The Gemara objects that a wife of a brother who existed in the world would not undergo yibbum due to a decree for a brother who never existed, but the Torah explicitly conditions yibbum on the brother's existence, which is well-known.

The Gemara objects that all women would not undergo yibbum due to a decree for an aylonit (איילונית), but an aylonit is uncommon, and similarly a mamzeret (ממזרת) or netinah (נתינה) is uncommon, so the decree is unnecessary.

items.text: Rava's third answer: decree due to second act
items.text_en: Rava's third answer: decree due to second act
items.desc_en: Rava says the decree is about the first act of relations (ביאה ראשונה) being permitted, but the second act (ביאה שניה) is forbidden. A baraita supports this: if he had relations, he acquires her in the first act, but may not keep her in the second act.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by explaining that the decree concerns the first act of relations (ביאה ראשונה) being permitted, but the second act (ביאה שניה) is forbidden.
A baraita supports Rava's distinction: if they had relations, they acquire her in the first act, but it is forbidden to keep her in the second act.

items.text: Rava's retraction and final conclusion
items.text_en: Rava's retraction and final conclusion
items.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Ashi) retracts, citing Resh Lakish: wherever there is a positive and negative commandment, if both can be fulfilled, that is best; otherwise, the positive commandment overrides the negative. Here, chalitzah fulfills both, so yibbum is not permitted. The baraita that says 'if he had relations, he acquires her' remains a difficulty (תיוובתא).

sub.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Ashi) retracts his earlier position, citing Resh Lakish's principle that when a positive and negative commandment conflict, if both can be fulfilled that is best, and here chalitzah fulfills both, so yibbum is not permitted.
The Gemara raises an objection from the baraita that says 'if they had relations, they acquire her,' leaving Rava's retraction as a difficulty (תיוובתא).

items.text: Dispute about a High Priest's yibbum with a widow
items.text_en: Dispute about a High Priest's yibbum with a widow
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar regarding whether a High Priest's yibbum with a widow (which is prohibited) exempts her rival from chalitzah or yibbum.

sub.desc_en: An amoraic dispute is recorded: regarding a Kohen Gadol's intercourse with a widow, one says it does not release her co-wife, and one says it does release her co-wife.
One of the disputants (Rabbi Yochanan or Rabbi Elazar) states that the High Priest's yibbum does not exempt the rival wife.
The other disputant (Rabbi Yochanan or Rabbi Elazar) states that the High Priest's yibbum does exempt the rival wife.

items.text: Dispute over widow from betrothal
items.text_en: Dispute over widow from betrothal
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is only about a widow from betrothal, not from marriage. One holds that a positive commandment can override a negative commandment, while the other holds it cannot since chalitzah is possible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that all agree regarding a widow from marriage: she does not exempt her rival, because a positive commandment cannot override a negative commandment combined with a positive one.
The Gemara clarifies that the dispute is specifically about a widow from betrothal: one opinion holds that a positive commandment can override a negative commandment, while the other holds it cannot.
The Gemara concludes that the second opinion holds the positive commandment cannot override because חליצה (release) is possible as an alternative.

items.text: Objection and Reish Lakish's response
items.text_en: Objection and Reish Lakish's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that if they had relations they acquire, which is a refutation. Reish Lakish defends his position by distinguishing that chalitzah is not a mitzvah in place of yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that if they had relations they acquire, presenting it as a refutation of Reish Lakish's position.
Reish Lakish defends his position by distinguishing that chalitzah is not a mitzvah in place of yibbum, so his ruling does not apply here.

items.text: Rava's derivation of secondaries from Torah
items.text_en: Rava's derivation of secondaries from Torah
items.desc_en: Rava derives that secondary forbidden relatives (שניות) are from the Torah, based on the verse 'כי את כל התועבות האל' where 'האל' implies severe ones, implying there are lenient ones, which are the secondaries. He supports this by showing 'האל' means severe.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by deriving that secondary forbidden relatives (שניות) have a hint from the Torah, citing the verse 'כי את כל התועבות האל' and interpreting 'האל' as severe, implying there are lenient ones, which are the secondaries.
Rava supports his interpretation by citing the verse 'וְאֶת אֵילֵי הָאָרֶץ לָקָח' to prove that 'האל' means severe.

items.text: Comparison with Rabbi Levi's statement
items.text_en: Comparison with Rabbi Levi's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rava's view conflicts with Rabbi Levi, who said punishment for middot is harsher than for arayot. It resolves that the verse 'אלה' in arayot excludes middot from karet, but the severity is that arayot cannot be rectified by repentance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rava's statement that the verse uses 'אֵל' for middot conflicts with Rabbi Levi's statement that punishment for middot is harsher than for arayot.
The Gemara objects that regarding arayot the verse also uses 'אֵלֶּה', and resolves that this excludes middot from karet.
The Gemara resolves that the greater severity of arayot is that they cannot be rectified by repentance, unlike middot.

items.text: Various derivations for secondaries
items.text_en: Various derivations for secondaries
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda, Rabbi Oshaya, Rav Ashi, and Rav Kahana each offer different verses as sources for secondary forbidden relatives. Abaye questions Rav Yosef whether these are Torah law, concluding they are rabbinic with a mere scriptural support.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites a verse from Kohelet (12:9) and, via Ulla citing Rabbi Elazar, explains that before Shlomo, the Torah was like a basket without handles, and Shlomo added 'handles' (fences) — a metaphor for secondary forbidden relatives.
Rabbi Oshaya cites Proverbs 4:15 as a source for secondary forbidden relatives, interpreting it as a warning to stay away from the boundary of forbidden relations.

Rav Ashi illustrates Rabbi Oshaya's verse with a parable of guarding an orchard from outside vs. inside, but the gemara dismisses Rav Ashi's version as fabricated (בדותא), noting that guarding from inside still protects the front, whereas without secondary relatives one would directly encounter the primary forbidden relative.
Rav Kahana cites Leviticus 18:30, interpreting 'make a guard for My guard' as a source for secondary forbidden relatives.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether the prohibition of secondary forbidden relatives is from the Torah (דאורייתא), noting that the rabbis merely explained it.

Rav Yosef objects that if the rabbis' explanation made it Torah law, then all Torah laws would be rabbinic; he concludes that secondary forbidden relatives are rabbinic (מדרבנן) with the verse as mere support (אסמכתא בעלמא).

items.text: List of secondary forbidden relatives and discussion
items.text_en: List of secondary forbidden relatives and discussion
items.desc_en: The baraita lists the secondary forbidden relatives. The Gemara questions why 'bat chorga' is included since it is Torah law, and explains it is because the tanna wanted to teach the statement about the wife of chorga. It then addresses why 'eshet chamiv' is not similarly stated.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the secondary forbidden relatives (שניות), including various maternal and paternal grandparents' wives and daughters-in-law, and states the permissibility of marrying the wife of one's father-in-law (חמיו) and the wife of one's stepson (חורגו), while forbidding the stepson's daughter (בת חורגו).
The baraita adds that the wife of one's stepson (אשת חורגו) may say to the man: 'I am permitted to you, but my daughter is forbidden to you.'
The Gemara questions why the baraita includes 'בת חורגו' (the stepson's daughter), since she is already forbidden by Torah law as a descendant of one's wife.

The Gemara answers that the tanna included 'בת חורגו' in the list because he wanted to teach the statement about 'אשת חורגו' (the wife of the stepson) in the continuation, so he also taught the beginning about the daughter.

The Gemara objects that the same reasoning should apply to 'אשת חמיו' (the wife of one's father-in-law), who could also say 'I am permitted to you, but my daughter (your wife's sister) is forbidden to you.'

The Gemara resolves that the cases differ: regarding 'אשת חמיו', the daughter (the man's wife's sister) is already severed from him (forbidden by Torah law), but regarding 'אשת חורגו', the daughter (the stepson's daughter) is not severed from him (since she is only a secondary forbidden relative).

items.text: Rav's list of women with a break and Ze'iri's addition
items.text_en: Rav's list of women with a break and Ze'iri's addition
items.desc_en: Rav states that four women have a break (הפסק), but he only holds three in his hand. Ze'iri adds the wife of his maternal grandfather. The Gemara explains why Rav omitted it and why Ze'iri includes it, and then discusses 'kallato'.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that four women have a break (הפסק) but only holds three in his hand: wife of his maternal uncle from the father, wife of his paternal uncle from the mother, and his daughter-in-law.
Ze'iri adds the wife of his maternal grandfather to Rav's list, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak provides a mnemonic sign.
The Gemara asks why Rav omitted the wife of his maternal grandfather from his list.
The Gemara answers that Rav omitted it because it might be confused with the wife of his paternal grandfather.
The Gemara asks why Ze'iri includes the wife of his maternal grandfather despite the potential confusion.

The Gemara answers that the wife of the paternal grandfather is common and one goes there, while the wife of the maternal grandfather is not common and one does not go there, so confusion is unlikely.
The Gemara begins to discuss the term 'kallato' (his daughter-in-law) from Rav's list.

items.text: Gemara's question on the daughter-in-law of one's son
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the daughter-in-law of one's son
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the daughter-in-law of one's son is considered a secondary forbidden relationship, given that the Torah explicitly forbids a daughter-in-law. It suggests it might refer to the daughter-in-law of one's daughter, but a baraita shows that the daughter-in-law of one's son is a secondary forbidden relationship.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the daughter-in-law of one's son is considered a secondary forbidden relationship, given that the Torah explicitly forbids a daughter-in-law, and suggests it might refer to the daughter-in-law of one's son.

The Gemara objects that the daughter-in-law of one's son has no interruption (i.e., it is a direct Torah prohibition), citing a baraita that lists the daughter-in-law of one's son as a secondary forbidden relationship.
The Gemara resolves that the secondary forbidden relationship is the daughter-in-law of one's daughter.

items.text: Rav Chisda's tradition and his reasoning
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's tradition and his reasoning
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda reports a tradition from Rabbi Ami that the prohibition of a daughter-in-law was only decreed because of the daughter-in-law of one's son. He then explains that he deduced on his own that the daughter-in-law of one's daughter was prohibited only because of the daughter-in-law of one's son.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda reports a tradition from Rabbi Ami that the prohibition of a daughter-in-law was only decreed because of the daughter-in-law of one's son.
Rav Chisda explains that he deduced on his own that the daughter-in-law of one's daughter was prohibited only because of the daughter-in-law of one's son.

items.text: Examples of the daughter-in-law of one's daughter
items.text_en: Examples of the daughter-in-law of one's daughter
items.desc_en: Abaye, Rav Pappa, and Rav Ashi each provide examples of cases where the daughter-in-law of one's daughter is prohibited because of the daughter-in-law of one's son, illustrating the principle with specific family relationships.

sub.desc_en: Abaye offers an example of a prohibited daughter-in-law of one's daughter: the daughter-in-law of Bar Tzeitai.
Rav Pappa provides his own example: the daughter-in-law of Rav Pappa bar Abba.
Rav Ashi gives his own example: the daughter-in-law of Mari bar Isak.

items.text: Inquiry about the wife of a maternal half-brother
items.text_en: Inquiry about the wife of a maternal half-brother
items.desc_en: A question is raised: is the wife of a maternal half-brother (where there is no paternal side) prohibited as a secondary forbidden relationship, or is it only prohibited when there is a paternal aspect?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: is the wife of a maternal half-brother (where there is no paternal side) prohibited as a secondary forbidden relationship, or is it only prohibited when there is a paternal aspect?

items.text: Rav Safra and Rava's discussion on decrees
items.text_en: Rav Safra and Rava's discussion on decrees
items.desc_en: Rav Safra objects that this would be a decree upon a decree, but Rava responds that all secondary forbidden relationships are decrees upon decrees, providing examples: the mother's mother, the father's wife's mother, and the wife of the father's brother from the mother, each explained by a common familial designation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra objects that the proposed prohibition of אשת אחי האם מן האם (wife of the mother's brother from the mother) would be a decree upon a decree, which is excessive.

Rava responds that all secondary forbidden relationships are decrees upon decrees, giving the example of the mother's mother and the mother's father's mother, all called 'דבי אימא רבתי' (the house of the great mother).

Rava provides another example: the wife of the father is a primary forbidden relationship, the wife of the father's father is a secondary one, and they decreed on the wife of the mother's father due to the wife of the father's father, all called 'דבי אבא רבה' (the house of the great father).

Rava gives a third example: the wife of the father's brother from the father is a primary forbidden relationship, the wife of the father's brother from the mother is secondary, and they decreed on the wife of the mother's brother from the father due to the wife of the father's brother from the mother, all called 'דבי דודי' (the house of my uncle).

items.text: Rav Yehuda bar Sheila's principle and Rava's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Sheila's principle and Rava's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Sheila reports a principle from the West: any female relative who is a primary forbidden relationship (ervah), the wife of the corresponding male relative is prohibited as a secondary. Rava challenges this with counterexamples (e.g., mother-in-law vs. wife of father-in-law). The Gemara then suggests that the principle was meant to include the wife of a maternal half-brother.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Sheila reports a principle from the West: any female relative who is a primary forbidden relationship (ערווה), the wife of the corresponding male relative is prohibited as a secondary (שנייה).

Rava challenges the principle with counterexamples: for several female relatives who are ערווה (e.g., mother-in-law, daughter of mother-in-law), the wife of the corresponding male relative is permitted, not prohibited.

The Gemara resolves that Rav Yehuda bar Sheila's principle was meant to include only the wife of a maternal half-brother (אשת אחי האם מן האם), where the female relative (the maternal half-sister) is a primary ערווה.

items.text: Distinction between the cases
items.text_en: Distinction between the cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the difference: in the cases Rava listed, the woman is close through one marriage bond, whereas in the cases where the principle applies, she is close only through two marriage bonds, hence the decree is necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the cases where the decree does not apply from the case where it does.
The Gemara answers that in the case where the decree applies, the woman is close through one marriage bond, whereas in the other cases she is close only through two marriage bonds.
