items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's prohibition might be a decree lest the yavam perform chalitzah for the first wife first, but rejects this because the Mishnah says 'they do not become yevamot' at all, indicating no yibum is possible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah teaches the prohibition לכתחילה (the ideal standard), not as a binding decree.
The Gemara asks why not say the prohibition is a decree lest the yavam perform חליצה (the release ceremony) for the first wife first.
The Gemara rejects the concern by noting the Mishnah says 'they do not become yevamot,' meaning there is no possibility of יבום (levirate marriage) here at all.

items.text: Rejecting the concern of death
items.text_en: Rejecting the concern of death
items.desc_en: Another suggestion is that the prohibition is a decree lest the yavam die, thereby nullifying the mitzvah of yibum, but Rabbi Yochanan does not worry about death.

sub.desc_en: The gemara proposes that the prohibition might be a decree lest the yavam die, thereby nullifying the mitzvah of yibum.
The gemara states that Rabbi Yochanan does not worry about the possibility of death.

items.text: Rejecting Rabbi Elazar's view
items.text_en: Rejecting Rabbi Elazar's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Elazar, who holds that once a woman stands in prohibition for an hour, she is forever forbidden, but notes that the latter clause is Rabbi Elazar, so the first clause is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah could be attributed to Rabbi Elazar, who holds that once a woman stands in prohibition for an hour, she is forever forbidden.
The Gemara rejects the attribution, noting that since the latter clause is Rabbi Elazar, the first clause cannot be his.

items.text: Rejecting Rabbi Yose HaGlili's view and the unknown order
items.text_en: Rejecting Rabbi Yose HaGlili's view and the unknown order
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the case involves two yevamot who fell simultaneously, following Rabbi Yose HaGlili who allows precise timing, but notes the Tanna does not rule like him. Then it suggests we do not know which fell first, but this leads to a difficulty with the Mishnah's ruling about those who married and must divorce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the case involves two yevamot who fell simultaneously, following Rabbi Yose HaGlili who holds that precise timing is possible.
The Gemara rejects this because the anonymous Tanna does not rule like Rabbi Yose HaGlili.
The Gemara suggests that the case is one where we do not know which yevama fell first.

items.text: Explaining the Mishnah's case of marrying first
items.text_en: Explaining the Mishnah's case of marrying first
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah says 'if they preceded and married, they must divorce': for the first wife, one can ask who permitted her, but for the second, she might claim her friend yibumed the second while she yibumed the first. This is why the Mishnah says 'I do not know who permitted sisters'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if so, why does the Mishnah say 'if they preceded and married, they must divorce' — for the first wife, one can ask who permitted her?
The Gemara answers: for the second wife, she might claim her friend yibumed the second while she yibumed the first, so the Mishnah says 'I do not know who permitted sisters'.

items.text: Analyzing the case of a mother-in-law
items.text_en: Analyzing the case of a mother-in-law
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one of the women is forbidden as an ervah, the yavam is forbidden to her but permitted to her sister, while the second yavam is forbidden to both. The Gemara questions why the son-in-law cannot first yibum the non-mother-in-law, making the mother-in-law a yevamah who was permitted and then forbidden and then permitted again. Rav Pappa answers that the non-mother-in-law fell first.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one woman is forbidden as an ervah to one yavam, he is forbidden to her but permitted to her sister, while the second yavam is forbidden to both.

The Gemara assumes the mother-in-law fell first and questions why the son-in-law cannot first perform yibum with the non-mother-in-law, making the mother-in-law a yevamah who was permitted, then forbidden, then permitted again, and thus revert to her original permitted status.
Rav Pappa answers that the case is where the non-mother-in-law fell first, so the son-in-law cannot perform yibum with her first because she is already the yevamah.

items.text: Analyzing the Tosefta on Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Analyzing the Tosefta on Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Eliezer reports that Beit Shammai say 'they may keep them' and Beit Hillel say 'they must divorce', while Rabbi Shimon says 'they may keep them' and Abba Shaul reverses the opinions. The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's position, concluding that he means there was no dispute in this case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Eliezer reports Beit Shammai say 'they may keep them' and Beit Hillel say 'they must divorce', while Rabbi Shimon says 'they may keep them' and Abba Shaul reverses the opinions.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's position, noting it aligns with neither Beit Shammai nor Beit Hillel as reported by others.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon means there was no dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel in this case.

items.text: Explaining the repetition of the sister case
items.text_en: Explaining the repetition of the sister case
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's case of a sister being a yevamah was already taught earlier, and explains that both are necessary: there, there is no second yavam to cause a decree, but here there is; conversely, here the second yavam provides a check, but there he does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah repeats the case of a sister being a yevamah, which was already taught earlier.
The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: there, there is no second yavam to cause a decree, but here there is; conversely, here the second yavam provides a check, but there he does not.

items.text: Introducing the next Mishnah
items.text_en: Introducing the next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's case of איסור מצוה was also already taught, and begins to introduce the next Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's case of איסור מצוה (a prohibition due to a commandment) was also already taught.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's distinction between issur mitzvah and issur ervah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's distinction between issur mitzvah and issur ervah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a woman forbidden by issur mitzvah (rabbinic prohibition) should not be permitted for yibbum, given that issur mitzvah is less severe. It explains that the case here involves both issur mitzvah and the sister of the yevama, and that the rabbis decreed to prevent violation of a biblical prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah distinguishes between a prohibition resulting from a mitzva alone and a case where both a prohibition resulting from a mitzva and her sister are involved.

The Gemara suggests that one might think the prohibition resulting from a mitzva should be treated like a prohibition against forbidden relatives, permitting the sister to enter into levirate marriage, but the Mishnah teaches that this is not the case.

The Gemara explains that the sister is forbidden because by Torah law the prohibited woman is still set before the yavam, and marrying the sister would violate the prohibition against the sister of a woman with a levirate bond; the Sages did not nullify their decree in this situation.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's repetition: 'One of them was...'
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's repetition: 'One of them was...'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah repeats the case of 'one of them was forbidden by issur ervah' when it already stated a similar case. It explains that the repetition is necessary to teach that even without a second witness (or without a second brother to prove the point), the ruling applies, and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah repeats the case of 'one of them was forbidden by issur ervah' when it already stated a similar case, questioning the difference between one brother and two.
The Gemara explains that the repetition is necessary because without a second brother to indicate the prohibition, one might think the ruling does not apply.
The Gemara adds that if only the case of two brothers were taught, one might think the opposite, so both cases are necessary.

items.text: Interpretation of 'This is what they said...' and exclusion of issur mitzvah for both
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'This is what they said...' and exclusion of issur mitzvah for both
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the phrase 'This is what they said' (zo hi she'amru) to exclude a case where both women are forbidden by issur mitzvah. It clarifies that the ruling applies only when one is forbidden by issur ervah and the other by issur mitzvah, and not when both are issur mitzvah, to prevent a decree due to a second brother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'zo hi' (this is) excludes, and answers that it excludes a case where both women are forbidden by איסור מצוה (a rabbinic prohibition).
The Gemara objects that this exclusion is redundant, since the same logic applies whether one or both women are forbidden by איסור מצוה.

The Gemara resolves that the exclusion is necessary to prevent a mistaken leniency: one might think that when there is no second brother to cause a decree, we could allow yibbum for both, but the mishnah teaches that even then, both must perform חליצה (release) and not yibbum.

items.text: Rav Yehuda, Abaye, and Rav Safra's interpretations of the Mishnah's scope
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda, Abaye, and Rav Safra's interpretations of the Mishnah's scope
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda (citing Rav and Rabbi Chiya) applies the principle to all cases where one woman is forbidden and the other permitted, but limits it to the six cases listed in the Mishnah. Abaye includes the case of a daughter from rape, while Rav Safra includes the case of a brother's wife who was never in the world (under Rabbi Shimon's view).

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rav and Rabbi Chiya
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav and Rabbi Chiya
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda, citing Rav and Rabbi Chiya, states that in all cases where one woman is forbidden and the other permitted, the sister who is the yevamah either performs חליצה (release) or יבום (levirate marriage).

Rav Yehuda limits the Mishnah's scope to the six cases from 'his mother-in-law' onward, excluding the first six cases because they involve a daughter from rape, which is not addressed in the Mishnah's context of marriage.

Abaye includes the case of a daughter from rape, since she can be acquired either through rape or marriage, but excludes the case of a brother's wife who was never in the world, as it depends on Rabbi Shimon's disputed view.

Rav Safra includes the case of a brother's wife who was never in the world, found in a scenario of six brothers under Rabbi Shimon's view, with the mnemonic 'died, was born, and performed יבום (levirate marriage).'

items.text: Illustrative case of Reuven, Shimon, Levi, and Yehuda to demonstrate the principle
items.text_en: Illustrative case of Reuven, Shimon, Levi, and Yehuda to demonstrate the principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a detailed example with four brothers and their wives to show how the principle works: when a woman is forbidden to one brother but permitted to another, the sister who is a yevama either performs chalitza or yibbum. It addresses potential objections about the necessity of certain details.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a detailed case with four brothers and their wives to illustrate the principle of when a woman forbidden to one brother is permitted to another.
The Gemara applies the principle: each woman forbidden to one brother is permitted to the other, and her sister as a yevama either performs חליצה (removing the shoe) or יבום (levirate marriage).
The Gemara questions why the case includes Yehuda's yibbum, since the same scenario could be found without it.
The Gemara answers that the detail is needed to address the case of a צרה (co-wife), and then raises a further question about a co-wife of a co-wife.
The Gemara resolves the question by adding that Gad and Asher also performed yibbum, creating a chain of co-wives.

items.text: Mishnah: Three brothers and the ruling of Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three brothers and the ruling of Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if two of three brothers are married to two sisters (or similar relations), the women perform chalitza but not yibbum. Rabbi Shimon exempts them entirely. The Gemara cites a baraita explaining Rabbi Shimon's reasoning from the verse 'You shall not take a woman to her sister to be rivals.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case of three brothers where two are married to two sisters or similar relations, ruling that the women perform חליצה (chalitza) but not ייבום (yibbum), and Rabbi Shimon exempts them entirely.

The Mishnah adds a second clause: if one woman is forbidden by איסור ערווה (incest prohibition), the brother is forbidden to her but permitted to her sister; if the prohibition is איסור מצוה (a rabbinic commandment prohibition) or איסור קדושה (sanctity prohibition), the women perform חליצה (chalitza) but not ייבום (yibbum).

A baraita is cited explaining Rabbi Shimon's reasoning from the verse 'וְאִשָּׁה אֶל אֲחוֹתָהּ לֹא תִקָּח לִצְרוֹר' (You shall not take a woman to her sister to be rivals), teaching that when they become rivals, you may not take even one of them.

items.text: Gemara: Why the Mishnah repeats 'One of them was...' for Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Gemara: Why the Mishnah repeats 'One of them was...' for Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah repeats the clause about one woman being forbidden by issur ervah, and explains that it is necessary for Rabbi Shimon's view, lest one think that since he exempts both sisters entirely, we should decree a prohibition even in cases of issur mitzvah to prevent confusion with the case of two sisters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah repeats the clause about one woman being forbidden by issur ervah, since it seems identical to the previous case.

The Gemara explains that the repetition is necessary for Rabbi Shimon's view, lest one think that since he exempts both sisters entirely, we should decree a prohibition even in cases of issur mitzvah to prevent confusion with the case of two sisters.
The Gemara cites the continuation of the Mishnah regarding issur mitzvah to show that the repetition is indeed needed.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Shimon and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Shimon and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's earlier statement that two sisters never perform halitzah or yibbum, given the Mishnah's case. It resolves by invoking a decree due to the general prohibition of a mitzvah, and distinguishes the case of ervah where people are fully aware.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Shimon's statement that two sisters never perform חליצה (halitzah) or יבום (yibbum), given the Mishnah's case.
The Gemara answers that the prohibition is a decree due to the general prohibition of a מצוה (mitzvah) of yibbum.
The Gemara questions why the sister of the woman who performed yibbum should also be prohibited.

The Gemara answers that the sister is prohibited due to a decree lest one confuse her case with the original, and distinguishes the case of ערוה (ervah) where people are fully aware and it is well-known.

items.text: Mishnah: Three brothers, two married to sisters, and a ma'amar
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three brothers, two married to sisters, and a ma'amar
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case of three brothers, two married to two sisters, and one unmarried. When one married brother dies and the unmarried brother performs ma'amar, then the second married brother dies, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute the status of the women.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of three brothers, two married to sisters, and one unmarried, where the unmarried brother performs ma'amar (a formal betrothal act) with the widow of the first brother who died.
Beit Shammai rules that the unmarried brother may keep his wife (the first widow), but the second widow must leave due to being the sister of his wife.

Beit Hillel rules that the brother must divorce his wife with a גט (bill of divorce) and perform חליצה (release ceremony) with her, and also perform חליצה with the second widow, lamenting his loss of both women.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying 'this is' to exclude Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying 'this is' to exclude Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'this is' comes to exclude, and answers that it excludes the case of Rabbi Yehoshua, meaning we do not follow his opinion but rather either Rabban Gamliel or Rabbi Elazar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'זוֹ הִיא' (this is) comes to exclude.
The Gemara answers that it excludes the case of Rabbi Yehoshua, meaning we do not follow his opinion but rather either Rabban Gamliel or Rabbi Elazar.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar: Ma'amar for Beit Shammai is not full acquisition
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar: Ma'amar for Beit Shammai is not full acquisition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that ma'amar for Beit Shammai does not effect a complete acquisition; rather, it only serves to push aside the tzarah (co-wife).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar clarifies that ma'amar for Beit Shammai does not effect a complete acquisition (קִנְיָן גָּמוּר), but only serves to push aside the tzarah (co-wife).

items.text: Rabbi Avin: Support from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin: Support from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin cites a Mishnah where Beit Shammai says 'they may keep them' (יקיימו), implying only after the fact, not ab initio, supporting Rabbi Elazar's view.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin cites a Mishnah where Beit Shammai says 'they may keep them' (יקיימו), implying only after the fact (בדיעבד), not לכתחילה (the ideal standard), supporting Rabbi Elazar's view.

items.text: Rejecting full acquisition and proposing partial rejection
items.text_en: Rejecting full acquisition and proposing partial rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers and rejects the possibility that ma'amar according to Beit Shammai is a full acquisition, as that would allow each brother to acquire the same woman. It then considers that ma'amar is a complete rejection, but notes that a permissible ma'amar can reject while a forbidden one cannot, leading to the conclusion that even for those who say ma'amar is a full acquisition, it only acquires when permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether ma'amar according to Beit Shammai is a full acquisition, as that would allow each brother to acquire the same woman.
The Gemara proposes that ma'amar is a complete rejection, allowing each brother to reject the yevama.
The Gemara resolves that a permissible ma'amar can reject or acquire, while a forbidden one cannot, applying this even to those who say ma'amar is a full acquisition.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's view: ma'amar rejects but leaves a remainder
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's view: ma'amar rejects but leaves a remainder
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that ma'amar according to Beit Shammai is not a complete rejection that exempts the rival wife from chalitzah, but rather a rejection that leaves a remainder. Rabbi Avin supports this from a mishnah where Beit Shammai say 'they shall fulfill' (implying bedi'eved, not lechatchilah), and if ma'amar were a complete rejection, each brother could make ma'amar and reject her.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's version of Rabbi Elazar's statement
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's version of Rabbi Elazar's statement
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi presents Rabbi Elazar's teaching that ma'amar according to Beit Shammai is not a complete rejection but a rejection that leaves a remainder.
Rabbi Avin cites a mishnah where Beit Shammai say 'they shall fulfill' (bedi'eved), implying ma'amar is not a complete rejection, otherwise each brother could make ma'amar and reject her.

items.text: Principle of partial viability
items.text_en: Principle of partial viability
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a principle: a yevamah who is fit for all brothers is fit for some, but one who is not fit for all is not fit for some.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a principle: a yevamah who is fit for all brothers is fit for some, but one who is not fit for all is not fit for some.

items.text: Rabba's inquiry: ma'amar as marriage or betrothal
items.text_en: Rabba's inquiry: ma'amar as marriage or betrothal
items.desc_en: Rabba asks whether ma'amar according to Beit Shammai constitutes marriage or betrothal. Abaye questions the practical difference, noting that for inheritance, impurity, and vow annulment, even a regular betrothal does not grant these rights. The issue is whether ma'amar requires a chuppah. Abaye argues that if without ma'amar the yavam can coerce her, with ma'amar it should certainly not require chuppah. Rabba responds that ma'amar removes the yevamah bond and replaces it with a betrothal bond.

sub.desc_en: Rabba asks whether ma'amar according to Beit Shammai constitutes marriage (נישואין) or betrothal (אירוסין).
Abaye asks Rabba what practical halachic difference this distinction makes.

sub.text: Abaye's objection regarding inheritance, impurity, and vows
sub.text_en: Abaye's objection regarding inheritance, impurity, and vows
sub.desc_en: Abaye argues that the practical difference cannot be inheritance, impurity, or vow annulment, since even a regular betrothed woman (ארוסה) does not grant these rights, as taught by Rabbi Chiyya.
Abaye suggests the practical difference is whether ma'amar requires a chuppah (מסירה לחופה) or not.

sub.text: Abaye's objection to the chuppah distinction
sub.text_en: Abaye's objection to the chuppah distinction
sub.desc_en: Abaye argues that if without ma'amar the yavam can coerce her to marry (based on 'יבמה יבוא עליה'), then with ma'amar it should certainly not require chuppah.
Rabba responds that ma'amar removes the yevamah bond (זיקת יבמין) and replaces it with a betrothal bond (זיקת אירוסין), leaving the question unresolved.

items.text: Proof from the mishnah of vow annulment for a shomeret yavam
items.text_en: Proof from the mishnah of vow annulment for a shomeret yavam
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer says a shomeret yavam can annul her vows, and Rabbi Ami explains this is a case of ma'amar according to Beit Shammai. If ma'amar constitutes marriage, annulment is understandable; if betrothal, the father should also be involved. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the annulment is in partnership (with the father). Rabbi Elazar, who holds ma'amar only rejects the rival wife, questions why there is any annulment, and the Gemara explains his view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a mishnah (Nedarim 74a) about vow annulment for a shomeret yavam, citing the positions of Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara analyzes the opinions: Rabbi Akiva holds no zikah, Rabbi Yehoshua holds zikah for one yavam but not two, and questions why Rabbi Eliezer allows annulment even with two yevamin.
רבי אמי בר אהבה (Rabbi Ami bar Ahava) explains that the mishnah deals with a case where one yavam performed ma'amar, and it follows Beit Shammai who hold that ma'amar is a full acquisition.
The Gemara infers: if ma'amar constitutes marriage, annulment is understandable; if only betrothal, how can he annul alone, since a betrothed woman requires her father's partnership?
רב נחמן בר יצחק (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak) answers that the mishnah means he annuls in partnership with the father.
The Gemara objects: according to Rabbi Elazar, who holds ma'amar only rejects the rival wife, why does he annul even in partnership?
רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) answers: his view that ma'amar only rejects the rival wife applies to the need for chalitza, but regarding vow annulment, he does not say it is ineffective.

items.text: Alternative explanation: court-ordered support and the principle of 'on da'at ba'al'
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: court-ordered support and the principle of 'on da'at ba'al'
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the case involves a shomeret yavam who stood in court and was awarded sustenance from the yavam, and she vows on his da'at (mindset), following Rav Pinchas in the name of Rava. This explains why the yavam can annul even without full marriage.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar objects to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution, noting that the mishna says 'יָפֵר (he nullifies)' in the singular, not 'יָפֵרוּ (they nullify)', implying the yavam acts alone.

The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the case involves a שומרת יבם (waiting yevama) who stood in court and was awarded sustenance from the yavam, and she vows on his דעת (mindset), following רב פנחס (Rav Pinchas) in the name of רבא (Rava). This explains why the yavam can annul even without full marriage.

items.text: First Mishnah: Case of three brothers
items.text_en: First Mishnah: Case of three brothers
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one of the brothers married to sisters dies, and the brother married to a non-relative marries the widow and then dies. The first widow is exempt due to being a sister-in-law, and the second due to being her tzarah. If he performed ma'amar, the non-relative performs halitzah but not yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case of three brothers, two married to sisters and one to a non-relative, and rules on the exemptions and halitzah requirements after successive deaths.

items.text: Gemara's inference and Rav Nachman's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's inference and Rav Nachman's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if he did not perform ma'amar, the non-relative would be permitted for yibbum. Rav Nachman says this indicates that there is no zikah, even with one brother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if he did not perform ma'amar, the non-relative would be permitted for yibbum.
Rav Nachman rules that this implies there is no זיקה (bond of yibbum), even with one brother.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Reversed case
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Reversed case
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a similar case but with the non-relative dying first, and one of the brothers married to sisters marrying her and then dying. The same ruling applies.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a second case where the non-relative dies first, then a brother married to a sister marries her and dies, with the same ruling.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about the order of Mishnayot
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about the order of Mishnayot
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the second Mishnah is needed, as it seems identical to the first. It answers that the Tanna first taught the case where the sister-in-law becomes a tzarah to the non-relative, which is more lenient, and then taught the stricter case where the non-relative becomes a tzarah to the sister-in-law. The order is due to the Tanna's preference for the lenient case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the second Mishnah is needed, arguing that the stricter case (non-relative becomes a tzarah to the sister-in-law) is already implied by the first Mishnah's lenient case.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna taught the lenient case first and then the stricter case, following a pattern of presenting the more permissible before the more forbidden.
The Gemara adds that because the lenient case was dear to the Tanna, he placed it first, and the Mishnah does not deviate from its established order.

items.text: Third Mishnah: Case where the yevamah was forbidden for an hour
items.text_en: Third Mishnah: Case where the yevamah was forbidden for an hour
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where the non-relative's wife dies after he marries the widow, and then he dies. The widow is forbidden forever because she was forbidden to him for one hour.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a third case where the non-relative's wife dies after he marries the widow, and then he dies, ruling the widow is permanently forbidden because she was forbidden for a moment.

items.text: Gemara's discussion: Rav's principle and its application
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion: Rav's principle and its application
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah says in the name of Rav that any yevamah who is not fit for yibbum at the time of falling is like a wife of a brother who has children and is forbidden. The Gemara questions what this adds, as the Mishnah already states this. It explains that one might think that if she was fit at the first falling, she would be permitted, but Rav teaches that she is still forbidden. The Gemara then cites a similar case from another Mishnah and explains that Rav's teaching is needed to counter the argument that since she is fit for the non-relative brother, she should be fit for this one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah says in the name of Rav that any יבמה (yevamah) who is not fit for יבום (levirate marriage) at the time of falling is like the wife of a brother who has children and is forbidden.
The Gemara asks what Rav's statement adds, since the Mishnah already states that she is forbidden forever because she was forbidden for one moment.
The Gemara explains that Rav's teaching is needed lest one think that if she was fit at the first falling she would be permitted; Rav teaches that she is still forbidden.
The Gemara objects that a similar case is already taught in another Mishnah about two brothers married to two sisters.
The Gemara resolves that Rav's teaching is needed to counter the argument that since she is fit for the non-relative brother, she should be fit for this brother as well.

items.text: Fourth Mishnah: Case of divorce and death
items.text_en: Fourth Mishnah: Case of divorce and death
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one of the brothers married to sisters divorces his wife, then the non-relative dies, and the divorcer marries the widow and dies. This is the case where it was said that if they die or are divorced, their tzarot are permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of three brothers where one divorces his wife, the non-relative brother dies, the divorcer marries the widow and dies, and rules that this is the case where their rival wives are permitted.

items.text: Gemara's inference and Rav Ashi's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's inference and Rav Ashi's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if he died first and then divorced, she is forbidden. Rav Ashi says this indicates that there is zikah, even with two brothers. The Gemara raises a contradiction with Rav Nachman's earlier statement, and Rav Ashi resolves it by saying that even without ma'amar, the non-relative would require halitzah, and the mention of ma'amar is to exclude Beit Shammai who say ma'amar acquires fully.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if the brother divorced first and then died, the yevamah is permitted, but if he died first and then divorced, she is forbidden.
Rav Ashi states that this inference proves there is זיקה (bond of yibbum) even when there are two brothers.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rav Ashi's position conflicts with Rav Nachman's earlier statement that there is no זיקה (bond of yibbum).

Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that even without מַאֲמָר (a formal declaration of yibbum), the non-relative yevamah requires חליצה (halitzah) and is forbidden for yibbum; the Mishnah's mention of מַאֲמָר is only to exclude Beit Shammai, who hold that מַאֲמָר fully acquires the yevamah.

items.text: Gemara's initial clarification of the Mishnah's phrase
items.text_en: Gemara's initial clarification of the Mishnah's phrase
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'this is' (זו היא) teaches that the ruling is not like Beit Shammai, implying a full acquisition (קנין גמור).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'this is' teaches a full acquisition (קנין גמור), not like Beit Shammai.

items.text: Resolving Rav Nachman's difficulty with Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Resolving Rav Nachman's difficulty with Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses Rav Nachman's difficulty with Rav Ashi's view. It considers two possibilities: either the Tanna holds like Rabbi Yirmeya that there are two distinct Tannaim (one for death, one for divorce), or like Rava that it is one Tanna using 'this and needless to say that'. Ultimately, it concludes that the Tanna must hold like Rabbi Yirmeya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises Rav Nachman's difficulty with Rav Ashi's view, and proposes that the Mishnah's phrase 'this is' excludes the case of marrying and then divorcing.
The Gemara considers the possibility that the Tanna holds like Rabbi Yirmeya, who posits two distinct Tannaim — one for death and one for divorce.
The Gemara objects that if the Tanna holds like Rava, who says it is one Tanna using 'this and needless to say that', then the phrase 'this is' would be superfluous.
The Gemara concludes that the Tanna must hold like Rabbi Yirmeya, as only his view resolves the difficulty.

items.text: Resolving Rava's difficulty with Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Resolving Rava's difficulty with Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: The Gemara similarly resolves Rava's difficulty: if he holds like Rav Ashi, the phrase excludes a case where the husband died without divorcing; if like Rav Nachman, it must be that he holds like Rav Ashi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rava's difficulty by showing that the phrase 'this is' must exclude a case where the husband died without divorcing if Rava holds like Rav Ashi, and if he held like Rav Nachman, the phrase would have no purpose, so he must hold like Rav Ashi.

items.text: Mishnah: Uncertain kiddushin and geirushin
items.text_en: Mishnah: Uncertain kiddushin and geirushin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that co-wives in cases of uncertain kiddushin or geirushin perform chalitzah but do not enter yibbum. It defines uncertain kiddushin as when a man throws a get close to her or close to him, and uncertain geirushin as a get lacking witnesses or date or having only one witness.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that co-wives in cases of uncertain kiddushin or geirushin perform chalitzah but do not enter yibbum, and defines uncertain kiddushin and geirushin.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why no 'close to him/her' for geirushin?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why no 'close to him/her' for geirushin?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not list the case of 'close to him or close to her' for geirushin, unlike for kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not list the case of 'close to him or close to her' for geirushin, as it does for kiddushin.

items.text: Raba's answer and Abaye's challenge
items.text_en: Raba's answer and Abaye's challenge
items.desc_en: Raba explains that a woman is presumed permitted to remarry, so we do not forbid her due to uncertainty. Abaye challenges that the same reasoning should apply to kiddushin, but Raba responds that there the stringency leads to a leniency: if we forbid the co-wife, the man might mistakenly marry the sister or the woman herself with valid kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not list a case of ספק גירושין (doubtful divorce) where the get is thrown close to him or close to her.
Raba explains that a woman stands in a חזקת היתר (presumption of permissibility) to remarry, so we do not forbid her due to uncertainty.
Abaye challenges that the same reasoning should apply to kiddushin (betrothal), where the woman stands in a חזקת היתר (presumption of permissibility) to the yavam (levir).

Raba responds that in the case of kiddushin, the stringency (חומרא) leads to a leniency (קולא): if we forbid the co-wife, the man might mistakenly marry the sister or the woman herself with valid kiddushin.

items.text: Challenge to the leniency of requiring ḥalitzah
items.text_en: Challenge to the leniency of requiring ḥalitzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if requiring ḥalitzah leads to the possibility of levirate marriage (a leniency), then the same should apply to a case of divorce where the woman is uncertainly divorced. The objection is that the assumption of permissibility should prevent any stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that since requiring ḥalitzah is known to be a stringency, the same logic should apply to a case of uncertain divorce, where requiring ḥalitzah would also be known as a stringency.

The objection counters that if you say she performs ḥalitzah, she may then enter levirate marriage (a leniency), but here the woman stands in a presumption of permissibility, so the leniency should not be introduced.

items.text: Abaye's objection from the case of a collapsed building
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from the case of a collapsed building
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a mishnah where a woman whose husband and brother-in-law died in a collapse, with the order unknown, must perform ḥalitzah and cannot enter levirate marriage. The Gemara questions why the same principle of assumption of permissibility does not apply, and answers that this stringency leads to a leniency (levirate marriage), so the Sages decreed only in common cases (divorce) but not in uncommon ones (collapse).

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a mishnah where a woman whose husband and brother-in-law died in a collapse, with the order unknown, must perform חליצה (ḥalitzah) and cannot enter levirate marriage, challenging the assumption of permissibility.
The Gemara asks why the same principle of חזקת היתר (presumption of permissibility) does not apply here, as the woman was in a permitted state and should not be forbidden due to doubt.
The Gemara answers that the stringency of requiring חליצה (ḥalitzah) leads to a leniency (levirate marriage), so the Sages decreed only in common cases (divorce) but not in uncommon ones (collapse).

items.text: Alternative explanation: concern about witnesses
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: concern about witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another reason: in divorce cases, the woman's ervah (forbidden relative) is present to testify, so people might mistakenly think the divorce is valid and permit levirate marriage. In a collapse, no such witness exists.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: in divorce cases, the ervah (forbidden relative) is present to testify, so people might mistakenly think the divorce is valid and permit levirate marriage, whereas in a collapse no such witness exists.

items.text: Challenge from the mishnah on get thrown in public domain
items.text_en: Challenge from the mishnah on get thrown in public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah where a get thrown in the public domain, equidistant between husband and wife, results in a doubt. The halakhah requires ḥalitzah for the co-wife, and the Gemara notes that there too the concern of leading to levirate marriage should apply, but it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: regarding divorce, is it not taught in a mishnah that a get thrown in the public domain, equidistant between husband and wife, results in a doubt (מגורשת ואינה מגורשת)?

The Gemara notes that the halakhah of that mishnah requires ḥalitzah for the co-wife, yet the concern that 'if you say she performs ḥalitzah, she might be taken for levirate marriage' is not raised there.

items.text: Resolution: distinction between one set and two sets of witnesses
items.text_en: Resolution: distinction between one set and two sets of witnesses
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain that the mishnah about the get involves two sets of witnesses (a Torah-level doubt), while our mishnah involves one set (a rabbinic doubt). The Gemara questions this, arguing that even with two sets, the doubt is rabbinic and the woman should be permitted, but concludes that the case of a shoteh (insane person) selling property shows that two sets create a Torah-level doubt.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef resolve the contradiction by distinguishing that the mishnah about the get involves two sets of witnesses (a Torah-level doubt), while our mishnah involves one set (a rabbinic doubt).
The Gemara questions how we know our mishnah involves one set of witnesses, suggesting that even if the kiddushin case involved two sets, the woman should be permitted to remarry.

The Gemara objects that even with two sets of witnesses, the doubt is rabbinic, as we apply the principle of 'אוֹקֵי תְּרֵי לְבַהֲדֵי תְּרֵי' (set two against two) and maintain the woman's presumptive status.

The Gemara cites the case of a shoteh (insane person) selling property, where Rav Ashi ruled that two sets of witnesses create a Torah-level doubt, supporting the distinction that two sets create a Torah-level doubt here as well.

items.text: Support from the case of a shoteh's property
items.text_en: Support from the case of a shoteh's property
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a case where two witnesses say a shoteh sold property while sane, and two say while insane. Rav Ashi rules that we set two against two, leaving the property in its presumptive state. This supports the distinction between one and two sets of witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a case where two witnesses say a shoteh sold property while sane and two say while insane, and Rav Ashi rules that we set two against two, leaving the property in its presumptive state, supporting the distinction between one and two sets of witnesses.

items.text: Rejection of the previous suggestion
items.text_en: Rejection of the previous suggestion
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that the land is established in the presumption of being a fool, implying that the previous explanation is insufficient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous suggestion by stating that the land is established in the presumption of being a fool, indicating the explanation is insufficient.

items.text: Abaye's explanation: יגיד עליו ריעו
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation: יגיד עליו ריעו
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Mishnah uses the principle of 'יגיד עליו ריעו' (its fellow clarifies it), and notes that the teaching in Kiddushin applies to Gittin and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Mishnah uses the principle of יגיד עליו ריעו (its fellow clarifies it), meaning that the teaching in Kiddushin applies to Gittin and vice versa.

items.text: Rava's question on 'zeh hu'
items.text_en: Rava's question on 'zeh hu'
items.desc_en: Rava questions Abaye: if the principle is 'יגיד עליו ריעו', then what is the meaning of the term 'zeh hu' that the Mishnah teaches?

sub.desc_en: Rava questions Abaye: if the principle is יגיד עליו ריעו (one topic illuminates the other), then what is the meaning of the term 'זהו' (this is it) that the Mishnah teaches?

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah means that whatever applies to kiddushin applies to gittin, but there are additional elements in gittin not in kiddushin. The 'zeh hu' in gittin is not precise, but is used because it appears in kiddushin, where it excludes time (zman) which does not apply to kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah's 'zeh hu' in gittin is not precise but borrowed from kiddushin, where it excludes time (zman) which does not apply to kiddushin.

items.text: Why time was not instituted for kiddushin
items.text_en: Why time was not instituted for kiddushin
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages did not institute a time (zman) for kiddushin. It considers two reasons: according to the view that it is due to produce (peirot), an arusah has no produce; according to the view that it is due to the daughter of his sister (bat achoto), the Gemara questions why time was not instituted. The answer is that because some betroth with money and some with a document, the Sages did not institute time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages did not institute a time limit (zman) for kiddushin (betrothal).

sub.text: First answer (according to the view of produce)
sub.text_en: First answer (according to the view of produce)
sub.desc_en: According to the view that the concern is about produce (peirot), an arusah (betrothed woman) has no produce, so no time is needed.

sub.text: Second answer (according to the view of the daughter of his sister)
sub.text_en: Second answer (according to the view of the daughter of his sister)
sub.desc_en: According to the view that the concern is about the daughter of his sister (bat achoto), the Gemara objects that a time should have been instituted.
The Gemara answers that because some betroth with money and some with a document, the Sages did not institute a time limit.

items.text: Challenge from the case of a slave
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of a slave
items.desc_en: Rav Acha the son of Rav Yosef challenges Rav Ashi: in the case of a slave, where acquisition can be by money or document, the Sages did institute time. The Gemara answers that there, the majority is by document, while here, the majority is by money.

sub.text: Rav Acha the son of Rav Yosef's challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Acha the son of Rav Yosef's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha challenges Rav Ashi: in the case of a slave, where acquisition can be by money or document, the Sages did institute time, so why not for betrothal?
The Gemara answers that there, the majority of slave acquisitions are by document, while here, the majority of betrothals are by money, so the concern about forged documents is minimal.

items.text: Alternative reason: impossibility
items.text_en: Alternative reason: impossibility
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: it is impossible to institute time for kiddushin because of practical difficulties. If the document is placed with her, she might erase it; if with him, he might conceal it if she is his sister's daughter; if with witnesses, they might testify from the writing, which is forbidden. The Gemara then asks why this reasoning does not apply to gittin, and answers that in gittin it comes for her benefit, while in kiddushin it comes for her detriment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative reason: it is impossible to institute a time for kiddushin because of practical difficulties — if the document is placed with her she might erase it, and if with him he might conceal it if she is his sister's daughter.
The Gemara adds that if the document is placed with witnesses, they might testify from the writing, which is forbidden by the verse 'מפיהם' (from their mouths) and not from their writing.
The Gemara asks why this reasoning does not apply to gittin (bills of divorce) as well.
The Gemara answers that in gittin the document comes for her benefit, while in kiddushin it comes for her detriment, so the concern about forgery is different.

items.text: Mishnah: Three brothers married to three converts
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three brothers married to three converts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if three brothers are married to three converts, one dies, the second performs ma'amar and then dies, the women must perform chalitzah and cannot enter yibbum, based on the verse that a yevamah has only one zikah. Rabbi Shimon says he may perform yibbum with whichever he wants and perform chalitzah with the second.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of three brothers married to three converts, where one dies, the second performs ma'amar and dies, and rules that the women must perform chalitzah and cannot enter yibbum because a yevamah has only one zikah.
The Mishnah cites the verse that a yevamah has only one zikah, not two.
Rabbi Shimon states that he may perform yibbum with whichever woman he wants and perform chalitzah with the second.

items.text: Gemara: The nature of the prohibition
items.text_en: Gemara: The nature of the prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the prohibition of zikat shnei yevamin is biblical or rabbinic. It concludes it is rabbinic, as a decree lest people say that two yevamot from one house can enter yibbum. The Gemara then asks why one cannot perform yibbum with one and chalitzah with the other, and answers that it is a decree lest people say that one house is partially built.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions that if the prohibition of זיקת שני יבמין (the bond of two yevamim) were biblical, even חליצה (the release ceremony) would not be required.
The Gemara answers that the prohibition is only rabbinic (מדרבנן), as a decree lest people mistakenly think that two yevamot from one house can enter יבום (levirate marriage).
The Gemara asks why one cannot perform יבום (levirate marriage) with one yevamah and חליצה (release) with the other.
The Gemara answers that it is a decree lest people say that one house is partially built (בית אחד מקצתו בנוי), implying that partial יבום is permitted.

items.text: Gemara's question on partial chalitza
items.text_en: Gemara's question on partial chalitza
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that if a yavam performed both yibum and chalitza with one of two sisters, the other sister is permitted. It explains that if he did yibum first and then chalitza, it is fine, but the concern is that he might do chalitza first and then yibum, violating the prohibition of 'asher lo yivneh'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling about partial chalitza, noting that if the yavam performed yibum first and then chalitza, it is understandable.
The Gemara explains that the concern is a decree lest he perform chalitza first and then yibum, violating the prohibition of 'אשר לא יבנה' (one who does not build shall not build again).

items.text: Rava's ruling on a get for ma'amar
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a get for ma'amar
items.desc_en: Rava states that if a yavam gave a get to his ma'amar (a formal betrothal of a yevamah), the co-wife is permitted. There are two versions: one says the yevamah herself remains forbidden due to confusion with a woman who received a get, while another version says even she is permitted because the ma'amar is nullified.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that if a yavam gave a get to his ma'amar, the co-wife is permitted, but the woman herself is forbidden because she might be confused with a woman who received a get.
An alternative version reports that Rava says even the woman herself is permitted, because what he did with her is already taken away.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on two brothers married to two sisters
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on two brothers married to two sisters
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if two brothers were married to two sisters, and one brother died, and then the wife of the second brother died, the surviving brother is forever forbidden to the surviving sister because she was forbidden to him for a moment. The Gemara questions why this is not obvious, and explains that the Tanna first taught a case where the woman was never permitted, then taught this case where she was initially permitted and then forbidden, and the Mishnah remains in its place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah's ruling is necessary, arguing that if a less severe case is forbidden, this more severe case should certainly be forbidden.

The Gemara explains that the Tanna taught the case where the woman was initially permitted and then became forbidden, and because she was beloved to him, he presented it first, but the Mishnah's order does not change the law.

The Gemara answers that the Tanna first taught a case where the woman was never permitted, then taught this case where she was initially permitted and then forbidden, and the Mishnah remains in its place.

items.text: Baraita on Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon's dispute
items.text_en: Baraita on Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon's dispute
items.desc_en: A Baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi Yosei says one who has relations with a woman who is both an yevamah and a sister of his wife is liable for both prohibitions, while Rabbi Shimon says he is liable only for one. A contradiction is noted in Rabbi Shimon's statements, and it is resolved by distinguishing between whether the living brother married first or the deceased brother married first.

sub.desc_en: The Baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Yosei holds one is liable for both prohibitions (אשת אח and אחות אשה), while Rabbi Shimon holds one is liable only for אשת אח.
The Gemara objects by citing a contradictory Baraita where Rabbi Shimon says one is liable only for אחות אשה, not אשת אח.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first Baraita (liable for אשת אח) refers to a case where the living brother married first, then the deceased brother married; the second Baraita (liable for אחות אשה) refers to the reverse order.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Shimon's view and Rav Ashi's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Shimon's view and Rav Ashi's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's view: if the prohibition of a sister of his wife does not take effect when the deceased married first, why can't the yavam perform yibum? Rav Ashi answers that the prohibition of a sister of his wife is pending; if the prohibition of a wife's brother falls away, the sister's prohibition takes effect, so it never falls away.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's view: if the prohibition of a sister of his wife (אחות אשה) does not take effect when the deceased married first, why can't the yavam perform yibum?

Rav Ashi answers that the prohibition of a sister of his wife (אחות אשה) is pending; if the prohibition of a wife's brother (אשת אח) falls away, the sister's prohibition takes effect, so it never falls away.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yosei from a Baraita on overlapping prohibitions
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yosei from a Baraita on overlapping prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yosei's view that one prohibition can take effect on another, citing a Baraita where Rabbi Yosei says a person is judged by the first prohibition that applies to him, not by the more severe one. Examples are given of a mother-in-law who becomes a married woman, or a married woman who becomes a mother-in-law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yosei's view that one prohibition can take effect on another (איסור חל על איסור).
A baraita is cited: for a transgression with two death penalties, one is judged by the stricter one, but Rabbi Yosei says one is judged by the first liability (זיקה) that came upon him.

The baraita elaborates: if a mother-in-law becomes a married woman, he is judged by the mother-in-law prohibition; if a married woman becomes a mother-in-law, he is judged by the married woman prohibition.

items.text: Analysis of איסור מוסיף regarding a living and deceased sister
items.text_en: Analysis of איסור מוסיף regarding a living and deceased sister
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu states that Rabbi Yosei concedes the principle of איסור מוסיף. The Gemara questions how this applies when one first marries a living sister and then a deceased one, and when one first marries a deceased sister and then a living one, suggesting the latter case involves איסור כולל rather than איסור מוסיף.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu states that Rabbi Yosei concedes the principle of איסור מוסיף (an added prohibition), and the Gemara explains that when one first marries a living sister and then a deceased one, the prohibition is added regarding the brothers and regarding himself.
The Gemara questions what איסור מוסיף (added prohibition) exists when one first marries a deceased sister and then a living one.
The Gemara objects that if one suggests the prohibition extends to all sisters, that is איסור כולל (a comprehensive prohibition), not איסור מוסיף (an added prohibition).

items.text: Rava and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the case
items.text_en: Rava and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the case
items.desc_en: Rava and Rabbi Yochanan rule that one who marries both a living and a deceased sister is considered as if he committed two acts but is only liable for one. The practical difference is for burial among the wicked.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that one who marries both a living and a deceased sister is considered as if he committed two acts but is only liable for one.
Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan independently rules the same as Rava.
The Gemara explains the practical difference between the two opinions is for burial among the wicked.

items.text: Dispute: Zar who served on Shabbat
items.text_en: Dispute: Zar who served on Shabbat
items.desc_en: A dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara regarding a non-priest who performed Temple service on Shabbat. Rabbi Chiyya holds he is liable for two (for זרות and Shabbat), while Bar Kappara holds he is liable for only one. Each swears they heard their ruling from Rabbi. They present logical arguments: Rabbi Chiyya argues both prohibitions apply, Bar Kappara argues only זרות applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara regarding a non-priest who performed Temple service on Shabbat, stating their opposing positions.
Rabbi Chiyya argues that since Shabbat was permitted only to priests in the Temple, a non-priest is liable for both זרות (non-priesthood) and Shabbat.
Bar Kappara argues that since Shabbat was permitted entirely in the Temple, only the prohibition of זרות (non-priesthood) applies.

items.text: Dispute: Ba'al Mum who served while impure
items.text_en: Dispute: Ba'al Mum who served while impure
items.desc_en: A dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara regarding a blemished priest who performed Temple service while impure. Rabbi Chiyya holds he is liable for two (for blemish and impurity), Bar Kappara holds he is liable for only one. Each swears they heard their ruling from Rabbi, and they present similar logical arguments.

sub.desc_en: The stam introduces a dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara regarding a blemished priest who served while impure: Rabbi Chiyya holds he is liable for two (for blemish and impurity), Bar Kappara holds he is liable for only one.
Rabbi Chiyya swears by the Temple service that he heard from Rabbi that the blemished priest is liable for two.
Bar Kappara swears by the Temple service that he heard from Rabbi that the blemished priest is liable for only one.
Rabbi Chiyya argues that since impurity was permitted only to unblemished priests in the Temple, both the prohibition of blemish and impurity apply here.
Bar Kappara argues that since impurity was permitted entirely in the Temple, only the prohibition of blemish applies.

items.text: Dispute: Zar who ate melikah
items.text_en: Dispute: Zar who ate melikah
items.desc_en: A dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara regarding a non-priest who ate a bird offering prepared by melikah. Rabbi Chiyya holds he is liable for two (for זרות and melikah), Bar Kappara holds he is liable for only one. Each swears they heard their ruling from Rabbi, and they present similar logical arguments.

sub.desc_en: The stam introduces the dispute: a non-priest who ate a bird offering prepared by melikah — Rabbi Chiyya says he is liable for two (for זרות and melikah), Bar Kappara says he is liable for only one.

Each rabbi swears he heard his ruling from Rabbi, and each presents a logical argument: Rabbi Chiyya argues that melikah was permitted only to priests, so both זרות and melikah apply; Bar Kappara argues that melikah was permitted entirely in the Temple, so only זרות remains.

items.text: Initial framing of the dispute
items.text_en: Initial framing of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara disagree about issur kolel according to Rabbi Yosei. Rabbi Chiyya holds that Rabbi Yosei would impose two liabilities for an issur kolel, while Bar Kappara holds he would impose only one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara frames the dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara as revolving around whether Rabbi Yosei applies איסור כולל (a prohibition that extends to include additional forbidden categories) to impose two liabilities or only one.

items.text: Analysis of issur kolel in this case
items.text_en: Analysis of issur kolel in this case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how issur kolel applies to a zar and a ba'al mum, but notes that melikah occurs at a single moment and cannot involve issur kolel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what איסור כולל (inclusive prohibition) exists in the case of melikah (pinching the neck of a bird-offering), and explains that for a zar (non-priest) and a ba'al mum (blemished priest), Shabbat or impurity add a new prohibition, but melikah occurs simultaneously and cannot involve איסור כולל.

The Gemara explains that for a בעל מום (blemished priest), impurity adds a prohibition on eating, which then includes the service prohibition, but notes that melikah (pinching the bird's neck) occurs at a single moment and cannot involve איסור כולל.

items.text: Revised framing: issur b'vat achat
items.text_en: Revised framing: issur b'vat achat
items.desc_en: The Gemara revises the dispute to be about issur b'vat achat according to Rabbi Yosei. Rabbi Chiyya holds that Rabbi Yosei would impose two liabilities, while Bar Kappara holds only one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara shifts the dispute to איסור בת אחת (a single act that simultaneously violates multiple prohibitions) according to Rabbi Yosei, with Rabbi Chiyya holding two liabilities and Bar Kappara holding one.

items.text: Examples of issur b'vat achat
items.text_en: Examples of issur b'vat achat
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides examples: a zar who served on Shabbat by bringing two hairs, and a ba'al mum who brought two hairs and became impure, or cut his finger with a contaminated knife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what איסור בת אחת (simultaneous prohibitions) exists here, and answers with examples: a zar serving on Shabbat by bringing two hairs, or a ba'al mum who brings two hairs and becomes impure, or one who cuts his finger with a contaminated knife.
The Gemara explains: a zar who served on Shabbat, e.g., by bringing two hairs on Shabbat, incurs both the prohibition of zarus (non-priestly service) and Shabbat simultaneously.
The Gemara gives another example: a ba'al mum (blemished priest) who brought two hairs and became impure, incurring both the prohibition of blemish and impurity simultaneously.
Alternatively, the Gemara suggests a case where a ba'al mum cut his finger with a contaminated knife, incurring both the blemish prohibition and impurity from the knife.

items.text: Challenge: consistency of Rabbi Chiyya's teaching
items.text_en: Challenge: consistency of Rabbi Chiyya's teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Chiyya taught Bar Kappara according to Rabbi Shimon, but taught himself according to Rabbi Yosei. This raises the question: is Bar Kappara accusing Rabbi Chiyya of lying?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: according to Bar Kappara's position, Rabbi Chiyya would have taught Bar Kappara according to Rabbi Shimon while teaching himself according to Rabbi Yosei, implying Rabbi Chiyya is lying — which is problematic.

items.text: Alternative: dispute according to Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Alternative: dispute according to Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the dispute is about issur b'vat achat according to Rabbi Shimon. For Rabbi Chiyya, he needed to take an oath to remove Rabbi Shimon from his presumption; for Bar Kappara, the oath is unnecessary, posing a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara shifts to framing the dispute according to Rabbi Shimon, noting that for Rabbi Chiyya the oath serves to remove Rabbi Shimon from his default position, but for Bar Kappara the oath is unnecessary — a difficulty.
The Gemara explains that for Rabbi Chiyya, the oath was needed to remove Rabbi Shimon from his presumption (חזקה).
The Gemara objects that for Bar Kappara, the oath would be unnecessary, posing a difficulty.

items.text: Challenge: consistency of Rabbi's teaching
items.text_en: Challenge: consistency of Rabbi's teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi taught Bar Kappara according to Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Chiyya according to Rabbi Yosei. This raises the question: is Rabbi Chiyya accusing Bar Kappara of lying?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: according to Rabbi Chiyya's position, Rabbi would have taught Bar Kappara according to Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Chiyya according to Rabbi Yosei, implying Bar Kappara is lying — which is problematic.
The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Chiyya taught Bar Kappara according to Rabbi Shimon, is Bar Kappara accusing Rabbi Chiyya of lying?

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya explains that when Rabbi taught Bar Kappara, he taught him two versions for exemption, implying that the teaching was not a lie but a different interpretation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya responds that when Rabbi taught Bar Kappara, he taught him two liabilities for exemption (i.e., that both prohibitions are exempt from punishment), not for liability.

items.text: Bar Kappara's search for a parallel to איסור בת אחת
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's search for a parallel to איסור בת אחת
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara sought a case of איסור בת אחת (simultaneous prohibitions) analogous to a non-priest eating a bird-offering (מליקה), but found only the case of a daughter (בת אחת). He concluded that just as that case involves a single act with multiple prohibitions, so too here; and just as those cases are exempt from multiple punishments, so too here.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that the Mishnah deals with איסור כולל (an inclusive prohibition) according to Rabbi Shimon, and Bar Kappara sought a parallel for a non-priest eating a bird-offering (מליקה) but found only the case of a daughter (בת אחת).

Bar Kappara reasoned that just as the daughter case involves a single act with simultaneous prohibitions, so too the bird-offering case; and just as those cases are exempt from multiple punishments, so too here.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita: Rabbi Yossi and Rabbi Shimon on overlapping prohibitions
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita: Rabbi Yossi and Rabbi Shimon on overlapping prohibitions
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a non-priest who served on Shabbat, and a blemished priest who served while impure — Rabbi Yossi holds there are four prohibitions (זרות, שבת, בעל מום, טומאה), while Rabbi Shimon says only two (זרות and בעל מום). The baraita omits מליקה. The Gemara argues this omission proves Rabbi Shimon would hold one liable for איסור בת אחת, contradicting Bar Kappara's position, and concludes Bar Kappara's view is refuted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a non-priest who served on Shabbat and a blemished priest who served while impure — Rabbi Yossi holds there are four prohibitions (זרות, שבת, בעל מום, טומאה), while Rabbi Shimon says only two (זרות and בעל מום), and the baraita omits מליקה.
The Gemara asks: for whom does the baraita omit מליקה? It argues it cannot be for Rabbi Yossi, who would certainly include it, so it must be for Rabbi Shimon.

The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon exempts only in cases of איסור כולל (an inclusive prohibition), but would hold one liable for איסור בת אחת (a single-act prohibition), thus refuting Bar Kappara's position.

items.text: Analysis of the non-priest's service on Shabbat: which act?
items.text_en: Analysis of the non-priest's service on Shabbat: which act?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what service the non-priest performed on Shabbat. Slaughter is valid by a non-priest; receiving and carrying are mere moving; burning (הקטרה) is only a negative prohibition per Rabbi Yossi. Rav Acha bar Yaakov suggests it was the slaughter of the High Priest's red heifer, which is invalid by a non-priest. But then even a common priest would be considered a 'non-priest' relative to the High Priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which service the non-priest performed on Shabbat, rejecting slaughter (valid by a non-priest) and receiving/carrying (mere moving).
The Gemara objects that burning (הקטרה) cannot be the act, since Rabbi Yossi holds that burning is only a negative prohibition, not a capital Shabbat violation.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that it was the slaughter of the High Priest's red heifer, which is invalid by a non-priest; the Gemara objects that even a common priest would be a 'non-priest' relative to the High Priest, and Rav Acha clarifies that the mishna means 'a non-priest relative to him.'

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection: the baraita counts prohibitions, not sin-offerings
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection: the baraita counts prohibitions, not sin-offerings
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects: the baraita lists prohibitions (איסורין), not sin-offerings. The practical difference is for burial among the wicked. This reframes the entire discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that the baraita counts prohibitions (איסורין), not sin-offerings, and the practical difference is for burial among the wicked.

items.text: Mishnah: Two men who exchanged wives at the wedding
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two men who exchanged wives at the wedding
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where two men betrothed two women, and at the wedding they accidentally exchanged wives. They are liable for adultery (אשת איש), and if brothers, for אשת אח; if sisters, for אשה אל אחותה; if menstruants, for נדה. They are separated for three months to check for pregnancy; minors are returned immediately; if the women are priestesses, they are disqualified from terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of two men who betrothed two women and accidentally exchanged wives at the wedding, listing the prohibitions violated: adultery, אשת אח (wife of a brother), אשה אל אחותה (a woman to her sister), and נדה (menstruant).

The Mishnah continues with the ruling that the women are separated for three months to check for pregnancy; minors are returned immediately; if the women are priestesses, they are disqualified from תרומה (priestly portion).

items.text: Gemara: The exchange was accidental (הוחלפו), not intentional
items.text_en: Gemara: The exchange was accidental (הוחלפו), not intentional
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah deals with intentional sinners (רשעי), since Rabbi Chiya's version lists sixteen sin-offerings, which would not apply to intentional acts. Rav Yehuda says to read 'they were exchanged' (הוחלפו). The Gemara supports this from the ruling that minors are returned immediately (since seduction of a minor is considered rape, permitted), and from the separation for three months — if intentional, they would not be permitted to return.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah deals with intentional sinners, since Rabbi Chiya's version lists sixteen sin-offerings, which would not apply to intentional acts.
Rav Yehuda answers that the Mishnah should be read as 'they were exchanged' (הוחלפו), implying an accident, not intentional sin.
The Gemara supports Rav Yehuda from the Mishnah's ruling that minors are returned immediately, explaining that seduction of a minor is considered rape and therefore permitted even if intentional.

The Gemara further supports from the Mishnah's requirement to separate for three months, arguing that if intentional, the women would not be permitted to return, so the exchange must have been accidental.

items.text: Identifying the tanna who holds issur kolel, issur mosif, and issur bat aḥat
items.text_en: Identifying the tanna who holds issur kolel, issur mosif, and issur bat aḥat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the tanna that holds the principles of issur kolel, issur mosif, and issur bat aḥat. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers that it is Rabbi Meir, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that one who eats a single forbidden item can be liable for four sin-offerings and one guilt-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the tanna that holds the principles of איסור כולל (a prohibition that encompasses additional items), איסור מוסיף (a prohibition that adds to an existing one), and איסור בת אחת (a single prohibition covering multiple items simultaneously).

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers that it is Rabbi Meir, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that one who eats a single forbidden item can be liable for four sin-offerings and one guilt-offering.
The baraita specifies the case: a ritually impure person who eats forbidden fat (חלב) that is leftover (נותר) from consecrated offerings on Yom Kippur.
Rabbi Meir adds that if it was Shabbat and he carried it out in his mouth, he is liable; the Sages respond that this case is not comparable.

items.text: Questioning Rabbi Meir's alignment with Rabbi Yehoshua or Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Questioning Rabbi Meir's alignment with Rabbi Yehoshua or Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which authority Rabbi Meir follows regarding liability for carrying on Shabbat. If he follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who exempts one who errs in a mitzva matter, that would contradict the baraita; therefore, he must follow Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which authority Rabbi Meir follows in the baraita, noting that if he follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who exempts one who errs in a mitzva matter, that would contradict the baraita.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Meir must follow Rabbi Eliezer, who holds one liable even for an error in a mitzva matter.

items.text: Alternative answer: Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Yehoshua with a distinction
items.text_en: Alternative answer: Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Yehoshua with a distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: Rabbi Meir could follow Rabbi Yehoshua, who exempts only when the error involves a mitzva with a pressing time (e.g., circumcision of infants), but here there is no such pressing time, so liability applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who exempts only when the error involves a pressing time (e.g., circumcision of infants), but here there is no such pressing time, so liability applies.

items.text: Objection from terumah and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from terumah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects from a mishna about terumah, where Rabbi Yehoshua exempts even though there is no pressing time. Rav Bibi bar Abbaye resolves that the case involves terumah on Passover eve, which has a pressing time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from a mishna about terumah, where Rabbi Yehoshua exempts even though there is no pressing time.
Rav Bibi bar Abbaye resolves that the case involves terumah on Passover eve, which has a pressing time.

items.text: Alternative resolution: issur bat aḥat according to Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: issur bat aḥat according to Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another resolution: the case involves issur bat aḥat, and the tanna is Rabbi Shimon, who holds that principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative resolution: the case involves איסור בת אחת (a single prohibition covering multiple acts) and follows Rabbi Shimon's view.

items.text: Finding a case of niddah in the mishnah's scenario
items.text_en: Finding a case of niddah in the mishnah's scenario
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to find a case of niddah within the mishnah's scenario of multiple forbidden relations. Rav Amram in the name of Rav answers: by having the women menstruate at intervals of thirteen days after thirteen days, or twelve after twelve, to create liability for the men or women respectively.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to find a case of niddah within the mishnah's scenario of multiple forbidden relations.
Rav Amram in the name of Rav answers: by having the women menstruate at intervals of thirteen days after thirteen days, or twelve after twelve, to create liability for the men or women respectively.

items.text: Addressing the impossibility of pregnancy from first intercourse and counting sin-offerings
items.text_en: Addressing the impossibility of pregnancy from first intercourse and counting sin-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that a woman cannot become pregnant from first intercourse, so Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha says they engaged in intercourse twice. It then questions the count of sixteen sin-offerings in a baraita of Rabbi Chiya, which should be thirty-two, and resolves that only the first intercourse is counted, similar to Rabbi Eliezer's counting only the first force.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a woman cannot become pregnant from first intercourse, challenging the assumption of a single act.

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman answers that they engaged in intercourse twice, so pregnancy could occur.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Chiya's baraita counts only sixteen sin-offerings when twice the number of acts should yield thirty-two.
The Gemara resolves that just as Rabbi Eliezer counts only the first force, here only the first intercourse is counted, so the count is correct.

items.text: Rava's question to Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Rava's question to Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: The daf ends with Rava addressing Rav Nachman, setting up the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rava begins a question to Rav Nachman, setting up the next discussion.

items.text: Explanation of Tamar's pregnancy and Er and Onan's behavior
items.text_en: Explanation of Tamar's pregnancy and Er and Onan's behavior
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Tamar became pregnant from first intercourse, and answers that she was a moca'at (one who conceives without full penetration). It then explains that Er and Onan engaged in unnatural intercourse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Tamar became pregnant from first intercourse.
The answer explains that Tamar conceived by pressing with her finger (a form of non-penetrative intercourse).
Rabbi Yitzchak supports the answer by noting that all women who conceive by pressing in Rabbi's house are called Tamar, after Tamar who pressed with her finger.
The Gemara objects that Er and Onan were also involved with Tamar.
The answer resolves that Er and Onan engaged in unnatural intercourse (שלא כדרכה), so Tamar did not conceive from them.

items.text: Distinction between Er and Onan's act and the permitted act
items.text_en: Distinction between Er and Onan's act and the permitted act
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer permits a certain practice for 24 months, and the Sages compare it to the act of Er and Onan.
