The Gemara clarifies that it is similar in that it involves wasting seed, but different because Er and Onan did it unnaturally, while here it is done naturally.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Eliezer permits threshing inside and winnowing outside for 24 months.
The Sages object that this practice is no different from the act of Er and Onan (wasting seed).

The Gemara resolves: it is similar to Er and Onan in wasting seed (as per the verse 'וְשִׁחֵת אַרְצָה'), but different because Er and Onan did it unnaturally (שֶׁלֹּא כְּדַרְכָּהּ), while here it is done naturally (כְּדַרְכָּהּ).

items.text: Source for Er's unnatural act and his motive
items.text_en: Source for Er's unnatural act and his motive
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know Er also engaged in unnatural intercourse, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives it from the verse that he died the same death as Onan. It then explains that Er's motive was to prevent Tamar from becoming pregnant and losing her beauty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted we know Onan's unnatural act from the verse, but from where do we derive that Er also engaged in such an act?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the verse 'וַיָּמֶת גַּם אוֹתוֹ' (and He also killed him) teaches that Er died the same death as Onan, implying the same sin.
The Gemara asks: granted Onan's motive was to avoid providing offspring for his brother, but what was Er's motive for doing the same?
The Gemara explains that Er's motive was to prevent Tamar from becoming pregnant and thereby losing her beauty.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding exceptions to the prohibition
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding exceptions to the prohibition
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the word 'otah' excludes a bride (Rabbi Yehuda) or unnatural intercourse (Sages). The Gemara explains their reasoning: the Sages derive both unnatural intercourse and foreplay from the verse, while Rabbi Yehuda derives unnatural intercourse from 'shichvat zera' and uses 'otah' to exclude a bride.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda)'s position that the word 'אוֹתָהּ' (with whom) excludes a כַּלָּה (bride) from the law of ritual impurity.
The חכמים (Sages) disagree, deriving from 'אוֹתָהּ' that sexual intercourse performed שלא כדרכה (in an atypical manner) is excluded.
הון בריה דרב נחמן (Hun son of Rav Nachman) asks רב נחמן (Rav Nachman) whether רבי יהודה's reasoning is that the Torah spared a bride's adornments.
רב נחמן answers that the real reason is that a woman does not become pregnant from the first act of ביאה (intercourse).

items.text: Rule about a woman who waited ten years and its exceptions
items.text_en: Rule about a woman who waited ten years and its exceptions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a woman who waited ten years after her husband's death and then remarried will not bear children. Rav Nachman qualifies this: only if she did not intend to remarry, but if she did, she can conceive. Rava's wife testifies that she intended to marry him. A woman who waited ten years and gave birth claims she was raped by a non-Jew.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) that a woman who waited ten years after her husband and then remarries will no longer bear children.
רב נחמן (Rav Nachman) qualifies the rule: it applies only when she did not intend to remarry, but if she did intend, she can conceive.
רבא (Rava) tells his wife בת רב חסדא (Bat Rav Chisda) that the sages gossip about her; she replies that her mind was on him, confirming the exception.
A woman who waited ten years and gave birth comes before רב יוסף (Rav Yosef); he warns her not to cast aspersions on the sages, and she confesses she was raped by a non-Jew.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on waiting period and its application to a minor convert
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on waiting period and its application to a minor convert
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that all women must wait three months before remarrying, except for a minor convert or freed slave. The Gemara questions this exception, noting that Shmuel already ruled that a minor who performs mi'un does not need to wait, but one who receives a get does. The Gemara concludes that the exception applies to a case of promiscuity.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that all women must wait three months before remarrying, except for a minor convert or freed slave, but a minor Israelite woman must wait.

The Gemara questions in which case the exception applies, noting that Shmuel already said a minor who performs mi'un does not need to wait, but one who receives a get does need to wait, implying no contradiction.
The Gemara answers that the exception applies to a case of promiscuity, not to the permitted cases already addressed.

items.text: Opening statement: the rabbis decreed a minor because of an adult
items.text_en: Opening statement: the rabbis decreed a minor because of an adult
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the rabbis decreed that a minor must wait three months because of an adult, to distinguish between children from different fathers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the rabbis decreed a minor woman must wait three months because of an adult woman.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Giddel's answer about a hora'at sha'ah
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Giddel's answer about a hora'at sha'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether we decree a minor because of an adult, citing a mishnah that minors who cannot give birth may remarry immediately. Rav Giddel answers that it was a hora'at sha'ah (an emergency ruling), and the case of a minor who can become pregnant is uncommon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether we decree a minor because of an adult, citing a baraita that minors who cannot give birth are returned immediately.
Rav Giddel in the name of Rav answers that it was a הוראת שעה (temporary ruling), and the case of a minor who can give birth is uncommon.

items.text: Alternative version: Shmuel's ruling on who must wait
items.text_en: Alternative version: Shmuel's ruling on who must wait
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Shmuel said all women must wait three months except for a convert or freed slave who is an adult. The Gemara clarifies that this applies to a case of promiscuity, not mi'un or get, since promiscuity is uncommon for a minor.

sub.text: Alternative version in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Alternative version in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Shmuel exempts a minor Israelite woman from waiting three months.
The Gemara questions in what case Shmuel's ruling applies, noting that for מיאון (refusal) Shmuel already said she does not wait, and for a גט (bill of divorce) she does wait.
The Gemara answers that the case is זנות (promiscuity), but promiscuity with a minor is uncommon.

items.text: Shmuel's opinion follows Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Shmuel's opinion follows Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Shmuel's ruling follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that a convert or freed slave may marry immediately because a promiscuous woman uses a contraceptive to avoid pregnancy. A baraita cites the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the rabbis did not decree a waiting period for a convert or freed slave, since promiscuity is common among them.
The Gemara answers that Shmuel follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that a promiscuous woman uses a מוך (absorbent cloth) to prevent pregnancy.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda requires a three-month wait for a convert, captive, or slave; Rabbi Yosei permits betrothal and marriage immediately.
Rabba explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning: a promiscuous woman uses a contraceptive (מוך) to avoid pregnancy.

items.text: Abaye's objection: convert and captive protect themselves
items.text_en: Abaye's objection: convert and captive protect themselves
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that a convert and a captive protect themselves to distinguish between seed conceived in holiness and not, but a slave freed through loss of a tooth or eye does not have such protection, so why does Rabbi Yosei permit her?

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that for a convert and captive the reasoning works, but for a slave freed by tooth or eye (שן ועין) the case is problematic.

items.text: Rejection: Rabbi Yosei also permits an raped or seduced woman
items.text_en: Rejection: Rabbi Yosei also permits an raped or seduced woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that Rabbi Yosei only permits those who protect themselves, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei permits a raped or seduced woman to marry immediately, even though she did not protect herself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if one says Rabbi Yosei agrees in a case that happens naturally, a baraita shows he permits a raped or seduced woman to marry immediately.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: a promiscuous woman twists to avoid pregnancy
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: a promiscuous woman twists to avoid pregnancy
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that a promiscuous woman twists her body to avoid pregnancy, but we worry she may not have twisted properly. This resolves the objection.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves that a promiscuous woman turns over to avoid pregnancy, but we worry she may not have turned properly.

items.text: Discussion of the mishnah: 'If they were priestesses'
items.text_en: Discussion of the mishnah: 'If they were priestesses'
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the mishnah's phrase 'if they were priestesses,' questioning whether it refers to priestesses married to Israelites, and cites Rav Amram and Rava to clarify that the mishnah discusses priestesses married to Israelites who become disqualified from terumah of their husbands' house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's phrase 'if they were priestesses,' asking why it specifies priestesses and not Israelite women.
The Gemara proposes that the mishnah should be read as 'if they were wives of priests,' not 'priestesses,' to clarify the distinction.

Rav Amram reports that Rav Sheshet taught a baraita: an Israelite woman who was raped, though permitted to her husband, is disqualified from the priesthood, supporting the need for the mishnah's specific wording.
Rava resolves the issue by explaining that the mishnah refers to priestesses married to Israelites who become disqualified from eating תרומה (the priestly portion) of their husbands' house.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Laws of a yavam who performed chalitzah or married a pregnant yevamah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Laws of a yavam who performed chalitzah or married a pregnant yevamah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases: a yavam who performed chalitzah and the yevamah was pregnant, a yavam who married her and she was pregnant, and a case of doubt about the paternity of the child. It rules on the permissibility of relatives and the status of the yevamah regarding kehunah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases: halitzah to a pregnant yevamah whose child survives, halitzah when the child does not survive, and marrying a pregnant yevamah with varying outcomes.

items.text: Gemara's opening dispute: Rabbi Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish on chalitzah of a pregnant yevamah
items.text_en: Gemara's opening dispute: Rabbi Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish on chalitzah of a pregnant yevamah
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds that chalitzah of a pregnant yevamah is valid chalitzah, so she does not need chalitzah from the other brothers; Reish Lakish holds it is not valid, so she does need chalitzah from them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding a yavam who performed halitzah to a pregnant yevamah who miscarried.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan considers halitzah and intercourse with a pregnant woman valid, while Reish Lakish considers them invalid.

items.text: Two explanations for the dispute: reasoning and scriptural derivation
items.text_en: Two explanations for the dispute: reasoning and scriptural derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two possible bases for the dispute: one based on reasoning (whether we say retroactive clarification) and one based on the verse 'וּבֵן אֵין לוֹ' (whether we require an 'examination' of the child).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what underlies the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, and offers two possible explanations: a verse or a logical reasoning.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan holds that the pregnancy is retroactively revealed to be nonexistent, so the halitzah was valid, while Reish Lakish rejects retroactive revelation.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'וּבֵן אֵין לוֹ' (and he has no son) literally, so the yavam has no son, while Reish Lakish interprets it as requiring examination of the child's viability.

items.text: First objection from the Mishnah: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish
items.text_en: First objection from the Mishnah: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from the Mishnah: if chalitzah of a pregnant woman is not valid, why does the Mishnah say she is disqualified from kehunah? Reish Lakish answers that it is a rabbinic stringency.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to Reish Lakish from the Mishnah: if halitzah is invalid, why does it disqualify the yevamah from the priesthood?
Reish Lakish answers that the disqualification is rabbinic, merely a stringency.

items.text: Alternative version: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Alternative version: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: In an alternative version, Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan: if chalitzah is valid, the Mishnah should have said she does not need chalitzah from the brothers. Rabbi Yochanan responds that the Mishnah only mentions the disqualification because it contrasts with the first clause.

sub.text: Alternative version: Reish Lakish's objection to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Alternative version: Reish Lakish's objection to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: In an alternative version, Reish Lakish objects to Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishnah should have stated 'she does not need halitzah from the brothers' if halitzah is valid, and Rabbi Yochanan responds that the Mishnah's phrasing is due to the parallel structure.

items.text: Second objection from the Mishnah: the case of 'yekayeim'
items.text_en: Second objection from the Mishnah: the case of 'yekayeim'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from the Mishnah's ruling 'yekayeim' (he may keep her). If intercourse with a pregnant woman is not valid, the Mishnah should have said 'yachzor veyiv'ol viyekayeim' (he must repeat intercourse). Reish Lakish explains that 'yekayeim' implies that. An alternative version reverses the challenge.

items.text: Third objection: the case of the tzarah (co-wife)
items.text_en: Third objection: the case of the tzarah (co-wife)
items.desc_en: A baraisa is cited: a co-wife of a pregnant yevamah may not remarry lest the child be viable. If intercourse with a pregnant woman is valid, why wouldn't the co-wife be exempt? Abaye clarifies that the dispute is only about chalitzah, not intercourse. Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish both agree that intercourse with a pregnant woman is not valid.

items.text: Rava's logical argument linking chalitzah and intercourse
items.text_en: Rava's logical argument linking chalitzah and intercourse
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the status of chalitzah and intercourse are logically linked: if intercourse is valid, chalitzah is valid; if intercourse is not valid, chalitzah is also not valid, based on a known principle.

items.text: Opening principle: all who rise for yibum rise for chalitza
items.text_en: Opening principle: all who rise for yibum rise for chalitza
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the general rule that any woman who is eligible for yibum is also eligible for chalitza, and one who is not eligible for yibum is not eligible for chalitza.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the general principle that any woman eligible for yibum is eligible for chalitza, and one ineligible for yibum is ineligible for chalitza.

items.text: Rava's explanation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava explains that if a man marries his yevama and she is found to be pregnant, her tzara may not marry, lest the child be viable; the yevama's intercourse and chalitza are not valid, and the child does not exempt until born.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains the Mishnah: if a man marries his yevama and she is found pregnant, her tzara may not marry lest the child be viable; the yevama's intercourse and chalitza are invalid, and the child does not exempt until born.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rava
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rava
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava's view: if a man marries his yevama and she is found pregnant, her tzara may not marry, lest the child be viable; only the child exempts, not intercourse or chalitza, and the child does not exempt until born.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava's view: if a man marries his yevama and she is found pregnant, her tzara may not marry, lest the child be viable; only the child exempts, not intercourse or chalitza, and the child does not exempt until born.

items.text: Challenge to Reish Lakish from the baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Reish Lakish from the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that the only reason the tzara is forbidden is lest the child be viable; if the child is not viable, the tzara is permitted, which contradicts Reish Lakish's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that the only reason the tzara is forbidden is lest the child be viable; if the child is not viable, the tzara is permitted, which contradicts Reish Lakish's position.

items.text: Reish Lakish's defense and reasoning
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's defense and reasoning
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish responds that the baraita should be read differently: the tzara may not marry lest the child not be viable, and chalitza and intercourse of a pregnant woman are not valid; even though most women give birth to viable children, the child does not exempt until born.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish reinterprets the baraita: the tzara may not marry because the child might not be viable, and both intercourse and chalitza of a pregnant woman are invalid.
The Gemara raises an objection: one should follow the majority of women who give birth to viable children.
Reish Lakish resolves that even though most women bear viable children, the child does not exempt the tzara until it is born into the world.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar finds a Mishnah supporting Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar finds a Mishnah supporting Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar wonders if Reish Lakish's view is not taught in a Mishnah, then finds one: a woman whose husband and tzara went overseas and was told 'your husband died' may not marry or undergo yibum until she knows if her tzara is pregnant.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar wonders whether Reish Lakish's view is not taught in a Mishnah.

Rabbi Elazar finds a Mishnah that supports Reish Lakish: a woman whose husband and tzara went overseas and was told 'your husband died' may not marry or undergo yibum until she knows if her tzara is pregnant.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah and the reason for not performing chalitza
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah and the reason for not performing chalitza
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the woman may not perform chalitza within nine months and marry later; Abaye and Rav Chinana explain that it is lest the child be viable and she would need a proclamation for the priesthood, and there is concern that someone present at chalitza but not the proclamation might permit a chalutza to a kohen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah forbids chalitza for a pregnant yevama, given that yibum is forbidden lest the child be viable, but chalitza could be performed within nine months and marriage after nine months.
The Gemara suggests that she could perform chalitza within nine months and marry after nine months.
The Gemara objects that even according to its own logic, she could simply perform chalitza and marry after nine months.

sub.text: Abaye bar Abba and Rav Chinana bar Abaye
sub.text_en: Abaye bar Abba and Rav Chinana bar Abaye
sub.desc_en: Abaye bar Abba and Rav Chinana bar Abaye explain that the concern is lest the child be viable, and she would then need a proclamation (כרוז) for the priesthood.
The Gemara resolves that the proclamation is necessary, but there is concern that someone present at the chalitza but not at the proclamation might mistakenly permit a חלוצה (chalutza) to a kohen.

items.text: Abaye's correction: the Mishnah says 'not marry' not 'not chalitza'
items.text_en: Abaye's correction: the Mishnah says 'not marry' not 'not chalitza'
items.desc_en: Abaye points out that the Mishnah says 'not marry and not undergo yibum', not 'not chalitza'; if he performed chalitza, she is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Abaye corrects the Mishnah's wording: it says 'not marry and not undergo yibum', not 'not chalitza', so if he performed חליצה (the release ceremony), she is permitted.

items.text: Baraita supporting Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Reish Lakish: if one performs chalitza with a pregnant woman and she miscarries, she requires chalitza from the brothers.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Reish Lakish: if one performs חליצה (chalitza) with a pregnant woman and she miscarries, she requires חליצה (chalitza) from the brothers.

items.text: Rava's ruling on three halachic matters
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on three halachic matters
items.desc_en: Rava states that the halakha follows Reish Lakish in three matters: the one just discussed, and two others regarding division of property and the status of a firstborn.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that the halakha follows Reish Lakish in three matters, beginning with the one just discussed.
Rava cites the second matter: a Mishnah about one who divides his property orally, giving more to one and less to another while equalizing the firstborn's share — his words stand.
Rava completes the citation: if he spoke in terms of inheritance his words are void, but if he wrote a gift document at any stage his words stand.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on a son's sale of inherited property
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on a son's sale of inherited property
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that a gift is not acquired until the donor says 'So-and-so and so-and-so shall inherit such-and-such field that I gave them as a gift and they shall inherit it.' The Gemara cites a mishnah about a father who writes all his property to his son after his death, and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish when the son sells the property during the father's lifetime and then dies. Rabbi Yochanan holds that the buyer does not acquire it because the father's right to the produce is considered like ownership of the body, while Reish Lakish disagrees.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that a gift is not acquired until the donor explicitly says 'So-and-so and so-and-so shall inherit such-and-such field that I gave them as a gift and they shall inherit it.'
The Gemara cites a mishnah about a father who writes all his property to his son after his death, where neither the father nor the son can sell the property during the father's lifetime.

The Gemara presents the dispute: if the son sold the property during the father's lifetime and then died, Rabbi Yochanan says the buyer does not acquire it, while Reish Lakish says the buyer does acquire it.
Rabbi Yochanan explains his position: the father's right to the produce (קניין פירות) is considered equivalent to ownership of the body (קניין הגוף), so the son's sale is invalid.
Reish Lakish explains his position: the father's right to the produce (קניין פירות) is not equivalent to ownership of the body (קניין הגוף), so the son's sale is valid.

items.text: Ruling of Rabbi Eliezer on a yevamah's child
items.text_en: Ruling of Rabbi Eliezer on a yevamah's child
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a yevamah gives birth to a child that is not viable (a 'kayyama'), the child is not considered a viable offspring. A baraita adds that in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, they said: He must divorce her with a get.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a child born to a yevamah that is not viable (a 'kayyama') is not considered a viable offspring.

sub.text: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: A baraita adds that in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, they said: He must divorce her with a גט (bill of divorce).

items.text: Rava's comparison of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer, and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rava's comparison of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer, and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rava claims that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer said the same thing: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling about the yevamah, and Rabbi Meir's ruling that one who marries a pregnant or nursing woman must divorce her permanently. Abaye objects, arguing that Rabbi Eliezer's stringency is due to a Torah prohibition (the yevamah might be forbidden as a brother's wife), while Rabbi Meir's ruling is rabbinic, and he might agree with the Sages there. Alternatively, Rabbi Meir's stringency is rabbinic, but here the Torah prohibition is explicit.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by asserting that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer said the same thing, referencing Rabbi Eliezer's known ruling.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Meir's position
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Meir's position
sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that one who marries a pregnant or nursing woman must divorce her permanently, while the Sages allow remarriage after the child is weaned.
Abaye objects that Rabbi Eliezer's stringency is due to a Torah prohibition (איסור אשת אח), while Rabbi Meir's ruling is rabbinic, so Rabbi Eliezer might agree with the Sages there.
Abaye alternatively argues that Rabbi Meir's stringency is rabbinic, but here the Torah prohibition is explicit, so Rabbi Meir would agree with the Sages.

items.text: Rava's ruling and Mar Zutra's support
items.text_en: Rava's ruling and Mar Zutra's support
items.desc_en: Rava states that according to the Sages, the husband must divorce her with a get. Mar Zutra notes that the language 'yotzi' (divorce) rather than 'yafrish' (separate) supports this.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that according to the Sages, the husband must divorce her with a גט (bill of divorce).
Mar Zutra notes that the Mishnah's use of 'יוציא' (divorce) rather than 'יפריש' (separate) supports Rava's ruling.

items.text: Dispute about a child who dies within thirty days and the yevamah's status
items.text_en: Dispute about a child who dies within thirty days and the yevamah's status
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that a child who survives thirty days is not a stillborn. If a child dies within thirty days, it is uncertain. The Gemara then discusses a case where a yevamah's child dies within thirty days and she remarries. Ravina in the name of Rava rules that if she is an Israelite's wife, she performs chalitzah; if a priest's wife, she does not. Rav Mesharshiya in the name of Rava rules that in both cases she performs chalitzah. Ravina questions Rav Mesharshiya.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites the mishnah of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that a child who survives thirty days is not a stillborn, implying that one who dies within thirty days is uncertain.
The Gemara presents the case: a yevamah's child dies within thirty days and she remarries.
Ravina reports Rava's ruling: if she is an Israelite's wife she performs חליצה (chalitzah); if a priest's wife she does not.

sub.text: Rav Mesharshiya in name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya in name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya reports a different ruling from Rava: in both cases she performs חליצה (chalitzah).
Ravina challenges Rav Mesharshiya's ruling, beginning a question.

items.text: Rava's retraction and the question about a pregnant or nursing woman married to a priest
items.text_en: Rava's retraction and the question about a pregnant or nursing woman married to a priest
items.desc_en: Rava initially stated one thing but retracted. The Gemara asks whether the Sages instituted a special enactment for a pregnant or nursing woman married to a priest.

sub.desc_en: The stam reports that Rava initially stated one thing in the evening but retracted in the morning, and then Rava challenges his interlocutor with a sarcastic wish.

items.text: Analysis of the enactment for a priest's wife
items.text_en: Analysis of the enactment for a priest's wife
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the difference between the case of a pregnant or nursing woman married to a priest and the earlier case. Since there are disputing opinions, it is unclear which authority to follow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the rabbinic enactment for a pregnant or nursing woman applies when she is married to a priest.
The Gemara answers that in the earlier case, since the Sages dispute Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the ruling follows the Sages because no alternative is possible.
The Gemara objects that here, neither Rabbi Meir's position (divorce permanently) nor the Sages' position (divorce with a get) can be followed without difficulty.

items.text: Dispute about one who betroths within three months and flees
items.text_en: Dispute about one who betroths within three months and flees
items.desc_en: Rav Acha and Rafram disagree about whether to excommunicate a man who betrothed a woman within three months of her husband's death and then fled. Rafram ruled that his flight suffices.

sub.desc_en: The stam reports a dispute between Rav Acha and Rafram about a man who betrothed a woman within three months and fled: one says to excommunicate him, the other says his flight suffices, and Rafram ruled accordingly.
Rav Acha argues that the man should be excommunicated for his action.
Rafram counters that the man's flight itself suffices as a penalty, so no excommunication is needed.
When the case actually occurred, Rafram ruled in practice that the man's flight suffices.

items.text: Rava and Rav Nachman debate the majority of women giving birth at nine months
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Nachman debate the majority of women giving birth at nine months
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether we follow the majority of women who give birth at nine months. Rav Nachman responds that local women give birth at seven months, but then refines the argument: most women give birth at nine months, but if the pregnancy was not recognizable at three months, the majority is weakened.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman why a guilt-offering for uncertainty is needed, since the majority of women give birth at nine months, so the child should be attributed to the first husband.
Rav Nachman responds that the women of his family give birth at seven months, so the majority does not apply.
Rava objects that the women of Rav Nachman's family do not constitute the majority of the world.

Rav Nachman refines his argument: although most women give birth at nine months, the pregnancy is recognizable at three months; since this woman's pregnancy was not recognizable then, the majority is weakened.
The Gemara objects that if every nine-month pregnancy is recognizable at three months, then this woman's child must be a seven-month child of the second husband, eliminating the uncertainty.

The Gemara resolves the objection by emending Rav Nachman's statement: only most women who give birth at nine months have recognizable pregnancies at three months, so the lack of recognition weakens the majority but does not eliminate uncertainty.

items.text: Dispute about the status of a first and second child from a remarriage
items.text_en: Dispute about the status of a first and second child from a remarriage
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that the first child is fit to be High Priest and the second is a doubtful mamzer. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says there is no doubtful mamzer. Abaye and Rava offer different interpretations of this dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that the first child is fit to be High Priest and the second is a doubtful mamzer; Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says there is no doubtful mamzer.
The Gemara asks what the baraita means.

Abaye interprets the baraita: the first child is fit to be High Priest, the second is a doubtful mamzer forbidden to marry a mamzeret; Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says he is a definite mamzer and permitted to marry a mamzeret.

Rava interprets the baraita oppositely: the first child is fit to be High Priest, the second is a definite mamzer permitted to marry a mamzeret; Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says he is a doubtful mamzer and forbidden to marry a mamzeret.

items.text: The dispute is linked to Rabbi Elazar's ruling and the conflicting traditions of Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: The dispute is linked to Rabbi Elazar's ruling and the conflicting traditions of Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The dispute between Abaye and Rava is based on Rabbi Elazar's ruling about certain and doubtful lineage. Rav ruled like Rabbi Elazar, but Shmuel cited Hillel's tradition that all ten genealogical classes may intermarry, contradicting Rabbi Elazar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between Abaye and Rava is based on Rabbi Elazar's ruling about certain and doubtful lineage.
The mishnah lists those with uncertain lineage: a child of unknown paternity, a foundling, and a Samaritan.
Rav Yehuda reports that Rav ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar.
Shmuel objects to Rav's ruling, citing Hillel's tradition that all ten genealogical classes may intermarry, which contradicts Rabbi Elazar's position.

items.text: Abaye and Rava reconcile the conflicting traditions
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava reconcile the conflicting traditions
items.desc_en: Abaye follows Shmuel's ruling that the halakha is like Hillel, and interprets Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov accordingly to avoid contradiction. Rava follows Rav's ruling that the halakha is like Rabbi Elazar, and interprets Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov to align with that.

sub.desc_en: Abaye holds like Shmuel that the halakha follows Hillel, and interprets Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov accordingly to avoid contradiction between halakhot.
Rava holds like Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar, and interprets Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov to align with that ruling, avoiding contradiction.

items.text: Abaye's proof that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov treats uncertainty as certainty
items.text_en: Abaye's proof that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov treats uncertainty as certainty
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov considers any uncertain case as definite, citing a baraita where he warns that multiple sexual encounters without identification could lead to incest and mamzerim. Rava counters that the baraita only refers to a specific case of 'this woman what is she'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a discussion about conflicting rulings (הלכתא אהלכתא).
Abaye asserts that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov treats any uncertainty (ספק) as certainty (ודאי).
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov warns that uncertain sexual encounters could lead to incest and mamzerim, implying he treats uncertainty as definite.
Rava counters that the baraita only addresses a specific case of 'this woman what is she' (זו מה היא), not a general principle of treating uncertainty as certainty.

An additional baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov forbids marrying in two different cities to prevent accidental sibling incest, further illustrating his concern for uncertain relationships.

items.text: Challenge from Rav and Rav Nachman's practice, and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav and Rav Nachman's practice, and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous ruling by noting that Rav and Rav Nachman would announce for women to marry them temporarily when visiting towns, seemingly contradicting the concern. The answer distinguishes rabbis who are well-known and send messengers to inform, or that they only designate the women privately.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous ruling by citing that Rav and Rav Nachman would publicly announce for women to marry them for a day when visiting towns.
The Gemara answers that rabbis are different because their names are well-known, so there is no concern of confusion.
The Gemara objects by citing Rava's ruling that a woman who was propositioned and agreed must wait seven clean days, implying that even rabbis' announcements would cause such a concern.

The Gemara answers that the rabbis would send messengers to inform the women in advance, or alternatively, they only designated the women privately, relying on the principle that one who has bread in his basket is not comparable to one who does not.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's additional ruling on marrying with intent to divorce
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's additional ruling on marrying with intent to divorce
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one should not marry a woman with the intention of divorcing her, based on the verse 'Do not plot harm against your neighbor who dwells trustingly with you'.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's ruling that one should not marry a woman with the intention of divorcing her, based on the verse 'Do not plot harm against your neighbor who dwells trustingly with you'.

items.text: Case of safek and yavam dividing the deceased's property
items.text_en: Case of safek and yavam dividing the deceased's property
items.desc_en: When a safek (uncertain child) and a yavam dispute over the deceased's estate, the safek claims to be the son and heir, while the yavam claims the safek is his son with no rights. This is a case of money in doubt, and they divide it equally.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents the case: a safek (uncertain child) and a yavam come to divide the deceased's property, each making conflicting claims.
The gemara rules that since the money is in doubt (ספק), the parties divide it equally.

items.text: Safek and the yavam's sons: dispute and Rav Mesharshiya's analysis
items.text_en: Safek and the yavam's sons: dispute and Rav Mesharshiya's analysis
items.desc_en: When a safek and the yavam's sons dispute over the deceased's property, the sons claim the safek is their brother with only a share. The rabbis initially compare it to a mishna where the safek does not inherit but they do, but Rav Mesharshiya distinguishes: there the claimants are certain and the safek is uncertain, here both are uncertain. He compares it instead to a case where the safek and the yavam's sons divide the yavam's own property.

sub.desc_en: The case is presented: a safek (child of uncertain status) and the yavam's sons dispute over the deceased's property; the safek claims he is the son of the deceased and sole heir, while the yavam's sons claim he is their brother and only entitled to a share.
The rabbis before Rav Mesharshiya thought to compare this case to a mishna (100a) where the safek does not inherit from the certain sons, but they inherit from him.
The rabbis note that the positions are reversed: in the mishna, the certain sons tell the safek to bring proof, while here the safek tells the yavam's sons to bring proof.
Rav Mesharshiya rejects the comparison: in the mishna, the claimants are certain and the safek is uncertain, but here both parties are uncertain.

items.text: Safek and yavam's sons dividing the yavam's property after division
items.text_en: Safek and yavam's sons dividing the yavam's property after division
items.desc_en: After the yavam divided the deceased's property, the safek and the yavam's sons dispute over the yavam's own property. The safek argues that regardless of his status, he deserves a share. Rabbi Abba citing Rav says the judgment stands, while Rabbi Yirmeya says the judgment is reversed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiyya offers a corrected analogy: the case of the safek and the yavam's sons dividing the yavam's own property is comparable to the mishna, where the definite claimants demand proof from the safek.
The Gemara frames the specific scenario: the safek and the yavam's sons come to divide the yavam's property after the yavam had already divided the deceased's property.

The yavam's sons demand proof from the safek that he is their brother; the safek counters with a 'whichever way you look at it' argument, claiming a share either as a brother or as the sole heir of the deceased.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba citing Rav vs. Rabbi Yirmeya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba citing Rav vs. Rabbi Yirmeya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba citing Rav rules that the original judgment stands, while Rabbi Yirmeya rules that the judgment is reversed.

items.text: Analysis of the dispute between Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Yirmeya via Admon and the Sages
items.text_en: Analysis of the dispute between Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Yirmeya via Admon and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Yirmeya parallels the dispute between Admon and the Sages regarding a lost path. Rava explains the case: when four people surround a field from four sides, all agree they can push him away; the dispute is when one comes from the power of four. Rabbi Abba says he holds even like Admon, who would agree here because the safek can argue 'from any angle, my path is with you'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Yirmeya parallels the dispute between Admon and the Sages regarding a lost path, citing the Mishnah.
The Gemara questions how Admon's position makes sense to the Sages, and Rav Yehuda citing Rav explains the case: four people surrounded the field from four sides.
The Gemara asks what Admon's reasoning is, and Rava answers that when four come from the power of four or one from the power of one, all agree they can push him away.

Rava explains that the dispute is when one comes from the power of four: Admon says he can claim 'from any angle, my path is with you', while the Sages say they can threaten to return the deed to the original owners.
The Gemara infers that Rabbi Abba holds like the Sages and Rabbi Yirmeya holds like Admon.
Rabbi Abba objects that he could even hold like Admon, because Admon only says his ruling there because the safek can argue 'from any angle, my path is with you'.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's defense of his position
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's defense of his position
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya explains that his earlier statement applies even to the Rabbis, because in that case the creditor could threaten to return the note, but here no such threat exists.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the earlier case of the disputed path is different because the claim there rests on clear facts, whereas here the son of uncertain descent cannot make such a claim.
Rabbi Yirmeya responds that his ruling applies even according to the Rabbis, since there the owner could threaten to return the bills of purchase, but here no such threat can be made.

items.text: Case of safek and yavam dividing grandfather's property
items.text_en: Case of safek and yavam dividing grandfather's property
items.desc_en: The safek claims he is the son of the deceased and entitled to half, while the yavam claims the safek is his son and has nothing. The yavam is certain and the safek is uncertain, so the certain party prevails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the case of a ספק (son of uncertain descent) and the יבם (yavam) coming to divide the grandfather's property, with each stating his claim.
The Gemara rules that the יבם has a definite claim while the ספק has only an uncertain claim, and an uncertain claim cannot extract property from a definite one.

items.text: Case of safek and yavam's sons dividing grandfather's property
items.text_en: Case of safek and yavam's sons dividing grandfather's property
items.desc_en: The safek claims he is the deceased's son, and the yavam's sons admit he is their brother. They divide the portion they admit, he takes the portion they admit, and the remaining portion is disputed and divided equally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a safek (doubtful son) and the yavam's sons come to divide the grandfather's property; the safek claims he is the deceased's son and entitled to half, while the yavam's sons admit he is their brother and has a share with them.
The Gemara rules: the yavam's sons take the half they admit, the safek takes the third they admit to him, and the remaining sixth is disputed money (ממון המוטל בספק) which they divide equally.

items.text: Cases of grandfather and yavam or safek in disputed property
items.text_en: Cases of grandfather and yavam or safek in disputed property
items.desc_en: When the grandfather and yavam dispute the safek's property, or the grandfather and safek dispute the yavam's property, it is disputed money and they divide it equally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents two cases: the grandfather and yavam dispute the safek's property, or the grandfather and safek dispute the yavam's property.
The Gemara rules that in both cases the property is disputed money (ממון המוטל בספק) and the parties divide it equally.

items.text: Mishnah: Shomeret yavam's property rights
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shomeret yavam's property rights
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that a shomeret yavam may sell and give away property that falls to her. If she dies, they dispute how her ketubah and property are divided. If he marries her, she is like his wife in all respects, provided her ketubah is on the first husband's property.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that a shomeret yavam (a widow awaiting yibbum) may sell and give away property that falls to her, and it is valid.
The Mishnah poses the question: if she dies, what is done with her ketubah and with property that enters and exits with her?
Beit Shammai rules that the heirs of the husband and the heirs of the father divide the property.
Beit Hillel rules that each asset remains in its presumptive ownership: the ketubah goes to the husband's heirs, and the property that enters and exits with her goes to the father's heirs.
The Mishnah concludes that if the yavam marries her, she is like his wife in all respects, provided her ketubah remains a lien on the first husband's property.

items.text: Gemara's question and Ulla's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Ulla's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the first clause has no dispute and the second clause has a dispute. Ulla answers that the first clause refers to property that fell while she was betrothed, and the second to when she was married. Ulla holds that the bond of betrothal creates a safek betrothal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the first clause of the Mishnah has no dispute while the second clause has a dispute.
Ulla answers that the first clause refers to property that fell to the yevama while she was betrothed, and the second clause to when she was married.
The Gemara explains that Ulla holds that the bond of betrothal (זיקת אירוסין) creates a ספק אירוסין (doubtful betrothal), which explains why the first clause is undisputed.

items.text: Gemara's initial analysis of the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's initial analysis of the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that the status of a yevamah is uncertain: a 'zikkat nesuah' creates a doubt of being married, and a 'zikkat arusah' creates a doubt of being engaged. This is derived from the fact that Beit Hillel would not allow a definite arusah to sell property, yet the Mishnah implies they do.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a zikkat nesuah (tie of a full marriage) creates a doubt of being married, and a zikkat arusah (tie of an engagement) creates a doubt of being engaged, because if it were a definite status, Beit Hillel would not allow her to sell property.

The Gemara cites a baraita about property that fell to her after marriage, where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree the husband can retrieve it, proving that zikkat nesuah creates a doubt of being married.

items.text: Rabbah's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rabbah's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbah objects that the dispute should be about the woman's lifetime and usufruct, not just after death. He explains that both cases involve property that fell when she was married, and the doubt of marriage applies. In the first clause, she is alive and certain, so doubt cannot remove from certainty; in the second clause, she dies, so the heirs divide.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah objects that the dispute should be about the woman's lifetime and usufruct, not just after death.

Rabbah explains that both clauses involve property that fell when she was married, and the doubt of marriage applies; in the first clause she is alive and certain, so doubt cannot remove from certainty.
Rabbah concludes that in the second clause, where she dies, the heirs divide the property.

items.text: Abaye's objection from a mishnah about a collapsed house
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from a mishnah about a collapsed house
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah's principle that doubt cannot remove from certainty, citing a mishnah where Beit Shammai rule that heirs and creditors divide property when there is doubt about who died first, even though the heirs are certain and the creditor is doubtful.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah's principle that doubt cannot remove from certainty, citing a mishnah about a collapsed house where Beit Shammai rule that heirs and creditors divide the property, even though the heirs are certain and the creditor is doubtful.
Abaye concludes his objection by noting that here, the heirs are certain and the creditor is doubtful, yet Beit Shammai allow the doubtful creditor to take half, contradicting Rabbah's principle.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: Beit Shammai consider a promissory note as already collected
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: Beit Shammai consider a promissory note as already collected
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Beit Shammai consider a document ready for collection as already collected, so the creditor is considered certain. This is supported by a mishnah about sotah where Beit Shammai allow the ketubah to be collected despite doubt, because the document is considered as collected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers Abaye's objection by stating that Beit Shammai consider a promissory note ready for collection as already collected, so the creditor is treated as certain.
The Gemara cites a mishnah about sotah where Beit Shammai allow the ketubah to be collected despite doubt, because the document is considered as collected.
The Gemara objects that the mishnah's phrase 'or they drink' is impossible since the husband is dead, and corrects it to 'since they do not drink, they do not collect their ketubah'.
The Gemara concludes that the sotah case proves Beit Shammai's principle: a document ready for collection is considered as collected, so the creditor is certain.

items.text: Abaye's alternative challenge and resolution regarding the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative challenge and resolution regarding the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: Abaye questions why the Gemara didn't cite the mishnah about ketubah directly, but the Gemara explains that the mishnah's case is different: the ketubah is separate from the property. The Mishnah's wording 'yachloku yorshei haba'al im yorshei ha'av' implies that the husband's heirs initiate the division, indicating they are the certain party.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks why the Gemara didn't object from the mishnah about ketubah, but the Gemara answers that a woman's marriage contract is different due to the consideration of חינא (desirability).
The Gemara objects that one could still object from the case of the marriage contract in the mishnah here.
The Gemara answers that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel do not disagree on that point, citing the mishnah's ruling about the marriage contract and property.

The Gemara resolves that the mishnah's statement about the marriage contract is left unresolved, and only the property that enters and leaves with her is discussed, with Beit Shammai ruling that the husband's heirs divide with the father's heirs.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof and Abaye's final distinction
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof and Abaye's final distinction
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi proves from the Mishnah's phrasing that the husband's heirs are the certain party. Abaye concludes that the first clause refers to property that fell when she was a shomeret yavam, and the second clause when she was under her husband.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi proves from the Mishnah's phrasing that the husband's heirs are the certain party, since it says 'the husband's heirs divide with the father's heirs' and not the reverse.
Abaye concludes that the first clause refers to property that fell when she was a שומרת יבם (widow waiting for yavam), and the second clause when she was under her husband.

items.text: Abaye and Rava dispute the effect of ma'amar according to Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava dispute the effect of ma'amar according to Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: Abaye holds that the yavam's hand is like her hand regarding property, while Rava distinguishes between property that fell to her while under the husband and while waiting for the yavam. Rava explains that according to Beit Shammai, ma'amar makes her a definite arusah and a doubtful nesu'ah. Two traditions are cited: one supports Rava, the other Abaye.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Abaye holds the principle that the yavam's hand is like her hand regarding property rights.
Rava objects to Abaye, arguing that when property falls to her while under the husband, everyone agrees the husband's hand is stronger than hers.
Rava distinguishes that the dispute concerns property that fell to her while she is waiting for the yavam, with the first clause where he did not perform ma'amar and the latter where he did.

sub.text: Rava's explanation of Beit Shammai's view
sub.text_en: Rava's explanation of Beit Shammai's view
sub.desc_en: Rava explains that according to Beit Shammai, ma'amar makes her a definite arusah (betrothed) to push off the rival wife, and a doubtful nesu'ah (married) to share in the property.
Two traditions are cited: one in the name of Rabbi Elazar supports Rava, and one in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina supports Abaye.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Elazar's position and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Elazar's position and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Elazar really holds like Rava, citing his statement that ma'amar only acquires to push off the rival wife. The Gemara resolves by either reversing the attribution or explaining that Rabbi Elazar only meant that ma'amar does not acquire for property division.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether Rabbi Elazar really holds like Rava, citing his own statement that ma'amar only acquires to push off the rival wife.
The Gemara resolves either by reversing the attribution or by explaining that Rabbi Elazar only meant that ma'amar does not acquire for property division.

items.text: Rav Pappa supports Abaye from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Pappa supports Abaye from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that the precise wording of the Mishnah supports Abaye, despite the difficulty of the word 'metah' (she died). He explains the terms 'entering' and 'leaving' as referring to the husband's and father's authority, and notes the difficulty that the dispute is about the body after death rather than about the produce during her lifetime.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa opens by asserting that the precise wording of the Mishnah supports Abaye, despite the difficulty posed by the word 'metah' (she died).
Rav Pappa explains that the Mishnah's terms 'entering' and 'leaving' refer to the husband's and father's authority respectively, supporting Abaye's position.
Rav Pappa notes the difficulty that the Mishnah discusses the dispute about the body after death rather than about the produce during her lifetime.
The gemara concludes the discussion with 'and nothing more,' indicating the matter is settled.

items.text: The halakhah of 'kenasah harei hi k'ishto'
items.text_en: The halakhah of 'kenasah harei hi k'ishto'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the purpose of the Mishnah's statement that once he marries her she is like his wife: to teach that he can divorce her with a get and remarry her. It addresses potential objections based on the verse 'ulkachah lo l'ishah v'yibmah' and the concern of an issur aishes ach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what halachic purpose is served by the Mishnah's statement that once he marries her she is like his wife.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina answers that it teaches that he can divorce her with a גט (bill of divorce) and remarry her.

The Gemara objects that the ability to divorce her with a גט (bill of divorce) is obvious, but then explains that without the Mishnah one might have thought that since the verse 'וּלְקָחָהּ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה וְיִבְּמָהּ' (and he takes her as a wife and performs yibbum) implies the first brother's yibbum obligation still applies, only חליצה (release) would be permitted, not a גט (bill of divorce); the Mishnah teaches otherwise.

The Gemara objects that the ability to remarry her is also obvious, but explains that without the Mishnah one might have thought that since he performed the מצוה (commandment) of yibbum, she would remain forbidden to him as אֵשֶׁת אָח (the wife of a brother); the Mishnah teaches that she is permitted.
The Gemara resolves the objection by citing the verse 'וּלְקָחָהּ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה' (and he takes her as a wife), teaching that once he takes her, she is like his wife for all purposes.

items.text: Reason for the condition regarding her ketubah
items.text_en: Reason for the condition regarding her ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the condition that her ketubah must be from the second husband is because the woman was given to him from Heaven, and if she has no ketubah from the first husband, the Sages instituted one from the second so that he will not find it easy to divorce her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah requires the yevamah's ketubah to be from the second husband, and explains that the woman was given to him from Heaven.
The Gemara explains that if she has no ketubah from the first husband, the Sages instituted one from the second so that he will not find it easy to divorce her.

items.text: Mishnah: The mitzvah of yibum falls on the eldest brother
items.text_en: Mishnah: The mitzvah of yibum falls on the eldest brother
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that the mitzvah of yibum is on the eldest brother. If he does not want to, they approach all the brothers. If they do not want to, they return to the eldest and tell him the mitzvah is on him: either chalitzah or yibum. If he delays for a minor or an absent brother, they do not listen to him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the mitzvah of yibum falls on the eldest brother; if he refuses, they approach all brothers, and if they refuse, they return to the eldest and tell him the mitzvah is on him: either chalitzah or yibum.

The Mishnah adds that if the brother delays for a minor, an absent brother, a deaf-mute, or an imbecile, the court does not listen to him but tells him the mitzvah is on him: either chalitzah or yibum.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: minor's yibum vs. adult's chalitzah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: minor's yibum vs. adult's chalitzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: one says a minor's yibum is preferable, the other says an adult's chalitzah is preferable. The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that the minor's yibum is preferable, but deflects the proof. It then raises a difficulty from the Mishnah's ruling that we do not wait for a minor to grow up, and resolves that we do not delay a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: one says a minor's yibum is preferable, the other says an adult's chalitzah is preferable.

The Gemara explains the rationale: the one who prefers a minor's yibum cites the mitzvah of yibum; the one who prefers an adult's chalitzah holds that in the presence of the adult, a minor's yibum is nothing.
The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that a minor's yibum is preferable, interpreting 'lo ratzah' as unwilling to do yibum but willing to do chalitzah.
The Gemara deflects the proof: 'lo ratzah' means unwilling to do either chalitzah or yibum, and the eldest is forced because the mitzvah is incumbent upon him.
The Gemara raises a difficulty: if a minor's yibum is preferable, why does the Mishnah rule that we do not wait for a minor to grow up?
The Gemara resolves: even according to the other opinion, we do not wait for an adult from overseas; the reason is that we do not delay a mitzvah, so no proof can be derived.

items.text: Debate on the preference of adult vs. minor halitza
items.text_en: Debate on the preference of adult vs. minor halitza
items.desc_en: An alternative version of the dispute: all agree that the yibbum of a minor is preferable, but they disagree about halitza. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi argue whether the halitza of an adult is superior or whether both are equal. The reasoning for the adult's superiority is the principle of 'mitzvah ba-gadol'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative version of the dispute: all agree that the yibbum of a minor is preferable, and they only disagree about the halitza of a minor.
The Gemara reports that Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi argue: one says the halitza of an adult is superior, and the other says they are equal.

The Gemara explains the reasoning: the one who says the adult's halitza is superior invokes the principle of 'מצוה בגדול (the mitzvah is performed by the elder)', while the other limits that principle to yibbum, not halitza.

items.text: Attempted proof from the Mishnah and its rejection
items.text_en: Attempted proof from the Mishnah and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove that adult halitza is preferable from the Mishnah's statement that if they did not want, they return to the adult. It suggests this means they did not want to perform yibbum but wanted halitza, and the Mishnah says they return to the adult, implying his halitza is superior. The Gemara rejects this: the case is that they did not want either halitza or yibbum, and they return to the adult because the mitzvah is incumbent upon him, so we coerce him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that adult halitza is preferable: the Mishnah says 'if they did not want, they return to the adult,' implying they wanted halitza but not yibbum, and the Mishnah directs them to the adult, showing his halitza is superior.
The Gemara rejects the proof: the case is that they did not want either halitza or yibbum, and they return to the adult because the mitzvah is incumbent upon him, so we coerce him.

items.text: Another attempted proof and its resolution
items.text_en: Another attempted proof and its resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if a yavam stipulates to wait for the adult from overseas, we do not listen to him. If adult halitza were superior, why not wait? The Gemara answers: the same applies to a minor — we do not wait for him to grow up and perform yibbum. The reason is that we do not delay the performance of a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where a yavam stipulates to wait for the adult from overseas and we do not listen to him, and challenges: if adult halitza were superior, why not wait for him to come and perform halitza?

The Gemara rejects the proof by analogy: just as we do not wait for a minor to grow up and perform yibbum, so too we do not wait for an adult from overseas, because we do not delay the performance of a mitzvah (כֹּל שַׁהוֹיֵי מִצְוָה לָא מְשַׁהֵינַן).

items.text: The Mishnah on priority of yibbum vs. halitza and Rav's ruling
items.text_en: The Mishnah on priority of yibbum vs. halitza and Rav's ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that originally, when the intention was for the mitzvah, yibbum preceded halitza; now that intentions are not pure, halitza precedes. Rav rules that we do not coerce: the yavam may choose either, as the Torah says 'if he does not desire' — implying if he desires, he may do either.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the original priority of yibbum over halitza, and the later reversal due to improper intentions.
Rav rules that we do not coerce the yavam; he may choose either yibbum or halitza, as the Torah implies choice.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's support and the halitza formula
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's support and the halitza formula
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda also holds that we do not coerce, as seen from the formula he instituted for the halitza document: the court tells the yavam 'if you wish to perform yibbum, do so; if not, extend your right foot.' The document describes the halitza procedure and the reading of the Torah passage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that Rav Yehuda also holds that we do not coerce, as evidenced by the halitza document he instituted, which includes the court's instruction to the yavam.
The document describes the physical halitza procedure: the yavam extends his right foot, the yevama removes his shoe and spits before the court.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Avya adds in the name of Rav Yehuda that the court also reads to them the Torah passage about halitza.

items.text: Dispute about the identification of the yavam
items.text_en: Dispute about the identification of the yavam
items.desc_en: A dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina: one says the identification of the yavam requires witnesses, the other says even a relative or a woman suffices. The halakha follows the latter, as it is merely revealing the matter.

sub.desc_en: Introduces the dispute between רב אחא (Rav Acha) and רבינא (Ravina): one requires witnesses for identifying the yavam, the other accepts even a relative or a woman.
Rules that the identification is merely revealing the facts, so even a relative or a woman is accepted.
Quotes the mishna from Bekhorot about the precedence of יבום (levirate marriage) or חליצה (halitza) depending on intent.

items.text: Return to the priority of yibbum and the dispute between Abba Shaul and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Return to the priority of yibbum and the dispute between Abba Shaul and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama quotes Rabbi Yitzchak that they reverted to saying yibbum precedes halitza. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak questions this. The Gemara explains: initially they held like Abba Shaul, who says that yibbum for ulterior motives is like incest, so halitza was preferred; later they held like the Rabbis, who permit yibbum in any case, so yibbum regained priority.

sub.text: Rami bar Chama citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rami bar Chama citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama cites Rabbi Yitzchak that they reverted to saying the מצוה (commandment) of יבום (levirate marriage) takes precedence over the מצוה of חליצה (ḥalitza).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges: could the later generations really have improved their spiritual level?
The Gemara answers: initially they held like אבא שאול (Abba Shaul), and in the end they held like the רבנן (Rabbis).

A baraita is cited: אבא שאול says one who consummates יבום for her beauty, for marital relations, or for another matter is like one who encounters a forbidden relation, and the offspring is nearly a ממזר (mamzer).
The חכמים (Sages) respond with the verse 'יבמה יבא עליה' (her brother-in-law will have intercourse with her), permitting יבום in any case.

items.text: Debate on the interpretation of 'yevamah yavo aleha'
items.text_en: Debate on the interpretation of 'yevamah yavo aleha'
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes a baraita that states 'yevamah yavo aleha' is a mitzvah. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi says it is Abba Shaul's view: the verse teaches that yibbum is a mitzvah, but if he wants for beauty etc., he may marry her. Rava says it could even be the Rabbis: the verse teaches that yibbum is a mitzvah, but he may choose to perform halitza instead. The Gemara questions this and refines the interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the tanna of the baraita that derives from 'יְבָמָהּ יָבֹא עָלֶיהָ' (her brother-in-law will have intercourse with her) that yibbum is a מִצְוָה (commandment), since she was initially permitted, then forbidden, then permitted again.

Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi answers that the baraita is in accordance with Abba Shaul, and explains that the verse teaches yibbum is a מִצְוָה (commandment), so that if he wishes for the sake of her beauty or for the sake of marital relations he may marry her.

sub.text: continuation of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi's explanation
sub.text_en: continuation of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi's explanation
sub.desc_en: The explanation continues: one might have thought she reverts to her original permitted status, so the verse teaches that it is only for the sake of the מִצְוָה (commandment).

Rava offers an alternative: the baraita can even accord with the Rabbis, teaching that yibbum is a מִצְוָה (commandment), and if he wishes he may marry her, and if he wishes he may choose not to marry her.
The Gemara objects to Rava's formulation: can it really be that if he wishes he does not marry her, given that she is bound to him by the levirate bond?

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by emending Rava's statement: rather, if he wishes he may marry her, and if he wishes he performs חליצה (ḥalitza) for her, and the verse teaches that yibbum is a מִצְוָה (commandment).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the verse 'matzot te'achel' according to Rava
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the verse 'matzot te'achel' according to Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rava's view that the verse teaches a mitzvah to eat matzah in a sacred place, even though it was initially permitted and then forbidden. It clarifies that the kohen may choose to eat it himself or have another kohen eat it.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that initially the flour was permitted, then forbidden, then permitted again, and the verse teaches it is a mitzvah to eat it.
The Gemara explains that according to Rava, the baraita teaches that the kohen may choose to eat or not eat the offering.
The Gemara objects that the kohen cannot choose not to eat, since the verse teaches that priests must eat the offerings for atonement.
The Gemara resolves that the choice is between the kohen eating it himself or another kohen eating it, and the verse teaches it is a mitzvah for the kohen who prepared it to eat it.

items.text: Gemara's analysis according to Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi and Abba Shaul
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis according to Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi and Abba Shaul
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi's view that the mishnah follows Abba Shaul, and explores possible distinctions between two types of eating. It rejects eating for appetite vs. gluttonous eating, and eating matzah vs. chametz, ultimately concluding that the distinction is between matzah and 'chalut' (a type of dough), and explains the halacha of chalut for Passover.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to רב יצחק בר אבדימי (Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi), who says the baraita follows אבא שאול (Abba Shaul), what two distinct manners of eating are there in the meal-offering clause?

The Gemara rejects the suggestion that the two options are eating with appetite versus gluttonous eating, since אכילה גסה (gluttonous eating) is not legally considered eating, as ריש לקיש (Reish Lakish) said one who eats gluttonously on יום הכפורים (Yom Kippur) is exempt.
The Gemara suggests instead that the two options are eating it as מצה (unleavened bread) or eating it as חמץ (leaven).
The Gemara rejects the חמץ option, since the verse forbids baking the priests' portion as חמץ, and concludes the two options are מצה versus חלוט (boiled dough).
The Gemara asks what the status of חלוט (boiled dough) is: if it is מצה it is simply permitted, and if it is not מצה the Torah requires מצות (unleavened bread).
The Gemara resolves that חלוט is indeed considered מצה, and the verse repeated the requirement of מצה in order to disqualify a boiled meal-offering.
The Gemara concludes that the relevance of חלוט being מצה is that one fulfills his obligation with it on פסח (Passover), since once it is baked in an oven it is called לחם עוני (bread of affliction).

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of inheritance after chalitzah and yibbum
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of inheritance after chalitzah and yibbum
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who performs chalitzah is like any other brother regarding inheritance, but if there is a father, the father inherits. One who marries his yevamah acquires his brother's property. Rabbi Yehuda says that in both cases, if there is a father, the father inherits.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: One who performs חליצה (the release ceremony) with his yevama is like one of the brothers regarding inheritance; if there is a father, the father inherits. One who marries his yevama acquires his brother's property. Rabbi Yehuda says: In either case, if there is a father, the father inherits.

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of the mishnah's rulings
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of the mishnah's rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the mishnah needed to state that the chalitzah brother is like any other brother, rejecting the notion that he might take all the property. It clarifies that the father inherits because he precedes all descendants, and the yavam who marries his yevamah acquires the property because the Torah says 'yikum al shem achiv'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah's ruling is necessary, since it seems obvious that the brother who performed חליצה (chalitzah) is like any other brother regarding inheritance.

The Gemara explains that one might have thought that חליצה (chalitzah) stands in place of יבום (yibbum) and the brother would take all the property, so the mishnah teaches that he is only like one of the brothers.
The Gemara objects that if the mishnah only meant to exclude taking all property, it should have said 'he is like one of the brothers' rather than 'he is as one of the brothers'.
The Gemara answers that one might have thought to penalize the brother because he caused the yevamah to lose יבום (yibbum), so the mishnah teaches that he is not penalized.
The Gemara explains that the mishnah's ruling that the father takes the property is based on the principle that the father precedes all descendants.

The Gemara explains that the brother who marries his yevamah acquires the property because the Torah says 'יָקוּם עַל שֵׁם אָחִיו' (he shall rise up on the name of his brother), and he has indeed risen.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and a challenge
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and a challenge
items.desc_en: Ulla and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha rule that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda, and explain his reasoning: just as a firstborn has no rights during the father's lifetime, so too the yavam has no rights during the father's lifetime. The Gemara challenges this by comparing the yavam to a firstborn who takes a double portion after the father's death, but deflects by noting the verse says 'al shem achiv' not 'al shem aviv'. A further challenge about the mitzvah of yibbum being dependent on inheritance is rejected.

sub.desc_en: Ulla and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha rule that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: just as a firstborn (בכור) has no rights during the father's lifetime, so too the yavam has no rights during the father's lifetime.
Objects that if the analogy to a firstborn is complete, the yavam should also take a double portion after the father's death.
Rejects the objection by noting the verse says 'יָקוּם עַל שֵׁם אָחִיו' (on his brother's name), not 'עַל שֵׁם אָבִיו' (on his father's name), so the analogy to a firstborn's inheritance is limited.
Objects further that if there is no father to inherit, the mitzvah of yibbum should be fulfilled, but if there is a father, the mitzvah should not be fulfilled.
Rejects the objection by stating that the mitzvah of yibbum is not dependent on inheritance; one performs yibbum regardless, and if there is inheritance he takes it, if not he does not.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute over the halacha and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute over the halacha and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina taught before Rabbi Yannai that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda, but Rabbi Yannai rejected this. A tanna taught before Rav Nachman that the halacha does not follow Rabbi Yehuda, and Rav Nachman questioned this, but the tanna explained that he had mistakenly taught the opposite and corrected himself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina, sitting before Rabbi Yannai, taught that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yannai rejected Rabbi Chanina's ruling, telling him to go read his studies outside, as the halacha does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.
A tanna taught before Rav Nachman that the halacha does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Nachman questioned the tanna, asking if the halacha follows the Sages, which is obvious since the rule is that the halacha follows the majority.
The tanna explained that he had mistakenly taught the opposite and corrected himself, and Rav Nachman affirmed that his correction was proper.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibitions after chalitzah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibitions after chalitzah
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who performs chalitzah with his yevamah is forbidden to her relatives, and she is forbidden to his relatives.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: One who performs חליצה (release) with his yevama is forbidden to her relatives, and she is forbidden to his relatives.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Forbidden relations after halitzah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Forbidden relations after halitzah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the relatives of the halutzah that the yavam is forbidden to marry, and those of the yavam that the halutzah is forbidden to marry. It also distinguishes between the rival wife of a close relative of the halutzah (permitted) and the rival wife of a close relative of the halutzah (forbidden).
