The Gemara concludes that the verse teaches that Jews may acquire even the body of a gentile, confirming Rav Avya's distinction.

items.text: Rav Acha's challenge: Perhaps it refers to purchase with money and immersion
items.text_en: Rav Acha's challenge: Perhaps it refers to purchase with money and immersion
items.desc_en: Rav Acha challenges Rav Avya's derivation, suggesting the verse might refer to acquisition through money and immersion, not the body itself. The Gemara notes this is a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha challenges Rav Avya's derivation, suggesting the verse might refer to acquisition through money and immersion, not the body itself, and the Gemara notes this is a difficulty.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling: One must force the slave into the water
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling: One must force the slave into the water
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that one must force the slave into the water. The Gemara illustrates with the case of Minyamin, slave of Rav Ashi, where Ravina and Rav Acha bar Rava ensured he did not immerse for freedom by placing a clod on his neck and later a pot of clay on his head, instructing him to go to his master's house.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one must force the slave into the water (to prevent him from immersing for freedom).
The Gemara illustrates Shmuel's ruling with the case of Minyamin, slave of Rav Ashi, where Ravina and Rav Acha bar Rava placed a clod on his neck to prevent him from immersing for freedom.
When Minyamin raised his head from the water, they placed a pot of clay on his head and told him to go to his master's house, ensuring he did not complete the immersion for freedom.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about those who pay poll tax for others
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about those who pay poll tax for others
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rava whether those who pay the poll tax for others and thereby subjugate them require a writ of manumission when they leave. Rava responds with Rav Sheshet's teaching: such subjugation is by royal decree, as the king says whoever does not pay tax is subjugated to the one who pays.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rava whether those who pay the poll tax for others and thereby subjugate them require a writ of manumission when they leave.
Rava responds that such subjugation is by royal decree, as the king says whoever does not pay tax is subjugated to the one who pays.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on converts who circumcised but did not immerse
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on converts who circumcised but did not immerse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba saw Jews in Gabla who were pregnant from converts who circumcised but did not immerse, and other halachic issues, but said nothing. Rabbi Yochanan told him to declare their children mamzerim, their wine as yayin nesekh, and their lupines as bishulei akum, because they are not bnei Torah. The Gemara explains each ruling and the dispute about bishulei akum.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba arrived in Gavla and observed several halachic irregularities but said nothing.

Rabbi Yochanan instructed him to declare their children mamzerim, their wine as יין נסך (wine of libation), and their lupines as בישולי גוים (gentile cooking), because they are not בְּנֵי תוֹרָה (Torah scholars).

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on mamzerim follows his own principles: a convert requires both circumcision and immersion, and a gentile or slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer.
The Gemara explains that the wine was prohibited as יין נסך (wine of libation) due to a precautionary principle, as illustrated by the maxim about the nazirite.

The Gemara questions why the lupines were prohibited due to בישולי גוים (gentile cooking), since according to Rav's criterion, lupines are not eaten raw and should be prohibited even for Torah scholars.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan follows the alternative version of Rav's statement: any food that does not appear on a king's table is not subject to the prohibition of בישולי גוים (gentile cooking), so lupines are permitted for Torah scholars but were prohibited for the locals due to their ignorance.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute: Is circumcision alone or immersion alone sufficient for conversion?
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute: Is circumcision alone or immersion alone sufficient for conversion?
items.desc_en: The Tannaim debate whether a convert who circumcised but did not immerse, or immersed but did not circumcise, is a valid convert. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua each derive from the patriarchs and matriarchs, while the Sages require both. The Gemara questions why they don't learn from the other, and cites a parallel dispute about the Passover offering.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says circumcision alone suffices, Rabbi Yehoshua says immersion alone suffices, and the Sages require both.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehoshua does not learn from the patriarchs and Rabbi Eliezer from the matriarchs, and suggests the principle that one cannot derive the possible from the impossible.
A baraita shows that Rabbi Eliezer does derive the possible from the impossible regarding the Passover offering, contradicting the proposed principle.
Rabbi Akiva objects that one cannot derive the possible from the impossible, but Rabbi Eliezer responds that it is a great proof and one may learn from it.
The Gemara signals a shift to reinterpret the baraita, as the previous objection remains unresolved.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on immersion for converts
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on immersion for converts
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that all agree immersion without circumcision is effective, but they dispute circumcision without immersion. Rabbi Eliezer derives immersion from the patriarchs, while Rabbi Yehoshua argues that the patriarchs also had immersion. The Gemara explores the source for immersion at Sinai and for the matriarchs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that all agree immersion without circumcision is effective, but they dispute circumcision without immersion; Rabbi Eliezer derives immersion from the patriarchs, while Rabbi Yehoshua argues that the patriarchs also had immersion.
The Gemara asks where Rabbi Eliezer derives immersion for the patriarchs, and proposes a kal vachomer from the Sinai revelation where washing clothes required immersion.
The Gemara objects that the washing might have been merely for cleanliness, not ritual immersion.
The Gemara provides a different source: Moses' sprinkling of blood at Sinai, which requires prior immersion as a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy).
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehoshua knows the matriarchs had immersion, and answers that it is logical: without immersion, how else would they have entered the covenant?

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that a convert must circumcise and immerse
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that a convert must circumcise and immerse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a convert is never a convert until he circumcises and immerses. The Gemara notes this is obvious since the halakha follows the majority (the Rabbis against Rabbi Yehoshua).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a convert is never a convert until he circumcises and immerses.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is necessary, since the הלכה (binding law) follows the majority (the Rabbis) against Rabbi Yehoshua.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei on immersing a convert on Shabbat
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei on immersing a convert on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the 'Rabbis' as Rabbi Yosei, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda allows immersing a convert who circumcised but did not immerse, while Rabbi Yosei forbids it. The Gemara explains the reasoning behind each opinion, particularly regarding the priority of circumcision versus immersion and the prohibition of fixing a person on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous 'Rabbis' in the earlier dispute as Rabbi Yosei.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda permits immersing a convert who circumcised but did not immerse, while Rabbi Yosei forbids it.
The baraita continues: therefore, Rabbi Yehuda allows immersing a convert on Shabbat, while Rabbi Yosei forbids it.
The Gemara questions why the baraita uses the term 'therefore' (לְפִיכָךְ), since Rabbi Yehuda's position seems obvious.

The Gemara explains: the baraita uses 'therefore' to teach that Rabbi Yehuda requires either circumcision or immersion, not that immersion alone is primary and thus prohibited on Shabbat as fixing a person.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yosei's ruling: since he requires both circumcision and immersion, it is obvious that one cannot fix a person on Shabbat by immersion alone.

The Gemara explains: the baraita teaches that Rabbi Yosei requires both circumcision and immersion, not that circumcision alone is primary and immersion would be permitted on Shabbat if circumcision was witnessed.

items.text: Practical case: convert who circumcised but did not immerse
items.text_en: Practical case: convert who circumcised but did not immerse
items.desc_en: Rabba recounts a case before Rabbi Chiyya bar Rabbi (or Rabbi Oshaya) where a convert came who had circumcised but not immersed. The rabbi told him to wait until the next day to immerse. The Gemara derives three halakhot: a convert needs three judges, a convert is not a convert until both circumcision and immersion, and a convert is not immersed at night. It questions whether expert judges are required.

sub.desc_en: Rabba recounts a case where a convert who had circumcised but not immersed came before Rabbi Chiyya bar Rabbi (or Rabbi Oshaya), who told him to wait until the next day for immersion.
The Gemara derives three halakhot from the story: a convert needs three judges, a convert is not a convert until both circumcision and immersion, and a convert is not immersed at night.
The Gemara questions whether expert judges are required, and answers that perhaps the judges who happened to be present were not necessarily experts.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan: convert requires three judges because 'judgment' is written
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan: convert requires three judges because 'judgment' is written
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explicitly states that a convert requires three judges, as the word 'mishpat' (judgment) is written regarding conversion.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a convert requires three judges because the word 'משפט' (judgment) is written regarding conversion.

items.text: Baraita: accepting a convert only with witnesses or established presence
items.text_en: Baraita: accepting a convert only with witnesses or established presence
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that if someone says 'I am a convert,' we do not accept him unless he is established with you (i.e., known to have converted). If he brings witnesses, we accept him, as derived from the verse 'And when a convert sojourns with you.'

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that a person claiming to be a convert is not accepted unless he is established with you, but if he brings witnesses he is accepted, citing the verse 'וכי יגור אתך גר בארצכם' (and when a convert sojourns with you in your land).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages on bringing proof for conversion
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages on bringing proof for conversion
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse that a convert in the Land of Israel must bring proof of conversion, but outside the Land, no proof is needed according to Rabbi Yehuda. The Sages argue that proof is required everywhere.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse that a convert in the Land of Israel must bring proof, and extends this to outside the Land via the word 'אִתְּךָ'.
Rabbi Yehuda explains that the verse specifies 'בָּאָרֶץ' to require proof only in the Land, but outside the Land no proof is needed.
The Sages argue that proof is required both in the Land and outside the Land.

items.text: Gemara's question on the need for the verse 'he and his witnesses'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the need for the verse 'he and his witnesses'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'he and his witnesses with him' is needed. Rav Sheshet explains that it addresses a case where the convert claims he converted in a specific court, and one might think his witnesses are not believed; the verse teaches they are believed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'he and his witnesses with him' is needed.
Rav Sheshet explains that the verse teaches that witnesses are believed when the convert claims he converted in a specific court.

items.text: Derivation from 'with you' and 'with you' (different word)
items.text_en: Derivation from 'with you' and 'with you' (different word)
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the word 'with you' (אִתְּךָ) is used for one derivation, and another word 'with you' (עִמָּךְ) is used for another derivation, so both verses are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the word 'אִתְּךָ' (with you) is used for one derivation and 'עִמָּךְ' (with you) for another, so both verses are needed.

items.text: Explanation of the Sages' position and the need for the verse 'in the land'
items.text_en: Explanation of the Sages' position and the need for the verse 'in the land'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Sages' view that proof is always needed, given the verse 'in the land'. It answers that the verse teaches that even in the Land of Israel, converts are accepted, countering the assumption that people convert only for the land's benefits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Sages' position that proof is always needed, given the explicit verse 'in the land' which seems to distinguish between the Land of Israel and outside.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'in the land' is needed to teach that even in the Land of Israel converts are accepted, countering the assumption that people convert only for the land's benefits.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan rules like the Sages
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules like the Sages
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that proof is always required, consistent with the majority opinion. The Gemara notes this is obvious, but it is stated to counter the possibility that Rabbi Yehuda's view is more logical because it is supported by verses.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows the Sages: both in the Land and outside the Land, proof is required.
The Gemara asks: this ruling is obvious, since the rule is that the majority opinion prevails over an individual opinion.
The Gemara explains: the ruling was necessary lest one think Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is more logical because it is supported by verses, so Rabbi Yochanan teaches us that the Sages' view prevails.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda on conversion in court vs. privately
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda on conversion in court vs. privately
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a convert who converts in a court is a valid convert, but one who converts privately is not. A story illustrates this: a man who converted privately came before Rabbi Yehuda, who ruled that he is believed to disqualify himself but not his sons.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites the verse 'וּשְׁפַטְתֶּם צֶדֶק' and reports Rabbi Yehuda's ruling: a convert who converts in a court is a valid convert, but one who converts privately is not.
A story illustrates the ruling: a man who converted privately came before Rabbi Yehuda, who ruled that he is believed to disqualify himself but not his sons.

items.text: Contradiction: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on sons vs. his own statement
items.text_en: Contradiction: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on sons vs. his own statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that a man is not believed to disqualify his sons, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says a man is believed to say 'this is my firstborn son' and to disqualify his son as a son of a divorced woman. The Sages disagree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that a man is not believed to disqualify his sons, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says a man is believed to say 'this is my firstborn son' and to disqualify his son as a son of a divorced woman, while the Sages disagree.

items.text: Resolutions by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and Ravina
items.text_en: Resolutions by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and Ravina
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that Rabbi Yehuda meant the man is a gentile and cannot testify. Ravina explains that he is believed to disqualify his sons but not his grandsons. A baraita supports Ravina, but the Gemara concludes the halakha follows Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that Rabbi Yehuda's statement to the convert meant: 'By your own admission you are a gentile (גוי), and a gentile cannot testify to disqualify his sons.'
Ravina explains that Rabbi Yehuda meant the convert is believed to disqualify his sons but not his grandsons (בני בנים).

A baraita supports Ravina: Rabbi Yehuda says a man is believed about his minor son but not his adult son, and Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that 'minor' means one who has sons, 'adult' means one without sons.

The Gemara rules the הלכה (binding law) follows Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, and explains that the baraita supporting Ravina was stated regarding the verse 'יַכִּיר' (the law of declaring a firstborn), not regarding conversion.

items.text: Procedure for accepting converts in the present time
items.text_en: Procedure for accepting converts in the present time
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the procedure: inform the prospective convert of the suffering of Israel, inform them of some light and severe commandments, their reward and punishment, and if they accept, they are accepted immediately.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by describing the initial step: when a convert comes to convert in the present time, the court informs them of Israel's suffering, and if they accept, they are accepted immediately.
The baraita details that the court informs the convert of some light and severe commandments, including the punishment for eating חלב (forbidden fat) and violating שבת (the Sabbath).

The baraita concludes by stating that just as the convert is informed of punishment, so too they are informed of reward — that the World to Come is only for the righteous, and Israel in the present time cannot receive it fully.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The conversion procedure
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The conversion procedure
items.desc_en: The Mishnah outlines the process for a male convert: he is informed of some light and severe commandments, circumcised immediately if he accepts, and immersed. For a female convert, women seat her in water and two scholars inform her of commandments. The same rules apply to a freed slave, and any interposition invalidates the immersion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a prospective male convert is informed of some light and severe commandments, but not excessively, and not with excessive scrutiny.

sub.text: Mishnah (Tanna Kamma) — procedure for male convert
sub.text_en: Mishnah (Tanna Kamma) — procedure for male convert
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah details the male convert's procedure: if he accepts, he is circumcised immediately, any obstructing flesh is recut, and after healing he is immersed with two scholars present, becoming fully Jewish.

sub.text: Mishnah (Tanna Kamma) — procedure for female convert
sub.text_en: Mishnah (Tanna Kamma) — procedure for female convert
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the female convert's procedure: women seat her in water up to her neck, and two scholars inform her of commandments from outside.
The Mishnah concludes that the same rules apply to a freed slave, and that any interposition invalidates immersion for a convert, a freed slave, and a menstruant woman.

items.text: Gemara: Reason for informing the convert and the prooftexts
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for informing the convert and the prooftexts
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why we inform the convert of some commandments: so that if he wants to withdraw, he can. Rabbi Chelbo says converts are as difficult for Israel as a scab, citing a verse. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains why we inform him of the laws of gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and pe'ah: a Noahide is executed for stealing less than a perutah, and it is not given for restitution. Rabbi Elazar cites a verse from Ruth to show we do not overwhelm the convert.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the reason for informing the convert of some commandments is so that if he wishes to withdraw, he may do so.
Rabbi Chelbo states that converts are as difficult for Israel as a scab (ספחת), citing the verse 'וְנִלְוָה הַגֵּר עֲלֵיהֶם וְנִסְפְּחוּ עַל בֵּית יַעֲקֹב'.

The Gemara asks why the convert is informed of the laws of gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and pe'ah, and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that a Noahide is executed for stealing less than a perutah, and it is not given for restitution.
Rabbi Elazar cites the verse from Ruth (וַתֵּרֶא כִּי מִתְאַמֶּצֶת הִיא לָלֶכֶת אִתָּהּ וַתֶּחְדַּל לְדַבֵּר אֵלֶיהָ) to show that we do not overwhelm the convert.

items.text: Gemara: The dialogue between Naomi and Ruth as a model
items.text_en: Gemara: The dialogue between Naomi and Ruth as a model
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the exchange between Naomi and Ruth, showing how Naomi informed Ruth of various commandments: the Sabbath boundary, prohibition of yichud, the 613 commandments, idolatry, the four death penalties, and two burial sites. Ruth's responses show her acceptance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins the dialogue between Naomi and Ruth, where Naomi informs Ruth of the Sabbath boundary (תחום שבת) and the prohibition of ייחוד (seclusion), and Ruth responds with acceptance.
Naomi continues informing Ruth of the 613 commandments, the prohibition of idolatry, the four death penalties, and the two burial sites, and Ruth responds with acceptance each time.
The Gemara concludes that immediately upon seeing Ruth's determination, Naomi ceased to dissuade her, citing the verse 'ותרא כי מתאמצת היא' (and she saw that she was determined).

items.text: Gemara: Clarifications on circumcision and immersion
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifications on circumcision and immersion
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why circumcision is done immediately: we do not delay a mitzvah. It defines the flesh that invalidates circumcision as that which covers most of the crown, citing Rav Yirmeya bar Abba in the name of Rav. Regarding immersion after healing, the Gemara notes that water aggravates the wound, so we wait until healed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that a convert is circumcised immediately upon acceptance.
The Gemara explains that circumcision is performed immediately because we do not delay a מצוה (commandment).
The Gemara cites a baraita defining the flesh that invalidates circumcision as that which covers most of the crown (עטרה).

sub.text: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba in the name of Rav specifies that the flesh must cover most of the height of the crown.
The Gemara notes that immersion is only performed after healing, not before.
The Gemara explains that water aggravates the wound, so immersion is delayed until the wound heals.

items.text: Gemara: The need for three judges and the status after immersion
items.text_en: Gemara: The need for three judges and the status after immersion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that two scholars stand over the convert, citing Rabbi Yochanan that a convert requires three. It resolves that Rabbi Yochanan taught the Tanna to say 'three'. It then asks about the practical implication of the convert being like a Jew: if he reverts and marries a Jewish woman, he is considered a Jewish apostate and his kiddushin is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's requirement of two scholars, citing Rabbi Chiyya quoting Rabbi Yochanan that a convert requires three judges.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan instructed the Tanna to teach 'three' instead of 'two'.
The Gemara asks about the practical halachic implication of the convert being like a Jew in all matters.
The Gemara answers that if the convert reverts and betroths a Jewish woman, he is considered a Jewish apostate and his kiddushin is valid.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute about a freed slave accepting commandments
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute about a freed slave accepting commandments
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah implies a freed slave must accept the yoke of commandments, but a baraita says a freed slave does not need to accept. Rav Sheshet resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, while the baraita follows the Rabbis. The baraita discusses a Canaanite maidservant: if she accepted, she is immersed and permitted immediately; Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says even if she did not accept, he forces her to immerse for slavery, then immerses her for freedom and frees her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one might think a freed slave must accept the yoke of commandments, but a baraita states that a freed slave does not need to accept.
Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the baraita to the Rabbis.
A baraita is cited: the Rabbis rule that a female slave who has not accepted immersion is delayed, but if she accepted, she is immersed and permitted immediately.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules that even if she did not accept, he forces her and immerses her for slavery, then immerses her again for freedom, and frees her.

items.text: Opening statement: immediate permission
items.text_en: Opening statement: immediate permission
items.desc_en: The segment states that a captive woman is permitted immediately after her captor's actions, setting the stage for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that a captive woman is permitted immediately after her captor's actions.

items.text: Rava explains Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's reasoning
items.text_en: Rava explains Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar derives from the verse 'כׇּל עֶבֶד אִישׁ' that a male slave is circumcised against his will, but not the son of a Jewish man against his will.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's reasoning: the verse 'כל עבד איש מקנת כסף' teaches that one may circumcise a male slave against his will but not a freeborn son against his will.

items.text: Rabbis' view and Ulla's explanation
items.text_en: Rabbis' view and Ulla's explanation
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that the Rabbis hold that just as one does not circumcise the son of a Jewish man against his will, so too one does not circumcise a male slave against his will. The verse 'כׇּל עֶבֶד אִישׁ' is needed for Shmuel's teaching about an owner who renounces ownership of his slave.

sub.desc_en: Ulla explains that the Rabbis derive from the same verse that just as one does not circumcise the son of a Jewish man against his will, so too one does not circumcise a male slave against his will.

The Gemara notes that the verse 'כׇּל עֶבֶד אִישׁ' is needed for Shmuel's teaching that an owner who renounces ownership of his slave frees him without a bill of manumission, as the verse defines a slave as one over whom the master has authority.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges the Rabbis' view, arguing that their leniency regarding the captive woman might not apply to a slave who is involved in commandments, suggesting that even the Rabbis would agree that a slave must be circumcised against his will.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges: the Rabbis' leniency regarding a יפת תואר (captive woman) who is not obligated in commandments does not apply to a slave who is obligated in commandments, where even the Rabbis would agree that circumcision is forced.

items.text: Baraita on accepting commandments and resolution
items.text_en: Baraita on accepting commandments and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that both a convert and one who buys a slave from a gentile must accept commandments, but one who buys from a Jew does not. The Gemara identifies this as the Rabbis' view, and resolves a contradiction regarding a freed slave by explaining that the baraita refers to immersion.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a convert and one who buys a slave from a gentile must accept commandments, but one who buys from a Jew does not.
The Gemara asks who authored the baraita, ruling out Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and concluding it must be the Rabbis.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that buying from a gentile requires accepting commandments, but buying from a Jew does not.
The Gemara objects that the baraita's mention of a convert alongside a freed slave creates a contradiction.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to immersion, not acceptance of commandments.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva on grooming
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva on grooming
items.desc_en: The Tannaim debate the meaning of 'וְעָשְׂתָה אֶת צִפׇּרְנֶיהָ': Rabbi Eliezer says she must cut them, Rabbi Akiva says she must let them grow. They each derive their view from a verbal analogy with the head, and a proof is brought from the case of Mephibosheth.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse and presents the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says she must cut (תָּקוֹץ) her nails, Rabbi Akiva says she must let them grow (תְּגַדֵּיל).
Rabbi Eliezer derives via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the head: just as 'עשייה' (doing) regarding the head means removal (העברה), so too regarding nails it means removal (cutting).

Rabbi Akiva derives via a different גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): just as 'עשייה' regarding the head means disfigurement (ניוול — letting hair grow long), so too regarding nails it means disfigurement (letting them grow).

A proof is brought from Mephibosheth: the verse says 'לֹא עָשָׂה רַגְלָיו' (he did not do his feet), and the gemara explains that 'עשייה' there means removal (העברה) — i.e., he did not trim his feet or mustache, supporting Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation.

items.text: Beginning of next baraita on weeping
items.text_en: Beginning of next baraita on weeping
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new baraita about the captive woman weeping for her parents, which continues the discussion of the captive woman's procedures.

sub.desc_en: A baraita begins citing the verse about the captive woman mourning her parents.

items.text: Opening Tannaitic dispute on biblical phrases
items.text_en: Opening Tannaitic dispute on biblical phrases
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer interprets 'her father' and 'her mother' literally, while Rabbi Akiva interprets them as idolatry. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar interprets 'a month of days' as ninety days.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer interprets 'her father' and 'her mother' literally as biological parents.
Rabbi Akiva interprets 'her father and her mother' as idolatry, citing a verse where people call a tree 'my father'.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar interprets 'a month of days' as ninety days: 'month' = thirty, 'days' = thirty, 'and afterward' = thirty.

items.text: Ravina's challenge to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.text_en: Ravina's challenge to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's interpretation, suggesting an alternative reading that would make the total ninety days but with a different structure, and declares it difficult.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's interpretation, suggesting that 'and afterward' might refer to the same thirty days, making the interpretation difficult.

items.text: Dispute on keeping uncircumcised slaves
items.text_en: Dispute on keeping uncircumcised slaves
items.desc_en: A Tannaitic source records a dispute: Rabbi Yishmael allows keeping uncircumcised slaves, while Rabbi Akiva forbids it. Rabbi Yishmael cites the verse 'and the son of your maidservant shall rest', which is explained to refer to an uncircumcised slave, as a circumcised slave is already mentioned elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: A Tannaitic source records the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael permits keeping uncircumcised slaves, while Rabbi Akiva forbids it.
Rabbi Yishmael cites the verse 'וְיִנָּפֵשׁ בֶּן אֲמָתְךָ' (and the son of your maidservant shall rest) to support his position.
Rabbi Akiva responds that the verse speaks of a case where one bought a slave at twilight and did not have time to circumcise him.
The Gemara notes that all agree the verse 'וְיִנָּפֵשׁ בֶּן אֲמָתְךָ' refers to an uncircumcised slave, and then explains the derivation from a baraita.

items.text: Interpretation of 'the stranger' as a resident alien
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'the stranger' as a resident alien
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the term 'the stranger' in the verse refers to a resident alien (ger toshav), not a righteous convert (ger tzedek), as the latter is already mentioned elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the term 'the stranger' in the verse refers to a resident alien (גר תושב), not a righteous convert (גר צדק), by citing the alternative verse 'and your stranger who is within your gates' which already covers the righteous convert.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling and Rav Pappa's defense
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling and Rav Pappa's defense
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that if a slave bought from a gentile refuses to be circumcised, the master may delay for up to twelve months, then sell him back. The rabbis suggest this contradicts Rabbi Akiva, but Rav Pappa defends it, saying Rabbi Akiva only forbids keeping a slave who never agreed, but if the slave initially agreed and then reneged, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a master who buys a slave from a gentile and the slave refuses to be circumcised may delay up to twelve months, and if still uncircumcised, must sell him back to gentiles.
The rabbis question before Rav Pappa whether this ruling contradicts Rabbi Akiva, who forbids keeping uncircumcised slaves.
Rav Pappa defends the ruling, explaining that Rabbi Akiva's prohibition applies only when the slave never agreed to circumcise, but if the slave initially agreed and then reneged, it is permitted.

items.text: Rav Kahana's report and Rav Zevid's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's report and Rav Zevid's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports the discussion to Rav Zevid, who challenges Rav Pappa's defense: if so, why did Rabbi Akiva only mention the case of buying a slave at twilight? He could have distinguished differently. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva gave one of two reasons.

sub.text: Rav Zevid's objection via Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid's objection via Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports: I stated this teaching before Rav Zevid of Nehardea, and he objected: If so, why didn't Rabbi Yishmael respond to Rabbi Akiva with this distinction?
Rav Kahana resolves: Rabbi Akiva gave one of two reasons (the purchase at twilight), so Rabbi Yishmael could not have responded with the distinction about definitive refusal.

items.text: Ravin's statement and further discussion on conditional sale
items.text_en: Ravin's statement and further discussion on conditional sale
items.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Ila'i that an uncircumcised slave may be kept only if the master stipulated at purchase that he would not be circumcised. The rabbis again question this against Rabbi Akiva, and Rav Pappa defends it by saying Rabbi Akiva only forbids when no stipulation was made. Rav Zevid challenges again, and the Gemara concludes that Rabbi Akiva gave one of multiple reasons.

sub.text: Ravin's report in the name of Rabbi Ila'i
sub.text_en: Ravin's report in the name of Rabbi Ila'i
sub.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Ila'i that the only uncircumcised slave one may keep is one purchased with the stipulation that he not be circumcised.
The rabbis question this ruling before Rav Pappa, noting it seems to contradict Rabbi Akiva's position that one may not keep an uncircumcised slave at all.
Rav Pappa answers that even according to Rabbi Akiva, the prohibition applies only when no stipulation was made, but when a stipulation was made it is permitted.

sub.text: Rav Kahana's report of Rav Zevid's challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana's report of Rav Zevid's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports that Rav Zevid objected: if Rabbi Akiva's earlier answer about a slave purchased at twilight is a separate reason, why didn't Rabbi Akiva simply give that answer instead of the stipulation-based one?
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Akiva gave one of multiple possible reasons, so the objection is not decisive.

items.text: Story of a city in Israel and a baraita on delaying circumcision
items.text_en: Story of a city in Israel and a baraita on delaying circumcision
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Papi, Rabbi Ami, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha relate a story of a city in Israel whose slaves refused circumcision; they delayed twelve months and then sold them. This aligns with a baraita: one may delay up to twelve months, but Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says in the Land of Israel one may not delay due to purity concerns, and near the border not at all lest the slave flee to the enemy.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Chanina bar Papi and colleagues
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chanina bar Papi and colleagues
sub.desc_en: A story: Rabbi Chanina bar Papi, Rabbi Ami, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha sat and discussed a city in Eretz Yisrael whose slaves refused circumcision; they negotiated for twelve months and then sold them to gentiles.
The Gemara asks: Whose opinion does this practice follow?

The Gemara answers: It follows this Tanna, as taught in a baraita: One who buys a slave from a gentile and he refuses to circumcise — negotiates for twelve months; if he still refuses, sells him back to gentiles. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds restrictions about delaying in Eretz Yisrael and border towns.

items.text: Reasons for the suffering of converts
items.text_en: Reasons for the suffering of converts
items.desc_en: A Tannaitic source records various opinions on why converts suffer: Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel says because they did not observe the seven Noahide laws before conversion; Rabbi Yose says a convert is like a newborn, but suffers due to lack of precision in mitzvot; Abba Chanan says because they act from fear, not love; others say because they delayed entering under the wings of the Shechinah. Rabbi Avahu or Rabbi Chanina cites a verse from Ruth.

sub.text: Rabbi Chananya, son of Rabban Gamliel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chananya, son of Rabban Gamliel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chananya, son of Rabban Gamliel, says: Why are converts in this age afflicted? Because they did not observe the שבע מצוות בני נח (Noahide laws).
Rabbi Yosei says: A convert is like a newborn child; rather, they are afflicted because they are not expert in the fine details of מצוות (commandments) like Israel.

sub.text: Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Abba Chanan says in the name of Rabbi Elazar: Because they do not act from love, but from fear.
Acherim (others) say: Because they delayed entering under the wings of the Shechinah.

Rabbi Avahu (or Rabbi Chanina) cites a verse: 'May the Lord repay your deed, and may your reward be complete from the Lord God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge' — supporting the idea that converts who delayed are rewarded despite their afflictions.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Definitions of a Mamzer
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Definitions of a Mamzer
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three opinions: Rabbi Akiva defines a mamzer as any offspring from a forbidden sexual relationship punishable by 'Lo Yavo'; Shimon HaTimni says it is any relationship punishable by karet; Rabbi Yehoshua says it is any relationship punishable by court-imposed death. The halakhah follows Shimon HaTimni.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking who is a mamzer, and presents Rabbi Akiva's opinion that it is any offspring from a forbidden sexual relationship punishable by 'Lo Yavo'.
Shimon HaTimni defines a mamzer as any offspring from a relationship punishable by karet, and the halakhah follows his view.
Rabbi Yehoshua defines a mamzer as any offspring from a relationship punishable by court-imposed death.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai's Supporting Evidence
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai's Supporting Evidence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai reports finding a genealogical scroll in Jerusalem that recorded a specific person as a mamzer from an adulterous relationship, supporting Rabbi Yehoshua's position that such offspring are mamzerim.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai reports finding a genealogical scroll in Jerusalem that recorded a specific person as a mamzer from an adulterous relationship, supporting Rabbi Yehoshua's position that such offspring are mamzerim.

items.text: Mishnah: Permitted Marriages After Wife's Death
items.text_en: Mishnah: Permitted Marriages After Wife's Death
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a man is permitted to marry his wife's sister after the wife dies, even if he divorced her or she married another man and then died. The same applies to a yevamah (brother's widow) after her death or after chalitzah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man is permitted to marry his wife's sister after the wife dies, and similarly for a yevamah (brother's widow) after her death or after chalitzah.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Akiva's Scriptural Basis
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Akiva's Scriptural Basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Akiva's reasoning: he interprets the verse 'Lo Yikach Ish et Eshet Aviv' as referring to a woman his father raped (following Rabbi Yehuda), which is a negative commandment. The adjacent verse 'Lo Yavo Mamzer' teaches that such a union produces a mamzer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Akiva's reasoning, and cites the verse 'לֹא יִקַּח אִישׁ אֶת אֵשֶׁת אָבִיו וְלֹא יְגַלֶּה כְּנַף אָבִיו' (a man shall not take his father's wife nor uncover his father's garment), interpreting 'garment' as something his father saw.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds the verse speaks of a woman his father raped, making the prohibition a negative commandment (חַיָּיבֵי לָאוִין).
The Gemara concludes that the adjacent verse 'לֹא יָבֹא מַמְזֵר' (a mamzer shall not enter the assembly of the Lord) teaches that from such a union a mamzer is produced.

items.text: Expanding the Scope: Rabbi Simai and Rabbi Yeshevav
items.text_en: Expanding the Scope: Rabbi Simai and Rabbi Yeshevav
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Simai extends mamzer status to other negative commandments not involving 'she'er basar', and Rabbi Yeshevav even includes positive commandments. They derive this from the extra 'vav' in the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the positions of Rabbi Simai, who extends mamzer status to other negative commandments not involving 'she'er basar', and Rabbi Yeshevav, who even includes positive commandments.
The Gemara explains that both Rabbi Simai and Rabbi Yeshevav derive their expansions from the extra 'vav' in the verse.

items.text: Shimon HaTimni's Scriptural Basis
items.text_en: Shimon HaTimni's Scriptural Basis
items.desc_en: Shimon HaTimni follows the Rabbis who interpret the verse as referring to a shomeret yavam (a yevamah waiting for levirate marriage), which is punishable by karet. The adjacent verse 'Lo Yavo Mamzer' teaches that such a union produces a mamzer.

sub.text: Stam's explanation of Shimon HaTimni's position
sub.text_en: Stam's explanation of Shimon HaTimni's position
sub.desc_en: Shimon HaTimni follows the Rabbis who interpret the verse as referring to a shomeret yavam (a yevamah waiting for levirate marriage), which is punishable by karet, and the adjacent verse 'Lo Yavo Mamzer' teaches that such a union produces a mamzer.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's Scriptural Basis
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's Scriptural Basis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua argues that the verse includes both 'Lo Yikach' and 'Lo Yegaleh', implying that only relationships between these two prohibitions (i.e., those punishable by death) produce a mamzer, but not additional ones.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents Rabbi Yehoshua's scriptural derivation: the verse includes both 'לֹא יִקַּח' and 'לֹא יְגַלֶּה', so only relationships between these two prohibitions produce a mamzer, not additional ones.

items.text: Abaye's Statement on Niddah
items.text_en: Abaye's Statement on Niddah
items.desc_en: Abaye begins a statement that all agree regarding one who has relations with a niddah, but the daf cuts off here, leaving the conclusion for the next amud.

sub.desc_en: Abaye begins a statement that all agree regarding one who has relations with a niddah, but the daf cuts off here, leaving the conclusion for the next amud.

items.text: Mishnah and baraita on mamzer from a sotah and niddah
items.text_en: Mishnah and baraita on mamzer from a sotah and niddah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a child from a sotah is not a mamzer. The Gemara explains that a niddah is excluded because kiddushin take effect with her, and similarly a sotah. A baraita confirms that all agree regarding a niddah, sotah, and shomeret yavam that the child is not a mamzer.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the offspring from a sotah is not a mamzer.
The Gemara explains that a niddah is excluded because kiddushin take effect with her, citing the verse 'וּתְהִי נִדָּתָהּ עָלָיו'.
The Gemara similarly explains that a sotah is excluded because kiddushin take effect with her.
A baraita confirms that all agree regarding a niddah, sotah, and shomeret yavam that the child is not a mamzer.

items.text: Abaye's uncertainty about shomeret yavam
items.text_en: Abaye's uncertainty about shomeret yavam
items.desc_en: Abaye is uncertain whether the status of a shomeret yavam follows Rav or Shmuel, indicating a dispute about whether her child is a mamzer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Abaye is uncertain whether the halakha regarding a shomeret yavam follows Rav or Shmuel, which is why he did not include her in his list.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai's scroll of genealogies
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai's scroll of genealogies
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai reports finding a scroll in Jerusalem that records a mamzer from a married woman, a teaching of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov as 'kav ve-naki', and that Menashe killed Yeshayahu.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai reports finding a scroll in Jerusalem that records a mamzer from a married woman, a teaching of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov as 'kav ve-naki', and that Menashe killed Yeshayahu.

items.text: Rava's account of Menashe's trial and killing of Yeshayahu
items.text_en: Rava's account of Menashe's trial and killing of Yeshayahu
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Menashe judged and killed Yeshayahu. Yeshayahu knew Menashe would not accept his words, so he hid. Menashe cited contradictions between Yeshayahu's prophecies and the Torah. Yeshayahu pronounced God's name and was swallowed in a cedar tree, which was sawed, and he died when the saw reached his mouth because he had said he dwells among a people of unclean lips.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that Menashe judged and killed Yeshayahu, then recounts Menashe's three contradictions between Yeshayahu's prophecies and the Torah.

Yeshayahu explains that he knew Menashe would not accept his words, so he pronounced God's name and was swallowed in a cedar tree; when the tree was sawed, he died at the mouth because he had said he dwells among a people of unclean lips.

items.text: Resolving contradictions between verses
items.text_en: Resolving contradictions between verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the contradictory verses can be reconciled. It answers: Yeshayahu saw through a dim lens while Moshe saw through a clear lens. The verse 'Seek God when He is found' applies to an individual during the Ten Days of Repentance, but to the community always. The verse about completing one's days is a dispute among Tanna'im.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the contradictory verses about seeing God and seeking Him can be reconciled.
The Gemara answers that Yeshayahu saw through a dim lens (אספקלריא שאינה מאירה) while Moshe saw through a clear lens (אספקלריא המאירה), as taught in a baraita.

sub.text: Second answer (Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha)
sub.text_en: Second answer (Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the verse 'דרשו ה׳ בהמצאו' (Seek God when He is found) applies to an individual during the Ten Days of Repentance, while the community is always answered.
The Gemara answers that the verse about completing one's days is a dispute among Tanna'im, as cited in a baraita.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on lifespan
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on lifespan
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages: if one merits, his years are completed (Rabbi Akiva) or increased (Sages); if not, they are decreased.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Akiva's position: if one merits, his years are completed; if not, they are decreased.
The Mishnah presents the Sages' position: if one merits, his years are increased; if not, they are decreased.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Akiva's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Akiva's answer
items.desc_en: The Sages challenge Rabbi Akiva from the verse where God added fifteen years to Hezekiah's life. Rabbi Akiva responds that those years were added from Hezekiah's own allotted time, as the prophecy about Josiah was given before Manasseh was born.

sub.desc_en: The Sages challenge Rabbi Akiva by citing the verse where God added fifteen years to Hezekiah's life, implying that years can be added beyond one's original allotment.
Rabbi Akiva responds that the added years were taken from Hezekiah's own allotted lifespan, proving this from the prophecy about Josiah given before Manasseh was born.

items.text: Sages' rebuttal
items.text_en: Sages' rebuttal
items.desc_en: The Sages counter that the prophecy about Josiah was not explicitly from Hezekiah, but only said 'to the house of David', so it could have been from another person.

sub.desc_en: The Sages object that the prophecy about Josiah was not explicitly from Hezekiah, but only said 'to the house of David', so it could have been from another person.

items.text: Transition to new Mishnah
items.text_en: Transition to new Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah about a wife or yevamah who died is unnecessary, and then concludes the chapter with 'Hadran alach haCholeitz'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: 'His wife who died... his yevamah who died...'.
Rav Yosef comments that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi taught a Mishnah that is unnecessary.
The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'Hadran alach haCholeitz' (we return to you, chapter haCholeitz).

items.text: New Mishnah: Sequential acts of yibbum and chalitzah
items.text_en: New Mishnah: Sequential acts of yibbum and chalitzah
items.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel rules that after a get, ma'amar, bi'ah, or chalitzah, no subsequent act of the same type is effective. The Sages disagree regarding get and ma'amar, but agree that after bi'ah or chalitzah, nothing further is effective.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel rules that after a get, ma'amar, bi'ah, or chalitzah, no subsequent act of the same type is effective.
The Sages disagree regarding get and ma'amar, but agree that after bi'ah or chalitzah, nothing further is effective.

items.text: Mishnah's examples of sequential acts
items.text_en: Mishnah's examples of sequential acts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details various sequences of ma'amar, get, bi'ah, and chalitzah, explaining which subsequent acts are effective and which require additional steps like get or chalitzah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins with the case of performing ma'amar (levirate betrothal) followed by a get (bill of divorce), requiring chalitzah; then ma'amar followed by chalitzah, requiring a get; then ma'amar followed by bi'ah (intercourse), which is the proper mitzvah.

The Mishnah continues with the case of giving a get followed by ma'amar, requiring both a get and chalitzah; then get followed by bi'ah, requiring both a get and chalitzah; then get followed by chalitzah, after which nothing is effective.
The Mishnah concludes with cases where chalitzah or bi'ah is performed first, followed by any other act, stating that nothing is effective after chalitzah or bi'ah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rules for a yavam with one or two yevamot
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rules for a yavam with one or two yevamot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists various sequences of ma'amar, get, bi'ah, and chalitzah performed by a yavam with one or two yevamot, specifying which combinations require additional gittin or chalitzah. It concludes with Rabbi Nechemya's opinion that both bi'ah and chalitzah, whether at the beginning, middle, or end, leave no subsequent effect.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the general rule for a yavam with one or two yevamot, then lists the first case: ma'amar in one and ma'amar in the other requires two gittin and chalitzah.
The Mishnah lists the second case: ma'amar in one and a get in the other requires a get and chalitzah.
The Mishnah lists the third case: ma'amar in one and bi'ah in the other requires two gittin and chalitzah.
The Mishnah lists the fourth case: ma'amar in one and chalitzah in the other, the first requires a get.
The Mishnah lists the fifth case: a get in one and a get in the other requires chalitzah from him.
The Mishnah lists the sixth case: a get in one and bi'ah in the other requires a get and chalitzah.
The Mishnah lists the seventh case: a get in one and ma'amar in the other requires a get and chalitzah.
The Mishnah lists the eighth case: a get in one and chalitzah in the other, nothing follows chalitzah.

The Mishnah lists the ninth case: chalitzah and chalitzah, or chalitzah and ma'amar, get and bi'ah, bi'ah and bi'ah, bi'ah and ma'amar, get and chalitzah — nothing follows chalitzah, whether one yavam with two yevamot or two yevamin with one yevamah.
The Mishnah repeats the rule for chalitzah and ma'amar, get and bi'ah, bi'ah and ma'amar, get and chalitzah — nothing follows chalitzah, whether at the beginning, middle, or end.
The Mishnah states the rule for bi'ah: when it is at the beginning, nothing follows it; when in the middle or end, something follows it.
Rabbi Nechemya says: both bi'ah and chalitzah, whether at the beginning, middle, or end, nothing follows them.

items.text: Gemara's initial observation: Dispute limited to multiple gittin or ma'amarim
items.text_en: Gemara's initial observation: Dispute limited to multiple gittin or ma'amarim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's dispute only applies to cases of multiple gittin or multiple ma'amarim, but a single get or a single ma'amar is effective.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's dispute is limited to cases of multiple gittin or multiple ma'amarim, but a single get or a single ma'amar is effective.

items.text: Reason for get being effective
items.text_en: Reason for get being effective
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages decreed a get is effective in yevamah because it is effective in the general world (for a regular wife). If it were not, people might think chalitzah is also ineffective, leading to bi'ah after chalitzah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages decreed that a get (bill of divorce) is effective for a yevamah (levirate widow).

The Gemara answers that the get is effective because it is effective in the general world (for a regular wife); otherwise, people might think chalitzah (removal of the shoe) is also ineffective, leading to bi'ah (intercourse) after chalitzah.

items.text: Reason for ma'amar being effective
items.text_en: Reason for ma'amar being effective
items.desc_en: Similarly, the Gemara explains that ma'amar is effective because it is effective in the general world (for betrothal). If not, people might think bi'ah is also ineffective, leading to bi'ah after bi'ah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages ruled that ma'amar (formal betrothal) is effective for a yevama (levirate widow).

The Gemara answers that ma'amar is effective because it is effective in the general world (for regular betrothal); otherwise, people might mistakenly think bi'ah (intercourse) is also ineffective, leading to bi'ah after bi'ah.

items.text: Reason for invalid bi'ah having subsequent effect
items.text_en: Reason for invalid bi'ah having subsequent effect
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Sages said that an invalid bi'ah has subsequent effect: it is a decree to prevent bi'ah after get (which might be confused with bi'ah after chalitzah) and bi'ah after ma'amar (which might be confused with bi'ah after bi'ah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages decreed that an invalid bi'ah (cohabitation) has subsequent effect (i.e., requires a get or chalitzah to nullify it).

The Gemara answers: if the bi'ah occurs after a get, it is a decree to prevent bi'ah after chalitzah (which would be ineffective); if after ma'amar, it is a decree to prevent bi'ah after bi'ah (which would be ineffective).

items.text: Reason for invalid chalitzah having no subsequent effect
items.text_en: Reason for invalid chalitzah having no subsequent effect
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why invalid chalitzah has no subsequent effect: there is no need to decree chalitzah after get due to chalitzah after chalitzah, and chalitzah after ma'amar requires a get for the ma'amar just as chalitzah after bi'ah requires a get for the bi'ah, so no confusion arises.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages ruled that an invalid chalitzah has no subsequent effect, and considers a possible decree of chalitzah after get due to chalitzah after chalitzah, but dismisses it.

The Gemara answers that there is no need to decree regarding chalitzah after ma'amar because it requires a get for the ma'amar, just as chalitzah after bi'ah requires a get for the bi'ah, so no confusion arises.

items.text: Rava's statement
items.text_en: Rava's statement
items.desc_en: Rava begins to speak, likely introducing a further analysis or conclusion, though the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Rava begins to speak, introducing a further analysis or conclusion, though the text cuts off.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabban Gamliel's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabban Gamliel's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabban Gamliel's view stems from uncertainty: he is unsure whether a get dismisses the yevama or not, and whether a ma'amar acquires her or not. This leads to the conclusion that a second get or ma'amar after the first is meaningless.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabban Gamliel's reasoning for his ruling that a second get or ma'amar is ineffective.

items.text: Abaye's objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges the uncertainty explanation by citing a baraita where Rabban Gamliel acknowledges that a get after a ma'amar and a ma'amar after a get are effective. If he were uncertain, then bi'ah (consummation) should also be effective after a get or ma'amar, but the baraita implies otherwise.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing a baraita where Rabban Gamliel acknowledges that a get after a ma'amar and a ma'amar after a get are effective, and also a get after bi'ah and ma'amar, and a ma'amar after bi'ah and get.

Abaye argues that if Rabban Gamliel were uncertain about the effectiveness of get and ma'amar, then bi'ah (consummation) should also be effective לכתחילה (the ideal standard), since the Mishnah teaches that initial bi'ah leaves nothing after it.

items.text: Abaye's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye revises the explanation: Rabban Gamliel is certain that a get dismisses and a ma'amar acquires, but the Sages decreed that a get after a get is ineffective because the first already dismissed, and a ma'amar after a ma'amar is ineffective because the first already acquired. However, a get after a ma'amar and a ma'amar after a get are effective because each serves a different function.

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces his alternative explanation that Rabban Gamliel is certain about the effects of a get and a ma'amar.

Abaye explains that the Sages decreed that a get after a get is ineffective because the first already dismissed, and a ma'amar after a ma'amar is ineffective because the first already acquired, but a get after a ma'amar and a ma'amar after a get are effective because each serves a different function.

items.text: The Rabbis' view and comparison of bi'ah to ma'amar
items.text_en: The Rabbis' view and comparison of bi'ah to ma'amar
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Rabbis' position: they instituted a get and a ma'amar for each yevama. It then compares a forbidden bi'ah to ma'amar, showing that bi'ah is superior in some respects (e.g., it is effective after a ma'amar) but inferior in others (e.g., it does not acquire the entire remnant of a get).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the rabbis instituted a get and ma'amar for a yevama, and that a forbidden ביאה (consummation) after a ma'amar is stronger than a ma'amar in some ways but weaker in others.
The Gemara compares a forbidden bi'ah to ma'amar, showing that bi'ah is superior (effective after ma'amar) but inferior (does not acquire the entire remnant of a get).

items.text: Baraita illustrating the rule of get after get and ma'amar after ma'amar
items.text_en: Baraita illustrating the rule of get after get and ma'amar after ma'amar
items.desc_en: A baraita is presented detailing the case of two yevamot and one yavam: if he gave a get to each, Rabban Gamliel says he must perform chalitzah for the first and is prohibited to her relatives but permitted to the second's, while the Rabbis say he is prohibited to both and must perform chalitzah for one. The same applies to two yevamim and one yevama. A similar case is given for ma'amar after ma'amar.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the case of two yevamot and one yavam who gave a get to each, presenting Rabban Gamliel's ruling that he performs chalitzah for the first and is prohibited to her relatives but permitted to the second's.
The baraita presents the Sages' ruling that he is prohibited to relatives of both and must perform chalitzah for one, and applies the same to two yevamim and one yevama.

The baraita presents a parallel case for ma'amar after ma'amar: Rabban Gamliel rules he gives a get to the first and performs chalitzah, while the Sages require a get for both and chalitzah for one, applying the same to two yevamim and one yevama.

items.text: Challenge to Shmuel from the baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Shmuel from the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita says Rabban Gamliel requires chalitzah for the first yevama, which seems to contradict Shmuel's view that chalitzah for the one who received a get does not exempt her rival. Shmuel defends himself by explaining that his ruling applies only to one who holds there is zikah, but Rabban Gamliel holds there is no zikah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita's ruling that Rabban Gamliel requires chalitzah for the first yevama and permits the relatives of the second.
The Gemara asks whether this baraita refutes Shmuel's statement that chalitzah for the one who received a get does not exempt her rival.

Shmuel explains that his ruling applies only to one who holds there is a substantial levirate bond (יש זיקה), but Rabban Gamliel holds there is no such bond (אין זיקה), so the baraita does not contradict him.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbah bar Rav Huna from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbah bar Rav Huna from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Rabbis hold there is zikah (bond of levirate ties), and the mishnah's ruling about two yevamin and one yevamah seems to contradict Rabbah bar Rav Huna's statement that a flawed chalitzah must be repeated for all brothers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling that a flawed chalitzah must be repeated for all brothers, citing the mishnah's case of two yevamin and one yevamah which implies the Rabbis hold there is זיקה (bond of levirate ties).

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's defense
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's defense
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna responds that both Rabban Gamliel and the Rabbis hold there is no zikah, and their dispute is about the validity of a get after a get or a ma'amar after a ma'amar.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna responds that both Rabban Gamliel and the Rabbis hold there is no זיקה (bond of levirate ties), and their dispute is only about the validity of multiple acts of מַאֲמָר (declaration of intent) and גט (bill of divorce).

items.text: Question on Rabban Gamliel's ruling
items.text_en: Question on Rabban Gamliel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabban Gamliel requires a get for the first woman if he holds that there is no ma'amar after a ma'amar, and answers that it is a decree lest one come to marry the second woman.

sub.text: Gemara's question on Rabban Gamliel's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabban Gamliel's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabban Gamliel requires a גט (bill of divorce) for the first woman if he holds there is no מַאֲמָר after מַאֲמָר (declaration after declaration), and answers it is a decree lest one come to perform יבום (levirate marriage) with the second woman.
The Gemara answers that the get is a decree (גזירה) lest one come to perform yibbum with the second woman.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's list of Tannaim who hold ma'amar is a full acquisition
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's list of Tannaim who hold ma'amar is a full acquisition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabban Gamliel, Beit Shammai, Rabbi Shimon, Ben Azzai, and Rabbi Nechemiah all hold that ma'amar is a full acquisition, and begins with Rabban Gamliel's case.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan lists five Tannaim who hold that מַאֲמָר (declaration of intent) effects a full acquisition, beginning with Rabban Gamliel whose view was already discussed.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabban Gamliel's case
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabban Gamliel's case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabban Gamliel's position is the one already discussed (the case of ma'amar in two sisters).

items.text: Beit Shammai's position
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah where Beit Shammai rules that a ma'amar by a free brother creates a full acquisition, such that the wife of the second brother is forbidden as a sister-in-law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah where Beit Shammai rules that a מַאֲמָר (declaration) by a brother-in-law to a sister-in-law who is also his wife's sister causes the second sister to be forbidden as a sister-wife, showing they view מַאֲמָר as a full acquisition.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's position
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon argues that if the first intercourse (of a nine-year-old) is considered intercourse, then the second is not; if not, then neither is, showing he treats such intercourse like a ma'amar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon argues that if the first act of ביאה (intercourse) by a nine-year-old is considered a valid act, the second is not; if the first is not valid, the second is also not, showing he treats such ביאה (which the Rabbis equated to מַאֲמָר) as a full acquisition.

items.text: Ben Azzai and Rabbi Nechemiah's positions
items.text_en: Ben Azzai and Rabbi Nechemiah's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Ben Azzai who holds there is ma'amar after ma'amar in the case of two yevamin and one yevamah, and Rabbi Nechemiah who rules that a flawed act of intercourse or chalitzah leaves no subsequent possibility, showing they treat ma'amar as a full acquisition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Ben Azzai rules that there is מַאֲמָר after מַאֲמָר (declaration after declaration) in the case of two yevamin and one yevamah, but not in the case of two yevamot and one yavam, showing he views מַאֲמָר as a full acquisition.

The Gemara cites a mishnah where Rabbi Nechemya rules that whether at the beginning, middle, or end, a single act of ביאה (intercourse) or חליצה (removal of the shoe) leaves nothing after it, showing he treats even flawed ביאה (which the Rabbis equated to מַאֲמָר) as a full acquisition.

items.text: Beginning of the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Beginning of the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara starts to quote the mishnah's case: 'How so? He performed ma'amar...'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins citing the mishnah's description of how the case of two yevamin and one yevamah is handled.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's phrase and supporting Rav Huna
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's phrase and supporting Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'get after get' means 'get after the get' and 'ma'amar after ma'amar' as previously stated. It then considers whether the case of performing ma'amar and then having intercourse supports Rav Huna's view that the mitzvah of yibum is to betroth first and then have intercourse, concluding that the Mishnah merely teaches that this too is a valid fulfillment of the mitzvah.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on yibum and the lashes for improper betrothal
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on yibum and the lashes for improper betrothal
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the mitzvah of yibum is to betroth and then have intercourse, but if one had intercourse without ma'amar, he acquires her. The Gemara objects that a baraita teaches he is lashed, and resolves that it is lashes of rebellion rabbinically.

items.text: List of those lashed by Rav and the Nehardeans' qualification
items.text_en: List of those lashed by Rav and the Nehardeans' qualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists those whom Rav would lash: one who betroths through intercourse, one who betroths in the marketplace, one who betroths without prior matchmaking, one who nullifies a get, one who delivers a declaration about a get, one who treats rabbinic emissaries lightly, one who delays a ban for thirty days without coming to court, and a groom who lives in his father-in-law's house. The Nehardeans say Rav only lashes for betrothal through intercourse and without matchmaking, and some say even with matchmaking due to licentiousness.

items.text: The form of ma'amar and the yevamah's ketubah
items.text_en: The form of ma'amar and the yevamah's ketubah
items.desc_en: The Tanna describes how ma'amar is performed: with money or its equivalent. Abaye clarifies that the question about a 'shtar' refers to the yevamah's ketubah document, which is written with a condition that her ketubah is on her first husband's property, and if she has none from him, the Sages instituted it from the second husband so he will not find it easy to divorce her.

items.text: The status of a get that does not fully release the yevamah
items.text_en: The status of a get that does not fully release the yevamah
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah about a get given to a yevamah with the statement 'you are divorced from me but you are not permitted to any man' – whether it is effective because it is a rabbinic get, or whether we fear confusion with a regular get. Rabbah answers that we fear confusion. Rabba bar Chanan objects that if so, giving her any paper would disqualify her, but Rabbah distinguishes because here it disqualifies her from kehunah, as taught in a baraita about the 'scent of a get' that disqualifies from kehunah.

items.text: A get written before marriage
items.text_en: A get written before marriage
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama cites a ruling: if one tells a scribe to write a get for his betrothed, to divorce her when he marries her, it is a valid get because he has the power to divorce her.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question about a get for a yevamah
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question about a get for a yevamah
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a get given to a yevamah (without ma'amar) is effective, comparing her to an arusah or not. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a get given to a yevamah (without ma'amar) is effective, comparing her to an arusah or not.
The question remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Rav Chananyah's question and Rava's precedent
items.text_en: Rav Chananyah's question and Rava's precedent
items.desc_en: Rav Chananyah asks about a get written for zikah but not ma'amar, or vice versa. The Gemara suggests resolving from Rava's ruling that a get for ma'amar permits the tzarah, but notes Rava's certainty vs. Rav Chananyah's doubt, ending with teiku.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chananyah asks whether a get written for the zikah (yibbum bond) but not for ma'amar (formal betrothal), or vice versa, is valid, considering whether ma'amar is superimposed on zikah (making it a partial divorce) or each stands independently.

The Gemara suggests resolving from Rava's ruling that a get for ma'amar permits the tzarah (co-wife), but notes that Rava was certain about his case while Rav Chananyah's question remains unresolved, concluding with תֵּיקוּ (let it stand).

items.text: Chalitzah followed by ma'amar: R. Akiva vs. Sages
items.text_en: Chalitzah followed by ma'amar: R. Akiva vs. Sages
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav states that if one performed chalitzah and then ma'amar, only R. Akiva (who holds that kiddushin does not take effect on those liable for lasin) would invalidate it, while the Sages say there is something after chalitzah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav introduces the case of performing חליצה (chalitzah) followed by מאמר (ma'amar), attributing the invalidation to Rabbi Akiva's position that קידושין (betrothal) does not take effect on those liable for lashes.
The Sages counter that there is something (i.e., validity) after חליצה (chalitzah), meaning the subsequent מאמר (ma'amar) takes effect.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah and R. Ashi's resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah and R. Ashi's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's case (get then ma'amar requiring get and chalitzah) contradicts R. Akiva, since after a get ma'amar should not take effect. R. Ashi answers that a yevamah's get is rabbinic, and the verse is merely an asmakhta.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's case (get then ma'amar requiring get and chalitzah) contradicts Rabbi Akiva, since after a get ma'amar should not take effect.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Akiva derives from a verse that a yevamah who received a get is forbidden to the yavam forever, supporting that ma'amar cannot take effect after a get.
Rav Ashi resolves the objection by explaining that a yevamah's get is only rabbinic, and the verse cited by Rabbi Akiva is merely an אסמכתא (scriptural support).

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi's distinction regarding intent
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi's distinction regarding intent
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi who says that the dispute (about chalitzah then ma'amar) applies only according to R. Akiva, but the Sages say there is something after chalitzah. Rabbi himself distinguishes: if he betrothed her for marriage, it takes effect; if for yevamah, it does not.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports the previous discussion, quoting Rabbi who states that the dispute (about chalitzah then ma'amar) applies only according to Rabbi Akiva's view.

Rabbi explains that Rabbi Akiva treats the חלוצה (a woman who underwent chalitzah) as an ערווה (forbidden relative), while the Sages hold that there is something (i.e., a valid marriage) after chalitzah.
Rabbi himself distinguishes: if he betrothed her for marriage (לשם אישות), it takes effect; if for yevamah (לשם יבמות), it does not.

items.text: Another baraita: Chalitzah then kiddushin
items.text_en: Another baraita: Chalitzah then kiddushin
items.desc_en: Another baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi says if one betrothed her for marriage, she needs a get; if for yevamah, no get. The Sages say she always needs a get.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi distinguishes between betrothal for marriage (needs a get) and for yevamah (no get), while the Sages require a get in both cases.

items.text: Rav Yosef's analogy and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's analogy and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains Rabbi's view by comparing to one who clears property thinking it belongs to a convert (not acquiring). Abaye objects: there he does not intend to acquire, but here he does. Abaye offers a different analogy: one who clears property thinking it belongs to another convert (acquires).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains Rabbi's view by comparing the ma'amar after chalitzah to one who clears a convert's property thinking it is his own, who does not acquire.

Abaye objects that the analogy fails because there the clearer does not intend to acquire, but here the yavam intends to acquire, and offers a corrected analogy: one who clears property thinking it belongs to another convert, who does acquire.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: ma'amar rides on zikah
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: ma'amar rides on zikah
items.desc_en: Abaye explains the case: he said 'be betrothed to me by ma'amar yevamin'. Rabbi holds ma'amar rides on zikah, and chalitzah uproots zikah, so ma'amar fails. The Rabbis hold each stands alone, so ma'amar works.

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces the case where the yavam said 'be betrothed to me by ma'amar yevamin' (a levirate betrothal).
Abaye explains that Rabbi holds ma'amar rides on zikah, and chalitzah uproots zikah, so the ma'amar fails.

sub.text: Abaye's explanation of the Rabbis' position
sub.text_en: Abaye's explanation of the Rabbis' position
sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Rabbis hold ma'amar and zikah stand independently, so the ma'amar remains effective even after chalitzah.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation: 'by zikah' vs. 'by ma'amar'
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation: 'by zikah' vs. 'by ma'amar'
