items.desc_en: Rava argues that if he said 'by ma'amar yevamin', all agree it works. The dispute is when he said 'by zikat yevamin'. Rabbi holds that zikah is uprooted by chalitzah, so the betrothal fails.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that if the yavam said 'by ma'amar yevamin', all agree the betrothal is effective.
Rava explains that the dispute is when he said 'by zikat yevamin', and Rabbi holds that since zikah is uprooted by chalitzah, the betrothal fails.

items.text: Gemara's question on zikah and chalitzah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on zikah and chalitzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that chalitzah removes zikah, presenting two views: one holds that zikah exists and chalitzah removes it, while the other holds that zikah does not exist, as even if one said 'be betrothed to me through the zikah of a yavam,' it would be effective.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether zikah (the bond between yavam and yevamah) exists and chalitzah removes it, presenting two views: one holds that zikah exists and chalitzah removes it, while the other holds that zikah does not exist, as even if one said 'be betrothed to me through the zikah of a yavam,' it would be effective.

items.text: Rav Sherevya's explanation: dispute over invalid chalitzah
items.text_en: Rav Sherevya's explanation: dispute over invalid chalitzah
items.desc_en: Rav Sherevya explains that all agree that if one said 'be betrothed through zikah,' it is ineffective; the dispute is about invalid chalitzah: one holds it is effective to release the yevamah, the other holds it is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sherevya answers that the dispute is about a valid chalitzah, where all agree that zikah does not take effect, but the Mishnah's dispute is about an invalid chalitzah: one holds that an invalid chalitzah is effective to release the yevamah, while the other holds it is not.
Rav Sherevya explains that the dispute is specifically about whether invalid chalitzah (חליצה פסולה) releases the yevamah or not.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation: dispute over condition in chalitzah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation: dispute over condition in chalitzah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that all agree invalid chalitzah does not release; the dispute is whether a condition can be made in chalitzah: one holds conditions are valid, the other holds they are not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that all agree an invalid chalitzah does not release, but the dispute is about whether a condition can be applied to chalitzah: one holds that a condition can be applied, while the other holds it cannot.

items.text: Ravina's explanation: dispute over double condition
items.text_en: Ravina's explanation: dispute over double condition
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that all agree conditions are valid in chalitzah; the dispute is whether a double condition (תנאי כפול) is required: one holds it is required, the other holds it is not.

sub.desc_en: Ravina answers that all agree a condition can be applied to chalitzah, but the dispute is about whether a double condition (תנאי כפול) is required: one holds it is required, while the other holds it is not.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's order
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's order
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not also teach 'there is nothing after intercourse' (אין אחר ביאה כלום). Abaye and Rava answer that it does teach this, but the Tanna prefers to emphasize the release of the yevamah to the public.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not also teach the case of 'after intercourse there is nothing' (i.e., that intercourse after ma'amar or get is ineffective).

Abaye and Rava answer that the Tanna does teach 'after intercourse there is nothing,' but the Tanna of our Mishnah prioritizes teaching the release of the yevamah to the general public (התרת יבמה לשוק).
The Gemara explains that the Tanna of our Mishnah prioritizes teaching the release of the yevamah to the public over the rule about intercourse.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah's case of two yevamot
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah's case of two yevamot
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling on one yavam and two yevamot contradicts Ben Azzai, who holds that there is ma'amar after ma'amar with two yevamin and one yevamah but not with two yevamot and one yavam. It then attempts to support Shmuel's view that chalitzah to a ma'amar wife does not release her rival, but Rav Yosef objects that the Mishnah uses 'chalatz' (past tense) not 'choleitz' (present), indicating it is only after the fact.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling on one yavam and two yevamot contradicts Ben Azzai, who holds that there is ma'amar after ma'amar with two yevamin and one yevamah but not with two yevamot and one yavam.
The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah supports Shmuel's view that chalitzah to a ma'amar wife does not release her rival.
Rav Yosef objects that the Mishnah uses 'חָלַץ' (past tense) not 'חוֹלֵץ' (present), indicating it is only after the fact, not a ruling for לכתחילה.

items.text: Support for Rabbah bar Rav Huna on invalid chalitzah
items.text_en: Support for Rabbah bar Rav Huna on invalid chalitzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's case of 'get to this one and get to that one' supports Rabbah bar Rav Huna's view that invalid chalitzah requires repeating with all brothers, but clarifies that 'need' means they need it in general (not that it is required).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah supports Rabbah bar Rav Huna, who said that an invalid chalitzah requires repeating with all the brothers, and explains that 'צְרִיכוֹת' means they are generally required.

items.text: Support for Shmuel and objection to Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Support for Shmuel and objection to Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Shmuel from the Mishnah's case of 'get to this one and chalitzah to that one,' and suggests it is a refutation of Rav Yosef, but again notes that the Mishnah uses 'chalatz' (past tense), indicating it is only after the fact.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah supports Shmuel and constitutes a refutation of Rav Yosef, but then notes that the Mishnah uses 'חָלַץ' (he performed chalitzah) rather than 'חוֹלֵץ' (he performs chalitzah), indicating an action already done.
The Gemara suggests that this Mishnah is also a refutation of Rav Yosef's position.
The Gemara rejects the support and refutation, noting that the Mishnah uses the past tense 'חָלַץ' (he performed chalitzah), indicating it is only after the fact (בדיעבד).

items.text: Repeated question on 'nothing after intercourse'
items.text_en: Repeated question on 'nothing after intercourse'
items.desc_en: The Gemara again asks why the Mishnah does not teach 'there is nothing after intercourse' in the case of 'chalatz and chalatz' etc. Abaye and Rava give the same answer: it is taught, but the Tanna prefers to emphasize the release of the yevamah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not also teach the case of 'after intercourse there is nothing' (i.e., that intercourse after chalitzah or ma'amar is ineffective).

Abaye and Rava answer that the Tanna does teach 'after intercourse there is nothing,' but the Tanna of our Mishnah prioritizes teaching the release of the yevamah to the general public (התרת יבמה לשוק).
The Gemara explains that the Tanna of our Mishnah prioritizes teaching the release of the yevamah to the public market over teaching the rule about intercourse.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the Mishnah's necessity
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the Mishnah's necessity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to teach the case of one yavam and two yevamot. For Rabbi Yochanan, who holds the entire household is under a negative commandment, it teaches that betrothal does not take effect for those liable for negative commandments. For Reish Lakish, who holds it is under karet, it teaches that betrothal does not take effect for those liable for karet. Reish Lakish counters that the same question applies to the Mishnah's case of 'ba'al and made ma'amar,' which teaches that betrothal does not take effect for a married woman. The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's structure is simply due to the Tanna's pattern of teaching cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to teach the case of one yavam and two yevamot, noting that for Rabbi Yochanan, who holds the entire household is under a negative commandment (לאו), it teaches that betrothal does not take effect for those liable for negative commandments.

The Gemara continues the question, noting that for Reish Lakish, who holds the entire household is under karet (כרת), the Mishnah teaches that betrothal does not take effect for those liable for karet.
Reish Lakish counters that the same question applies to the Mishnah's case of 'ba'al and made ma'amar,' which teaches that betrothal does not take effect for a married woman.

The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's structure is simply due to the Tanna's pattern of teaching cases, teaching the case of two yevamot and one yavam because it taught the case of one yavam and one yevamah, and teaching the case of two yevamim and one yevamah because it taught the case of two yevamot and one yavam.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's cases
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah includes the case of 'chalatz and gave a get' when it seems unnecessary, and similarly for 'ba'al and made ma'amar'. It resolves that these are included for symmetry with the other cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah includes the case of 'חָלַץ וְנָתַן גֵּט' (chalatz and gave a get) when the case of 'חָלַץ וְעָשָׂה מַאֲמָר' (chalatz and made ma'amar) already teaches the needed principle.
The Gemara raises a parallel objection: by the same logic, the case of 'בָּעַל וְעָשָׂה מַאֲמָר' (ba'al and made ma'amar) in the latter clause seems unnecessary.

The Gemara resolves that the extra cases are included for symmetry: since the Mishnah listed 'חָלַץ וְעָשָׂה מַאֲמָר', it also listed 'בָּעַל וְעָשָׂה מַאֲמָר', and since it wanted to list 'בָּעַל וְנָתַן גֵּט', it also listed 'חָלַץ וְנָתַן גֵּט'.

items.text: Dispute about the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Dispute about the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling that chalitzah after bi'ah has no effect is not like the Tanna who holds that both bi'ah and chalitzah at the beginning have no effect, but in the middle or end they do. Three opinions are presented: Tanna Kamma distinguishes between bi'ah and chalitzah, Rabbi Nechemya holds no decree is needed, and Abba Yosef ben Yochanan agrees with the Sages who decree for bi'ah and extends the decree to chalitzah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara observes that the Mishnah's ruling does not align with the Tanna cited in the baraita.

sub.text: Baraita citation: Abba Yosef ben Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Baraita citation: Abba Yosef ben Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: The baraita states that both bi'ah and chalitzah at the beginning have no effect, but in the middle or end they do.

The Gemara explains the three opinions: Tanna Kamma distinguishes between bi'ah and chalitzah regarding the decree, Rabbi Nechemya holds no decree is needed for bi'ah either, and Abba Yosef ben Yochanan agrees with the Sages who decree for bi'ah and extends the decree to chalitzah.

items.text: Mishnah: The one who has bi'ah with his yevamah
items.text_en: Mishnah: The one who has bi'ah with his yevamah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who has bi'ah with his yevamah, whether intentionally or unintentionally, under duress or willingly, even if one is mistaken and the other intentional, acquires her. This applies to all cases of bi'ah with a yevamah and similarly to bi'ah with forbidden relatives, disqualifying her.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the heading 'We return to you, Rabban Gamliel'.

The Mishnah states that one who has bi'ah with his yevamah, whether unwittingly, intentionally, under duress, or willingly, even if one is mistaken and the other intentional, acquires her, and does not distinguish between types of bi'ah.
The Mishnah extends the same principle to one who has bi'ah with any forbidden relative or unfit woman, disqualifying her, without distinguishing between types of bi'ah.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of 'even'
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of 'even'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'even' in the Mishnah includes, and explains that it is not necessary to state cases where one intends a mitzvah, but even when both do not intend a mitzvah, he acquires. Rabbi Chiya adds that even if both are mistaken, both intentional, or both under duress, the same applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'אפילו (even)' in the Mishnah is meant to include.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is stated in the style of 'needless to say', and even when both do not intend a mitzvah, the yavam acquires the yevama.
רבי חייא (Rabbi Chiya) teaches a baraita that even if both are unwitting, both intentional, or both coerced, the yavam acquires the yevama through intercourse.

items.text: Clarification of 'ones' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Clarification of 'ones' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how 'ones' (duress) applies in the Mishnah, suggesting it cannot be when Gentiles force him, as Rava said there is no duress for forbidden relations. Instead, it refers to a case where he is asleep, but then cites Rav Yehudah's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the case of duress (אונס) in the Mishnah is possible, since Rava ruled that there is no duress for forbidden relations.
Rava's principle is cited: there is no duress for forbidden relations because arousal requires intent.
The Gemara proposes that the case of duress in the Mishnah refers to a sleeping man, but then cites Rav Yehudah's statement that challenges this.

items.text: Clarifying the case of 'sleeping' and 'forced' yibbum
items.text_en: Clarifying the case of 'sleeping' and 'forced' yibbum
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that a sleeping man does not acquire his yevamah. It distinguishes between a case where he fell and was accidentally wedged (which does not effect acquisition) and a case where he intended for his wife but was seized by his yevamah or by gentiles who forced them together (which does effect acquisition, as both are considered forced).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a sleeping man does not acquire his yevamah, citing Rabbah's principle that one who falls from a roof and becomes wedged is liable for damages but does not acquire his yevamah.

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by distinguishing the Mishnah's case: it refers to a man who intended for his wife but was seized by his yevamah and had relations with her, where both are considered forced (אנוסים).

The school of Rabbi Chiyya provides a parallel example: a man who intended for his wife but was seized by gentiles who forced them together, and he had relations with her, where both are considered forced.

items.text: Source that yibbum is effective even unintentionally or under duress
items.text_en: Source that yibbum is effective even unintentionally or under duress
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraisa that derives from the verse 'yevamah yavo aleha' that yibbum is a mitzvah, and alternatively that it applies whether the act is unintentional, intentional, forced, or willing. The Gemara explains that the mitzvah aspect is derived from another verse, leaving this verse to teach about all modes of intercourse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the rule that yibbum is effective even unintentionally or under duress.
A baraita derives from the verse 'יְבָמָהּ יָבֹא עָלֶיהָ' that the act of yibbum is a מצוה (commandment).
The same baraita alternatively derives from the verse that yibbum applies whether the act was unwitting or intentional, coerced or willing.
The Gemara objects that the verse was already used to derive that yibbum is a מצוה (commandment), so how can it also teach the other rule?
The Gemara resolves that the מצוה (commandment) aspect is derived from the verse 'וְאִם לֹא יַחְפּוֹץ הָאִישׁ', leaving the other verse to teach that yibbum applies in all modes.

items.text: Another baraisa: yibbum must be 'in its natural way' and other derivations
items.text_en: Another baraisa: yibbum must be 'in its natural way' and other derivations
items.desc_en: A second baraisa expounds the same verse to teach that yibbum must be 'in its natural way' (vaginal intercourse), that 'ul'kachah' teaches unnatural intercourse is invalid, that 'veyibem' teaches that intercourse alone completes acquisition (not money or document), and that 'veyibmah' teaches it can be against her will. The Gemara again notes that the 'natural way' is derived from another verse, so this verse teaches about all modes of intercourse.

sub.desc_en: A second baraita expounds 'יְבָמָהּ יָבֹא עָלֶיהָ' (her brother-in-law will have intercourse with her) to teach that yibbum must be performed in its natural way, i.e., vaginal intercourse.
The baraita derives from 'וּלְקָחָהּ' (and take her) that even atypical, i.e., anal, intercourse effects the levirate acquisition.
The baraita derives from 'וְיִבֵּם' (and consummate the levirate marriage) that sexual intercourse alone completes the acquisition, unlike money or a marriage document.
The baraita derives from 'וְיִבְּמָהּ' (and consummate the levirate marriage with her) that the acquisition is effective even if performed against her will.
Alternatively, the baraita expounds the same verse to teach that levirate marriage is effected whether the parties acted unwittingly or intentionally, whether due to coercion or willingly.
The Gemara challenges: but you already derived from this verse that yibbum must be performed in its natural way, so how can the same verse also teach the other halakhot?

The Gemara answers that the requirement of natural intercourse is derived from 'לְהָקִים לְאָחִיו שֵׁם' (to establish a name for his brother), so the verse 'יְבָמָהּ יָבֹא עָלֶיהָ' teaches that levirate marriage is effected regardless of intent or coercion.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's statement about a sleeping man and the resolution with the baraisa
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's statement about a sleeping man and the resolution with the baraisa
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that a sleeping man does not acquire his yevamah because the verse requires intention for the act of intercourse. The Gemara challenges this with a baraisa that explicitly includes both awake and sleeping. The resolution is that the baraisa refers to a drowsy state (mitnamen), which is defined by Rav Ashi as half-asleep, half-awake.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that a sleeping man does not acquire his yevamah because the verse requires intention for the act of intercourse.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraisa that explicitly includes both awake and sleeping cases, seemingly contradicting Rav Yehuda.
The Gemara first suggests that the baraisa refers to the woman (awake or asleep), not the man.
The Gemara objects again, citing another baraisa that explicitly includes both the man awake or asleep and the woman awake or asleep.
The Gemara resolves that the baraisa refers to a drowsy state (mitnamen), defined by Rav Ashi as half-asleep, half-awake, thus reconciling the contradiction.

items.text: Rabbah's and Rava's rulings on accidental and misdirected intercourse
items.text_en: Rabbah's and Rava's rulings on accidental and misdirected intercourse
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that one who falls from a roof and becomes wedged is liable for four types of damages (but not shame) but does not acquire his yevamah. Rava adds that if one intended to strike the wall but struck his yevamah, he does not acquire; but if he intended to strike an animal and struck his yevamah, he does acquire because he had general intent for intercourse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that one who falls from a roof and becomes wedged is liable for four types of damages (nezek, tza'ar, shevet, ripui) but not for shame (boshet), and does not acquire his yevamah.

Rava adds that if one intended to strike the wall but struck his yevamah, he does not acquire; but if he intended to strike an animal and struck his yevamah, he does acquire because he had general intent for intercourse.

items.text: Deriving ha'ara'ah (partial penetration) for all forbidden relations
items.text_en: Deriving ha'ara'ah (partial penetration) for all forbidden relations
items.desc_en: Ulla states that ha'ara'ah is a valid act of intercourse from the Torah, derived from the verse regarding a niddah. The Gemara then attempts to extend this to other forbidden relations (e.g., wife of a brother, aunt, etc.) through various analogies, but each is refuted. Ultimately, the Gemara considers combining two sources, but Rav Acha bar Rav Ika objects that niddah and wife of a brother have no permit during the lifetime of the one who forbids them, unlike a married woman who may be permitted after divorce. Rav Acha from Difti counters that niddah and wife of a brother also have no permit after the fact, but the Gemara cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that ha'ara'ah (partial penetration) is derived from the Torah from the verse regarding a niddah.
The Gemara asks: we found niddah, but from where do we derive ha'ara'ah for other forbidden relations?
The Gemara objects that one cannot learn from niddah because niddah has the unique stringency of imparting ritual impurity to her partner.
The Gemara proposes deriving ha'ara'ah from the wife of a brother, using the analogy 'niddah hi' (she is like a niddah).
The Gemara objects that the wife of a brother is unique because the brother could potentially marry many women, making the analogy flawed.
The Gemara proposes deriving ha'ara'ah from the aunt (sister of father or mother), using the verse that includes the term 'he'erah'.
The Gemara objects that the aunt is unique because her prohibition is inherent (not dependent on marriage), unlike a married woman.
The Gemara attempts to derive ha'ara'ah from two sources together: wife of a brother and aunt, but objects that both are forbidden due to familial relation (שאר).
The Gemara attempts to derive from niddah and aunt, but objects that both have inherent prohibition.
The Gemara finally attempts to derive from niddah and wife of a brother, asking what objection could be raised.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika objects that niddah and wife of a brother have no permit during the lifetime of the one who forbids them, unlike a married woman who may be permitted through divorce.
Rav Acha from Difti counters that niddah and wife of a brother also have no permit after the fact, but the Gemara cuts off mid-sentence.

items.text: Rejection of the previous comparison
items.text_en: Rejection of the previous comparison
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous attempt to derive the law of ha'ara'ah for all arayot from niddah and yevamah, because those have a unique leniency: their prohibitions are not lifted by the same person who forbids them. The Gemara then proposes a new comparison to eshet ish, whose prohibitor is also her permitter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous comparison to niddah and yevamah because their prohibitions are not lifted by the same person who forbids them, and proposes a new comparison to eshet ish, whose prohibitor is also her permitter.

items.text: Rabbi Yona's derivation from a verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Yona's derivation from a verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yona (or Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua) cites a verse that equates all arayot to niddah, teaching that just as niddah is prohibited by ha'ara'ah, so too are all arayot.

sub.text: Rabbi Yona (or Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yona (or Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yona (or Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua) cites a verse that equates all arayot to niddah, teaching that just as niddah is prohibited by ha'ara'ah, so too are all arayot.

items.text: The purpose of the word 'niddah' regarding yevamah
items.text_en: The purpose of the word 'niddah' regarding yevamah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah writes 'niddah' specifically regarding eshet ach (yevamah). It first suggests it teaches that yevamah is forbidden during her husband's lifetime, but the Gemara objects that this could be derived logically. The verse is then explained to teach that just as niddah, though permitted later, is punishable by karet during her prohibition, so too is eshet ach punishable by karet during her husband's lifetime.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah writes the word 'niddah' specifically regarding eshet ach (yevamah), and suggests it hints that yevamah is forbidden during her husband's lifetime.
The Gemara objects that the prohibition during the husband's lifetime is logical: since the Torah permits her after the husband's death, it implies she is forbidden during his lifetime.

The Gemara rejects the logical inference, suggesting that perhaps after the husband's death it is a מצוה (commandment) but during his lifetime it is merely permitted, or that the inference from a positive commandment yields only a positive commandment, not a prohibition punishable by karet.

The Gemara resolves that the verse teaches a comparison to niddah: just as niddah, though permitted later, is punishable by karet during her prohibition, so too eshet ach is punishable by karet during her husband's lifetime.

items.text: The purpose of 'ha'ara'ah' regarding a paternal and maternal aunt
items.text_en: The purpose of 'ha'ara'ah' regarding a paternal and maternal aunt
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah writes 'ha'ara'ah' specifically regarding achot av and achot em, since they are already included in the general derivation. It answers that this teaches the law of ha'ara'ah with an animal, as asked by Ravina from Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah writes 'ha'ara'ah' specifically regarding a paternal aunt and a maternal aunt, since they are already included in the general derivation.
Ravina asks Rava about the status of one who performs ha'ara'ah with a male, but the Gemara notes that the verse already specifies 'the lyings of a woman' for a male.
Rava answers that the superfluous 'ha'ara'ah' regarding a paternal and maternal aunt teaches the law of ha'ara'ah with an animal, since it is not needed for the aunts themselves.

items.text: Why the law of bestiality is written among karet punishments
items.text_en: Why the law of bestiality is written among karet punishments
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the law of ha'ara'ah with an animal is written among the karet punishments, since bestiality is a capital crime. It answers that since the entire verse comes for exposition, it also includes this matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the law of ha'ara'ah with an animal is written among the karet punishments, since bestiality is a capital crime and should be written among the capital punishments.
The Gemara answers that since the entire verse comes for exposition, it also includes this matter of ha'ara'ah with an animal for exposition.

items.text: Exposition: 'achot av' includes both paternal and maternal half-sisters
items.text_en: Exposition: 'achot av' includes both paternal and maternal half-sisters
items.desc_en: The Gemara expounds the verse 'achot avicha' to include both a paternal and maternal half-sister, using a logical argument and a concluding verse. The same is said for 'achot imecha'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what exposition is derived from the extra verse, and cites a baraita that 'achot avicha' includes both a paternal and maternal half-sister.

items.text: Why both 'achot av' and 'achot em' are written
items.text_en: Why both 'achot av' and 'achot em' are written
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains that both verses are necessary: if only 'achot av' were written, one might think the law applies only there because she has a paternal lineage (חייס), but not to 'achot em'; conversely, if only 'achot em' were written, one might think it applies only there because she is a definite relative, but not to 'achot av'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why both 'achot av' and 'achot em' are written in the Torah.
Rabbi Avahu states that both verses are necessary.
If only 'achot av' were written, one might think the law applies only there because she has a paternal lineage (חייס), but not to 'achot em'.
If only 'achot em' were written, one might think the law applies only there because she is a definite relative (ודאית), but not to 'achot av'.
Rabbi Avahu concludes that both verses are indeed necessary.

items.text: Source that 'dodo' (paternal uncle) is only from the father's side
items.text_en: Source that 'dodo' (paternal uncle) is only from the father's side
items.desc_en: Rava derives from a verbal analogy (gezeirah shavah) between the word 'dodo' here and in the context of redemption, that a paternal uncle is only from the father's side, not the mother's. The source for that is the verse 'mimishpachto yiga'alenu', which defines family as the father's family.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where does the Tanna derive that 'dodato' (paternal aunt) refers only to the father's side and not the mother's?
Rava derives via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'דודו' (his uncle) used in the redemption context that 'dodo' refers only to the father's side.
The Gemara explains the source for the redemption context: the verse 'ממשפחתו יגאלנו' teaches that only the father's family is called 'משפחה' (family), not the mother's.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of marrying sisters after a wife's death
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of marrying sisters after a wife's death
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a man married sisters in sequence after each wife's death, specifying which marriages are permitted and which are forbidden, and which wives exempt their rivals from yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces a case where a man marries sisters in sequence after each wife's death, listing the first four marriages.
The Mishnah rules that the first, third, and fifth wives are permitted and exempt their rivals, while the second and fourth are forbidden and do not exempt their rivals.
The Mishnah adds that if he had relations with the second wife after the first's death, the second and fourth become permitted and exempt their rivals, while the third and fifth become forbidden.

items.text: Derivation that a wife's sister is forbidden from both father and mother
items.text_en: Derivation that a wife's sister is forbidden from both father and mother
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a wife's sister is forbidden whether from the father or mother, derived from one's own sister. It asks why not derive from the aunt (דודתו) who is only from the father, and answers that it is more logical to derive relatives of oneself from relatives of oneself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a wife's sister is forbidden whether from the father or mother, derived from one's own sister.

items.text: Alternative derivations and resolution for sister-in-law
items.text_en: Alternative derivations and resolution for sister-in-law
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers deriving from the aunt (דודתו) because it involves kiddushin, but then rejects that in favor of deriving from the sister-in-law (אשת אח), which involves both kiddushin and relatives of oneself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes deriving the law of the sister-in-law from the aunt (דודתו), which would limit the prohibition to the father's side only.
The Gemara answers that it is more logical to derive from the sister (אחותו), since both involve relatives of oneself (קרובי עצמו).
The Gemara objects that deriving from the aunt (דודתו) is more appropriate because both involve a relationship established through kiddushin (קידושין).
The Gemara resolves that the derivation is from the sister-in-law (אשת אח), which shares both characteristics: it involves kiddushin and relatives of oneself.

items.text: Derivation that sister-in-law is forbidden from both father and mother
items.text_en: Derivation that sister-in-law is forbidden from both father and mother
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraitha that derives from the verse 'ערוות אשת אחיך לא תגלה' that it applies whether from the father or mother, using a logical comparison to one's own sister and rejecting the comparison to the aunt. The verse 'ערוות אחיך היא' concludes the derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive the prohibition of a sister-in-law (אשת אח) itself?
A baraita is cited: The verse 'ערוות אשת אחיך לא תגלה' includes both a paternal and maternal brother's wife.
The Gemara raises an objection: Perhaps the verse only applies to a paternal brother, but a logical comparison to one's sister suggests it includes both.
Alternatively, one might compare to the aunt (דודתו), which only applies to a paternal brother, limiting the prohibition.
The verse concludes with 'ערוות אחיך היא', teaching that the prohibition applies whether the brother is from the father or the mother.

items.text: Clarifying the need for multiple verses regarding sister-in-law
items.text_en: Clarifying the need for multiple verses regarding sister-in-law
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why two verses are needed for sister-in-law from the father, considering cases of having children or not. It explores various possibilities and concludes that the additional verse 'ערוות אחיו גילה' is necessary to teach that the prohibition applies even after the brother's death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that both verses might refer to a sister-in-law from the father, one for when she has children during her husband's lifetime and one for when she has none, but rejects this because the latter case is already derived from Rav Huna's ruling.
The Gemara suggests another possibility: both verses refer to a sister-in-law from the father, one for children during the husband's lifetime and one for children after his death.
The Gemara rejects this, arguing that a verse for children after death is unnecessary because the Torah's rule that a childless woman is permitted implies that a woman with children is forbidden.

The Gemara objects that the inference is not straightforward, suggesting alternative interpretations: the childless woman might be forbidden to all but permitted to the yavam, or the mitzvah might be optional.

The Gemara raises another objection: perhaps the childless woman is permitted and the one with children is forbidden, but the prohibition derived from a positive commandment is merely a positive commandment.

The Gemara concludes that the additional verse 'ערוות אחיו גילה' (he uncovered his brother's nakedness) is necessary to teach that the prohibition applies even after the brother's death, resolving the need for two verses.

items.text: Sister-in-law from the mother remains forbidden after death
items.text_en: Sister-in-law from the mother remains forbidden after death
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers that sister-in-law from the mother might be permitted after the brother's death like from the father, but the verse 'היא' teaches that she remains in her prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a brother's wife from the mother is permitted after the husband's death like from the father.
The Gemara answers that the verse says 'הִיא' (she) to indicate she remains in her original state.

items.text: Purpose of karet for one's sister
items.text_en: Purpose of karet for one's sister
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah specified karet for one's sister, and answers according to Rabbi Yochanan that it teaches liability for each act in one lapse of awareness, and according to Rabbi Yitzchak that it teaches that the punishment is karet rather than lashes. The division between multiple women is derived from the verse 'ואל אשה בנדת טומאתה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah specified karet (excision) for the prohibition of one's sister.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the karet clause teaches liability for each act even within a single lapse of awareness.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the karet clause teaches that the punishment is karet rather than lashes.
The Gemara asks from where the division between multiple women is derived.
The Gemara answers that the division is derived from the verse 'ואל אשה בנדת טומאתה' (and to a woman in her menstrual impurity), teaching liability for each woman.

items.text: Purpose of 'ערירים יהיו' for the aunt
items.text_en: Purpose of 'ערירים יהיו' for the aunt
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the two expressions 'ערירים יהיו' and 'ערירים ימותו' are both necessary: one teaches that the punishment applies from the time of the sin onward, and the other that it applies even after the sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote the phrase 'ערירים יהיו' (they shall be childless) specifically regarding the aunt.

Rabbah resolves the apparent contradiction between the two phrases 'ערירים יהיו' and 'ערירים ימותו' by explaining that one applies to one who has children (they will bury them) and the other to one who has no children (he will remain childless).

The Gemara explains that both phrases are necessary: 'ערירים יהיו' teaches that the punishment applies from the time of the sin onward, and 'ערירים ימותו' teaches that it applies even after the sin, and each alone would have been insufficient.

items.text: Source for העראה in prohibitions of negative commandments and positive commandments
items.text_en: Source for העראה in prohibitions of negative commandments and positive commandments
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source that העראה (partial intercourse) is prohibited for negative commandments. It derives from the case of the designated maidservant (שפחה חרופה) that העראה is considered a full act for negative commandments. Rav Ashi argues that if not, the verse would be superfluous. For negative commandments of priests, it is derived via a verbal analogy of 'קיחה'. The Gemara then asks about positive commandments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that העראה (partial intercourse) is a prohibited act for negative commandments (חייבי לאוין)?

The Gemara answers: it is derived from the fact that the Torah specified 'שִׁכְבַת זֶרַע' (emission of seed) regarding the designated maidservant (שפחה חרופה), implying that for other negative commandments, העראה (partial intercourse) suffices.

The Gemara objects: on the contrary, from the fact that the Torah revealed העראה (partial intercourse) regarding חייבי כריתות (those liable to excision), it implies that for negative commandments, full intercourse (גמר ביאה) is required.

Rav Ashi rejects the objection: if so, the verse regarding the designated maidservant (שפחה חרופה) would be superfluous, proving that for negative commandments, העראה (partial intercourse) is the standard.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that העראה (partial intercourse) is prohibited for negative commandments specific to priests (חייבי לאוין דכהונה)?
The Gemara answers: it is derived via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of the word 'קיחה' (taking) from the case of the designated maidservant.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that העראה (partial intercourse) is prohibited for positive commandments (חייבי עשה)?

items.text: Derivation of forbidden relations via גזירה שוה
items.text_en: Derivation of forbidden relations via גזירה שוה
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that a יבמה is forbidden to the public through a verbal analogy of 'ביאה' from a shifchah charufah, and that a married woman is forbidden to her husband through a verbal analogy of 'קיחה' from betrothal.

items.text: Rava's question on the need for multiple 'שכבת זרע' verses
items.text_en: Rava's question on the need for multiple 'שכבת זרע' verses
items.desc_en: Rava asks why the Torah writes 'שכבת זרע' in three places: shifchah charufah, eshet ish, and sotah. He explains that for eshet ish it excludes a dead person (or a dead woman), and for shifchah charufah it is as previously stated.

items.text: Debate on the meaning of 'דבר אחר' in sotah
items.text_en: Debate on the meaning of 'דבר אחר' in sotah
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates what 'דבר אחר' excludes in the sotah verse. Rav Sheishes says it excludes a case where the husband warned her in an unnatural way, but Rava objects citing 'משכבי אשה'. Rava then suggests it excludes warning via limbs, but Abaye objects that the Torah forbids licentiousness. Abaye suggests it excludes a kiss, but this is challenged. Finally, the Gemara concludes that Rava's view is correct but needs to be stated to counter a possible assumption.

items.text: Shmuel's definition of העראה as a kiss
items.text_en: Shmuel's definition of העראה as a kiss
items.desc_en: Shmuel defines העראה as a kiss, comparing it to placing a finger on the mouth where the flesh is pressed.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's first tradition: גמר ביאה is insertion of the corona
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's first tradition: גמר ביאה is insertion of the corona
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah reports that Rabbi Yochanan says גמר ביאה in the context of a shifchah charufah is insertion of the corona. Rav Sheishes challenges with a baraita about 'שכבת זרע' being only for completion, and the Gemara resolves that completion refers to the corona.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's second tradition and reconciliation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's second tradition and reconciliation
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yochanan says העראה is insertion of the corona, contradicting Rabba bar bar Chanah. The Gemara reconciles that from a kiss to insertion of the corona is all called העראה, so there is no dispute with Shmuel.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's final tradition distinguishing העראה from גמר ביאה
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's final tradition distinguishing העראה from גמר ביאה
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehudah reports that Rabbi Yochanan says העראה is insertion of the corona, while גמר ביאה is actual completion.

items.text: Clarifying the baraita: does 'and so' include all cases?
items.text_en: Clarifying the baraita: does 'and so' include all cases?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita that says 'and so' regarding a raped woman, asking whether it means that whether the act was accidental, intentional, or forced, she is disqualified from kehuna.

items.text: Rejecting the initial interpretation and offering alternatives
items.text_en: Rejecting the initial interpretation and offering alternatives
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that 'and so' refers to all cases, and instead suggests it refers to 'העראה' (initial contact) in the context of forbidden relations, then to unnatural intercourse, and finally to unnatural intercourse with those liable for negative commandments.

items.text: Rava's statement: a kohen's raped wife is liable for 'zonah'
items.text_en: Rava's statement: a kohen's raped wife is liable for 'zonah'
items.desc_en: Rava states that a kohen who has relations with his raped wife is liable for the prohibition of 'zonah', but the Gemara clarifies that he also means she is liable for 'tum'ah'.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's objection from the verse 'and she was not seized'
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's objection from the verse 'and she was not seized'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects by citing a verse that implies a raped woman is permitted, but a kohen's wife is forbidden even if seized, and notes that this is a positive commandment derived from a positive commandment.

items.text: Rabbah's resolution: the verse distinguishes Israelite from kohen's wife
items.text_en: Rabbah's resolution: the verse distinguishes Israelite from kohen's wife
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the verse 'and she was not seized' applies only to an Israelite woman, implying that a kohen's wife remains forbidden even if seized, as she was already in the category of 'zonah'.

items.text: Alternative version: Rabbah says the kohen is liable for 'tum'ah' not 'zonah'
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rabbah says the kohen is liable for 'tum'ah' not 'zonah'
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rabbah says a kohen is liable for 'tum'ah' but not 'zonah' in the case of rape, and Rabbi Zeira's objection is answered by Rava who explains that the verse 'after she is defiled' includes all, and the exception for the Israelite woman shows the kohen's wife remains forbidden.

items.text: Mishnah: widows and divorcees married to priests and their terumah status
items.text_en: Mishnah: widows and divorcees married to priests and their terumah status
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a widow married to a High Priest, or a divorcee or chalutzah to a regular priest, from betrothal may not eat terumah; Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon permit it. If widowed or divorced after marriage, they are disqualified; from betrothal they are fit.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Meir's kal vachomer and the dispute with Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Meir's kal vachomer and the dispute with Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir argues by kal vachomer that betrothal through transgression cannot permit terumah, but the Sages counter that a regular betrothal has no alternative place to eat, while a transgressive betrothal does. Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya applies this dispute to a wounded priest who betroths an Israelite woman.

items.text: Rejection of the initial proof from Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rejection of the initial proof from Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the attempted proof that a פצוע דכא כהן may feed his wife terumah because Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's ruling there applies only when he can feed her elsewhere, which is not the case here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the attempted proof by distinguishing the case of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon, where the husband can feed her elsewhere, from the present case where he cannot.

items.text: Rejection of the possibility of feeding her through a בת גרים
items.text_en: Rejection of the possibility of feeding her through a בת גרים
items.desc_en: The Gemara dismisses the suggestion that he could feed her through a בת גרים, noting that Rabbi Yochanan asked this very question of Rabbi Oshaya and received no answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the suggestion that he could feed her through a בת גרים (daughter of converts), noting that Rabbi Yochanan asked this question of Rabbi Oshaya and received no answer.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's explanations for why she eats
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's explanations for why she eats
items.desc_en: Abaye says she eats because he can feed her without her knowledge; Rava says because he can feed her through his Canaanite slaves. Each explains why the other's reasoning is rejected, with a further debate about whether prior eating matters.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Abaye says she eats because he can feed her without her knowledge.
Rava says she eats because he can feed her through his Canaanite slaves.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of Abaye's rejection of Rava
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Abaye's rejection of Rava
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that Abaye rejects Rava's reasoning because one cannot derive the acquisition of a wife (קִנְיָן דְּאִישׁוּת) from the acquisition of slaves (קִנְיָן דַּעֲבָדִים).

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of Rava's rejection of Abaye
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rava's rejection of Abaye
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that Rava rejects Abaye's reasoning because there the woman already ate, unlike here where the acquisition has not lapsed; Abaye counters that the fact of prior eating is not a decisive distinction, as a bat Yisrael who married a kohen and then died would also eat, but Rava distinguishes because there the acquisition lapsed.

items.text: The original inquiry of Rabbi Yochanan from Rabbi Oshaya
items.text_en: The original inquiry of Rabbi Yochanan from Rabbi Oshaya
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Yochanan asked Rabbi Oshaya whether a פצוע דכא כהן who married a בת גרים may feed her terumah. Rabbi Oshaya was silent, but later answered a different question from Resh Lakish, leading Rabbi Yehuda Nesia to question his silence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Yochanan asked Rabbi Oshaya whether a פצוע דכא כהן who married a בת גרים may feed her terumah; Rabbi Oshaya was silent, but later answered a different question from Resh Lakish, leading Rabbi Yehuda Nesia to question his silence.

items.text: Analysis of the question according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Analysis of the question according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the question is irrelevant according to Rabbi Yehuda (she never eats) and Rabbi Yosei (she always eats), so it must be according to a third Tanna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks according to which Tanna the question applies, noting that for Rabbi Yehuda the woman never eats terumah.

The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, whether the woman is within her husband's sanctity or not, she does not eat: if within, she is like a daughter of a חלל (disqualified priest); if not, the congregation of converts is called a congregation, disqualifying her.

The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yosei, the woman always eats terumah: if within her husband's sanctity, her daughter is fit for the priesthood; if not, the congregation of converts is not called a congregation.

items.text: The question according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.text_en: The question according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov as the relevant Tanna, and frames the question: does her fitness for priesthood increase (allowing her to eat) or does her sanctity increase (preventing her from eating)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov as the relevant Tanna, citing his Mishnah that a woman who is a daughter of converts may not marry into the priesthood unless her mother is from Israel.

The Gemara frames the question: does her fitness for priesthood (כַּשְׁרוּת) increase, allowing her to eat תרומה (priestly portion), or does her sanctity (קְדוּשָּׁה) increase, preventing her from eating?

items.text: Resolution via a baraita brought by Rabbi Acha bar Chinana
items.text_en: Resolution via a baraita brought by Rabbi Acha bar Chinana
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that explicitly states a פצוע דכא כהן may feed his בת גרים wife terumah, based on a verse. The Gemara confirms this applies to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, concluding that her fitness increases and she eats.

sub.text: Baraita brought by Rabbi Acha bar Chinana
sub.text_en: Baraita brought by Rabbi Acha bar Chinana
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chinana brings a baraita that provides a verse-based source for a פצוע דכא כהן (a priest with crushed or severed reproductive organs) who married a בת גרים (daughter of converts) to feed her תרומה (priestly portion).
The Gemara asks which Tanna the baraita aligns with, first considering Rabbi Yehuda and rejecting him because he holds the woman does not eat תרומה in either case.
The Gemara rejects Rabbi Yosei as the Tanna because he already permits her to eat without needing a verse.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita aligns with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, and deduces that her fitness (כשרות) increases, so she eats תרומה.

items.text: Introduction of Rav's statement
items.text_en: Introduction of Rav's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new statement attributed to Rav, which will be discussed further.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new statement attributed to Rav, setting up the next discussion.

items.text: Opening dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Opening dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rav holds that there is a valid ḥuppah for disqualified women, while Shmuel denies it. This sets up the central debate of the daf.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with the dispute: Rav holds that there is a valid ḥuppah (marital canopy) for disqualified women (פסולות), while Shmuel denies it.
Shmuel adds that Rav (called 'Abba') concedes to him regarding a girl less than three years and one day old, since she cannot engage in intercourse (ביאה), she has no ḥuppah.

Rava cites a supporting baraita: a girl of three years and one day can be betrothed through intercourse, and if a yavam (levir) has relations with her, he acquires her, and she is subject to the laws of a married woman.
The baraita continues: if she marries a priest, she may eat תרומה (priestly portion); if a disqualified person (פסול) has relations with her, he disqualifies her from the priesthood.

The gemara infers from the baraita: only a girl of three years and one day, who is disqualified through intercourse, is also disqualified through ḥuppah; a younger girl, who is not disqualified through intercourse, is also not disqualified through ḥuppah — thus supporting Shmuel's position.

Rami bar Chama shifts the discussion: the dispute about 'יש חופה לפסולות' (whether there is a valid ḥuppah for disqualified women) actually stems from a Tannaitic disagreement between Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Shmuel's concession regarding a minor girl
items.text_en: Shmuel's concession regarding a minor girl
items.desc_en: Shmuel concedes that even he agrees with Rav in the case of a girl under three years and one day, because she is not yet fit for intercourse, so ḥuppah has no effect.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel concedes that even Rav agrees with him regarding a minor girl under three years and one day, because she is not fit for intercourse, so ḥuppah has no effect.

items.text: Rava's proof from a baraita
items.text_en: Rava's proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita that discusses a girl of three years and one day, who can be acquired through intercourse and can be disqualified by a pasul. The baraita implies that only a girl who can be disqualified by intercourse can be disqualified by ḥuppah, supporting Shmuel's position.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by citing a baraita about a girl of three years and one day, detailing her halachic status regarding acquisition through intercourse, yibbum, and impurity.
The baraita continues, stating that if such a girl marries a priest she eats תרומה (priestly portion), and if a pasul (disqualified person) has intercourse with her, she becomes disqualified.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that only a girl who can be disqualified through intercourse can be disqualified through חופה (ḥuppah), thereby supporting Shmuel's position.

items.text: Rami bar Ḥama's analysis
items.text_en: Rami bar Ḥama's analysis
items.desc_en: Rami bar Ḥama suggests that the dispute between Rav and Shmuel about ḥuppah for disqualified women actually hinges on a prior dispute among Tannaim: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Ḥama asserts that the dispute about whether there is ḥuppah (a nuptial canopy) for disqualified women (פסולות) maps onto a Tannaitic disagreement among Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Initial inference from the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Initial inference from the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that kiddushin disqualifies a yevamah from terumah, chuppah should also disqualify her. Conversely, according to Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon, who hold that kiddushin does not disqualify, chuppah should not disqualify either.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that kiddushin disqualifies a yevamah from terumah, chuppah should also disqualify her; according to Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon, who hold that kiddushin does not disqualify, chuppah should not disqualify either.

items.text: Rejection of the inference: possible distinctions
items.text_en: Rejection of the inference: possible distinctions
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, suggesting that Rabbi Meir might only disqualify through kiddushin because it acquires her, but not through chuppah which does not acquire her. Alternatively, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon might only permit through kiddushin because it is not close to intercourse, but chuppah, which is close to intercourse, might disqualify.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the inference is not necessary, because Rabbi Meir might only disqualify through קידושין (betrothal) which acquires her, but not through חופה (chuppah) which does not acquire her.
Alternatively, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon might only permit through קידושין (betrothal) because it is not close to intercourse, but חופה (chuppah), which is close to intercourse, might disqualify.

items.text: Alternative source: the baraita about entering chuppah
items.text_en: Alternative source: the baraita about entering chuppah
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute might be found among Tannaim in a baraita. The baraita states that if two women (one fit and one unfit) entered chuppah but were not intimate, they eat from his property and from terumah. The Gemara clarifies that 'entered' implies actual marriage, but then reinterprets it as entering chuppah without intimacy, and the baraita teaches that they eat terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute might be found among Tannaim in a baraita, which states that if two women (one fit and one unfit) entered chuppah but were not intimate, they eat from his property and from terumah.
The Gemara questions the baraita's wording, noting that 'entered' implies actual marriage, which would be problematic.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to entering chuppah without intimacy, and teaches that they eat terumah.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's statement and its analysis
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's statement and its analysis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka states that if intimacy permits her to eat terumah, then chuppah also permits her; if intimacy does not permit her, chuppah does not permit her. The Gemara questions whether this aligns with Rabbi Meir's view, and suggests that Rabbi Yishmael should have said 'money' instead of 'chuppah', but he used 'chuppah' because the first Tanna did.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka states that if intimacy permits a woman to eat תרומה (priestly portion), then חופה (wedding canopy) also permits her; if intimacy does not permit her, חופה does not permit her.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yishmael's statement necessarily reflects a unique position, suggesting he might simply follow Rabbi Meir's view that betrothal disqualifies her from eating תרומה.

The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Yishmael follows Rabbi Meir, he should have said 'her money' (betrothal money) rather than 'her חופה (wedding canopy)', since the disqualification stems from betrothal.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yishmael used the term 'חופה (wedding canopy)' because the first Tanna in the baraita spoke of חופה, and he simply continued the same terminology.

items.text: Rav Amram's teaching: chuppah exists for disqualified women
items.text_en: Rav Amram's teaching: chuppah exists for disqualified women
items.desc_en: Rav Amram reports that Rav Sheshet taught and illuminated their eyes from a Mishnah: there is a concept of chuppah for disqualified women. This is derived from the Sotah passage where a woman swears she did not stray as an arusah or nesu'ah, a yevamah or a married woman.

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram reports that Rav Sheshet taught and illuminated their eyes from a Mishnah: there is a concept of chuppah for disqualified women, derived from the Sotah oath that includes an arusah, nesu'ah, shomeret yavam, and married woman.

items.text: Analysis of the Sotah case: chuppah for an arusah
items.text_en: Analysis of the Sotah case: chuppah for an arusah
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the case of an arusah mentioned in the Sotah passage. It cannot be that he warned her as an arusah and made her drink as an arusah, because an arusah does not drink. It also cannot be that he warned her as an arusah and made her drink as a nesu'ah, because the husband must be free of sin. Rather, it must be that he warned her as an arusah, she secluded herself, and then entered chuppah without intimacy, proving that chuppah exists for disqualified women.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the case of an arusah in the Sotah passage is possible, since an arusah does not drink the bitter waters.
The Gemara objects that if he warned her as an arusah and made her drink as a nesu'ah, the waters would not test her because the husband is not free of sin.
The Gemara resolves that he warned her as an arusah, she secluded herself, and then entered chuppah without intimacy, proving that chuppah exists for disqualified women.

items.text: Rava's objection and resolution via a baraita
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution via a baraita
items.desc_en: Rava objects that the resolution is not straightforward, citing a baraita brought by Rabbi Acha bar Chanina from the South: the verse 'from under your husband' implies that the husband's intimacy must precede the lover's. Rami bar Chama resolves that the case is where her arus came upon her in her father's house, and similarly for a yevamah, where the yavam came upon her in her father-in-law's house.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that the previous resolution is not straightforward, citing a baraita brought by Rabbi Acha bar Chanina from the South.

sub.text: Baraita cited by Rabbi Acha bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Baraita cited by Rabbi Acha bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: The baraita interprets the verse 'מבלעדי אישך' (from under your husband) to require that the husband's intimacy precede the lover's.

Rami bar Chama resolves that the case is where her arus (betrothed) came upon her in her father's house, and similarly for a yevamah (levirate widow), where the yavam (levir) came upon her in her father-in-law's house.

items.text: Gemara's question: Is shomeret yavam like a wife?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Is shomeret yavam like a wife?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a shomeret yavam is called a wife, citing Rav and Shmuel's dispute about acquisition through ma'amar. It resolves that the case involves ma'amar and follows Beit Shammai, who view ma'amar as full acquisition, and distinguishes between one's own arusah and another's shomeret yavam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a shomeret yavam is called a wife, citing Rav and Shmuel's dispute about acquisition through ma'amar.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves ma'amar and follows Beit Shammai, who view ma'amar as full acquisition.
The Gemara distinguishes between one's own arusah and another's shomeret yavam, resolving the apparent contradiction.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanations
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanations
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa attributes the ruling to a tannaitic source that distinguishes between an arusah and a nesu'ah for sotah. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains it through gilgul (rolling over of the sotah oath).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa attributes the ruling to a specific tannaitic source that distinguishes between an arusah (betrothed woman) and a nesu'ah (married woman) regarding the sotah (suspected adulteress) procedure.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the ruling through the principle of גלגול (rolling over) of the sotah oath, whereby the oath taken for the husband's suspicion extends to cover the yavam's (levir's) concerns as well.

items.text: Rav Chanina's statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rav Chanina's statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina reports that Rabbi Yochanan said: one who performs ma'amar with his yevamah, even if both are priests, disqualifies her from terumah. The Gemara questions to whom this applies, considering Rabbi Meir's view that a shomeret for a disqualifying intercourse does not eat terumah even rabbinically, and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's view that she does eat even biblically.

sub.text: Rav Chanina in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Chanina in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanina reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled: one who performs ma'amar (formal betrothal) with his yevamah (sister-in-law awaiting levirate marriage), even if both are priests, disqualifies her from eating תרומה (priestly portion).

The Gemara asks to which Tanna this ruling applies: if to Rabbi Meir, who holds that a shomeret (guardian) for a disqualifying intercourse does not eat תרומה even biblically, then the rabbinic disqualification is already obvious; if to Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon, who hold she eats even biblically, then the rabbinic disqualification is a novel question.

items.text: Ravin's version and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Ravin's version and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Ravin clarifies the dispute: if one performed ma'amar, all agree she eats; if he has a brother who is a chalai, all agree she does not eat; the dispute is when he gave her a get. Rabbi Yochanan says she eats, even according to Rabbi Meir, because the disqualification is only rabbinic. Reish Lakish says she does not eat, even according to Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon, because he cannot feed her elsewhere and she is bound to him.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports the dispute: after ma'amar all agree she eats; if the brother is a חלל (disqualified priest), all agree she does not eat; the dispute is only when he gave her a גט (bill of divorce).
Rabbi Yochanan rules she eats, even according to Rabbi Meir, because the disqualification is only rabbinic (דרבנן), not biblical (דאורייתא).
Reish Lakish rules she does not eat, even according to Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon, because he cannot feed her elsewhere and she is bound to him.
The Gemara objects that perhaps he could feed her through a חוזרת (a woman who returns to her husband's house), but rejects this because she is already bound to him (אגידא ביה).

items.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's question to Shmuel
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's question to Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef asks Shmuel about a High Priest who betrothed a minor and she reached majority under him, regarding the continuation of the Mishnah about widows or divorcees.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's question to Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's question to Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef asks Shmuel about a High Priest who betrothed a minor and she reached majority under him, regarding the continuation of the Mishnah about widows or divorcees.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry: Does the High Priest's prohibition depend on the stage of marriage?
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: Does the High Priest's prohibition depend on the stage of marriage?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a widow's disqualification for a High Priest follows the stage of marriage (nissuin) or betrothal (erusin). A proof is brought from a mishnah stating that widows from nissuin are disqualified, while those from erusin are permitted. The Gemara clarifies that the question is about the requirement of 'taking' (kicha) for betrothal or marriage, and a further proof is offered from a case where a man betroths a widow and then becomes High Priest. The discussion concludes with a distinction based on whether the woman's body changed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the High Priest's prohibition regarding a widow follows the stage of nissuin (marriage) or erusin (betrothal).
The interlocutor cites a mishnah that widows from nissuin are disqualified, while those from erusin are permitted, implying the prohibition follows nissuin.
The Gemara clarifies that the question is not about creating a חללה (profaned woman) through intercourse, but about the requirement of 'taking' (קיחה) for betrothal or marriage.
The interlocutor offers another proof from a mishnah: if a man betroths a widow and then becomes High Priest, he may marry her, showing that betrothal is permitted.
The Gemara objects that the verse 'יִקַּח אִשָּׁה' (he shall take a woman) teaches 'one and not two', distinguishing the case.
The Gemara resolves the distinction: in one case the woman's body changed (through nissuin), in the other it did not (through erusin).

items.text: Mishnah: High Priest's marriage restrictions
items.text_en: Mishnah: High Priest's marriage restrictions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a High Priest may not marry a widow, whether from betrothal or marriage, nor a bogeret (matured maiden). Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon permit a bogeret, and the Mishnah also prohibits marrying a woman who has been struck by wood (mukat etz).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a High Priest may not marry a widow (from betrothal or marriage), nor a bogeret (matured maiden), with Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon permitting a bogeret, and also prohibits marrying a woman struck by wood (mukat etz).

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of widow from betrothal or marriage
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of widow from betrothal or marriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraisa that teaches the verse 'almanah lo yikach' includes both widows from betrothal and marriage. It questions why this is not obvious, and suggests that one might have thought to learn from Tamar that only a widow from marriage is meant. The Gemara rejects this by comparing to a divorcee, who is disqualified from both stages.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'אלמנה לא יקח' (a widow he shall not take) includes both a widow from betrothal and a widow from marriage.
The Gemara asks why this is obvious, suggesting one might have thought to learn a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from Tamar that only a widow from marriage is meant.
The Gemara rejects the analogy by comparing to a divorcee (גרושה), who is disqualified from both betrothal and marriage, so a widow is likewise disqualified from both stages.

items.text: Dispute over the bogeret: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Dispute over the bogeret: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraisa where Rabbi Meir derives from the verse 'vehu ishah bivtuleha yikach' that a bogeret, whose virginity has faded, is excluded. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon permit her. The Gemara explains their dispute: Rabbi Meir interprets 'betulah' to include partial virginity, 'betuleha' to require all virginity, and 'bivtuleha' to require normal intercourse. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon interpret 'betulah' as complete virginity, 'betuleha' to include partial virginity, and 'bivtuleha' to require all virginity to be intact, whether through normal or abnormal intercourse.

sub.desc_en: The baraisa cites the verse 'וְהוּא אִשָּׁה בִבְתוּלֶיהָ יִקָּח' and reports that Rabbi Meir excludes a bogeret (whose virginity has faded), while Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon permit her.

The Gemara asks what underlies the dispute, and explains that Rabbi Meir interprets 'בְּתוּלָה' to include partial virginity, 'בְּתוּלֶיהָ' to require all virginity, and 'בִּבְתוּלֶיהָ' to require normal intercourse (בִּכְדַרְכָּהּ), excluding abnormal intercourse.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon interpret 'בְּתוּלָה' to mean complete virginity, 'בְּתוּלֶיהָ' to include partial virginity, and 'בִּבְתוּלֶיהָ' to require all virginity to be intact, whether through normal or abnormal intercourse.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on non-vaginal intercourse and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on non-vaginal intercourse and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav rules that a woman who engaged in non-vaginal intercourse (she'lo k'darkah) is disqualified from marrying a priest. Rava objects from a verse that excludes a widow for a High Priest and a divorcee for a common priest, arguing that if the case is normal intercourse, the disqualification would be due to being a 'be'ulah' (non-virgin), not a widow. Thus, the verse must refer to non-vaginal intercourse, where only a widow is disqualified, not a be'ulah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that a woman who engaged in non-vaginal intercourse (שלא כדרכה) is disqualified from marrying a priest.
Rava objects by citing a baraita that derives from the verse 'ולו תהיה לאשה' that a woman must be fit for the priest, excluding a widow for a High Priest and a divorcee or חלוצה for a common priest.

The Gemara analyzes Rava's objection: if the baraita referred to normal intercourse, the disqualification would be due to being a בעולה (non-virgin), not a widow; therefore it must refer to non-vaginal intercourse, where only a widow is disqualified but not a בעולה.

items.text: Identifying the Mishnah's author
items.text_en: Identifying the Mishnah's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah's ruling as following Rabbi Meir, and notes that Rav's statement aligns with Rabbi Elazar's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah's author as Rabbi Meir and notes that Rav's statement aligns with Rabbi Elazar's view.

items.text: Question on Rabbi Elazar's view
items.text_en: Question on Rabbi Elazar's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'be'ulah' (a woman who had intercourse) if it follows Rabbi Elazar, who holds that a bachelor who has intercourse with an unmarried woman for non-marital purposes makes her a zonah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'be'ulah' (a woman who had intercourse) if it follows Rabbi Elazar, who holds that a bachelor who has intercourse with an unmarried woman for non-marital purposes makes her a zonah.

items.text: Rav Yosef's answer: bestiality
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's answer: bestiality
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef answers that the case involves a woman who had intercourse with an animal, where she becomes a be'ulah but not a zonah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef answers that the case involves a woman who had intercourse with an animal, where she becomes a be'ulah but not a zonah.

items.text: Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that if she is a be'ulah, she is also a zonah; if not a zonah, she is not a be'ulah. He dismisses the possibility of unnatural intercourse (mukat etz) as it would disqualify all women.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects with a dilemma: if she is a be'ulah (non-virgin), she is also a zonah (harlot); if not a zonah, she is not a be'ulah, and the possibility of unnatural intercourse (מוכת עץ, a woman injured by wood) is dismissed because it would disqualify all women.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's answer: a minor who refuses marriage
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's answer: a minor who refuses marriage
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that the case involves a minor who refuses marriage (mema'enet), who is considered a be'ulah but not a zonah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves a minor who refuses marriage (ממאנת), who is considered a בעולה (one who has had intercourse) but not a זונה (harlot).

items.text: Support for bestiality case and a story
items.text_en: Support for bestiality case and a story
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya states that a woman who had intercourse with an animal is eligible for priesthood, supported by a baraita. Rav Dimi recounts a story where Rabbi declared such a woman eligible for priesthood, and Shmuel adds she is even eligible for a high priest.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya states that a woman who had intercourse with an animal is eligible for priesthood.
A baraita supports Rav Shimi bar Chiyya's ruling, stating that a woman who had intercourse with a non-human (even though it is a capital offense) is eligible for priesthood.
Rav Dimi recounts a story where a woman was mounted by a dog from behind while cleaning, and Rabbi declared her eligible for priesthood.
Shmuel adds that such a woman is even eligible for a high priest.
The Gemara objects that in Rabbi's time there was no high priest, questioning how Shmuel's statement applies.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel meant she is eligible for a high priest in principle, not that one existed at that time.

items.text: Source for no bestiality zonah
items.text_en: Source for no bestiality zonah
items.desc_en: Rava of Parzakya asks Rav Ashi for the source that there is no zonah from bestiality, citing the verse about the hire of a harlot and the price of a dog, and a Mishnah that allows both when exchanged.

sub.text: Rava of Parzakya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rava of Parzakya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rava of Parzakya asks Rav Ashi for the source of the rabbinic principle that there is no זנות (illicit sexual status) from bestiality.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's answer citing a verse and a Mishnah
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer citing a verse and a Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites the verse 'לֹא תָבִיא אֶתְנַן זוֹנָה וּמְחִיר כֶּלֶב' (Deut 23:19) and the Mishnah that permits an exchange of a dog's hire for a harlot's price, interpreting 'גַּם שְׁנֵיהֶם' to mean only two forbidden categories, not four, thus excluding bestiality from the definition of זונה.

items.text: Baraita on raped/seduced women and their offspring
items.text_en: Baraita on raped/seduced women and their offspring
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a man marrying his own raped or seduced woman, and another's; Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says the child is a chalai, while the Sages say the child is fit. Rav Huna says he must divorce her, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains the phrase 'if he married, he is married' means he may keep her.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that a man may not marry his own raped or seduced woman, but if he married, he is married; for another's raped or seduced woman, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says the child is a חלל (disqualified from the priesthood), while the Sages say the child is fit.
The Gemara notes that Rav Huna citing Rav says that if he married, he must divorce her with a גט (bill of divorce).
The Gemara objects: if he must divorce her, what does the baraita mean by 'if he married, he is married'?
Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains that the phrase 'if he married, he is married' means that the marriage is valid and he may keep her, contradicting Rav Huna's statement.

items.text: Gemara's challenge from Rav and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from Rav and Rabbi Yochanan
