items.desc_en: Rav G'viha from Bei Katil presents a teaching before Rav Ashi, citing Rav and Rabbi Yochanan who both say that a bogeret or one wounded by wood may not be married initially, but if married, the marriage is valid. This implies that since she will eventually become a bogeret or wounded by wood under him, similarly here she will eventually become a non-virgin under him, creating a contradiction.

sub.text: Rav G'viha's challenge before Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav G'viha's challenge before Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav G'viha presents a teaching before Rav Ashi, citing Rav and Rabbi Yochanan who both rule that a bogeret or one wounded by wood may not be married initially but if married the marriage is valid, and argues that since she will eventually become a bogeret or wounded by wood under him, similarly here she will eventually become a non-virgin under him, creating a contradiction.

items.text: Mishnah on raped/seduced woman of another and the dispute
items.text_en: Mishnah on raped/seduced woman of another and the dispute
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one may not marry the raped or seduced woman of another. If he did marry her, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says the child is a halal, and the Sages say the child is fit. Rav Huna and Rav Giddel both rule in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that one may not marry the raped or seduced woman of another.
The mishnah presents the dispute: if he did marry her, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says the child is a חלל (disqualified from the priesthood).
The Sages say the child is כשר (fit, not disqualified).
Rav Huna reports in the name of Rav that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
Rav Giddel similarly states in the name of Rav that the הלכה follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

items.text: Attempt to explain Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's reasoning and the contradiction
items.text_en: Attempt to explain Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's reasoning and the contradiction
items.desc_en: Some say Rav Huna explained that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds like Rabbi Elazar. But this is contradicted by the fact that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's mishnah is clean, yet Rav Amram said the halakha is not like Rabbi Elazar. This is a difficulty.

sub.text: Some say (איכא דאמרי) version of Rav Huna's statement
sub.text_en: Some say (איכא דאמרי) version of Rav Huna's statement
sub.desc_en: Some say that Rav Huna said in the name of Rav: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's reasoning is that he holds like Rabbi Elazar.

The Gemara objects: Does Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov really hold like Rabbi Elazar? But we know that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's mishnah is clean, yet Rav Amram said the halakha is not like Rabbi Elazar — this is a difficulty.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution: dispute over whether there is a halal from positive commandments
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution: dispute over whether there is a halal from positive commandments
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says they dispute whether there is a halal from those liable to positive commandments. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds there is, the Rabbis hold there is not. The Gemara explains the scriptural derivation and a baraita that aligns with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, ending with a difficulty about the placement of 'these'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the dispute by stating that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Rabbis disagree over whether there is a halal (profaned offspring) from those liable to positive commandments.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's scriptural derivation
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's scriptural derivation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derives his position from the verse 'אלמנה וגרושה וחללה זונה את אלה לא יקח כי אם בתולה' and the subsequent verse 'ולא יחלל זרעו בעמיו', applying the profanation to all the forbidden women listed.

The Rabbis object that the word 'אלה' (these) interrupts the context, limiting the application; Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov counters that 'אלה' serves to exclude a menstruating woman (niddah) from the profanation.

The Gemara cites a baraita that aligns with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, stating that from 'אלה' one creates a halal but not from a niddah, and then raises a difficulty about why 'אלה' is not written at the end of the verse.

items.text: Baraita on a priest's impurity for his sister
items.text_en: Baraita on a priest's impurity for his sister
items.desc_en: The baraita discusses a priest's impurity for his sister: for an arusah, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda say he may become impure, Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon say not. For an anusah or mefutah, all agree he may not. For one wounded by wood, Rabbi Shimon says not, as he holds that only a woman fit for a High Priest may be impure for. For a bogeret, all agree he may become impure.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing the dispute about a priest's impurity for his sister: for an arusah, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda permit impurity, while Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon forbid it; for an anusah or mefutah, all agree impurity is forbidden; for a mukkat etz, Rabbi Shimon forbids it based on her fitness for a High Priest.
The baraita concludes that for a bogeret, all agree a priest may become impure for her.

items.text: Reasoning of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Reasoning of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: They derive from the verse 'and to his sister the virgin' that anusah and mefutah are excluded. One might think to exclude even one wounded by wood, but the verse 'who has not been with a man' includes her. 'The close one' includes the arusah, and 'to him' includes the bogeret. The Gemara questions why a verse is needed for bogeret, since Rabbi Meir holds 'virgin' includes even a partial virgin, and answers that otherwise one might learn from another verse that it means a na'arah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, and explains that they derive from the verse 'וְלַאֲחוֹתוֹ הַבְּתוּלָה' (and to his sister the virgin) to exclude an anusah (raped woman) and a mefutah (seduced woman).

The Gemara continues the derivation: one might think to exclude even a mukkat etz (woman wounded by wood), but the verse 'אֲשֶׁר לֹא הָיְתָה לְאִישׁ' (who has not been with a man) includes her; 'הַקְּרוֹבָה' (the close one) includes the arusah (betrothed woman); and 'אֵלָיו' (to him) includes the bogeret (adult woman).
The Gemara questions why a verse is needed for bogeret, since Rabbi Meir holds that 'בְּתוּלָה' (virgin) includes even a partial virgin.
The Gemara answers that the verse is necessary, because otherwise one might learn from another verse that 'בְּתוּלָה' means a na'arah (young woman), so the verse teaches us otherwise.

items.text: Reasoning of Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Reasoning of Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: They derive differently: 'and to his sister the virgin' excludes anusah, mefutah, and one wounded by wood; 'who has not been' excludes the arusah; 'the close one' includes a divorced arusah; 'to him' includes the bogeret. The baraita continues with 'the close one' to include a divorced arusah.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon derive their positions by interpreting the verse 'וְלַאֲחוֹתוֹ הַבְּתוּלָה' (and to his sister the virgin) to exclude an אֲנוּסָה (raped woman), מְפוּתָּה (seduced woman), and מוּכַּת עֵץ (one wounded by wood); 'אֲשֶׁר לֹא הָיְתָה' (who has not been) to exclude an אֲרוּסָה (betrothed woman); 'הַקְּרוֹבָה' (the close one) to include a divorced אֲרוּסָה; and 'אֵלָיו' (to him) to include the בּוֹגֶרֶת (mature woman).

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rabbi Shimon's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rabbi Shimon's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's earlier distinction between a woman fit for a High Priest (who may become impure for her) and one not fit (who may not). It argues that if the distinction is based on the word 'קרובה', then a מוּכַּת עֵץ (a woman who lost her virginity through an accident) should also be excluded, but the Gemara distinguishes between a case where an act occurred and where it did not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Shimon's distinction between a woman fit for a High Priest (who may become impure for her) and one not fit (who may not), noting that the distinction is based on the word 'קרובה' (close relative).
The Gemara answers that a מוּכַּת עֵץ (a woman who lost her virginity through an accident) is excluded because an act occurred, unlike the case of a woman who never had an act at all.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's derivation from 'לא הייתה לאיש'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's derivation from 'לא הייתה לאיש'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei, who disagrees with his colleague, must hold like Rabbi Meir regarding a מוּכַּת עֵץ. This is derived from the phrase 'לא הייתה לאיש', which is expounded to teach two separate laws: one from 'לא הייתה' and one from 'לאיש'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Since Rabbi Yosei disagrees with his colleague, implying he holds like Rabbi Meir regarding a מוּכַּת עֵץ (a woman who suffered a wooden injury), from where does he derive this law? The answer is from the phrase 'לֹא הָיְתָה לְאִישׁ'.
The Gemara responds: But you already used that verse! It explains that the verse yields two laws: one from 'לֹא הָיְתָה' and one from 'לְאִישׁ'.

items.text: Derivation of 'אליו' to include a bogeret
items.text_en: Derivation of 'אליו' to include a bogeret
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the word 'אליו' in the verse comes to include a bogeret (a post-pubescent virgin) in the prohibition for a High Priest. Rabbi Shimon's reasoning that 'בתולה' implies a complete virgin is derived from the fact that the verse needed 'אליו' to include the bogeret.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the word 'אליו' (to him) in the verse comes to include a bogeret (post-pubescent virgin) in the prohibition for a High Priest.
The Gemara questions how Rabbi Shimon can derive the inclusion of a bogeret from 'אליו', given that he holds 'בתולה' implies a complete virgin.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Shimon's own reasoning is derived from here: since 'אליו' is needed to include the bogeret, it implies that 'בתולה' means a complete virgin.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's ruling on a young convert and the scriptural basis
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's ruling on a young convert and the scriptural basis
items.desc_en: A beraita states that Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai rules a female convert under three years and one day is eligible for the priesthood, citing the verse from the Midianite war where Pinchas was with them. The Gemara questions the Rabbis' interpretation and resolves a contradiction in verses through Rav Huna's explanation that the verse speaks of one fit for intercourse.

sub.desc_en: A beraita cites Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's ruling that a female convert under three years and one day is eligible for the priesthood, based on the verse from the Midianite war where Pinchas was with them.
The Gemara objects: how do the Rabbis interpret the verse, and why would a three-year-old not also be included?

Rav Huna resolves the contradiction between two verses by showing that the verse about 'knowing a man' refers to those fit for intercourse, while the verse about 'the young girls' includes all minors.
The Gemara concludes that the verse speaks of one fit for intercourse, not one who has actually engaged in it.

items.text: Supporting beraita for Rav Huna's interpretation
items.text_en: Supporting beraita for Rav Huna's interpretation
items.desc_en: A beraita explicitly states that the verse 'וכל אשה יודעת איש' speaks of one fit for intercourse, not one who actually experienced it, as proven by the continuation of the verse.

sub.desc_en: A beraita explicitly supports Rav Huna's interpretation that the verse 'וכל אשה יודעת איש' speaks of one fit for intercourse, not one who actually experienced it, as proven by the continuation of the verse.

items.text: Methods to determine fitness for intercourse and the use of the Tzitz
items.text_en: Methods to determine fitness for intercourse and the use of the Tzitz
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Bizna explains that the Midianite women were passed before the Tzitz to determine fitness, with a green face indicating fitness. Rav Nachman notes a general sign for sin. A parallel case from Yavesh Gilead uses a wine barrel test. The Gemara questions why the Tzitz wasn't used there, and Rav Kahana answers that the Tzitz is for favor, not punishment, but for gentiles it can be used for punishment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Midianite women knew whether a young girl was fit for intercourse (and therefore to be killed).

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Bizna quoting Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Bizna quoting Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida answers that the women were passed before the Tzitz (the high priest's forehead plate); a girl whose face turned green was known to be fit for intercourse, while one whose face did not turn green was known to be unfit.
Rav Nachman observes a general sign: a sin (like illicit intercourse) causes the face to turn green (the pallor of one who is flushed out or stricken).
The Gemara brings a parallel case: in Yavesh Gilead, the men determined virginity by seating the girls on a wine barrel — a married woman's smell would waft, while a virgin's would not.
The Gemara asks why the men of Yavesh Gilead did not simply pass the girls before the Tzitz as was done in the Midianite case.

sub.text: Rav Kahana bar Rav Natan's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana bar Rav Natan's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana bar Rav Natan answers that regarding the Tzitz it is written 'לְרָצוֹן לָהֶם' (for favor for them) — the Tzitz is for favor (determining who is fit for the Temple service) and not for punishment (determining who to kill).
The Gemara objects: if the Tzitz is only for favor and not punishment, then why was it used in Midian to determine which girls to kill (a punishment)?
Rav Ashi resolves the objection by noting a distinction: 'לָהֶם' (for them) — for Israel the Tzitz is only for favor, not punishment; but for גויים (gentiles) it can be used even for punishment.

items.text: Halachic ruling and clarification of Rabbi Shimon's position
items.text_en: Halachic ruling and clarification of Rabbi Shimon's position
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi reports that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ruled the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai. Rabbi Zeira asks whether this was heard explicitly or inferred. The Gemara explores the inference from a case where Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reported that Rabbi permitted a young convert, but questions whether that case was different because she was already married. Rav Safra had difficulty with this inference and resolved it differently.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi reports that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi whether he heard the ruling explicitly (בפירוש) or inferred it (מכללא).

Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi explains the inference: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reported that Rabbi (the Patriarch) permitted a young female convert under three years old to marry a priest, implying the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai.

The Gemara objects that the inference is weak: perhaps the case was different because the convert was already married (הואיל ואינסיב — since she married, she stays married), and Rabbi's ruling was only בדיעבד (after the fact), not לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

The Gemara rejects the objection: the parallel to a bogeret (adult virgin) or מוכת עץ (one whose hymen was broken by wood) is inapt, because a convert under three who later has relations would become a זונה (harlot) forbidden to a priest, so Rabbi would not have permitted even בדיעבד (after the fact).
Rav Safra taught the tradition as an inference (מכללא) but found it difficult, and resolved it differently (the text does not specify his resolution here).

items.text: Practical case and final ruling
items.text_en: Practical case and final ruling
items.desc_en: A certain priest married a convert under three years old. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenged him, and the priest cited Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi's ruling. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak threatened to excommunicate Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi if the priest did not divorce her. The daf ends with a beraita repeating Rabbi Shimon's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a certain priest married a female convert under three years old.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges the priest, asking what he thinks he is doing.
The priest defends himself by citing Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi's tradition that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's lenient ruling.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak threatens to excommunicate Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi if the priest does not divorce the convert.
The daf concludes with a beraita that repeats Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's ruling, reinforcing the earlier tradition.

items.text: Gentile graves and impurity under a tent
items.text_en: Gentile graves and impurity under a tent
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a baraita stating that gentile graves do not impart impurity under a tent, based on the verse 'You are called Adam, but gentiles are not called Adam.' It then addresses objections from verses that seem to refer to gentiles as 'Adam,' explaining that those refer to animals or Israelites. Ravina raises a question about whether the exclusion applies only to impurity under a tent or also to contact and carrying.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that gentile graves do not impart impurity under a tent, citing the verse 'You are called Adam, but gentiles are not called Adam.'
An objection is raised from a verse that refers to gentiles as 'Adam,' and the answer is that the term refers to animals.
Another objection is raised from a verse that calls gentiles 'Adam,' and again the answer is that it refers to animals.

A third objection is raised from a verse about purification from corpse impurity, and the Gemara answers that it might refer to an Israelite, with additional explanations from the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai.
Ravina questions whether the exclusion of gentiles from the term 'Adam' applies only to impurity under a tent or also to impurity through contact and carrying.

items.text: Mishnah: High Priest betrothing a widow
items.text_en: Mishnah: High Priest betrothing a widow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a common priest betrothed a widow and was then appointed High Priest, he may marry her. It recounts the case of Yehoshua ben Gamla who betrothed Marta bat Baitos and was appointed High Priest. However, if a yevama fell to a common priest who was then appointed High Priest, even if he performed ma'amar, he may not marry her.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule: if a common priest betrothed a widow and was then appointed High Priest, he may marry her.
The Mishnah recounts the case of Yehoshua ben Gamla, who betrothed Marta bat Baitos and, after being appointed High Priest by the king, married her.
The Mishnah adds a contrasting case: if a yevama fell to a common priest who was then appointed High Priest, even if he performed ma'amar, he may not marry her.

items.text: Gemara: Source for the Mishnah and the story of Yehoshua ben Gamla
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for the Mishnah and the story of Yehoshua ben Gamla
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita deriving from the verse 'He shall take a woman' that a High Priest may marry a widow he betrothed before his appointment, but not a yevama. It then discusses the story of Yehoshua ben Gamla, noting that the Mishnah says he was appointed (by the king), implying that if he merely became High Priest on his own, he could not marry her. Rav Yosef comments on the bribe Marta gave King Yannai to appoint Yehoshua.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse 'יִקַּח אִשָּׁה' (he shall take a woman) that a High Priest may marry a widow he betrothed before his appointment, but not a yevama (יְבָמָה).

The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's phrase 'מִנָּהוּ הַמֶּלֶךְ' (the king appointed him) implies that only if he was appointed (by the king) may he marry her, but if he merely became High Priest on his own (נִתְמַנָּה), he may not.
Rav Yosef observes that Marta bat Baitos bribed King Yannai with a tarqaba (תַּרְקַבָּא) of dinars to appoint Yehoshua ben Gamla as a High Priest (בְּכָהֲנֵי רַבְרְבֵי).

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: High Priest's brother dies
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: High Priest's brother dies
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a High Priest's brother dies, the High Priest performs chalitzah but not yibbum. The Gemara questions why this applies even if the brother was only betrothed, since the positive commandment of yibbum should override the prohibition. It answers that this is a decree to prevent confusion with the case of a married woman.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a High Priest's brother dies, the High Priest performs חליצה (the release ceremony) and does not perform יבום (levirate marriage).

The Gemara questions why the Mishnah rules the same for both betrothal and marriage, since in the case of betrothal the positive commandment of יבום (levirate marriage) should override the negative prohibition.
The Gemara answers that the prohibition is a decree: the first marital act (from betrothal) is treated like the second (from marriage) to prevent confusion.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Common priest marrying an aylonit
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Common priest marrying an aylonit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a common priest may not marry an aylonit unless he already has a wife and children. Rabbi Yehuda prohibits it entirely, considering her a zonah. The Sages define zonah as a convert, freed slave, or one who engaged in forbidden relations. The Gemara records a discussion between the Exilarch and Rav Huna about the rationale for the Mishnah's first clause.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by ruling that a common priest may not marry an aylonit (a woman incapable of bearing children) unless he already has a wife and children.
Rabbi Yehuda prohibits it entirely, arguing that an aylonit is considered a זונה (forbidden woman) as defined in the Torah.
The Sages define a זונה (forbidden woman) as a convert, a freed slave, or one who engaged in forbidden relations, thereby excluding an aylonit from that category.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Kohen with children may not marry an aylonit
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Kohen with children may not marry an aylonit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a kohen who already has children may not marry an aylonit, as she is considered a zona. The Gemara clarifies that the prohibition of zona applies specifically to kohanim, not to Israelites.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a kohen who already has children may not marry an aylonit, because she is considered a zona, and the Gemara clarifies that the prohibition of zona applies only to kohanim, not to Israelites.

items.text: Rav Huna explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.text_en: Rav Huna explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains Rabbi Yehuda's view that an aylonit is a zona, based on the verse 'they ate but were not satisfied, they engaged in promiscuity but did not increase'—any intercourse without potential for increase is promiscuous.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning that an aylonit is a zona, based on the verse 'they ate but were not satisfied, they engaged in promiscuity but did not increase'—any intercourse without potential for increase is promiscuous.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling and Rav Chisda's inquiry
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling and Rav Chisda's inquiry
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Eliezer says a kohen may not marry a minor. Rav Chisda tells Rabba to investigate this, as Rav Huna will ask about it. Rabba concludes that Rabbi Eliezer holds like Rabbi Meir (concerned for minority cases) and like Rabbi Yehuda (that an aylonit is a zona).

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that Rabbi Eliezer rules a kohen may not marry a minor girl.
Rav Chisda tells Rabba to investigate the baraita, as Rav Huna will ask about it later.
Rabba investigates and concludes that Rabbi Eliezer holds like Rabbi Meir (concerned for minority cases) and like Rabbi Yehuda (that an aylonit is a zona).
The gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer follows Rabbi Meir's concern for minority cases and Rabbi Yehuda's definition of an aylonit as a zona.

items.text: Objection: Does Rabbi Eliezer really hold like Rabbi Meir?
items.text_en: Objection: Does Rabbi Eliezer really hold like Rabbi Meir?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer actually follows Rabbi Meir, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir says a minor cannot perform chalitzah or yibbum due to concern they might be a saris or aylonit, while Rabbi Eliezer says a minor girl may undergo yibbum but not chalitzah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer actually holds like Rabbi Meir, given a baraita that seems to contradict this.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that a minor boy and girl cannot perform חליצה (chalitzah) or יבום (yibbum).
The Sages object to Rabbi Meir, agreeing that חליצה (chalitzah) is impossible for a minor, but questioning why יבום (yibbum) is also forbidden.
Rabbi Meir answers that a minor boy might be a סריס (saris, sterile male) and a minor girl might be an אילונית (aylonit, sterile female), leading to an incestuous union.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer rules that a minor girl may undergo יבום (yibbum) but not חליצה (chalitzah), contradicting the earlier assumption.

items.text: Objection: Does Rabbi Eliezer really hold like Rabbi Yehuda?
items.text_en: Objection: Does Rabbi Eliezer really hold like Rabbi Yehuda?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer follows Rabbi Yehuda, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer defines a zona literally, while Rabbi Yehuda says a zona is an aylonit. Other opinions include Rabbi Akiva (a promiscuous woman), Rabbi Matya ben Charash (one who commits adultery), and Rabbi Elazar (a single man with a single woman not for marriage).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer actually holds like Rabbi Yehuda, given the baraita that follows.
The baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer defining a zona literally (an adulteress), contradicting Rabbi Yehuda's definition.
Rabbi Akiva defines a zona as a promiscuous woman available to all.
Rabbi Matya ben Charash says a woman becomes a zona if her husband had intercourse with her on the way to drink the bitter waters.
Rabbi Yehuda defines a zona as a sexually underdeveloped woman (aylonit).
The Sages define a zona as a convert, a freed maidservant, or one who engaged in licentious intercourse.
Rabbi Elazar says an unmarried man who has intercourse with an unmarried woman not for marriage makes her a zona.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's resolution: High Priest
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's resolution: High Priest
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah resolves the contradiction by saying the case involves a High Priest, who may only marry a virgin. A minor girl, when she grows up, is no longer a virgin, so he cannot marry her.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah resolves the issue by stating that the case involves a High Priest, who may only marry a virgin; a minor girl, when she grows up, is no longer a virgin, so he cannot marry her.

items.text: Rava's objection and alternative resolution: Concern for seduction
items.text_en: Rava's objection and alternative resolution: Concern for seduction
items.desc_en: Rava objects: if her father betrothed her, he acquires her immediately; if she betroths herself, that is only Rabbi Eliezer's view. Rava instead says the case is an ordinary kohen, and we are concerned she might be seduced. The Gemara asks: an Israelite also? Answer: seduction of a minor is coercion, and coercion is permitted for an Israelite.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to the previous resolution: if her father betrothed her, he acquires her immediately; if she betroths herself, that is only Rabbi Eliezer's view, not the Rabbis'.
Rava instead says the case is an ordinary kohen, and we are concerned she might be seduced.
The Gemara asks: if the concern is seduction, then an Israelite also should be prohibited.
The Gemara answers: seduction of a minor is coercion, and coercion is permitted for an Israelite.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolutions: High Priest and the definition of 'naarah'
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolutions: High Priest and the definition of 'naarah'
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says the case is a High Priest, citing a baraita that a 'betulah' must be a naarah (between minority and majority). Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita that 'betulah' means naarah, as in the verse about Rebecca.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the difficulty by identifying the case as a High Priest, citing a baraita that defines 'בתולה' (virgin) as a naarah (adolescent) who has left minority but not yet reached majority.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative resolution, citing a baraita that 'בתולה' (virgin) exclusively means a naarah, as demonstrated by the verse describing Rebecca as both a naarah and a betulah.

items.text: Rav Amram rules against Rabbi Elazar's definition of zona
items.text_en: Rav Amram rules against Rabbi Elazar's definition of zona
items.desc_en: Rav Amram states that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Elazar, who said a single man with a single woman not for marriage makes her a zona.

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram rules that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Elazar's definition of a zona as a single man with a single woman not for marriage.

items.text: Mishnah: Obligation of procreation
items.text_en: Mishnah: Obligation of procreation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not refrain from procreation unless he already has children. Beit Shammai says two males, Beit Hillel says a male and a female, based on the verse 'male and female He created them'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the obligation of procreation: one may not refrain unless he has children, with Beit Shammai requiring two males and Beit Hillel requiring a male and a female, citing the verse 'male and female He created them'.

items.text: Gemara: Does having children exempt one from marriage?
items.text_en: Gemara: Does having children exempt one from marriage?
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether having children exempts one from marriage. One version supports Rav Nachman citing Shmuel that one must still marry. Another version says he is exempt from both, but the Gemara resolves that if he has children, he marries a woman not fit for children; the practical difference is selling a Torah scroll for children.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that having children exempts one from the obligation of פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה (procreation) but not from the obligation of marriage.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rav Nachman citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rav Nachman citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Nachman citing Shmuel that even with children, one is forbidden to be without a wife, based on the verse 'לֹא טוֹב הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ' (it is not good for man to be alone).
An alternative version states that having children exempts one from both procreation and marriage.
The Gemara objects that this alternative version would be a refutation of Rav Nachman citing Shmuel.
The Gemara resolves that if one has children, he marries a woman not fit for children; the practical difference is selling a Torah scroll for children.

items.text: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel's sources for procreation
items.text_en: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel's sources for procreation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Beit Shammai's reasoning: they learn from Moses, who had two sons. Beit Hillel learn from the creation of the world. The Gemara asks why Beit Shammai don't learn from creation, and answers that one cannot derive a possible case from an impossible one.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Beit Shammai's position (two males) and Beit Hillel's position (male and female, from creation).
The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of Beit Shammai.
The Gemara explains that Beit Shammai learn from Moses, who had two sons.
The Gemara explains that Beit Hillel learn from the creation of the world.
The Gemara objects: why don't Beit Shammai also learn from creation?
The Gemara resolves that one cannot derive a possible case (human procreation) from an impossible one (creation ex nihilo).

items.text: Moses' celibacy as a precedent for Beis Hillel
items.text_en: Moses' celibacy as a precedent for Beis Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Beis Hillel does not learn from Moses that one may refrain from procreation. It answers that Moses acted on his own reasoning, and the Gemara lists three things Moses did on his own and with which God agreed: separating from his wife, breaking the tablets, and adding one day to the revelation. Each is explained with a kal vachomer derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Beis Hillel does not learn from Moses' example of celibacy.
The Gemara answers that Moses acted on his own reasoning, and cites a baraita listing three things Moses did on his own with which God agreed.

sub.text: Tanna's explanation of Moses' separation from his wife
sub.text_en: Tanna's explanation of Moses' separation from his wife
sub.desc_en: The Tanna explains Moses' kal vachomer reasoning for separating from his wife, and that God agreed, as per the verse.

sub.text: Tanna's explanation of Moses' breaking the tablets
sub.text_en: Tanna's explanation of Moses' breaking the tablets
sub.desc_en: The Tanna explains Moses' kal vachomer reasoning for breaking the tablets, and Resh Lakish adds that God approved.

sub.text: Tanna's explanation of Moses' adding one day
sub.text_en: Tanna's explanation of Moses' adding one day
sub.desc_en: The Tanna explains Moses' reasoning for adding one day to the revelation, and that God agreed by not resting the Shechinah until Shabbos.

items.text: Rabbi Natan's first baraita on Beis Shammai's opinion
items.text_en: Rabbi Natan's first baraita on Beis Shammai's opinion
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Natan reporting that Beis Shammai requires two males and two females for procreation, while Beis Hillel requires a male and a female. Rav Huna explains Rabbi Natan's reasoning for Beis Shammai based on verses about Kayin and Hevel, each having a twin sister. The Rabbis (Sages) interpret those verses as mere acknowledgment.

sub.desc_en: A baraita reports Rabbi Natan's tradition that Beis Shammai requires two males and two females for procreation, while Beis Hillel requires a male and a female.

Rav Huna explains Rabbi Natan's reasoning for Beis Shammai's position, deriving from verses that Kayin and Hevel each had a twin sister, while the Rabbis interpret those verses as mere acknowledgment.

items.text: Rabbi Natan's second baraita on Beis Hillel's opinion
items.text_en: Rabbi Natan's second baraita on Beis Hillel's opinion
items.desc_en: Another baraita cites Rabbi Natan reporting that Beis Shammai requires a male and a female, while Beis Hillel requires either a male or a female. Rava explains Rabbi Natan's reasoning for Beis Hillel from the verse 'Lo sohu vera'ah' — God created the world for habitation, so even one child suffices.

sub.desc_en: A second baraita cites Rabbi Natan reporting Beis Shammai's opinion requiring a male and a female, and Beis Hillel's opinion requiring either a male or a female.

Rava explains Rabbi Natan's reasoning for Beis Hillel from the verse 'לֹא תֹהוּ בְרָאָהּ לָשֶׁבֶת יְצָרָהּ' (He did not create it a waste, but formed it for habitation), so even one child suffices for habitation.

items.text: Dispute: children born before conversion
items.text_en: Dispute: children born before conversion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish argue whether a convert who had children before conversion fulfills the mitzvah of procreation. Rabbi Yochanan says yes, because he had children; Resh Lakish says no, because a convert is like a newborn. The Gemara notes this parallels their dispute about the firstborn's inheritance, and explains why both cases are necessary to teach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds a convert who had children before conversion fulfills procreation; Resh Lakish holds he does not, because a convert is like a newborn.
The Gemara notes that this dispute parallels their earlier dispute about a convert's firstborn inheritance, where Rabbi Yochanan says he has no firstborn and Resh Lakish says he does.
The Gemara explains why both cases (procreation and inheritance) are necessary to teach: each case alone might have led to a different concession, so both are needed to fully establish the positions.

items.text: Proof from Merodach-baladan and the status of slaves
items.text_en: Proof from Merodach-baladan and the status of slaves
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Resh Lakish from the verse about Merodach-baladan, who is called 'ben Baladan' even after conversion. Resh Lakish answers that converts have lineage but not pity. Rav states that all agree a slave has no lineage, citing 'im hachamor'. An objection from Tziva's fifteen sons is answered by Rav Acha bar Yaakov, and the Gemara distinguishes cases where names are given with patronymics.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Resh Lakish by citing the verse that calls Merodach-baladan 'ben Baladan' even after conversion, implying converts retain lineage.
Resh Lakish answers that converts have lineage (חַיִיס) while in their gentile state, but after conversion they lose it.
Rav states that all agree a slave has no lineage, citing the verse 'שבו לכם פה עם החמור' (stay here with the donkey), interpreting 'עם' as a people comparable to a donkey.
An objection is raised from the verse that Tziva had fifteen sons and twenty slaves, implying slaves have lineage.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the term 'בנים' (sons) there is like 'כפר בן בקר' (a village named 'son of cattle'), meaning it is a descriptive name, not actual lineage.
The Gemara objects that if so, the same reasoning could apply to Merodach-baladan, but the distinction is that there the names are given with patronymics, while here they are not.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the lineage of converts is recorded elsewhere with full patronymics, citing the verse about Ben Hadad ben Tabrimmon ben Hezyon.

items.text: Dispute: children who died
items.text_en: Dispute: children who died
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan argue whether a person who had children who died fulfills procreation. Rav Huna says yes, based on Rav Asi's teaching that all souls must be born before Mashiach. Rabbi Yochanan says no, because the verse 'lashevet yetsarah' requires the children to inhabit the world. The Gemara begins an objection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the dispute: Rav Huna says a person who had children who died fulfills procreation, Rabbi Yochanan says he does not.

sub.text: Rav Huna's position with Rav Asi's support
sub.text_en: Rav Huna's position with Rav Asi's support
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna supports his view with Rav Asi's teaching that all souls must be born before Mashiach, while Rabbi Yochanan counters that the verse 'לשבת יצרה' (He created it to be inhabited) requires the children to actually inhabit the world.
The Gemara begins to raise an objection against one of the positions.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Huna's statement about grandchildren
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Huna's statement about grandchildren
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Huna's statement that grandchildren are considered children for the mitzvah of procreation, citing a baraita that says if a grandchild dies or is found to be a eunuch, the grandfather has not fulfilled the mitzvah. This is presented as a conclusive refutation of Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Huna's statement that grandchildren are considered children for the mitzvah of procreation, citing a baraita that says if a grandchild dies or is found to be a eunuch, the grandfather has not fulfilled the mitzvah.
The Gemara concludes that this is a conclusive refutation of Rav Huna's position.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's discussion on grandchildren fulfilling procreation
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's discussion on grandchildren fulfilling procreation
items.desc_en: Abaye thought that grandchildren fulfill the mitzvah only if they are from a son or daughter, but not from a daughter via a son. Rava countered that the verse 'He created it to be inhabited' requires that there be offspring, and here there is. The Gemara then discusses whether two grandchildren from one child suffice, citing an incident with Rav Sheishet who deflected a question about his grandchildren.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asserts that grandchildren fulfill the procreation mitzvah only if they descend from a son or daughter, but not from a daughter via a son.
Rava objects that the verse 'לָשֶׁבֶת יְצָרָהּ' (He created it to be inhabited) requires offspring, and here there is offspring, so Abaye's limitation is invalid.
The Gemara questions whether everyone agrees that two grandchildren from one child do not fulfill the mitzvah.
The Gemara cites an incident where the rabbis told Rav Sheishet to marry and have children, and he deflected by saying his daughter's children are his children.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Sheishet was merely deflecting the question, as he had been uprooted from Rav Huna's lecture (i.e., he was infertile).

items.text: Source for grandchildren being like children
items.text_en: Source for grandchildren being like children
items.desc_en: Rabba asks Rava bar Mari for the source of the rabbinic statement that grandchildren are like children. After rejecting a proof from Jacob's statement to Laban, he derives it from the verse about Hezron marrying the daughter of Machir, showing that Machir's grandchildren were called 'lawgivers' like Judah.

sub.text: Rabba's question to Rava bar Mari
sub.text_en: Rabba's question to Rava bar Mari
sub.desc_en: Rabba asks Rava bar Mari for the source of the rabbinic statement that grandchildren are considered like children.

sub.text: Rabba's rejected proof from Jacob's statement
sub.text_en: Rabba's rejected proof from Jacob's statement
sub.desc_en: Rabba proposes a proof from Jacob's statement 'the daughters are my daughters and the sons are my sons,' but rejects it because the parallel phrase 'the flock is my flock' refers to acquisition, not lineage.

sub.text: Rava bar Mari's derivation from the verse about Hezron and Machir
sub.text_en: Rava bar Mari's derivation from the verse about Hezron and Machir
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Mari derives the principle from the verse about Hezron marrying the daughter of Machir, showing that Machir's grandchildren were called 'lawgivers' like Judah.

items.text: Mishnah not in accordance with Rabbi Yehoshua; story of Rabbi Akiva's students
items.text_en: Mishnah not in accordance with Rabbi Yehoshua; story of Rabbi Akiva's students
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehoshua, who says one should marry and have children in both youth and old age. Rabbi Akiva says the same about Torah study and students. The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Akiva had 12,000 pairs of students who all died in one period because they did not treat each other with respect, and the world was desolate until he taught five rabbis who revived the Torah. Rav Mattana rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehoshua.
A baraita is cited in which Rabbi Yehoshua rules that one should marry and have children in both youth and old age, citing the verse 'בבקר זרע את זרעך' (in the morning sow your seed).
Rabbi Akiva applies the same principle to Torah study and students, citing the same verse.
The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Akiva had 12,000 pairs of students who all died in one period because they did not treat each other with respect.
The world was desolate until Rabbi Akiva taught five rabbis who revived the Torah.
A tanna adds that they all died between Passover and Shavuot, and Rav Chama bar Abba (or Rabbi Chiya bar Avin) says they died a bad death, identified by Rav Nachman as croup (אסכרה).
Rav Mattana rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua.

items.text: A man without a wife lacks joy, blessing, goodness, Torah, protection, and peace
items.text_en: A man without a wife lacks joy, blessing, goodness, Torah, protection, and peace
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum says in the name of Rabbi Chanilai that a man without a wife lacks joy, blessing, and goodness, citing verses. In the West they add that he lacks Torah and a wall (protection). Rava bar Ulla says he lacks peace, citing a verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Chanilai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Chanilai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Chanilai states that a man without a wife lacks joy, blessing, and goodness, each supported by a verse.
The sages in the West add that a man without a wife also lacks Torah and a wall (protection), each supported by a verse.
Rava bar Ulla adds that a man without a wife lacks peace, citing a verse.

items.text: Duty to be intimate with one's wife before a journey
items.text_en: Duty to be intimate with one's wife before a journey
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says one who knows his wife is God-fearing and does not visit her (be intimate) is called a sinner, and one must visit his wife before going on a journey. The Gemara questions the source, suggesting it is from the verse about the woman's desire, but Rav Yosef says it is needed only when close to her expected menstrual period. Rava defines the time as one 'onah (a set period), and notes that for a mitzvah journey, one is preoccupied.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that one who knows his wife is God-fearing and does not visit her (be intimate) is called a sinner, citing the verse 'וְיָדַעְתָּ כִּי שָׁלוֹם אׇהֳלֶךָ' (and you shall know that your tent is at peace).
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that a man is obligated to visit his wife (be intimate) when he goes on a journey, citing the same verse.

The Gemara questions the source, suggesting it should be derived from the verse 'וְאֶל אִישֵׁךְ תְּשׁוּקָתֵךְ' (and your desire shall be for your husband), which teaches that a woman longs for her husband when he goes on a journey.
Rav Yosef answers that the verse from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi is needed only for a case close to her expected menstrual period (וסתה), where the woman's desire alone would not suffice.
Rava defines the time frame for this obligation as one 'עונה' (a set period, typically a day or night).
Rava concludes that this obligation applies only for a discretionary journey (דבר הרשות), but for a mitzvah journey (דבר מצוה), one is preoccupied and exempt.

items.text: Praise for one who loves and honors his wife and family
items.text_en: Praise for one who loves and honors his wife and family
items.desc_en: The baraita lists praiseworthy behaviors: loving one's wife as oneself, honoring her more than oneself, guiding children in the right path, and marrying them off close to their maturity. Such a person merits the verse 'And you shall know that your tent is at peace.'

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists praiseworthy behaviors: loving one's wife as oneself, honoring her more than oneself, guiding children in the right path, and marrying them off close to their maturity, promising the verse 'And you shall know that your tent is at peace.'

items.text: Opening statement on lending to the poor
items.text_en: Opening statement on lending to the poor
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a verse about lending to the poor in their time of need, promising that God will answer their call.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing a verse promising that one who lends to the poor in their distress will be answered by God.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar: A man without a wife or land is not a man
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar: A man without a wife or land is not a man
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that a man without a wife is not considered a man, citing the verse 'male and female He created them and called their name Adam'. Similarly, a man without land is not a man, citing 'the earth He gave to the children of man'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that a man without a wife is not a man, citing the verse 'male and female He created them and called their name Adam', and similarly a man without land is not a man, citing 'the earth He gave to the children of man'.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar: 'Ezer kenegdo' interpreted
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar: 'Ezer kenegdo' interpreted
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains the verse 'Ezer kenegdo' (a helpmate opposite him): if he merits, she helps him; if not, she opposes him. An alternative version says she fights against him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse 'Ezer kenegdo' (a helpmate opposite him): if a man merits, she helps him; if not, she opposes him.

An alternative version presents Rabbi Elazar as noting a discrepancy between the written and read forms of 'kenegdo', and interpreting: if he merits, she is opposite him; if not, she fights against him.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei and Elijah: How does a woman help?
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei and Elijah: How does a woman help?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei asks Elijah how a woman helps a man. Elijah responds that a man brings wheat but cannot chew it, flax but cannot wear it; she enlightens his eyes and sets him on his feet.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei asks Elijah how a woman helps a man, citing the verse 'I will make him a helper'.
Elijah answers that a man brings wheat but cannot chew it, flax but cannot wear it; the woman enlightens his eyes and sets him on his feet.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar: Adam's satisfaction only with Eve
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar: Adam's satisfaction only with Eve
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that Adam cohabited with every animal and beast but was not satisfied until he cohabited with Eve, as per the verse 'This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that Adam cohabited with every animal and beast but was only satisfied after cohabiting with Eve, citing the verse 'This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh'.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar: Blessings through Israel
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar: Blessings through Israel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that God told Abraham He would bless him with two good blessings: Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite. All families of the earth are blessed only for Israel's sake, even ships from Gaul to Spain.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse 'וְנִבְרְכוּ בְךָ כֹּל מִשְׁפְּחֹת הָאֲדָמָה' (and all families of the earth shall be blessed through you) as God telling Abraham He will bless him with two good blessings: Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite.
Rabbi Elazar explains that 'כֹּל מִשְׁפְּחוֹת הָאֲדָמָה' (all families of the earth) includes even families dwelling on the land, and they are blessed only for Israel's sake.
Rabbi Elazar further explains that 'כׇּל גּוֹיֵי הָאָרֶץ' (all nations of the earth) includes even ships coming from Gaul to Spain, and they are blessed only for Israel's sake.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar: Craftsmen and land
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar: Craftsmen and land
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says all craftsmen will stand on land, citing a verse. He adds that no craft is lower than working the land. Rabbi Elazar saw a man plowing widthwise and advised him to plow lengthwise or engage in business instead.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that all craftsmen will eventually stand on land, citing the verse about sailors and oarsmen standing on the earth.
Rabbi Elazar adds that no craft is lower than working the land, as the verse uses the term 'וְיָרְדוּ' (they will descend).
Rabbi Elazar sees a man plowing widthwise and advises him to plow lengthwise or engage in business instead.

items.text: Rav and Rava: Business vs. land
items.text_en: Rav and Rava: Business vs. land
items.desc_en: Rav saw people winnowing and advised them to engage in business instead. Rava says 100 zuz in business yields meat and wine daily, while 100 zuz in land yields salt and grass, and also causes worry and disputes.

sub.desc_en: Rav sees people winnowing and tells them that engaging in business is better than their current work.
Rava contrasts the yield of 100 zuz in business (meat and wine daily) versus land (salt and grass), adding that land brings worry and disputes.

items.text: Rav Papa: Practical advice on farming and selling
items.text_en: Rav Papa: Practical advice on farming and selling
items.desc_en: Rav Papa advises: sow but do not buy; even if equal, these are blessed. Sell but do not discount; this applies to silk garments, but not to cloaks.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa advises that one should sow rather than buy, because even if the yield is equal, the homegrown produce is blessed.
Rav Papa advises that one should sell at full price rather than discount, applying this rule to silk garments but not to cloaks.

items.text: Proverbs on building and marriage
items.text_en: Proverbs on building and marriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara gives proverbs: plaster but do not smooth; smooth but do not build, for building leads to poverty. Buy land quickly, marry slowly. Go down a step to marry, go up a step to choose a best man.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a series of proverbs about building, marriage, and choosing a best man.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Avina: Punishment for Israel's sake
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Avina: Punishment for Israel's sake
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Avina says punishment comes to the world only for Israel's sake, citing verses about destroying nations and the call for Israel to fear God.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Avina states that punishment comes to the world only for Israel's sake, citing verses about destroyed nations and the call for Israel to take reproof.

items.text: Rav and Rabbi Chiyya: The bitterness of a bad wife
items.text_en: Rav and Rabbi Chiyya: The bitterness of a bad wife
items.desc_en: Rav parted from Rabbi Chiyya, who blessed him to be saved from something worse than death. Rav found the verse 'I find more bitter than death the woman'. Rav's wife vexed him by reversing his requests.

sub.desc_en: Rav was taking leave of Rabbi Chiyya, who blessed him to be saved from something worse than death.
The gemara asks: Is there indeed anything worse than death?
Rav went out, examined Scripture, and found the verse 'I find more bitter than death the woman' (Ecclesiastes 7:26).
Rav's wife vexed him by reversing his requests: when he asked for lentils (טְלוֹפְחֵי), she made him chickpeas (חִימְצֵי), and vice versa.

items.text: Chiyya's son reverses the wife's actions
items.text_en: Chiyya's son reverses the wife's actions
items.desc_en: When Chiyya grew up, he reversed his mother's actions. Rav told him not to do so, citing the verse about teaching one's tongue to speak falsehood.

sub.desc_en: The narrative reports that when Chiyya grew up, he reversed his mother's actions toward his father Rav.
Rav objects, saying 'Your mother is better than you!' and Chiyya clarifies that he himself reversed her actions.

sub.text: Rav's resolution with a proverb and a verse
sub.text_en: Rav's resolution with a proverb and a verse
sub.desc_en: Rav cites the folk saying 'one who comes from you teaches you a reason' and then forbids Chiyya from continuing, citing the verse 'לִמְּדוּ לְשׁוֹנָם דַּבֶּר שֶׁקֶר הַעֲוֵה' (they taught their tongue to speak falsehood, to do wrong).

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya's patience with his wife
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya's patience with his wife
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya's wife vexed him, but he would wrap things in his scarf and bring them to her. Rav asked why, and Rabbi Chiyya replied that it is enough that they raise our children and save us from sin.

sub.desc_en: The narrative introduces that Rabbi Chiyya's wife vexed him, yet he would wrap things in his scarf and bring them to her.
Rav asks Rabbi Chiyya why he brings gifts to his wife when she vexes him.
Rabbi Chiyya answers that it is enough that wives raise our children and save us from sin.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's contradictory teachings about women
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's contradictory teachings about women
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda teaches his son Rav Yitzchak a verse about the bitterness of women, then later teaches a verse about the joy of a first wife. When asked for examples, he points to his own mother, causing confusion.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's teaching to his son
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's teaching to his son
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda teaches his son Rav Yitzchak the verse 'וּמוֹצֶא אֲנִי מַר מִמָּוֶת אֶת הָאִשָּׁה' and identifies his own mother as the example of a bitter woman.

Rav Yehuda then teaches his son a verse about the joy of a first wife, again citing his own mother, creating a contradiction that the gemara notes by describing her as both harsh and pregnant with words.

items.text: Definition of a bad wife
items.text_en: Definition of a bad wife
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava offer contrasting descriptions of a bad wife: Abaye says she prepares the bed and table but turns her back, while Rava says she prepares the bed but turns her back.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the definition of a bad wife?
Abaye defines a bad wife as one who prepares the bed and table for her husband but turns her back on him.
Rava defines a bad wife as one who prepares the bed but turns her back on him.

items.text: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina on marriage and sin
items.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina on marriage and sin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina teaches that when a man marries, his sins are pardoned, citing the verse 'He who finds a wife finds good'. The Gemara notes that in the West, they ask whether the verse is 'found' or 'finds'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina teaches that when a man marries, his sins are pardoned, citing the verse 'He who finds a wife finds good'.
The Gemara notes that in the West, when a man marries, they ask whether the verse is 'found' (מצא) or 'finds' (מוצא), referencing the contrasting verses.

items.text: Rava's teachings on good and bad wives
items.text_en: Rava's teachings on good and bad wives
items.desc_en: Rava states that a bad wife should be divorced, and that a bad wife with a large ketubah is like a rival wife. He also compares a bad wife to a rainy day. He then contrasts the good wife, praised by Scripture, with the bad wife, compared to Gehinnom.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that a bad wife is a mitzvah to divorce, citing a verse.
Rava adds that a bad wife with a large ketubah is like a rival wife, as people say.
Rava compares a bad wife to a rainy day, citing a verse.
Rava concludes by contrasting the good wife, praised by Scripture, with the bad wife, compared to Gehinnom.

items.text: Interpretations of biblical verses about bad wives
items.text_en: Interpretations of biblical verses about bad wives
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman, Rav Chisda, and Rav Chanan bar Rava interpret various verses as referring to a bad wife with a large ketubah. Rabbi Eliezer interprets one verse as referring to heretics.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha interprets the verse 'הנני מביא רעה אשר לא יוכלו לצאת ממנה' (Behold I bring evil from which they cannot escape) as referring to a bad wife with a large ketubah.

sub.text: Rav Chisda citing Mar Ukva bar Chiyya
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Mar Ukva bar Chiyya
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva bar Chiyya interprets the verse 'נתנני ה' בידי לא אוכל קום' (The Lord has given me into hands from which I cannot rise) as referring to a bad wife with a large ketubah.
The Western sages interpret the same verse as referring to one whose sustenance depends on his money (i.e., a dependent situation).

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava in the name of Rav interprets the verse 'בניך ובנותיך נתונים לעם אחר' (Your sons and daughters are given to another people) as referring to a father's wife (a stepmother).

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava in the name of Rav interprets the verse 'בגוי נבל אכעיסם' (With a vile nation I will anger them) as referring to a bad wife with a large ketubah.
Rabbi Eliezer interprets the same verse as referring to heretics (מינים), citing the verse 'אמר נבל בלבו אין אלהים' (The fool said in his heart: There is no God).

items.text: Interpretations of 'a foolish nation'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'a foolish nation'
items.desc_en: A baraita interprets 'a foolish nation' as the people of Barbaria and Martnai who walk naked. Rabbi Yochanan interprets it as the 'chaverim' (associates), and a story is told about them in Babylonia.

sub.desc_en: A baraita interprets 'a foolish nation' as the people of Barbaria and Martnai who walk naked in the market.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'a foolish nation' as the 'chaverim' (associates), and a story is told about them in Babylonia where they fell and were accused of bribery.

items.text: Decrees and the digging of graves
items.text_en: Decrees and the digging of graves
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses decrees made for various reasons, and then explains that the dead are dug up because the living rejoice on their festival days, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a general principle that decrees were enacted for three matters because of three corresponding concerns: meat because of priestly gifts, bathhouses because of ritual immersion.

The Gemara explains that the dead are dug up because the living rejoice on their festival days, citing a verse and a statement by Rabbah bar Shmuel that in the sin of the living, the dead are disinterred.

items.text: Rava's question about the fate of the wicked
items.text_en: Rava's question about the fate of the wicked
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari about a contradiction in verses regarding the fate of the wicked, and is answered that death is chosen for the wicked to prevent them from sinning further.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari about a contradiction between two verses: one says the wicked will not be gathered or buried, and the other says death is chosen over life.
Rabbah bar Mari answers that death is chosen for the wicked so they will not live in this world and sin further, and thus fall into Gehinnom.

items.text: Quotes from Ben Sira about women
items.text_en: Quotes from Ben Sira about women
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites several proverbs from the book of Ben Sira about good and bad wives, and advice about avoiding temptation and not worrying about tomorrow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Ben Sira's proverbs about a good wife being a good gift and a bad wife being leprosy, with the remedy of divorce.
The Gemara continues citing Ben Sira's warnings against temptation from a charming woman and the prevalence of deceit.
The Gemara concludes the Ben Sira citation with advice not to worry about tomorrow and to limit confidants.

items.text: The importance of procreation
items.text_en: The importance of procreation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi says the son of David will not come until all souls in the body are finished. Tannaitic sources debate whether one who does not procreate is considered a murderer, diminishes the divine image, or both. Ben Azzai, who did not marry, defends himself by saying his soul loves the Torah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi states that the son of David (the Messiah) will not come until all the souls in the body (the treasury of souls) are exhausted, citing a verse.

A baraita is cited: Rabbi Eliezer says that one who does not engage in procreation (פריה ורביה) is as if he sheds blood, linking the verse 'one who sheds blood' with the command 'be fruitful and multiply'.
Rabbi Yaakov says that one who does not procreate is as if he diminishes the divine image (הדמות), citing the verse about man being made in God's image followed by the command to be fruitful.
Ben Azzai says that one who does not procreate is as if he both sheds blood and diminishes the divine image, citing the same verse.
The Sages object to Ben Azzai: some preach well and act well, some act well but do not preach well, but Ben Azzai preaches well yet does not act well (since he never married).
Ben Azzai defends himself: his soul loves the Torah, and the world can be sustained through others (who do procreate).

items.text: A baraita on the verse 'Return, O Lord'
items.text_en: A baraita on the verse 'Return, O Lord'
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a baraita interpreting the verse 'Return, O Lord, the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita begins by citing the verse 'Return, O Lord, the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel'.

items.text: Opening argument: refraining from procreation causes the Shekhinah to depart
items.text_en: Opening argument: refraining from procreation causes the Shekhinah to depart
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if Israel is just short of 22,000 and one person does not engage in procreation, that person causes the Divine Presence to depart. Abba Ḥanan cites Rabbi Eliezer that such a person is liable to death, citing Nadav and Avihu. Others say he causes the Shekhinah to depart, citing the verse about God being a God to you and your seed after you.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if Israel is just short of 22,000 and one person refrains from procreation, that person causes the Divine Presence (שכינה) to depart from Israel.
Abba Ḥanan reports in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that one who does not engage in procreation is liable to death (חייב מיתה), citing the verse about Nadav and Avihu who had no children.
Others say that such a person causes the Divine Presence (שכינה) to depart from Israel, citing the verse about God being a God to you and your seed after you.

items.text: Mishnah: ten childless years obligates divorce
items.text_en: Mishnah: ten childless years obligates divorce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a man marries a woman and waits ten years without children, he may not neglect the mitzva of procreation. If he divorces her, she may marry another, and the second husband may also wait ten years. If she miscarries, the count begins from the miscarriage.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a man who marries and waits ten childless years must divorce, and the count resets after a miscarriage.

items.text: Gemara: baraita on the ten-year rule and exceptions
items.text_en: Gemara: baraita on the ten-year rule and exceptions
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that if a man marries and waits ten childless years, he must divorce and pay the ketubah, lest he not merit children from her. The proof is from Abraham's ten-year stay in Canaan, teaching that time outside the Land does not count. If either spouse is ill or imprisoned, that time does not count.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that a man who marries and waits ten childless years must divorce and pay the ketubah, lest he not merit children from her.
The baraita cites Abraham's ten-year stay in Canaan as a mnemonic, teaching that time outside the Land does not count toward the ten-year waiting period.
The baraita adds that if either spouse is ill or imprisoned, that time does not count toward the ten-year period.

items.text: Rava's question: why not learn from Isaac?
items.text_en: Rava's question: why not learn from Isaac?
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Naḥman why we do not learn from Isaac, who married at 40 and had children at 60, implying a 20-year wait. Rav Naḥman answers that Isaac was barren.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Naḥman why we do not learn from Isaac, who married at 40 and fathered children at 60, implying a 20-year waiting period.
Rav Naḥman answers that Isaac was barren, so his case is not a precedent for a normal couple.

items.text: Objection: Abraham was also barren, but his years are used for Jacob's chronology
items.text_en: Objection: Abraham was also barren, but his years are used for Jacob's chronology
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Abraham was also barren, yet his years are not used for the ten-year rule. Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba says in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan that Ishmael's years were counted to establish Jacob's chronology.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Isaac's barrenness explains why his years are not used, then Abraham was also barren, so his years should similarly be excluded.
The Gemara answers that Abraham's years are needed for a different purpose: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan that Ishmael's years were counted to establish Jacob's chronology.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzḥak: Isaac was barren, and the verse teaches both were barren
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzḥak: Isaac was barren, and the verse teaches both were barren
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzḥak states that Isaac was barren, as the verse says 'before his wife' rather than 'for his wife', implying both were barren. The Gemara questions why the verse says 'He was entreated for him' rather than 'for them', and answers that the prayer of a righteous son of a righteous person is not like that of a righteous son of a wicked person.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzḥak asserts that Isaac was barren, proving from the verse's wording 'לְנֹכַח אִשְׁתּוֹ' (before his wife) rather than 'עַל אִשְׁתּוֹ' (for his wife), which implies both were barren.
The Gemara objects: if both were barren, the verse should have said 'וַיֵּעָתֵר לָהֶם' (He was entreated for them) rather than 'לוֹ' (for him).

The Gemara answers that the prayer of a righteous son of a righteous person (Isaac) is not comparable to that of a righteous son of a wicked person (Abraham), so the verse focuses on Isaac's prayer alone.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzḥak and Rabbi Ammi: why the Patriarchs were barren and the power of prayer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzḥak and Rabbi Ammi: why the Patriarchs were barren and the power of prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzḥak explains that the Patriarchs were barren because the Holy One desires the prayers of the righteous, and compares prayer to a pitchfork that overturns produce, so prayer overturns God's attribute of anger to mercy. Rabbi Ammi adds that Abraham and Sarah were tumtumim, citing the verse 'Look to the rock from which you were hewn'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzḥak asks why the Patriarchs were barren and answers that God desires the prayers of the righteous.
Rabbi Yitzḥak explains that the prayer of the righteous is compared to a pitchfork (עתר) that overturns produce, so prayer overturns God's attribute of anger to mercy.
Rabbi Ammi adds that Abraham and Sarah were tumtumim (of indeterminate sex), citing the verse 'Look to the rock from which you were hewn'.

items.text: Sarah was an Aylonit
items.text_en: Sarah was an Aylonit
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Rabbah bar Avuha that Sarah was an aylonit (incapable of bearing children), based on the verse 'and Sarai was barren, she had no child' — implying she lacked even a womb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses from Isaiah about being hewn from a rock and looking to Abraham and Sarah.

sub.text: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Rabbah bar Avuha that Sarah was an aylonit (incapable of bearing children), based on the verse 'and Sarai was barren, she had no child' — implying she lacked even a womb.

items.text: Duration of pregnancy in different generations
items.text_en: Duration of pregnancy in different generations
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah and Rabbah debate the minimum pregnancy duration: Rav Yehudah says 2.5 years for later generations, while Rabbah says 3 years, corresponding to the three 'visitations' (Rosh Hashanah) when Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah were remembered.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav states that the rule of a short pregnancy applies only to early generations with long lives, but for later generations with shorter lives the minimum is two and a half years, corresponding to three pregnancy terms.
Rabbah in the name of Rav Nachman gives a different minimum of three years, corresponding to the three 'visitations' (Rosh Hashanah) when Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah were remembered.

items.text: Objection to the rules and the woman's responsibility
items.text_en: Objection to the rules and the woman's responsibility
items.desc_en: Rabbah objects to the above rules, noting that in David's time lifespans were already short (70 years), contradicting the distinction between early and later generations. The Gemara then questions whether the woman is punished for not having children, concluding she is not since she is not commanded to procreate.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah objects to the earlier rules by pointing out that in David's time lifespans were already short (70 years), contradicting the distinction between early and later generations.
The Gemara questions whether the woman is punished for not having children, given the earlier phrase 'perhaps he was not worthy to be built from her'.
The Gemara answers that the woman is not punished because she is not commanded regarding פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה (procreation).

items.text: Stories of Sages who were childless
items.text_en: Stories of Sages who were childless
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Abba bar Zavda, Rav Giddel, Rabbi Chelbo, Rav Sheshet, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov were all childless due to being 'uprooted' from Rav Huna's study hall. Rav Acha bar Yaakov was saved by wisdom, as per the verse 'wisdom preserves its owner'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier claim that a childless man is not punished, citing the story where the Rabbis told Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to marry and have children.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Abba bar Zavda was merely deflecting the Rabbis, as he was actually 'uprooted' (איעקר) from Rav Huna's study hall and thus could not have children.

The Gemara lists Rav Giddel, Rabbi Chelbo, Rav Sheshet, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov as also being 'uprooted' from Rav Huna's study hall, with Rav Acha bar Yaakov saved by wisdom as per the verse 'wisdom preserves its owner'.

items.text: Mishnah and dispute on circumcision after deaths
items.text_en: Mishnah and dispute on circumcision after deaths
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman's second husband dies, she may not marry a third. The Gemara identifies this as Rabbi's opinion, citing a beraita where Rabbi says after two sons die from circumcision, the third should not be circumcised, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the third may be circumcised but not the fourth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman's second husband dies, she may not marry a third.

The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as Rabbi's opinion, citing a beraita where Rabbi says after two sons die from circumcision the third should not be circumcised, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the third may be circumcised but not the fourth.

items.text: Contradictory beraita and the principle of chazakah
items.text_en: Contradictory beraita and the principle of chazakah
items.desc_en: A contradictory beraita is cited. Rabbi Yochanan relates a case in Tzippori where four sisters married and three died, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel told the fourth not to circumcise. The Gemara questions whether he would have said the same for the third, and concludes that the story teaches that sisters establish a chazakah (presumption).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradictory beraita and asks which version is authoritative.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba relates a story in the name of Rabbi Yochanan about four sisters in Tzippori, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel told the fourth not to circumcise after three died.
The Gemara objects that perhaps Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel would have said the same to the third sister, undermining the proof.
The Gemara resolves that the story's point is to teach that sisters establish a חֲזָקָה (presumption), not to decide the halacha for the third sister.

items.text: Rava's ruling and a conflicting incident
items.text_en: Rava's ruling and a conflicting incident
items.desc_en: Rava rules that since sisters establish a chazakah, one should not marry into a family of epileptics or lepers after three instances. However, Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef reports that Rabbi Yochanan circumcised a third son on Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbat, contradicting the chazakah.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that since sisters establish a chazakah (presumption), one should not marry into a family of epileptics or lepers after three instances.
Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef reports that Rabbi Yochanan circumcised a third son on Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbat, contradicting the chazakah.

items.text: Abaye's risky marriage and Rava's criticism
items.text_en: Abaye's risky marriage and Rava's criticism
items.desc_en: Abaye warns about the danger, then himself marries a woman from a family where two previous husbands died, and he also dies. Rava criticizes this, citing a distinction between Avin (who is reliable) and Yitzchak Sumaka (who is not), and questions whether the dispute applies to marriage as well as circumcision.

sub.desc_en: Abaye warns Rava that his action ties a prohibition and a danger.
Abaye ignores his own warning, marries a woman from a dangerous family, and dies.
Rava objects that Abaye acted against his own principle, citing the distinction between Avin and Yitzchak Sumaka, and questions whether the dispute applies to marriage as well as circumcision.

items.text: Dispute on marriage after deaths and the cause
items.text_en: Dispute on marriage after deaths and the cause
items.desc_en: A beraita states that after two husbands die, a woman may not marry a third (Rabbi) or may marry a third but not a fourth (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel). The Gemara explains the reason: for circumcision it is due to blood types, but for marriage, Rav Huna says 'a spring causes it' (the woman's body), while Rav Ashi says 'mazal causes it'. The difference is if she was betrothed and he died, or if he fell from a palm tree.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi rules that after two husbands die, a woman may not marry a third; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules she may marry a third but not a fourth.
The Gemara asks: regarding circumcision, the reason is blood-type tendencies, but what is the reason for the marriage restriction?

sub.text: Rav Mordechai citing Avimi from Hagronya in the name of Rav Huna
