sub.text_en: Rav Mordechai citing Avimi from Hagronya in the name of Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai reports to Rav Ashi: Avimi from Hagronya said in the name of Rav Huna that 'a spring causes it' (the woman's body is the cause), while Rav Ashi himself says 'mazal causes it' (astrological fate).

The Gemara explains the practical difference between the two views: a case where she was betrothed and he died (not married, so no 'spring' effect), or where he fell from a palm tree (accidental death, not mazal-related).

items.text: Halakhic conclusion and examples
items.text_en: Halakhic conclusion and examples
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks Rava about the halakha, and Rava initially jokes, then clarifies: for marriage and lashes, the halakha follows Rabbi; for sotah and goring ox, it follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Examples are given: a woman who married twice and husbands died (marriage), one who was lashed twice (lashes), and the beginning of the mishnah on sotah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks Rava whether the halakha follows Rabbi or Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and Rava initially jokes by answering 'yes' to both.
Rava clarifies that the halakha follows Rabbi for marriage and lashes, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel for sotah and the goring ox.
The gemara cites the mishnah about lashes and the beginning of the mishnah on sotah as examples supporting Rava's ruling.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and related Tosefta
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and related Tosefta
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman establishes a fixed menstrual cycle only after three occurrences, and a goring ox becomes mu'ad only after three warnings. The Gemara then cites a Tosefta: a woman who married twice and had no children may only marry a third man who already has children; if she marries one without children, she leaves without a ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a woman establishes a fixed menstrual cycle only after three occurrences, and a goring ox becomes mu'ad only after three warnings.
The Gemara cites a Tosefta: a woman who married twice and had no children may only marry a third man who already has children; if she marries one without children, she leaves without a ketubah.

items.text: First inquiry: Can previous husbands demand return of ketubah?
items.text_en: First inquiry: Can previous husbands demand return of ketubah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if a woman married a third husband and still had no children, can the first two husbands demand their ketubah payments back, claiming she was the cause? The Gemara suggests she can argue that her fertility only waned now, not earlier.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: if a woman married a third husband and still had no children, can the first two husbands demand their ketubah payments back, or can she argue that her fertility only waned now?
The Gemara resolves that it is reasonable for her to claim that her fertility only diminished now, so the previous husbands cannot reclaim their ketubah payments.

items.text: Second inquiry: Can the third husband be sued after she has children?
items.text_en: Second inquiry: Can the third husband be sued after she has children?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if she married a fourth husband and had children, can she then demand her ketubah from the third husband? The Gemara suggests he can argue that her silence at the time of divorce indicated acceptance, so she cannot now claim he was at fault.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: if she married a fourth husband and had children, can she then demand her ketubah from the third husband?
The Gemara suggests that the third husband can argue that her silence at the time of divorce indicated acceptance, so she cannot now claim he was at fault.

items.text: Rav Pappa's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects: if she remained silent, the get would be invalid and her children would be mamzerim. Therefore, the Gemara concludes that she can claim her fertility was restored only now.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects that if the woman remained silent, the get would be invalid and her children would be mamzerim.
The Gemara resolves that she can claim her fertility was restored only now, avoiding the problem of the get being invalid.

items.text: Credibility of the wife's claim about virility
items.text_en: Credibility of the wife's claim about virility
items.desc_en: When a husband claims he is not the father and the wife claims he is, Rabbi Ammi rules that the wife is believed because she knows whether he 'shoots like an arrow' (i.e., is fertile), while he does not know this about himself.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents the case: the husband claims the child is not from him, and the wife claims it is from him.
Rabbi Ammi rules that the wife is believed in matters between them, because she knows whether he 'shoots like an arrow' (is fertile), while he does not know this about himself.

items.text: Marrying another woman to test fertility
items.text_en: Marrying another woman to test fertility
items.desc_en: If a husband says he will marry another woman to test his fertility, Rabbi Ammi rules he must divorce and pay the ketubah, as one who marries a second wife while still married must divorce and pay. Rava disagrees, allowing a man to marry multiple wives as long as he can support them.

sub.desc_en: The husband declares he will marry another woman to test his own fertility.
Rabbi Ammi rules that even in this case the husband must divorce and pay the ketubah.
Rabbi Ammi cites his general principle that anyone who marries a second wife while still married must divorce and pay the ketubah.
Rava objects, asserting that a man may marry multiple wives while still married to his first wife.
Rava qualifies his ruling, stating that this is only permitted if the husband has the means to support all his wives.

items.text: Credibility of a woman regarding miscarriages
items.text_en: Credibility of a woman regarding miscarriages
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses cases where a husband and wife disagree about the number of miscarriages. Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar rule that the woman is believed because she would not establish a reputation for herself as a miscarrier or as one who miscarries frequently if it were not true.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a husband claims his wife miscarried within ten years, and she denies it.
Rabbi Ammi rules that the woman is believed, because she would not establish a reputation for herself as a miscarrier if it were not true.
The Gemara presents a second case where a woman is established as a miscarrier, and the husband claims two miscarriages while she claims three.
Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar reports that in the study hall they ruled the woman is believed, because she would not establish a reputation for herself as a miscarrier if it were not true.

items.text: Mishnah: Obligation of procreation
items.text_en: Mishnah: Obligation of procreation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man is commanded to procreate, but not a woman. Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka argues that both are commanded, citing the verse where God blessed them and said 'Be fruitful and multiply'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man is commanded to procreate, but not a woman; Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka argues that both are commanded, citing the verse 'Be fruitful and multiply'.

items.text: Gemara: Source for the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the biblical source for the Mishnah's ruling. Rabbi Ila'a quotes Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon that the verse 'and subdue it' implies a man's way to subdue, not a woman's. An objection is raised that 'subdue it' could imply two, but Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains it is written defectively. Rav Yosef cites another verse where God addresses only the man.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of the Mishnah's ruling that a man is commanded regarding procreation but not a woman.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a cites Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon that the verse 'וּמִלְאוּ אֶת הָאָרֶץ וְכִבְשׁוּהָ' (fill the earth and subdue it) implies a man's way to subdue, not a woman's.
The Gemara objects that the word 'וְכִבְשׁוּהָ' (subdue it) is in the plural, implying both man and woman are commanded.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the verse is written defectively as 'וְכׇבְשֶׁהָ' (subdue her), in the singular, referring only to the man.
Rav Yosef cites another verse where God addresses only the man in the singular 'פְּרֵה וּרְבֵה' (be fruitful and multiply), not the plural 'פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ'.

items.text: Laws of rebuke and altering truth for peace
items.text_en: Laws of rebuke and altering truth for peace
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a quotes Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon that it is a mitzvah to say something that will be heard and not to say something that will not be heard. Rabbi Abba says it is an obligation. Rabbi Ila'a further states that it is permitted to alter the truth for the sake of peace, citing the example of Jacob's sons. Rabbi Natan says it is a mitzvah, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that peace is so great that even God altered the truth.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon states that just as it is a מצוה (commandment) to say something that will be heard, so too it is a מצוה not to say something that will not be heard.

Rabbi Abba upgrades the rule from a מצוה (commandment) to a חובה (obligation), citing the verse 'אַל תּוֹכַח לֵץ פֶּן יִשְׂנָאֶךָּ הוֹכַח לְחָכָם וְיֶאֱהָבֶךָּ' (Do not rebuke a scoffer lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man and he will love you).

sub.text: Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon rules that it is מותר (permitted) for a person to alter the truth for the sake of peace, citing the verse where Jacob's sons told Joseph 'אָבִיךְ צִוָּה... כֹּה תֹאמְרוּ לְיוֹסֵף אָנָּא שָׂא נָא' (Your father commanded... thus shall you say to Joseph: Please forgive...).
Rabbi Natan says it is a מצוה (commandment) to alter the truth for peace, citing the verse where Samuel said 'אֵיךְ אֵלֵךְ וְשָׁמַע שָׁאוּל וַהֲרָגָנִי' (How can I go? Saul will hear and kill me).

The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught that peace is so great that even the Holy One, blessed be He, altered the truth, as initially it is written 'וַאֲדוֹנִי זָקֵן' (and my master is old) and finally it is written 'וַאֲנִי זָקַנְתִּי' (and I have grown old).

items.text: Dispute about the halakha of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
items.text_en: Dispute about the halakha of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
items.desc_en: There is a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi about whether the halakha follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka. It is concluded that Rabbi Yochanan himself said the halakha is not like him, as evidenced by Rabbi Avahu's statement which was rejected by Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi. Another version attributes the statement to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, and Rav Pappa questions why they did not simply tell him that Rabbi Yochanan did not say that.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi about whether the halakha follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.

The gemara infers that Rabbi Yochanan himself said the halakha is not like Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, based on an incident where Rabbi Avahu cited him saying 'halakha' and Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi rebuffed him.

sub.text: Alternative version and Rav Pappa's question
sub.text_en: Alternative version and Rav Pappa's question
sub.desc_en: An alternative version attributes the statement to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, and Rav Pappa questions why they did not simply tell him that Rabbi Yochanan did not say that.

items.text: Practical ruling: Woman who claims ketubah
items.text_en: Practical ruling: Woman who claims ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks a practical ruling. Rabbi Acha bar Chanina quotes Rabbi Avahu quoting Rabbi Assi that a case came before Rabbi Yochanan in the synagogue of Caesarea, and he ruled that the husband must divorce and give the ketubah. This implies the woman is commanded, otherwise why would she get a ketubah? The Gemara deflects that perhaps she came with a claim. Stories are brought of women who came before Rabbi Ammi and Rav Nachman, who initially said they are not commanded but then forced the husband to give the ketubah when the woman argued she would be left without support.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what conclusion was reached about the halakhic dispute.

sub.text: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina quoting Rabbi Avahu quoting Rabbi Assi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina quoting Rabbi Avahu quoting Rabbi Assi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled in Caesarea that a husband must divorce and give the ketubah, implying the woman is commanded.
The Gemara deflects that perhaps the woman came with another claim, not because she is commanded.

sub.text: Story of a woman before Rabbi Ammi
sub.text_en: Story of a woman before Rabbi Ammi
sub.desc_en: A woman came before Rabbi Ammi; he initially said she is not commanded, but when she argued about old age, he forced the husband to give the ketubah.

sub.text: Story of a woman before Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Story of a woman before Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: A woman came before Rav Nachman; he initially said she is not commanded, but when she argued about needing support and burial, he forced the husband to give the ketubah.

items.text: Story of Yehudit and the sterility potion
items.text_en: Story of Yehudit and the sterility potion
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Yehudit, the wife of Rabbi Chiyya, suffered from childbirth pain. She asked Rabbi Chiyya if a woman is commanded to procreate, and he said no. She then took a sterility potion. Later, when the matter was revealed, Rabbi Chiyya expressed regret, saying she could have borne him another set of twins like Yehuda and Chizkiya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Yehudit, wife of רבי חייא (Rabbi Ḥiyya), suffered severe birthing pain, disguised herself, asked him whether a woman is commanded to be fruitful and multiply, and upon hearing 'no', drank a sterility potion.
When the matter was revealed, רבי חייא (Rabbi Ḥiyya) expressed regret, saying she could have borne him another set of twins like Yehuda and Ḥizkiyya, and Pazi and Tavi.

items.text: Opening question about a half-slave woman
items.text_en: Opening question about a half-slave woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a previous statement about a half-slave, half-free woman, citing a story where the court forced her master to free her. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that they treated her as ownerless.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a brief word linking to the previous discussion.
The Gemara questions whether women are commanded to be fruitful and multiply, citing a story where the court forced a master to free his half-slave woman.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the court freed her not for procreation but because she was treated as ownerless due to promiscuity.
The Gemara signals a return to the main topic of the mishna.

items.text: Mishnah: Slaves of a widow or divorcee married to a priest
items.text_en: Mishnah: Slaves of a widow or divorcee married to a priest
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a widow married to a High Priest, or a divorcee or chalutzah to an ordinary priest, brings עבדי מלוג (who do not eat terumah) and עבדי צאן ברזל (who do eat). It defines these categories and adds cases of a bat Yisrael married to a priest and a bat kohen married to a Yisrael.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a widow married to a High Priest, or a divorcee or חלוצה (ḥalutza) to a common priest, brings עבדי מלוג (usufruct slaves) who do not eat תרומה (teruma) and עבדי צאן ברזל (guaranteed investment slaves) who do eat.

The Mishnah defines עבדי מלוג (usufruct slaves) as those whose loss or gain belongs to the wife, and עבדי צאן ברזל (guaranteed investment slaves) as those whose loss or gain belongs to the husband, who therefore eat תרומה (teruma).
The Mishnah adds that a בת ישראל (Israelite woman) married to a priest brings slaves who eat תרומה (teruma), while a בת כהן (priest's daughter) married to an Israelite brings slaves who do not eat.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Why don't עבדי מלוג eat terumah?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Why don't עבדי מלוג eat terumah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why עבדי מלוג do not eat terumah, citing a baraita that a priest's acquired slaves eat terumah, and a principle that one who eats can feed others, while one who does not eat cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why עבדי מלוג (usufruct slaves) do not eat תרומה (priestly portion), proposing they should be considered like the priest's acquisition who acquired an acquisition.

The Gemara cites a ברייתא (baraita) that derives from the verse 'וְכֹהֵן כִּי יִקְנֶה נֶפֶשׁ קִנְיַן כַּסְפּוֹ' (Leviticus 22:11) that a priest's wife's slaves and a priest's slaves' slaves also eat תרומה (priestly portion).
The Gemara answers with the principle that only one who himself eats תרומה (priestly portion) can enable others to eat, and since the forbidden wife does not eat, her slaves also do not eat.

items.text: Objection and resolution: The principle of 'one who eats feeds'
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: The principle of 'one who eats feeds'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that an uncircumcised person or a mamzer cannot eat terumah but can feed others. Ravina resolves that the principle applies only to a 'kinyan' (acquired property) that itself eats.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the principle 'one who eats feeds' by citing uncircumcised people (ערל) and all impure people who cannot eat terumah but can feed it to others.
The Gemara rejects the objection by explaining that those people are physically pained (their mouths hurt) and therefore not considered 'eaters' in the relevant sense.
The Gemara objects further by citing a mamzer (bastard) who cannot eat terumah but can feed it to others.
Ravina resolves the objection by clarifying that the principle applies only to a 'kinyan' (acquired property) that itself eats; a kinyan that eats feeds, but one that does not eat does not feed.

items.text: Rava's explanation: Rabbinic decree to prevent suspicion
items.text_en: Rava's explanation: Rabbinic decree to prevent suspicion
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the slaves could eat terumah by Torah law, but the Sages decreed they should not, to prevent the woman from saying 'I do not eat, my slaves do not eat' and thus appearing as a zonah to her husband.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that by Torah law the slaves may eat, but the Sages decreed they should not, to prevent the woman from saying 'I do not eat, my slaves do not eat' and thus appearing as a zonah to her husband.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation and refinement
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation and refinement
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi initially suggests a decree lest she feed the slaves after her husband's death, but the Gemara objects that this would apply to a bat Yisrael married to a priest. Rav Ashi then refines: the decree applies specifically to a widow who was a bat kohen, who might mistakenly think she returns to her father's house and eat terumah there, not realizing she becomes a chalalah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi proposes a decree: lest the widow feed the slaves terumah after her husband's death.
The Gemara objects: if the decree applies, then a bat Yisrael married to a priest should also be forbidden to feed her slaves, which is not the case.

Rav Ashi refines: the decree applies specifically to a widow who is a bat kohen, who might mistakenly think she returns to her father's house and eat terumah there, not realizing she becomes a חללה (profaned woman).
The Gemara concludes: the decree is limited to a widow who is a bat kohen; for a widow who is a bat Yisrael, the rabbis do not dispute that she may feed her slaves.

items.text: Transition to a new dispute: The wife's claim to her utensils
items.text_en: Transition to a new dispute: The wife's claim to her utensils
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute about a woman who brings property into her marriage and later claims her utensils, while the husband offers to pay their value. Rav Yehuda begins to state his opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute about a woman who brings property into her marriage and later claims her utensils, while the husband offers to pay their value, and begins to state Rav Yehuda's opinion.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Ami on the law of shevach beit aviha
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Ami on the law of shevach beit aviha
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda holds that the increase belongs to the wife, while Rabbi Ami holds it belongs to the husband because he bears responsibility for losses. Rav Safra clarifies that the mishna does not say 'they are his' but rather 'since he is responsible for them'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that the law is with the wife, because the increase (שבח בית אביה) belongs to her.
Rabbi Ami rules that the law is with the husband, because since he bears responsibility for losses (אחריות), he also eats the increase.
Rav Safra clarifies that the mishna does not say 'they are his' but rather 'since he is responsible for them', implying the increase is not actually his property.

items.text: Gemara's objection from the mishna of a hired cow and terumah
items.text_en: Gemara's objection from the mishna of a hired cow and terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether responsibility for loss always permits feeding terumah, citing a mishna where an Israelite who hires a cow from a priest cannot feed it terumah even though he bears responsibility. It then distinguishes between a hirer and a borrower, concluding that only a borrower (who bears full liability) may feed terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether bearing responsibility for loss always permits feeding תרומה (priestly portion), citing a mishna where an Israelite who hires a cow from a priest cannot feed it תרומה even though he bears responsibility.
The Gemara distinguishes between a hirer (who bears only limited liability) and a borrower (who bears full liability), concluding that only a borrower who appraises the cow may feed it תרומה.

items.text: Two baraitot supporting each opinion
items.text_en: Two baraitot supporting each opinion
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef sit and state that there is a baraita supporting Rabbi Ami (regarding tzon barzel going out with a tooth or eye for the husband) and another supporting Rav Yehuda (regarding a wife's property that the husband cannot sell).

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef sit at the conclusion of Rav Naḥman's sermon and state that there is a baraita supporting Rav Yehuda and another supporting Rabbi Ami.
The baraita states that slaves of guaranteed investment go free for a tooth or eye only when the husband strikes them, not the wife, indicating they belong to the husband.

The baraita rules that a husband cannot sell property his wife brought in as guaranteed investment, and even his own gift added to her dowry cannot be sold; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel ruled that the husband repossesses from purchasers.

items.text: Rava cites Rav Nachman's ruling in favor of Rav Yehuda
items.text_en: Rava cites Rav Nachman's ruling in favor of Rav Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rava reports that Rav Nachman rules the halakha follows Rav Yehuda. When Rava objects that a baraita supports Rabbi Ami, Rav Nachman explains that Rav Yehuda's reasoning is more compelling because the increase belongs to her father's house.

sub.desc_en: Rava reports that Rav Nachman rules the halakha follows Rav Yehuda.
Rava objects that a baraita supports Rabbi Ami's position.
Rav Nachman explains that despite the baraita, Rav Yehuda's reasoning is more compelling because the increase belongs to her father's house.

items.text: Case of a widow's garment sold for burial expenses
items.text_en: Case of a widow's garment sold for burial expenses
items.desc_en: A woman brought a woolen cloak as part of her ketubah; her husband died, and the orphans sold it for burial expenses. Rava rules that the burial acquired it. When challenged that Rav Nachman ruled like Rav Yehuda, Rava's son explains that Rav Yehuda concedes that property not yet collected is still in the husband's domain.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a woman brought a woolen cloak as part of her ketubah; her husband died, and the orphans sold it for burial expenses.
Rava rules that the burial acquired the cloak, meaning the orphans are not liable to the widow for its value.
Naanai objects to Rav Kahana: but Rava himself cited Rav Nachman that the halacha follows Rav Yehuda, who holds the wife retains rights to her property.
Rav Kahana resolves: Rav Yehuda concedes that property not yet collected (מחוסר גוביינא) is still in the husband's domain, so the burial's acquisition stands.

items.text: Transition to a new topic: Rava's principle
items.text_en: Transition to a new topic: Rava's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion, noting that Rava holds a consistent principle regarding hekdesh and chametz, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rava's consistent principle regarding hekdesh and chametz, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on appreciation of property
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on appreciation of property
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that if a woman brought two items worth 1000 zuz and they appreciated to 2000, she takes one in her ketubah and pays for the other, because the appreciation belongs to her father's house. The Gemara questions why this is repeated, and explains it teaches that even when she pays and takes, the appreciation is hers.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that a woman who brought two items worth 1000 zuz that appreciated to 2000 takes one in her ketubah and pays for the other, because the appreciation belongs to her father's house.
The Gemara questions why Rav Yehuda repeats this ruling, since he already stated that the appreciation belongs to her father's house.
The Gemara explains that the repetition teaches that even when she pays and takes the item, the appreciation is still hers.

items.text: Mishnah: Fetus of a bat Yisrael married to a kohen
items.text_en: Mishnah: Fetus of a bat Yisrael married to a kohen
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a bat Yisrael married to a kohen dies pregnant, her slaves may not eat terumah because of the fetus's portion, as a fetus disqualifies but does not enable. The Sages extend this to a bat kohen married to a kohen.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a bat Yisrael married to a kohen dies pregnant, her slaves may not eat terumah because of the fetus's share, as a fetus disqualifies but does not enable, per Rabbi Yosei.
The Sages argue that since Rabbi Yosei testified about a bat Yisrael, the same should apply to a bat kohen married to a kohen who dies pregnant.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry into Rabbi Yossi's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry into Rabbi Yossi's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yossi's ruling is because a fetus in a non-priestess's womb is a non-priest, or because a born child enables but an unborn one does not. The practical difference is for a fetus in a priestess's womb. Rabbah holds the former, Rav Yosef the latter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: is Rabbi Yosei's reasoning that a fetus in a non-priestess's womb is a non-priest, or that a born child enables but an unborn one does not?
The Gemara asks: what is the practical difference between the two possible reasons? It is the case of a fetus in the womb of a priestess.
Rabbah states that Rabbi Yosei's reasoning is that a fetus in the womb of a non-priest is a non-priest.
Rav Yosef says that Rabbi Yosei's reasoning is that only a born child enables others to partake of teruma, but an unborn one does not.

items.text: Supporting objection from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Supporting objection from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where the Sages asked Rabbi Yossi about a bat kohen, and he said he only heard the ruling for a bat Yisrael. This supports Rabbah's view that a fetus in a non-priestess is a non-priest, as it explains why he didn't extend the ruling. If the reason were about birth, the cases would be identical and the objection would stand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where the Sages asked Rabbi Yossi about a בת כהן (daughter of a priest) married to a priest, and he replied that he only heard the ruling for a בת ישראל (Israelite woman).

The Gemara explains that if Rabbi Yossi's reason is that a fetus in a non-priestess is a non-priest, his distinction between the cases is logical; but if the reason is that only a born child enables, the cases are identical and the objection stands.

items.text: Shmuel's clarification and dispute with Rabbi Yossi
items.text_en: Shmuel's clarification and dispute with Rabbi Yossi
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says the Mishnah is only Rabbi Yossi's view, but the Sages say slaves eat terumah due to the husband's relatives. The Gemara questions whether Shmuel agrees with Rabbi Yossi, and concludes he does not, as he holds that one can acquire for a fetus. Rabbi Zakkai objects that the Sages agreed with Rabbi Yossi, but Rav Ashi explains they only acknowledged his reasoning, not accepted it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel declares that the Mishnah's ruling is only Rabbi Yossi's view, but the Sages say slaves eat terumah due to the husband's relatives.
The Gemara questions whether Shmuel agrees with Rabbi Yossi, citing Shmuel's own statement that one can acquire for a fetus.
The Gemara concludes that Shmuel does not agree with Rabbi Yossi; rather, he is informing us that the Sages dispute Rabbi Yossi's view.
Rabbi Zakkai objects that the Sages actually agreed with Rabbi Yossi, citing a tradition that they acknowledged his testimony.
Rav Ashi resolves that the Sages only acknowledged the reasoning of Rabbi Yossi, not accepted his ruling as binding.

items.text: Baraita: Details of who eats terumah
items.text_en: Baraita: Details of who eats terumah
items.desc_en: A Baraita elaborates: if the husband left children, all slaves eat; if only a fetus, none eat; if both, melog slaves eat but tzon barzel slaves do not due to the fetus. Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yossi says a daughter enables but a son does not. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says males eat but females do not, lest a male fetus be found and daughters have no share. The Gemara questions why he mentions only a male fetus, and explains he adds that a female also disqualifies.

sub.desc_en: The Baraita opens by stating the general rule: if the husband left children, all slaves eat; if only a fetus, none eat; if both, melog slaves eat but tzon barzel slaves do not, because the fetus disqualifies but does not enable, according to Rabbi Yossi.
Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yossi cites his father: a daughter enables the slaves to eat terumah, but a son does not.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai rules: male children enable the slaves to eat, but female children do not, lest a male fetus be found and the daughters have no share.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai mentions only a male fetus, since a female fetus also disqualifies the daughters.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is making two points: first, a female fetus also disqualifies; second, a male fetus would leave the daughters with no share at all.
The Gemara objects: if males eat, what about the fetus that disqualifies them?
The Gemara begins to explain Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's reasoning, but the explanation is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Two alternative resolutions for the dispute about the fetus and the daughter's inheritance
items.text_en: Two alternative resolutions for the dispute about the fetus and the daughter's inheritance
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two resolutions to the earlier dispute: either we are not concerned about the minority (the fetus being a male), or we are concerned but apply Rav Nachman's remedy of appointing a guardian. It then questions whether Rav Nachman's ruling is a subject of Tannaic dispute, concluding that all agree with Rav Nachman and the dispute is about being concerned for the minority.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers the first resolution: we are not concerned about the minority (the possibility that the fetus is a male).
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: we are concerned about the minority, but we apply Rav Nachman's remedy of appointing a guardian to protect the fetus's share.

Rav Nachman cites Shmuel's ruling that for orphans dividing their father's estate, the court appoints a guardian who selects a good portion, and the orphans can later protest; Rav Nachman himself adds that once they mature they cannot protest, to preserve the court's authority.
The Gemara asks whether Rav Nachman's ruling is itself a subject of Tannaic dispute.
The Gemara resolves that all agree with Rav Nachman, and the dispute is actually about whether we are concerned for the minority.

items.text: Abaye's explanation of Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi's ruling about a daughter and a fetus
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation of Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi's ruling about a daughter and a fetus
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi rules that a daughter can feed terumah to her mother but a son cannot. The Gemara questions why a daughter should feed terumah given the fetus's potential share. Abaye explains that the case involves limited assets and a son already present, so the fetus cannot be worse than the existing son; the daughter eats by rabbinic enactment only after birth.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi states in his father's name that a daughter feeds terumah to her mother but a son does not.
The Gemara questions why a daughter should feed terumah given the fetus's potential share, just as a son cannot due to the fetus's share.
Abaye explains that the case involves limited assets with a son already present, so the fetus cannot be worse than the existing son; the daughter eats only by rabbinic enactment after birth.

items.text: Challenge to Abaye's explanation and resolution with the mother
items.text_en: Challenge to Abaye's explanation and resolution with the mother
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's explanation by noting that the latter clause of the Mishnah refers to abundant assets, not limited ones. It then questions why the daughter would inherit in limited assets, citing Rabbi Asi's ruling that orphans who sold limited assets have their sale valid. The Gemara resolves that the 'daughter' in the Mishnah is actually the mother, and the entire statement is from Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's explanation: if the Mishnah deals with limited assets (נְכָסִים מוּעָטִים), the latter clause about the daughter inheriting nothing contradicts this, as it refers to abundant assets.

The Gemara objects further: if the assets are limited, why would the daughter inherit at all, given Rabbi Asi's ruling that orphans who sold limited assets have their sale valid (i.e., the daughter has no claim)?
The Gemara resolves that the 'daughter' in the Mishnah is actually the mother, and the entire statement is from Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi, not a dispute with Rabbi Yosi.

items.text: Mishnah: Those who disqualify but do not enable eating terumah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those who disqualify but do not enable eating terumah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five categories: a fetus, a yavam, an arusah, a deaf person, and a nine-year-old boy, who disqualify a woman from eating terumah but do not enable her to eat. It also discusses cases of doubt regarding the nine-year-old's age or puberty, and a case where a building collapsed on a man and his brother's daughter, requiring halitzah without yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five categories that disqualify a woman from eating terumah but do not enable her to eat.
The Mishnah discusses cases of doubt regarding the nine-year-old's age or puberty.
The Mishnah presents a case where a building collapsed on a man and his brother's daughter, requiring חליצה (halitzah) without יבום (yibbum).

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's first three categories
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's first three categories
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains each category: a fetus disqualifies a bat kohen married to a Yisrael from eating terumah (based on 'her youth'), and does not enable a bat Yisrael married to a kohen to eat. A yavam disqualifies based on 'she returns to her father's house', and does not enable because the yavam's acquisition is his brother's. An arusah disqualifies a bat kohen married to a Yisrael.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a fetus disqualifies a בת כהן (daughter of a priest) married to an ישראל (Israelite) from eating תרומה (priestly portion) based on the verse 'כנעוריה' (in her youth) excluding a pregnant woman, and does not enable a בת ישראל (daughter of an Israelite) married to a כהן (priest) to eat, because one who is born enables but one not yet born does not.

The Gemara explains that a יבם (levir) disqualifies a בת כהן (daughter of a priest) married to an ישראל (Israelite) based on the verse 'ושבה אל בית אביה' (and returns to her father's house) excluding a שומרת יבם (widow waiting for levirate marriage), and does not enable a בת ישראל (daughter of an Israelite) married to a כהן (priest) to eat because the Torah says 'קנין כספו' (the purchase of his money) and this woman is his brother's acquisition.
The Gemara begins to explain that a מאורס (betrothed man) disqualifies a בת כהן (daughter of a priest) married to an ישראל (Israelite) from eating תרומה (priestly portion).

items.text: Clarification of the deaf man's case
items.text_en: Clarification of the deaf man's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the mishnah's ruling about a deaf man: if he marries a bat kohen to a Yisrael, he disqualifies her from terumah because his acquisition is rabbinic; if he marries a bat Yisrael to a kohen, he does not enable her to eat because he lacks the capacity for acquisition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the mishnah's ruling about a deaf man: if he marries a bat kohen to a Yisrael, he disqualifies her from terumah because his acquisition is rabbinic; if he marries a bat Yisrael to a kohen, he does not enable her to eat because he lacks the capacity for acquisition.

items.text: Initial question about the nine-year-old
items.text_en: Initial question about the nine-year-old
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: the mishnah discusses a nine-year-old boy in the context of a shomeret yavam. Whether for disqualifying or enabling, the case seems problematic because a minor can disqualify but not enable, and an adult can do both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's case of a nine-year-old boy, asking whether it refers to disqualifying or enabling a shomeret yavam, since a minor can disqualify but not enable, and an adult can do both.

items.text: Abaye's answer: the nine-year-old as yavam
items.text_en: Abaye's answer: the nine-year-old as yavam
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the case involves a nine-year-old yavam who had relations with his yevamah. Although Torah law gives him acquisition, the Sages treated his act like a ma'amar of an adult, so he does not enable her to eat terumah.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the case involves a nine-year-old yavam who had relations with his yevamah; although Torah law gives him acquisition, the Sages treated his act like a ma'amar of an adult, so he does not enable her to eat terumah.

items.text: Rava's objection to Abaye
items.text_en: Rava's objection to Abaye
items.desc_en: Rava objects: if the case is about a definite nine-year-old yavam, then the mishnah's later clause about a doubtful nine-year-old is redundant, because if a definite one does not enable, certainly a doubtful one does not.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's explanation: if the mishnah deals with a definite nine-year-old yavam, then the later clause about a doubtful nine-year-old is redundant, because if a definite one does not enable her to eat, certainly a doubtful one does not.

items.text: Rava's alternative: the nine-year-old among disqualifiers
items.text_en: Rava's alternative: the nine-year-old among disqualifiers
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the mishnah's case is about a nine-year-old boy among the disqualifiers (e.g., a mamzer, Chalal) who disqualify a woman from kehunah through their relations. The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction between the first and second parts of the baraita by distinguishing between disqualifiers from the congregation and disqualifiers from kehunah.

sub.desc_en: Rava reinterprets the baraita as referring to a nine-year-old boy among the disqualifiers (e.g., mamzer, Chalal) who disqualify a woman from kehunah through their relations.
The Gemara objects that the baraita's second clause implies the first clause does not deal with disqualifiers at all.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between disqualifiers from the congregation (קהל) and disqualifiers from kehunah (כהונה).

items.text: Baraita on disqualifiers and Tannaic disputes
items.text_en: Baraita on disqualifiers and Tannaic disputes
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the full baraita listing those who disqualify a woman from kehunah through relations, followed by the opinions of Rabbi Yosei and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding the principle of who disqualifies.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists those who disqualify a woman from kehunah through relations: a nine-year-old boy, a convert, an Ammonite, Moabite, Egyptian, Edomite, a Kutite, a Netin, a ḥalal, and a mamzer.
Rabbi Yosei rules that only one whose offspring is disqualified from kehunah can disqualify a woman through relations.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that one whose daughter you may marry, you may also marry his widow; otherwise, you may not marry his widow.

items.text: Scriptural source for disqualification
items.text_en: Scriptural source for disqualification
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav derives the law that a bat kohen who has relations with a disqualifier is disqualified from terumah, based on the verse "and a bat kohen who is to a zar." The Gemara clarifies that this verse teaches a negative commandment, while the allowance for her to return to her father's house is derived from another verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that a bat kohen who has relations with a disqualifier is disqualified from terumah) derived?
Rav Yehudah citing Rav answers: The verse 'וּבַת כֹּהֵן כִּי תִהְיֶה לְאִישׁ זָר' teaches that once she is violated by a disqualifier, she is disqualified from terumah.
The Gemara objects: This verse is needed to teach that a bat kohen married to a zar (a non-priest) may not eat terumah — it is not available for the disqualification case.

The Gemara rejects the objection: That law (the bat kohen married to a zar does not eat) is derived from the verse 'וְשָׁבָה אֶל בֵּית אָבִיהָ ... תֹּאכֵל', which implies that initially she did not eat.

The Gemara resolves: If only from that verse, one might think the prohibition is only a positive commandment (עשה), so the Torah wrote the verse about a zar to establish a negative commandment (לאו); the disqualification for a bat kohen who is violated by a disqualifier is derived from 'וְכָל זָר לֹא יֹאכַל קֹדֶשׁ'.

items.text: Question on the need for the second "vechol zar"
items.text_en: Question on the need for the second "vechol zar"
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the second "vechol zar" is necessary, suggesting it might be needed for its own context, but notes that two instances of "vechol zar" are written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the second instance of 'vechol zar' is needed, noting that two instances are written in the Torah.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the second "vechol zar" is needed for Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's teaching that "zar" implies estrangement (zarut) but not mourning (aninut), which is derived from "zar" and "vechol zar".

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the second 'vechol zar' is needed for Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's teaching that 'zar' implies estrangement (zarut) but not mourning (aninut).
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's derivation comes from the two occurrences of 'zar' and 'vechol zar'.

items.text: Derivation for the bat kohen returning to terumah
items.text_en: Derivation for the bat kohen returning to terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the verse is needed for the teaching that when a bat kohen returns from marriage to a zar, she returns to terumah but not to the breast and thigh. Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Rav Sheila explains the verse: "ubat kohen ki tihyeh le'ish zar hi biterumat hakodashim lo tochel" teaches two things.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that when a bat kohen returns from marriage to a zar, she returns to eating תרומה (priestly portion) but not to the breast and thigh.

sub.text: Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Rav Sheila
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Rav Sheila
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Rav Sheila explains the verse 'וּבַת כֹּהֵן...' teaches that she may not eat from the elevated portion of the sacred offerings (the breast and thigh).
The Gemara resolves that the verse's extra wording 'בִּתְרוּמַת הַקֳּדָשִׁים' teaches two things: the return to תרומה (priestly portion) and the exclusion from the breast and thigh.

items.text: Source for a leviah or yisre'elit
items.text_en: Source for a leviah or yisre'elit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we derive the same law for a leviah or yisre'elit. Rabbi Abba citing Rav says from the extra "bat" and "ubat" — here too we use "bat" and "ubat". The Gemara notes this follows Rabbi Akiva who expounds vavs, but even the Rabbis agree since the entire "ubat" is an extra verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we found the source for a kohenet (priest's daughter) — from where do we derive the same law for a leviah (Levite's daughter) or yisre'elit (Israelite's daughter)?
Rabbi Abba citing Rav answers: just as we derived the law for a kohenet from the extra 'בת' and 'ובת' (bat and ubat), here too we use 'בת' and 'ובת'.
The Gemara objects: this follows Rabbi Akiva, who expounds the vavs (the letter vav as an extra word) — but what about the Rabbis who do not?
The Gemara resolves: even if you say the Rabbis (רבנן) disagree, here the entire word 'ובת' (ubat) is an extra verse, so even the Rabbis would agree.

items.text: Derivation for disqualification from kehunah
items.text_en: Derivation for disqualification from kehunah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we derive disqualification from kehunah (not just terumah). It first considers that a leviah or yisre'elit is also being included for kehunah, since they don't eat terumah themselves. The Gemara then proposes a kal vachomer from a gerushah: just as a gerushah, permitted in terumah, is forbidden to kehunah, so too this woman, forbidden in terumah, should be disqualified from kehunah. The Gemara objects that we do not derive prohibitions from a kal vachomer, but answers it is merely a giluy milta (revealing the matter).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we derive disqualification from kehunah (priesthood) for a woman who had relations with a pasul, noting that a leviah or yisre'elit is also being included for kehunah, since they do not eat terumah themselves.
The Gemara answers that one can find a case where a leviah or yisre'elit eats terumah for the sake of her son.

The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if a kohenet, who eats terumah due to her own sanctity, is disqualified, then a leviah or yisre'elit, who eats only for her son, should certainly be disqualified.
The Gemara objects that the kal vachomer is flawed: a kohenet, whose body is sanctified, is disqualified, but a leviah or yisre'elit, whose body is not sanctified, is not disqualified.

The Gemara instead proposes a kal vachomer from a gerushah (divorcée): just as a gerushah, permitted in terumah, is forbidden to kehunah, so too this woman, forbidden in terumah, should be disqualified from kehunah.
The Gemara objects that we do not derive prohibitions from a kal vachomer (אין מזהירין מן הדין).
The Gemara resolves that the kal vachomer is merely a גילוי מילתא (revealing the matter), not a formal derivation of a prohibition.

items.text: Exclusion of chayavei keritot and inclusion of a non-Jew or slave
items.text_en: Exclusion of chayavei keritot and inclusion of a non-Jew or slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a woman who is violated by one liable to karet is not disqualified, and answers that the verse says "ki tihyeh" — those who have a status of marriage (havayah), but chayavei keritot are not subject to havayah. It then asks why a non-Jew or slave should disqualify, and answers from Rabbi Yishmael's teaching that a non-Jew or slave who has relations with a bat Yisrael, kohen, or levi disqualifies her, as derived from the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a woman violated by one liable to karet is not disqualified, and answers that the verse says 'כי תהיה' (ki tihyeh) — only those who have a status of marriage (havayah) are included, but chayavei keritot are not subject to havayah.

The Gemara asks why a non-Jew or slave should disqualify, and answers from Rabbi Yishmael's teaching that a non-Jew or slave who has relations with a bat Yisrael, kohen, or levi disqualifies her, as derived from the verse.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who has the possibility of widowhood or divorce (i.e., a bat Yisrael married to a Kohen) eats terumah, but a non-Jew or slave, who lack that possibility, does not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the principle that a woman who can become a widow or divorcee eats terumah, while a non-Jew or slave who cannot does not.

items.text: Derivation for Levite and Israelite women
items.text_en: Derivation for Levite and Israelite women
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that a Levite or Israelite woman (married to a Kohen) also eats terumah. Rabbi Abba bar Rav derives it from the double expression "bat" and "ubat" in the verse, similar to Rabbi Akiva's exegesis, but even the Rabbis agree that the extra "ubat" is superfluous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that a Levite or Israelite woman married to a Kohen also eats terumah, and cites Rabbi Abba bar Rav's derivation from the double expression 'בת' and 'ובת'.
The Gemara objects that this derivation follows Rabbi Akiva's method of expounding the letter 'vav', but even the Rabbis agree that the extra 'ובת' is superfluous.

items.text: Alternative interpretation rejected
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation rejected
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative: perhaps the Mishnah means that a woman who has the possibility of widowhood or divorce eats only when she has no children, but one without that possibility eats even with children. This is rejected because then the inclusion of Levite and Israelite women would be unnecessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative interpretation: a woman who can experience widowhood or divorce eats only when she has no children, but one who cannot eats even when she has children.
The Gemara rejects this proposal: if so, the inclusion of Levite and Israelite women in the Mishnah's rule would be superfluous.

items.text: The need for both widow and divorcee
items.text_en: The need for both widow and divorcee
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah mentions both widow and divorcee, given Rabbi Akiva's view that a woman who has relations with a man forbidden by a negative commandment is not betrothed. The Gemara explains that both are needed: the widow to be stringent, the divorcee to be lenient, and they are necessary because one might have thought otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to mention both widow and divorcee, given Rabbi Akiva's view that betrothal does not take effect with those forbidden by a negative commandment.
The Gemara answers that both are needed: the widow to impose stringency and the divorcee to impose leniency, and they are necessary because one might have thought otherwise.

items.text: Excluding a man who remarries his divorcee
items.text_en: Excluding a man who remarries his divorcee
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a woman who has relations with a man who remarries his divorcee (a pasul) is not disqualified. The answer is that the Torah says "to a stranger" — one who was initially a stranger to her, excluding this man who was not initially a stranger. The Gemara then asks about a חלל, who is not initially a stranger, and answers that the verse "he shall not profane his seed" equates his seed to him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a woman who has relations with a man who remarries his divorcee (a pasul) is not disqualified from eating תרומה (priestly portion).
The Gemara answers that the Torah says 'to a stranger' (לאיש זר), meaning one who was initially a stranger to her, excluding this man who was not initially a stranger.
The Gemara objects that if the criterion is initial strangeness, then a חלל (chalal), who is not initially a stranger, should not disqualify her.
The Gemara resolves that the verse 'לֹא יְחַלֵּל זַרְעוֹ בְּעַמָּיו' (he shall not profane his seed among his people) equates his seed to him, so just as he disqualifies, his seed also disqualifies.

items.text: The moment of disqualification
items.text_en: The moment of disqualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether disqualification takes effect from the moment of the forbidden act (ביאה) or requires both the act and the marriage (הויה). It concludes that it is only from the act, analogous to a High Priest with a widow, where disqualification is solely by the act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether disqualification takes effect from the moment of marriage (הויה) rather than from the act of intercourse (ביאה).
The Gemara answers that disqualification is only from the act of intercourse, analogous to a High Priest with a widow where disqualification is solely by the act, not requiring marriage.

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei says that only one whose own seed is disqualified disqualifies a bat Kohen. Rabbi Yochanan explains that the difference between them is a second-generation Egyptian or Edomite convert. Both derive their rulings from the case of a High Priest with a widow: the first Tanna focuses on the act being a transgression, while Rabbi Yosei focuses on the seed being disqualified.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states the principle that only one whose own seed is disqualified disqualifies a bat Kohen from eating תרומה (priestly portion).
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the first Tanna and Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the difference lies in the case of a second-generation Egyptian or Edomite convert.

The Gemara explains that both derive their rulings from the case of a High Priest with a widow: the first Tanna focuses on the act being a transgression, while Rabbi Yosei focuses on the seed being disqualified, excluding a second-generation Egyptian or Edomite convert whose seed is not disqualified.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that one whose daughter you may marry disqualifies. Ulla explains that the difference is an Ammonite or Moabite convert. Both derive from the High Priest: Rabbi Yosei requires that all his seed be disqualified, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires that all his seed be disqualified, excluding Ammonites and Moabites whose females are permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's principle: one whose daughter you may marry, you may marry his widow.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rabbi Yosei's position and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position.
Ulla answers that the difference is an Ammonite or Moabite convert, and both derive their rulings from the High Priest marrying a widow.
Ulla explains that Rabbi Yosei derives: just as the High Priest's seed is disqualified and he disqualifies, so anyone whose seed is disqualified disqualifies.

sub.text: Ulla's explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Ulla's explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: Ulla explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires all of one's seed to be disqualified, excluding Ammonites and Moabites whose females are permitted.

items.text: Mishnah: Those who do not disqualify
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those who do not disqualify
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists an אונס (rapist), מפתה (seducer), and שוטה (imbecile) as not disqualifying a bat Kohen from terumah nor enabling her to eat. However, if they are unfit to enter the congregation, they do disqualify. An example is given: an Israelite who has relations with a bat Kohen allows her to eat terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an אונס (rapist), מפתה (seducer), and שוטה (imbecile) do not disqualify a bat Kohen from terumah nor enable her to eat, but if they are unfit to enter the congregation they do disqualify, giving the example of an Israelite who has relations with a bat Kohen allowing her to eat terumah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rules of terumah for pregnant women and offspring
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rules of terumah for pregnant women and offspring
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a woman's terumah eligibility changes based on pregnancy, childbirth, and the status of her child. It then introduces the categories of a slave, a mamzer, and a High Priest who can affect their mother's or grandmother's terumah status.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that a pregnant woman who became pregnant while married to an Israelite may not eat terumah, but if the fetus is miscarried she may eat; it then contrasts the power of the son over the father.
The Mishnah presents the case of a slave who disqualifies his grandmother from terumah through his birth from a maidservant, showing the rule of paternal lineage.
The Mishnah presents the case of a mamzer who both disqualifies and enables his grandmother's terumah eligibility, depending on her original status.
The Mishnah presents the case of a High Priest who sometimes disqualifies his grandmother from terumah, concluding that his power exceeds that of a regular High Priest's son.

items.text: Gemara's opening: Baraita on a fool or minor
items.text_en: Gemara's opening: Baraita on a fool or minor
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a fool or minor who married and died, exempting their wives from chalitzah and yibbum, setting the stage for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that the wives of a fool or minor who married and died are exempt from חליצה (chalitzah) and ייבום (yibbum).

items.text: Gemara's question: Why is a pregnant woman forbidden terumah immediately?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why is a pregnant woman forbidden terumah immediately?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a woman who became pregnant from an Israelite is forbidden terumah immediately, asking why we do not suspect she might be pregnant earlier, citing a baraita about separating for three months.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a pregnant woman is forbidden terumah immediately, asking why we do not suspect she might be pregnant earlier, citing a baraita about separating for three months.

items.text: First answer: Rabba bar Rav Huna distinguishes lineage vs. terumah
items.text_en: First answer: Rabba bar Rav Huna distinguishes lineage vs. terumah
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna initially answers that the Sages were stringent for lineage but not for terumah. When challenged with a baraita about a get, he revises: they were stringent for marriage but not for promiscuity.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna's initial answer
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna's initial answer
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna answers that the Sages were stringent (חָשְׁשׁוּ) regarding lineage (יוּחֲסִין) but not regarding terumah (תְּרוּמָה).
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita about a get (גט) that shows the Sages were indeed stringent regarding terumah immediately.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna's revised answer
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna's revised answer
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna revises his answer: the Sages were stringent regarding marriage (נִישּׂוּאִין) but not regarding promiscuity (זְנוּת).

items.text: Second answer: Rav Chisda's forty-day rule
items.text_en: Second answer: Rav Chisda's forty-day rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even in marriage we are not stringent, citing a baraita where a widow immerses and eats terumah the same evening. Rav Chisda answers that she may eat until forty days, as before that the fetus is merely water.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Chisda's position that we are stringent in marriage cases, citing a baraita where a widow immerses and eats terumah the same evening.
Rav Chisda answers that she may eat until forty days, as before that the fetus is merely water.

items.text: Abaye's challenge: The case of recognized pregnancy
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge: The case of recognized pregnancy
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Chisda from the Mishnah's case where the fetus is recognized, arguing that the woman is retroactively disqualified, but only from forty days.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Chisda by citing the Mishnah's case of a recognized fetus, arguing that the woman is retroactively disqualified only from forty days.

items.text: Debate: The child of a betrothed woman who had relations
items.text_en: Debate: The child of a betrothed woman who had relations
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where a man had relations with his betrothed in his father-in-law's house. Rav says the child is a mamzer, Shmuel says a shetuki. Rava supports Rav with a proof from the Mishnah, but Abaye objects, arguing that if she was promiscuous with her fiancé, she might be promiscuous with others. An alternative version limits the dispute to a case where she became pregnant without known relations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rav says the child of a man who had relations with his betrothed in his father-in-law's house is a mamzer, while Shmuel says the child is a shetuki.
Rava supports Rav's position, arguing that if the woman was promiscuous with others, the child is a mamzer, but if she was only promiscuous with her fiancé, the child is attributed to him.

Rava proves his point from the Mishnah: if a woman gave birth, she may eat terumah, implying the child is attributed to the father; a fortiori, in a case of one prohibition and one permission, the child is attributed to the father.

Abaye objects: even if she was promiscuous only with her fiancé, Rav still says the child is a mamzer, because once she was promiscuous with her fiancé, she might be promiscuous with others, and the Mishnah's case involved both being imprisoned together.

An alternative version limits the dispute to a case where the betrothed woman became pregnant without known relations, with Rav and Shmuel disagreeing, and Rava supporting Rav's position that the child is a mamzer if she was promiscuous with others but not with her fiancé.

items.text: Rava's proof that a slave follows his master's status
items.text_en: Rava's proof that a slave follows his master's status
items.desc_en: Rava argues that even if a slave has some independent lineage, he is assigned to his master's status. He proves this from the mishnah where a slave's child eats terumah, implying that even if the slave has lineage from elsewhere, he follows his master.

sub.desc_en: The stam introduces the principle that a slave who has lineage from elsewhere is still assigned to his master's status.
Rava proves his principle from the mishnah: if a slave's child eats terumah even when the slave has lineage from elsewhere, then certainly a slave with mixed prohibitions follows his master.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rav rules the child is a mamzer when the slave has lineage from elsewhere, so the mishnah must refer to a slave with no independent lineage at all.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rav's ruling that the child is a mamzer applies only when the slave has lineage from elsewhere, so the mishnah must refer to a slave with no independent lineage at all.

items.text: The slave disqualifies through intercourse
items.text_en: The slave disqualifies through intercourse
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that a slave disqualifies a woman from terumah through intercourse, derived from the verse 'the woman and her children shall be'.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that a slave disqualifies a woman from terumah through intercourse, citing the verse 'the woman and her children shall be' as the source.

items.text: Derivation of who is disqualified from terumah
items.text_en: Derivation of who is disqualified from terumah
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'and she has no seed' to include grandchildren and even invalid seed (mamzerim) as disqualifying. The Gemara clarifies that grandchildren are already included by a general principle, so the verse is needed only for invalid seed.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְזֶרַע אֵין לָהּ' (and she has no seed) to derive that grandchildren disqualify a woman from eating תרומה (priestly portion).
The baraita extends the derivation to include invalid seed (ממזר) as disqualifying, using the same verse.
The Gemara resolves that grandchildren are already included by the principle 'בני בנים הרי הן כבנים' (grandchildren are like children), so the verse is only needed to include invalid seed.

items.text: Resh Lakish's question about the mamzer ruling
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's question about the mamzer ruling
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan whether the baraita follows Rabbi Akiva (who holds there is a mamzer from a lav) or the Rabbis. The Gemara answers that even the Rabbis agree in the case of a gentile or slave, citing Rav Dimi's tradition.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan whether the baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a child from a relationship violating a negative commandment is a mamzer.

Rabbi Yochanan answers that even the Rabbis, who generally disagree with Rabbi Akiva, concede in the case of a gentile or slave, citing Rav Dimi's tradition that a gentile or slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer.

items.text: The High Priest's disqualifying effect
items.text_en: The High Priest's disqualifying effect
items.desc_en: A baraita illustrates that a High Priest can sometimes disqualify his wife from terumah, as in the case of a daughter who marries a non-priest.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that a High Priest sometimes disqualifies his wife from partaking of תרומה (priestly portion).

A baraita illustrates the mishnah's point: a woman expresses willingness to atone for her daughter's son who is a mamzer, because he enables her to eat תרומה, but not for her daughter's son who is a High Priest, because he disqualifies her.
The Gemara concludes the chapter with the formula 'we return to you, widow' (הדרן עלך אלמנה), marking the end of the mishnah discussion.

items.text: Mishnah: The uncircumcised and others disqualified from terumah
items.text_en: Mishnah: The uncircumcised and others disqualified from terumah
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists who may not eat terumah: the uncircumcised, all impure persons, and a petzu'a daka or kerut shofchah, with exceptions for their wives and slaves under certain conditions.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that an uncircumcised priest and all impure persons may not eat תרומה (priestly portion), but their wives and slaves may eat.
The mishnah continues: a פצוע דכא (crushed testicles) or כרות שפכה (severed penis) priest and his slaves may eat תרומה, but his wife may not unless she did not have relations after his injury.
The mishnah defines פצוע דכא as one whose testicles (even one) are wounded, and כרות שפכה as one whose member is cut off; if any corona remains, he is still fit.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation that an arel may not eat terumah
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation that an arel may not eat terumah
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer's gezerah shavah from 'toshav ve-sakhir' in Passover to terumah, and Rabbi Akiva's alternative derivation from 'ish ish'. The Gemara analyzes the need for the gezerah shavah to be 'mufneh' (free for exposition), concluding that the Passover verse is mufneh.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar opens with a baraita deriving that an ערל (uncircumcised man) may not eat תרומה (priestly portion) via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the words 'תושב ושכיר' (resident and hired worker) used in both Passover and terumah contexts.
Rabbi Akiva counters that no verbal analogy is needed, because the verse 'איש איש' (any man) already includes the ערל (uncircumcised man) as prohibited from eating terumah.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Eliezer's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Eliezer's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara repeats Rabbi Eliezer's statement of the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between Passover and terumah regarding the terms 'תושב ושכיר' (resident and hired worker).

sub.text: Gemara's question about the verbal analogy being mufneh
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the verbal analogy being mufneh
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verbal analogy must be מופנה (free for exposition), otherwise one could refute it by noting that Passover carries additional penalties of פיגול (pigul), נותר (notar), and טמא (tamei) which terumah does not, but concludes that it is indeed מופנה (free).

sub.text: Gemara's question: which verse is mufneh?
sub.text_en: Gemara's question: which verse is mufneh?
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which verse is מופנה (free), and suggests that the terumah verse cannot be free because both words 'תושב' (resident) and 'שכיר' (hired worker) are needed to teach distinct laws about קניין עולם (permanent acquisition) and קניין שנים (temporary acquisition).

sub.text: Gemara's objection: one word could suffice
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection: one word could suffice
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one could have derived the law from only the word 'תושב' (resident), since if a permanently acquired slave does not eat, a temporarily acquired one certainly should not eat, making 'שכיר' (hired worker) seemingly redundant and thus available for the verbal analogy.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution: both words are needed
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution: both words are needed
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that both words are necessary: without 'שכיר' (hired worker), one might have thought 'תושב' (resident) refers to a temporary acquisition and a permanent acquisition would permit eating, so 'שכיר' teaches that even a permanent acquisition does not permit eating.

sub.text: Gemara's conclusion: the Passover verse is mufneh
sub.text_en: Gemara's conclusion: the Passover verse is mufneh
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Passover verse is the one that is מופנה (free), because the terms 'תושב ושכיר' (resident and hired worker) in the Passover context cannot be taken literally — since if they were literal, they would exempt such a person from Passover, but we already know that such a person does not eat terumah, so the verse must be available for the verbal analogy.

items.text: Establishing the gezerah shavah as fully free
items.text_en: Establishing the gezerah shavah as fully free
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that since the verse about the Passover offering is not needed for its own context, it can be used for a gezerah shavah that is free from both sides, allowing for learning and rebuttal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that the master does not acquire the slave for himself, so the verse about the Passover offering is free for a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy).
The Gemara objects that the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) is only free from one side, and Rabbi Elazar holds that such an analogy can be rebutted.
The Gemara resolves that since the verse is not needed for its own context, it is considered free from both sides, making the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) fully free for learning and rebuttal.

items.text: The gezerah shavah analogy
items.text_en: The gezerah shavah analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the analogy: just as an onen is prohibited from eating the Passover offering, so too an onen is prohibited from eating terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): just as an אונן (one in acute mourning) is forbidden from eating the Passover offering, so too an אונן is forbidden from eating תרומה (priestly portion).

items.text: Rejecting aninut and preferring arlah
items.text_en: Rejecting aninut and preferring arlah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina derives from the verse 'zar' that only a stranger (non-priest) is prohibited, not an onen. The Gemara then considers whether arlah should be included instead, and lists reasons why arlah is more fitting to be derived from the Passover offering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina derives from the verse 'זָר' (stranger) that only a non-priest is prohibited from eating תרומה (priestly portion), not an אונן (one in acute mourning).
The Gemara asks why the verse should not be interpreted to exclude ערלה (uncircumcision) instead of אנינות (mourning).
The Gemara answers that the verse already excludes ערלה (uncircumcision) via the terms 'תושב ושכיר' (a resident alien and a hired laborer), which refer to an uncircumcised person.
The Gemara asks why one should prefer to derive the exclusion of אנינות (mourning) over ערלה (uncircumcision) from the Passover offering.

The Gemara lists reasons why ערלה (uncircumcision) is more fitting to be derived: it involves an action, is performed on one's own body, carries the penalty of כרת (excision), existed before the giving of the Torah, and the circumcision of one's males and slaves is a prerequisite for eating the Passover offering.
The Gemara objects that אנינות (mourning) could be considered more fitting to derive because it applies at all times, to both men and women, and one cannot remedy it by his own action.
The Gemara resolves that the reasons for preferring ערלה (uncircumcision) are more numerous, outweighing the objection.

items.text: Rava's objection to the preference for arlah
items.text_en: Rava's objection to the preference for arlah
items.desc_en: Rava argues that even without the multiple reasons, one cannot derive arlah from the Passover offering because the Passover itself learns the law of aninut from ma'aser, not from its own verse.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that even without the many reasons favoring aninus over arlah, one cannot derive arlah from the Passover offering because the Passover itself learns the law of aninus from ma'aser, not from its own verse.

items.text: Deriving circumcision of slaves for terumah
items.text_en: Deriving circumcision of slaves for terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive that circumcision of male slaves is required for terumah from the Passover offering, but a verse limits this requirement to the Passover only.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the Passover offering to terumah, suggesting that circumcision of male slaves should be required for eating terumah just as it is for the Passover.

The Gemara rejects the proposal by citing the verse 'וּמַלְתָּה אוֹתוֹ אָז יֹאכַל בּוֹ' (and you shall circumcise him, then he shall eat of it), which limits the requirement of circumcision of male slaves to the Passover offering alone, not to terumah.

items.text: Excluding the uncircumcised from terumah
items.text_en: Excluding the uncircumcised from terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether an uncircumcised person is prohibited from terumah based on the verse 'kol arel lo yochal bo', but concludes that only personal arlah is excluded, not that of others, and the verse 'toshav v'sachir' already teaches the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse 'כל ערל לא יאכל בו' (no uncircumcised person may eat of it) implies that an uncircumcised person may eat terumah, since the verse only restricts the paschal offering.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'תושב ושכיר' (a resident alien or hired laborer) already teaches the prohibition of an uncircumcised person from eating terumah.

The Gemara asks why one would prioritize excluding personal arlah (uncircumcision of oneself) over the circumcision of one's males and slaves, and answers that personal arlah involves an act on one's body and carries the penalty of karet.
The Gemara objects that the circumcision of one's males and slaves should be prioritized because it applies at all times.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that the reasons for personal arlah are more numerous.

The Gemara offers an alternative answer: even without the numerous reasons, one cannot argue that the uncircumcision of others (his males and slaves) would be a greater impediment than his own uncircumcision.

items.text: Questioning the need for 'ben nechar'
items.text_en: Questioning the need for 'ben nechar'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since 'bo' is used for a derivation, why is the phrase 'kol ben nechar lo yochal bo' needed?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since the word 'בּוֹ' (in it) is already used for a derivation, why is the additional phrase 'כׇּל בֶּן נֵכָר לֹא יֹאכַל בּוֹ' (no alien shall eat in it) needed?

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Apostasy invalidates, but not for tithe
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Apostasy invalidates, but not for tithe
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that apostasy invalidates one from eating the Paschal offering, but does not invalidate for tithe. This sets up the discussion about who is excluded.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that apostasy invalidates one from eating the Paschal offering, but does not invalidate for tithe.

items.text: Gemara: Why the extra verse for ערל?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why the extra verse for ערל?
