items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah needed both 'ערל' and 'כל בן נכר' to exclude the uncircumcised. It explains that each term addresses a different reason for exclusion: one for being repulsive, the other for not having a heart for Heaven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'כל ערל לא יאכל בו' (no uncircumcised person may eat of it) is needed, since it already teaches that he may not eat the Pesach offering but may eat matzah and maror.

The Gemara explains that both terms 'ערל' and 'כל בן נכר' are necessary: 'ערל' excludes one who is repulsive, while 'בן נכר' excludes one whose heart is not directed to Heaven, and each alone would not cover the other case.

items.text: The word 'מִמֶּנּוּ' for Rabba bar Rav Yitzchak
items.text_en: The word 'מִמֶּנּוּ' for Rabba bar Rav Yitzchak
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the repeated word 'מִמֶּנּוּ' in the verse is used for a teaching of Rabba bar Rav Yitzchak, which will be explained later.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah repeats the word 'מִמֶּנּוּ' (from it) in the verse.
The Gemara answers that the repetition is for a teaching of Rabba bar Rav Yitzchak, which will be explained later.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's derivation: 'איש איש' includes the ערל
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's derivation: 'איש איש' includes the ערל
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva says the verse 'איש איש' includes the uncircumcised person. The Gemara questions why it doesn't include an אונן (mourner), and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina answers that 'זר' implies strangeness, not mourning. A debate ensues about which inclusion is more logical, with Rava concluding that 'איש איש' refers to something specific to men, i.e., circumcision.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Akiva's position that the verse 'איש איש' includes the uncircumcised person (ערל) in the prohibition.
The Gemara questions why the inclusion should not apply to an אונן (mourner) instead of an ערל.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina answers that the verse 'וכל זר' implies strangeness (זרות), not mourning (אנינות), so the inclusion is for the ערל.
The Gemara objects that the same logic could exclude ערלות (uncircumcision) as well, but the verse 'איש איש' already includes it.

The Gemara argues that it is more logical to include ערלות because it involves an action, is a cutting, is in a matter (of the covenant), applies to a slave, is lacking an action, is an action on the body, carries the penalty of כרת (excision), exists before the giving of the Torah, and the circumcision of males and slaves is a prerequisite.
The Gemara counters that אנינות (mourning) is more logical to include because it applies at all times, applies to both men and women, and the mourner cannot remedy his state.
Rava resolves the debate by noting that the verse 'איש איש' refers to something specific to men, i.e., circumcision (ערלות), which does not apply to women, unlike אנינות.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's use of 'תושב ושכיר' and Rabbi Eliezer's view
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's use of 'תושב ושכיר' and Rabbi Eliezer's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Akiva does with the verse 'תושב ושכיר'. Rav Shemaya answers it includes a circumcised Arab or Gibeonite. A difficulty is raised from a mishna about vows, leading to a reinterpretation: it includes a convert who was circumcised but not immersed, and a child born circumcised. Rabbi Eliezer holds that such a convert is valid and such a child needs no blood of the covenant, and he interprets 'איש איש' as the Torah speaking in human language.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Akiva does with the verse 'תושב ושכיר' (a resident alien and a hired hand), since he already derived the prohibition for an uncircumcised person from 'איש איש'.
Rav Shemaya answers that the verse includes a circumcised Arab or a circumcised Gibeonite, who are circumcised but not valid converts.

The Gemara objects that these are considered circumcised (מולין), citing a mishna about vows that distinguishes between 'uncircumcised' (including circumcised Jews) and 'circumcised' (including circumcised gentiles).
The Gemara revises the answer: the verse includes a convert who was circumcised but not yet immersed, and a child born circumcised, who require a drop of blood of the covenant (דם ברית).

sub.text: Stam's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's position
sub.text_en: Stam's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Eliezer consistently holds that a convert circumcised but not immersed is a valid convert, and a child born circumcised does not need a drop of blood of the covenant, so he interprets 'איש איש' as the Torah speaking in human language.

items.text: Rav Chama bar Ukva's question: Does untimely circumcision invalidate?
items.text_en: Rav Chama bar Ukva's question: Does untimely circumcision invalidate?
items.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Ukva asks whether a minor who is uncircumcised may be anointed with terumah oil, questioning if untimely circumcision (ערלות שלא בזמנה) is a valid impediment. Rabbi Zeira attempts to prove from a baraitha that it is, but Rava rejects this, explaining the case involves a child weakened by fever. The Gemara discusses giving him all seven days to recover and the timing of circumcision.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Ukva asks whether a minor who is uncircumcised may be anointed with terumah oil, questioning if untimely circumcision (ערלות שלא בזמנה) is a valid impediment.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's attempted proof from a baraitha
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's attempted proof from a baraitha
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira attempts to prove from a baraitha that untimely circumcision is a valid impediment, arguing that a child born between the making of the Paschal lamb and its eating must be circumcised.
Rava rejects the proof, explaining that the case involves a child weakened by fever (חלצתו חמה) who is not fit for circumcision, not a case of untimely circumcision.
The Gemara discusses giving the child all seven days to recover, citing Shmuel's ruling, and questions why the circumcision cannot be performed in the morning, concluding with an unresolved inquiry.

items.text: Comparison of day of creation to day of birth
items.text_en: Comparison of day of creation to day of birth
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the day of creation is like the day of birth regarding the requirement of 'from time to time' (me'eyt le'eyt). It cites a baraita from the school of Lud that states the day of creation is like the day of birth, and attempts to infer that just as the day of birth does not require 'from time to time', so too the day of creation does not. The Gemara rejects this, arguing that the day of creation is more stringent than the day of birth, as the day of birth does not require 'from time to time' but the day of creation does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating the requirement of waiting 'from time to time' (מעת לעת) for a full seven-day period after the child's recovery before circumcision.

The Gemara cites a baraita from the school of Lud that states 'the day of his healing is like the day of his birth' and asks whether this implies that, just as the day of birth does not require 'from time to time', so too the day of healing does not.

The Gemara rejects the inference, arguing that the day of healing is more stringent than the day of birth: the day of birth does not require 'from time to time', but the day of healing does require a full seven-day period from time to time.

items.text: Scenarios for circumcision between the eighth day and the first opportunity
items.text_en: Scenarios for circumcision between the eighth day and the first opportunity
items.desc_en: Various Amoraim present scenarios where a child is circumcised between the eighth day and the first opportunity (bein u'vein). Rav Pappa suggests a case where the child had an eye ailment and was healed in the interim. Rava suggests a case where the parents were imprisoned. Rav Kahana bar Rav Nechemya suggests a case of a tumtum who was torn and found to be a male in the interim. Rav Sherevya suggests a case where the child's head emerged outside the prozdor (vestibule).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa presents a scenario where a child had an eye ailment and recovered between the preparation and eating of the Paschal lamb.
Rava presents a scenario where the parents were imprisoned at the time of preparation and released before the eating.
Rav Kahana bar Rav Nechemya presents a scenario where a tumtum was torn and found to be a male in the interim.
Rav Sherevya presents a scenario where the child's head emerged outside the prozdor (vestibule) in the interim.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding the viability of a child whose head emerged
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding the viability of a child whose head emerged
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Sherevya's scenario, citing a baraita that once a child emerges into the air of the world, the sealed openings open and the open ones seal, without which the child cannot live even an hour. The Gemara resolves that the case is where the child was sustained by fire (ishata), specifically the mother's fire (ishata d'imeih). Alternatively, it says that the baraita applies when the child is not deformed, but if deformed, it can live.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Sherevya's scenario by citing a baraita that once a child emerges into the air of the world, the sealed openings open and the open ones seal, without which the child cannot live even an hour.
The Gemara resolves that the case is where the child was sustained by fire (אִישָּׁתָא), specifically the mother's fire (אִישָּׁתָא דְּאִימֵּיהּ), not his own.
Alternatively, the Gemara says that the baraita applies when the child is not deformed, but if deformed, it can live.

items.text: Uncircumcised person receiving sprinkling
items.text_en: Uncircumcised person receiving sprinkling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Bena'ah states that an uncircumcised person (arel) can receive sprinkling (haza'ah), as we find with our ancestors who received sprinkling while uncircumcised, based on the verse about the tenth of the month. The Gemara questions whether they might not have performed the Passover at all, but rejects this due to the verse 'and they performed the Passover'. Mar Zutra objects that it might have been a Passover brought in impurity, but Rav Ashi cites a baraita that they circumcised, immersed, and performed their Passover in purity.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Bena'ah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Bena'ah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Bena'ah rules that an uncircumcised person (ערל) can receive sprinkling (הזאה), citing the precedent of the ancestors who received sprinkling while uncircumcised, based on the verse about the tenth of the month.
The Gemara infers that since they did not circumcise on the tenth due to travel weakness, the sprinkling must have been performed while they were still uncircumcised.
The Gemara objects that perhaps they did not perform the Passover at all, but rejects this because the verse explicitly states 'and they performed the Passover'.
Mar Zutra objects that perhaps it was a Passover brought in impurity (פסח הבא בטומאה), which would not require purity.
Rav Ashi resolves by citing a baraita that explicitly states they circumcised, immersed, and performed their Passover in purity (בטהרה).

items.text: Requirement of peri'ah (uncovering) for circumcision
items.text_en: Requirement of peri'ah (uncovering) for circumcision
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Yitzchak quoting Rav states that the requirement of peri'ah (uncovering) was not given to Abraham our father, based on the verse where God told Joshua to make flint knives and circumcise the Israelites again a second time. The Gemara questions whether this refers to those who were uncircumcised, but the verse says they were circumcised. It concludes that 'again' refers to peri'ah, and 'second time' teaches that the end of circumcision is like the beginning: just as the beginning is indispensable, so the end is indispensable. Ravina or Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba quoting Rav defines the flesh that covers the majority of the height of the corona (basar hachofeh et rov govhah shel atarah).

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Yitzchak quoting Rav states that the requirement of peri'ah (uncovering) was not given to Abraham, citing the verse where God told Joshua to make flint knives.
The Gemara questions whether the verse refers to those who were uncircumcised, citing that the text says all who left Egypt were circumcised.
The Gemara argues that if the verse referred to the uncircumcised, why does it say 'again' and 'a second time', implying the circumcision was already performed but incomplete.

The Gemara resolves that 'a second time' teaches that the end of circumcision is like the beginning: just as the beginning is indispensable, so the end is indispensable, citing the Mishnah about flesh covering the majority of the corona.

sub.text: Ravina (or Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba) quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Ravina (or Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba) quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Ravina or Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba quoting Rav defines the flesh that covers the majority of the height of the corona (בָּשָׂר הַחוֹפֶה אֶת רוֹב גּוֹבְהָהּ שֶׁל עֲטָרָה).

items.text: Reason for not circumcising in the desert
items.text_en: Reason for not circumcising in the desert
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Israelites were not circumcised in the desert, and offers an answer: due to the weakness of the journey (chulsha d'orchah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Israelites were not circumcised during their forty years in the desert.
The Gemara answers that the Israelites were not circumcised due to חולשא דאורחא (the weakness of the journey).

items.text: Reason for the north wind's absence in the desert
items.text_en: Reason for the north wind's absence in the desert
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two explanations for why the north wind did not blow during Israel's forty years in the wilderness: either because they were rebuked, or to prevent the clouds of glory from scattering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation that the north wind did not blow during the forty years in the wilderness, citing a baraita.
The Gemara gives two possible reasons: either because the Israelites were rebuked, or to prevent the clouds of glory from scattering.

items.text: Rav Pappa's practical ruling on cloudy and windy days
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's practical ruling on cloudy and windy days
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that on a cloudy or windy day one should not circumcise or perform the peri'ah, but nowadays since many people are accustomed to it, 'the Lord protects the simple.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that on a cloudy or windy day one should not circumcise or perform peri'ah, but nowadays since many are accustomed to it, 'the Lord protects the simple.'

items.text: Baraita on the north wind blowing at midnight
items.text_en: Baraita on the north wind blowing at midnight
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that during the forty years in the desert, the north wind blew every night at midnight, as derived from the verse about the plague of the firstborn, indicating that this is a time of divine favor.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that during the forty years in the desert, the north wind blew every midnight, citing the verse about the plague of the firstborn to show this is a time of divine favor.

items.text: Debate on whether a man with a retracted foreskin eats terumah
items.text_en: Debate on whether a man with a retracted foreskin eats terumah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that a man with a retracted foreskin (משוך) may eat terumah by Torah law, but the Sages decreed against it because he appears uncircumcised. The Gemara challenges this with a baraita requiring him to be circumcised, and analyzes whether the source is biblical or a rabbinic support.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that by Torah law a man with a retracted foreskin (משוך) may eat תרומה (priestly portion), but the Sages decreed against it because he appears uncircumcised.
The Gemara objects with a baraita that says a man with a retracted foreskin must be circumcised, implying it is a Torah requirement, and questions the meaning of 'צריך' (needs).

The Gemara cites the continuation of the baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says he should not circumcise due to danger, but the Sages respond with a proof from the verse 'הִמּוֹל יִמּוֹל' (he shall surely be circumcised) and 'אֶת בְּרִיתִי הֵפַר' (he has broken My covenant) to include the retracted foreskin.

The Gemara explains the phrase 'ואומר' (and it says): if you think 'הִמּוֹל יִמּוֹל' includes only the obstructing shreds of skin, then the second verse 'אֶת בְּרִיתִי הֵפַר' teaches that it also includes the retracted foreskin.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Huna thought the baraita's citation of a verse proves it is Torah law, but in truth it is only rabbinic, and the verse is merely an אסמכתא (supportive allusion).

items.text: Refutation of Rav Huna from a baraita
items.text_en: Refutation of Rav Huna from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly states that a man with a retracted foreskin (משוך) and one born circumcised may eat terumah, which contradicts Rav Huna's position. The Gemara declares this a conclusive refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing who may eat terumah, including a man with a retracted foreskin (משוך) and one born circumcised, which contradicts Rav Huna's position.
The Gemara declares that the baraita is a conclusive refutation (תיוובתא) of Rav Huna's position.

items.text: Analysis of the tumtum's wives and the baraita's structure
items.text_en: Analysis of the tumtum's wives and the baraita's structure
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a tumtum can have wives, with Abaye explaining that his testicles are externally visible, and Rava interpreting 'his wives' as his mother. The Gemara then reconciles the baraita's statements about tumtum and the definite uncircumcised person.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that a tumtum does not eat terumah, but his wives and slaves do.
The Gemara questions how a tumtum can have wives, considering the possibility that his betrothal might be invalid.
Abaye answers that the tumtum's testicles are externally visible, confirming his male status.
Rava interprets 'his wives' as his mother, teaching that even a tumtum who cannot father children still enables his mother to eat terumah.
The Gemara cites a baraita to support Abaye's view, showing that the first clause refers to a definite uncircumcised person and the latter to a doubtful one.
The Gemara objects to Rava's interpretation, questioning why the baraita needs to mention tumtum in the latter clause if it simply means an uncircumcised person.
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita means: just as a definite uncircumcised person does not eat, so too a tumtum (who is a doubtful uncircumcised person) does not eat.

items.text: Introduction of a Tannaitic dispute on circumcision timing
items.text_en: Introduction of a Tannaitic dispute on circumcision timing
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a Tannaitic dispute about who must be circumcised only during the day, including a man with a retracted foreskin, a convert born circumcised, and one who delayed his circumcision, with Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon offering a different opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaitic dispute listing those who must be circumcised only during the day, including a man with a retracted foreskin, a convert born circumcised, one who delayed, and others.
Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon states that one who delayed his circumcision may be circumcised even at night, differing from the first Tanna.

items.text: Dispute over the nature of a delayed circumcision
items.text_en: Dispute over the nature of a delayed circumcision
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the dispute in the Mishnah is about whether a child who is a 'משוך' (whose foreskin is drawn back) is a Torah prohibition or a rabbinic one. It then rejects this, concluding that all agree a 'משוך' is rabbinic and a child past his time is Torah, and the real dispute is over whether we expound the word 'וּבַיּוֹם'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's dispute is about whether a 'משוך' (drawn-back foreskin) is a Torah prohibition or a rabbinic one.
The Gemara objects: can anyone hold that a child past his time is only rabbinic?
The Gemara concludes: all agree a 'משוך' is rabbinic and a child past his time is Torah law; the real dispute is whether we expound the word 'וּבַיּוֹם'.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's teaching and Rabbi Elazar's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's teaching and Rabbi Elazar's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that leftover sacrificial meat (נותר) is burned only by day in its time, but at any time if past its time. Rabbi Elazar objects by citing a baraita that derives from 'וּבַיּוֹם' that circumcision on the eighth day is only by day, and includes later days. The Gemara notes that even one who does not expound a 'ו' does expound 'ו' and 'הי', and Rabbi Yochanan was silent.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that leftover sacrificial meat (נותר) is burned only by day when in its time, but by day or night when past its time.
Rabbi Elazar objects by citing a baraita that derives from 'וּבַיּוֹם' that circumcision on the eighth day is only by day, and includes later days.
The Gemara notes that even one who does not expound a 'ו' does expound 'ו' and 'הי', and Rabbi Yochanan was silent.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan praises Rabbi Elazar, Resh Lakish corrects him
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan praises Rabbi Elazar, Resh Lakish corrects him
items.desc_en: After Rabbi Elazar leaves, Rabbi Yochanan praises him to Resh Lakish, saying he sits and teaches like Moses from the Almighty. Resh Lakish retorts that it is not his own teaching but a baraita from Torat Kohanim. Rabbi Elazar then reviews it in three days and masters it in three months.

sub.desc_en: After Rabbi Elazar leaves, Rabbi Yochanan praises him to Resh Lakish, comparing his teaching to Moses from the Almighty.
Resh Lakish objects that Rabbi Elazar's teaching is not original but a baraita from Torat Kohanim.
Rabbi Elazar reviews the baraita in three days and masters it in three months, demonstrating his diligence.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on an uncircumcised man sprinkling the red heifer
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on an uncircumcised man sprinkling the red heifer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that an uncircumcised man who sprinkles the red heifer water is valid. He compares him to a טבול יום (one who immersed that day), who is forbidden in terumah but valid for the red heifer. The Gemara supports this with a baraita and a precedent where the Sages validated such sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that an uncircumcised man who sprinkles the red heifer water is valid, comparing him to a טבול יום (one who immersed that day), who is forbidden in תרומה (priestly portion) but valid for the red heifer.
The Gemara objects that the comparison to a טבול יום is flawed, since a טבול יום is permitted in מעשר (tithe), unlike an uncircumcised man.

The Gemara clarifies that the comparison is about נגיעה (touching), not eating: just as a טבול יום, forbidden in touching תרומה, is valid for the red heifer, so an uncircumcised man, permitted in touching, should certainly be valid.
A baraita supports Rabbi Elazar's ruling, stating that an uncircumcised man's sprinkling is valid and citing a precedent where the Sages validated such sprinkling.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about a tumtum and an uncircumcised man
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about a tumtum and an uncircumcised man
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states a tumtum (whose sex is unknown) who sanctifies the red heifer water is invalid because he is a ספק ערל (doubtfully uncircumcised), and an uncircumcised man is invalid to sanctify. Rav Yosef answers that this baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, who includes an uncircumcised man as impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that a tumtum (whose sex is unknown) who sanctifies the red heifer water is invalid because he is a ספק ערל (doubtfully uncircumcised), and an uncircumcised man is invalid to sanctify.
Rav Yosef answers that this baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, who includes an uncircumcised man as impure via the verse 'איש איש' (any man).

items.text: Rava's question and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's question and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava questions why the baraita did not explicitly state 'הערל והטמא' and attribute it to Rabbi Akiva. The Gemara answers that in another baraita, 'הערל והטמא' are exempt from pilgrimage, but there the reason is because they are repulsive, not because of impurity.

sub.desc_en: Rava questions why the baraita did not explicitly state 'הערל והטמא' and attribute it to Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara answers that in another baraita, 'הערל והטמא' are exempt from pilgrimage, but there the reason is because they are repulsive, not because of impurity.

items.text: Dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda on who is fit to sanctify
items.text_en: Dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda on who is fit to sanctify
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda regarding who is fit to sanctify the red heifer water. The Rabbis derive from 'וְלָקְחוּ' that those unfit for gathering are unfit for sanctification, while Rabbi Yehuda argues that 'וְלָקְחוּ' includes even those unfit there. The Gemara clarifies the scriptural nuances.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda by citing a baraita about who is fit to sanctify the red heifer water.
The Rabbis derive from the verse 'וְלָקְחוּ' that those unfit for gathering the ashes are also unfit for sanctification, while those fit for gathering are fit for sanctification.

Rabbi Yehuda objects that if the Rabbis' reasoning were correct, the verse should have said 'וְלָקַח' (singular); the plural 'וְלָקְחוּ' teaches that even those unfit for gathering are fit for sanctification.

The Gemara asks Rabbi Yehuda: if the plural 'וְלָקְחוּ' includes those unfit for gathering, why does the verse not also include women, since it says 'וְנָתַן' (masculine) and not 'וְנָתְנָה' (feminine)?

The Rabbis answer that the Torah wrote both 'וְלָקְחוּ' (plural) and 'וְנָתַן' (singular) to teach that even if two people take the ashes, one may give them, thereby excluding women who cannot take at all.

items.text: Opening derivation from the verse about the red heifer
items.text_en: Opening derivation from the verse about the red heifer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse that teaches that a טבול יום is valid for the red heifer, establishing a principle of derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'וְהִזָּה הַטָּהוֹר עַל הַטָּמֵא' (the pure one shall sprinkle upon the impure) and derives that a טבול יום (one who immersed but awaits sunset) is valid for the red heifer.

items.text: Question about the uncircumcised man and ma'aser
items.text_en: Question about the uncircumcised man and ma'aser
items.desc_en: The students ask Rav Sheshet whether an ערל is prohibited from eating ma'aser, posing two possibilities: either ma'aser learns from pesach regarding ערלות just as pesach learns from ma'aser regarding אנינות, or the derivation only works from the stringent to the lenient.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Rav Sheshet whether an ערל (uncircumcised man) is prohibited from eating ma'aser, proposing that just as pesach learns from ma'aser regarding אנינות (mourning), ma'aser might learn from pesach regarding ערלות (uncircumcision).
The students raise an alternative: perhaps the derivation only works from the stringent (חמור) to the lenient (קל), but not from the lenient to the stringent, so ma'aser cannot learn from pesach.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's answer from a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's answer from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet responds by citing a baraita that lists the laws of terumah and bikurim, including that they are subject to death and the fifth, forbidden to non-priests, etc., and notes that these laws do not apply to ma'aser.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet responds by citing a baraita that lists the laws of תרומה (priestly portion) and ביכורים (first fruits), including that they are subject to death and the fifth, forbidden to non-priests, etc., and notes that these laws do not apply to מעשר (tithe).

items.text: Objection: why not mention ערל?
items.text_en: Objection: why not mention ערל?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the baraita intended to exclude ma'aser from the law of ערל, it should have explicitly stated that an ערל is forbidden in terumah and bikurim but not in ma'aser.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the baraita intended to exclude ma'aser from the law of ערל (uncircumcised), it should have explicitly stated that an ערל is forbidden in terumah and bikurim but not in ma'aser.

items.text: Resolution: the baraita omitted some laws
items.text_en: Resolution: the baraita omitted some laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the baraita is not exhaustive; it omitted the law of ערל, as it also omitted other laws like the requirement to bring ma'aser to the Temple, the confession, and the prohibition for an אונן, which are listed in the continuation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the baraita omitted some laws, and then asks what exactly it omitted.
The Gemara specifies that the baraita omitted the laws of bringing ma'aser to the Temple, the confession, the prohibition for an אונן, and the obligation of ביעור, as listed in the continuation.
The Gemara adds that the baraita also omitted the prohibition of burning terumah and bikurim in a state of טומאה (ritual impurity).

items.text: Opening observation: Tanna omitted terumah from the list
items.text_en: Opening observation: Tanna omitted terumah from the list
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Tanna included bikurim in the list of items that are eaten in tum'ah and liable for lashes, but did not include terumah, implying the Tanna taught and omitted something.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Tanna included bikurim in the list of items eaten in tum'ah with lashes, but omitted terumah, implying the Tanna taught and omitted something.

items.text: Bikurim and onen: dispute between Sages and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Bikurim and onen: dispute between Sages and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the source for bikurim being forbidden to an onen: a verse links bikurim to ma'aser, which is forbidden to an onen. Rabbi Shimon argues that bikurim are called terumah, and terumah is permitted to an onen.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that bikurim are forbidden to an onen, while Rabbi Shimon permits them.
The Gemara asks: what is the source for the Sages' position that bikurim are forbidden to an onen?

The Gemara explains that the verse (Deut 12:17) links bikurim to ma'aser, and as ma'aser is forbidden to an onen, bikurim are likewise forbidden, based on a teaching by Mar that 'תרומת ידך' refers to bikurim.
Rabbi Shimon argues that since the Torah calls bikurim 'תרומה' (terumah), and terumah is permitted to an onen (by virtue of its own אונן law), bikurim are likewise permitted to an onen.

items.text: Bikurim and bi'ur: dispute between Sages and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Bikurim and bi'ur: dispute between Sages and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that bikurim are subject to bi'ur (removal), but Rabbi Shimon exempts them. The dispute hinges on whether bikurim are linked to ma'aser or to terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that bikurim (first fruits) are subject to bi'ur (removal), but Rabbi Shimon exempts them.
The Gemara explains the dispute: one authority (Mar) links bikurim to ma'aser (tithe), requiring bi'ur, while the other does not link them.

items.text: Source for prohibition of eating bikurim while tamei
items.text_en: Source for prohibition of eating bikurim while tamei
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the prohibition of eating bikurim in a state of tum'ah. It cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse 'Lo vi'arti mimenu b'tamei' that one must not eat bikurim when either the person or the fruit is tamei. The Gemara then clarifies that the question is about tum'at atzmo (the fruit's own impurity), and derives it from a comparison to ma'aser.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the prohibition against burning bikurim in a state of tum'ah and the liability for eating them in a state of tum'at atzmo.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse 'לֹא בִעַרְתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ בְּטָמֵא' that one must not eat bikurim when either the person or the fruit is tamei.

The Gemara notes that the source for the prohibition of eating bikurim when the person is tamei is already explicit in the verse, so the question must be about tum'at atzmo (the fruit's own impurity).

The Gemara clarifies that the question is about tum'at atzmo, and derives it from a comparison to ma'aser: just as ma'aser is permitted to be eaten by a tamei person, bikurim are forbidden, as the verse 'בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ תֹּאכְלֶנּוּ' teaches that bikurim are not like ma'aser in this regard.

items.text: Source for terumah being excluded from the prohibition of burning in tum'ah
items.text_en: Source for terumah being excluded from the prohibition of burning in tum'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why terumah is not included in the prohibition of burning bikurim in tum'ah. Rabbi Avahu quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the verse 'mimenu' excludes terumah. The Gemara then questions why kodashim (sacred items) are not also excluded, and answers with a kal vachomer. A further objection is raised that terumah should also be excluded by kal vachomer, but the verse 'mimenu' teaches otherwise. The Gemara then debates which category is more stringent, using the mnemonic פנקעכ״ס for kodashim and מחפ״ז for terumah, concluding that the stringencies of kodashim are more numerous, or that karet is more severe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that terumah is excluded from the prohibition of burning bikurim in tum'ah.
Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse 'לֹא בִעַרְתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ בְּטָמֵא' to show that 'מִמֶּנּוּ' excludes terumah from the prohibition.
The Gemara objects that the same verse could exclude kodashim (sacred items) rather than terumah.
The Gemara rejects the objection with a kal vachomer: if the lenient maaser is prohibited, then the stringent kodashim certainly is.
The Gemara objects that terumah should also be excluded by kal vachomer, but the verse 'מִמֶּנּוּ' teaches otherwise.
The Gemara answers that kodashim is not excluded because it has more stringencies (mnemonic פנקעכ״ס: piggul, notar, korban, me'ilah, karet, and aninut).
The Gemara objects that terumah also has stringencies (mnemonic מחפ״ז: death, fifth, no redemption, and forbidden to non-priests).
The Gemara resolves that kodashim's stringencies are more numerous, or alternatively that karet is more severe than terumah's stringencies.

items.text: Terumah: prohibition but no lashes for eating in tum'ah
items.text_en: Terumah: prohibition but no lashes for eating in tum'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that while terumah is not subject to lashes for eating in tum'ah, there is still a prohibition derived from the verse 'Bish'arecha tochalenu', which implies a positive commandment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah states one receives lashes for eating bikurim in a state of personal tum'ah, unlike terumah, and asks: from where do we derive that terumah has at least a prohibition?

The Gemara answers that the verse 'בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ תֹּאכְלֶנּוּ' (in your gates you shall eat it) implies a positive commandment for terumah, and a prohibition derived from a positive commandment is merely a positive commandment, not a negative prohibition carrying lashes.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof that the Tanna omitted items
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof that the Tanna omitted items
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi concludes that from the beginning we can infer that the Tanna taught and omitted something, because the Tanna did not include terumah in the list of items that are eaten in tum'ah and liable for lashes.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi concludes that from the beginning we can infer that the Tanna taught and omitted something, because the Tanna did not include terumah in the list of items that are eaten in tum'ah and liable for lashes.

items.text: Initial inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Initial inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to infer from the Mishnah's statement that second tithe has no redemption in other years of the Sabbatical cycle, unlike first tithe, that an ערל is prohibited from ma'aser. The inference is presented as 'שמע מינה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's statement that second tithe has no redemption in other years, unlike first tithe, that an ערל (uncircumcised man) is prohibited from ma'aser.

items.text: Baraita about remaining foreskin and clarification of ma'aser
items.text_en: Baraita about remaining foreskin and clarification of ma'aser
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one with remaining foreskin that impedes circumcision may not eat terumah, Passover, sacrifices, or ma'aser. The Gemara initially assumes ma'aser means grain tithe, but then considers animal tithe. It rejects animal tithe as redundant with sacrifices, and concludes it must be first tithe according to Rabbi Meir, who prohibits first tithe to non-priests.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one with remaining foreskin that impedes circumcision may not eat terumah, Passover, sacrifices, or ma'aser.
The Gemara asks: does 'ma'aser' in the baraita refer to grain tithe? It answers: no, it is animal tithe.
The Gemara objects: animal tithe is the same as sacrifices, so why list both?
The Gemara resolves: it must be first tithe, and the baraita follows Rabbi Meir, who prohibits first tithe to non-priests.

items.text: Support from Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Midifti
items.text_en: Support from Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Midifti
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Midifti taught that an ערל is prohibited from two tithes. The Gemara initially thinks these are grain tithe and animal tithe, but again explains it refers to first tithe according to Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Midifti that an ערל (uncircumcised man) is prohibited from two tithes, and asks whether these are grain tithe and animal tithe.
The Gemara rejects the initial understanding and explains that here too it refers to first tithe according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that first tithe is forbidden to non-priests.

items.text: Challenge from the law of an onein and the school of Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of an onein and the school of Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: A baraita lists prohibitions for an onein, tevul yom, and mechusar kippurim regarding terumah, parah, and ma'aser, but does not mention an ערל. The Gemara explains that this tanna is from the school of Rabbi Akiva, who includes an ערל as like a tamei person, so the prohibition is already covered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the view that an ערל (uncircumcised man) is prohibited in ma'aser by citing a baraita that lists prohibitions for an onein, tevul yom, and mechusar kippurim regarding terumah, parah, and ma'aser, but does not mention an ערל, implying he is permitted.
The Gemara answers that this tanna is from the school of Rabbi Akiva, who includes an ערל as like a tamei person, so the prohibition is already covered and need not be listed separately.

items.text: Identifying the opposing tanna: Rabbi Yosef HaBavli
items.text_en: Identifying the opposing tanna: Rabbi Yosef HaBavli
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Akiva as Rabbi Yosef HaBavli, who holds that an onein's burning is valid but a mechusar kippurim's is invalid, implying a different view on the status of an ערל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the opposing tanna as Rabbi Yosef HaBavli, who holds that an onein's burning is valid but a mechusar kippurim's is invalid.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's gezeirah shavah and its exposition
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's gezeirah shavah and its exposition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak derives that an ערל is prohibited from ma'aser via a גזירה שווה from the word 'מִמֶּנּוּ' used in both Passover and ma'aser. The Gemara discusses the superfluity of the three instances of 'מִמֶּנּוּ' in Passover and in ma'aser, and addresses objections about the validity of the analogy, including a counter-argument from Mar Zutra and resolutions by Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua and Rav Ashi.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak asserts that an ערל (uncircumcised man) is prohibited from eating ma'aser, deriving it via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'מִמֶּנּוּ' used in both Passover and ma'aser.

The Gemara objects that the גזירה שווה requires both instances of 'מִמֶּנּוּ' to be מוּפְנֶה (free for analogy), otherwise one could refute it by noting that Passover carries additional penalties (pigul, notar, tum'ah) that ma'aser lacks.

Rava explains in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak that three instances of 'מִמֶּנּוּ' appear in the Passover section: one for its own context, one for the גזירה שווה, and one for the dispute about whether the verse gives a positive command after a prohibition or a second morning for burning the leftover.

The Gemara states that three instances of 'מִמֶּנּוּ' appear in the ma'aser section: one for its own context, one for the teaching of Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan, and one for the teaching of Reish Lakish.

Reish Lakish cites Rabbi Simai that from the verse 'וְלֹא נָתַתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ לְמֵת' one derives that second tithe that became impure may be used for anointing, since the verse permits giving it to the living in a manner similar to the dead.
Mar Zutra objects that perhaps the verse permits buying a coffin and shrouds for the dead, not just anointing.

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua resolves that the word 'מִמֶּנּוּ' implies from the body itself, excluding items like a coffin.
Rav Ashi resolves by comparing 'לֹא נָתַתִּי' to 'לֹא אָכַלְתִּי', concluding that just as eating is from the body itself, so too the giving is from the body itself.

items.text: Addressing the 'one-sided' analogy and Rabbi Avahu's derivation
items.text_en: Addressing the 'one-sided' analogy and Rabbi Avahu's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the גזירה שווה might be one-sided (מופנה מצד אחד), which is acceptable to those who say 'learn and do not respond', but problematic for those who say 'learn and respond'. It then cites Rabbi Avahu's derivation from Rav Nachman that two terumot (pure and impure) are discussed, and the verse 'לְךָ' permits the impure one for heating under one's cooking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) is only מופנה מצד אחד (one-sided), which is acceptable to those who say 'learn and do not respond' but problematic for those who say 'learn and respond'.

sub.text: Gemara's answer via Rabbi Avahu and Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer via Rabbi Avahu and Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Rabbi Avahu's derivation from Rav Nachman that the verse 'וַאֲנִי הִנֵּה נָתַתִּי לְךָ אֶת מִשְׁמֶרֶת תְּרוּמֹתָי' refers to two terumot (pure and impure), and the word 'לְךָ' permits the impure one for heating under one's cooking.

items.text: Source for all impure persons being prohibited from eating terumah
items.text_en: Source for all impure persons being prohibited from eating terumah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael cites a verse to derive that all impure individuals (like a leper or zav) are prohibited from eating terumah, establishing the general principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that all impure persons are prohibited from eating תרומה (priestly portion).

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yishmael derives the prohibition from the verse 'איש איש מזרע אהרן והוא צרוע או זב' (any man of Aaron's seed who is a leper or zav), which includes all impure individuals.

items.text: Initial question about terumah and the chalalah
items.text_en: Initial question about terumah and the chalalah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether terumah can be eaten by a chalalah (a disqualified priestly descendant), concluding that she is not considered 'seed of Aaron' and thus cannot eat terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the verse 'in the seed of Aaron' refers to terumah (תרומה) or to the priestly gifts of the breast and thigh (חזה ושוק).
The Gemara answers that a chalalah (חללה) cannot eat terumah because she is not considered 'seed of Aaron', resolving the question.

items.text: Derivation that 'until he becomes pure' means sunset, not atonement
items.text_en: Derivation that 'until he becomes pure' means sunset, not atonement
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the phrase 'until he becomes pure' refers to sunset, not bringing an atonement offering, based on a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael comparing a zav with two sightings and a quarantined leper to a 'tamei nefesh' (corpse-impure person) who does not require atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how we know that the phrase 'until he becomes pure' (עַד אֲשֶׁר יִטְהָר) means until sunset, rather than until he brings an atonement offering.

The Gemara rejects the possibility, citing a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that compares a zav with two sightings and a quarantined leper to a 'tamei nefesh' (corpse-impure person), who does not require atonement, to show that the phrase refers to sunset.

items.text: Challenge: perhaps atonement is needed for those who require it
items.text_en: Challenge: perhaps atonement is needed for those who require it
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the previous derivation only applies to those who do not need atonement, but for one who does need atonement, perhaps they must bring it before eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the previous derivation only applies to those who do not need atonement, but for one who does need atonement, perhaps they must bring it before eating.

items.text: Rava and Rav Chisda's three verses for ma'aser, terumah, and kodashim
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Chisda's three verses for ma'aser, terumah, and kodashim
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about the stages of eating (ma'aser after immersion, terumah after sunset, kodashim after atonement) and Rava quoting Rav Chisda derives these from three verses: one for immersion, one for sunset, and one for atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the mishnah's stages: eating ma'aser after immersion, terumah after sunset, and kodashim after atonement.
Rava in the name of Rav Chisda answers by citing three verses: one for immersion (ma'aser), one for sunset (terumah), and one for atonement (kodashim).

items.text: Debate over which is more stringent: terumah or ma'aser
items.text_en: Debate over which is more stringent: terumah or ma'aser
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether terumah is more stringent than ma'aser (due to the acronym מחפ״ז) or ma'aser is more stringent (due to הד״ס ט״ב), concluding that death (mentioned in terumah) makes it more stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the assignment of the verses could be reversed, and then suggests that תרומה (terumah) is more stringent based on the acronym מחפ״ז.
The Gemara objects that מעשר (ma'aser) is more stringent based on the acronym הד״ס ט״ב.
The Gemara concludes that despite the counter-argument, the fact that תרומה (terumah) involves death makes it more stringent.

items.text: Rava's proof that ma'aser is for all souls
items.text_en: Rava's proof that ma'aser is for all souls
items.desc_en: Rava argues that even without the death argument, one cannot reverse the assignment because the verse says 'nefesh' (soul), indicating something equal for all souls, which is ma'aser.

sub.desc_en: Rava argues that even without the death argument, one cannot reverse the assignment because the verse says 'נפש' (soul), indicating something equal for all souls, which is מעשר (tithe).

items.text: Challenge: perhaps atonement is still needed for kodashim
items.text_en: Challenge: perhaps atonement is still needed for kodashim
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the previous derivation only applies to those who do not need atonement, but for kodashim, perhaps atonement is required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the previous derivation only applies to those who do not need atonement, but for kodashim, perhaps atonement is required.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's derivation for terumah vs. kodashim from a yoledet
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's derivation for terumah vs. kodashim from a yoledet
items.desc_en: Abaye cites two verses about a yoledet (woman after childbirth) to distinguish terumah (after full days) from kodashim (after atonement). Rava adds a proof that the verse 'and the priest shall atone... and she shall be pure' refers to terumah, not kodashim, because kodashim would be forbidden if touched by a tamei.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by citing two verses about a yoledet (woman after childbirth) to distinguish between terumah (after full days) and kodashim (after atonement).
The Gemara objects that one could reverse the assignment, arguing that kodashim is more stringent (חמור) based on the mnemonic פנקעכ״ס.
The Gemara counters that terumah is more stringent, based on the mnemonic מחפ״ז, and notes that those stringencies are more numerous.

Rava resolves the objection by citing the verse 'וְכִפֶּר עָלֶיהָ הַכֹּהֵן וְטָהֵרָה' (and the priest shall atone... and she shall be pure), arguing that since the verse implies she was still impure before atonement, it must refer to terumah, because touching kodashim while impure is forbidden by the verse 'וְהַבָּשָׂר אֲשֶׁר יִגַּע בְּכׇל טָמֵא לֹא יֵאָכֵל' (the flesh that touches any impure thing shall not be eaten).

items.text: Rav Shisha's objection and Rava's response
items.text_en: Rav Shisha's objection and Rava's response
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi objects that the verse about a yoledet includes converts and freed maidservants, who cannot eat terumah, so it must refer to kodashim. Rava dismisses this objection with 'And not?'

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi objects that the verse about a yoledet includes converts and freed maidservants, who cannot eat תרומה (priestly portion), so it must refer to קדשים (sacred offerings).
Rava dismisses the objection with a rhetorical 'And not?' implying the objection is invalid.

items.text: Gemara's question on the need for multiple verses regarding terumah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the need for multiple verses regarding terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why multiple verses are needed to teach the laws of impurity for terumah. It explains that each verse serves a specific purpose: one teaches that impurity ends at sunset, another that a sacrifice is needed for those requiring atonement, and a third that immersion is required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a verse prohibiting contact with holy things is needed, since it already includes terumah, and answers that the verse merely lists categories.
The Gemara asks why three verses about terumah are needed, and explains that one verse teaches that impurity ends at sunset.
The Gemara explains that a second verse is needed to teach that one who requires atonement must bring a sacrifice.
The Gemara explains that a third verse is needed to teach that immersion is required.

items.text: Question for the Tanna who disagrees with the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Question for the Tanna who disagrees with the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why two verses are needed for sacrifices according to the Tanna who holds that the verse 'עד אשר יטהר' refers to a zav with three sightings and a confirmed leper, requiring atonement. It explains that one verse is needed for a woman after childbirth and another for a zav, as each has unique leniencies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why two verses are needed for sacrifices according to the Tanna who disagrees with the school of Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that the verse 'עַד אֲשֶׁר יִטְהָר' refers to a zav with three sightings and a confirmed leper, requiring atonement.

The Gemara answers that both verses are necessary: one for a woman after childbirth and another for a zav, because each has unique leniencies that might otherwise exempt it from the requirement of atonement.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's derivation for the prohibition of touching terumah
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's derivation for the prohibition of touching terumah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that the verse 'במים יובא וטמא עד הערב' teaches the prohibition of touching terumah. A baraita is cited showing that 'וטמא' and 'וטהר' together indicate that one is impure for terumah but pure for ma'aser. The Gemara supports this by noting that just as eating terumah is more stringent than eating ma'aser, so too touching terumah is more stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what purpose the verse 'במים יובא וטמא עד הערב' serves.
Rabbi Zeira answers that the verse teaches the prohibition of touching terumah.
A baraita is cited showing that 'וטמא' and 'וטהר' together indicate impurity for terumah but purity for ma'aser.
The Gemara resolves the direction of the baraita by reasoning that just as eating terumah is more stringent than eating ma'aser, so too touching terumah is more stringent.

items.text: Alternative derivation for the prohibition of touching terumah
items.text_en: Alternative derivation for the prohibition of touching terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: the verse 'בכל קדש לא תגע' is a warning for the eater, not the toucher. It proves this by comparing 'קדש' to 'מקדש', showing that just as entering the Temple involves a capital offense, so too eating terumah involves a capital offense, but touching does not. Thus, 'נגיעה' here means eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative derivation: the verse 'בכל קדש לא תגע' is a warning for the eater, not the toucher, and questions whether it might instead refer to the toucher.

The Gemara cites a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'קדש' and 'מקדש', showing that just as entering the Temple involves a capital offense, so too eating terumah involves a capital offense, but touching does not.
The Gemara resolves that the verse uses the term 'נגיעה' to mean eating, equating touching with eating in this context.

items.text: Dispute regarding a woman who guards herself from forbidden relations
items.text_en: Dispute regarding a woman who guards herself from forbidden relations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a woman who guards herself from forbidden relations (משמרת לביאה פסולה) and whether she may eat terumah. Rabbi Elazar says this is a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon, while Rabbi Yochanan says even Rabbi Meir would permit because she already ate. Rabbi Elazar rejects this reasoning, citing a case of a bat Yisrael married to a kohen who died.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah regarding a woman who guards herself from forbidden relations (משמרת לביאה פסולה) and whether she may eat terumah.
Rabbi Elazar answers that the Mishnah is taught in a dispute, and it follows Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon who would forbid her to eat terumah.
Rabbi Yochanan says that even according to Rabbi Meir, the case is different because she has already eaten terumah before becoming forbidden.
Rabbi Elazar objects that the reasoning of 'already ate' is not accepted, citing the case of a bat Yisrael married to a kohen who died, who would then eat terumah based on that logic.
Rabbi Yochanan responds that in the case of the widow, her husband's acquisition (קניין) has lapsed, but here the acquisition has not lapsed, so the cases are different.

items.text: Definition of פצוע דכא and the case of a pierced testicle
items.text_en: Definition of פצוע דכא and the case of a pierced testicle
items.desc_en: The rabbis define פצוע דכא as one whose testicles are wounded, even one, even pierced, even decayed, even missing. Rabbi Yishmael's son reports that in Yavneh, they said one with only one testicle is like a סריס חמה and is valid. The Gemara questions whether a pierced testicle prevents reproduction, citing a story of a man who climbed a palm tree.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines פצוע דכא as one whose testicles are wounded, even one, even pierced, even decayed, even missing.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael reports that in Yavneh, the sages said one with only one testicle is like a סריס חמה (congenital eunuch) and is valid.
The Gemara objects that a man with one testicle cannot literally be a סריס חמה (congenital eunuch), and corrects the statement to mean he is like a סריס חמה and is valid.
The Gemara questions whether a pierced testicle prevents reproduction, citing a story of a man who climbed a palm tree.

items.text: Opening anecdote about a bird that produced offspring
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about a bird that produced offspring
items.desc_en: A story is told about a bird that was injured and still produced offspring, leading Shmuel to send a message to Rav questioning the status of the offspring.

sub.desc_en: A story is told about a bird that was injured and still produced offspring, leading Shmuel to send a message to Rav questioning the status of the offspring.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on פצוע דכא בידי שמים
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on פצוע דכא בידי שמים
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that a פצוע דכא caused by Heaven (natural causes) is valid. Rava explains the linguistic nuance of the term.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that a פצוע דכא (crushed testicle) caused by Heaven (natural causes) is valid for marriage.
Rava explains the linguistic nuance: the term is 'פצוע' (indefinite) not 'הפצוע' (definite), implying a natural condition rather than a deliberate act.

items.text: Baraita comparing פצוע to ממזר
items.text_en: Baraita comparing פצוע to ממזר
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that just as a ממזר is disqualified only when caused by human action, so too a פצוע is disqualified only when caused by human action.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'פצוע' and 'ממזר', concluding that just as a ממזר is disqualified only when caused by human action, so too a פצוע is disqualified only when caused by human action.

items.text: Rava's definition of פצוע, דך, and כרות
items.text_en: Rava's definition of פצוע, דך, and כרות
items.desc_en: Rava explains that each term (פצוע, דך, כרות) applies to injuries of the penis, testicles, or the tubes of the testicles.

sub.desc_en: Rava declares that each of the three terms (פצוע, דך, כרות) applies to injuries of the penis, testicles, or the tubes of the testicles.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on the location of the injury
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on the location of the injury
items.desc_en: A rabbi asks Rava how we know that פצוע דכא refers to the reproductive organ and not the head. Rava answers from the fact that it does not disqualify descendants. The Gemara then questions this and brings a proof from the term כרות שפכה, which is explained to mean the place where one emits semen, not the lip or nose.

sub.text: One of the rabbis to Rava
sub.text_en: One of the rabbis to Rava
sub.desc_en: A rabbi asks Rava how we know that פצוע דכא refers to the reproductive organ and not the head.
Rava answers that the proof is from the fact that the disqualification does not extend to descendants, indicating it refers to the reproductive organ.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the disqualification applies only to the man himself, but his descendants are permitted, so the proof is not conclusive.
The Gemara brings a proof from the term כרות שפכה, which is understood to refer to the same location, establishing a verbal analogy.
The Gemara questions how we know that כרות שפכה itself refers to the reproductive organ, suggesting it might refer to the lip.
The Gemara answers that the word 'שפכה' indicates the place where one emits semen, not the lip.
The Gemara objects that perhaps it refers to the nose, but then rejects this by noting the specific form of the word.
The Gemara resolves that the phrase 'כרות שפכה' means one who emits semen due to cutting, excluding the nose or lip where emission is not affected by cutting.

items.text: Baraita confirming the location
items.text_en: Baraita confirming the location
items.desc_en: Another baraita teaches that just as a ממזר is disqualified from the place of reproduction, so too a פצוע דכא is disqualified from that place.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that just as a ממזר (bastard) is disqualified from the place of reproduction, so too a פצוע דכא (wounded testicles) is disqualified from that place.

items.text: Discussion on the corona and the ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Discussion on the corona and the ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba thought to validate a puncture below the corona, but Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that any missing part of the corona invalidates. Then Ravina asks about the measure of 'the width of a thread' and Rava Tosfa'ah answers that it is over most of its circumference.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba considered validating a puncture below the corona whose corresponding area above the corona is intact.

sub.text: Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi rejects the validation, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that any missing part of the corona invalidates.
Ravina asks whether the measure of 'the width of a thread' applies to the entire corona or most of it.
Rava Tosfa'ah answers that the measure is over most of its circumference and toward the head.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda about the shape of the wound
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda about the shape of the wound
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a wound like a quill (קולמוס) is valid, but like a spout (מרזב) is invalid, while Rav Chisda says the opposite. Rava supports Rav Huna. Finally, Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa rules that both are valid, but the issue is whether the wound is above or below the corona.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a wound shaped like a quill (קולמוס) is valid, but like a spout (מרזב) is invalid, explaining that air penetrates the former but not the latter.
Rav Chisda reverses the ruling, arguing that a spout-shaped wound scrapes (גריד) properly while a quill-shaped one does not.
Rava supports Rav Huna, reasoning that air penetration is the decisive factor, and scraping is irrelevant like a barrel spout.

sub.text: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa rules that both shapes are valid, but the wound must be below the corona; Ravina's question to Marimar was merely to confuse him.

items.text: Two practical cases and a third case
items.text_en: Two practical cases and a third case
items.desc_en: Two cases are brought: one in Machseya where Mar bar Rav Ashi shaped the wound like a quill and validated it, and one in Pumbedita where the seminal vesicle was blocked and Rav Bibi bar Abaye thought to validate it, but Rav Papi objected. The text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts a case in Machseya where Mar bar Rav Ashi shaped the wound like a quill and validated the man.
The gemara recounts a second case in Pumbedita where the seminal vesicle was blocked and fluid emerged from the place of small [organs].
Rav Bibi bar Abaye thought to validate the man.
Rav Papi objects, beginning to explain why the man should be invalidated, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Opening Aramaic saying about cooking in place
items.text_en: Opening Aramaic saying about cooking in place
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a cryptic Aramaic statement about cooking in its place versus not in its place, possibly a metaphor for the discussion that follows.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a cryptic Aramaic metaphor about cooking in its place versus not in its place, setting the stage for the discussion.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel on a perforation that sealed
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel on a perforation that sealed
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that if the organ was perforated and then sealed, the ruling depends on whether the seal would tear if the organ were cut. Rava questions where this applies, concluding it refers to the corona itself. Rav Mari bar Mar confirms this version.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that if the organ was perforated and then sealed, the ruling depends on whether the seal would tear if the organ were cut.
Rava asks where this perforation occurred, concluding it refers to the corona itself.

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Mar citing Mar Ukva citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Mar citing Mar Ukva citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Mar confirms this version, citing Mar Ukva who reports Shmuel's explicit statement that the perforation was in the corona itself.

items.text: Practical test for the seal: hot barley bread
items.text_en: Practical test for the seal: hot barley bread
items.desc_en: Rava son of Rabbah asks Rav Yosef how to test the seal. Rav Yosef instructs to place hot barley bread on the area and observe whether it causes the seal to tear.

sub.text: Rava son of Rabbah's question to Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Rava son of Rabbah's question to Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rava son of Rabbah asks Rav Yosef how to practically test the seal on a perforated organ.
Rav Yosef instructs to bring hot barley bread, place it on the area, and observe whether it causes the seal to tear.

items.text: Abaye and Rava reject the test: not all are like Jacob or Barzilai
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava reject the test: not all are like Jacob or Barzilai
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that not every man is like Jacob who never had a seminal emission, so the test is unreliable. He suggests using colored garments to induce arousal. Rava counters that not everyone is like Barzilai the Gileadite, and instead recommends a whitening test as originally done.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that not every man is like Jacob our father, who never had a seminal emission, so the arousal test is unreliable.
Abaye proposes using colored garments to induce arousal as a more reliable test.
Rava objects that not every man is like Barzilai the Gileadite, who was immune to such arousal.
Rava resolves that the original whitening test (מחוורתא) should be used instead.

items.text: Baraita: perforated is invalid, sealed is valid, and the exception
items.text_en: Baraita: perforated is invalid, sealed is valid, and the exception
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a perforated organ is invalid because urine drips, but if sealed it is valid because it can still produce offspring. This is a disqualification that can be reversed, excluding a membrane that forms from a wound, which is not considered a valid seal.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a perforated organ is invalid because urine drips, but if sealed it is valid because it can still produce offspring.
The gemara asks what the word 'זהו' (this is) in the baraita comes to exclude.
The gemara answers that it excludes a membrane that forms from a wound, which is not considered a valid seal.

items.text: Rav Idi bar Avin's practical procedure for testing
items.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin's practical procedure for testing
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin sends to Abaye a detailed method: scratch with a bristle, apply fat, then use a large ant to bite the area, and cut off its head. This works only with a bristle, not metal, and only for a small child; for an adult, the skin folds.

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin's inquiry to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin's inquiry to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin sends to Abaye a detailed method for testing a פצוע דכא (crushed or wounded male): scratch with a bristle, apply fat, use a large ant to bite, and cut off its head, specifying that only a bristle works, not metal.
Rav Idi bar Avin qualifies that this procedure applies only to a small child, because for an adult the skin folds and the test is unreliable.

items.text: Rava rejects Rav Huna's rulings on dual urination and women's licentiousness
items.text_en: Rava rejects Rav Huna's rulings on dual urination and women's licentiousness
items.desc_en: Rava states that the halakha follows neither the son (Rav Huna's son) regarding a man who urinates from two places being invalid, nor the father (Rav Huna) regarding women who rub against each other being invalid for the priesthood. Even Rabbi Elazar's view that a bachelor who has sex with an unmarried woman makes her a zonah does not apply to women, as it is mere licentiousness.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules that a man who urinates from two places is invalid for the priesthood.
Rava rejects both the son's ruling (Rabbah bar Rav Huna) and the father's ruling (Rav Huna) that women who rub against each other are invalid for the priesthood.

Rava clarifies that even according to Rabbi Elazar, who says a bachelor having sex with an unmarried woman makes her a זונה (harlot), this applies only to a man, but a woman's act is mere licentiousness and does not disqualify her from the priesthood.

items.text: Mishnah: פצוע דכא and כרות שפכה are permitted to converts and freed slaves
items.text_en: Mishnah: פצוע דכא and כרות שפכה are permitted to converts and freed slaves
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man with crushed or severed reproductive organs is permitted to marry a convert or freed slavewoman, but is prohibited from entering the assembly, as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a man with crushed or severed reproductive organs is permitted to marry a convert or freed slavewoman, but is prohibited from entering the assembly, as per the verse.

items.text: Gemara: Does a kohen with פצוע דכא retain his sanctity regarding converts?
items.text_en: Gemara: Does a kohen with פצוע דכא retain his sanctity regarding converts?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a kohen who is פצוע דכא may marry a convert or freed slavewoman. Rav Sheshet proves from a baraita that an Israelite with this condition may marry a נתינה, implying he is not sanctified. Rava initially argues the prohibition is due to idolatry, not sanctity, and that converts are permitted. The Gemara then questions whether this logic would permit a mamzer, but concludes that the rabbinic decree applies only to kosher individuals, not to those already disqualified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav Sheshet whether a kohen who is פצוע דכא (wounded in the testicles) retains his sanctity such that he is forbidden to marry a convert or freed slavewoman, or whether he is no longer in his sanctity and thus permitted.

Rav Sheshet answers by citing a baraita: an Israelite who is פצוע דכא is permitted to marry a נתינה (descendant of Gibeonites), implying that if he retained sanctity, the prohibition of 'לֹא תִתְחַתֵּן בָּם' would apply.

Rava objects that the prohibition against marrying a נתינה is not due to sanctity but because the child might be led to idolatry; once they convert, the concern is removed, and the rabbis decreed a prohibition only for those capable of procreation.

The Gemara objects that if the rabbinic decree applies only to those capable of procreation, then a mamzer (bastard), who is capable of procreation, should also be forbidden to marry a נתינה, yet the Mishnah permits mamzerim and נתינים to marry each other.

The Gemara resolves that the rabbinic decree applies only to kosher (fit) individuals, not to those already disqualified (like mamzerim), so a פצוע דכא kohen, being a כשר, remains forbidden to marry a convert.

items.text: Rava retracts and Rav Yosef objects with Solomon's marriage
items.text_en: Rava retracts and Rav Yosef objects with Solomon's marriage
items.desc_en: Rava retracts his earlier statement, asserting that gentiles have no marriage relationship, but converts do. Rav Yosef objects citing Solomon's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter, who converted, but the Gemara notes that converts were not accepted in Solomon's time, implying the marriage was for political reasons.

sub.desc_en: Rava retracts his earlier statement, asserting that gentiles have no marriage relationship (חתנות), but converts do.
Rav Yosef objects by citing Solomon's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter, implying she converted and thus had marriage relationship.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that converts were not accepted in Solomon's time, implying the marriage was for political reasons (לשולחן מלכים).

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the contradiction about Solomon's marriage
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the contradiction about Solomon's marriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a contradiction: Solomon married an Egyptian woman, yet the verse says he did not marry from forbidden nations. It resolves that the verse considers him as if he married her due to his excessive love, but he did not actually marry her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the verse was not actually needed for Solomon.
The Gemara questions: since the Egyptian woman was a first-generation Egyptian, she should be forbidden; perhaps the verse refers to later generations.

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda reports a first-generation Egyptian convert who married a first-generation Egyptian woman and planned to marry his son to a second-generation Egyptian so the grandson could enter the congregation.
Rav Pappa objects: why raise a difficulty from Solomon? The verse says he did not marry forbidden nations, only clung to them in love.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: the verse says 'וַיִּתְחַתֵּן' (he married into them).
The Gemara resolves: because of his excessive love for her, Scripture considers him as if he married her, but he did not actually marry her.

items.text: Ravina's question about a wounded testicles convert and a Netinah
items.text_en: Ravina's question about a wounded testicles convert and a Netinah
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi about a mishnah that permits a פצוע דכא to marry a convert or freedwoman, implying a Netinah is forbidden. Rav Ashi counters that the latter clause permits Netinah, so no inference can be drawn.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: the mishnah permits a פצוע דכא (wounded testicles man) to marry a convert or freedwoman, implying a Netinah is forbidden.
Rav Ashi counters: the latter clause permits a Netinah, so no inference can be drawn from the mishnah.

items.text: Mishnah: Ammonite, Moabite, Egyptian, and Edomite restrictions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Ammonite, Moabite, Egyptian, and Edomite restrictions
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that Ammonite and Moabite males are permanently forbidden, but their females are immediately permitted. Egyptian and Edomite males and females are forbidden only for three generations. Rabbi Shimon permits Egyptian and Edomite females immediately via a kal vachomer, and the Sages respond that if it is a tradition they accept, but if logical, there is a refutation. Rabbi Shimon insists it is a tradition.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that Ammonite and Moabite males are permanently forbidden, but their females are immediately permitted.
The mishnah continues that Egyptian and Edomite males and females are forbidden only for three generations.
Rabbi Shimon permits Egyptian and Edomite females immediately.
Rabbi Shimon argues via a kal vachomer (a fortiori) that if in a stricter case (Ammon/Moab) females are permitted, then in a lighter case (Egypt/Edom) they should certainly be permitted immediately.
The Sages respond that if Rabbi Shimon's ruling is a tradition (הלכה) they accept it, but if it is based on logical reasoning (דין), there is a refutation.
Rabbi Shimon insists that his ruling is based on tradition (הלכה), not logic.

items.text: Gemara: Source for Ammonite and Moabite prohibition from David's lineage
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for Ammonite and Moabite prohibition from David's lineage
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives the prohibition from Saul's question about David's father. Saul wondered if David was from Peretz (fit for kingship) or Zerach (merely important). Doeg the Edomite questioned David's fitness to enter the congregation due to his descent from Ruth the Moabite. Abner responded with the tradition that 'Ammoni' excludes Ammonite women, and 'Moavi' excludes Moabite women.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the prohibition against Ammonite and Moabite men entering the congregation, and Rabbi Yochanan cites a verse.
Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse where Saul asks Abner about David's lineage, setting up the narrative.
The Gemara objects that Saul already knew David, as David was his armor-bearer.
The Gemara resolves that Saul was asking about David's father, not about David himself.
The Gemara objects that Saul should have known Jesse, who was a prominent elder.
The Gemara explains that Saul was asking whether David descended from Peretz (fit for kingship) or Zerach (merely important).
The Gemara explains why Saul asked about David's lineage, citing that Saul's armor fit David, indicating David's stature.
Doeg the Edomite objects that Saul should first question whether David is fit to enter the congregation due to his Moabite descent.
Abner responds that the tradition 'Moavi' excludes Moabite women, so Ruth's descendant is permitted.

items.text: Abner's proof and the resolution of the halakhah
items.text_en: Abner's proof and the resolution of the halakhah
items.desc_en: Abner cites the mishnah that 'Ammoni' excludes Ammonite women, and 'Moavi' excludes Moabite women. The Gemara distinguishes Egyptian and Edomite, where the reason is that men typically offer bread and water, not women. Saul then tells Abner to ask in the study hall, where they confirm the tradition.

sub.desc_en: Abner cites the mishna that 'עַמּוֹנִי' (Ammonite) excludes Ammonite women, and 'מוֹאָבִי' (Moabite) excludes Moabite women, and explains that 'מַמְזֵר' (mamzer) is written as a compound 'מוּם זָר' (strange blemish), applying to both genders.

Doeg objects that if the rule applies to 'מִצְרִי' (Egyptian) but not 'מִצְרִית' (Egyptian woman), the reason given (men go out to meet guests, women do not) is insufficient, since men could have met men and women met women.
Abner is silent, unable to respond to Doeg's objection.
