Saul tells Doeg that the halakha is hidden from him and instructs him to go and inquire in the study hall.
Doeg asks in the study hall and they confirm the tradition: 'עַמּוֹנִי' (Ammonite) excludes Ammonite women, and 'מוֹאָבִי' (Moabite) excludes Moabite women.

items.text: Doeg's challenge and the tradition from Samuel's court
items.text_en: Doeg's challenge and the tradition from Samuel's court
items.desc_en: Doeg challenges the sages with many questions, and they are silent. He seeks to proclaim against them, but Amasa invokes a tradition from Samuel's court that 'Ammoni' excludes Ammonite women and 'Moabi' excludes Moabite women.

sub.desc_en: Doeg challenges the sages with many questions, they are silent, and Amasa invokes a tradition from Samuel's court that 'עַמּוֹנִי' excludes Ammonite women and 'מוֹאָבִי' excludes Moabite women.

items.text: Questioning the reliability of the tradition
items.text_en: Questioning the reliability of the tradition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Amasa's statement can be accepted, given the rule that a scholar who rules after the fact is not listened to. It answers that this case is different because Samuel and his court are established.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects: how can Amasa's tradition be trusted, given Rav's rule that a Torah scholar who rules after the fact is not listened to?
The gemara answers: this case is different because Samuel and his court were still alive and authoritative.

items.text: Alternative explanations for the exclusion of women
items.text_en: Alternative explanations for the exclusion of women
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the tradition still seems problematic, and offers two alternative derivations: one from 'All glorious is the king's daughter within' and another from the verse about Sarah.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects further: the difficulty remains, and offers two resolutions — one from the verse 'כׇּל כְּבוּדָּה בַת מֶלֶךְ פְּנִימָה' and another from the verse 'וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֵלָיו אַיֵּה שָׂרָה אִשְׁתֶּךָ'.
The Gemara offers the first alternative derivation from the verse 'All glorious is the king's daughter within' to explain the exclusion of women.
The Gemara presents a second alternative derivation from the verse about Sarah, attributed to Rabbi Yitzchak.

items.text: The Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: The Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds that 'Ammoni' excludes Ammonite women and 'Moabi' excludes Moabite women, while Rabbi Shimon derives the exclusion from the fact that men typically offer food and water, not women.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda says 'עַמּוֹנִי' excludes Ammonite women and 'מוֹאָבִי' excludes Moabite women, while Rabbi Shimon derives the exclusion from the verse about not greeting with bread and water, noting it is a man's way to greet.

Rabbi Shimon derives the exclusion from the verse 'עַל דְּבַר אֲשֶׁר לֹא קִדְּמוּ אֶתְכֶם בַּלֶּחֶם וּבַמַּיִם' (because they did not meet you with bread and water), arguing that it is the way of a man to offer food and water, not a woman.

items.text: Rava's homilies on David and the converts
items.text_en: Rava's homilies on David and the converts
items.desc_en: Rava delivers three homilies: David thanks God for removing two bonds (Ruth and Naamah), Rehoboam learns that two verses apply to him and David, and David discovers that his coming was foretold in the scroll.

sub.desc_en: Rava expounds that David thanked God for removing two bonds: Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite.
Rava expounds that Rehoboam, sitting in David's lap, said that two verses apply to him and David.
Rava expounds that David said he came without knowing that his coming was foretold in the scroll, citing the verse 'I found David My servant, with My holy oil I anointed him.'

items.text: Ulla's ruling on the daughter of an Ammonite convert
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling on the daughter of an Ammonite convert
items.desc_en: Ulla states in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the daughter of a male Ammonite convert is fit for the priesthood. Rava bar Ulla questions whether this follows Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Yosei, and concludes it must be according to Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: Ulla says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the daughter of a male Ammonite convert is fit for the priesthood, and Rava bar Ulla questions whether this follows Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Yosei.

sub.text: Rava bar Ulla's question to Ulla
sub.text_en: Rava bar Ulla's question to Ulla
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Ulla asks Ulla whether his ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Yosei, noting that if it follows Rabbi Yosei it is obvious.
Ulla's position is clarified: it must follow Rabbi Yosei, since Rabbi Yehuda would disqualify the daughter of a male convert.

items.text: Debate on the daughter of an Ammonite convert who is unfit to enter the congregation
items.text_en: Debate on the daughter of an Ammonite convert who is unfit to enter the congregation
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the ruling applies only to those fit to enter the congregation, but for an Ammonite who is unfit, perhaps his daughter is unfit. It attempts to derive this from a comparison to a High Priest with a widow, but the derivation is refuted. Ultimately, it is clarified that the case is an Ammonite who married an Israelite woman, and his daughter is still fit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: perhaps the ruling that a daughter of a male convert is fit applies only to those fit to enter the congregation, but for an Ammonite convert who is unfit, how do we know his daughter is also fit?
The Gemara proposes deriving the disqualification from the case of a High Priest with a widow, noting that both involve a forbidden union (ביאה בעבירה).
The Gemara objects that a חלל (profaned priest) can disprove the analogy, since his very creation is through a forbidden union yet his daughter is fit.
The Gemara counters that the High Priest case can also disprove the חלל, and the argument cycles back.

The Gemara attempts to establish a common denominator (צד השוה) between the High Priest and the חלל: both are excluded from the majority of the congregation, and their daughters are unfit, so the same should apply to an Ammonite convert.
The Gemara objects that the common denominator is flawed because both cases involve an element of transgression (צד עבירה), which the Ammonite convert lacks.
The Gemara clarifies that the case is an Ammonite who married an Israelite woman, and despite the forbidden union, his daughter is still fit.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: When Ravin came, he reported a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan rules that the daughter of an Ammonite convert or a second-generation Egyptian is fit for the priesthood, while Reish Lakish rules she is unfit, deriving it from the case of a High Priest with a widow.

sub.text: Ravin citing Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Ravin citing Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: Ravin reports a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says the daughter of a male Ammonite convert is fit for the priesthood, while Resh Lakish says she is disqualified, deriving it from the case of a High Priest with a widow.
Rabbi Yochanan explicitly states that the daughter is fit (כשרה).
Reish Lakish objects, ruling the daughter is unfit (פסולה), deriving this from the case of a High Priest with a widow.
Rabbi Yochanan reaffirms his ruling that the daughter is fit, concluding the dispute.

items.text: Opening dispute between Rabbi Zakkai and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Opening dispute between Rabbi Zakkai and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zakkai teaches that a convert from her nation is eligible for the priesthood. Rabbi Yochanan objects, citing his own tradition that the verse includes a virgin from two nations, not just a convert.

items.text: Clarification of 'two nations'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'two nations'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'two nations' refers to an Ammonite who married an Israelite woman, not an Ammonite who married an Ammonite, as the latter is simply a convert.

items.text: Alternative version of Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.desc_en: Some say Rabbi Yochanan's tradition includes a virgin from a nation that has two nations within it, again rejecting the simple convert interpretation.

items.text: Derivation for the daughter of a second-generation Egyptian
items.text_en: Derivation for the daughter of a second-generation Egyptian
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive the eligibility of a second-generation Egyptian's daughter for the priesthood through analogies, but the argument cycles through comparisons and returns to the starting point.

items.text: Rav Yosef and Rav Yehuda's tradition on Ammonite converts
items.text_en: Rav Yosef and Rav Yehuda's tradition on Ammonite converts
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef recalls Rav Yehuda's teaching about 'from his people' without understanding it. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda clarifies the halakha: an Ammonite woman is eligible, her son from an Ammonite is disqualified, but her daughter from an Ammonite is eligible for the priesthood. The Gemara refines this with Rabbi Yochanan's correction.

items.text: The Gemara's response to the Mishnah's ruling on Egyptians and Edomites
items.text_en: The Gemara's response to the Mishnah's ruling on Egyptians and Edomites
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the 'answer' is to the Mishnah's statement that Egyptians and Edomites are not prohibited forever. Rabbi Yochanan provides a response based on an analogy with forbidden relations and mamzerim, concluding that the common element is that both are prohibited for males and females, but the Gemara objects that the common element includes a dimension of karet.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's ruling and the derivation from 'sons'
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's ruling and the derivation from 'sons'
items.desc_en: The Rabbis derive from the case of a חלל from a positive commandment, following Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. Rabbi Shimon argues that the halakha is that 'sons' excludes daughters, supported by a scriptural verse.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's and Rabbi Yochanan's final clarification
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's and Rabbi Yochanan's final clarification
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states 'sons' not 'daughters'. Rabbi Yehuda argues that the verse ties the prohibition to birth. Rabbi Yochanan praises Rabbi Yehuda's insight, noting that without it he would have been lost in the study hall, and concludes that a congregation of converts is called a congregation.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a second-generation Egyptian convert can become pure, suggesting the verse uses 'if' for prohibition but not for permission. It addresses counterexamples like the mamzer and the one who remarries his divorcee.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how a second-generation Egyptian convert can become pure, suggesting the verse uses 'דְּאִי' (if) only for prohibition, not for permission.
The Gemara objects that the verse uses 'דְּאִי' for the mamzer, but answers that 'דְּאִי' is written for prohibition, not for permission.
The Gemara objects that the verse uses 'דְּאִי' for permission in the case of one who remarries his divorcee, but answers that there it is written because of the underlying prohibition.

items.text: Baraita on 'banim' and 'dorot'
items.text_en: Baraita on 'banim' and 'dorot'
items.desc_en: A baraita explains why the Torah wrote both 'banim' and 'dorot': 'banim' alone would limit the prohibition to first and second sons, while 'dorot' alone would apply to those at Sinai. Both are needed for the correct law.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by questioning why the Torah wrote both 'banim' and 'dorot', and explains that 'banim' alone would limit the prohibition to first and second sons.
The baraita continues by explaining that 'dorot' alone would apply to those at Sinai, so both terms are needed for the correct law.

items.text: Exegesis of 'lahem' and 'asher yivaledu'
items.text_en: Exegesis of 'lahem' and 'asher yivaledu'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the need for both 'lahem' and 'asher yivaledu' in the verse, and why 'lahem' is written here and 'lo' by the mamzer. Each phrase prevents a mistaken inference about lineage or purity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the exegesis of 'lahem', explaining that it means to count from them and to follow their disqualification.
The Gemara explains why both 'lahem' and 'asher yivaledu' are necessary, each preventing a mistaken inference about lineage.
The Gemara explains why 'lahem' is written here and 'lo' by the mamzer, each preventing a mistaken inference about purity.
The Gemara explains that if only 'lahem' were written, one might think the rule applies only to those from a flawed drop, but not to a mamzer from a kosher drop.
The Gemara concludes that both verses are necessary, as each prevents a mistaken inference about the other case.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's first statement and challenges
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's first statement and challenges
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan that a second-generation Egyptian who marries a first-generation Egyptian has a third-generation child, implying lineage follows the father. Rav Yosef and Rava challenge this with sources showing lineage follows the mother, but the Gemara deflects.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that a second-generation Egyptian who marries a first-generation Egyptian produces a third-generation child, implying lineage follows the father.
Rav Yosef challenges Rabbi Yochanan by citing Rabbi Tarfon's teaching that a mamzer who marries a maidservant produces a child who follows the mother's status, implying lineage follows the mother.
The Gemara deflects the challenge by distinguishing the case of a maidservant, where the verse explicitly ties the child to the mother's owner.

Rava challenges Rabbi Yochanan by citing Rabbi Yehuda's story of a first-generation Egyptian who married a first-generation Egyptian and planned for his son to marry a second-generation Egyptian, implying lineage follows the mother.
The Gemara deflects by noting that Rabbi Yochanan himself instructed the Tanna to teach 'first-generation' in the baraita, implying the child follows the father.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's second statement and Abaye's challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's second statement and Abaye's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Yochanan saying the child is second-generation, following the mother. Abaye challenges this with Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a pregnant sin-offering, which assumes the fetus is not a limb of the mother. Rabbi Yochanan is silent, then deflects by citing the verse 'asher yivaledu'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Yochanan's statement that a second-generation Egyptian who marries a first-generation Egyptian woman produces a second-generation child, following the mother.
Abaye challenges Rabbi Yochanan by citing his own ruling about a pregnant sin-offering (חטאת מעוברת), where the owner may choose to atone with either the mother or the offspring.
Abaye argues that if the fetus is not considered a limb of the mother (עובר לאו ירך אמו), the ruling aligns with Rav Oshaya's principle of two sin-offerings set aside for contingency.
Abaye argues that if the fetus is a limb of the mother (עובר ירך אמו), the offspring would be considered a 'born sin-offering' (ולד חטאת) which must die, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.

Rabbi Yochanan is silent, then deflects by citing the verse 'אֲשֶׁר יִוָּלְדוּ' (those who are born), and Abaye mockingly remarks that he saw Rabbi Yochanan's head between the pillars when he made this statement.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a pregnant convert and conclusion
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a pregnant convert and conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that without the verse, lineage follows the father, but then questions Rava's ruling that a pregnant convert's child needs no immersion. It suggests an answer from Rabbi Yitzchak about interposition, but the argument is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that without the verse 'אֲשֶׁר יִוָּלְדוּ' (who are born), lineage would follow the father.
The Gemara questions Rava's ruling that a pregnant convert's child needs no immersion.
The Gemara suggests an answer based on Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that a majority that is not cared about does not interpose.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of Rav Kahana's statement regarding the fetus
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of Rav Kahana's statement regarding the fetus
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between a majority and the entire body, explaining that a fetus is different because it is its natural growth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rav Kahana said that only a majority of the body interposes, but the entire body certainly interposes, yet a fetus is considered part of the mother's body.
The Gemara resolves that a fetus is different because it is its natural growth, so it does not interpose.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's rule: Follow the male among nations, the flawed among converts
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's rule: Follow the male among nations, the flawed among converts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that regarding nations, one follows the male parent, but if they convert, one follows the more flawed parent. The Gemara explains the first part with a baraita about purchasing a child born to a non-Jew and a Canaanite, and questions the second part with examples of Ammonite and Egyptian.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states the rule: among nations, follow the male parent; among converts, follow the more flawed parent.
A baraita supports the first part of the rule, deriving from a verse that a child born to a non-Jewish father and a Canaanite mother can be purchased as a slave.
The baraita adds that a child born to a Canaanite father and a non-Jewish mother cannot be purchased as a slave, reinforcing that the male parent determines status among nations.
The Gemara questions the second part of the rule, asking in what case it applies, and challenges the example of an Egyptian man marrying an Ammonite woman, since Ammonite women are not prohibited.

The Gemara resolves the question by citing the case of an Ammonite man marrying an Egyptian woman: a male child follows the Ammonite father (prohibited), a female child follows the Egyptian mother (prohibited as well).

items.text: Mishnah: Mamzerim and Netinim are forever forbidden
items.text_en: Mishnah: Mamzerim and Netinim are forever forbidden
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that mamzerim and Netinim are forbidden, and their prohibition is eternal, applying to both males and females.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that mamzerim and Netinim are forbidden, and their prohibition is eternal, applying to both males and females.

items.text: Resh Lakish's argument: Female mamzeret permitted after ten generations
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's argument: Female mamzeret permitted after ten generations
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish uses a גזירה שווה to argue that a female mamzeret is permitted after ten generations, like Ammonite and Moabite women. The Gemara objects from the Mishnah, and resolves the contradiction by attributing the views to different opinions on whether to derive from the source and apply it fully or only partially.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish opens by asserting that a female mamzeret is permitted after ten generations, deriving this via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the words 'עֲשִׂירִי' (tenth) used for Ammonite and Moabite women.

The Gemara objects that if the analogy is exact, the female mamzeret should be permitted immediately, not after ten generations; it answers that the גזירה שווה applies only from the tenth generation onward.
The Gemara objects from the Mishnah which states that mamzerim are forbidden forever, both males and females.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to the view that one derives from the source and applies it fully (דּוּן מִינַּהּ וּמִינַּהּ), and Resh Lakish's view to the opinion that one derives from the source but leaves it in its place (דּוּן מִינַּהּ וְאוֹקֵי בְּאַתְרָא).

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer and Rav Huna: A mamzer does not live long
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer and Rav Huna: A mamzer does not live long
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer says he would purify a third-generation mamzer, implying mamzerim do not live. Rav Huna agrees. Rabbi Zeira explains that a known mamzer lives, an unknown one does not, and a partially known one lives up to three generations. A story illustrates this with Rabbi Ami.

sub.desc_en: The questioners ask Rabbi Eliezer about the status of a mamzeret (female mamzer) after ten generations.
Rabbi Eliezer responds that he would purify a third-generation mamzer, implying that mamzerim do not live long.

sub.text: Gemara's inference and Rav Huna's statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's inference and Rav Huna's statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that Rabbi Eliezer holds that a mamzer does not live, and cites Rav Huna who explicitly states the same.
The Gemara objects by citing the Mishnah that mamzerim are forbidden with an eternal prohibition, contradicting the idea that they do not live.
Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction by distinguishing: a known mamzer lives, an unknown one does not, and a partially known one lives up to three generations.
A story is told of a neighbor of Rabbi Ami who was proclaimed a mamzer; Rabbi Ami told him 'I have given you life,' illustrating that a known mamzer lives.

items.text: David's decree against the Netinim (Gibeonites)
items.text_en: David's decree against the Netinim (Gibeonites)
items.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Ada states that David decreed against the Netinim. The Gemara explains the reason: a three-year famine led David to investigate sins, and ultimately he consulted the Urim and Thummim. The famine was due to Saul's killing of the Gibeonites, and the Gemara elaborates on the verses and the connection to Saul's actions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Ada states that David decreed against the Netinim, citing the verse about the Gibeonites.
The Gemara asks why David decreed against the Netinim, and explains the three-year famine and David's investigation into possible sins, finding none in the first year.
In the second year, David investigated whether there were sinners among the people, citing the verse about withheld rain due to harlotry, but found none.
In the third year, David investigated whether there were those who pledged charity publicly but did not give, citing the verse about false promises, but found none.
David concluded the famine was due to his own failure, and Resh Lakish explains that he consulted the Urim and Thummim.
Rabbi Elazar derives that David consulted the Urim and Thummim via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'פני' (face) used in both verses.

The Gemara explains that the verse attributes the famine to Saul's killing of the Gibeonites, and clarifies that Saul's sin was killing Nov, the city of priests, who provided for the Gibeonites, which is considered as if he killed them directly.
The Gemara objects that the verse seems to demand both for Saul's improper eulogy and for killing the Gibeonites, and Resh Lakish resolves that God's judgment is where His justice is carried out.
David declares that Saul's descendants are excluded from the community, establishing the decree against the Netinim.

items.text: David's attempt to appease the Gibeonites
items.text_en: David's attempt to appease the Gibeonites
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that David tried to appease the Gibeonites with money, but they refused, citing the verse where they demanded seven of Saul's descendants to be hanged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that David mourned for twelve months, which was not his usual practice.
The Gemara recounts that David summoned the Gibeonites and offered appeasement, but they refused money and demanded seven of Saul's descendants to be hanged.

items.text: The three signs of the Jewish people
items.text_en: The three signs of the Jewish people
items.desc_en: David identifies three characteristics of the Jewish people: merciful, bashful, and kind. He cites verses to support each trait and concludes that anyone with these signs is fit to join the nation.

sub.desc_en: David states that the Jewish people have three distinguishing signs: merciful, bashful, and kind.
David cites three verses to support each trait: mercy (Deut 13:18), bashfulness (Exod 20:17), and kindness (Gen 18:19).
David concludes that anyone possessing these three signs is fit to join the Jewish nation.

items.text: The selection of Saul's descendants for execution
items.text_en: The selection of Saul's descendants for execution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why specific descendants were chosen and Rav Huna explains that they were passed before the Ark; those the Ark accepted were put to death, and those it rejected were spared.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why specifically these seven descendants of Saul were chosen for execution.
Rav Huna explains that the descendants were passed before the Ark; those the Ark accepted were put to death, and those it rejected were spared.

items.text: The case of Mephibosheth and the Ark
items.text_en: The case of Mephibosheth and the Ark
items.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Katina objects that David spared Mephibosheth, implying favoritism. The Gemara resolves that the Ark accepted him, but David prayed for mercy and the Ark released him, or that David prayed that the Ark not accept him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Katina objects from the verse that David spared Mephibosheth, implying he was not passed before the Ark.
The Gemara questions whether there is favoritism in the matter.
The Gemara answers that the Ark accepted Mephibosheth, but David prayed for mercy and the Ark released him.
The Gemara again questions whether there is favoritism, since David's prayer itself seems to show special treatment.
The Gemara resolves that David prayed that the Ark not accept Mephibosheth at all, so no favoritism was shown.

items.text: Justification for executing sons for fathers' sins
items.text_en: Justification for executing sons for fathers' sins
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the violation of the verse 'Fathers shall not be put to death for children.' Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that it is better to uproot one letter of the Torah than to desecrate God's name publicly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how David could execute the Gibeonites' sons, given the verse forbidding putting fathers to death for children.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that it is better to uproot one letter of the Torah than to allow a public desecration of God's name.

items.text: Rizpah's vigil and the sanctification of God's name
items.text_en: Rizpah's vigil and the sanctification of God's name
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rizpah could leave the bodies hanging, violating the law against leaving a corpse overnight. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochatzadak explains that it is better to uproot one letter of the Torah to sanctify God's name publicly, as passersby would inquire and learn about the Gibeonites' grievance, leading to admiration for Israel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rizpah could leave the bodies hanging overnight, given the biblical prohibition against leaving a corpse on the tree overnight.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochatzadak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochatzadak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that it is better to uproot one letter of the Torah to sanctify God's name publicly, as passersby would inquire and learn about the Gibeonites' grievance, leading to admiration for Israel.

items.text: The influx of converts after the event
items.text_en: The influx of converts after the event
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that 150,000 converts joined Israel as a result, citing the verse about Solomon's laborers. It clarifies that these were not Israelites but gerim, as proven by the explicit verse about Solomon's census of the gerim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that 150,000 converts joined Israel as a result, citing the verse about Solomon's laborers.
The Gemara objects that perhaps those laborers were Israelites, but rejects this because the verse explicitly says Solomon did not make Israelites slaves.

The Gemara raises a further objection that perhaps the verse about Solomon's census refers to a different group, but then cites the explicit verse about the census of the gerim (גרים) to prove they were converts.

items.text: David's decree on the Nethinim compared to Moses and Joshua
items.text_en: David's decree on the Nethinim compared to Moses and Joshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether David decreed on the Nethinim, noting that Moses already decreed on them. It explains that Moses decreed for his generation, while David decreed for all generations. Similarly, Joshua decreed when the Temple stood, but David decreed for when the Temple would not stand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether David decreed on the Nethinim, noting that Moses already decreed on them.
The Gemara answers that Moses decreed for his generation, while David decreed for all generations.
The Gemara objects that Joshua also decreed on them, citing the verse that Joshua assigned them as woodcutters and water drawers for the congregation and the altar.
The Gemara resolves that Joshua decreed when the Temple stood, while David decreed for when the Temple would not stand.

items.text: Opening discussion about Nethinim
items.text_en: Opening discussion about Nethinim
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that in the days of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, they sought to permit Nethinim (descendants of Gibeonites). Rabbi argued that if we permit their share in the congregation, who will permit their share for the altar? This is disputed by Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan, who distinguishes between the share of the congregation (always forbidden) and the share of the altar (forbidden only when the Temple stands).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that in the days of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi they sought to permit Nethinim, and Rabbi argued that if they permit their share in the congregation, who will permit their share for the altar.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan disputes Rabbi's position, distinguishing between the share of the congregation (always forbidden) and the share of the altar (forbidden only when the Temple stands).

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute about saris and halitzah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute about saris and halitzah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Yehoshua states he heard that a saris (eunuch) performs halitzah and his wife performs halitzah, but a saris does not perform halitzah nor does his wife perform halitzah, and he cannot explain. Rabbi Akiva explains: a saris adam (by human action) performs halitzah because he had a time of fitness; a saris chamah (by nature) does not because he never had a time of fitness. Rabbi Eliezer reverses the ruling, arguing that a saris chamah has a cure, while a saris adam does not. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira testified about a case supporting Rabbi Akiva. The Mishnah concludes with general rules: a saris does not perform halitzah or yibbum, and if he performed halitzah it is valid but if he had relations it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states he heard a contradictory tradition about a saris (eunuch) performing halitzah and cannot explain it.
Rabbi Akiva explains the distinction: a saris adam (by human action) performs halitzah because he had a time of fitness, but a saris chamah (by nature) does not.
Rabbi Eliezer reverses the ruling, arguing that a saris chamah has a cure and thus performs halitzah, while a saris adam does not.

sub.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira's testimony
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira's testimony
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira testifies about a case of a saris adam in Jerusalem whose wife was taken for yibbum, supporting Rabbi Akiva's position.
The Mishnah states the general rule: a saris does not perform halitzah or yibbum, and similarly an aylonit (sterile woman) does not perform halitzah or undergo yibbum.

sub.text: Mishnah: Consequence of halitzah or relations
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Consequence of halitzah or relations
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes that if a saris performed halitzah it is valid, but if he had relations it invalidates her because it is a forbidden union.

items.text: Gemara's first question and answer regarding Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and answer regarding Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Akiva's ruling: since he holds that prohibitions punishable by lashes are like those punishable by karet (and thus a saris adam is forbidden to marry a Jewess), how can he allow halitzah? Rabbi Ammi answers that the case involves a brother who married a convert, and Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Yosi that converts do not constitute a 'congregation' (קהל). The Gemara then asks why he doesn't also permit yibbum, and answers that since Rabbi Yehoshua said 'he performs halitzah', Rabbi Akiva also says 'he performs halitzah' (but yibbum is also permitted). This is supported by the testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Akiva's ruling that a saris adam performs halitzah, given that Rabbi Akiva holds prohibitions punishable by lashes are like those punishable by karet, and those liable for karet are not subject to halitzah or yibbum.

Rabbi Ammi answers that the case involves a brother who married a convert, and Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Yosi's view that converts do not constitute a 'congregation' (קהל), so the prohibition of 'לֹא יָבֹא פְצוּעַ דַּכָּא... בִּקְהַל ה׳' does not apply.
The Gemara objects: if the prohibition does not apply, why does Rabbi Akiva only permit halitzah and not also yibbum?
The Gemara answers that indeed yibbum is also permitted, but since Rabbi Yehoshua said 'he performs halitzah', Rabbi Akiva also says 'he performs halitzah' (without mentioning yibbum).

The Gemara cites the testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira about ben Megusat, who was a saris adam and whose wife was taken for yibbum, confirming that yibbum is indeed permitted according to Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Objection from a Baraita about petzua daka
items.text_en: Objection from a Baraita about petzua daka
items.desc_en: Rabbah raises an objection from a Baraita that states a petzua daka (wounded in the testicles) and a saris adam either perform halitzah or yibbum, and if they had relations they acquire the yevamah, but they are forbidden to keep her due to the verse 'No petzua daka shall enter the assembly of the Lord.' This implies that the case involves a congregation (קהל), contradicting Rabbi Ammi's explanation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah objects by citing a Baraita that rules a petzua daka (wounded in the testicles) and a saris adam either perform halitzah or yibbum, and if they had relations they acquire the yevamah but are forbidden to keep her due to the verse 'לֹא יָבֹא פְצוּעַ דַּכָּא... בִּקְהַל ה (No petzua daka shall enter the assembly of the Lord),' implying the case involves a congregation (קהל), contradicting Rabbi Ammi's explanation.

items.text: Rabbah's first answer and Abaye's challenge
items.text_en: Rabbah's first answer and Abaye's challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbah answers that the case is where the yevamah fell to him (for yibbum) and then he became petzua. Abaye challenges: why doesn't the prohibition of petzua override the positive commandment of yibbum? He cites a case where the prohibition of a sister-wife overrides the positive commandment, so here too the prohibition should override. This refutes Rabbah's answer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah answers that the case is where the yevamah fell to him (for yibbum) and then he became a פצוע דכא (a crushed or wounded person).

Abaye challenges: why doesn't the prohibition of a פצוע דכא (a crushed or wounded person) override the positive commandment of yibbum, just as the prohibition of a sister-wife overrides it, as cited from Rabban Gamliel's ruling?

items.text: Rav Yosef's answer: the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's answer: the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef answers that the Tanna of this Baraita is from the school of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a mamzer is only produced from prohibitions punishable by lashes that involve incest (שאר), not from other prohibitions. The Gemara then questions: but the verse says 'to establish his brother's name', and this man is not capable of that?

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef answers that the Tanna of this Baraita is from the school of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a mamzer is only produced from prohibitions punishable by lashes that involve incest (שאר), not from other prohibitions.
The Gemara objects: but the verse says 'to establish his brother's name', and this man is not capable of that.

items.text: Rava's challenge and resolution regarding Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Rava's challenge and resolution regarding Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Rava argues that if so, no woman would be fit for yibbum, since every husband might have been a saris chamah for one hour before death. The Gemara notes that this is a challenge to Rabbi Eliezer's position. It answers that there, it is a weakness that began in him (not a permanent condition). The daf ends with a definition of saris chamah from Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Rabbi Eliezer's position by arguing that if a temporary condition before death could disqualify a husband, then no woman would be fit for yibbum, since every husband might have been a סריס חמה (sun-made eunuch) for one hour before death.
The Gemara notes that Rava's statement is actually a challenge (פירכא) to Rabbi Eliezer, not a resolution.
The Gemara answers that in the case of a dying man, the weakness is a temporary decline that began in him (כחישותא דאתחילה ביה), not a permanent condition of סריס חמה (sun-made eunuch).

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The daf ends with Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan to define what constitutes a סריס חמה (sun-made eunuch).

items.text: Identifying a congenital eunuch
items.text_en: Identifying a congenital eunuch
items.desc_en: Abaye explains how to identify a סריס חמה: one who urinates without forming an arch, and whose mother was exposed to heat and drank strong beer. Rav Yosef adds a tradition from his mother about a defect from the womb.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks how to identify a congenital eunuch (סריס חמה) who never had a moment of halachic fitness.
Abaye provides two signs: the man urinates without forming an arch, and his mother was exposed to heat and drank strong beer.
Rav Yosef adds a tradition from his mother that a congenital eunuch is one who was defective from the womb, though he did not know the precise meaning.

items.text: Concern for interim healing
items.text_en: Concern for interim healing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether we should worry that the person might have healed between birth and now, but concludes that since the defect is continuous from start to finish, we do not worry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that the person might have healed between birth and the present moment.
The Gemara resolves that since the defect is continuous from start to finish, we do not worry about interim healing.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus
items.desc_en: Rav Mari objects based on a baraita where Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus says we examine the person three times within eighty days. The Gemara resolves that we worry about a single limb healing, but not the entire body.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus requires examining the person three times within eighty days, challenging the assumption that we never worry about healing.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing between a single limb, where we worry about healing, and the entire body, where we do not.

items.text: Contradiction regarding Rabbi Eliezer's ruling
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding Rabbi Eliezer's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer rules differently from Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai regarding the age of majority for a סריס and אילונית, and notes a contradiction with his earlier statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer rules that a male סריס (sterile male) follows Beit Hillel's age of twenty, and a female אילונית (sterile female) follows Beit Shammai's age of eighteen, because a woman matures faster.

items.text: Did Rabbi Eliezer retract?
items.text_en: Did Rabbi Eliezer retract?
items.desc_en: Rami bar Dikulei quotes Shmuel that Rabbi Eliezer retracted his opinion, citing a baraita where he rules that a סריס חמה performs חליצה. Rabbi Elazar argues he never retracted, and the earlier ruling was only regarding punishments.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Dikulei reports in the name of Shmuel that Rabbi Eliezer retracted his earlier opinion.
The gemara asks: from which of his statements did he retract?

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer rules that a סריס חמה (congenital eunuch) performs חליצה (levirate release) and his wife may be released, because such eunuchs are healed in Alexandria of Egypt.
Rabbi Elazar objects that Rabbi Eliezer never retracted at all.
Rabbi Elazar resolves that the earlier ruling (where Rabbi Eliezer appeared to forbid) was only regarding punishments (עונשין), not regarding the permissibility of חליצה itself.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on retroactive status
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on retroactive status
items.desc_en: A case is presented of someone who ate forbidden fat between ages 12 and 18 and later developed signs of סריס. Rav says he retroactively becomes a סריס, while Shmuel says he was a minor at that time. Rav Yosef challenges Rav's view regarding an אילונית, and Abaye responds that she leaves minority at the onset of adulthood. Rav Yosef praises this teaching, citing a baraita about a סריס not being judged as a rebellious son and an אילונית not as a betrothed girl.

sub.desc_en: A case is presented: someone ate forbidden fat (חלב) between ages 12 and 18 and later developed signs of a סריס (congenital eunuch); Rav rules he retroactively becomes a סריס, while Shmuel rules he was a minor at that time.

Rav Yosef challenges Rav's position: according to Rav, an אילונית (congenitally sterile woman) should also be subject to the fine (קנס) for seduction according to Rabbi Meir, since she would retroactively be considered an adult.

Abaye answers that an אילונית is different: she leaves minority (קטנות) directly into adulthood (בגר) at the onset of her signs, so she never passes through the intermediate stage of נערות (adolescence) where the fine applies.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's praise and supporting baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's praise and supporting baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef praises Abaye's teaching and cites a baraita: a סריס is not judged as a rebellious son (בן סורר ומורה) because that judgment requires lower beard growth, and an אילונית is not judged as a betrothed girl (נערה המאורסה) because she leaves minority directly into adulthood.

items.text: Age requirement for acting on signs
items.text_en: Age requirement for acting on signs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu rules that signs of סריס, אילונית, and a בן שמונה (premature infant) are not acted upon until age 20. The Gemara questions whether a בן שמונה can live, citing a baraita that such an infant is like a stone and may not be moved, but his mother may bend over and nurse him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu rules that signs of a סריס (congenital eunuch), אילונית (congenital sterile woman), and a בן שמונה (premature infant) are not acted upon until age 20.
The Gemara questions whether a בן שמונה (premature infant) can live at all, challenging the premise of acting on its signs.
A baraita is cited stating that a בן שמונה (premature infant) is like a stone and may not be moved, but his mother may bend over and nurse him, indicating he is considered non-viable.

items.text: Clarifying the case of the eight-month infant
items.text_en: Clarifying the case of the eight-month infant
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the earlier mishnah's concern about danger applies when the infant's signs (hair and nails) have fully developed, indicating it is a seven-month infant that was merely delayed. This is based on a baraita where Rabbi says that unfinished signs prove it is an eight-month infant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In what case does the mishnah's concern about danger apply?
The Gemara answers: When his signs (hair and nails) have fully developed.
A baraita is cited: Who is an eight-month infant? One whose months were not completed; Rabbi says signs prove it — his hair and nails are unfinished.
The Gemara resolves: The reason is that if signs are unfinished it is an eight-month infant, but if finished we say it is a seven-month infant that was merely delayed.

items.text: Rava's ruling and its support from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Rava's ruling and its support from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a case where Rava Tosfa'ah permitted a woman whose husband was delayed twelve months to remarry, following Rabbi's view that delay is possible. It then notes that since Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel also holds that a delay of thirty days indicates viability, Rava acted in accordance with the majority.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: Rava Tosfa'ah performed a practical ruling permitting a woman whose husband was delayed twelve months to remarry, and asks whose view he followed — that of Rabbi, who holds that a delay is possible.

The Gemara answers that since Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel also holds that a delay of thirty days indicates viability, Rava acted in accordance with the majority, citing a baraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that any infant that survives thirty days is not a stillborn.

items.text: Baraita on signs of a saris and aylonit
items.text_en: Baraita on signs of a saris and aylonit
items.desc_en: A baraita lists the signs of a saris (sterile male) and aylonit (sterile female), including age twenty without two pubic hairs, and various physical signs. Multiple opinions are cited, including Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and others.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by defining a saris chamah (naturally sterile male) as one who reaches age twenty without two pubic hairs, and lists initial physical signs: no beard, thin hair, and smooth skin.

sub.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Rabbi Yehuda ben Yair
sub.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Rabbi Yehuda ben Yair
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds, in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Yair, that another sign is that his urine does not produce foam.
Multiple anonymous opinions list further signs: urine that does not form an arch, semen that is thin, and urine that does not ferment.
Acherim state that a sign is that after bathing in the rainy season, his skin does not steam.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that a sign is a weak voice, indistinguishable between male and female.

items.text: Signs of an aylonit
items.text_en: Signs of an aylonit
items.desc_en: The baraita continues with the definition and signs of an aylonit: a woman who reaches twenty without two pubic hairs, and even if she later grows them, she remains an aylonit. Signs include lack of breasts, difficulty during intercourse, and other physical indicators.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines an אַיְלוֹנִית (naturally sterile female): one who is twenty years old and has not grown two pubic hairs; even if she grows them later, she is considered an aylonit for all purposes.

sub.text: Baraita's list of signs for Aylonit
sub.text_en: Baraita's list of signs for Aylonit
sub.desc_en: The baraita lists signs: one who has no breasts and is rough during intercourse.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: One who does not have a lower abdomen like women.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: One whose voice is thick and is not distinguishable between female and male.

items.text: Dispute: all signs or any one sign?
items.text_en: Dispute: all signs or any one sign?
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether the signs of a saris require all of them or even one suffices. They agree that if he has grown two pubic hairs on his beard, all signs are needed; the dispute is when he has not grown them.

sub.desc_en: It was stated: Regarding signs of a sterile male, Rav Huna says: Until all of them are present.
Rabbi Yochanan says: Even with one of them.
The Gemara resolves: Where he grew two pubic hairs on the beard, everyone agrees that all signs are required; they disagree only where he did not grow them.
The Gemara clarifies that both agree that if he has grown two pubic hairs on his beard, all signs are required; the dispute is only when he has not grown them.

items.text: Rav Nachman's case and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's case and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a case where Rabbah bar Avuh told the rabbis to examine Rav Nachman: if his flesh does not produce vapor, he may marry a woman. This seems to follow Rav Huna (all signs needed). The Gemara answers that Rav Nachman had a beard, so the dispute does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: But what about the case where Rabbah bar Avuh told the rabbis: Examine Rav Nachman; if his flesh steams, seat him as head of the academy?
The Gemara answers: Whose opinion does this follow? Rav Huna's (who requires all signs).
The Gemara rejects: No, Rav Nachman had beard stubble (so the sign of no beard was absent, and the test was about a different sign).

items.text: Mishnah: saris and aylonit do not perform chalitzah or yibbum
items.text_en: Mishnah: saris and aylonit do not perform chalitzah or yibbum
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the mishnah compares a saris to an aylonit: just as an aylonit is a heavenly condition, so too a saris must be a heavenly condition (saris chamah). This anonymous mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva, who distinguishes between a human-made and heavenly-made condition.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah is cited: A sterile male does not perform חליצה (removal of the shoe) nor יבום (levirate marriage), and similarly an aylonit.
The Gemara infers: The mishnah teaches a sterile male analogous to an aylonit: just as an aylonit is by Heaven's hand, so too a sterile male is by Heaven's hand.
The Gemara notes: The anonymous mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva, who says: By human hand — yes (the law applies), by Heaven's hand — no.

items.text: Mishnah: saris who performed chalitzah does not disqualify
items.text_en: Mishnah: saris who performed chalitzah does not disqualify
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah states a saris who performed chalitzah does not disqualify his yevamah, implying that if he is the husband (ba'al), it is different. This sets up a contrast with another case.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah is cited: A sterile male who performed חליצה for his yevamah did not disqualify her.
The Gemara infers: The reason is that he is her husband (and his חליצה is invalid), but if another (a valid yavam) performed חליצה — no (she would be disqualified).

items.text: Challenge to Rav Hamnuna and support for Rabbi Yehudah
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Hamnuna and support for Rabbi Yehudah
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the Mishnah's ruling about an aylonit who was not married by her yevamim disproves Rav Hamnuna's statement that a shomeret yavam who committed adultery is disqualified from her yavam. It deflects by saying the same applies to others. Then it notes that the Mishnah's condition 'if they had relations' implies that without relations she is not disqualified, which contradicts Rabbi Yehudah who considers an aylonit a zonah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah's ruling about an aylonit who was not married by her yevamim disproves Rav Hamnuna's statement that a shomeret yavam who committed adultery is disqualified from her yavam.
The Gemara deflects the challenge by stating that the same disqualification applies even to others, and the Mishnah's phrasing is merely parallel to its earlier clause.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's condition 'if they had relations' implies that without relations she is not disqualified, which contradicts Rabbi Yehudah's view that an aylonit is a zonah.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah must be following a position other than Rabbi Yehudah, since he would consider an aylonit a zonah regardless of relations.

items.text: Mishnah: Seris chamah and androgynos kohen
items.text_en: Mishnah: Seris chamah and androgynos kohen
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a seris chamah kohen who marries a bat Yisrael may feed her terumah. Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon extend this to an androgynos kohen. Rabbi Yehudah rules that a tumtum found to be a male may not perform chalitzah because he is like a seris. Rabbi Eliezer says an androgynos is liable for stoning as a male.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a seris chamah kohen who marries a bat Yisrael may feed her terumah.
Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon extend the rule to an androgynos kohen who marries a bat Yisrael.
Rabbi Yehudah rules that a tumtum found to be a male may not perform chalitzah because he is like a seris.
Rabbi Yehudah adds that an androgynos may marry a woman but may not be married as a woman.
Rabbi Eliezer rules that an androgynos is liable for stoning as a male.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's first ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's first ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needed to state that a seris chamah kohen feeds his wife terumah, since it is obvious. It explains that one might have thought only one who can father children feeds terumah, so the Mishnah teaches that even a seris chamah, who cannot father children, feeds terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needed to state that a seris chamah kohen feeds his wife terumah, since it is obvious, and explains the potential mistaken assumption that only one who can father children feeds terumah.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah teaches that even a seris chamah, who cannot father children, feeds terumah.

items.text: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on androgynos
items.text_en: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on androgynos
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that an androgynos kohen feeds his wife terumah but not the breast and thigh offerings. Rabbi Yochanan argues that he may even feed her breast and thigh. The Gemara questions Reish Lakish's distinction, since both terumah and breast and thigh are Torah laws.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that an androgynos kohen feeds his wife תרומה (priestly portion) but not the חזה ושוק (breast and thigh) offerings.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that an androgynos kohen may even feed his wife the breast and thigh offerings.
The Gemara questions Reish Lakish's distinction, since both תרומה and חזה ושוק are דאורייתא (Torah laws).

items.text: Resolution: Reish Lakish refers to rabbinic terumah
items.text_en: Resolution: Reish Lakish refers to rabbinic terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish's ruling applies to terumah in the present time, which is rabbinic. However, when the Temple stood, he would not feed her breast and thigh. The Gemara questions why the Mishnah did not explicitly distinguish between biblical and rabbinic terumah. It concludes that Reish Lakish means that even with rabbinic terumah, he does not feed her breast and thigh, lest one come to feed her biblical terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that Reish Lakish's ruling refers to rabbinic terumah in the present time, not biblical terumah.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah did not explicitly distinguish between biblical and rabbinic terumah.
The Gemara concludes that Reish Lakish means that even with rabbinic terumah, he does not feed her breast and thigh, lest one come to feed her biblical terumah.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge and the dispute about bitul
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge and the dispute about bitul
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish's assumption that terumah nowadays is rabbinic, citing a Mishnah about round cakes of kilayim that are nullified in a majority. Reish Lakish counters with a Mishnah about a piece of forbidden fat that is not nullified. They debate whether the principle is 'anything that is countable' or 'that which is countable'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish's assumption that terumah nowadays is rabbinic, and Reish Lakish responds by citing a Mishnah that round cakes of kilayim are nullified in a majority.

Reish Lakish counters with a Mishnah about a piece of forbidden fat that is nullified in a majority, and clarifies that the principle is 'that which is countable' (אֶת שֶׁדַּרְכּוֹ לִימָּנוֹת), not 'anything that is countable' (כׇּל שֶׁדַּרְכּוֹ לִימָּנוֹת).

The Gemara explains the source of Reish Lakish's principle by citing a Mishnah about bundles of kilayim of the vineyard that must be burned, and if they become mixed with other bundles, the rule of nullification applies.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Meir says all items that are normally counted (for sale) render a mixture forbidden, while the Sages limit this to six specific items. Rabbi Akiva adds a seventh. The list includes nuts, pomegranates, sealed jugs, etc., and the items are subject to the laws of orlah and kil'ayim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Meir's position that all items normally counted render a mixture forbidden, and the Sages' counter-position that only six specific items do so.
Rabbi Akiva adds a seventh item to the Sages' list.
The Mishnah lists the six (or seven) items and states that they are subject to the laws of orlah and kil'ayim.

items.text: Gemara's dispute: wording of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's dispute: wording of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish disagree about the precise wording of the Mishnah: whether it says 'that which is normally counted' or 'everything that is normally counted'. This distinction affects the scope of the rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rabbi Yochanan holds the Mishnah reads 'אֶת שֶׁדַּרְכּוֹ לִימָּנוֹת' (that which is normally counted), while Resh Lakish holds it reads 'כֹּל שֶׁדַּרְכּוֹ לִימָּנוֹת' (everything that is normally counted).

items.text: Baraita about a sacred piece mixed with others
items.text_en: Baraita about a sacred piece mixed with others
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: a piece of a sin-offering or a loaf of showbread that is impure and mixed with pure ones of the same type can be nullified in a hundred. However, if the sacred piece is pure and mixed with pure non-sacred pieces, all agree it cannot be nullified.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a piece of a sin-offering or showbread that is impure and mixed with pure ones of the same type can be nullified in a hundred, but Rabbi Yehuda disagrees.
The baraita adds that if the sacred piece is pure and mixed with pure non-sacred pieces, all agree it cannot be nullified.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Chiyya's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Chiyya's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita's first clause says the impure piece 'ascends' (is nullified), but this seems to contradict the Mishnah's rule. Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Huna answers that the case is where the piece is ground into a powder, so it is no longer a discrete item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the baraita's first clause can say the impure piece 'ascends' (is nullified), given the Mishnah's rule that items whose way is to be counted are not nullified.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Huna answers that the case is where the piece is ground into a powder (נימוחה), so it is no longer a discrete item and can be nullified.

items.text: Gemara's follow-up question about Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's follow-up question about Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the piece is ground, why does Rabbi Yehuda still say it does not ascend? This sets up the next stage of the argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If the piece is ground, what is Rabbi Yehuda's reason for saying it does not ascend (is not nullified)?

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's consistent position on nullification
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's consistent position on nullification
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling in the Mishnah aligns with his general view that a substance of the same type is not nullified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling in the Mishnah aligns with his general view that a substance of the same type (מין במינו) is not nullified.

items.text: Question on the Mishnah's omission of a case where the piece is not dissolved
items.text_en: Question on the Mishnah's omission of a case where the piece is not dissolved
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah did not distinguish between a dissolved and undissolved piece in the case of a pure chatat piece mixed with pure chullin, and answers that the Tanna preferred to teach about pure with pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah did not teach a case where the piece is not dissolved, and suggests that the Tanna should have distinguished within the same case.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna preferred to teach about pure items mixed with pure items, rather than distinguishing dissolved from undissolved.

items.text: Reish Lakish's distinction between rabbinic and biblical tumah
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's distinction between rabbinic and biblical tumah
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explains that for Reish Lakish, the first clause deals with rabbinic tumah (liquids) and the second with biblical tumah (creeping animals). The Gemara again asks why the Tanna did not make the distinction explicit, and answers that he preferred to teach pure with pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Reish Lakish distinguishes between the first and second clauses of the Mishnah.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explains that the first clause deals with rabbinic tumah (liquids) and the second with biblical tumah (creeping animals).
The Gemara asks why the Tanna did not make the distinction explicit in the Mishnah itself.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna preferred to teach pure with pure (טהורה בטהרות).

items.text: Rabbah's distinction between a negative commandment and karet
items.text_en: Rabbah's distinction between a negative commandment and karet
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the first clause involves a prohibition of a negative commandment (לאו) and the second involves karet. The Gemara objects that Rabbah himself holds that in biblical law, there is no difference between these categories.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah distinguishes the two clauses: the first involves a prohibition of a negative commandment (לאו), the second involves a prohibition punishable by karet (כרת).
The Gemara objects that Rabbah himself holds that in biblical law (דאורייתא), there is no difference between a negative commandment and karet, so his distinction is inconsistent.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation of 'something that has permitter'
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation of 'something that has permitter'
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the second clause involves a substance that has a permitter (דבר שיש לו מתירין), which is never nullified even in a thousand. The Gemara challenges this as a fabrication, since for a kohen it is permitted and for an Israelite it is always forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the second clause involves a substance that has a permitter (דבר שיש לו מתירין), which is never nullified even in a thousand.
The Gemara challenges Rav Ashi's explanation as a fabrication, since for a kohen the substance is permitted and for an Israelite it is always forbidden.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on terumah in the present era
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on terumah in the present era
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan holds that terumah nowadays is biblical, citing a baraita about two baskets where Rabbi Yochanan says chullin need not outnumber terumah, while Reish Lakish requires a majority. The Gemara resolves that the baraita follows the Rabbis, not Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan holds that תרומה (terumah) in the present era is biblical, citing a baraita about two baskets where the mixture is permitted based on a presumption.
The baraita records Reish Lakish's position that chullin must outnumber terumah, and Rabbi Yochanan's position that no majority is required.
The Gemara objects that while Reish Lakish's view is consistent (requiring a majority even for rabbinic law), Rabbi Yochanan's lenient position is difficult if he holds terumah is biblical.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita follows the Rabbis (who hold terumah is rabbinic), not Rabbi Yochanan's own view.

items.text: Rabbi Yose's view on inheritance
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose's view on inheritance
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the previous statement was said in accordance with Rabbi Yose, as taught in Seder Olam that the land of Israel was inherited only in the first and second generations, not the third. Rabbi Yochanan identifies the author of Seder Olam as Rabbi Yose.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that his own opinion aligns with that of רבי יוסי (Rabbi Yosei).

A baraita from סדר עולם (Seder Olam) is cited, interpreting the verse 'אֲשֶׁר יָרְשׁוּ אֲבוֹתֶיךָ וִירִשְׁתָּהּ' (which your fathers inherited and you shall inherit it) to mean that there were only two inheritances of the land, not a third.
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) identifies the author of סדר עולם (Seder Olam) as רבי יוסי (Rabbi Yosei).

items.text: Question about Rabbi Yochanan's view on rabbinic law
items.text_en: Question about Rabbi Yochanan's view on rabbinic law
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan holds that rabbinic laws require a biblical derivation, citing a mishnah about a mikveh and Rabbi Yochanan's statement that it is valid until most of the water is removed. The Gemara clarifies that this means as long as most remains, not that most must remain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan holds that rabbinic laws do not require a majority, citing a mishnah about a mikveh and Rabbi Yochanan's statement that it is valid until most of the water is removed.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's statement means that most must not be removed, not that most must remain.

items.text: Alternative answer: distinction due to 'I can say'
items.text_en: Alternative answer: distinction due to 'I can say'
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the case of the androgynos is different because there is a possibility to say 'I can say' (that the androgynos is male), which allows leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the case of the androgynos is different because there is a possibility to say 'I can say' (that the androgynos is male), which allows leniency.

items.text: Dispute over the mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Dispute over the mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah says 'an androgynos marries' (in the present tense), implying it is permitted initially. The Gemara suggests reading it as 'if he married' (past tense), but then questions the phrase 'but he may not be married' (passive), concluding that both phrases refer to after the fact.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the mishnah's wording 'an androgynos marries' (נוֹשֵׂא, present tense, implying לכתחילה), and suggests reading it as 'if he married' (אִם נָשָׂא, past tense, implying בדיעבד).

The Gemara objects that the mishnah explicitly says 'נוֹשֵׂא' (present tense), and then points out that the phrase 'but he may not be married' (אֲבָל לֹא נִישָּׂא) also appears, which is passive and implies בדיעבד.
The Gemara resolves that both 'נִישָּׂא' (passive) and 'נוֹשֵׂא' (active) refer to בדיעבד (after the fact), not לכתחילה.

items.text: Rejection: 'marries' implies initially
items.text_en: Rejection: 'marries' implies initially
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous interpretation, stating that 'marries' implies initially, while 'but he may not be married' means even after the fact it is not allowed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous interpretation, asserting that the term 'נוֹשֵׂא' (marries) implies לכתחילה (the ideal standard), while 'but he may not be married' means even בדיעבד (after the fact) it is not permitted.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Eliezer's statement
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Eliezer's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that from the fact that Rabbi Eliezer says an androgynos is stoned as a male, it implies that the first tanna is in doubt about the androgynos's sex.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rabbi Eliezer's statement that an androgynos is stoned as a male that the first tanna (תנא קמא) is in doubt about the androgynos's sex.

items.text: Dispute about stoning from two places
items.text_en: Dispute about stoning from two places
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both opinions are certain about the androgynos's sex, but they disagree about whether he is stoned from two places (as a doubtful case) or as a male.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute by stating that both opinions are certain about the androgynos's sex, but they disagree about whether he is stoned from two places (as a doubtful case) or as a male.

items.text: Rav's statement
items.text_en: Rav's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a statement by Rav, which is cut off at the end of the page.

sub.desc_en: Rav begins to speak, but the statement is cut off at the end of the page.

items.text: Debate over authority of Mishnah vs. baraita regarding androgynos
items.text_en: Debate over authority of Mishnah vs. baraita regarding androgynos
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the Mishnah is not authoritative against the baraita where Rabbi Yosei calls the androgynos a unique creation. It then counters that the baraita is not authoritative against the Mishnah, since Rabbi Yosei abandoned his colleague, implying he retracted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah is not authoritative against the baraita, citing Rabbi Yosei's statement that the androgynos is a unique creation about which the sages did not decide its sex.
The Gemara counters that the baraita is not authoritative against the Mishnah, since Rabbi Yosei abandoned his colleague, implying he retracted his position.

items.text: Shmuel's position and the Gemara's resolution
items.text_en: Shmuel's position and the Gemara's resolution
items.desc_en: Shmuel says the baraita is not authoritative against the Mishnah. The Gemara objects that Shmuel elsewhere defers to an individual opinion, but resolves that he only does so when the Mishnah is not uprooted, but here it is uprooted.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that the baraita is not authoritative before the Mishnah.
The Gemara objects that, on the contrary, the Mishnah should yield to the baraita, since Shmuel elsewhere defers to an individual opinion.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel only defers to an individual when the Mishnah is not uprooted, but here the Mishnah is uprooted, so he does not defer.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel rule on four matters
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel rule on four matters
items.desc_en: The school of Rav says in Rav's name that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei regarding androgynos and grafting. Shmuel says the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei regarding difficult birth and קידוש (kilayim of vines over grain).

sub.text: School of Rav in Rav's name
sub.text_en: School of Rav in Rav's name
sub.desc_en: The school of Rav reports in Rav's name that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei regarding androgynos and grafting.
Shmuel states that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei regarding difficult birth and קידוש (kilayim of vines over grain).

items.text: Elaboration on grafting (הרכבה)
items.text_en: Elaboration on grafting (הרכבה)
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the ruling on grafting by citing a Mishnah about planting and grafting before the Sabbatical year, with disputes between Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon. Rav Nachman bar Abba then clarifies the required days for each opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the topic of grafting (הרכבה) by citing a Mishnah that discusses the required days before the Sabbatical year for planting and grafting, with disputes among Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon.

Rav Nachman bar Abba clarifies the required days for each opinion: for the one who says thirty days, one needs thirty plus thirty; for three days, three plus thirty; for two weeks, two weeks plus thirty.

items.text: Elaboration on difficult birth (קושי)
items.text_en: Elaboration on difficult birth (קושי)
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Shmuel's ruling on קושי by citing a Mishnah about the duration of a difficult birth, with opinions from Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Shmuel's ruling on קושי (difficult birth) and cites a Mishnah as the source.

The Mishnah records three opinions on the duration of a difficult birth: Rabbi Meir says 40 or 50 days, Rabbi Yehuda says her month suffices, and Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon say no more than two weeks.

items.text: Elaboration on קידוש (kilayim of vines)
items.text_en: Elaboration on קידוש (kilayim of vines)
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Shmuel's ruling on קידוש by citing a Mishnah about one who trellises his vine over a friend's grain, which renders the grain forbidden (קידוש), with a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the concept of קידוש (forbidden mixture of vine and grain) by citing a Mishnah about one who trellises his vine over a friend's grain, stating Rabbi Meir's position that it renders the grain forbidden and the trelliser is liable.
The Mishnah records the dissenting view of Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon, who disagree with Rabbi Meir regarding the status of the grain.

items.text: Opening principle: No one prohibits what is not his
items.text_en: Opening principle: No one prohibits what is not his
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the general principle that a person cannot forbid something that does not belong to him, setting the stage for the ensuing inquiries.

items.text: Inquiries about Shmuel and Rav's rulings on androgynos, hybrid, difficulty, and kiddush
items.text_en: Inquiries about Shmuel and Rav's rulings on androgynos, hybrid, difficulty, and kiddush
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises four questions: what Shmuel said about an androgynos, about hybrid grafting, what Rav said about difficulty (koshi), and about kiddush. It brings evidence from Shmuel's statements and a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Adda regarding the halakha like Rabbi Yosi.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda on tumtum and the case of the tumtum of Bei Re'i
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda on tumtum and the case of the tumtum of Bei Re'i
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami questions Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about a tumtum, citing a case where a tumtum was torn and fathered seven children. Rabbi Yehuda responds that the children's origin is uncertain.

items.text: Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda's concern and the difference between the opinions
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda's concern and the difference between the opinions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda rules that a tumtum should not perform chalitzah lest he be found a seris chamah. The Gemara clarifies his meaning and Rava explains the practical difference between the two opinions: disqualifying in the presence of brothers versus performing chalitzah without brothers.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rav: Androgynos is liable for stoning from two places, and the support from Rabbi Simai
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav: Androgynos is liable for stoning from two places, and the support from Rabbi Simai
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that an androgynos is liable for stoning from two places. An objection is raised from Rabbi Eliezer who says it is only liable as a male. The Gemara then aligns Rav's view with Rabbi Simai, who derives this from the verse 'and with a male you shall not lie' referring to one with two forms.

items.text: The Sages' counter-argument and derivation of male and female
items.text_en: The Sages' counter-argument and derivation of male and female
items.desc_en: The Sages argue that even with two forms, the verse says 'et zakhar' (a male). They derive the prohibition of a regular male from 'ishah' and of unnatural intercourse from 've'ishah'.

items.text: Rav Chisda: Rabbi Eliezer does not consider androgynos a complete male, and the dispute about impurity
items.text_en: Rav Chisda: Rabbi Eliezer does not consider androgynos a complete male, and the dispute about impurity
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that Rabbi Eliezer does not consider an androgynos a complete male, otherwise it would sanctify consecrated animals. The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer excludes tumtum and androgynos from imparting impurity to garments at the throat, unlike the Sages who include them.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's support from a Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's support from a Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a Mishnah that supports Rabbi Eliezer's position regarding tumtum and androgynos.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Samuel's explanation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Samuel's explanation
