items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists kil'ayim, tereifah, yotzei dofen, tumtum, and androgynos as animals that are neither consecrated nor effect consecration. Samuel explains that 'not consecrated' refers to temurah and 'not effecting consecration' refers to one who makes temurah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five categories of animals that are neither consecrated nor effect consecration.
Shmuel explains that 'not consecrated' refers to temurah and 'not effecting consecration' refers to one who makes temurah.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's statement and Rabbi's anecdote
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's statement and Rabbi's anecdote
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer says that an androgynos is liable for stoning like a male. Rabbi recounts that when he went to study with Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua, his students crowded him like chickens of Beit Bukya and only allowed him to learn one thing: that Rabbi Eliezer says an androgynos is liable for stoning like a male.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that an androgynos is liable for stoning like a male.

Rabbi recounts that when he went to study with Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua, his students crowded him like chickens of Beit Bukya and only allowed him to learn one thing: that Rabbi Eliezer says an androgynos is liable for stoning like a male.

items.text: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.desc_en: This segment marks the end of the previous chapter with the phrase 'We have returned to you, O arel'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'We have returned to you, O arel'.

items.text: Mishnah: Women permitted or forbidden to husband and yavam
items.text_en: Mishnah: Women permitted or forbidden to husband and yavam
items.desc_en: The Mishnah categorizes women into four groups: those permitted to their husbands but forbidden to their yevamim, those permitted to yevamim but forbidden to husbands, those forbidden to both, and those permitted to both. It lists specific cases involving priests, chalals, Israelites, and mamzerim, and discusses secondary prohibitions, ketubah, and forced divorce.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by announcing four categories of women regarding their permissibility to husband and yavam.

The Mishnah lists cases of women permitted to their husbands but forbidden to their yevamim: a common priest who married a widow (brother High Priest), a חלל (disqualified priest) who married a fit woman, an Israelite who married an Israelite woman (brother a mamzer), and a mamzer who married a mamzeret (brother an Israelite).

The Mishnah lists cases of women permitted to their yevamim but forbidden to their husbands: High Priest who betrothed a widow (brother common priest), a fit man who married a חללה (disqualified woman), an Israelite who married a mamzeret (brother a mamzer), and a mamzer who married a fit Israelite woman (brother an Israelite).

sub.text: Mishnah third and fourth categories list
sub.text_en: Mishnah third and fourth categories list
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases of women forbidden to both husband and yavam (e.g. High Priest who married a widow, brother a High Priest) and concludes that all other women are permitted to both.

The Mishnah addresses women forbidden by rabbinic decree (שניות): a שניה (secondary forbidden relation) to the husband but not the yavam is forbidden to the husband and permitted to the yavam, and vice versa, and if she is a שניה to both, she is forbidden to both.

sub.text: Mishnah penalty clause for forbidden marriages
sub.text_en: Mishnah penalty clause for forbidden marriages
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for these rabbinically forbidden marriages, the woman receives no marriage contract (כתובה), produce (פירות), sustenance (מזונות), or worn garments (בלָאות), the child is fit, and the husband is compelled to divorce her.

sub.text: Mishnah concluding list of marriages with a ketubah
sub.text_en: Mishnah concluding list of marriages with a ketubah
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists marriages (e.g. widow to High Priest, divorcee to common priest, etc.) that, despite being forbidden, still merit a marriage contract (כתובה).

items.text: Gemara: Why does the Mishnah say 'married' rather than 'betrothed'?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why does the Mishnah say 'married' rather than 'betrothed'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah uses the term 'married' (nasa) instead of 'betrothed' (kidesh). It considers and rejects the possibility that betrothal would allow an aseh to override a lo ta'aseh, then explains that the Mishnah uses 'married' because of the latter cases where marriage creates a chalalah, and also because of the middle case of a High Priest who betrothed a widow. It further questions why the Mishnah specifies 'widow' rather than 'virgin'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah uses the term 'nasa' (married) instead of 'kidesh' (betrothed).

The Gemara considers and rejects the possibility that betrothal would allow an עשה (positive commandment) to override a לא תעשה (negative commandment), noting that the entire chapter involves both an עשה and a לא תעשה, and an עשה does not override a לא תעשה.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah uses 'nasa' because of the latter case of a High Priest who married a widow, where marriage creates a חללה (chalalah), whereas betrothal would permit her; therefore the Tanna also uses 'nasa' in the first clause.
The Gemara objects that if the reason is the latter case, why not teach based on the middle case of a High Priest who betrothed a widow, which would require the term 'kidesh'?

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah uses 'nasa' because of the 'bat bukta' (the case of a חלל (chalal) who married a כשרה (kasherah)), where marriage creates a חללה (chalalah), whereas betrothal would permit her; therefore the Tanna uses 'nasa'.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies 'widow' (אלמנה) rather than 'virgin' (בתולה).

items.text: Rejecting the first explanation of the Mishnah's omission
items.text_en: Rejecting the first explanation of the Mishnah's omission
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the suggestion that the Tanna holds that first marriages cause disqualification, citing the case of a חלל who married a kosher woman where that principle does not apply. It then explains that the Mishnah's wording is due to the need to teach the case of a High Priest who married a widow, specifying 'widow' to exclude a virgin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the suggestion that the Tanna holds that first marriages cause disqualification, citing the case of a חלל (a disqualified priest) who married a kosher woman, where that principle does not apply.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's wording is due to the need to teach the case of a High Priest who married a widow, specifying 'widow' to exclude a virgin.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge and the missing case
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge and the missing case
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges the Mishnah's omission, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling about a second-generation Egyptian who married a first-generation Egyptian woman. He argues that the Mishnah should have included a similar case involving two Egyptian women, with various scenarios of permissibility and prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges the Mishnah's omission, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that a second-generation Egyptian who married a first-generation Egyptian woman produces a second-generation child, and argues that the Mishnah should have included a similar case.

Rav Pappa proposes a case: a second-generation Egyptian married two Egyptian women (one first-generation, one second-generation) and had children from both; if the marriages were performed in the normal order, the wives are permitted to their husbands but forbidden to their yevamim.

Rav Pappa adds that if the order is reversed, the wives are permitted to their yevamim and forbidden to their husbands; those permitted to both are converts, and those forbidden to both are aylonit (infertile women).

items.text: The Gemara's response: the Tanna omitted and left out
items.text_en: The Gemara's response: the Tanna omitted and left out
items.desc_en: The Gemara responds that the Tanna indeed omitted some cases, and asks what was omitted. It suggests the case of a פצוע דכא (a man with crushed testicles).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Tanna omitted some cases, asks what was omitted, and answers that the case of a פצוע דכא (a man with crushed testicles) was omitted.

items.text: Defending the omission and proving the Tanna omitted
items.text_en: Defending the omission and proving the Tanna omitted
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a פצוע דכא is not a true omission because the Tanna already taught cases of those liable for negative commandments. It then defends that the Tanna needed to teach certain cases for specific reasons, but ultimately concludes that the Tanna did omit, as shown by the case of an Israelite who married a mamzeret.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a פצוע דכא (wounded or crushed testicles) is not a true omission because the Tanna already taught cases of those liable for negative commandments.

The Gemara counters that the Tanna indeed repeated cases of those liable for negative commandments, citing the examples of a common priest who married a widow and a חלל (profaned priest) who married a fit woman.
The Gemara answers that those cases were necessary to teach the principle of Rav Yehuda citing Rav: that fit women were not warned against marrying those unfit for the priesthood.

The Gemara objects further that the Tanna also taught the case of an Israelite who married a daughter of Israel and has a mamzer brother, which teaches about a לאו שאינו שוה בכל (a prohibition not equally applicable to all).
The Gemara concludes that the Tanna indeed omitted cases, as shown by the case of an Israelite who married a mamzeret, and thus the Tanna did omit.

items.text: Analyzing Rav Yehuda's statement about kosher women
items.text_en: Analyzing Rav Yehuda's statement about kosher women
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines Rav Yehuda's statement that kosher women are not warned against marrying disqualified men. It attempts to prove this from the Mishnah's case of a חלל who married a kosher woman, but concludes that the Mishnah's 'kosher' refers to an Israelite woman, not a priestess, and the case is ambiguous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda's statement in the name of Rav that kosher women (כְּשֵׁרוֹת) were not warned against marrying disqualified men (פְּסוּלִין).
The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's case of a חלל (halal) who married a 'kosher woman' supports Rav Yehuda, suggesting that 'kosher' means a priestess (כֹּהֶנֶת) fit for the priesthood.
The Gemara rejects the support, explaining that 'kosher' here means an Israelite woman (יִשְׂרְאֵלִית) fit for the congregation (כְּשֵׁרָה לַקָּהָל), not a priestess.

The Gemara objects: if 'kosher' means fit for the congregation, then the Mishnah's phrase 'he has a kosher brother' implies the brother is fit for the congregation, but the halal himself is disqualified from the congregation — which is inconsistent.

The Gemara resolves: the halal is a priest (כֹּהֵן), so his wife is a priestess (כֹּהֶנֶת), but the term 'kosher' in the Mishnah is ambiguous — each case stands on its own (הָא כִּדְאִיתָא וְהָא כִּדְאִיתָא), and the attempted proof is inconclusive.

items.text: Ravin's objection and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Ravin's objection and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Ravin bar Nachman objects with a verse that teaches that a woman is warned through the man. Rava explains that wherever the man is warned, the woman is warned, but Rav Yehuda's statement applies only to prohibitions that are not equal for both. The Gemara then cites a source from Rav Yehuda and the school of Rabbi Yishmael that equates women to men for all punishments, but clarifies that this applies only to prohibitions that are equal for all.

sub.desc_en: Ravin bar Nachman objects by citing a verse that teaches that a woman is warned through the man, contradicting Rav Yehuda's statement that women were not warned.
Rava answers that wherever the man is warned, the woman is warned, and wherever he is not warned, she is not warned, thus limiting the scope of the verse.
The Gemara questions why the principle is derived from this verse, when it could be derived from Rav Yehuda's statement and the baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that equates women to men for all punishments in the Torah.

The Gemara resolves that from that baraita one might have thought the principle applies only to prohibitions that are equal for all, but Rav Yehuda's statement teaches that even for prohibitions not equal for all, the woman is warned through the man.

items.text: Gemara's question on women's obligation in impurity
items.text_en: Gemara's question on women's obligation in impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether women would be obligated in impurity if not for the verse 'sons of Aaron' excluding daughters. It considers whether this derives from Rav Yehuda's statement or from the verse 'lo yikachu'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: regarding טומאה (ritual impurity), which is not a law equally applicable to all, if not for the verse 'בני אהרן' (sons of Aaron) excluding daughters, would women be obligated — is this not because of Rav Yehuda's statement?
The Gemara answers: no, the obligation derives from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) with the verse 'לֹא יִקָּחוּ' (they shall not take).
An alternative version states: the word 'קיחה' (taking) was necessary for him, as one might have thought to learn from impurity — so the verse teaches us otherwise.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's inquiry about fit women marrying unfit men
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's inquiry about fit women marrying unfit men
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua ask whether fit women are warned against marrying unfit men. Rav Pappa cites a Mishna about yichusin, and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explains why a priestess to a chalai is not listed. Rav Idi bar Avin rules in the name of Rav that they are not warned.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna's question
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua arrived at Hinzvu and asked: were fit women (כשרות) warned against marrying those disqualified from the priesthood (פסולין) or not?

Rav Pappa answered: you have learned the baraita of the ten genealogical classes that ascended from Babylonia, which lists permissible marriages but does not include a כהנת (priest's daughter) marrying a חלל (disqualified priest).
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua objected: wherever the classes intermarry, the baraita lists them; but a כהן (priest) cannot marry a חללה (female disqualified priest), so it is not listed.
They came before Rav Idi bar Avin, who ruled in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Rav: fit women were not warned against marrying those disqualified from the priesthood.

items.text: Inquiry about a secondary forbidden woman's ketubah from the yavam
items.text_en: Inquiry about a secondary forbidden woman's ketubah from the yavam
items.desc_en: The Benei Beirei ask Rav Sheshet whether a woman who is a secondary forbidden relative to the husband but not to the yavam has a ketubah from the yavam. Rav Sheshet cites a baraita that her ketubah is on the first husband's property, and if she is secondary to the husband, she has nothing even from the yavam. The Gemara clarifies the baraita's wording.

sub.desc_en: The Benei Beirei ask Rav Sheshet whether a woman who is a secondary forbidden relative to the husband but not to the yavam has a ketubah from the yavam, presenting the first side of the dilemma based on the principle that her ketubah is on the first husband's property.
The Benei Beirei present the alternative possibility that since the Sages instituted a ketubah from the second husband when there is none from the first, she might have a ketubah from the yavam.
Rav Sheshet cites a baraita that her ketubah is on the first husband's property, and if she is secondary to the husband, she has nothing even from the yavam.

The Gemara clarifies that the baraita is incomplete and teaches that if she has no ketubah from the first husband, they institute one from the second, but if she is secondary to the husband, she has nothing even from the yavam.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's inquiry about sustenance for a widow to a high priest
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's inquiry about sustenance for a widow to a high priest
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Yochanan whether a widow married to a high priest or a divorcee to a common priest is entitled to sustenance if the husband went overseas and she borrowed and ate. Rabbi Yochanan rules she has no sustenance. The Gemara reconciles a contradictory baraita by distinguishing between during the husband's lifetime and after his death.

sub.desc_en: רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) asks רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) whether a widow married to a high priest or a divorcee to a common priest has a right to sustenance.
The Gemara clarifies the case: if she dwells under his roof, he is in a 'stand and divorce' situation, so the question only arises when he went overseas and she borrowed and ate.
The Gemara poses the dilemma: is sustenance a stipulation of the marriage contract, so she has it, or is it withheld to prevent her from lingering with him?
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) answers that she has no right to sustenance.
The Gemara objects with a baraita that says she has sustenance, and resolves that the baraita refers to after his death.
An alternative version of the discussion is presented, where the objection and resolution are phrased differently but lead to the same conclusion.

items.text: Baraita on the rights of a widow to a high priest and secondary forbidden women
items.text_en: Baraita on the rights of a widow to a high priest and secondary forbidden women
items.desc_en: A baraita lists the entitlements of a widow to a high priest or a divorcee to a common priest: she has a ketubah, produce, sustenance, and worn garments, but she is unfit and her child is unfit, and he is compelled to divorce her. Secondary forbidden women have none of these, but she is fit and her child is fit. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar explains the reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that a widow married to a High Priest or a divorcée/ḥalutza to a common priest has a marriage contract, produce, sustenance, and worn garments, but she is disqualified and her offspring is disqualified, and the court forces him to divorce her.

The Tanna Kamma contrasts the case of secondary forbidden relatives: they have no marriage contract, produce, sustenance, or worn garments, but they are fit and their offspring is fit, and the court forces him to divorce her.

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar explains that the widow to a High Priest has a marriage contract because both he and she are disqualified, and wherever both are disqualified, the marriage contract is granted.

items.text: Mishnah: Distinction between primary and secondary forbidden marriages
items.text_en: Mishnah: Distinction between primary and secondary forbidden marriages
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for primary forbidden marriages (where both are unfit), the man is penalized by losing his ketubah obligation, while for secondary rabbinic marriages (where both are fit), the woman is penalized by losing her ketubah.

items.text: Rabbi's explanation: Torah vs. rabbinic laws
items.text_en: Rabbi's explanation: Torah vs. rabbinic laws
items.desc_en: Rabbi offers two reasons: first, Torah laws need no reinforcement, but rabbinic laws do; second, in the primary case the man entices her, while in the secondary case she entices him.

items.text: Alternative attribution: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.text_en: Alternative attribution: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.desc_en: Some say the Mishnah is taught by Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who explains the rationale as: in the primary case the man entices her, in the secondary case she entices him.

items.text: Alternative attribution: Rabbi and the challenge of the חלוצה
items.text_en: Alternative attribution: Rabbi and the challenge of the חלוצה
items.desc_en: Others say Rabbi himself taught the Mishnah, and he was troubled by the case of a חלוצה (a rabbinic prohibition) who still receives a ketubah; he therefore explained the distinction based on who entices whom.

items.text: Practical difference between the two attributions
items.text_en: Practical difference between the two attributions
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks a practical difference between Rabbi and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. Rav Chisda suggests a mamzeret or netinah marrying an Israelite; Rav Yosef suggests a divorcée remarried to her first husband; Rav Pappa suggests a woman who had relations with a High Priest; Rav Ashi suggests a suspected sotah who was not actually unfaithful; Mar bar Rav Ashi suggests a definite sotah. Each case tests whether the woman is considered the enticer.

items.text: New Mishnah: Terumah and ma'aser eligibility for women
items.text_en: New Mishnah: Terumah and ma'aser eligibility for women
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a woman, despite her connection to a priest or Levite, may not eat terumah or ma'aser due to her marital status or the status of her child.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about ma'aser
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about ma'aser
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a non-Levite woman (a zar) cannot eat ma'aser, and Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that first tithe is forbidden to non-Levites.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute over first tithe
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute over first tithe
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir says terumah is for the priest and first tithe for the Levite; Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah permits it to the priest. The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Elazar permits it, not that there is an additional prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Meir's position that terumah is for the priest and first tithe for the Levite, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah permits it to the priest.
The Gemara questions the wording 'permits it,' implying there is someone who forbids it.
The Gemara resolves that the correct phrasing is 'he gives it even to a priest,' not 'permits it.'

items.text: Gemara's derivation for Rabbi Meir's position
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation for Rabbi Meir's position
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rabbah cites a derivation: just as terumah is forbidden to non-priests, so is first tithe. The Gemara rejects the comparison regarding the death penalty and the additional fifth, citing verses that limit these to terumah. The Rabbis derive that first tithe renders the produce tevel, like terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning behind Rabbi Meir's position that first tithe is given only to a Levite.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rabbah citing the Gemara
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rabbah citing the Gemara
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rabbah cites a derivation from the verse 'כי את מעשר בני ישראל אשר ירימו לה׳ תרומה' (for the tithe of the children of Israel which they raise as a heave-offering to the Lord): just as תרומה (terumah) is forbidden to non-priests, so first tithe is forbidden to non-Levites.
The Gemara objects: if the analogy is complete, then just as one is liable to death and the additional fifth for eating תרומה (terumah), so too for first tithe — but this is not the case.
The Gemara rejects the objection by citing verses that limit the death penalty and the additional fifth specifically to תרומה (terumah), not to first tithe.
The Rabbis derive that just as תרומה (terumah) renders the produce טבל (tevel, untithed), so first tithe also renders the produce טבל (tevel).

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei: Tevel includes all tithes
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei: Tevel includes all tithes
items.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Yosei teaches that the prohibition of eating tevel applies even if only one tithe has not been separated, including first tithe, second tithe, and poor man's tithe. The Gemara notes that without the derivation from Rabbi Meir, one might think the prohibition is only a negative commandment, not punishable by death.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei's baraita opens by stating that one might think the prohibition of tevel applies only when no tithe at all has been removed, and then asks: from where do we derive that it applies even if only first tithe, second tithe, or poor man's tithe remains?

The baraita derives the law via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'שעריך' (your gates) used in the context of poor man's tithe, concluding that the prohibition 'לֹא תוּכַל' (you may not eat) applies to all tithes.

The Gemara explains that without the derivation from Rabbi Meir, one might think the prohibition from the baraita is only a negative commandment (לאו), not punishable by death; therefore the earlier derivation teaches that it carries the death penalty.

items.text: Alternative formulation: Derivation from Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Alternative formulation: Derivation from Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative formulation: the fact that first tithe renders tevel is derived from Rabbi Yosei's baraita, but without the derivation from Rabbi Meir, one might think it is only a negative commandment, not punishable by death. The derivation teaches that it is indeed punishable by death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative formulation: the fact that first tithe renders tevel is derived from Rabbi Yosei's baraita.
The Gemara objects that from that baraita alone one might think the prohibition is only a negative commandment (לאו), not punishable by death.
The Gemara resolves that the derivation from Rabbi Meir teaches that it is indeed punishable by death.

items.text: Question on the Mishnah's ruling for an arusah
items.text_en: Question on the Mishnah's ruling for an arusah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a bat Levi arusah to a Kohen or a bat Kohen arusah to a Levi may not eat terumah or ma'aser, asking what 'strangeness' is involved. Rav Sheshet explains that 'she does not eat' means she does not give permission to tithe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a bat Levi arusah to a Kohen or a bat Kohen arusah to a Levi may not eat terumah or ma'aser, asking what 'strangeness' is involved.
Rav Sheshet explains that 'she does not eat' means she does not give permission to tithe.

items.text: Proof that a nesu'ah gives permission to tithe
items.text_en: Proof that a nesu'ah gives permission to tithe
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that a nesu'ah does give permission, citing a baraita that a bat Yisrael married to a Kohen gives permission to tithe. The baraita derives this from the verse 'And you shall eat it in every place, you and your household,' teaching that a nesu'ah gives permission, not just to eat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the mishna implies that a married woman (נשואה) does give permission to tithe.
The Gemara answers yes, citing a baraita that derives from the verse 'ואכלתם אותו בכל מקום אתם וביתכם' that a married Israelite woman gives permission to tithe.

The baraita raises the possibility that the verse might only teach that she may eat, not that she gives permission, but then rejects this because if she may eat the stringent תרומה (priestly portion), she certainly may eat the lenient מעשר (tithe).
The baraita concludes that the verse must teach that a married Israelite woman gives permission to tithe, not merely that she may eat.

items.text: Mar bar Ravana's explanation and the Gemara's challenge
items.text_en: Mar bar Ravana's explanation and the Gemara's challenge
items.desc_en: Mar bar Ravana explains that the Mishnah means that an arusah does not receive ma'aser at the granary. The Gemara challenges this based on the reasons for the decree (yichud or gerushah) and concludes that the decree applies even to a nesu'ah, but the Mishnah only mentions arusah because the first clause did.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ravana explains that the Mishnah means that an arusah does not receive ma'aser at the granary.
The Gemara objects that this explanation works for the reason of yichud but not for the reason of gerushah, since a bat Levi divorcée may eat ma'aser.
The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that the decree applies even to a bat Kohen divorcée due to concern for a bat Yisrael divorcée.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah mentions arusah even though the halakhah applies to nesu'ah as well, because the first clause used arusah.

items.text: Second version of the Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's dispute
items.text_en: Second version of the Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a second version of the Mishnah where the dispute is between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, with Rabbi Akiva stating that terumah is for the priest and first tithe for the Levite.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a second version of the Mishnah, stating that terumah is for the priest and first tithe for the Levite, according to Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah states his opposing view, though the baraita is cut off here; the full position is implied from context.

items.text: Dispute over Levites and ma'aser rishon
items.text_en: Dispute over Levites and ma'aser rishon
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether ma'aser rishon is given only to priests or also to Levites. Rabbi Akiva holds it is only for Levites, citing the verse addressing Levites. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi argues that priests are sometimes called Levites, citing a verse. The Gemara then explains Rabbi Akiva's position based on the phrase 'you may eat it in any place,' which excludes priests who cannot eat in a cemetery.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse refers to a priest or a Levite, suggesting it might include a priest.
Rabbi Akiva explains that the verse explicitly addresses Levites, not priests.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites that in twenty-four places priests are called Levites, including one verse.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Akiva cannot apply his reasoning here because the verse says 'in every place,' excluding a priest who cannot eat in a cemetery.
The Gemara resolves that a priest can eat maaser anywhere because it does not require a walled city, and if he eats while impure he is not lashed.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: A story is told about a garden from which Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya took ma'aser rishon. Rabbi Akiva surrounded it with graves, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya rebuked him, saying 'Akiva, you carry a sack, and I am alive?'

sub.text: Story about Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: A story is told about a garden from which Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya took first tithe, and Rabbi Akiva redirected its entrance to a cemetery, prompting a complaint.

items.text: Reason for penalizing Levites with ma'aser
items.text_en: Reason for penalizing Levites with ma'aser
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses why Levites were penalized regarding ma'aser rishon. Two opinions are given: one says because they did not ascend in Ezra's time, another says to allow priests to rely on it during their impurity. The Gemara clarifies that the second opinion actually agrees with the first, and the dispute is about whether the penalty goes to the poor or to priests in their impurity, who are considered poor.

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi Akiva's action
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi Akiva's action
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Akiva's action of surrounding the garden with graves. According to the view that the penalty goes to the poor, this prevented the priest from eating there. According to the view that it goes to priests, Rabbi Akiva told Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya: if you come as a penalty, you have a share; if as an allotment, you have none.

items.text: Proof that Levites did not ascend in Ezra's time
items.text_en: Proof that Levites did not ascend in Ezra's time
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides a proof from the verse in Ezra that no Levites were found among those who returned. Rav Chisda adds that initially, officers were appointed from Levites, but now they are appointed from Israelites.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the Levites did not ascend in Ezra's time.
A verse from Ezra is cited showing that among the returnees, no Levites were found.
Rav Chisda adds that initially officers were appointed only from Levites, but now from Israelites, as a consequence of the Levites' absence.

items.text: Mishnah: Who eats terumah and ma'aser
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who eats terumah and ma'aser
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules: a bat Yisrael married to a priest eats terumah; if she has a son from him, she continues. Married to a Levite, she eats ma'aser; with a son, continues. Married to an Israelite, she eats neither. If her son from an Israelite dies, she eats ma'aser; if from a Levite dies, she eats terumah; if from a priest dies, she eats neither.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for a bat Yisrael married to a priest, Levite, or Israelite regarding eating terumah and maaser.
The Mishnah continues with the rules after the death of her son from each type of husband.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for a bat kohen who marries an Israelite, a Levite, or a kohen: she may or may not eat terumah or ma'aser depending on her marital status and children. After the death of her child from a kohen or Levite, she loses the right to eat terumah or ma'aser, but if her child from an Israelite dies, she returns to her father's house and may eat from his bread, as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for a bat kohen who marries an Israelite, a Levite, or a kohen: she may or may not eat terumah or ma'aser depending on her marital status and children.

items.text: Gemara's derivation for the bat kohen's return to terumah
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation for the bat kohen's return to terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that a bat kohen whose son from a Levite dies may eat terumah. Rabbi Abba says in the name of Rav that it is derived from the extra 'vav' in the word 'וּבַת' (and a daughter). The Gemara then questions whether this follows Rabbi Akiva's method of expounding vavs, and concludes that even the Rabbis agree because the entire word 'וּבַת' is an extra verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that a bat kohen whose son from a Levite dies may eat terumah.
Rabbi Abba says in the name of Rav that the derivation is from the extra 'vav' in the word 'וּבַת' (and a daughter).
The Gemara questions whether this derivation follows Rabbi Akiva's method of expounding vavs.
The Gemara concludes that even the Rabbis agree because the entire word 'וּבַת' is an extra verse.

items.text: Baraita on returning to terumah but not to breast and thigh
items.text_en: Baraita on returning to terumah but not to breast and thigh
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that when a bat kohen returns to her father's house, she returns to eat terumah but not the breast and thigh (the priestly gifts from peace offerings). Rav Chisda and Ravina bar Sheila derive this from the verse 'הִיא בִּתְרוּמַת הַקֳּדָשִׁים לֹא תֹאכֵל', meaning she may not eat from the elevated part of the offerings. Rav Nachman and Rabbah bar Avuha derive it from 'מִלֶּחֶם', implying not all bread, excluding breast and thigh.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that when a bat kohen returns to her father's house, she returns to eat terumah but not the breast and thigh.

sub.text: Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Sheila
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Sheila
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Sheila derives the exclusion from the verse 'הִיא בִּתְרוּמַת הַקֳּדָשִׁים לֹא תֹאכֵל', interpreting it as 'from the elevated part of the offerings she may not eat'.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha derives the exclusion from 'מִלֶּחֶם', meaning 'not all bread', thereby excluding breast and thigh.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's objection and Rava's answer regarding annulment of vows
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's objection and Rava's answer regarding annulment of vows
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama objects: perhaps the exclusion from 'מִלֶּחֶם' refers to the annulment of vows, not breast and thigh. Rava answers that the tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael already resolved this: the verse 'וְנֵדֶר אַלְמָנָה וּגְרוּשָׁה יָקוּם עָלֶיהָ' teaches that once a woman leaves her father's domain, he can no longer annul her vows, even if she returns. This is derived from the case of a woman who was handed over to the husband's agents and then widowed or divorced on the way.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama objects that the exclusion from 'מִלֶּחֶם' might refer to the annulment of vows rather than breast and thigh.

Rava answers that the tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael already resolved this: the verse 'וְנֵדֶר אַלְמָנָה וּגְרוּשָׁה יָקוּם עָלֶיהָ' teaches that once a woman leaves her father's domain, he can no longer annul her vows, even if she returns, as derived from the case of a woman handed over to the husband's agents and then widowed or divorced on the way.

items.text: Rav Safra, Rav Pappa, and Rava's alternative derivations
items.text_en: Rav Safra, Rav Pappa, and Rava's alternative derivations
items.desc_en: Rav Safra derives from 'מִלֶּחֶם אָבִיהָ תֹּאכֵל' that she may eat bread but not meat. Rav Pappa derives that it refers to bread acquired by her father, excluding breast and thigh which come from the Most High's table. Rava derives from the verse 'וְאֵת חֲזֵה הַתְּנוּפָה... תֹּאכְלוּ אַתָּה וּבָנֶיךָ וּבְנוֹתֶיךָ אִתָּךְ' that the breast and thigh are only eaten when the daughter is 'with you' (i.e., living with her father), not when she returns after marriage.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra derives from the verse 'מִלֶּחֶם אָבִיהָ תֹּאכֵל' that she may eat bread (i.e., תרומה) but not meat (i.e., breast and thigh).
Rav Pappa derives that the verse refers to bread acquired by her father, excluding breast and thigh which come from the Most High's table.
Rava derives from the verse that the breast and thigh are only eaten when the daughter is 'with you' (i.e., living with her father), not when she returns after marriage.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's baraita and Rav Mordechai's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's baraita and Rav Mordechai's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava teaches a baraita: when a bat kohen returns to her father's house, she returns to terumah but not to breast and thigh; but for the sake of her son (from a kohen), she returns even to breast and thigh. Rav Mordechai reports this teaching before Rav Ashi, who asks: from where is this derived? From 'וּבַת'? Is she more privileged than her mother? There, exclusions are written; here, no exclusions are written.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava teaches a baraita: when a bat kohen returns to her father's house, she returns to תרומה (terumah) but not to breast and thigh; but for the sake of her son (from a kohen), she returns even to breast and thigh.
Rav Mordekhai reports the teaching before Rav Ashi, who asks: from where is this derived? From 'וּבַת'? Is she more privileged than her mother?
The Gemara answers: there, exclusions are written; here, no exclusions are written.

items.text: Derivation of exceptions for a yevamah and a pregnant woman
items.text_en: Derivation of exceptions for a yevamah and a pregnant woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the Mishnah and cites a baraita: 'וְשָׁבָה אֶל בֵּית אָבִיהָ' excludes a woman awaiting yibbum; 'כִּנְעוּרֶיהָ' excludes a pregnant woman. A logical argument is presented: if in the case of yibbum, where a child from the first husband is not like a child from the second to exempt from yibbum, yet a fetus is considered like a born child; then in the case of terumah, where a child from the first is like a child from the second to disqualify from terumah, should not a fetus be considered like a born child? The Gemara refutes this: in yibbum, the dead are considered alive, but in terumah, the dead are not considered alive. Therefore, the verse 'כִּנְעוּרֶיהָ' excludes a pregnant woman. The Gemara then explains why both 'וְזֶרַע אֵין לָהּ' and 'כִּנְעוּרֶיהָ' are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְשָׁבָה אֶל בֵּית אָבִיהָ' to exclude a woman awaiting yibbum, and 'כִּנְעוּרֶיהָ' to exclude a pregnant woman.
The Gemara proposes a logical argument (קל וחומר) that since in yibbum a fetus is treated as born, it should also be treated as born for terumah.
The Gemara refutes the argument: in yibbum the dead are considered alive, but in terumah the dead are not considered alive, so the analogy fails.
The Gemara concludes that the verse 'כִּנְעוּרֶיהָ' excludes a pregnant woman, as the logical argument is refuted.
The Gemara explains why both 'וְזֶרַע אֵין לָהּ' and 'כִּנְעוּרֶיהָ' are necessary, as each addresses a different case.

items.text: Clarification of the earlier Mishnah's logic
items.text_en: Clarification of the earlier Mishnah's logic
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needed to state 'she has no seed' separately, arguing that without it one might think the case is different when the body was initially empty and remains empty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's phrase 'she has no seed' is necessary, because without it one might think the case of a woman whose body was initially empty and remains empty is exempt from yibbum.

items.text: Siman for the following arguments
items.text_en: Siman for the following arguments
items.desc_en: A mnemonic sign lists the topics of the four kal va-chomer arguments that follow: not making the dead like the living for levirate marriage, making the dead like the living for terumah, making a child from the first like a child from the second for levirate marriage, and not making a child from the first like a child from the second for terumah.

sub.desc_en: The mnemonic sign lists the four kal va-chomer arguments that follow, concerning levirate marriage and terumah.

items.text: First kal va-chomer: not making the dead like the living for levirate marriage
items.text_en: First kal va-chomer: not making the dead like the living for levirate marriage
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda from Diskarta proposes to Rava a kal va-chomer: if in a case where a child from the first husband is treated like a child from the second to disqualify her from terumah, the dead are not treated like the living, then in a case where a child from the first is not treated like a child from the second to exempt her from levirate marriage, certainly the dead should not be treated like the living. The verse 'Her ways are ways of pleasantness' rejects this logic.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda miDiskarta's proposal to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda miDiskarta's proposal to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda miDiskarta proposes a kal va-chomer to Rava: if in the case of terumah, where a child from the first husband is treated like a child from the second to disqualify her, the dead are not treated like the living, then in the case of levirate marriage, where a child from the first is not treated like a child from the second to exempt her, certainly the dead should not be treated like the living.

The gemara rejects the kal va-chomer by citing the verse 'Her ways are ways of pleasantness and all her paths are peace', indicating that the Torah's laws are not derived by such logic when they would lead to harshness.

items.text: Second kal va-chomer: making the dead like the living for terumah
items.text_en: Second kal va-chomer: making the dead like the living for terumah
items.desc_en: A kal va-chomer argues: if in a case where a child from the first is not treated like a child from the second to exempt her from levirate marriage, the dead are treated like the living, then in a case where a child from the first is treated like a child from the second to disqualify her from terumah, certainly the dead should be treated like the living. The verse 'And she has no seed' rejects this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal va-chomer (a fortiori argument) to make the dead like the living for terumah (priestly portion) disqualification.
The Gemara rejects the kal va-chomer by citing the verse 'וְזֶרַע אֵין לָהּ' (and she has no seed), indicating that the dead are not treated like the living for terumah.

items.text: Third kal va-chomer: making a child from the first like a child from the second for levirate marriage
items.text_en: Third kal va-chomer: making a child from the first like a child from the second for levirate marriage
items.desc_en: A kal va-chomer argues: if in a case where the dead are not treated like the living for terumah, a child from the first is treated like a child from the second, then in a case where the dead are treated like the living for levirate marriage, certainly a child from the first should be treated like a child from the second. The verse 'And he has no son' rejects this.

sub.desc_en: The gemara proposes a kal va-chomer (a fortiori argument) that a child from the first husband should be treated like a child from the second husband for levirate marriage (ייבום), based on the analogy with terumah (priestly portion).
The gemara rejects the kal va-chomer by citing the verse 'וּבֵן אֵין לוֹ' (and he has no son), indicating that the child from the first husband is not considered a son for levirate marriage.

items.text: Fourth kal va-chomer: not making a child from the first like a child from the second for terumah
items.text_en: Fourth kal va-chomer: not making a child from the first like a child from the second for terumah
items.desc_en: A kal va-chomer argues: if in a case where the dead are treated like the living to exempt her from levirate marriage, a child from the first is not treated like a child from the second, then in a case where the dead are not treated like the living for terumah, certainly a child from the first should not be treated like a child from the second. The verse 'She has no [seed]' rejects this, as she does have.

sub.desc_en: The gemara proposes a kal va-chomer (a fortiori argument): if in a case where the dead are treated like the living to exempt her from levirate marriage, a child from the first is not treated like a child from the second, then in a case where the dead are not treated like the living for terumah, certainly a child from the first should not be treated like a child from the second.
The gemara rejects the kal va-chomer with the verse 'She has no [seed]', arguing that she does have a child, so the premise fails.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter 'Yesh Mutarot' with the phrase 'Hadaran alach Yesh Mutarot'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter 'Yesh Mutarot' with the standard concluding formula.

items.text: Mishnah: The woman who remarried based on testimony of her husband's death
items.text_en: Mishnah: The woman who remarried based on testimony of her husband's death
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case of a woman whose husband went overseas, witnesses said he died, she remarried, and then her husband returned. She must leave both husbands, needs a get from both, has no ketubah or other rights, and the child is a mamzer from both. Various rulings are given about her status and the obligations of the husbands. Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Shimon offer dissenting opinions. The Mishnah concludes with the distinction between marrying with court permission (exempt from a sacrifice) and without (liable).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a woman who remarried based on testimony of her husband's death and then he returns, stating she must leave both husbands and needs a גט (bill of divorce) from each.
The Mishnah rules that she has no כתובה (marriage contract), produce, sustenance, or worn garments from either husband, and must return anything she took.
The Mishnah states that the child is a ממזר (illegitimate) from both, and neither husband may become impure for her, nor are they entitled to her found property, earnings, or annulment of her vows.

The Mishnah details further consequences: a daughter of Israel is disqualified from the priesthood, a Levite from tithes, a priest's daughter from תרומה (priestly portion); neither husband's heirs inherit her כתובה; and if they die, their brothers perform חליצה (removal of the shoe) but not יבום (levirate marriage).
Rabbi Yose says her כתובה is a lien on the property of the first husband.
Rabbi Elazar says the first husband is entitled to her found property, earnings, and annulment of her vows.
Rabbi Shimon says her marital relations or חליצה with the first husband's brother exempts her rival wife, and the child from him is not a ממזר.
The Mishnah distinguishes: if she married without court permission she may return to her first husband; if she married with court permission she must leave but is exempt from a sacrifice.

The Mishnah concludes: if she married without court permission she must leave and is liable for a sacrifice; the court's power is beautified as it exempts her from a sacrifice, but if she went and corrupted herself after their permission she is liable.

items.text: Gemara: Proof that a single witness is credible from the Torah
items.text_en: Gemara: Proof that a single witness is credible from the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's wording that the first case involved court permission and a single witness, proving a single witness is credible. It brings supporting Mishnayot and a baraita from the verse 'or his sin be made known to him' to show that a single witness is believed from the Torah when the accused does not deny it. The Gemara then questions whether silence is considered admission, and cites a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about two witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's wording that the first case involved court permission and a single witness, proving that a single witness is credible.
The Gemara brings a supporting Mishnah that courts would marry off a woman based on a single witness, confirming the credibility of a single witness.
The Gemara brings another Mishnah where a single witness about eating forbidden fat is believed if the accused is silent, showing Torah-level credibility.
The Gemara cites a baraita from the verse 'אוֹ הוֹדַע אֵלָיו חַטָּאתוֹ' (or his sin be made known to him) to prove that a single witness is believed from the Torah when the accused does not deny it.
The Gemara questions whether the single witness's credibility is due to his testimony or because the accused's silence is considered an admission.

The Gemara cites the continuation of the Mishnah where two witnesses testify and the accused denies, and Rabbi Meir argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori) that two witnesses should obligate a sacrifice, showing the issue is about testimony, not silence.
The Sages object to Rabbi Meir's argument, noting that the accused could claim he acted intentionally (מזיד), which would exempt him from a sacrifice.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Rabbis' reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Rabbis' reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Rabbis require the woman to leave the second husband, suggesting it might be because the witness is believed, but then notes that even two witnesses are believed against her denial. It concludes that the reason is her silence, which is like an admission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Rabbis require the woman to leave the second husband, considers that it might be because the witness is believed, rejects this because even two witnesses are believed against her denial, and concludes that the reason is her silence, which is like an admission.

items.text: Analogy to a piece of fat and its rejection
items.text_en: Analogy to a piece of fat and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an analogy: a piece of uncertain fat and suet, where one witness is believed. It rejects this because there is no established prohibition, unlike here where the woman is established as a married woman, and matters of ervah require two witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an analogy: a piece of uncertain fat and suet, where one witness is believed.
The Gemara rejects the analogy because here the woman is established as a married woman (אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ), and matters of ערוה (forbidden relations) require two witnesses.

items.text: Analogy to definite fat and its rejection
items.text_en: Analogy to definite fat and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another analogy: a piece of definite fat where one witness says it is suet, and he is not believed. This is rejected because there, even a hundred witnesses would not be believed, but here, since two witnesses would be believed, one should also be believed, based on the principle of tevel, hekdesh, and konamot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an analogy to a piece of definite fat (חתיכה דוודאי חלב) where one witness claims it is suet and is not believed.

The Gemara rejects the analogy: there, even a hundred witnesses would not be believed, but here, since two witnesses would be believed, one should also be believed, based on the principle of tevel (טבל), hekdesh (הקדש), and konamot (קונמות).

items.text: Analysis of the tevel, hekdesh, and konamot analogy
items.text_en: Analysis of the tevel, hekdesh, and konamot analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the analogy to tevel, hekdesh, and konamot. It questions the source for believing one witness in each case, considering whether the item belongs to the witness or another, and whether the witness can rectify the situation himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the case of tevel (untithed produce): if it belongs to the witness, he is credible because he can fix it himself; if it belongs to another, what does the Sage hold?

The Gemara analyzes two possibilities: if the Sage holds that one can separate tithes for another without the owner's knowledge, the witness is credible because he can fix it; if he holds that the owner's knowledge is required, and the witness merely claims to know it was already tithed, the source for this halakha is unclear.

The Gemara similarly questions the case of hekdesh (consecrated property): if it is sanctity of value, the witness can redeem it; if it is inherent sanctity and belongs to another, the source for believing the witness is unclear.

The Gemara questions the case of konamot (vows): if there is misuse of consecrated objects, the witness can redeem it; if not, and it belongs to another, the source for believing the witness is unclear.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's explanation and the Gemara's conclusion
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's explanation and the Gemara's conclusion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira suggests that the leniency is due to the stringency at the end (the woman would be forbidden to both husbands), but the Gemara rejects this as inconsistent. Instead, the Gemara concludes that the Rabbis were lenient due to agunah (the woman's distress from being chained to a missing husband).

sub.desc_en: רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) proposes that the leniency of accepting one witness is justified by the stringency imposed on the woman at the end (if the husband returns), creating a balance.
The Gemara rejects Rabbi Zeira's reasoning, arguing that consistency would require either both stringency and leniency or neither, not one without the other.
The Gemara concludes that the Sages were lenient due to the distress of a deserted wife (עיגונא), accepting one witness to prevent her from being chained to a missing husband.

items.text: Rav's ruling on remarriage based on two witnesses
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on remarriage based on two witnesses
items.desc_en: Rav rules that the Mishnah's case of 'she shall leave this one and that one' applies only when she remarried based on one witness, but if based on two witnesses, she does not leave. The Gemara in the West questions this, and Rav's statement is clarified: the two witnesses did not know the husband's identity, but they testify that they were with him from when he left until now, and he changed appearance (like Joseph's brothers). The Gemara notes that this results in a tie between two sets of witnesses.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the Mishnah's case of 'she shall leave this one and that one' applies only when she remarried based on one witness, but if based on two witnesses, she does not leave.
The Gemara in the West objects: if the husband stands before us alive, how can Rav say she does not leave?
The Gemara clarifies that Rav's case is where the two witnesses do not know the husband's identity.
The Gemara asks: if the witnesses do not know the husband, why would she leave based on one witness?
The Gemara explains that the two witnesses testify they were with him from when he left until now, and he changed appearance (like Joseph's brothers, as Rav Chisda taught about the beard).
The Gemara notes that this results in a tie between two sets of witnesses (two saying he died, two saying he is alive).

items.text: Gemara's initial objection and Rav Sheshet's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection and Rav Sheshet's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the woman herself is in a state of uncertainty, and Rav Sheshet explains the case is when she married one of the witnesses, but the Gemara counters that she herself is still uncertain, so the case must be when she says 'it is clear to me'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the man who marries her is in a state of uncertain guilt (אשם תלוי).
Rav Sheshet explains that the case is when she married one of the witnesses, so the man is not in uncertainty.

items.text: Clarification of the dispute between Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei and the Sages
items.text_en: Clarification of the dispute between Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that even Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei only says she must leave when witnesses came before she married, but if she married first and then witnesses came, she does not leave. A baraita is cited detailing the dispute: two say 'died' and two say 'did not die' — she may not marry, but if she did, she does not leave; Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei says she leaves only if witnesses came first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the woman claims certainty, what is the novelty of the earlier statement?
The Gemara answers: even Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei only requires her to leave when witnesses came before she married, but if she married first, she does not leave.

A baraita is cited detailing the dispute: two say 'died' and two say 'did not die' — she may not marry, but if she did, she does not leave; Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei says she leaves only if witnesses came first.

items.text: Rav's ruling aligned with the Sages against Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei
items.text_en: Rav's ruling aligned with the Sages against Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rav's ruling is specifically when witnesses came before she married, to exclude Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei's opinion. An alternative version says that if she married first and then witnesses came, she does not leave, but if witnesses came first, she does leave, in accordance with Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rav's ruling also applies when witnesses came before marriage, to exclude Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yosei's position.
An alternative version states that Rav's leniency is only when she married before witnesses came, but if witnesses came first she must leave, aligning with Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Rava's objection from the law of a priest's wife
items.text_en: Rava's objection from the law of a priest's wife
items.desc_en: Rava raises an objection from a baraita that a priest's wife who remarried must leave her second husband even against his will, citing 'and you shall sanctify him'. The Gemara analyzes the case: if she did not marry a witness and does not claim certainty, it is obvious; rather, it must be that she married one of the witnesses and claims certainty, yet the baraita says she must leave, proving that she is taken from him.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises an objection from a baraita that a priest's wife who remarried must leave her second husband even against his will, citing the verse 'and you shall sanctify him'.
The Gemara questions the case: if she did not marry one of the witnesses and does not claim certainty, is it necessary to state that she is forced to leave?
The Gemara concludes that the case must be where she married one of the witnesses and claims certainty, yet the baraita says she must leave, proving that she is taken from him.

items.text: Three answers to Rava's objection
items.text_en: Three answers to Rava's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers three answers: the case of a priest's wife is different due to the stringency of priestly lineage; alternatively, 'let him force her' means with witnesses; or the case is when witnesses came before marriage and follows Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: the prohibition of priestly marriage is different (so the baraita does not apply to a regular woman).
Alternatively, the Gemara says: 'compel him' means compel him with witnesses (to divorce her, not to stay married).
Alternatively, the baraita refers to when witnesses came before marriage, and it follows Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yosei who says she must leave.

items.text: Rav Ashi's interpretation of Rav's 'does not leave'
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's interpretation of Rav's 'does not leave'
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that Rav's 'does not leave' means she does not leave her first husband's permission, i.e., she remains permitted to him. The Gemara notes that Rav already said this once regarding a mishna about a woman who married without permission, and it was stated as one of several rulings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that Rav's statement 'she does not leave' means she does not leave her first husband's permission, i.e., she remains permitted to him.
The Gemara notes that Rav already stated this ruling once regarding a mishna about a woman who married without permission, and it was stated as one of several rulings.

items.text: Shmuel's distinction and Ulla's principle applied to disqualified witnesses
items.text_en: Shmuel's distinction and Ulla's principle applied to disqualified witnesses
items.desc_en: Shmuel says the ruling that she does not leave applies only if she does not contradict the witness, but if she contradicts him, she does leave. The Gemara questions this: if there are two witnesses, contradiction is irrelevant; if one witness, why would silence matter? Ulla's principle that wherever the Torah believed one witness, here there are two, is cited. The Gemara resolves that the case involves disqualified witnesses, as per Rabbi Nechemiah who says to follow the majority of opinions, treating two women as two men.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel distinguishes the Mishnah's ruling: if she does not contradict the witness, she does not leave; if she contradicts him, she does leave.
The Gemara questions the case: if there are two witnesses, contradiction is irrelevant.
If it is one witness, why would silence matter? The Gemara implies that silence should not make her leave.
Ulla's principle is cited: wherever the Torah believed one witness, here there are two, and one witness's words cannot stand against two.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves disqualified witnesses, and cites Rabbi Nechemiah who says to follow the majority of opinions, treating two women as two men.

items.text: Alternative explanation with a single qualified witness and Rabbi Nechemiah's corrected version
items.text_en: Alternative explanation with a single qualified witness and Rabbi Nechemiah's corrected version
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation: if a single qualified witness came initially, even a hundred women are like one witness. The case is when a woman came initially. The Gemara then corrects Rabbi Nechemiah's statement: he said to follow the majority, treating two women regarding one woman as two men regarding one man, but two women regarding one man are considered equally divided.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: wherever a single qualified witness came initially, even a hundred women are considered like one witness.
The Gemara specifies that the case is where a woman came initially (as the first witness).

The Gemara corrects Rabbi Nechemiah's statement: he said to follow the majority, treating two women regarding one woman as two men regarding one man, but two women regarding one man are considered equally divided.

items.text: Question about requiring a get from the second husband and Rav Huna's decree
items.text_en: Question about requiring a get from the second husband and Rav Huna's decree
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a get is needed from both husbands; from the first is understandable, but from the second is mere promiscuity. Rav Huna says it is a decree lest people say 'this one divorced and that one married', and a married woman would leave without a get. The Gemara objects that in a similar case in the mishna where she married after being told her husband died and he returns, she may return to him, so why not fear the same?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a get is needed from the second husband, since the second marriage is merely promiscuity.
Rav Huna explains that the requirement for a get from the second husband is a decree lest people say 'this one divorced and that one married', and a married woman would leave without a get.
The Gemara objects that in a similar case in the mishna where she married after being told her husband died and he returns, she may return to him, so why not fear the same decree there?

items.text: Resolution with Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar's opinion
items.text_en: Resolution with Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that she always requires a get, but then the problem arises that this would be returning a divorced woman after betrothal. This is resolved according to Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar, who says that from marriage it is forbidden, but from betrothal it is permitted. The text cuts off mid-sentence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that she always requires a גט (bill of divorce) from the second husband.
The Gemara objects that this would mean the first husband is returning his divorced wife after she was betrothed to another, which is forbidden.

sub.text: Resolution according to Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar
sub.text_en: Resolution according to Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar, who holds that returning a divorced woman is forbidden only from marriage (נישואין) but permitted from betrothal (אירוסין).
The Gemara begins to note that the continuation of the Mishnah (סֵיפָא) supports this, but the text cuts off mid-sentence.

items.text: Distinction between first and second marriage in mistaken marriage
items.text_en: Distinction between first and second marriage in mistaken marriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the later husband's get does not disqualify her from kehunah if she needs a get, and answers that the second marriage was a mistake. It then asks why the first marriage is treated differently, and explains that the first involved a transgression so the rabbis penalized her, while the second did not.

items.text: Reason for no ketubah
items.text_en: Reason for no ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the woman has no ketubah: the ketubah was instituted to prevent a husband from easily divorcing his wife, but here she is already divorced.

items.text: No fruits, sustenance, or worn garments
items.text_en: No fruits, sustenance, or worn garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the woman also does not receive the benefits of the ketubah's conditions, as they are like the ketubah itself.

items.text: Taking from both husbands
items.text_en: Taking from both husbands
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that if she seized property from both, it is not taken from her, teaching that seizure is effective.

items.text: Comparison to terumah from impure on pure
items.text_en: Comparison to terumah from impure on pure
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares the child's status as a mamzer to the law of terumah from impure on pure, citing Rav Chisda and Rav Nathan bar Oshaya's dispute about whether the terumah is valid at all or only for the remainder. It then distinguishes between intentional and unintentional acts.

items.text: Contradiction between unintentional cases
items.text_en: Contradiction between unintentional cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two mishnayot about unintentional terumah: one says it is valid, the other says he must return and tithe again. It resolves that the latter case is close to intentional, as he should have tasted it.

items.text: Contradiction between intentional cases
items.text_en: Contradiction between intentional cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two mishnayot about intentional terumah: one says it is invalid, the other says he must return and tithe again. It resolves that the latter case involves two vessels where the sound is heard, unlike one vessel.

items.text: Rav Nathan bar Oshaya's view on terumah
items.text_en: Rav Nathan bar Oshaya's view on terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rav Nathan bar Oshaya, who says the terumah is valid for the remainder, the intentional case would still be problematic.

items.text: Distinguishing the case from the Mishnah of terumah from defective produce
items.text_en: Distinguishing the case from the Mishnah of terumah from defective produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the case of a husband who remarries his ex-wife is different from the Mishnah where one separates terumah from defective produce for good produce, where the terumah is valid but cannot be eaten until additional terumah and ma'aser are separated. It answers that here, the terumah is actually valid on a Torah level, as derived from Rabbi Il'ai's teaching that terumah from bad for good is valid.

items.text: Rabbah's challenge to Rav Chisda's position
items.text_en: Rabbah's challenge to Rav Chisda's position
items.desc_en: Rabbah challenges Rav Chisda, who holds that the husband's action is entirely void and even the se'ah of produce returns to its untithed state. Rabbah asks: since the terumah is valid on a Torah level, how can the rabbis uproot it due to a concern that he might neglect to separate? Can a court uproot a Torah law?

items.text: Rav Chisda's counterexample: the child from a woman who remarried after her husband's death
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's counterexample: the child from a woman who remarried after her husband's death
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda responds by citing a Mishnah where a child from a woman who remarried after her husband's death is a mamzer from both husbands. He questions why the child is a mamzer from the first husband, since the first husband was permitted to her. The Gemara answers that Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan say the first husband is forbidden to marry a mamzeret, and the term 'mamzer' is used to prohibit him from marrying a Jewish woman.

items.text: Rav Chisda's proof from the inheritance of a minor wife
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's proof from the inheritance of a minor wife
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda sends a message to Rabbah via Rav Acha bar Rav Huna, citing a baraita where Beit Shammai, Beit Hillel, and Rabbi Eliezer debate when a husband inherits his minor wife. The baraita states that the husband inherits her, becomes impure for her, and she eats terumah on his account. The Gemara notes that Torah law gives inheritance to the father, yet the rabbis give it to the husband, proving the principle of 'hefker beit din hefker.' Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Elazar provide scriptural sources for this principle.

items.text: Addressing the impurity for a minor wife as a met mitzvah
items.text_en: Addressing the impurity for a minor wife as a met mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the husband can become impure for his minor wife, since Torah law requires the father to become impure. It answers that this is because she is a met mitzvah (a corpse with no one to bury it). The Gemara then questions whether she qualifies as a met mitzvah, citing a baraita that a met mitzvah is one with no buriers. Since her relatives do not inherit her, they do not respond to her call, making her a met mitzvah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah reference and initial question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah reference and initial question
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about one who eats impure terumah and pays with pure hullin, and then discusses the dispute between Sumchos in the name of Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding whether payment with impure hullin is valid.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Mishnah and baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Mishnah and baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing a Mishnah about eating impure terumah and then brings a baraita with the dispute between Sumchos in the name of Rabbi Meir and the Sages about payment with impure hullin.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's statement about eating terumah refers to rabbinic terumah.
The Gemara attempts to prove the claim by saying 'Come and hear' a baraita.

items.text: Gemara's question on Sumchos' ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Sumchos' ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Sumchos' statement that in the case of intentional violation the payment is not valid, arguing that the one who ate impure terumah benefits by paying with something he could have eaten during his impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Sumchos says that intentional payment with impure produce is invalid, noting that the payer actually benefits the priest by giving him something usable during his impurity.

items.text: Rava's correction of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rava's correction of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava (or some say Kedi) explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause: it first discusses one who ate impure terumah and pays any amount, then one who ate pure terumah and pays with pure hullin, and then the dispute about paying with impure hullin.

sub.desc_en: Rava corrects the baraita, teaching that it originally distinguished between eating impure terumah (pays any amount), eating pure terumah (pays pure hullin), and the dispute over paying with impure hullin.

items.text: Gemara's objection: Torah law vs. rabbinic decree
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: Torah law vs. rabbinic decree
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to Torah law, the payment with impure hullin is valid (since a kohen can betroth a woman with them), yet Rabbi Meir says the payment is not valid, effectively tying a married woman to the world (i.e., creating a prohibition).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to Torah law, payment with impure hullin is valid (a kohen can betroth a woman with them), yet the Rabbis say it is not payment, effectively tying a married woman to the world.

items.text: Resolution: the meaning of 'no payment' and the distinction between intentional and unintentional
items.text_en: Resolution: the meaning of 'no payment' and the distinction between intentional and unintentional
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir's 'no payment' means he must repay with pure hullin, but this would make Sumchos identical to the Sages. Rav Acha bar Rav Ika resolves that the difference is that the Sages penalize the intentional violator but not the unintentional one, while Rabbi Meir penalizes both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Meir means by 'no payment', and objects that if it means he must repay with pure hullin, then Sumchos's view would be identical to the Sages.
Rav Acha bar Rav Ika resolves that the difference between Sumchos and the Sages is whether they penalize the unwitting violator due to the intentional violator.

items.text: Second case: blood that became impure
items.text_en: Second case: blood that became impure
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a second case: blood that became impure and was sprinkled, where if done unintentionally it is accepted, but if intentionally it is not accepted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about blood that became impure and was sprinkled: if done unwittingly it is accepted, if intentionally it is not accepted.

items.text: Objection: the Tzitz atones even for intentional impurity
items.text_en: Objection: the Tzitz atones even for intentional impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to Torah law, the Tzitz atones for impure blood even when intentionally offered, yet the Sages say it is not accepted, and this would cause hullin to be brought into the Temple courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to Torah law the Tzitz atones for impure blood even when intentionally offered, yet the Sages say it is not accepted, which would cause hullin to be brought into the Temple courtyard.

items.text: Resolution: 'not accepted' means only regarding eating the meat
items.text_en: Resolution: 'not accepted' means only regarding eating the meat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina explains that 'not accepted' means only that the meat is not permitted for consumption, but the owners achieve atonement. The Gemara objects that this undermines the requirement for priests to eat the meat for atonement, and the answer is that the case is different (since it is a rabbinic decree).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina explains that the statement 'the offering is not accepted' means only regarding permitting the meat for consumption, but the owners do attain atonement.
The Gemara objects that the requirement for priests to eat the meat for atonement is still uprooted, citing the verse that the priests eat and the owners are atoned.
The answer distinguishes the case of 'sit and refrain from action' (שב ואל תעשה), where the sages can uproot a positive Torah command by inaction.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: all cases are passive violations
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: all cases are passive violations
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier distinction between active and passive violations by listing several cases (uncircumcised man performing sprinkling, a linen garment with tzitzit, etc.) that are all passive (שב ואל תעשה) and thus should be permitted if the court can uproot a Torah law passively.
