sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier distinction by listing cases (uncircumcised man performing sprinkling, a linen garment with tzitzit, etc.) that are all passive violations (שב ואל תעשה) and thus should be permitted if the court can uproot a Torah law passively.

items.text: Proof from Elijah on Mount Carmel and distinction
items.text_en: Proof from Elijah on Mount Carmel and distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from the verse 'אליו תשמעון' that one must obey a prophet even to violate a Torah commandment temporarily, as Elijah did. It distinguishes this case as a 'fence' (מיגדר מילתא) rather than a general principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one must listen to a prophet even if he says to violate a mitzvah temporarily, as with Elijah on Mount Carmel, but distinguishes that case as a temporary fence (מיגדר מילתא).
The Gemara distinguishes this case as a 'fence' (מיגדר מילתא) rather than a general principle, because the verse explicitly commands obedience to a prophet.

items.text: Court's power to annul a get and the principle of 'כוח בית דין יפה'
items.text_en: Court's power to annul a get and the principle of 'כוח בית דין יפה'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where a court annuls a get, permitting the woman to remarry even though the get is valid by Torah law. Ravina asks Rav Ashi about betrothal through intercourse, and the answer is that the rabbis make such intercourse into licentiousness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about annulling a get (bill of divorce) where the court's power (מה כח בית דין) permits a married woman to remarry, and discusses the case of betrothal by intercourse (ביאה) where the rabbis retroactively make the intercourse an act of licentiousness (בעילת זנות).
The Gemara questions how the court can permit a married woman to remarry based on the principle of 'מה כח בית דין יפה' (the power of the court is great), given that the get is valid by Torah law.
The answer explains that one who betroths a woman does so on condition of rabbinic approval, and the rabbis retroactively annul the betrothal.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if the betrothal was through intercourse (ביאה) rather than money, how can the rabbis annul it?
Rav Ashi answers that the rabbis render his intercourse an act of licentiousness (זנות), thereby retroactively invalidating the betrothal.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov's testimony on emergency court actions
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov's testimony on emergency court actions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov testifies that courts may punish beyond Torah law for the sake of a fence, citing cases of a man riding on Shabbat and a man having relations with his wife under a fig tree. The Gemara again distinguishes these as 'מיגדר מילתא'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita from Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov that a court may punish beyond Torah law as a fence (סייג), with examples of a man riding a horse on Shabbat and a man having intercourse with his wife under a fig tree, but distinguishes these as temporary measures (מיגדר מילתא).

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov's testimony (second case)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov's testimony (second case)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov adds a second case of a man who had relations with his wife under a fig tree and was flogged.
The Gemara distinguishes these cases as 'מיגדר מילתא' (a fence-making measure), which is exceptional and not a general precedent.

items.text: Source that a kohen does not become impure for his disqualified wife
items.text_en: Source that a kohen does not become impure for his disqualified wife
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from verses that a kohen may become impure for his kosher wife but not for his disqualified wife, explaining the mishnah's ruling that neither husband nor ex-husband defiles her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that neither the husband who divorces nor the one who remarries her may become impure for her, deriving from the verse 'כי אם לשארו' (only to his close relative) that a priest may become impure only for his kosher wife, not for a disqualified one.
The Gemara cites the verse 'כי אם לשארו הקרוב אליו' (for his close relative) and the teaching of Mar that 'שארו' refers to his wife.
The Gemara cites another verse 'לא יטמא בעל בעמיו להחלו' and deduces that a kohen may become impure for his kosher wife but not for his disqualified wife.

items.text: Reasons for the mishnah's rulings on found property, earnings, and vows
items.text_en: Reasons for the mishnah's rulings on found property, earnings, and vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why neither husband acquires her found property or earnings, and neither can annul her vows: the usual reasons (avoiding enmity, supporting her, preventing disgrace) do not apply here, and in fact the opposite is true.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah rules that neither husband acquires her found property, and notes the usual reason for a husband acquiring found property is to avoid enmity (איבה).

The Gemara answers that here, since the husband does not support her, the usual reasons (avoiding enmity, supporting her) do not apply, and in fact the opposite is true: he would have enmity, and since she does not receive sustenance, her earnings are not his.

The Gemara explains that the husband cannot annul her vows because the Torah gave the husband the power to annul vows to prevent her from being disgraced, but here she would be disgraced anyway, so the power does not apply.

items.text: Mishnah's continuation: daughter of Israel disqualified from priesthood
items.text_en: Mishnah's continuation: daughter of Israel disqualified from priesthood
items.desc_en: The segment introduces the next clause of the mishnah: if the woman was a bat Yisrael, she is disqualified from marrying a kohen.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah continues with the case of a daughter of Israel who becomes disqualified from the priesthood.

items.text: Penalty for a Levite woman who ate tithe after forbidden relations
items.text_en: Penalty for a Levite woman who ate tithe after forbidden relations
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a Levite woman who engaged in forbidden relations is disqualified from eating tithe, citing a baraita that she may still eat. Rav Sheshet explains that the disqualification is a penalty (קנסא).

items.text: Penalty for a priest's daughter and inheritance of ketubah
items.text_en: Penalty for a priest's daughter and inheritance of ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses that a priest's daughter is penalized even regarding rabbinic terumah. It then clarifies that the ketubah mentioned in the mishnah refers to the ketubah of sons (כתובת בנין דיכרין), and explains that the penalty applies only to her, not to her children.

items.text: Levirate marriage and chalitzah for brothers of both husbands
items.text_en: Levirate marriage and chalitzah for brothers of both husbands
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that the brothers of each husband perform chalitzah but not yibbum. The Gemara explains the reasoning: the brother of the first husband performs chalitzah by Torah law and refrains from yibbum by rabbinic law; the brother of the second husband performs chalitzah by rabbinic law and refrains from yibbum entirely.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Elazar on penalties
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Elazar on penalties
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a series of disputes: Rav Huna states that later authorities concede to earlier ones but not vice versa. Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar disagree about whether a penalty applies to the woman's found property and earnings versus forbidden relations. Both concede to Rabbi Yosei regarding property she holds during his lifetime. Rabbi Yochanan reverses the concession pattern, and further debates ensue about the scope of penalties.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling and Rav Nachman's objection
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling and Rav Nachman's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Huna quotes Rav that the halakha follows the mishnah. Rav Nachman criticizes him for being indirect, suggesting he should explicitly state that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon in the latter clause. The Gemara notes a difficulty with this formulation.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's challenge and resolution regarding the need for a get
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's challenge and resolution regarding the need for a get
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet questions the need for a get if the woman was forced, citing a baraita that only a woman who remarried based on a court ruling needs a get, not one based on witnesses. The Gemara initially assumes this baraita follows the Rabbis, but then reinterprets it according to Rabbi Shimon, distinguishing between intentional and unintentional acts. Rav Ashi explains that the baraita deals with prohibition, not the need for a get.

items.text: Ravina's distinction between court and witness error
items.text_en: Ravina's distinction between court and witness error
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the Mishnah's case is about a korban: if the court erred in their ruling, it is like intentional sin and no korban is brought; if based on witnesses, it is like an unintentional sin and a korban is brought.

sub.desc_en: Ravina explains that the Mishnah's case is about a korban: if the court erred in their ruling, it is like intentional sin and no korban is brought; if based on witnesses, it is like an unintentional sin and a korban is brought.

items.text: Alternative explanation: the first Mishnah is Rabbanan
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: the first Mishnah is Rabbanan
items.desc_en: An alternative answer is offered: the first Mishnah follows the Rabbanan, and should be resolved by saying 'except for a married woman who remarried based on a court ruling'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the first Mishnah follows the Rabbanan, and the resolution is that the exception is a married woman who remarried based on a court ruling.

items.text: Ulla's objection from a mishna about a get with improper dating
items.text_en: Ulla's objection from a mishna about a get with improper dating
items.desc_en: Ulla challenges the principle 'what could she have done?' by citing a mishna where a get written with improper dating (e.g., for an inappropriate kingdom) renders the woman a 'yotzei mi-zeh u-mi-zeh' and all the ways are upon her, even though she could have had the get read to her.

sub.desc_en: Ulla challenges the principle 'what could she have done?' by citing a mishna about a get written with improper dating, which penalizes the woman despite her possible oversight.

The gemara notes that the mishna declares the woman a 'yotzei mi-zeh u-mi-zeh' and asks why the principle 'what could she have done?' does not apply, answering that she could have had the get read to her.

items.text: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's objection from a yevama who was an aylonit
items.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's objection from a yevama who was an aylonit
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi brings a baraita: if a man married his yevama and her rival wife remarried, and the yevama turned out to be an aylonit, the rival wife must leave both husbands and all the ways are upon her, even though she could have waited.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects by citing a baraita: if a man married his yevama and her rival wife remarried, and the yevama turned out to be an aylonit, the rival wife must leave both husbands and all the ways are upon her, even though she could have waited.

items.text: Abaye's objection from all arayot who are ayloniyot
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from all arayot who are ayloniyot
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita: all arayot who exempt their rival wives, if the rival wives remarried and the arayot turned out to be ayloniyot, the rival wives must leave both husbands and all the ways are upon them, even though they could have waited.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita: all arayot who exempt their rival wives, if the rival wives remarried and the arayot turned out to be ayloniyot, the rival wives must leave both husbands and all the ways are upon them, even though they could have waited.

items.text: Rava's objection from a scribe's error with get and shover
items.text_en: Rava's objection from a scribe's error with get and shover
items.desc_en: Rava brings a baraita: if a scribe wrote a get for the husband and a receipt for the wife, and mistakenly gave the get to the wife and the receipt to the husband, and they exchanged them, and later the get emerges from the husband's hand and the receipt from the wife's, she must leave both and all the ways are upon her, even though she could have had the get read.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita where a scribe mistakenly exchanged a get and a receipt, and the woman is penalized despite her claim of ignorance.
Rava asks why the woman is penalized, since she could have had the get read to her to discover the error.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection from changed names
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection from changed names
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites a baraita: if the names of the husband and wife or their cities were changed, the woman must leave both husbands and all the ways are upon her, even though she could have had the get read.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites a baraita about changed names to object to the principle of 'what could she have done'.

items.text: Ravina's objection from a get kere'ach
items.text_en: Ravina's objection from a get kere'ach
items.desc_en: Ravina brings a baraita: if a man married her with a get kere'ach, she must leave both husbands etc., and she could have had the get read.

sub.desc_en: Ravina cites a baraita about a woman married with a get kere'ach (a defective get) who must leave both husbands, arguing that she could have had the get read and thus should have known.

items.text: Rav Pappa's attempted ruling and Rav Huna's objection
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's attempted ruling and Rav Huna's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa was about to rule based on the principle 'what could she have done?' but Rav Huna bar Yehoshua told him that all these baraitot are taught. Rav Pappa replied that they were resolved (shinninhu), but Rav Huna asked if one can rely on such resolutions, and the matter was decided (u-fasak).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa intended to rule based on the principle 'what could she have done?'.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objected that all these baraitot are taught (contradicting the principle).
Rav Pappa replied that they (the baraitot) were resolved (shinninhu).
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua asked whether one can rely on such resolutions.
The matter was decided (u-fasak) — the principle was rejected.

items.text: Rav Ashi's ruling: we do not worry about a rumor
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's ruling: we do not worry about a rumor
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that we do not worry about a rumor (kala). The Gemara asks which rumor, and suggests it is a rumor after marriage, but Rav Ashi already said that once.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that we do not worry about a rumor (קלא).
The Gemara asks which rumor is being referred to.
The Gemara suggests it is a rumor after marriage, but notes that Rav Ashi already stated this once before.

items.text: Gemara's question about the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a rumor that arises after marriage should be disregarded, and suggests that if the court already permitted her, it might be considered like a pre-marriage rumor and thus forbid her. The Gemara concludes that it is not a concern.

items.text: Dispute between Ze'iri and Rav Nachman about the nature of the court's ruling
items.text_en: Dispute between Ze'iri and Rav Nachman about the nature of the court's ruling
items.desc_en: Ze'iri argues that the Mishnah's case is not a formal ruling but an error, based on a baraita about the sun setting and rising. Rav Nachman counters that it is a ruling, citing the fact that a single witness is believed here. Rava objects, comparing it to a court that permits forbidden fats and then retracts, showing it is an error.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's view and the Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's view and the Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Eliezer also considers it an error, as he says the woman must bring a sin offering. The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer might hold that an individual who acts on a court's ruling is liable, but then asks why he would say 'let the law pierce the mountain'.

items.text: Dispute about the meaning of 'kilkela' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Dispute about the meaning of 'kilkela' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says 'kilkela' means she committed adultery, while Rabbi Yochanan says it means she married a forbidden relative like a widow to a High Priest. The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yochanan, adultery is excluded because she can claim the court made her available.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan and dispute about liability
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan and dispute about liability
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan, stating that if a woman remarries based on a court ruling and then violates a prohibition, she is liable for a sacrifice for each act. Rabbi Elazar holds she is liable for each act, while the Sages say one sacrifice covers all, but they agree that if she married multiple men, she is liable for each.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of mistaken reports about husband and son
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of mistaken reports about husband and son
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a woman is told her husband and son died in different orders, leading to remarriage or yibbum, and later the report is reversed. The rulings specify when she must leave and whether the children are mamzerim. It also discusses a case where she remarries and then the husband returns, and the status of her children.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah and dispute about mamzer status
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah and dispute about mamzer status
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'first' and 'last' refer to, and explains that the Mishnah's phrasing is due to the later clause. It then cites a baraita where Rabbi Akiva holds that a child from a yevama is a mamzer, while the Sages say there is no mamzer from a yevama. The Gemara identifies the Tanna as one who distinguishes between different types of negative commandments.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's dispute on yevamah betrothal
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's dispute on yevamah betrothal
items.desc_en: Rav states that betrothal does not take effect on a yevamah, citing the verse 'lo tihyeh eshet hamet hachutza l'ish zar'. Shmuel is uncertain whether the verse teaches a prohibition or that betrothal does not take effect, and therefore requires a get.

items.text: Halakha like Shmuel and its practical consequence
items.text_en: Halakha like Shmuel and its practical consequence
items.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rachel reports to Rav Ashi that Ameimar ruled the halakha follows Shmuel. Rav Ashi then deduces that if the yavam is a kohen, he must perform chalitzah and then she is permitted to him; but an objection is raised that this would make a sinner profit, so instead if the yavam is an Israelite, he gives her a second get and she is permitted to him.

items.text: Rav's statement on betrothal vs. marriage in yevamah
items.text_en: Rav's statement on betrothal vs. marriage in yevamah
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel quotes Rav Chiyya bar Yosef quoting Rav: a yevamah has no betrothal but has marriage. The Gemara questions this, then offers two resolutions: either 'marriage' refers to illicit relations (as per Rav Hamnuna), or it refers to a case where she is mistaken for a woman whose husband went overseas.

items.text: Rabbi Yannai's ruling and Rabbi Yochanan's comment
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai's ruling and Rabbi Yochanan's comment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai reports that a group voted and concluded that betrothal does not take effect on a yevamah. Rabbi Yochanan asks if this is not already taught in a Mishnah about conditional betrothal after chalitzah. Rabbi Yannai responds that without Rabbi Yochanan's insight, one would not find the pearl beneath the potsherd.

items.text: Reish Lakish's objection and the Mishnah's attribution
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's objection and the Mishnah's attribution
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish tells Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that betrothal does not take effect for those liable for negative commandments. The Gemara then objects: if it is Rabbi Akiva, why does the Mishnah say betrothal after chalitzah does not take effect, since Rabbi Akiva holds that one can acquire something not yet in the world?

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about annulling a vow
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about annulling a vow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a woman vows that her hands are dedicated to their maker. The first opinion holds that the husband need not annul such a vow, while Rabbi Akiva argues that he must annul it, lest she produce more than is fitting for him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first opinion: a woman who vows 'konam that I do for your mouth' does not require her husband to annul the vow.
Rabbi Akiva argues that the husband must annul the vow, lest she produce more than is fitting for him.

items.text: Gemara's explanation: The vow refers to hands
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation: The vow refers to hands
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explains that the Mishnah's case is where the woman says 'my hands are consecrated to their maker,' since hands exist in the world. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak disputes this, linking Rav Huna's view through a chain of authorities back to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that one can transfer ownership of something not yet in the world.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explains that the Mishnah's case is where the woman says 'my hands are consecrated to their maker,' since hands exist in the world.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak disputes Rav Huna's view, tracing it through a chain of authorities back to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that one can transfer ownership of something not yet in the world.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on selling future produce
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on selling future produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies Rav Huna's position: one who sells dates from a palm tree before they have grown can retract before they come into the world, but cannot retract after they appear. Rav Nachman disagrees, holding that even after they appear the seller can retract, though if the buyer consumes them the court does not extract payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the case of Rav Huna's ruling that is being referenced?
Rav Huna rules that one who sells future dates from a palm tree can retract before they appear, but cannot retract after they come into the world.
Rav Nachman disagrees, holding that even after the dates appear the seller can retract.
Rav Nachman qualifies that if the buyer consumes the dates, the court does not extract payment from him.

items.text: Rav's ruling: Acquisition of a future field
items.text_en: Rav's ruling: Acquisition of a future field
items.desc_en: Rav Huna citing Rav rules that if one says to another, 'This field that I will purchase, when I purchase it, it is acquired by you from now,' the buyer acquires it immediately.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna reports in Rav's name that if one says to another, 'This field that I will purchase, when I purchase it, it is acquired by you from now,' the buyer acquires it immediately.

items.text: Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Chiyya: Tithing from produce not yet tithed
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Chiyya: Tithing from produce not yet tithed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai had a tenant who brought him a basket of produce every Friday. One Friday the tenant was late, so Rabbi Yannai took ten pieces from his own produce to cover the tithe. Rabbi Chiyya approved, citing a verse about learning to fear God on Shabbat and festivals, and questioning whether a verse is needed to permit rabbinic handling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Yannai had a tenant who brought him a basket of produce every Friday; one Friday the tenant was late, so Rabbi Yannai took ten pieces from his own produce to cover the tithe, and then came before Rabbi Chiyya.

Rabbi Chiyya approved Rabbi Yannai's action, citing a baraita that interprets the verse 'לְמַעַן תִּלְמַד לְיִרְאָה אֶת ה׳' (to learn to fear God) as referring to Shabbatot and festivals, and rhetorically questions whether a verse is needed to permit rabbinic handling (טִלְטוּל דְּרַבָּנַן).

items.text: Opening anecdote about a dream
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about a dream
items.desc_en: A brief exchange about a dream involving a 'bruised reed' (קנה רצוץ), interpreted as either a rebuke or a promise of mercy.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks whether the dream of a 'bruised reed' (קנה רצוץ) is a rebuke, citing the verse about trusting in a broken reed.
The gemara answers that the dream is actually a promise of mercy, citing the verse that God will not break a bruised reed or extinguish a dim wick.

items.text: Supporting sources for delayed effect (ברירה)
items.text_en: Supporting sources for delayed effect (ברירה)
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites four Tannaitic opinions (Rabbi, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, Rabbi Akiva) that support the concept of a conditional act taking effect retroactively or upon fulfillment of a condition, relevant to the earlier discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi cites a baraita on the verse 'לֹא תַסְגִּיר עֶבֶד' (do not hand over a slave), interpreting it as referring to a buyer who purchases a slave conditionally to free him, with Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explaining the formula: 'when I acquire you, you are retroactively your own from now.'
Rabbi Meir holds that a conditional betrothal (קידושין) — e.g., 'you are betrothed to me after I convert' — is valid, supporting the concept of retroactive effect (ברירה).

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules that a conditional designation of תרומה (priestly portion) from detached to attached produce, contingent on the attached reaching a third of growth and being detached, takes effect retroactively.
Rabbi Akiva rules that a husband must annul (יָפֵר) his wife's vow of 'קונם' (a form of vow) because she might have added more than is proper, implying a conditional effect.

items.text: Question about a single witness in yibbum
items.text_en: Question about a single witness in yibbum
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a single witness is believed in yibbum (to permit the yevamah to marry another), based on two possible rationales for why a single witness is believed in other cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav Sheishet whether a single witness is believed in yibbum, presenting two possible rationales for why a single witness is believed in other cases and questioning which applies here.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's proof from a Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's proof from a Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a Mishnah where contradictory pairs of witnesses cause the woman to leave and the child to be a mamzer, implying that a single witness is believed unless contradicted by two.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a Mishnah where witnesses tell a woman her son died then her husband died, and she entered yibbum, but later reversed testimony.
The Gemara objects that the child should be a safek mamzer (doubtful mamzer), but the Mishnah's precise language shows it is definite.
Rav Sheshet concludes that the Mishnah refers to a single witness, who is believed unless contradicted by two.

items.text: Refined question: permitting the yevamah to the public
items.text_en: Refined question: permitting the yevamah to the public
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the question is not about the woman herself (who is believed), but about permitting the yevamah to marry anyone, and restates the two possible rationales.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara refines the question: the woman herself is believed based on the Mishnah, so the question is about permitting the yevamah to marry anyone.

The Gemara restates the two possible rationales for the credibility of a single witness: either because a matter destined to be revealed is not lied about, or because the woman investigates carefully before marrying, and here she does not investigate because she is repulsive to him.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's case of contradictory testimony
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's case of contradictory testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a child is a definite mamzer when two pairs of witnesses contradict each other. It suggests that the case must involve witnesses who were later found to be conspiring (edim zomemim), not just contradicting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case: if two pairs of witnesses contradict each other, why rely on one pair? The child should only be a doubtful mamzer (ספק ממזר), not a definite one.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the Mishnah is imprecise, because the later clause distinguishes between first and last child, showing precision.

The Gemara resolves: the case involves one witness contradicted by two, and the child is a definite mamzer because the two witnesses are later found to be conspiring (עדי הזמה), not merely contradicting.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's case is also about conspiring witnesses (עדי הזמה), applying Rav Acha bar Minyomi's principle.

items.text: Proof from a baraita about a woman's testimony
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about a woman's testimony
items.desc_en: Rav Mordechai and Rav Acha bring a baraita to prove that a single witness is believed for a yevama. The Gemara distinguishes between a woman's own testimony (not believed) and a single witness (believed), and explains that the baraita was necessary for Rabbi Akiva's view.

sub.text: Rav Mordechai and Rav Acha to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Mordechai and Rav Acha to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai and Rav Acha bring a baraita to Rav Ashi as proof that a single witness is believed for a yevama, since the baraita says the woman herself is not believed but a single witness is.

The Gemara objects: if the baraita's logic were simple, the same inference would apply to a man's testimony about his brother's death, but there is no leniency of עיגונא (agunah distress) for a man, so the baraita must be explained differently.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita was necessary only for Rabbi Akiva's view, who holds that a woman would worry about her offspring's status (ממזר) and thus be careful, so the baraita teaches she only worries about her own disgrace, not her offspring's.

items.text: Rava's kal vachomer argument and its refutation
items.text_en: Rava's kal vachomer argument and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rava argues that a single witness should be believed for a yevama through a kal vachomer: if a witness is believed for a prohibition punishable by karet, certainly for a mere negative prohibition. A rabbi refutes this by pointing out that the woman herself is not believed for a negative prohibition despite being believed for karet, showing the kal vachomer is flawed.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens with a kal vachomer argument: if a single witness is believed for a prohibition punishable by karet (the yevama's original prohibition), then certainly for a mere negative prohibition (the yevama's prohibition to marry a stranger).

sub.text: A certain rabbi's objection to Rava
sub.text_en: A certain rabbi's objection to Rava
sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi objects: the woman herself disproves the kal vachomer, because she is believed for a karet prohibition but not for a negative prohibition, showing the kal vachomer is invalid.

The Gemara explains the distinction: the woman herself is not believed because she might hate the yavam and not investigate carefully (לא דייק), but a single witness has no such bias, so the kal vachomer stands refuted.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Matya's midrash and Rav Yehuda's critique
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Matya's midrash and Rav Yehuda's critique
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav criticizing Rabbi Elazar ben Matya for missing a precious interpretation (margalita) and instead teaching a worthless one (chaspah). The precious interpretation is that the verse 'a woman divorced from her husband' implies even a mere rumor of divorce (rei'ach ha-get) disqualifies a woman from kehuna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah's reference to Rabbi Elazar ben Matya's midrash.
Rav Yehuda reports that Rav criticized Rabbi Elazar ben Matya for missing a precious interpretation (מרגניתא) and teaching a worthless one (חספא).
The Gemara explains the precious interpretation: the verse 'a woman divorced from her husband' teaches that even a mere rumor of divorce (ריח הגט) disqualifies a woman from kehuna.

items.text: Opening Mishnah of the next chapter
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah of the next chapter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case: a man whose wife went overseas, was told she died, married her sister, and then his wife returns. The Mishnah rules that the wife is permitted to return to him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a case: a man whose wife went overseas, was told she died, married her sister, and then his wife returns — she is permitted to return to him.

items.text: Mishnah: Case of marrying sister after wife's reported death
items.text_en: Mishnah: Case of marrying sister after wife's reported death
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a man married his wife's sister after being told his wife died, then later learned the wife was alive but died later. The first child is a mamzer, the second is not. Rabbi Yosei adds a principle about who is disqualified.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule that one is permitted to marry the relatives of the second wife, and the second wife is permitted to marry his relatives; if the first wife dies, he is permitted to the second.

The Mishnah presents a case where witnesses reported the wife's death, the man married her sister, and later it was discovered the wife was alive but then died; the first child is a mamzer (ממזר, illegitimate child) and the second is not.
Rabbi Yosei adds a general principle: one who disqualifies others through his actions also disqualifies himself, and one who does not disqualify others does not disqualify himself.

items.text: Gemara's question: Does this Mishnah reject Rabbi Akiva?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does this Mishnah reject Rabbi Akiva?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that even though the wife and brother-in-law went overseas, the sister-in-law is forbidden but the wife is permitted. It suggests this Mishnah might not follow Rabbi Akiva, who requires a get for a sister-in-law, making her a rival wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara observes that even though the wife and brother-in-law went overseas, the sister-in-law is forbidden but the wife is permitted.
The Gemara questions whether this Mishnah rejects Rabbi Akiva's position.
A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi Akiva requires a get for a sister-in-law, making her a rival wife.

items.text: Rav's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's cases
items.text_en: Rav's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's cases
items.desc_en: Rav explains that Rabbi Akiva's cases involve betrothal, not marriage, where people assume there was a condition. The Gemara questions whether such a condition can apply to marriage.

sub.text: Rav Giddel citing Rav Chiyya bar Yosef citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Giddel citing Rav Chiyya bar Yosef citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav explains that Rabbi Akiva's case of אשת אח (a brother's wife) involves a situation where the brother betrothed a woman and went overseas, and the other brother married her upon hearing of his death, because people assume the first betrothal had a condition.
The Gemara questions whether such a conditional assumption can apply to marriage (נישואין) as opposed to betrothal (קידושין).

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection: Why not include mother-in-law?
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection: Why not include mother-in-law?
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks that if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva, it should also include the case of a mother-in-law, since Rabbi Akiva exempts her from burning after death.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva, it should also include the case of a mother-in-law (חמותו), since Rabbi Akiva exempts her from burning after death.

sub.text: Supporting baraita on Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita on Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva dispute the interpretation of the verse 'באש ישרפו אותו ואתהן' (they shall burn him and them), with Rabbi Akiva ruling that both women are burned, implying the mother-in-law is exempt from burning after death.

items.text: Resolution: Mother-in-law is forbidden even if not burned
items.text_en: Resolution: Mother-in-law is forbidden even if not burned
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rava, the dispute is about burning after death, but the prohibition remains. The Gemara concludes that the case of a wife who went overseas is different because the prohibition is only rabbinic in cases of error.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Abaye, the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is about interpreting the verse as one or two burnings, which works well.
The Gemara objects that according to Rava, the dispute is about the mother-in-law after death, so the Mishnah should also list the mother-in-law.
Rav Ashi answers that although the verse excludes the mother-in-law from burning, it does not exclude her from the prohibition.
The Gemara resolves that the case of a wife who went overseas is different because the prohibition is only rabbinic in cases of error, unlike the mother-in-law.

items.text: Opening statement: sister of a wife is not prohibited by Torah
items.text_en: Opening statement: sister of a wife is not prohibited by Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a sister of a wife is not prohibited by Torah law even intentionally, and certainly the Sages did not decree a prohibition for an unwitting act. It cites a baraita deriving from 'אותה' that only her own sexual intercourse prohibits her, not that of her sister.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a sister of a wife is not prohibited by Torah law even intentionally, and the Sages did not decree a prohibition for an unwitting act.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the word 'אותה' (her) that only her own sexual intercourse prohibits her, not that of her sister.

items.text: Kal vachomer argument for prohibiting the wife
items.text_en: Kal vachomer argument for prohibiting the wife
items.desc_en: A logical argument is proposed: if in a case of a light prohibition the one who causes the prohibition becomes forbidden, then in a case of a severe prohibition (like a sister of a wife) the one who causes the prohibition should certainly be forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if a light prohibition causes the one who triggers it to become forbidden, then a severe prohibition (like a sister of a wife) should certainly cause the one who triggers it to become forbidden.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei about the cases
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei about the cases
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that one who has relations with his mother-in-law disqualifies his wife, but disagree about the sister of his wife. Rabbi Yosei reverses the positions: they agree that the sister does not disqualify, but disagree about the mother-in-law.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that one who has relations with his mother-in-law disqualifies his wife, and they disagree only about the sister of his wife.
Rabbi Yosei reverses the positions: they agree that the sister does not disqualify, but disagree about the mother-in-law.

items.text: Explanation of the kal vachomer and derivation for intentional acts
items.text_en: Explanation of the kal vachomer and derivation for intentional acts
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the logic: initially each is permitted to all, but marriage creates mutual prohibitions. A kal vachomer shows that if a woman who is forbidden to all men does not become forbidden to her husband when she errs with a forbidden man, then certainly a man who only forbids himself to her relatives should not be forbidden to his wife when he errs. For intentional acts, the verse 'אותה' teaches the same.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the initial state of mutual permissibility and how marriage creates asymmetric prohibitions: the husband forbids his wife to all men, while she only forbids him to her relatives.

The Gemara poses a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if a woman who is forbidden to all men does not become forbidden to her husband when she errs with a forbidden man, then certainly a man who only forbids himself to her relatives should not be forbidden to his wife when he errs.

The Gemara resolves that the kal vachomer applies to unintentional acts (שוגג), and for intentional acts (מזיד) it derives from the verse 'אותה' that only her own sexual relations forbid her, not relations with her sister.

items.text: Rabbi Ami citing Resh Lakish on Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami citing Resh Lakish on Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami quotes Resh Lakish explaining Rabbi Yehuda's position: the verse 'באש ישרפו אותו ואתהן' implies that the wife is also prohibited, as the superfluous word 'אתהן' teaches an additional prohibition beyond burning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi quotes Resh Lakish explaining Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: the verse 'באש ישרפו אותו ואתהן' implies that the wife is also prohibited, as the superfluous word 'אתהן' teaches an additional prohibition beyond burning.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: halakha not like Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: halakha not like Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yehuda. A story illustrates: a man who had relations with his mother-in-law was lashed by Rav Yehuda, who told him that were it not for Shmuel's ruling, he would have prohibited the man's wife forever.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yehuda, and illustrates with a story where he lashed a man who had relations with his mother-in-law, telling him that without Shmuel's ruling he would have prohibited the man's wife forever.

items.text: Identifying the 'light prohibition' in the kal vachomer
items.text_en: Identifying the 'light prohibition' in the kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks to identify the case of 'light prohibition' mentioned earlier. Rav Chisda suggests it is one who takes back his divorced wife after she remarried. Resh Lakish proposes a yevama, but difficulties arise. Rabbi Yochanan suggests a sotah, but that is a severe prohibition. The discussion remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the 'light prohibition' referred to in the earlier kal vachomer.
Rav Chisda proposes that the light prohibition is one who takes back his divorced wife after she remarried.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Chisda's case
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Chisda's case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that in Rav Chisda's case, if one man has relations with her, she becomes forbidden to the other.
The Gemara objects that Rav Chisda's case is not a light prohibition because it involves bodily defilement, a majority-based prohibition, and a permanent prohibition.
Resh Lakish proposes that the light prohibition is a yevama (a widow awaiting levirate marriage).
The Gemara asks to whom the yevama is forbidden.

sub.text: Gemara's first clarification of Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Gemara's first clarification of Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Resh Lakish means she is forbidden to another man, citing Rav Hamnuna's ruling that a yevama who committed adultery is forbidden to her yavam.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to the first clarification
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to the first clarification
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that this case also involves bodily defilement and a majority-based prohibition, so it is not light.

sub.text: Gemara's second clarification of Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Gemara's second clarification of Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets Resh Lakish to mean the yevama is forbidden to the other brothers (the yevamin).

sub.text: Gemara's question on the second clarification
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on the second clarification
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the case specifies the second brother having relations, since even a mere declaration of intent (מאמר) by the second brother should also forbid her to the first.
The Gemara resolves that this follows Rabban Gamliel's view that one declaration of intent (מאמר) cannot follow another, so only actual relations cause the prohibition.
The Gemara objects that even a get (bill of divorce) or chalitzah (release) from the second brother should also forbid her to the first, making the case not uniquely about relations.
Rabbi Yochanan proposes that the light prohibition is a sotah (a suspected adulteress).
The Gemara asks to whom the sotah is forbidden.

sub.text: Gemara's first clarification of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Gemara's first clarification of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yochanan means the sotah is forbidden to her husband, and if the husband has relations with her, she becomes forbidden to the adulterer.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to the first clarification
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to the first clarification
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even giving a get or refusing to administer the bitter water should also forbid her, not just relations.

sub.text: Gemara's second clarification of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Gemara's second clarification of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets Rabbi Yochanan to mean the sotah is forbidden to the adulterer (the one who had relations with her).
The Gemara objects that this is not a light prohibition but a severe one, since it involves a married woman (אשת איש).

items.text: Rava and Rabbi Yochanan's principle and the kal vachomer
items.text_en: Rava and Rabbi Yochanan's principle and the kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rava and Rabbi Yochanan state that a married woman is a 'light prohibition' because the one who forbids her does not forbid her for all his days. A baraita supports this. The Gemara then poses a kal vachomer: if one who has relations with a light prohibition becomes forbidden to the one who forbids her, then for a severe prohibition it should certainly be so. The verse 'otah' teaches that only her own intercourse forbids her, not her sister's.

sub.desc_en: Rava and Rabbi Yochanan state that a married woman (אשת איש) is a 'light prohibition' because the one who forbids her (her husband) does not forbid her for all his days; a supporting baraita from Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar is cited.

The Gemara poses a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if one who has relations with a light prohibition becomes forbidden to the one who forbids her, then for a severe prohibition it should certainly be so.
The Gemara resolves the kal vachomer by citing the verse 'אותה' (her), teaching that only her own intercourse forbids her, not her sister's intercourse.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Yosei's statement
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Yosei's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yosei means. It first suggests he argues with the Tanna Kamma that if the wife is permitted, the wife of the brother-in-law should also be permitted. The Gemara objects that the phrasing 'one who does not disqualify' is problematic. It then suggests the opposite: that if the brother-in-law's wife is forbidden, the wife should also be forbidden, but again the wording is problematic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yosei means, suggesting he argues with the Tanna Kamma that if the wife is permitted, the wife of the brother-in-law should also be permitted.
The Gemara objects that the phrasing 'one who does not disqualify' is problematic, as it should be reversed.
The Gemara suggests the opposite interpretation, that if the brother-in-law's wife is forbidden, the wife should also be forbidden, but again the wording is problematic.

items.text: Rabbi Ami's explanation of Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami's explanation of Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami explains the case: if a woman remarried on the authority of a court, she must leave but is exempt from a sacrifice; if on the authority of witnesses, she must leave and is liable. The Tanna Kamma holds that in both cases the brother-in-law's wife is permitted. Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: on court authority, where he disqualifies others, he disqualifies himself; on witness authority, where he does not disqualify others, he does not disqualify himself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami states the general rule: a woman who remarried on court authority must leave but is exempt from a sacrifice; on witness authority she must leave and is liable.
The Tanna Kamma holds that in both cases (witnesses or court) the brother-in-law's wife is permitted.
Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: on court authority, where he disqualifies others, he disqualifies himself; on witness authority, where he does not disqualify others, he does not disqualify himself.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's explanation of Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's explanation of Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha explains that the dispute is about the end of the mishnah, distinguishing between a wife and an arusah (betrothed woman). The Tanna Kamma holds that in both cases the brother-in-law's wife is forbidden and the wife is permitted. Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: for a wife, where there is no possibility of a condition in the marriage, he does not disqualify himself; for an arusah, where there could be a condition in the betrothal, he disqualifies himself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha asserts that the dispute is always about the end of the mishnah, distinguishing between cases of a wife and an arusah (betrothed woman) going to a Mediterranean country with the brother-in-law, and the Tanna Kamma rules that in both cases the brother-in-law's wife is forbidden and his own wife is permitted.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's explanation of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's explanation of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: for a wife, where there is no possibility of a condition in the marriage, he does not disqualify himself; for an arusah, where there could be a condition in the betrothal, he disqualifies himself.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel and the objection from the yevama dispute
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel and the objection from the yevama dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says Shmuel ruled that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei. Rav Yosef objects, citing a dispute between Rav and Shmuel about a yevama: Rav says she is like a married woman and forbidden to the yavam, Shmuel says she is permitted. Abaye deflects, questioning whether Shmuel's ruling was on Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's version or Rabbi Ami's, and whether it was on the 'disqualifies' clause.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports that Shmuel ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Yosef objects, citing a dispute between Rav and Shmuel about a yevama where Shmuel permits her, contradicting the ruling attributed to him.
The gemara clarifies that Rav considers the yevama forbidden like a married woman, while Shmuel permits her to the yavam.
Abaye deflects the objection by questioning whether Shmuel's ruling was on Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's version or Rabbi Ami's, and whether it was on the 'disqualifies' clause.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rav Huna's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rav Huna's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Huna's statement about a yevamah being disqualified by adultery is valid, suggesting instead that the dispute between Rav and Shmuel might be about whether a yevamah is like an eshet ish or about whether kiddushin can take effect on a yevamah. It notes that these disputes were already stated elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Huna's statement about disqualification is valid, suggesting that perhaps the dispute between Rav and Shmuel is about Rav Hamnuna's ruling.

The Gemara explains Rav Hamnuna's statement that a yevamah who committed adultery is forbidden to the yavam, and suggests that Rav and Shmuel dispute whether she is like an eshet ish (married woman) in this regard.
The Gemara offers an alternative: the dispute between Rav and Shmuel might be about whether kiddushin (betrothal) can take effect on a yevamah.
The Gemara objects that these disputes were already stated elsewhere, and resolves that one was stated as a general principle from which the other is derived.

items.text: Mishnah: Marrying sisters after being told wife died
items.text_en: Mishnah: Marrying sisters after being told wife died
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a man is told his wife died and marries her sister, then is told again and marries another sister, etc. If all wives are found alive, he is permitted to the first, third, and fifth and they exempt their co-wives, but forbidden to the second and fourth. It then discusses the law of a nine-year-old boy who can disqualify a yevamah through bi'ah, and the brothers can disqualify through various actions.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a man who marries a series of sisters based on false reports of his wife's death, and rules that he is permitted to the first, third, and fifth wives, who exempt their co-wives.
The Mishnah states that he is forbidden to the second and fourth wives, and relations with them do not exempt their co-wives.
The Mishnah adds that if he had relations with the second wife after the first wife's actual death, he is permitted to the second and fourth, but forbidden to the third and fifth.
The Mishnah introduces the law of a nine-year-old boy who disqualifies his brothers from the yevamah through bi'ah, while the brothers disqualify him whether first or last.
The Mishnah explains how the nine-year-old boy disqualifies his brothers through bi'ah, and the brothers disqualify him through bi'ah, ma'amar, get, or chalitzah.

items.text: Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's timing
items.text_en: Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's timing
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that the Mishnah's case of marrying after being told 'your wife died' is certainly after the death of the first wife, addressing a potential redundancy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether all the cases in the Mishnah are not after the death of the first wife, implying a redundancy.
Rav Sheshet clarifies that the Mishnah's case is certainly after the definite death of the first wife, not a mere rumor.

items.text: Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between beginning and end
items.text_en: Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between beginning and end
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that a nine-year-old boy disqualifies only at the beginning, citing a beraita where he disqualifies even at the end through bi'ah. It resolves by saying the Mishnah is missing a clause: the rule about beginning only applies to ma'amar, but bi'ah disqualifies even at the end.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's claim that a nine-year-old boy disqualifies only at the beginning, citing a beraita of Rav Zevid bar Rav Oshaya where he disqualifies even at the end through bi'ah.

The Gemara initially answers that bi'ah disqualifies even at the end, while ma'amar disqualifies only at the beginning, but then objects that the Mishnah's examples show the boy disqualifying only at the beginning even with bi'ah.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is missing a clause: the rule about beginning only applies to ma'amar, but bi'ah disqualifies even at the end.

items.text: Gemara questions whether a nine-year-old has ma'amar at all
items.text_en: Gemara questions whether a nine-year-old has ma'amar at all
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a nine-year-old boy has the power of ma'amar at all, citing a beraita that he only disqualifies through bi'ah, while the brothers disqualify through bi'ah, ma'amar, get, and chalitzah. It concludes that bi'ah is established as disqualifying both at the beginning and end, but ma'amar at the beginning only is not established.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a nine-year-old boy has the power of ma'amar (formal betrothal-like act) at all, citing a beraita that says he disqualifies through one thing (bi'ah) while the brothers disqualify through four things (bi'ah, ma'amar, get, chalitzah).

The Gemara resolves that bi'ah is established as disqualifying both at the beginning and end, but ma'amar, which disqualifies only at the beginning and not at the end, is not established for the nine-year-old.

items.text: Supporting statements about ma'amar and get for a nine-year-old
items.text_en: Supporting statements about ma'amar and get for a nine-year-old
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel and Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi state that a nine-year-old has a get and ma'amar, and a beraita supports this in the name of Rabbi Meir. The Gemara then questions Rabbi Meir's view based on another beraita, and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua resolves that he has it but it is minor (zutar).

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel and Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi state that a nine-year-old has a get and ma'amar.
A beraita supports this ruling in the name of Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Meir's view based on another beraita that compares the nine-year-old's chalitza to a get, not to a get of a minor.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua resolves that the nine-year-old has a get but it is minor (זוטר), explaining the distinction.

items.text: Distinction between Rabban Gamliel and the Rabbis regarding get after get
items.text_en: Distinction between Rabban Gamliel and the Rabbis regarding get after get
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabban Gamliel, who says there is no get after a get, this applies only to an adult after an adult or a minor after a minor, but an adult after a minor is effective. According to the Rabbis, who say there is a get after a get, this applies to an adult after an adult or a minor after a minor, but a minor after an adult is not effective.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabban Gamliel, who holds there is no get after a get, this applies only to an adult after an adult or a minor after a minor, but an adult after a minor is effective.
The Gemara explains that according to the Rabbis, who hold there is a get after a get, this applies to an adult after an adult or a minor after a minor, but a minor after an adult is not effective.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Nine-year-old's intercourse with yevama
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Nine-year-old's intercourse with yevama
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a nine-year-old boy has intercourse with his yevama, and then his nine-year-old brother does so, the second brother disqualifies the first. Rabbi Shimon disagrees. Similarly, if the same boy then has intercourse with the yevama's rival, he disqualifies himself, but Rabbi Shimon disagrees.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a nine-year-old boy who has intercourse with his yevama, and then his nine-year-old brother does so — the second brother disqualifies the first.
Rabbi Shimon disagrees, stating that the second brother does not disqualify the first.
The Mishnah presents a second case: a nine-year-old boy who has intercourse with his yevama and then with her rival disqualifies himself.
Rabbi Shimon again disagrees, ruling that the boy does not disqualify himself.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's argument to the Sages
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's argument to the Sages
items.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Shimon's argument: if the first intercourse is valid, the second is not; if the first is invalid, the second is also invalid. This is a logical challenge to the Mishnah's ruling.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Shimon's logical argument to the Sages: if the first intercourse is valid, the second is not; if the first is invalid, the second is also invalid.

items.text: Gemara: The Mishnah is not like Ben Azzai
items.text_en: Gemara: The Mishnah is not like Ben Azzai
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling does not align with Ben Azzai, who holds that there can be a ma'amar (formal betrothal) after another ma'amar in the case of two yevamin and one yevama, but not in the case of two yevamot and one yavam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Mishnah's ruling does not align with Ben Azzai's position.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Ben Azzai rules that there can be a ma'amar (formal betrothal) after another ma'amar in the case of two yevamin and one yevama, but not in the case of two yevamot and one yavam.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Cases of a nine-year-old's marriage and death
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Cases of a nine-year-old's marriage and death
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases: if a nine-year-old has intercourse with his yevama and dies, she performs chalitzah but not yibbum. If he marries a woman and dies, she is exempt. If he later marries another woman and dies, the first wife does chalitzah, the second may do chalitzah or yibbum. Rabbi Shimon allows yibbum to either and chalitzah to the other. This applies to a nine-year-old and a twenty-year-old without two pubic hairs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the first case: a nine-year-old who had intercourse with his yevama and died — she performs חליצה (chalitzah) but not יבום (yibbum); if he married a woman and died, she is exempt; if he later married another woman after growing up, the first wife does חליצה and the second may do either.

Rabbi Shimon states that he may perform יבום (yibbum) with whichever he wishes and perform חליצה (chalitzah) to the other, and this applies equally to a nine-year-old and a twenty-year-old without two pubic hairs.

items.text: Gemara: Rava's explanation of the rule for two yevamin
items.text_en: Gemara: Rava's explanation of the rule for two yevamin
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Sages' rule that a woman with two yevamin does chalitzah but not yibbum applies even without a rival wife, as shown in the Mishnah's first case where there is no rival, yet she still does chalitzah.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the Sages' rule that a woman with two yevamin does chalitzah but not yibbum applies even without a rival wife, as shown in the Mishnah's first case.

items.text: Gemara: The case of a minor who married and died
items.text_en: Gemara: The case of a minor who married and died
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that the wives of a deaf-mute or a minor who married and died are exempt from both chalitzah and yibbum, which aligns with the Mishnah's second case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that the wives of a deaf-mute or a minor who married and died are exempt from both חליצה (chalitzah) and ייבום (yibbum), which aligns with the Mishnah's second case.

items.text: Gemara: Debate on whether a nine-year-old's intercourse is like a ma'amar
items.text_en: Gemara: Debate on whether a nine-year-old's intercourse is like a ma'amar
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the rival wife is not exempt from yibbum, given that the nine-year-old's intercourse should be like a ma'amar of an adult. Rav says it is not, while Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan say it is. The Gemara resolves that this is a dispute between tannaim: one tanna (from the case of four brothers) decrees due to the rival wife, and the other does not. The Mishnah's tanna holds that it is like a ma'amar and does not decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the rival wife is not exempt from yibbum, given that the nine-year-old's intercourse should be treated like a ma'amar (formal betrothal) of an adult.
Rav answers that the Sages did not equate the nine-year-old's intercourse with an adult's ma'amar.
Shmuel answers that they did equate the nine-year-old's intercourse with an adult's ma'amar.
Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Shmuel that the nine-year-old's intercourse is treated like an adult's ma'amar.
The Gemara resolves the dispute by attributing it to a tannaitic disagreement: the tanna of the case of four brothers decreed due to the rival wife, and the Mishnah's tanna did not.

The Gemara clarifies that the tanna of the four brothers taught the case of an adult, but the same rule applies to a minor, and the reason for mentioning the adult is that the discussion was about an adult.

The Gemara clarifies that the tanna of our Mishnah holds that the nine-year-old's intercourse is like a ma'amar and does not decree due to the rival wife, and he taught the case of a minor because the discussion was about a minor.

items.text: Story: Rabbi Elazar's teaching without attribution and Rabbi Yochanan's anger
items.text_en: Story: Rabbi Elazar's teaching without attribution and Rabbi Yochanan's anger
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar taught a halachah in the study hall without attributing it to Rabbi Yochanan, who became angry. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi tried to appease him with a story about a dispute in Tiberias that led to a Torah scroll being torn. Rabbi Yochanan remained angry until Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi explained that just as Yehoshua taught without attribution, so too Rabbi Elazar's teaching was understood to be from Rabbi Yochanan. Rabbi Yochanan then questioned why they could not appease him like Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi. The Gemara explains Rabbi Yochanan's anger based on a verse about David's desire to dwell in God's tent in both worlds.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar taught a halachah in the study hall without attributing it to Rabbi Yochanan, and Rabbi Yochanan became angry.

sub.text: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi's appeasement attempt
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi's appeasement attempt
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi tried to appease Rabbi Yochanan by recounting a story of a dispute in Tiberias over a bolt with a globe, where Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei argued so fiercely that a Torah scroll was torn, and Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma predicted the synagogue would become idolatrous.
Rabbi Yochanan became even more angry, exclaiming that even the companionship (of Rabbi Elazar) was being used against him.

Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi appeased Rabbi Yochanan by citing a verse about Joshua teaching without attribution, arguing that just as everyone knew Joshua's teaching was from Moses, so too everyone knew Rabbi Elazar's teaching was from Rabbi Yochanan.

Rabbi Yochanan questioned why the others could not appease him like Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi, and the Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan's anger stemmed from a verse about David's desire to dwell in God's tent in both worlds, indicating a concern for proper attribution in both this world and the next.

items.text: The lips of the righteous move in the grave
items.text_en: The lips of the righteous move in the grave
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai teaches that when a Torah scholar's teaching is cited in this world, his lips move in the grave. Rabbi Yitzchak ben Ze'ira (or Shimon Nazira) cites a verse from Song of Songs to support this, and a metaphor of a cluster of grapes is used to illustrate how the lips move when touched.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the concept that a Torah scholar's lips move in the grave when his teaching is cited, citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Ze'ira / Shimon Nazira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Ze'ira / Shimon Nazira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Ze'ira (or Shimon Nazira) cites a verse from Song of Songs to support the idea that the lips of the righteous move in the grave.
The Gemara provides a metaphor of a pile of grapes to illustrate how the lips of Torah scholars move when their teachings are cited.

items.text: Contradiction regarding a twenty-year-old without signs of puberty
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding a twenty-year-old without signs of puberty
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita: a twenty-year-old who has not grown two pubic hairs must bring proof that he is twenty, and he is considered a saris (eunuch) who does not perform halitzah or yibbum. Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak says this applies only if he has developed signs of being a saris. Rava confirms this from the wording of the baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that a twenty-year-old without two pubic hairs must bring proof of age and is considered a סריס (eunuch) who may not perform חליצה (halitzah) or יבום (yibbum), contradicting the mishna which treats him like a nine-year-old.
The Gemara answers that Rav said the baraita applies only if the person developed signs of being a סריס (eunuch).
Rava provides linguistic support: the baraita explicitly says 'and he is the סריס (eunuch)', confirming that Rav's interpretation is correct.

items.text: The age limit for signs of saris
items.text_en: The age limit for signs of saris
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if he did not develop signs of being a saris, until what age does he wait? The school of Rabbi Chiyya teaches: until most of his years (i.e., 36). Rava would instruct litigants to either fatten or thin the person, as these signs can fall due to thinness or fatness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if he did not develop signs of being a saris, until what age does he wait?
The school of Rabbi Chiyya teaches: until most of his years (i.e., 36).
Rava would instruct litigants to either fatten or thin the person to determine if signs appear.
The Gemara explains: these signs can fall due to thinness or fatness.

items.text: Mishnah: Marrying a raped or seduced woman's relatives
items.text_en: Mishnah: Marrying a raped or seduced woman's relatives
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may marry the daughter of a woman he raped or seduced, but if he marries a woman, he is liable for marrying her daughter. One may marry his father's or son's rape or seduction victim. Rabbi Yehuda prohibits marrying his father's rape victim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one may marry the relatives of a woman he raped or seduced, but if he marries a woman, he is liable for marrying her daughter.
The Tanna Kamma rules that a man may marry his father's or son's rape or seduction victim.
Rabbi Yehuda prohibits marrying a woman raped or seduced by one's father.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's leniency
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's leniency
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: a baraita says one who rapes a woman may marry her daughter, but another baraita says one who is suspected with a woman is forbidden to marry her mother, daughter, or sister (a rabbinic decree). The Gemara asks: how can the Mishnah permit this initially if there is a rabbinic prohibition? It answers: the Mishnah speaks after the woman's death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one who rapes a woman may marry her daughter, but one who marries her is prohibited.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita that one suspected with a woman is forbidden to marry her mother, daughter, or sister, by rabbinic decree.
The Gemara objects: how can the Mishnah teach that one may marry לכתחילה (the ideal standard) if there is a rabbinic prohibition?
The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah speaks after the woman's death, where the rabbinic concern no longer applies.

items.text: Source for the distinction between rape and marriage
items.text_en: Source for the distinction between rape and marriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the biblical source: the Torah uses 'taking' (kicha) in the context of a woman and her daughter, implying that only through marriage (kiddushin) is it forbidden, not through rape. Rav Pappa challenges Abaye: regarding one's sister, the Torah also uses 'taking'—does that mean only marriage is forbidden? Abaye answers: the Torah uses 'taking' generically; what is appropriate for marriage is forbidden via marriage, and what is appropriate for intercourse is forbidden via intercourse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of the distinction between rape and marriage regarding relatives, citing a baraita that the Torah uses 'taking' (קיחה) rather than 'lying' (שכיבה) to indicate that only through marriage is it forbidden.

Rav Pappa objects to Abaye: if the use of 'taking' implies only marriage is forbidden, then regarding one's sister, where the Torah also uses 'taking' (איש אשר יקח את אחותו), would that mean only marriage is forbidden but non-marital intercourse is permitted?

Abaye answers that the Torah uses 'taking' generically; it is interpreted according to context: what is appropriate for marriage (קידושין) is forbidden via marriage, and what is appropriate only for intercourse is forbidden via intercourse.

items.text: Rava's alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Rava derives the leniency from a different verse: the Torah forbids uncovering the nakedness of one's granddaughter, but permits the daughter of one's daughter (i.e., the woman's daughter) in the case of rape. The Gemara asks why not reverse the interpretation, and answers: the term 'she'er' (flesh) is used for forbidden relations, which applies only in marriage, not rape.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens his alternative derivation: from the verse 'ערוות בת בנך... לא תגלה' (the nakedness of your son's daughter... you shall not uncover), he infers that the daughter of the woman's own daughter is permitted (i.e., uncovered), establishing the leniency for rape.
The Gemara cites the contradictory verse 'ערוות אשה ובתה לא תגלה' (the nakedness of a woman and her daughter you shall not uncover) and asks: how can both verses be reconciled?
The Gemara answers: the first verse (permitting the daughter) refers to rape, while the second verse (prohibiting the daughter) refers to marriage.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the interpretation should be reversed, making the daughter of a rape victim forbidden and the daughter of a wife permitted.

The Gemara rejects the objection: the term 'שאר' (kinship/flesh) is used for forbidden relations, which applies only in marriage (where there is kinship), not in rape (where there is no kinship), thus the original resolution stands.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and the Sages' response
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and the Sages' response
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel explains Rabbi Yehuda's position: the verse 'He shall not take his father's wife, nor uncover his father's wing' implies he may not uncover a wing (i.e., a woman) that his father has seen (i.e., raped). The Sages argue that the verse is not adjacent to the rape passage; rather, it refers to a yevamah (levirate widow) of his father, as per Rav Anan. The Gemara then asks why not also prohibit due to his aunt (dodato) or a yevamah to the public, and answers that these add additional prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel cites Rav to explain Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: the verse 'לֹא יִקַּח... וְלֹא יְגַלֶּה כְּנַף אָבִיו' (he shall not uncover his father's wing) means he may not uncover a woman his father has seen (i.e., raped).
The Gemara supports that the verse refers to rape, citing the adjacent verse about the rapist paying fifty silver shekels to the girl's father.

The Sages object: if the verse were adjacent to the rape passage, it would support Rabbi Yehuda, but since it is not, it must refer to a שומרת יבם (levirate widow) of his father, as per Rav Anan citing Shmuel.
The Gemara asks: why not derive the prohibition from the fact that she is his aunt (דודתו)? The answer: to add a second prohibition.

The Gemara asks: why not also derive from the prohibition of יבמה לשוק (a yevamah to a stranger)? The answer: to add a third prohibition, or alternatively, the verse refers to after the father's death.

items.text: Riddles of complex family relationships among converts
items.text_en: Riddles of complex family relationships among converts
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama introduces a series of riddles describing convoluted family relationships that can only occur among converts or gentiles, where a person can be both a brother and a father, etc. Each riddle is followed by an explanation of the specific scenario that produces such a relationship.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama introduces the first riddle: a person is a brother from the father but not the mother, and is also the husband of the mother, and the speaker is the daughter of his wife, noting this scenario is not according to Rabbi Yehuda of the Mishnah.
The Gemara explains the second riddle — 'He is my brother and my son, and I am his sister who carries him on my shoulders' — which occurs in a gentile who had relations with his daughter.
The Gemara explains the third riddle — 'Greetings to you my son, I am your aunt' — which occurs in a gentile who had relations with his granddaughter.

The Gemara explains the fourth riddle — 'May the bucket-drawers fall and break their bones: the one I carry is my son, and I am his father's daughter' — which occurs in a gentile who had relations with his son's daughter.

The Gemara explains the fifth riddle — 'My uncle, my uncle from my brother, and he is a father, and a husband, and a stepson, and my mother's husband, and I am his wife's daughter, and he does not give bread to his brother's orphaned granddaughters' — which occurs in a gentile who had relations with his mother, fathered a daughter, then had relations with that daughter, and then an old man had relations with her and fathered sons.

The Gemara explains the sixth riddle — 'I and you are brothers, I and your father are brothers, I and your mother are brothers' — which occurs in a gentile who had relations with his mother and fathered two daughters, then had relations with one daughter and fathered a son, and the mother's sister addresses him accordingly.

The Gemara explains the seventh riddle — 'I and you are cousins, I and your father are cousins, I and your mother are cousins' — which can also occur among permitted relationships, such as Reuven having two daughters, Shimon marrying one, and Levi marrying the other, and Shimon's son speaking to Levi's grandson.

items.text: Mishnah: Convert woman and her sons
items.text_en: Mishnah: Convert woman and her sons
