items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a convert woman who converted with her sons, even if one son was conceived before conversion and born after, and another conceived and born after conversion, they do not perform chalitzah or yibbum with each other. The same applies to a freed slave woman and her sons.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a convert woman who converted with her sons, even if one son was conceived before conversion and born after, and another conceived and born after conversion, they do not perform חליצה (release) or יבום (levirate marriage) with each other, and the same applies to a freed slave woman and her sons.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov permits freed slaves to marry each other's wives
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov permits freed slaves to marry each other's wives
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that when the sons of Yudan the maidservant were freed, Rav Acha bar Yaakov permitted them to marry each other's wives. Rava objects, citing Rav Sheshet who forbade it, but Rav Acha bar Yaakov asserts his own authority to permit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that the sons of Yudan the maidservant were freed, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov permitted them to marry each other's wives.
Rava objects, citing Rav Sheshet who forbade such marriages.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov asserts his own authority to permit, disregarding Rav Sheshet's prohibition.

items.text: Dispute about siblings from father vs. mother among converts
items.text_en: Dispute about siblings from father vs. mother among converts
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the dispute: all agree that siblings from the father only are permitted, and from the mother only are forbidden. The dispute is about siblings from both father and mother: Rav Acha bar Yaakov permits, following the father's lineage, while Rav Sheshet forbids, noting they are also called by the mother's name. An alternative version says Rav Acha bar Yaakov even permits siblings from the mother only, since a convert is like a newborn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes the undisputed cases: siblings from the father only are permitted, and from the mother only are forbidden.

The Gemara identifies the dispute: siblings from both father and mother, where Rav Acha bar Yaakov permits based on paternal lineage and Rav Sheshet forbids because they are also called by the mother's name.
An alternative version states that Rav Acha bar Yaakov even permits siblings from the mother only, because a convert is like a newborn.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Does the Mishnah prove prohibition or permission?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Does the Mishnah prove prohibition or permission?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that converts do not perform chalitzah or yibbum implies they are forbidden to each other or simply exempt. Two versions of the argument are presented: one concludes they are permitted, the other concludes they are forbidden, each interpreting the word 'even' in the Mishnah differently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that converts do not perform חליצה (chalitzah) or יבום (yibbum) is because they are forbidden to each other.
The first answer rejects the implication, explaining that the Mishnah means they are exempt from the laws of חליצה (chalitzah) and יבום (yibbum) and are permitted to marry each other's wives.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah uses the word 'אפילו (even)', which is problematic if the converts are permitted, and asks what 'even' would add.
The first answer explains that 'אפילו (even)' means that even though both were born in sanctity, which might lead to confusion with native Jews, they are still permitted.
An alternative version states that it is reasonable that they are permitted, and again questions what 'אפילו (even)' would add if they were forbidden.

The alternative answer explains that 'אפילו (even)' means that even though the first son was not conceived in sanctity and the second was, making them like sons of two mothers, they are still forbidden.

items.text: Supporting baraita: Twin converts and liability for sister-in-law
items.text_en: Supporting baraita: Twin converts and liability for sister-in-law
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: twin converts or freed slaves do not perform chalitzah or yibbum and are not liable for marrying their brother's wife. If conceived before conversion but born after, they are still exempt from chalitzah and yibbum but are liable for marrying their brother's wife. If conceived and born after conversion, they are like full Israelites. The Gemara notes that the baraita explicitly says there is no liability, implying they are permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about twin converts and freed slaves, detailing their exemption from חליצה (ḥalitza) and יבום (levirate marriage) and their liability for אשת אח (brother's wife), and infers that lack of liability implies permission.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the Mishnah's phrasing
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the Mishnah's phrasing
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's statement 'they are not liable' is only because the Tanna wanted to teach the latter clause 'but they are liable', not because there is no prohibition at all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's phrase 'they are not liable' implies there is still a prohibition (איסור), challenging the notion that there is no prohibition at all.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's wording is merely a stylistic choice: the Tanna used 'they are not liable' only to parallel the later clause 'but they are liable', but in truth there is no prohibition either.

items.text: Rava's principle: no paternal lineage for a gentile
items.text_en: Rava's principle: no paternal lineage for a gentile
items.desc_en: Rava states that the rabbinic principle 'a gentile has no father' applies even when the father is known, because the Torah considers a gentile's seed as abandoned, as proven by the case of twin brothers who cannot perform levirate marriage.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the rabbinic principle 'a gentile has no father' applies even when the father is known, not only due to promiscuity.
The Gemara proves Rava's principle from the case of twin brothers who cannot perform levirate marriage, showing the Torah considers a gentile's seed as abandoned.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Yosei's story of Niftayim the convert
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Yosei's story of Niftayim the convert
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei relates that a convert married his half-brother's wife from the mother's side, and the Sages said 'a convert has no marital bond' (אֵין אִישׁוּת לַגֵּר), which is reinterpreted as 'no prohibition of a brother's wife for a convert'. The Gemara initially assumes the brother married her after conversion, but concludes it was while still a gentile, to avoid decreeing against the case of conversion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story of Rabbi Yosei about a convert who married his half-brother's wife from the mother's side, and the Sages said 'a convert has no marital bond' (אֵין אִישׁוּת לַגֵּר), which the Gemara reinterprets as 'no prohibition of a brother's wife for a convert'.
The Gemara asks: does this not imply that the brother married her after conversion (כְּשֶׁהוּא גֵּר), which would prove that a convert has no prohibition of a brother's wife?

The Gemara answers: no, the brother married her while still a gentile (כְּשֶׁהוּא גּוֹי), and the case teaches that we do not decree a prohibition for the gentile case lest it lead to a decree for the conversion case.

items.text: Proof from Ben Yasyan's story of Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Proof from Ben Yasyan's story of Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Ben Yasyan reports that Rabbi Akiva ruled a convert may marry his half-brother's wife from the mother's side. The Gemara again assumes the brother married after conversion, but concludes it was while still a gentile, to avoid decreeing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story of Ben Yasyan who found a convert who married his half-brother from the mother's side, citing Rabbi Akiva's ruling that a convert may do so, and challenges that this implies the brother married after conversion.
The Gemara asks whether the case is that the brother married the woman after conversion, which would prove the convert may marry his half-brother's wife from the mother's side.
The Gemara rejects the challenge, explaining that the brother married the woman while still a gentile, and the ruling teaches that we do not decree a concern for the case of conversion to forbid it.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Akiva's authority and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Akiva's authority and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Akiva's ruling is reliable, citing Rav's rule that a scholar who rules after the fact is not listened to unless he stated it before the event. Three answers are given: he stated it before, or he cited a precedent of a woman and seven sons, or he also cited another incident.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Akiva's reliability by citing Rav's rule that a scholar who rules after the fact is not listened to unless he stated it before the event.
The first answer suggests that Rabbi Akiva stated his ruling before the incident occurred, satisfying Rav's condition.
The second answer argues that Rabbi Akiva's ruling is reliable because he cited a precedent of a woman and seven sons.
The third answer distinguishes this case because Rabbi Akiva also cited another incident alongside his ruling.

items.text: Discussion of Jonah's prophecy
items.text_en: Discussion of Jonah's prophecy
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the statement that God spoke to Jonah only twice, citing a verse about Jonah prophesying the restoration of Israel's borders. Ravina and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explain that the second prophecy refers to Nineveh, and the restoration was a separate matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the statement that God spoke to Jonah only twice, citing a verse about Jonah prophesying the restoration of Israel's borders.
Ravina answers that the second prophecy refers to Nineveh, not the restoration.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the verse about restoration is not a separate prophecy but a comparison: just as Nineveh was turned from evil to good, so too in Jeroboam's days Israel was turned from evil to good.

items.text: Baraita on a convert's maternal vs paternal relationships
items.text_en: Baraita on a convert's maternal vs paternal relationships
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a convert whose conception was not in holiness but birth was in holiness has maternal lineage but not paternal lineage, so he must divorce a maternal half-sister but may keep a paternal half-sister.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that a convert with birth in holiness but not conception has maternal lineage but not paternal lineage, so he must divorce a maternal half-sister but may keep a paternal half-sister.

items.text: Mishnah: Forbidden and permitted relatives for a convert
items.text_en: Mishnah: Forbidden and permitted relatives for a convert
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists which maternal and paternal relatives a convert must divorce or may keep, and permits marriage to certain relatives like the wife of his maternal brother or paternal uncle.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that a convert may keep a maternal sister from the father's side but must divorce one from the mother's side, and permits marriage to the wife of his maternal brother.
Rabbi Meir rules that any forbidden relation due to maternal kinship must be divorced, but paternal kinship may be kept.
The Sages disagree and permit keeping the maternal sister from the father's side.
The mishnah concludes that a convert is permitted to marry the wife of his maternal brother and the wife of his paternal uncle, and adds the wife of his father as an additional permitted relative.

items.text: Mishnah: Marrying a woman and her daughter
items.text_en: Mishnah: Marrying a woman and her daughter
items.desc_en: If a convert married a woman and her daughter, he must divorce one and may keep the other; initially he should not marry both. After his wife dies, there is a dispute about whether he is permitted to his mother-in-law.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: if a convert married a woman and her daughter, he must divorce one and may keep the other, but initially he should not marry both.
The Mishnah records a dispute: after his wife dies, some say he is permitted to his mother-in-law, and an alternative tradition says he is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the case of the wife of his brother
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the case of the wife of his brother
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the mishnah's permission to marry the wife of his brother refers to a case where the brother married her as a convert or as a gentile, and concludes it refers to when the brother married her as a gentile, to avoid a decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the mishnah's permission to marry the wife of his brother refers to a case where the brother married her as a convert (גר) or as a gentile.
The Gemara answers that it refers to when the brother married her as a gentile, to avoid a decree that would conflate the gentile case with the convert case.

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of the ruling on marrying a woman and her daughter
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of the ruling on marrying a woman and her daughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's phrasing: if he must divorce one, why mention that initially he should not marry? It explains that the mishnah means that even where the Sages said he may keep her, initially he should not marry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah's ruling that if one marries a woman and her daughter, he must divorce one, and initially he should not marry.
The Gemara questions why the mishnah mentions the initial prohibition when it already requires divorce after the fact.
The Gemara explains that the mishnah means that even where the Sages said he may keep her, initially he should not marry.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute about the mother-in-law after the wife's death
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute about the mother-in-law after the wife's death
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the two traditions about the mother-in-law: one forbids, following Rabbi Yishmael who holds the prohibition remains strong; the other permits, following Rabbi Akiva who holds the prohibition weakens after the wife's death, and the Sages did not decree for a convert.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites two conflicting traditions regarding the mother-in-law after the wife's death: one permits, one forbids.

The Gemara explains that the forbidding tradition follows Rabbi Yishmael, who holds the prohibition remains strong after death and the Sages decreed for a convert, while the permitting tradition follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds the prohibition weakens and the Sages did not decree for a convert.

items.text: Mishnah: Five women with intermingled children
items.text_en: Mishnah: Five women with intermingled children
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents a case of five women whose children became intermingled; when the children grow up and marry, if they die, four perform chalitzah for each widow and one performs yibbum, resulting in four chalitzot and one yibbum for each.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the case of five women whose children were intermingled; when the children grow up, marry, and die, four perform חליצה (chalitzah) for each widow and one performs יבום (yibbum).

The mishnah clarifies that each man and three others perform חליצה (chalitzah) for one widow, and one performs יבום (yibbum), resulting in four חליצות (chalitzot) and one יבום (yibbum) for each widow.

items.text: Gemara: Order of chalitzah and yibbum, and explanation of the procedure
items.text_en: Gemara: Order of chalitzah and yibbum, and explanation of the procedure
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that chalitzah must precede yibbum to avoid violating a yevamah in the public domain, and explains that each of the four brothers performs yibbum for one widow to avoid the possibility of marrying his own sister.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that chalitzah must precede yibbum, because performing yibbum first would violate the yevamah in the public domain.
The Gemara explains that the mishnah's phrase 'he and three perform chalitzah for one' means each brother performs yibbum for a different widow, to avoid the possibility of marrying his own sister.

items.text: Gemara: Cases of mixed paternal and maternal brothers, and priests
items.text_en: Gemara: Cases of mixed paternal and maternal brothers, and priests
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when some are paternal brothers and some maternal, the maternal brothers perform chalitzah and the paternal perform yibbum; when some are priests, the priests perform chalitzah; when both categories apply, all perform chalitzah only.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'some are brothers and some are not brothers'.

Rav Safra explains that the Mishnah refers to cases where some are paternal brothers and some are maternal brothers: maternal brothers perform חליצה (chalitzah) and paternal brothers perform ייבום (yibbum).
The Mishnah adds that when some are priests, the priests perform חליצה (chalitzah); when both categories (priests and maternal brothers) apply, all perform only חליצה (chalitzah).

items.text: First Baraita: חליצה מספק for mother, sister, and daughter
items.text_en: First Baraita: חליצה מספק for mother, sister, and daughter
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma teaches that one performs חליצה out of doubt for his mother, sister, and daughter in cases of intermingled births. Three scenarios are given: one for mother, one for sister, and one for daughter, each involving hidden births and marriages that create uncertainty about the yevamah's identity.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states the general rule: one performs חליצה (the release ceremony) out of doubt for his mother, sister, and daughter in cases of intermingled births.

The baraita explains the scenario for the mother: two women with hidden twin sons, each son marries the other's mother, and upon their childless death each brother performs חליצה (the release ceremony) to both widows, resulting in each performing חליצה (the release ceremony) to his own mother out of doubt.

The baraita explains the scenario for the sister: two women give birth to hidden daughters, half-brothers marry them, and upon the brothers' childless death each brother performs חליצה (the release ceremony) to both widows, resulting in performing חליצה (the release ceremony) to his own sister out of doubt.

The baraita explains the scenario for the daughter: two women give birth to hidden daughters, brothers marry them, and upon the brothers' childless death each brother performs חליצה (the release ceremony) to both widows, resulting in each performing חליצה (the release ceremony) to his own daughter out of doubt.

items.text: Second Baraita: Rabbi Meir's case of five nations
items.text_en: Second Baraita: Rabbi Meir's case of five nations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir teaches that a man and woman can produce offspring of five different national/status categories: a convert, a gentile, a slave, a mamzer, and an Israelite. The Gemara asks what this teaches, and answers that a gentile or slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir teaches that a man and woman can produce offspring of five different national/status categories: a convert, a gentile, a slave, a mamzer, and an Israelite.
The Gemara asks what novel halachic point this baraita teaches.
The Gemara answers that the baraita teaches that a gentile or slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer.

items.text: Third Baraita: Selling one's father to collect mother's ketubah
items.text_en: Third Baraita: Selling one's father to collect mother's ketubah
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one can sell his father (a slave) to enable his mother to collect her ketubah. The Gemara explains that this follows Rabbi Meir's view that a slave is considered movable property, and movable property is liened for a ketubah. Alternatively, it teaches that a slave is considered like land.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one may sell his father (a slave) to enable his mother to collect her ketubah.
The Gemara asks what novel point this baraita teaches.
The Gemara answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Meir's view that a slave is movable property (מִטַּלְטְלֵי), and movable property is liened for a ketubah.
Alternatively, the Gemara answers that the baraita teaches that a slave is considered like land (מְקַרְקַע), which is always liened for a ketubah.

items.text: Mishnah: Intermingled offspring and levirate obligations
items.text_en: Mishnah: Intermingled offspring and levirate obligations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a case where a woman's child is mixed up with her daughter-in-law's child. When the mixed-up children grow up, marry, and die childless, the rules of יבום and חליצה vary: the daughter-in-law's sons perform חליצה only, while the elder woman's sons may perform either. Further cases involve the death of the 'kosher' children and a priestess whose child is mixed with her maidservant's child, who eat terumah and share one portion at the threshing floor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a woman whose child is mixed with her daughter-in-law's child, and states that the daughter-in-law's sons perform חליצה only, not יבום, due to the doubt.
The Mishnah states that the elder woman's sons may either perform חליצה or יבום, because the doubt involves both a brother's wife and a brother's son's wife.
The Mishnah presents a second case: if the 'kosher' children die, the mixed-up children of the elder woman perform only חליצה, while those of the daughter-in-law have one perform חליצה and one יבום.
The Mishnah concludes with the case of a priestess whose child is mixed with her maidservant's child: they eat תרומה and share one portion at the threshing floor.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of a mixture of kosher and disqualified priests
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of a mixture of kosher and disqualified priests
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the restrictions that apply to a mixture of kosher priests and disqualified priests (such as a חלל) until they are separated or freed. These include not becoming impure for the dead, not marrying certain women, and various limitations regarding terumah and sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the restrictions that apply to a mixture of kosher and disqualified priests, including prohibitions on impurity for the dead, marriage, terumah consumption, and receiving priestly gifts.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's language
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's language
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'the kosher ones died' and suggests that the disqualification is due to the mixture itself. Rav Pappa proposes an emendation: 'the definite ones died' (meaning those whose status is certain).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'the kosher ones died' by asking whether the disqualification is simply due to the mixture itself.
Rav Pappa proposes an emendation to the Mishnah: read 'the definite ones died' (those whose status is certain) instead of 'the kosher ones died'.

items.text: Gemara's inference regarding the order of halitza and yibum
items.text_en: Gemara's inference regarding the order of halitza and yibum
items.desc_en: The Gemara deduces from the Mishnah's phrase 'one performs halitza and then yibum' that one must perform halitza first and only then yibum, but not yibum first, because that would be encountering a yevama in the marketplace (a prohibited act).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's phrase 'one performs halitza and then yibum' as the basis for its inference.
The Gemara deduces that the Mishnah mandates halitza first and then yibum, not yibum first, because performing yibum first would involve encountering a yevama in the marketplace (a prohibited act).

items.text: Gemara's emendation of the Mishnah's phrase
items.text_en: Gemara's emendation of the Mishnah's phrase
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'one portion' (חֵלֶק אֶחָד) as being obvious, and suggests it should read 'a portion as one' (חֵלֶק כְּאֶחָד), meaning they receive a single portion together.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says 'one portion' (חֵלֶק אֶחָד), as it is obvious that they receive a portion.
The Gemara emends the Mishnah to read 'a portion as one' (חֵלֶק כְּאֶחָד), meaning they receive a single portion together.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei regarding terumah for a slave
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei regarding terumah for a slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah follows the opinion that terumah is not given to a slave unless his master is with him. A baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda requires the master's presence, while Rabbi Yosei allows the slave to claim terumah for himself if he is a priest, or for his master if he is a slave. The Gemara notes the practical difference in their locales regarding lineage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the Mishnah follows the opinion that terumah is not given to a slave unless his master is with him.
A baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda requires the master's presence, while Rabbi Yosei allows the slave to claim terumah for himself if he is a priest, or for his master if he is a slave.
The Gemara notes the practical difference: in Rabbi Yehuda's locale they would infer lineage from terumah distribution, but in Rabbi Yosei's locale they would not.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok and the elevation of a slave to the priesthood
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok and the elevation of a slave to the priesthood
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok testifies that he once testified and they elevated a slave to the priesthood based on his testimony. The Gemara objects that this cannot be, as God would not bring a stumbling block through the righteous. It explains that they only sought to elevate him, and that Rabbi Elazar testified in the locale of Rabbi Yehuda about a case from Rabbi Yosei's locale.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok testifies that he once gave a single testimony, and they elevated a slave to the priesthood based on it.
The Gemara objects that it is impossible for a slave to actually be elevated to the priesthood through Rabbi Elazar's testimony, since God would not bring a stumbling block through the righteous.
The Gemara resolves that they only sought to elevate the slave, and Rabbi Elazar testified in the locale of Rabbi Yehuda about a case from Rabbi Yosei's locale.

items.text: Baraita: Ten who do not receive terumah at the threshing floor
items.text_en: Baraita: Ten who do not receive terumah at the threshing floor
items.desc_en: A baraita lists ten categories of people who do not receive terumah at the threshing floor, including a deaf-mute, an imbecile, a minor, a tumtum, an androgynous, a slave, a woman, an uncircumcised person, a ritually impure person, and one who marries a woman unfit for him. All except the impure and the one who marries an unfit woman may have terumah sent to their homes. The Gemara begins to explain the reasons for the exclusion of the first categories.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists ten categories of people who do not receive תרומה (priestly portion) at the threshing floor, with the exception that all except the impure and one who marries an unfit woman may have it sent to their homes.
The Gemara begins to explain the reasons for the exclusion of the first categories, starting with the deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor who lack understanding, and then the tumtum and androgynous.

items.text: Debate on why a woman does not receive terumah at the granary
items.text_en: Debate on why a woman does not receive terumah at the granary
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a woman, unlike a slave, an uncircumcised priest, a defiled priest, and one who marries an inappropriate woman, is not given terumah at the granary. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna dispute the reason: one says it is due to the concern that she might be a divorced woman (and thus not entitled), and the other says it is due to the prohibition of seclusion (yichud) with the male distributors. The difference between them is whether the granary is near the town (where people are not commonly found) or far (where people are found).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a woman, unlike a slave, an uncircumcised priest, a defiled priest, and one who marries an inappropriate woman, is not given תרומה (priestly portion) at the granary.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna dispute
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna dispute
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna dispute the reason: one says it is due to concern that she might be a divorced woman (גרושה), and the other says it is due to the prohibition of seclusion (יחוד) with the male distributors.
The Gemara explains the practical difference between the two opinions: whether the granary is near the town (where people are not commonly found) or far (where people are found).

items.text: Reason for sending terumah to the uncircumcised priest but not to the defiled priest
items.text_en: Reason for sending terumah to the uncircumcised priest but not to the defiled priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that all those mentioned (slave, uncircumcised, defiled, and one who marries an inappropriate woman) are sent terumah to their homes, except for the defiled priest and the one who marries an inappropriate woman. It questions why the uncircumcised priest is sent terumah, answering that he is forced (an object of circumstance), whereas the defiled priest is also forced but his constraint is greater (since defilement is more common).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the uncircumcised priest is sent terumah (priestly portion) to his home, unlike the defiled priest.
The Gemara answers that the uncircumcised priest is forced (an object of circumstance), but the defiled priest's constraint is greater since defilement is more common.

items.text: Baraita on giving terumah to a woman first
items.text_en: Baraita on giving terumah to a woman first
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a slave and a woman do not receive terumah at the granary, but in a place where they do give, they give to the woman first and release her immediately. The Gemara clarifies that this refers to the poor tithe (ma'aser ani), and the reason is due to her dignity (ziluta), to avoid her being shamed by waiting.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a slave and a woman do not receive terumah at the granary, but where they do give, they give to the woman first and release her immediately.
The Gemara asks what the baraita means, since terumah is not given to women at the granary.
The Gemara clarifies that the baraita refers to poor tithe (מעשר עני), and the reason for giving to the woman first is due to her dignity (זילותא), to avoid her being shamed by waiting.

items.text: Rava's practice of prioritizing women in judgment
items.text_en: Rava's practice of prioritizing women in judgment
items.desc_en: Rava relates that initially, when a man and a woman came before him for judgment, he would first hear the man's case because the man is obligated in mitzvot. But after hearing this baraita, he would first hear the woman's case due to her dignity (ziluta).

sub.desc_en: Rava states that initially, when a man and woman came before him for judgment, he would first hear the man's case because the man is obligated in mitzvot (מצוות).
Rava explains that after hearing the baraita about giving terumah to a woman first due to her dignity (זילותא), he changed his practice to hear the woman's case first.

items.text: Coercing slaves in a mixed group to free each other
items.text_en: Coercing slaves in a mixed group to free each other
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when mixed groups of slaves (from different owners) grow up, they may or may not free each other. The Gemara questions why they are not forced to free each other, since they cannot marry a maidservant (as they are half-free) nor a free woman. Rava says the Mishnah means we force them to free each other.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when mixed groups of slaves grow up, they may free each other but are not forced to.
The Gemara questions why the slaves are not forced to free each other, since they cannot marry a maidservant (as half-free) nor a free woman.
Rava resolves the difficulty by reinterpreting the Mishnah: it means we force them to free each other.

items.text: Halakhic implications of the mixed group's offerings
items.text_en: Halakhic implications of the mixed group's offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the practical halakha of the mixed group's offerings: Rav Pappa explains that their meal-offering is treated like that of an Israelite (the handful is offered) but not eaten like that of a priest (the remainder is burned). The Gemara then cites Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi that this follows Rabbi Elazar's view that one may burn the remainder for the sake of wood. For the Rabbis, it follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who says the handful is offered and the remainder is scattered on the ash-pile, and even the Rabbis agree here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical halakhic implication arises from the Mishnah's ruling that the mixed group is subject to the stringencies of both Israelites and priests.

Rav Pappa answers that the meal-offering of the mixed group is treated like that of an Israelite (the handful is offered) but not eaten like that of a priest (the remainder is burned), so the handful is offered alone and the remainder is burned alone.

A baraita is cited stating that anything from which a portion is offered on the altar is subject to the prohibition of 'בל תקטירו' (you shall not burn) — supporting the need to burn the remainder separately.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi's explanation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi explains that the ruling follows Rabbi Elazar, who permits burning the remainder for the sake of wood, as derived from the verse 'לְרֵיחַ נִיחוֹחַ' (for a pleasing aroma).
The Gemara asks what the Rabbis, who disagree with Rabbi Elazar, would say about this case.

The Gemara answers that the ruling follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who says the handful is offered and the remainder is scattered on the ash-pile, and even the Rabbis agree here because this meal-offering is not fit for offering like the sinner's meal-offering of a priest.

items.text: Mishnah: Woman who remarries within three months and uncertain paternity
items.text_en: Mishnah: Woman who remarries within three months and uncertain paternity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman did not wait three months after her husband (before remarrying) and then gives birth, and it is unknown whether the child is nine months from the first husband or seven from the second, then the children from the first and second marriages perform chalitzah but not yibbum. Similarly, the child himself performs chalitzah but not yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law for a woman who remarries within three months and gives birth with uncertain paternity: the children from both marriages and the child himself perform חליצה (chalitzah) but not יבום (yibbum).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a man with brothers from different mothers, detailing the laws of levirate marriage and inheritance. It then lists the restrictions and privileges of a child of uncertain paternity, including priestly duties and penalties.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a man who has half-brothers from two different fathers, and rules that he performs חליצה (ḥalitza) or יבום (levirate marriage) with their widows, and they do the same with his wife.

The Mishnah lists the restrictions and privileges of a child of uncertain paternity when one possible father is an Israelite and the other a priest: he may marry a woman fit for a priest, may not become impure, but if he does he is not lashed; he may not eat תרומה (teruma) but if he does he does not repay; he sells his own תרומה (teruma) and keeps the money.

The Mishnah continues with further restrictions: he does not receive a share of sacred offerings, his own offerings are not taken, he is exempt from priestly gifts, his firstborn animal grazes until blemished, and he is subject to the stringencies of both priests and Israelites.

The Mishnah rules that if both possible fathers are priests, the child mourns for each and they mourn for him, but none may become impure for the other; he does not inherit from them but they inherit from him.

The Mishnah concludes: the child is exempt from punishment for striking or cursing either possible father; he serves in the priestly watch of both but does not receive a share unless both are in the same watch, in which case he takes one share.

items.text: Gemara's initial inference
items.text_en: Gemara's initial inference
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrasing that the man must perform חליצה before יבום, not the reverse, to avoid encountering a forbidden woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrasing that the man must perform חליצה (ḥalitza) before יבום (levirate marriage), not the reverse, to avoid encountering a forbidden woman.

items.text: Shmuel's statement on a child of uncertain paternity
items.text_en: Shmuel's statement on a child of uncertain paternity
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that if ten priests stand and one has relations, the child is a שְׁתוּקִי, silenced from priestly rights. The Gemara explains the term and cites a verse requiring the child to be attributed to the father.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that if ten priests stand and one has relations, the child is a שְׁתוּקִי (silenced one).
The Gemara asks what the term שְׁתוּקִי means, and rejects the possibility that it refers to being silenced from inheritance, since the father is unknown.
The Gemara concludes that the child is silenced from the rights of priesthood.
The Gemara explains the reason: the verse requires the seed to be attributed after the father, which is impossible here.

items.text: Rav Pappa's objection
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects by comparing to Abraham, where the verse requires the seed to be after him, but the Gemara explains that this refers to not marrying a gentile or maidservant.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects by comparing to Abraham, where the verse requires the seed to be after him, but the Gemara explains that this refers to not marrying a gentile or maidservant.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel from the Mishnah that a firstborn can be a High Priest, implying the child is attributed. It resolves that the requirement is rabbinic, and the verse is a mere support; the rabbis only decreed in cases of זְנוּת, not marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel from the Mishnah that a firstborn can be a High Priest, implying the child is attributed, contradicting the requirement of 'זַרְעוֹ מְיוּחָס אַחֲרָיו' (his seed traced after him).

The Gemara resolves that the requirement of attributed lineage is only rabbinic (דְּרַבָּנַן), and the verse is merely a support (אַסְמַכְתָּא); the rabbis only decreed in cases of זְנוּת (promiscuity), not in marriage.

items.text: Further challenge and refutation of Shmuel
items.text_en: Further challenge and refutation of Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether the rabbis decreed even in cases of זְנוּת, citing a Mishnah about a woman who remarries within three months. After analyzing the case, it concludes that the Mishnah deals with זְנוּת, and the ruling contradicts Shmuel, leading to a תְּיוּבְתָּא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether the rabbis decreed even in cases of זְנוּת (promiscuity), citing a Mishnah about a woman who remarries within three months and gives birth.
The Gemara questions the meaning of 'after her husband' in the Mishnah, first interpreting it as after the husband's death, but then pointing out a contradiction in the ruling about mourning.
The Gemara reinterprets the case as involving a divorcee, but then raises a difficulty: why is the child forbidden from becoming impure for the first husband?

The Gemara objects that the child should be permitted to become impure for the first husband regardless of paternity, since if he is the son it is proper, and if he is the son of the second he is a חָלָל (disqualified priest) who may become impure.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah must deal with a case of זְנוּת (promiscuity), and this constitutes a תְּיוּבְתָּא (conclusive refutation) of Shmuel's position.

items.text: Rav Shmaya's resolution and final discussion
items.text_en: Rav Shmaya's resolution and final discussion
items.desc_en: Rav Shmaya suggests the case involves a מְמָאֶנֶת, but the Gemara objects that a minor does not give birth. It then resolves with קִידּוּשֵׁי טָעוּת, citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel from Rabbi Yishmael, where a woman who was not captured is forbidden, but one with mistaken kiddushin is permitted even if she has a child.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shmaya answers the challenge to Shmuel by proposing the case involves a מְמָאֶנֶת (a minor who refuses her marriage).

The Gemara objects that a minor who מְמָאֶנֶת (refuses marriage) cannot give birth, citing a baraita about three women who use a contraceptive device, including a minor who is too young to conceive safely.

The Gemara resolves that the case involves קִידּוּשֵׁי טָעוּת (mistaken betrothal), citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel from Rabbi Yishmael: a woman with mistaken kiddushin is permitted even if she has a child, and she may refuse and leave.

items.text: Dispute about liability for simultaneous or sequential acts
items.text_en: Dispute about liability for simultaneous or sequential acts
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where if two priests each struck or cursed, whether simultaneously or sequentially, they are liable. Rabbi Yehuda holds that simultaneous acts incur liability but sequential ones do not. A contradiction is noted from another baraita where Rabbi Yehuda exempts in simultaneous cases, resolved by saying there are two Tannaic versions of his opinion.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that two priests who struck or cursed, whether simultaneously or sequentially, are liable, but Rabbi Yehuda holds simultaneous acts liable and sequential ones exempt.
The Gemara objects by citing a contradictory baraita where Rabbi Yehuda exempts in simultaneous cases.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating there are two Tannaic versions of Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.

items.text: Reason for exemption: analogy from blessing above
items.text_en: Reason for exemption: analogy from blessing above
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina explains the reasoning of the one who exempts: just as the blessing above (by God) has no partnership, so too below (by priests) there should be no partnership. The verse links striking and cursing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning of the Tanna who exempts one who strikes or curses two priests simultaneously.

Rabbi Chanina explains the exemption by a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): just as God's blessing above involves no partnership, so too the priestly blessing below must involve no partnership, and striking is linked to cursing.

items.text: Why a disqualified priest ascends the platform
items.text_en: Why a disqualified priest ascends the platform
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a priest who is not eligible to serve still ascends the platform for the priestly blessing. The Gemara questions why he would ascend if he does not receive a portion, and answers that it is due to family blemish (to avoid shame).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a disqualified priest would ascend the platform for the priestly blessing if he does not receive a portion.
The Gemara rejects its own question, noting that the Mishnah uses the present tense 'עוֹלֶה' (ascends) implying compulsion, not voluntary desire to perform a מצוה (commandment).
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the disqualified priest ascends due to פְּגַם מִשְׁפָּחָה (family blemish), to avoid shaming his family.

items.text: Distinction between two watches and one watch
items.text_en: Distinction between two watches and one watch
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between two watches (where the priest is rejected) and one watch (where he is not). Rav Pappa explains that if both priests are from the same watch and same paternal house, he receives one portion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishna distinguishes between two watches (where the priest gets no share) and one watch, since even in one watch he could be rejected by each paternal house.
Rav Pappa explains that the mishna means: if both uncertain fathers are from the same watch and same paternal house, he receives one share.
The Gemara signals the end of the chapter with the concluding formula 'הדרן עלך נושאין על האנוסה'.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of chalitzah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of chalitzah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that chalitzah requires three judges, even laymen. It details the types of footwear that are valid or invalid, and other conditions for the chalitzah ceremony.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that chalitzah requires three judges, even laymen, and specifies that a soft shoe (מנעל) is valid while a cloth shoe (אנפיליא) is invalid.
The Mishnah rules that a sandal with a heel is valid for chalitzah, but one without a heel is invalid.
The Mishnah states that if the yavam's leg is amputated from the knee down, chalitzah is valid; from the knee up, it is invalid.
The Mishnah rules that chalitzah is valid if performed with a sandal not belonging to the yavam, a wooden sandal, or a left sandal on the right foot.
The Mishnah concludes that chalitzah is valid with a shoe too large but walkable, or too small but covering most of the foot.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of three judges and the dispute with Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of three judges and the dispute with Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah mentions judges if even laymen suffice: to teach that they must know how to read the verses. It then derives the number of judges from the verse 'elders' (two) plus one, while Rabbi Yehuda derives five from the double mention of 'elders'. The Tanna Kamma uses the extra word to include even laymen, and Rabbi Yehuda derives laymen from the word 'before their eyes', excluding the blind.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies 'judges' if even three laymen suffice.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that the three must know how to read the verses like judges.
A baraita is cited supporting that the three must know how to read the verses like judges.
Rabbi Yehuda states that chalitzah requires five judges.
The Gemara explains the Tanna Kamma's derivation: 'elders' (זקנים) implies two, plus one to avoid an even court, totaling three.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's derivation: the double mention 'זִקְנֵי' and 'זְקֵנִים' yields four, plus one to avoid an even court, totaling five.
The Gemara asks what the Tanna Kamma does with the extra word 'זִקְנֵי'.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna Kamma uses 'זִקְנֵי' to include even three laymen.
The Gemara asks from where Rabbi Yehuda derives that laymen are valid.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda derives laymen from the word 'לְעֵינֵי' (before their eyes), which excludes the blind.
The Gemara concludes that since 'לְעֵינֵי' is needed to exclude the blind, it implies that even laymen are valid, and supports this with Rav Yosef's teaching that a court must be free of blemishes.

items.text: Derivation of the requirement for judges in chalitzah
items.text_en: Derivation of the requirement for judges in chalitzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'לְעֵינֵי הַזְּקֵנִים' teaches that judges must see the spittle, and 'בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל' excludes a court of converts. Additional derivations are given for the requirement that all present respond 'חלוץ הנעל'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing a verse and then explains that Rava derives from 'לְעֵינֵי' that judges must see the spittle during חליצה.
The Gemara asks: does the other opinion also need the verse for Rava's derivation? It answers that the requirement for ordinary judges is derived from 'בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל' — any Israelite.
The Gemara asks what the other opinion does with the word 'יִשְׂרָאֵל', and answers that it excludes a court of converts, as taught by Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda.
The Gemara asks about the other opinion's use of the second 'בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל', and answers that it is needed for Rabbi Yehuda's teaching that all present respond 'חלוץ הנעל'.
The Gemara concludes that the requirement for the response is derived from the word 'וְנִקְרָא'.

items.text: Challenge from the verses 'וְקָרְאוּ' and 'וְדִבְּרוּ'
items.text_en: Challenge from the verses 'וְקָרְאוּ' and 'וְדִבְּרוּ'
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if each verb implies multiple people, the count would be too high. It answers that these verses teach that the court gives appropriate advice to the yavam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if each verb implies multiple people, the count would be too high (nine for Rabbi Yehuda, seven for the Rabbis).
The Gemara answers that these verses teach that the court gives appropriate advice to the yavam, not that multiple people are required.

items.text: Halakhic ruling: chalitzah requires three judges
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling: chalitzah requires three judges
items.desc_en: Rava quotes Rav Nachman that the halakhah follows the anonymous mishnah requiring three judges for chalitzah. The Gemara compares this to mi'un and resolves a contradiction between multiple anonymous mishnayot, concluding that Rabbi Yehuda retracted his opinion.

sub.desc_en: Rava reports Rav Nachman's ruling that the halakhah requires three judges for חליצה (chalitzah), citing an anonymous mishnah that supports this.
Rava challenges Rav Nachman: if the anonymous mishnah is decisive, then the same logic should apply to מיאון (mi'un), which also appears in an anonymous mishnah requiring three.

The Gemara objects: but a baraita records a dispute about mi'un, with Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agreeing on three, while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei permit two, and Rav Nachman himself ruled like that pair.
The Gemara distinguishes: there (mi'un) there is only one anonymous mishnah, but here (chalitzah) there are two anonymous mishnayot supporting three judges.
The Gemara rejects the previous distinction, noting that mi'un also has two anonymous mishnayot, and chalitzah has three, but the number of anonymous sources alone is not a principled criterion.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves: the anonymous mishnah about chalitzah was taught in a place of dispute (regarding semikhah and eglah arufah), and since Rabbi Yehuda did not dispute the chalitzah clause, he must have retracted his earlier position.

items.text: Practice of adding extra judges for publicity
items.text_en: Practice of adding extra judges for publicity
items.desc_en: Rava states that judges must sit in a designated place. Rav Papa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua performed chalitzah with five judges, following Rabbi Yehuda's opinion for publicity, even though he retracted.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that judges must sit in a designated place, citing the verse 'וְעָלְתָה יְבִמְתּוֹ הַשַּׁעְרָה אֶל הַזְּקֵנִים' (and his yevamah shall go up to the gate to the elders).

sub.text: Narrative of Rav Papa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Narrative of Rav Papa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rav Papa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua performed חליצה (chalitzah) with five judges, following Rabbi Yehuda's opinion even though he retracted.
The Gemara explains that they added extra judges for publicity (לפרסומי מילתא), not as a matter of strict law.

items.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's disqualification as a judge due to being a convert
items.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's disqualification as a judge due to being a convert
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda asked Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda to join a court of five, but he declined because he was a convert, citing the verse that excludes a court of converts. Rav Yehuda then said he would rely on Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda to invalidate documents.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda invites Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda to join a court of five for publicity.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda declines, citing the baraita that a court must be of Israelites, not converts, and noting that he is a convert.
Rav Yehuda initially says he would extract money based on Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's testimony, but the gemara objects that this contradicts the requirement of two witnesses.
The gemara rejects the idea of extracting money based on one witness, and Rav Yehuda clarifies that he would only invalidate documents based on Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's testimony.

items.text: Beginning of Rava's next statement
items.text_en: Beginning of Rava's next statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new statement by Rava, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rava begins a new statement, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Ger's qualifications for judging and chalitzah
items.text_en: Ger's qualifications for judging and chalitzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a ger can judge another ger based on the verse about appointing a king, but not a Jew unless his mother is Jewish. For chalitzah, both parents must be Jewish, as derived from the verse 'and his name shall be called in Israel'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a ger (convert) can judge another ger by Torah law, based on the verse about appointing a king, and if his mother is Jewish he can judge even a born Jew.
The Gemara concludes that for chalitzah (the ritual of releasing a yevamah), both parents must be Jewish, as derived from the verse 'and his name shall be called in Israel'.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef regarding Elijah's ruling on chalitzah footwear
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef regarding Elijah's ruling on chalitzah footwear
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef dispute what would happen if Elijah came to rule about chalitzah. Rabbah says if Elijah says to perform chalitzah with a shoe (min'al), we listen, but if he says not with a sandal, we don't listen because the people have already adopted the sandal. Rav Yosef says the opposite: if Elijah says not with a shoe, we listen, but not with a sandal. The difference between them is whether a shoe is permitted initially (lechatchilah).

sub.text: Rabbah citing Rav Kahana citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah citing Rav Kahana citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbah states that if Elijah comes to rule, we listen regarding performing חליצה (chalitzah) with a shoe (מנעל) but not regarding forbidding a sandal (סנדל), because the people have already adopted the sandal.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rav Kahana citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rav Kahana citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef gives the opposite ruling: we listen if Elijah forbids the shoe, but not if he forbids the sandal, since the sandal is already customary.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two positions, and answers that the difference is whether a shoe (מנעל) is permitted לכתחילה (as an ideal standard) for חליצה (chalitzah).

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding the initial permissibility of a shoe
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding the initial permissibility of a shoe
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the view that a shoe is permitted initially, citing a mishnah that says if a woman performed chalitzah with a shoe, it is valid, implying only after the fact (di'avad) but not initially. The Gemara resolves that the mishnah's wording is due to the latter clause about a felt shoe (anpilya) being invalid even after the fact, so the first clause also uses the language of after the fact.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the view that a shoe is permitted לכתחילה (the ideal standard), citing a mishnah that says if a woman performed חליצה (chalitzah) with a shoe, it is valid, implying only בדיעבד (after the fact) but not initially.
The Gemara resolves that the mishnah's wording is due to the latter clause about a felt shoe (אנפיליא) being invalid even after the fact, so the first clause also uses the language of after the fact.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about the initial permissibility of a shoe
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about the initial permissibility of a shoe
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosi recounts meeting an elder who said he saw many chalitzot performed, but only with a sandal, not a shoe, citing the Torah's word 'na'alo' (shoe) and not 'min'alo' (his shoe). Rabbi Yaakov says in his name that one may perform chalitzah with a shoe initially. The Gemara then asks what is the reason for the one who says it is not permitted initially.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a tannaitic dispute regarding whether a shoe (מנעל) is permitted for chalitzah לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yosi recounts meeting an elder in Netzivin who said he saw many chalitzot performed only with a sandal (סנדל), not a shoe (מנעל), citing the Torah's word 'נעלו' (his shoe) and not 'מנעלו' (his shoe).

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov's ruling in the name of the elder
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov's ruling in the name of the elder
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov says in the elder's name that one may perform chalitzah with a shoe (מנעל) לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
The Gemara asks: what is the reason for the one who says a shoe (מנעל) is not permitted for chalitzah לכתחילה (the ideal standard)?

items.text: Reasons for prohibiting a shoe initially
items.text_en: Reasons for prohibiting a shoe initially
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers possible reasons for prohibiting a shoe initially: because it has a double layer (panta me'al ve'arketa me'al), but the Torah requires 'me'al' (on the foot) and not 'me'al d'me'al' (on top of another layer). This is rejected because it would invalidate even after the fact. Instead, the reason is a decree due to a patched shoe (min'al merupat) or a half-shoe (chatzi min'al).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the prohibition of a shoe (מנעל) initially is because it has a double layer (panta me'al ve'arketa me'al), violating the Torah's requirement of 'מעל' (on the foot) and not 'מעל דמעל' (on top of another layer).
The Gemara rejects this suggestion, arguing that if the reason were the double layer, it would invalidate the chalitzah even after the fact (בדיעבד), which is not the case.
The Gemara offers an alternative reason: the prohibition is a decree (גזירה) due to a patched shoe (מנעל מרופט), which might be mistaken for a proper shoe.
The Gemara offers another alternative reason: the prohibition is due to a half-shoe (חצי מנעל), which is not a complete shoe for chalitzah.

items.text: Rav's practice and the sign for releasing a yevamah
items.text_en: Rav's practice and the sign for releasing a yevamah
items.desc_en: Rav says that had he not seen his friend perform chalitzah with a sandal that has straps (shintzin), he would only perform chalitzah with an Arab sandal that is tightly bound. He adds that even with our sandal, which has a thick sole, we tie a belt (mitna) to ensure the chalitzah is proper. Rav Yehudah says in the name of Rav that the release of a yevamah to the public (i.e., to marry) requires the removal of most of the heel.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that had he not seen his friend perform חליצה (chalitzah) with a sandal that has straps (שינצין), he would only perform it with a tightly bound Arab sandal, and that even with our thick-soled sandal, they tie a belt (מיתנא) to ensure the חליצה is proper.
Rav Yehudah says in the name of Rav that the release of a יבמה (yevamah) to the public requires the removal of most of the heel (רוב העקב).

items.text: Discussion on the requirement of removing most of the foot or heel
items.text_en: Discussion on the requirement of removing most of the foot or heel
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that says if the straps were untied or most of the foot slipped out, the chalitzah is invalid. This implies that if she slipped it out (shamtah hi), it is valid, and it specifies 'most of the foot' but not 'most of the heel'. The Gemara resolves that 'most of the foot' is the same as 'most of the heel', and explains the terminology. It then cites Rabbi Yannai who says that whether he untied and she slipped, or she untied and he slipped, the chalitzah is invalid until she unties and slips it herself. Rabbi Yannai then raises a question about tearing or burning the shoe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that says if the straps were untied or most of the foot slipped out, the chalitzah is invalid, implying that if she slipped it out it is valid, and specifying 'most of the foot' but not 'most of the heel'.
The Gemara resolves that 'most of the foot' is the same as 'most of the heel', and explains the terminology: the entire force of the foot rests on the heel.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yannai who says that whether he untied and she slipped, or she untied and he slipped, the chalitzah is invalid until she unties and slips it herself.

Rabbi Yannai raises a question about tearing or burning the shoe: whether the requirement is to reveal the foot (which is satisfied) or to perform chalitzah (which is not), and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Question about two shoes worn one on top of the other
items.text_en: Question about two shoes worn one on top of the other
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nechemyah asks Rabbah about a case where two shoes are worn one on top of the other. If she removed the upper shoe and the lower one remains, it is invalid because the Torah requires 'me'al' (on the foot) and not 'me'al d'me'al'. But if she tore the upper shoe and removed the lower one, while the upper one remains, what is the law? Do we require chalitzah, which exists, or do we require uncovering the foot, which is not achieved? The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nechemyah asks Rabbah about the law when two shoes are worn one on top of the other.
The Gemara clarifies that if she removed the upper shoe and the lower remains, it is invalid because the Torah requires 'מעל' (on the foot) and not 'מעל דמעל' (on top of something on the foot).
Rabbi Nechemyah refines the case: she tore the upper shoe and removed the lower one while the upper remains; what is the law?

sub.text: Gemara's presentation of the unresolved dilemma
sub.text_en: Gemara's presentation of the unresolved dilemma
sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the unresolved dilemma: do we require the act of חליצה (removing the shoe), which exists, or do we require uncovering the foot, which is not achieved?

items.text: Yevamah who grew up among the brothers and intent in chalitzah
items.text_en: Yevamah who grew up among the brothers and intent in chalitzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a yevamah who grew up among the brothers is permitted to marry one of them, given the concern that she might have performed chalitzah with one of them. Rav Yehuda says that if we did not see it, we do not suspect, but if we saw it, we suspect. The Gemara then reconciles this with a baraita that requires intent for chalitzah to be valid, explaining that even if we see her removing a sandal, we do not suspect they intended chalitzah. An alternative version states that if we see it, we do suspect, and the requirement of intent is only to permit her to marry others, but for the brothers she is disqualified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether such a case existshare, and answers that the rabbis saw Rav Yehuda going out to the market with five zuz.
Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that a yevamah who grew up among the brothers is permitted to marry one of them, and we do not suspect she performed חליצה (chalitzah) unless we saw it.
The Gemara objects with a baraita that requires intent (כוונה) from both parties for חליצה (chalitzah) to be valid.
The Gemara resolves that even if we see her removing a sandal, we do not suspect they intended חליצה (chalitzah).
An alternative version states that if we see it, we do suspect, and the requirement of intent applies only to permit her to marry others, but for the brothers she is disqualified.

items.text: Sandal sewn with linen
items.text_en: Sandal sewn with linen
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that one may not perform chalitzah with a sandal sewn with linen, based on the verse 'Va'enchalech tachash'. The Gemara questions why other materials are not derived from the repetition of 'na'al', and then asks what the verse 'tachash' teaches us.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that one may not perform חליצה (chalitzah) with a sandal sewn with linen, citing the verse 'וָאֶנְעֲלֵךְ תָּחַשׁ' (I shod you with tachash).
The Gemara asks: perhaps only a sandal made of tachash (תחש) is valid, but not any other material?
The Gemara answers that the repetition of the word 'נַעַל' (shoe) in the verse expands the category to include other materials.
The Gemara objects: if the repetition of 'נַעַל' expands the category, then even any item (like a cloth shoe) would be valid, which is not the case.
The Gemara resolves: if so, what does the word 'תָּחַשׁ' (tachash) teach us? It limits the expansion to materials similar to tachash (i.e., leather), excluding cloth.

items.text: Sandal with leather sole and hair straps
items.text_en: Sandal with leather sole and hair straps
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rav whether a sandal with a leather sole and hair straps is valid for chalitzah. Rav responds by citing the verse 'Va'enchalech tachash', implying it is valid. Rabbi Elazar then questions whether a sandal entirely made of hair would also be valid, and Rav explains that such an item is called a 'kurka' (a type of felt shoe) and is not considered a sandal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rav whether a sandal with a leather sole and hair straps is valid for חליצה (chalitzah).
Rav answers by citing the verse 'וָאֶנְעֲלֵךְ תָּחַשׁ' (I shod you with tachash), implying the sandal is valid because the verse mentions a shoe made of tachash, which is leather.
Rabbi Elazar objects: if the verse validates any shoe, then a sandal entirely made of hair should also be valid.
Rav explains that a sandal entirely made of hair is called a 'קורקָא' (a felt shoe) and is not considered a sandal for חליצה (chalitzah).

items.text: Meaning of 'chalatzah' – removal or tying?
items.text_en: Meaning of 'chalatzah' – removal or tying?
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Shmuel whether the word 'chalatzah' in the context of chalitzah means removal (as in removing stones from a house) or tying (as in equipping for battle). Through a series of verses, the Gemara concludes that it means removal, based on the phrase 'me'al raglov' (from upon his foot), which implies removal, not tying.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Shmuel whether the word 'חלצה' in the chalitzah verse means removal, citing the verse about removing stones from a house.
Shmuel objects that the word might mean equipping for battle, citing the verse 'החלצו מאתכם אנשים לצבא', but the Gemara explains that even there it means removal from the house to battle.
The Gemara objects with the verse 'יחלץ עני בעניו', and explains that it means God will rescue the poor from Gehinnom as a reward for their poverty.
The Gemara objects with the verse 'חונה מלאך ה' סביב ליראיו ויחלצם', and explains that it means rescue from Gehinnom as a reward for fearing God.

sub.text: Gemara's objection with Rabbi Elazar and Rava
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection with Rabbi Elazar and Rava
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with the verse 'ועצמותיך יחליץ', where Rabbi Elazar says it refers to the best of blessings and Rava says it means strengthening bones, but the Gemara notes that the word can mean both; however, for chalitzah, if it meant tying, the verse would have said 'ברגלו' (on his foot) rather than 'מעל רגלו' (from upon his foot).

The Gemara resolves that the phrase 'מעל רגלו' (from upon his foot) proves the word means removal, because if it meant tying, the Torah would have written 'ברגלו' (on his foot); the extra 'מעל' indicates removal from the foot, and even from the leg.

items.text: Heretic's challenge to Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: Heretic's challenge to Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: A heretic challenges Rabban Gamliel by citing a verse that says 'chalatz meihem' (He removed from them), implying that God removed Himself from the Jewish people. Rabban Gamliel responds by pointing out that the verse says 'meihem' (from them), not 'lahem' (to them), and that in the case of a yevamah, the brothers perform chalitzah for her, not from her.

sub.desc_en: A heretic challenges Rabban Gamliel by citing the verse 'חָלַץ מֵהֶם' (He removed from them), claiming it shows God abandoned Israel.

Rabban Gamliel rebukes the heretic, noting the verse says 'חָלַץ מֵהֶם' (removed from them), not 'חָלַץ לָהֶם' (removed for them), and contrasts this with the yevamah for whom brothers perform חליצה (removal of the shoe) for her benefit.

items.text: Status of an 'anpilya' (sock) for chalitzah
items.text_en: Status of an 'anpilya' (sock) for chalitzah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that chalitzah with an 'anpilya' is invalid, implying it is not considered a 'na'al'. The Gemara brings a contradiction from a baraita that includes 'anpilya' in the prohibition of wearing shoes on Yom Kippur. Abaye and Rava resolve the contradiction by distinguishing between an 'anpilya' of leather (which is considered a shoe) and one of cloth (which is not). This is supported by another baraita about Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that chalitzah performed with an anpilya (sock) is invalid.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that an anpilya is not considered a na'al (shoe).
A baraita about the Temple supports this: a priest entering to separate תרומה (the priestly portion) may not wear an anpilya, just as he may not wear a shoe or sandal.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about Yom Kippur that includes anpilya in the prohibition of wearing shoes.
Abaye and Rava resolve the contradiction by distinguishing between an anpilya of leather (considered a shoe) and one of cloth (not considered a shoe), supported by a baraita about Yom Kippur.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rava's distinction
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rava's distinction
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava's distinction, listing various types of footwear that are invalid for chalitzah, including an 'anpilya' of leather, but not one of cloth.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava's distinction, listing various invalid footwear for חליצה (chalitzah), including an 'אנפיליא' (slipper) of leather but not one of cloth.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Valid and invalid chalitzah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Valid and invalid chalitzah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists conditions under which chalitzah is valid (standing, sitting, lying down, or from a blind man) and invalid (with a torn shoe that doesn't cover most of the foot, a sandal that doesn't hold most of the foot, with a wooden stump, a cloth shoe, or from a minor).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the conditions for valid and invalid chalitzah, including the shoe's material and the yavam's physical state.

items.text: Identifying the author of the Mishnah's ruling on the wooden stump
items.text_en: Identifying the author of the Mishnah's ruling on the wooden stump
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the ruling about the wooden stump (קַב הַקִּיטֵּעַ) follows Rabbi Meir, as taught in a baraita: a person with an amputated leg may go out with his wooden stump according to Rabbi Meir, but Rabbi Yosei prohibits it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the Mishnah's ruling on the wooden stump (קַב הַקִּיטֵּעַ) follows Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir permits and Rabbi Yosei prohibits going out with a wooden stump.

items.text: Debate about the cloth shoe: Abaye and Rava
items.text_en: Debate about the cloth shoe: Abaye and Rava
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that since the latter clause (cloth shoe) follows the Rabbis, the entire Mishnah is according to the Rabbis, and the first clause refers to a shoe covered with leather. Rava objects that if so, the Mishnah should have distinguished within the same case. Rava instead argues that the first clause follows Rabbi Meir and the latter clause also follows Rabbi Meir, but the difference is that one provides protection and the other does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's ruling on a cloth shoe (אנפיליא של בגד) aligns with the earlier dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis.
Abaye argues that since the latter clause (cloth shoe) follows the Rabbis, the entire Mishnah is according to the Rabbis, and the first clause refers to a shoe covered with leather.
Rava objects that if Abaye were correct, the Mishnah should have distinguished within the same case of a shoe, rather than introducing a separate cloth shoe clause.
Rava resolves that both clauses follow Rabbi Meir, but the difference is that one shoe provides protection (מגין) and the other does not.

items.text: Amemar's rulings on pressing the foot and walking on the heel
items.text_en: Amemar's rulings on pressing the foot and walking on the heel
items.desc_en: Amemar rules that one who performs chalitzah must press his foot (into the shoe). Rav Ashi objects from the Mishnah that allows various postures, and Amemar explains that even then he presses his foot. Amemar also rules that one who walks on the heel of his foot may not perform chalitzah; Rav Ashi objects from a baraita about 'support of the feet', and Amemar explains that refers to giving the shoe to another to perform chalitzah.

sub.desc_en: Amemar rules that one who performs חליצה (chalitzah) must press his foot into the shoe.
Rav Ashi objects from the Mishnah that allows various postures (standing, sitting, reclining) for חליצה (chalitzah), implying no pressing is required.
Amemar explains that even in those postures, one must still press his foot into the shoe.
Amemar rules that one who walks on the heel of his foot may not perform חליצה (chalitzah).
Rav Ashi objects from a ברייתא (baraita) that mentions 'support of the feet', implying such a person could perform חליצה (chalitzah).
Amemar explains that the baraita refers to giving the shoe to another person to perform חליצה (chalitzah), not to the one walking on his heel.

items.text: Rav Ashi's summary of Amemar's rulings
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's summary of Amemar's rulings
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that according to Amemar, one who has a clubfoot (בר אובא) or a flat foot (בר קיפוף) may not perform chalitzah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi summarizes Amemar's position: one with a clubfoot (בר אובא) or a flat foot (בר קיפוף) may not perform חליצה (chalitzah).

items.text: Definition of the foot: from the knee and below
items.text_en: Definition of the foot: from the knee and below
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that chalitzah is performed from the knee and below. The Gemara raises a contradiction from a verse that excludes those with stumps (בעלי קבין). It resolves that the verse says 'from upon his foot' (מֵעַל רַגְלוֹ), implying the foot itself, not above the knee. Rav Papa concludes that the shin bone (אִיסְתָּוִירָא) descends to the ground; if it were severed, the stump would be 'upon' and the leg 'above upon'. Rav Ashi counters that even if severed, what is attached to the foot is considered like the foot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says chalitzah is from the knee and below, but a verse (Deut 25:10) uses 'feet' (רְגָלִים) which excludes those with stumps (בעלי קבין), implying the foot itself, not the leg.
The Gemara resolves: here the verse says 'מֵעַל רַגְלוֹ' (from upon his foot), which implies the foot itself, not above the knee; 'upon' excludes 'above upon' (i.e., above the knee).
Rav Papa concludes that the shin bone (אִיסְתָּוִירָא) descends to the ground; if it were severed, the stump would be 'upon' and the leg 'above upon', which is excluded.
Rav Ashi counters that even if the shin bone is severed, what is attached to the foot is considered like the foot itself, so the stump is still valid for chalitzah.

items.text: Proofs that 'feet' can refer to the thigh area
items.text_en: Proofs that 'feet' can refer to the thigh area
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges the Mishnah's ruling that chalitzah is from the knee and above (invalid) by citing verses where 'feet' refers to the thigh area (e.g., the placenta emerging between the feet). Abaye explains that when a woman crouches to give birth, she presses her heels into her thighs. Other verses (about Saul and Sisera) are dismissed as euphemisms. Rabbi Yochanan interprets a verse about Sisera to mean he had seven relations, and questions whether one benefits from sin; he cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that the good of the wicked is...

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges the Mishnah's ruling that chalitzah above the knee is invalid by citing a verse where 'feet' (בין רגליה) refers to the thigh area, implying the term can include the upper leg.
Abaye explains that when a woman crouches to give birth, she presses her heels into her thighs, so 'between her feet' actually refers to the area near the thighs, not the foot itself.
The Gemara cites a verse about Saul's feet (referring to his thighs) as another proof that 'feet' can mean the thigh area, but dismisses it as a euphemism (לישנא מעליא).
The Gemara cites another verse where Saul's 'feet' refers to his thighs (for relieving himself), but again dismisses it as a euphemism.
The Gemara cites a verse about Eglon's 'feet' (referring to his thighs), but dismisses it as a euphemism.
The Gemara cites the verse about Sisera's 'feet' (between her feet) as another proof, but dismisses it as a euphemism.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse about Sisera to mean he had seven relations with Yael, based on the repeated verbs in the verse.
The Gemara questions how Yael could benefit from sin (the relations), implying a moral difficulty.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's principle that the good of the wicked is (incomplete), beginning an answer to the moral difficulty.

items.text: The serpent's impurity and its effect on Jews and Gentiles
items.text_en: The serpent's impurity and its effect on Jews and Gentiles
