items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the serpent's interaction with Eve is considered evil even when it speaks good, citing a verse. It then clarifies that the evil is the injection of זוהמא (impurity), which ceased for Israel at Sinai but not for Gentiles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the serpent's speaking good to Jacob is considered evil, citing the verse that warns Jacob not to speak with Laban from good to evil.
The Gemara objects that in the case of Laban, the evil might be mentioning idolatry, but here with the serpent, what evil is there?
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the serpent injected זוהמא (impurity) into Eve, which ceased for Israel at Sinai but not for Gentiles.

items.text: Source for chalitzah with any shoe
items.text_en: Source for chalitzah with any shoe
items.desc_en: A baraisa derives from the verse that chalitzah may be performed with any shoe, not just the yavam's own. However, the word 'his shoe' limits it to a shoe that fits him properly, excluding a shoe too large, too small, or one without a heel.

sub.desc_en: The baraisa cites the verse 'נעלו' (his shoe) and derives that any shoe (נעל) is valid for חליצה (chalitzah).
The baraisa resolves the apparent redundancy: 'נעלו' limits the shoe to one that fits him properly, excluding a shoe too large, too small, or one without a heel.

items.text: Abaye's incident with Rav Yosef regarding a left shoe
items.text_en: Abaye's incident with Rav Yosef regarding a left shoe
items.desc_en: Abaye, standing before Rav Yosef, was asked to give his shoe for a yevamah to perform chalitzah. He gave his left shoe, and Rav Yosef questioned whether the rabbis' allowance for a shoe not belonging to the yavam applies only after the fact, not initially. Abaye then clarified that he meant to give the shoe and transfer ownership.

sub.desc_en: Abaye was standing before Rav Yosef when a yevamah came for chalitzah; Rav Yosef asked Abaye for his shoe, and Abaye gave his left shoe.
Rav Yosef questioned whether the rabbis' allowance for a shoe not belonging to the yavam applies only בדיעבד (after the fact), not לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
Abaye clarified that he intended to give the shoe and transfer ownership to the yavam, so it would be considered the yavam's own shoe.

items.text: The Tanna behind the wooden sandal
items.text_en: The Tanna behind the wooden sandal
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Tanna who permits chalitzah with a wooden sandal as Rabbi Meir, based on a mishnah about a amputee going out with a wooden leg. Shmuel's father adds that this is only if it is covered with leather, and all agree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna is the source for the mishnah's ruling that a wooden sandal is valid for חליצה (chalitzah).
Shmuel identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Meir, citing a mishnah where Rabbi Meir permits an amputee to go out with a wooden leg (קַב).
The Gemara cites the mishnah in Shabbat where Rabbi Meir permits and Rabbi Yosi forbids an amputee going out with a wooden leg, showing Rabbi Meir's lenient approach to wooden footwear.
Avuh d'Shmuel qualifies that the wooden sandal is valid only if it is covered with leather (מחופה עור), and on this point all agree.

items.text: Dispute about the closed and declared sandal
items.text_en: Dispute about the closed and declared sandal
items.desc_en: Rav Pappi in the name of Rava rules that a closed sandal (מוסגר) renders chalitzah valid after the fact, while a declared sandal (מוחלט) renders it invalid. Rav Pappa in the name of Rava disagrees, holding that both are valid after the fact.

sub.text: Rav Pappi in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappi in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappi in the name of Rava rules that a closed sandal (מוסגר) renders chalitzah valid after the fact, while a declared sandal (מוחלט) renders it invalid.

sub.text: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava disagrees, holding that both a closed and a declared sandal are valid after the fact.

items.text: Challenges to Rav Pappa's view from impurity laws
items.text_en: Challenges to Rav Pappa's view from impurity laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the laws of a house afflicted with leprosy, where a closed house is different from a declared one. It attempts to compare the sandal to a garment with leprosy, but concludes that we cannot derive prohibitions from impurity laws. The Gemara then cites a final ruling by Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the laws of a house afflicted with leprosy, where a quarantined house and a confirmed house both impart impurity through entry.
The Gemara questions: if a confirmed leprous house is considered as if already crushed, how can it impart impurity through entry, since the verse requires a house?
The Gemara answers that the verse 'וְנָתַץ אֶת הַבַּיִת' (and he shall break down the house) teaches that even during demolition it is still called a house.
The Gemara brings a baraita about a rag with leprosy that imparts impurity when most of it enters a pure house, and questions whether it refers to a confirmed or quarantined rag.
The Gemara challenges: if the baraita refers to a quarantined rag, why does the latter clause treat an olive-bulk of the rag like a corpse, which is only true for a confirmed leprous rag?
The Gemara answers that for a garment with leprosy, the verse 'וְשָׂרַף אֶת הַבֶּגֶד' (and he shall burn the garment) teaches that even during burning it is still called a garment.
The Gemara rejects the comparison, stating that we cannot derive a halakha of prohibition from a halakha of ritual impurity.

items.text: Rava's final ruling on various sandals
items.text_en: Rava's final ruling on various sandals
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a closed sandal, a declared sandal, and a sandal used for idolatry all render chalitzah valid after the fact, but not initially. The text begins to discuss a sandal of an idolatrous offering.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a closed sandal (מוסגר), a declared sandal (מוחלט), and a sandal used for idolatry (עבודה זרה) all render חליצה (chalitzah) valid after the fact (בדיעבד) but not initially (לכתחילה), and the text begins to mention a sandal of an idolatrous offering (תקרובת עבודה זרה).

items.text: Halitzah with a shoe of an idolatrous city or an elder's shoe
items.text_en: Halitzah with a shoe of an idolatrous city or an elder's shoe
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that halitzah with a shoe from an idolatrous city or from an elder's honorific shoe is invalid. Ravina asks Rav Ashi why an elder's shoe is invalid because it is not made for walking, while a court shoe is also not made for walking. Rav Ashi answers that a court messenger may walk in it without the judge objecting.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that halitzah with a shoe from an idolatrous city (עיר הנדחת) or an elder's honorific shoe is invalid.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi: why is an elder's shoe invalid because it is not made for walking, when a court shoe is also not made for walking?
Rav Ashi answers that a court messenger may walk in the court shoe without the judge objecting, distinguishing it from the elder's shoe.

items.text: Halitzah at night and with the left foot
items.text_en: Halitzah at night and with the left foot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute: halitzah at night is valid according to the Sages but invalid according to Rabbi Elazar; halitzah with the left foot is invalid according to the Sages but valid according to Rabbi Elazar. The Gemara suggests the dispute is about whether we compare halitzah to the beginning of judgment or the end, but rejects the idea that it is about comparing judgments to plagues.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dispute: halitzah at night is valid for the Sages but invalid for Rabbi Elazar; halitzah with the left foot is invalid for the Sages but valid for Rabbi Elazar.
The Gemara suggests the dispute is about whether we compare disputes (ריבים) to plagues (נגעים) for the requirement of daytime.

The Gemara rejects that comparison, explaining that all agree we do not compare disputes to plagues; rather, the dispute is whether halitzah is like the beginning of judgment (תחילת דין) which can be done at night, or like the end of judgment (גמר דין) which must be by day.

items.text: Rabbah bar Chiyya's ruling and the dispute about a single judge
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Chiyya's ruling and the dispute about a single judge
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Chiyya performed halitzah with a wooden shoe, with a single judge, and at night. Shmuel praised him for acting like an individual authority. The Gemara explains that the difficulty was with the single judge, as the Mishnah records a dispute about halitzah with two or three judges, and Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yochanan the Sandal-maker validate it even with one. Rav Yosef bar Minyomei says the halakhah does not follow that pair, but alternatively all those cases are taught as individual opinions, citing Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi who saw Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha do so.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Chiyya performed halitzah with a wooden shoe, a single judge, and at night; Shmuel praised him for acting like an individual authority.
The Gemara asks what was difficult about Rabbah bar Chiyya's actions, noting that the wooden shoe and night are taught anonymously in the Mishnah.
The Gemara explains that the difficulty was with the single judge, citing the Mishnah's dispute where Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yochanan the Sandal-maker validate halitzah even with one judge.
A story is cited about a man who performed halitzah alone with the woman in prison, and Rabbi Akiva validated it.
Rav Yosef bar Minyomei says in the name of Rav Nachman that the halakhah does not follow that pair (Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yochanan the Sandal-maker).

Alternatively, all those cases are taught as individual opinions, citing Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi who saw Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha perform halitzah with a wooden shoe, a single judge, and at night.

items.text: The left foot dispute and the scriptural analogy
items.text_en: The left foot dispute and the scriptural analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Sages' reason for requiring the right foot: a verbal analogy from 'regel' to 'regel' from the metzora, where the right foot is used. It questions why Rabbi Elazar does not accept this analogy, given he uses a similar analogy for ear piercing. Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef says the positions are reversed, but Rava says the analogy for ear is free (mufneh) while for foot it is not, allowing a refutation that the metzora requires cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reason of the Sages for requiring the right foot in חליצה (the release ceremony).
Ulla answers that the Sages derive a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'regel' to 'regel' from the metzora (leper), where the right foot is used, so here too the right foot is required.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Elazar should accept this analogy, since he himself uses a similar גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'אוזן' (ear) to 'אוזן' for the ear-piercing ceremony requiring the right ear.
Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the positions are reversed: Rabbi Elazar actually requires the right foot and the Sages permit the left.

Rava rejects the reversal, explaining that the analogy for ear is מופנה (free for derivation) while the analogy for foot is not, so Rabbi Elazar can consistently accept the ear analogy but reject the foot analogy.
The Gemara asks what refutation is available against the non-free analogy.
The Gemara answers that one can refute the analogy by noting that the metzora requires cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool, which חליצה (the release ceremony) does not, so the analogy is not valid.

items.text: Halitzah without spitting
items.text_en: Halitzah without spitting
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman performed halitzah and spat but did not recite, it is valid; if she recited and spat but did not perform halitzah, it is invalid; if she performed halitzah and recited but did not spit, Rabbi Eliezer invalidates and Rabbi Akiva validates.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first case: halitzah with spitting but without recitation is valid.
The Mishnah states the second case: recitation and spitting without halitzah is invalid.
The Mishnah presents the third case: halitzah and recitation without spitting, with Rabbi Eliezer invalidating and Rabbi Akiva validating.

items.text: Opening dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Opening dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that the phrase 'כָּכָה יֵעָשֶׂה' implies that any action (ma'aseh) is essential. Rabbi Akiva counters that the verse 'כָּכָה יֵעָשֶׂה לָאִישׁ' refers only to actions performed on the man.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that the phrase 'כָּכָה יֵעָשֶׂה' (thus shall be done) teaches that any action (ma'aseh) is essential and delays the halitza.
Rabbi Akiva objects, citing the full verse 'כָּכָה יֵעָשֶׂה לָאִישׁ' (thus shall be done to the man), arguing it only refers to actions performed on the man, not any action.

items.text: Mishnah: Invalid chalitzah cases
items.text_en: Mishnah: Invalid chalitzah cases
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where chalitzah is invalid: a deaf man who performed chalitzah, a deaf woman who performed chalitzah, a woman who performed chalitzah with a minor, and a minor who performed chalitzah. It also discusses a case where one witness was found to be a relative or invalid, with Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar validating it. A story is told of a man who performed chalitzah in private in prison, and Rabbi Akiva validated it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing invalid cases of חליצה (chalitzah): a deaf man, a deaf woman, and a woman performing it with a minor.
The Mishnah rules that a minor who performed חליצה must repeat it after reaching majority, otherwise it is invalid.
The Mishnah states that if a witness was found to be a relative or invalid, the חליצה is invalid, but Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar validate it.
The Mishnah recounts a story of a man who performed חליצה in private in prison, and Rabbi Akiva validated it.

items.text: Rava's first statement: Reading is not essential
items.text_en: Rava's first statement: Reading is not essential
items.desc_en: Rava states that since reading (קְרִיאָה) is not essential, a mute man or woman who performed chalitzah is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that since reading (קְרִיאָה) is not essential, a mute man or woman who performed chalitzah is valid.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and Rava's response
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and Rava's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava from the Mishnah: why is a deaf person's chalitzah invalid? Is it because they cannot read? The Gemara answers that it is because they lack understanding (דֵעָה). Rava responds that mutes have understanding, but their mouths hurt, preventing speech.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava from the Mishnah: is the reason a deaf person's chalitzah is invalid because they cannot read (קְרִיָּיה)?
The Gemara rejects that reasoning and answers that the invalidity is because deaf people lack understanding (דֵעָה).
The Gemara objects: if the reason is lack of understanding, then mutes should also be invalid.
Rava responds that mutes have understanding (דֵעָה), but their mouths hurt, preventing speech.

items.text: Reassessment: Rava's statement applied to the latter clause
items.text_en: Reassessment: Rava's statement applied to the latter clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the statement of the school of Rabbi Yannai (based on the verses 'אָמַר' and 'וְאָמְרָה') contradicts Rava. It resolves that Rava's statement was actually said about the latter clause of the Mishnah (the case of a minor). Rava then concludes that since reading is essential, a mute's chalitzah is invalid, and the Mishnah follows Rabbi Zeira.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the school of Rabbi Yannai derives from the verses 'אָמַר' and 'וְאָמְרָה' that reading is essential for חליצה (chalitzah), contradicting Rava's earlier leniency for a mute.

The Gemara resolves that Rava's statement was actually said about the latter clause of the Mishnah (the case of a deaf person and a minor), where the disqualification is due to lack of understanding, not lack of reading.
Rava now concludes that since reading is essential (מעכבא), a mute's חליצה (chalitzah) is invalid.
The Gemara states that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Zeira's principle that one who is fit for the act of mixing (בילה) has the mixing not impede, but one unfit for mixing has it impede.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's principle
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's principle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira states: For anyone fit for mixing (בִּילָּה), mixing does not impede; for anyone unfit for mixing, mixing does impede.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira states a general principle: for anyone fit for mixing (בִּילָּה), mixing does not impede; for anyone unfit for mixing, mixing does impede.

items.text: Discussion on spitting disqualifying the yevamah
items.text_en: Discussion on spitting disqualifying the yevamah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a ruling sent to the father of Shmuel: if a yevamah spat (without completing chalitzah), she must perform chalitzah, implying she is disqualified from the brothers. The Gemara analyzes which Tanna holds this view, considering Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi. It cites a baraita about the lambs of Shavuot and the bread, where Rabbi holds that slaughter for their sake sanctifies the bread even if the blood is not thrown for their sake, while Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon requires both. The Gemara begins to question whether Rabbi Akiva holds that spitting does not disqualify.

sub.text: Anonymous ruling sent to the father of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Anonymous ruling sent to the father of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: A ruling is sent to the father of Shmuel: if a yevamah spat (without completing chalitzah), she must perform chalitzah, implying she is disqualified from the brothers.

The Gemara asks who holds this view, and rejects Rabbi Akiva: if he holds that spitting does not disqualify even in the context of the mitzvah (where the limbs are present), how could it disqualify from the brothers?
The Gemara considers Rabbi Elazar, but objects: spitting and chalitzah are two permitting factors (שני דברים המתירין), and one cannot operate without the other.

The Gemara concludes it is according to Rabbi, citing a baraita about the lambs of Shavuot: Rabbi holds that slaughter for their sake sanctifies the bread even if the blood is not thrown for their sake.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon disagrees, requiring both slaughter and blood throwing for their sake to sanctify the bread.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Akiva indeed holds that spitting does not disqualify, citing a baraita that begins 'חָלְצָה וְלֹא' (she performed chalitzah but did not...).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Cases of halitzah with missing elements
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Cases of halitzah with missing elements
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three scenarios: if she spat but did not recite, the halitzah is valid; if she spat but did not perform halitzah or recite, it is invalid; if she recited but did not spit or perform halitzah, there is no concern.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three cases of halitzah (חליצה) involving missing elements: spitting without recitation is valid; spitting without halitzah or recitation is invalid; recitation without spitting or halitzah is of no concern.

items.text: Gemara's question: Who is the Tanna?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Who is the Tanna?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah. It rejects Rabbi Eliezer because he holds that the act of halitzah is indispensable. It concludes it must be Rabbi Akiva, and then questions the ruling that if she spat but did not perform halitzah or recite, the halitzah is invalid: to whom is she forbidden? It answers: to the brothers, not to the world.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah, and rejects Rabbi Eliezer because he holds that the act of halitzah is indispensable.
The Gemara concludes it must be Rabbi Akiva, and then questions to whom the invalid halitzah forbids her.
The Gemara answers that she is forbidden to the brothers, not to the world, and concludes with 'שמע מינה' (learn from this).

items.text: Why distinguish between spitting and recitation?
items.text_en: Why distinguish between spitting and recitation?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why, according to Rabbi Akiva, spitting is treated differently from recitation. It answers: recitation appears both at the beginning and end of the process, so it is not confused; spitting appears only at the end, so people might mistakenly think it is not required and permit the yevamah to the brothers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why, according to Rabbi Akiva, spitting (רקיקה) is treated differently from recitation (קריאה) in the halacha of חליצה.

The Gemara answers: recitation appears both at the beginning and end of the process, so it is not confused; spitting appears only at the end, so people might mistakenly think it is not required and permit the yevamah to the brothers.

items.text: Alternative version and the story of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Abba
items.text_en: Alternative version and the story of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Abba
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that if the yevamah spat, she should perform halitzah and need not spit again. A story illustrates this: a woman spat before halitzah before Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Abba. Rabbi Abba objected that spitting must be done in order, but Rabbi Ami ruled that the order is not indispensable. Rabbi Abba later found a baraita supporting this.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that if the yevamah spat, she should perform halitzah and need not spit again.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Abba
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Abba
sub.desc_en: A story illustrates the ruling: a woman spat before halitzah before Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Abba, and Rabbi Ami ruled that she should perform halitzah and be permitted.
Rabbi Abba objects that spitting must be done in order, and that requiring her to spit again would lead to a leniency regarding the yevamah's status.

sub.text: Rabbi Ami's response and supporting baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ami's response and supporting baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami responds that the order is not indispensable, and Rabbi Abba later finds a baraita that supports this: whether halitzah preceded spitting or spitting preceded halitzah, what was done is valid.

items.text: Levi's questions: amputee and spitting blood
items.text_en: Levi's questions: amputee and spitting blood
items.desc_en: Levi went to the villages and was asked: may an amputee perform halitzah? And what about a yevamah who spat blood? The answer from the study hall: the Torah does not require a hand or actual spittle, so both are valid.

sub.desc_en: Levi was asked two questions: whether an amputee may perform halitzah, and whether a yevamah who spat blood is valid.
Levi did not have an answer, so he asked the study hall, which replied that the Torah does not require a hand or actual spittle, so both are valid.

items.text: Digression: The seal of a decree and the power of Torah
items.text_en: Digression: The seal of a decree and the power of Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the verse 'But I will tell you what is inscribed in the writing of truth,' implying there is a writing that is not true. It resolves that a decree with an oath is not torn, but one without an oath is. Rabba and Abaye debate atonement through Torah and kindness. A story about Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and a family that died young shows that Torah study can annul a decree. Finally, it discusses that a communal decree can be torn even after being sealed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the verse 'But I will tell you what is inscribed in the writing of truth,' implying there is a writing that is not true.
The Gemara resolves that a decree with an oath is not torn, but one without an oath is.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Ami citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Ami citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Ami in the name of Rabbi Yonatan cites a verse to prove that a decree with an oath is not torn.
Rabba and Abaye debate that atonement (כפרה) is achieved through Torah study and kindness, and their own lifespans reflect this.
A story about Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and a family that died young shows that Torah study can annul a decree.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Unya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Unya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Unya in the name of Rav questions how a communal decree can be unsealed, citing a verse that implies it is sealed.
The Gemara resolves that a communal decree can be torn even after being sealed, distinguishing between an individual and a community.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabba bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabba bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avuha specifies that the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are the time when an individual's decree can be torn.

items.text: Spitting blood: resolution and objection
items.text_en: Spitting blood: resolution and objection
items.desc_en: They sent to Shmuel's father: a yevamah who spat blood should perform halitzah because blood cannot be without some saliva. An objection is raised from a baraita that blood from the mouth is pure. The Gemara resolves: here it refers to blood from sucking (which has saliva), there it refers to blood that flows freely.

sub.text: The court's message to Shmuel's father
sub.text_en: The court's message to Shmuel's father
sub.desc_en: They sent to Shmuel's father that a yevamah who spat blood should perform halitzah because blood cannot be without some saliva.
An objection is raised from a baraita that blood from the mouth is pure, contradicting the assumption that it contains saliva.
The Gemara resolves: here it refers to blood from sucking (which has saliva), there it refers to blood that flows freely.

items.text: Beginning of next Mishnah: A deaf-mute who performed halitzah
items.text_en: Beginning of next Mishnah: A deaf-mute who performed halitzah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins discussing the case of a deaf-mute who performed halitzah, but the Gemara's analysis is not included in this segment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the case of a deaf-mute who performed halitzah, setting up the topic for the Gemara's discussion.

items.text: Halitzah of a minor male and female
items.text_en: Halitzah of a minor male and female
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that the Mishnah's ruling that a minor's halitzah is invalid is only according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages hold that a minor's halitzah is meaningless. For a minor female, Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav again attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi Meir, who derives from the word 'ish' that a woman is equated to a man, but the Sages say that only 'ish' is written, so a woman—whether adult or minor—is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that the Mishnah's ruling on a minor male's halitzah is only according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages hold that a minor's halitzah is meaningless.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav attributes the Mishnah's ruling on a minor female to Rabbi Meir, who derives from the word 'איש' (man) that a woman is equated to a man.
The Sages respond that only 'איש' is written in the passage, so a woman—whether adult or minor—is valid for halitzah.

items.text: Who are the Sages? A story about prayer and Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Who are the Sages? A story about prayer and Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Sages as Rabbi Yosei, relating a story where Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi debated whether one's eyes should be directed downward or upward during prayer. Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei then arrived and reconciled both verses by saying one's eyes should be downward and one's heart upward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who the Sages are, and answers that it is Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara relates a story where Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi debated whether one's eyes should be directed downward or upward during prayer, each citing a verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei's resolution
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei arrives and reconciles the two verses by saying one's eyes should be downward and one's heart upward.

items.text: The incident with Abadan and the halitzah ruling
items.text_en: The incident with Abadan and the halitzah ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi arrived at the study hall; Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei stepped over the heads of the students due to his honor. Abadan rebuked him, leading to a sharp exchange. When a yevamah came before Rabbi, he sent Abadan to examine her, but Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei privately ruled that a woman—whether adult or minor—is valid for halitzah. Rabbi then told him it was unnecessary as the elder had already ruled. Abadan was humiliated, and the Gemara recounts his punishment: he became a leper, his sons drowned, and his daughters-in-law performed mi'un.

sub.desc_en: The narrator describes Rabbi arriving at the study hall while Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei steps over the heads of the students due to his honor.
Abadan rebukes Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei for stepping over the heads of the holy people and questions his worthiness to learn from Rabbi.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei's retort
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei's retort
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei retorts by comparing himself to Moses and Abadan's teacher to God, and Rav Yosef notes that Abadan disrespected Rabbi by saying 'your teacher' instead of 'my teacher'.
A yevamah comes before Rabbi; Rabbi sends Abadan to examine her, but Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei privately rules that a woman—whether adult or minor—is valid for halitzah.
Rabbi tells Abadan that the elder had already ruled, and Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei rebukes Abadan for stepping over the heads of the holy people when he is not needed.

sub.text: Narrator (Stam) and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Narrator (Stam) and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi orders Abadan to his place; the Tanna recounts that Abadan became a leper, his sons drowned, and his daughters-in-law performed mi'un, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak blesses God for shaming Abadan in this world.

items.text: The age for a minor female to perform halitzah
items.text_en: The age for a minor female to perform halitzah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami learns from the words of bar Rabbi (Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei) that a minor female may perform halitzah even at a very young age (pe'utut). Rava says until she reaches the age of vows (onat nedarim). The halakhah is until she grows two pubic hairs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami derives from the words of bar Rabbi (Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei) that a minor female may perform halitzah even at a very young age (pe'utut).
Rava qualifies that the minor female must have reached the age of vows (onat nedarim) to perform halitzah.
The halakhah is established that the minor female must have grown two pubic hairs (brought two hairs) to perform halitzah.

items.text: Halitzah with two judges is invalid
items.text_en: Halitzah with two judges is invalid
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomei in the name of Rav Nachman states that the halakhah does not follow that pair (the one who said halitzah is valid with two). The Gemara questions why this was necessary, since Rav Nachman already said halitzah requires three. The Gemara explains that both statements are needed: one to teach that even after the fact two are invalid, and the other to teach that initially five are not required.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyomei in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomei in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomei reports in Rav Nachman's name that the halakhah does not follow the pair who permit halitzah with two judges.
The Gemara questions why Rav Nachman needed to repeat this ruling, since he already stated that halitzah requires three judges.
The Gemara explains that both statements are necessary: the first teaches that initially five are not required, and the second teaches that even after the fact two are invalid.

items.text: The case of halitzah in private and the location of the incident
items.text_en: The case of halitzah in private and the location of the incident
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions a case where halitzah was performed between him and her alone. The Gemara asks how we know about it, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that witnesses saw from outside. A further inquiry arises: was the incident that occurred between him and her outside (in public) and brought before Rabbi Akiva in prison, or did it happen in prison? Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav resolves that the incident happened in prison and the case was brought to prison.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Mishnah could know about a halitzah performed in private between the yavam and yevamah alone.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that witnesses saw the halitzah from outside.
The Gemara raises a doubt: was the halitzah performed outside and brought before Rabbi Akiva in prison, or was it performed inside the prison itself?

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav resolves that the halitzah occurred in prison and the case was brought to the prison.

items.text: Definition of mistaken halitzah
items.text_en: Definition of mistaken halitzah
items.desc_en: The baraita states that a mistaken halitzah is valid. Resh Lakish defines it as when they tell the yavam: 'Perform halitzah, and by doing so you will marry her.' Rabbi Yochanan objects, citing a mishnah that halitzah requires mutual intent; otherwise it is invalid. The Gemara then redefines mistaken halitzah as when they say: 'Perform halitzah on condition that she gives you 200 zuz.'

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that a mistaken halitzah is valid, and Resh Lakish defines it as when they tell the yavam: 'Perform halitzah, and by doing so you will marry her.'
Rabbi Yochanan objects, citing a mishnah that halitzah requires mutual intent; otherwise it is invalid, and challenges Resh Lakish's definition.
The Gemara redefines mistaken halitzah as when they say: 'Perform halitzah on condition that she gives you 200 zuz,' and cites a supporting baraita.

items.text: Supporting story with Rabbi Chiyya
items.text_en: Supporting story with Rabbi Chiyya
items.desc_en: A story is brought to support the definition: a woman fell before an unsuitable yavam, and they told him to perform halitzah on condition of receiving 200 zuz. The case came before Rabbi Chiyya, who validated the halitzah.

sub.desc_en: A story is brought to support the definition: a woman fell before an unsuitable yavam, they told him to perform halitzah on condition of receiving 200 zuz, and Rabbi Chiyya validated the halitzah.

items.text: Case of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
items.text_en: Case of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
items.desc_en: A man came before Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba. The woman refused to stand for halitzah, claiming her sitting was her standing. She said she knew the yavam but he wanted her money. Rabbi Chiyya told the yavam to perform halitzah and thereby marry her. After he did so, Rabbi Chiyya told him to perform a proper halitzah to free her for others, since she was now forbidden to him.

sub.desc_en: A man came before Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba; the woman refused to stand, claiming her sitting was her standing, and said she knew the yavam but he wanted her money.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba instructed the yavam to perform halitzah (חליצה) to marry her, then after he did so, told him to perform a proper halitzah to free her for others.

items.text: Case of Rav Pappa's daughter-in-law
items.text_en: Case of Rav Pappa's daughter-in-law
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa's daughter-in-law fell before an unsuitable yavam. Abaye told the yavam to perform halitzah and thereby marry her. Rav Pappa questioned Abaye about Rabbi Yochanan's ruling. Abaye then told the yavam to perform halitzah on condition of receiving 200 zuz. After halitzah, Abaye told the woman to pay, but the yavam said she was mocking him. The Gemara supports this with a baraita about a prisoner crossing a river: if the ferryman says he was mocking, he only gets his wages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of Rav Pappa's daughter-in-law who fell before an unsuitable yavam; Abaye initially instructs the yavam to perform חליצה (ḥalitza) and thereby marry her, and Rav Pappa questions Abaye about Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.
Abaye responds by instructing the yavam to perform חליצה (ḥalitza) on condition that she give him 200 zuz; after the act, Abaye tells the woman to pay, but the yavam claims she was mocking him.
The Gemara cites a baraita about a prisoner crossing a river: if he offers a dinar but the ferryman says he was mocking, the ferryman only gets his usual wages.
The Gemara concludes that just as the ferryman can claim he was mocking, here too the woman can claim she was mocking, so she is exempt from paying the 200 zuz.

items.text: Abaye's inquiry about the yavam's parents
items.text_en: Abaye's inquiry about the yavam's parents
items.desc_en: Abaye asked the yavam where his father and mother were; he replied they were in the town. Abaye then cast his eyes upon them and they died, implying the yavam was now free to marry the woman.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks the yavam where his father is, and the yavam responds that he is in the town.
Abaye asks the yavam where his mother is, and the yavam responds that she is also in the town.
Abaye casts his eyes upon the yavam's parents, and they die, implying the yavam is now free to marry the woman.

items.text: Comparison of mistaken and coerced halitzah and get
items.text_en: Comparison of mistaken and coerced halitzah and get
items.desc_en: A baraita states: mistaken halitzah is valid, mistaken get is invalid; coerced halitzah is invalid, coerced get is valid. The Gemara clarifies: if he says 'I am willing,' even halitzah is valid; if not, even a get is invalid. The true meaning: mistaken halitzah is always valid, mistaken get always invalid; coerced halitzah and get are sometimes valid, sometimes invalid, depending on whether he says 'I am willing.' This is derived from a verse about offerings: they coerce him until he says 'I am willing.'

sub.desc_en: A baraita states the rules: mistaken halitzah is valid, mistaken get is invalid; coerced halitzah is invalid, coerced get is valid.
The Gemara questions the baraita's distinction: if the man says 'I am willing,' even halitzah should be valid; if not, even a get should be invalid.
The Gemara resolves: mistaken halitzah and get are always as stated; coerced halitzah and get are sometimes valid, sometimes invalid, depending on whether he says 'I am willing.'
A baraita from the verse about offerings teaches that coercion is applied until he says 'I am willing,' and the same applies to gittin.

items.text: Dispute about recognizing parties for halitzah
items.text_en: Dispute about recognizing parties for halitzah
items.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Sehora in the name of Rav Huna says: we perform halitzah even if we do not recognize the parties, and we write the document of halitzah only if we do recognize them, due to concern for mistaken courts. Rava himself says: we only perform halitzah if we recognize them, and therefore we write the document even if we do not recognize them, as we are not concerned for mistaken courts.

sub.text: Rava citing Rav Sehora citing Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rav Sehora citing Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Sehora in the name of Rav Huna rules that we perform halitzah (חליצה) and mi'un (מיאון) even without recognizing the parties.

sub.text: Rava citing Rav Sehora citing Rav Huna (continued)
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rav Sehora citing Rav Huna (continued)
sub.desc_en: Therefore, we only write the document of halitzah (גט חליצה) or mi'un (גט מיאון) if we recognize the parties, due to concern for mistaken courts (בית דין טועין).

Rava himself disagrees: we only perform halitzah (חליצה) and mi'un (מיאון) if we recognize the parties, and therefore we write the documents even without recognition, as we are not concerned for mistaken courts.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Procedure of Ḥalitzah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Procedure of Ḥalitzah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the basic procedure of ḥalitzah: the yavam and yevamah come to court, the court advises them, and the yevamah recites verses, removes the shoe, spits, and declares 'Thus shall be done to the man who does not build his brother's house'. Initially, only these verses were recited, but after Rabbi Hurkanos read the entire passage, it became the practice. The Mishnah also notes that the declaration 'ḥalutz ha-na'al' is a mitzvah for the judges, while Rabbi Yehudah says it is a mitzvah for all present.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing the basic procedure of חליצה (ḥalitzah): the yavam and yevamah come to court, the court advises them, and the yevamah recites verses, removes the shoe, spits, and declares the prescribed formula.

The Mishnah notes that initially only these verses were recited, but after Rabbi Hurkanos read the entire passage under the terebinth in Kfar Eitam, it became the practice to complete the entire passage.

The Mishnah concludes with the ruling that the declaration 'בית חלוץ הנעל' (the house of the one whose shoe was removed) is a מצוה (commandment) for the judges, while Rabbi Yehudah says it is a מצוה for all present to say 'חלוץ הנעל' (the one whose shoe was removed).

items.text: Gemara: Order of Actions in Ḥalitzah
items.text_en: Gemara: Order of Actions in Ḥalitzah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah states the order of ḥalitzah: the yevamah recites, the yavam recites, she removes the shoe, spits, and recites again. The Gemara questions why this is necessary, as it is already in the Mishnah. It explains that Rav Yehudah teaches that this is the proper order, but if one reverses the order, it is still valid. A baraita supports this, stating that whether spitting precedes ḥalitzah or vice versa, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah states the order of ḥalitzah: the yevamah recites, the yavam recites, she removes the shoe, spits, and recites again.
The Gemara questions why Rav Yehudah's statement is necessary, since the Mishnah already teaches the order.
The Gemara answers that Rav Yehudah teaches that this is the proper order (לכתחילה), but if one reverses the order, it is still valid (בדיעבד).
A baraita supports this, stating that whether spitting precedes ḥalitzah or vice versa, it is valid.

items.text: Abaye and Rava: Proper Recitation of Verses
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava: Proper Recitation of Verses
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that when reciting the verses for the yevamah, one should not pause between 'lo' and 'avah yevami' to avoid implying 'avah yevami' (he desires to marry me). Similarly, for the yavam, one should not pause between 'lo' and 'ḥafatzti' to avoid implying 'ḥafatzti lekachtah' (I desire to take her). Rava disagrees, arguing that a pause is a separate matter and is not a concern.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that when reciting the halitzah verses for the yevamah, one should not pause between 'לֹא' and 'אָבָה יַבְּמִי' to avoid implying 'אָבָה יַבְּמִי' (he desires to marry me).
Abaye similarly rules that for the yavam, one should not pause between 'לֹא' and 'חָפַצְתִּי' to avoid implying 'חָפַצְתִּי לְקַחְתָּהּ' (I desire to take her).
Rava disagrees, arguing that a pause is a separate matter and is not a concern.

items.text: Rav Ashi and Rav Kahana: Practical Application of Rava's View
items.text_en: Rav Ashi and Rav Kahana: Practical Application of Rava's View
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi finds Rav Kahana struggling while reciting 'lo avah yevami' and asks if he does not accept Rava's view. Rav Kahana responds that Rava concedes regarding 'lo avah yevami'. Abaye then gives instructions for writing the get ḥalitzah document, specifying which verses to recite for each party.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi finds Rav Kahana struggling while reciting 'לֹא אָבָה יַבְּמִי' and asks if he does not accept Rava's view that one may pause between words.
Rav Kahana responds that Rava concedes regarding the phrase 'לֹא אָבָה יַבְּמִי' that it must be recited without pause.

sub.text: Abaye's instructions for writing the get ḥalitzah
sub.text_en: Abaye's instructions for writing the get ḥalitzah
sub.desc_en: Abaye gives instructions for writing the get ḥalitzah document, specifying which verses to recite for each party.

items.text: Mar Zutra and Mar bar Idi: Writing the Entire Passage
items.text_en: Mar Zutra and Mar bar Idi: Writing the Entire Passage
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra would rule lines and write the entire passage of ḥalitzah. Mar bar Idi objects because the passage is not permitted to be written (as a Torah scroll). The halakhah follows Mar Zutra.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra would rule lines and write the entire passage (of the חליצה verses).
Mar bar Idi objects that the entire passage was not given to be written (as a חליצה document).
The Gemara rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Mar Zutra's practice.

items.text: Abaye and Rava: Requirements for Spitting
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava: Requirements for Spitting
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that if the yevamah spat and the wind carried the spittle away, it is invalid because the spittle must reach the yavam's face. If the yavam is tall and she is short, the wind carrying it still satisfies 'in his face'. If she is tall and he is short, it must reach his face and then go. Rava adds that if she ate garlic or a gourd and then spat, it is invalid because the spitting must be from her own saliva. Rava also requires the judges to see the spittle leaving her mouth, as per the verse 'before the elders... and she shall spit'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that if the yevamah spat and the wind carried the spittle away, the act is invalid because the spittle must reach the yavam's face.
Abaye explains the reason: the Torah requires spitting 'in his face', so the spittle must reach his face.
Abaye resolves that if the yavam is tall and she is short, wind carrying the spittle still satisfies 'in his face'; but if she is tall and he is short, it must reach his face and then go.
Rava adds that if she ate garlic or a gourd and then spat, it is invalid because the spitting must be from her own saliva.
Rava further requires the judges to see the spittle leaving her mouth, as derived from the verse 'before the elders... and she shall spit'.

items.text: Rabbi Yehudah: The Declaration 'Ḥalutz Ha-Na'al'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehudah: The Declaration 'Ḥalutz Ha-Na'al'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehudah recounts that when sitting before Rabbi Tarfon, a yevamah came for ḥalitzah, and Rabbi Tarfon instructed all present to say 'ḥalutz ha-na'al' three times, supporting his view that the mitzvah applies to all standing there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that the declaration 'בית חלוץ הנעל' is a מצוה for the judges and not for the students.

sub.text: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Yehudah's story
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Yehudah's story
sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Rabbi Yehudah said: once we were sitting before Rabbi Tarfon, and a yevamah came for חליצה, and he told us all to respond 'חלוץ הנעל' three times.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Three disputes on mi'un
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Three disputes on mi'un
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three disagreements between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel: whether mi'un applies only to betrothed or also to married women; whether it applies to the husband or also to the yavam; and whether it must be done in his presence and in court. Beit Hillel then argue that a minor may perform mi'un multiple times, while Beit Shammai respond that this would make Jewish women hefker, so she should wait until she grows up.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai rules that מיאון (mi'un, the refusal of a minor to remain married) applies only to betrothed women, while Beit Hillel rules it applies to both betrothed and married women.
Beit Shammai rules that מיאון applies only to the husband and not to the yavam (levir), while Beit Hillel rules it applies to both the husband and the yavam.
Beit Shammai rules that מיאון must be performed in the husband's presence and in court, while Beit Hillel rules it may be done in his presence or not, and in court or not.
Beit Hillel argues that a minor may perform מיאון multiple times, even four or five times, contradicting Beit Shammai's restrictive view.
Beit Shammai responds that allowing repeated מיאון would make Jewish women הפקר (ownerless), so she should wait until she grows up, then perform מיאון once and remarry.

items.text: First explanation: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
items.text_en: First explanation: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains Beit Shammai's reasoning: there is no condition in marriage, so if a married woman could perform mi'un, it would imply that marriage is conditional. The Gemara raises objections: what about a woman who entered the chuppah but was not yet intimate? Shmuel answers that there is no condition in chuppah either. What about when the father handed her over to the husband's agents? The Gemara says the Rabbis did not distinguish in that case.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that Beit Shammai's reasoning is that there is no condition in marriage (אֵין תְּנַאי בְּנִשּׂוּאִין), so allowing a married woman to perform מיאון (mi'un) would imply that marriage is conditional.
The Gemara raises an objection: what about a woman who entered the chuppah (חוּפָּה) but was not yet intimate — how does Beit Shammai's reasoning apply?
Shmuel answers that there is no condition in chuppah (אֵין תְּנַאי בְּחוּפָּה) either, so the same logic applies.
The Gemara further objects: what about when the father handed her over to the husband's agents — how does Beit Shammai's reasoning apply?
The Gemara resolves that the Rabbis did not distinguish (לָא פְּלוּג רַבָּנַן) in that case, meaning the same reasoning applies uniformly.

items.text: Second explanation: Rabbah and Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Second explanation: Rabbah and Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef both state that Beit Shammai's reason is that a man does not want his intercourse to be an act of zenut. The Gemara raises the same objections about chuppah and agents, and answers similarly. Beit Hillel, however, hold that since there are kiddushin and a ketubah, people will not think the intercourse is zenut.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef both state that Beit Shammai's reason is that a man does not want his intercourse to be an act of זנות (forbidden sexual union).
The Gemara raises the objection: if the girl entered the חופה (canopy) but was not yet intimate, what can be said — why would Beit Shammai still forbid her to perform מיאון (refusal)?
The Gemara answers: the man is not pleased that his חופה (canopy) should be one of prohibition, so he would not want her to refuse after חופה alone.
The Gemara raises another objection: if the father handed the girl over to the husband's agents, what can be said — why would Beit Shammai forbid her to refuse?
The Gemara answers: the Sages did not distinguish (between cases) — the decree applies uniformly.
Beit Hillel hold that since there are קידושין (betrothal) and a כתובה (marriage contract), people will not think the intercourse is an act of זנות (forbidden union).

items.text: Third explanation: Rav Pappa on produce
items.text_en: Third explanation: Rav Pappa on produce
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains both opinions based on produce (peirot). Beit Shammai argue that if a married woman could perform mi'un, the husband would consume her produce since she will eventually leave. Beit Hillel counter that if she can perform mi'un, the husband will improve the produce, fearing her relatives might otherwise pressure her to leave.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa introduces a third explanation for both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel based on the issue of produce (פֵּירֵי).

sub.text: Rav Pappa's explanation for Beit Shammai
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation for Beit Shammai
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that Beit Shammai forbids mi'un for a married woman because if she could perform mi'un, the husband would consume her produce (פֵּירֵי) since she will eventually leave him.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's explanation for Beit Hillel
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation for Beit Hillel
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that Beit Hillel permits mi'un for a married woman because the husband will improve the produce (פֵּירֵי), fearing that her relatives might otherwise pressure her to leave him.

items.text: Fourth explanation: Rava on the wedding feast
items.text_en: Fourth explanation: Rava on the wedding feast
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Beit Shammai's reason is that a man does not trouble to prepare a feast and then lose it. Beit Hillel say that both parties are pleased, so that a rumor of marriage will go out about them.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that Beit Shammai's reasoning is that a man does not trouble to prepare a wedding feast (סעודה) and then lose it through the wife's מיאון (refusal).
Rava explains that Beit Hillel holds that both parties are pleased with the marriage, so that a rumor of marriage (קלא דאישות) will go out about them.

items.text: Discussion on mi'un for yavam: Rabbi Oshaya and Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Discussion on mi'un for yavam: Rabbi Oshaya and Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the second Mishnaic dispute: whether mi'un applies to the yavam. Rabbi Oshaya states that a minor can perform mi'un to nullify the ma'amar (declaration of yibum) but not the zikah (levirate bond). Rav Chisda explains that ma'amar is by her consent, so she can uproot it, but zikah is against her will, so she cannot. The Gemara then questions whether the same applies to bi'ah (intercourse with the yavam), which is also against her will.

sub.desc_en: רבי אושעיא (Rabbi Oshaya) states that a minor yevama may perform מיאון (refusal) to nullify the מאמר (levirate betrothal) but not the זיקה (levirate bond).
רב חסדא (Rav Chisda) explains the reasoning: the מאמר (levirate betrothal) is by her consent, so she can uproot it, but the זיקה (levirate bond) applies against her will, so she cannot uproot it.
The Gemara questions whether the same logic applies to ביאה (intercourse with the yavam), which is also against her will, implying she should not be able to nullify it through מיאון (refusal).

items.text: Ulla's position: mi'un annuls even the levirate bond
items.text_en: Ulla's position: mi'un annuls even the levirate bond
items.desc_en: Ulla argues that a minor can perform mi'un to annul even the levirate bond (zikka) because she is uprooting the first marriage, not the bond imposed by Heaven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: a minor can annul the marriage she contracted herself, but can she annul the levirate bond (zikka) imposed by Heaven?
Ulla rules that a minor can perform mi'un even against the levirate bond, because she is uprooting the original marriage, not the bond itself.

items.text: Rava's objection and resolution: the case of a tzarat erva
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution: the case of a tzarat erva
items.desc_en: Rava objects from a baraita: if a minor could annul the levirate bond, her tzarat erva could remarry through levirate marriage after mi'un. The Gemara answers that the case involves a tzarat erva, where the minor appears as her daughter-in-law at the time of the levirate bond, making mi'un ineffective.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Ulla's position by citing a baraita: if a minor can perform mi'un and does not, her tzarah (co-wife) must perform חליצה (release) and cannot enter levirate marriage; but if the minor could annul the bond now, why should the tzarah not remarry through יבום (levirate marriage)?
The Gemara resolves: the case involves a tzarat erva (co-wife of a forbidden relative), where the minor appears as her daughter-in-law at the time of the levirate bond, so mi'un is ineffective.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel debate: mi'un to one brother and its effect on others
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel debate: mi'un to one brother and its effect on others
items.desc_en: Rav holds that mi'un to one brother renders her forbidden to all brothers, analogous to a divorcée (ba'alat ha-get). Shmuel disagrees, arguing that since she initiates the refusal, she is permitted to other brothers, as she says 'I do not want you' but implies she wants another.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a minor who performs מיאון (refusal) against one brother becomes forbidden to all brothers, analogizing her to a divorcée (בעלת הגט) who is forbidden to all the brothers after divorce.
Shmuel disagrees with Rav, ruling that the minor is permitted to other brothers because she initiates the refusal, saying 'I do not want you' but implying she wants another.

items.text: Rav Asi's lenient view: mi'un permits even the same brother
items.text_en: Rav Asi's lenient view: mi'un permits even the same brother
items.desc_en: Rav Asi rules that mi'un to one brother permits her even to that same brother, but the Gemara limits this to a case of two yevamin, where mi'un cannot apply to half a zikka.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi rules: she is even permitted to the yavam with whom she performed mi'un, because we are dealing with two yevamim and mi'un cannot annul a half-levirate bond.
The Gemara asks whether Rav Asi's view aligns with Rabbi Oshaya's position that mi'un cannot annul the zikka.
The Gemara answers that in the case of a single yavam, she can indeed annul the zikka, so Rav Asi's case must involve two yevamin.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves two yevamin, where mi'un cannot apply to half a zikka, so Rav Asi's leniency stands.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and dispute over who disagreed
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and dispute over who disagreed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that mi'un to one brother permits her to the other brothers, but some disagreed. Abaye identifies Rav as the dissenter, Rava says it was Rabbi Oshaya, and others say Rav Asi.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement reported by Ravin
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement reported by Ravin
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules: a minor who performs mi'un with one yavam is permitted to the other brothers, but the sages did not agree with him.
The Gemara asks: who are the sages who did not agree with Rabbi Yochanan?
Abaye says Rav; Rava says Rabbi Oshaya; some say Rav Asi.
Rava counters that the dissenter was Rabbi Oshaya, not Rav.
An alternative tradition identifies Rav Asi as the dissenter.

items.text: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on mi'un in the husband's presence
items.text_en: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on mi'un in the husband's presence
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records Beit Shammai requiring mi'un in the husband's presence; Beit Hillel cites the case of Pishon the camel-driver whose wife performed mi'un not in his presence. The Gemara explains that Pishon was punished measure for measure, and notes that the case involved a married woman, which Beit Shammai normally forbids, but here they made an exception.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah records Beit Shammai requiring mi'un in the husband's presence, and Beit Hillel citing the case of Pishon the camel-driver whose wife performed mi'un not in his presence.
Beit Shammai responds that Pishon was punished measure for measure for his own crooked dealings.
The Gemara infers from the fact that Pishon consumed the fruit of his wife's property that she was a married woman (נשואה), not merely an arusah (betrothed).
The Gemara objects: Beit Shammai normally holds that a married woman (נשואה) cannot perform mi'un, so why did they accept the case of Pishon's wife?
The Gemara resolves that Pishon was doubly crooked, so Beit Shammai made an exception and allowed mi'un even for a married woman in his case.

items.text: The requirement of three judges for mi'un
items.text_en: The requirement of three judges for mi'un
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that mi'un requires three judges. Rabba attributes this to Beit Shammai, while Abaye says even Beit Hillel require three, just not experts. A baraita confirms that both agree on three, though Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon permit two. Rav Nachman rules like the latter pair.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that mi'un requires three judges, citing the general rule that חליצה (release from levirate marriage) and מיאונין (refusal of marriage) are performed before three.
The Gemara asks which Tanna is the author of this Mishnah.
Rabba answers that the Mishnah reflects the view of Beit Shammai.
Abaye counters that even Beit Hillel require three judges, but they do not require expert judges (מומחין).
A baraita confirms that both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that three judges are required for mi'un.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon permit mi'un with only two judges.
Rav Nachman rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows the lenient pair who permit two judges.

items.text: Interpretation of 'until she grows up' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'until she grows up' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says a minor can perform mi'un until she grows up. Shmuel explains she must say she wants the first mi'un, while Ulla says the Mishnah means she can either mi'un and grow up and marry, or mi'un and marry immediately. The Gemara notes a textual difficulty with Shmuel's interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'until she grows up,' noting that mi'un is a one-time act, so why mention growth?
Shmuel explains that 'until she grows up' means until she is old enough to declare that she still wants her first mi'un.
Ulla explains that the Mishnah teaches two possibilities: either she performs mi'un and grows up and marries, or she performs mi'un and marries immediately.
The Gemara notes a textual difficulty: according to Ulla the Mishnah's wording fits, but according to Shmuel it should have said 'until she grows up and says,' not 'until she grows up and marries.'

items.text: Mishnah: which minor needs mi'un and related opinions
items.text_en: Mishnah: which minor needs mi'un and related opinions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a minor who needs mi'un as one married off by her mother or brothers with her consent; if without consent, no mi'un is needed. Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus adds that a girl who cannot guard her kiddushin does not need mi'un. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov offer further rulings on the status of such marriages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a minor who needs mi'un as one married off by her mother or brothers with her consent; without consent, no mi'un is needed.
Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonos adds that a girl who cannot guard her kiddushin does not need mi'un.
Rabbi Elazar rules that a minor's marriage is void, treating her as a seduced woman, with implications for terumah (priestly portion) eligibility.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov distinguishes between impediments from the husband, which preserve marital status, and those not from the husband, which nullify it.

items.text: Gemara: the text of the get mi'un
items.text_en: Gemara: the text of the get mi'un
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda that originally the get mi'un was written with a long formula, but later shortened due to verbosity.

sub.text: Gemara citation about the get mi'un formula
sub.text_en: Gemara citation about the get mi'un formula
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda or a baraita reports: originally they wrote a get mi'un with a verbose formula, then they shortened it.
The Gemara explains that because the formula was verbose, the Sages later shortened it.

items.text: Definition of מיאון and expansions by Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
items.text_en: Definition of מיאון and expansions by Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by explaining the formula for a bill of refusal (גט מיאון). It then cites a baraita defining מיאון as the minor saying 'I do not want my husband' or 'I do not want the kiddushin my mother and brothers gave me.' Rabbi Yehuda expands this to include a case where she says this while in the bridal chamber or while serving guests, and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda further expands it to when she sends a messenger to refuse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the formula for a bill of refusal (גט מיאון) was instituted to prevent confusion with a regular divorce document (גט).
The baraita defines מיאון as the minor saying 'I do not want my husband' or 'I do not want the kiddushin my mother and brothers gave me.'
Rabbi Yehuda expands the definition to include a case where the minor says 'I do not want my husband' while in the bridal chamber (אפריון) on the way to her husband's house.
Rabbi Yehuda further expands the definition to include a case where the minor says 'I do not want my husband' while serving guests in her husband's house.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda expands the definition to include a case where the minor sends a messenger to refuse while her husband sends her to a shopkeeper.

items.text: Halakha like Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus and the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
items.text_en: Halakha like Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus and the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the halakha follows Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus (from the Mishnah). It then cites a baraita: a minor who did not refuse and then married, according to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, her marriage itself constitutes her refusal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's opening statement of Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus.
Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus.
A baraita is cited: a minor who did not refuse and then married — according to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, her marriage itself constitutes her refusal (מיאון).

items.text: Question about kiddushin as refusal
items.text_en: Question about kiddushin as refusal
items.desc_en: A question is raised: if the minor was betrothed (not married), does that also constitute refusal? The Gemara answers with a baraita: according to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, her betrothal is her refusal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if the minor was betrothed (not married), does that also constitute refusal?
The Gemara answers by citing a baraita: according to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, her betrothal is her refusal.

items.text: Series of inquiries about the dispute and halakha regarding Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
items.text_en: Series of inquiries about the dispute and halakha regarding Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a series of questions: do the Sages disagree with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira? If so, is the dispute only regarding betrothal or also marriage? Is the halakha like him? It then brings a proof from Shmuel that the Sages do disagree, and from a story about Rabbi's daughters-in-law that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira even in the case of marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a series of nested questions: whether the Sages disagree with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, whether the dispute applies to betrothal or marriage, whether the halakha follows him, and in which scenario.

sub.text: Proof from Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Proof from Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, which implies that the Sages disputed his view.
The Gemara asks whether the story about Rabbi's daughters-in-law involved a marriage or merely betrothal, and begins to recount the story.
Rabbi declares there is no greater act of מיאון (refusal) than this, and the Gemara resolves that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira even in the case of marriage.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's view on the minor wife's status
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's view on the minor wife's status
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Elazar's opinion (from the Mishnah) and Shmuel's comment that he found no one who equated the minor's status like Rabbi Elazar, who treated her as one who strolls with him in the courtyard, able to immerse and eat terumah in the evening.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Elazar's opinion from the Mishnah that a minor wife who refuses her husband may immerse and eat תרומה (priestly portion) in the evening.

Shmuel states that he found no sage who equated the minor's status like Rabbi Elazar, who treated her as one who strolls with him in the courtyard, able to immerse and eat תרומה (priestly portion) in the evening.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on the minor wife's status
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on the minor wife's status
items.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says the minor's actions are void and she is not considered his wife in any respect except requiring מיאון. Rabbi Yehoshua says she is like his wife in all respects except she leaves through מיאון. Rabbi comments that Rabbi Eliezer's view is more consistent, but the Gemara questions the logic of both positions.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that a minor's marriage is void: the husband has no rights to her found property, earnings, vows, inheritance, or impurity, and she is not his wife except that she requires מיאון (refusal) to leave.
Rabbi Yehoshua argues that the minor is fully his wife in all respects, except that she leaves through מיאון (refusal) rather than a גט (bill of divorce).
Rabbi comments that Rabbi Eliezer's view is more consistent, but the Gemara questions Rabbi Yehoshua's logic: if she is truly his wife, why does she not require a גט (bill of divorce)?
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer's position is also inconsistent: if she is not his wife at all, why should she need even מיאון (refusal)? She should simply leave without any formal act.

items.text: Definition of 'restraint from the husband' and 'restraint not from the husband'
items.text_en: Definition of 'restraint from the husband' and 'restraint not from the husband'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's distinction between a restraint that is from the husband and one that is not. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel defines it based on the woman's stated reason. Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chanina bar Avin define it based on whether he gave a get (restraint from the husband) or she refused (restraint not from the husband), with different legal consequences. The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's statement is merely explanatory.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definition of 'restraint from the husband' and 'restraint not from the husband' mentioned in the Mishnah.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel defines the distinction based on the woman's stated reason: if she blames her husband, it is restraint from him; if she blames other unsuitable men, it is not from him.

sub.text: Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chanina bar Avin
sub.text_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chanina bar Avin
sub.desc_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chanina bar Avin define the distinction based on the legal action: if he gave a גט (bill of divorce), it is restraint from him with severe consequences; if she performed מיאון (refusal), it is not from him with lenient consequences.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah itself already states the same distinction between מיאון (refusal) and giving a גט (divorce), so the Amoraim's definition seems redundant.
The Gemara resolves that the Amoraim are merely explaining the Mishnah's distinction, not adding new law.

items.text: Mishnah: Consequences of מיאון vs. get, and remarriage after return
items.text_en: Mishnah: Consequences of מיאון vs. get, and remarriage after return
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: a woman who refuses is permitted to her husband's relatives, but if he gave a get, they are forbidden. It then discusses cases where a get was given and she was remarried, or she refused and was remarried, and the rules for returning to the first husband.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the basic rule: a woman who performs מיאון (refusal) is permitted to her husband's relatives, but if he gave a get, they are forbidden, and she is disqualified from the priesthood.

The Mishnah continues with cases of remarriage after a get or מיאון, stating that after a get and remarriage to another, she may return to the first husband, but after מיאון and remarriage, she is forbidden to return.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rule of get after ma'un and ma'un after get
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rule of get after ma'un and ma'un after get
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states a general rule: if a woman receives a get after having performed ma'un (refusal) with a previous husband, she is forbidden to return to him; but if she performs ma'un after receiving a get, she is permitted to return. It then elaborates on a case where a woman refuses one husband, marries another, and is divorced or refuses again, reiterating the rule that any relationship ended by get forbids return, while ma'un permits it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: a get after ma'un forbids return, but ma'un after a get permits return.
The Mishnah elaborates with a case sequence, reiterating that any exit by get forbids return, while ma'un permits it.

items.text: Gemara's initial contradiction: Does ma'un nullify get?
items.text_en: Gemara's initial contradiction: Does ma'un nullify get?
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's first clause that ma'un after get nullifies the get, allowing return. But it cites a baraita (the second clause) that seems to contradict this, implying that another man's ma'un does not nullify one's own get.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's first clause that ma'un (refusal) after a get nullifies the get, allowing the woman to return to the first husband.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita (the second clause of the Mishnah) which implies that another man's ma'un does not nullify one's own get.

items.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: Two different Tannaim
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: Two different Tannaim
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel resolves the contradiction by asserting that the two clauses were taught by different Tannaim, so they do not conflict.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel resolves the contradiction by asserting that the two conflicting clauses were taught by different Tannaim, so they do not conflict.

items.text: Rava's challenge: Why not distinguish between one's own ma'un and another's?
items.text_en: Rava's challenge: Why not distinguish between one's own ma'un and another's?
items.desc_en: Rava questions the need for two Tannaim: perhaps the rule is that one's own ma'un nullifies one's own get, but another's ma'un does not, because the woman is familiar with the first husband's hints and might be persuaded to return. The Gemara counters that if so, even one's own ma'un should not nullify the get for the same reason, but the Mishnah already shows that it does, so the distinction fails.

sub.desc_en: Rava questions the contradiction, proposing that one's own ma'un (refusal) nullifies one's own get (bill of divorce), but another's ma'un does not.
The Gemara objects that if the woman is familiar with the first husband's hints, even his own ma'un should not nullify the get, yet the Mishnah shows it does.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah already tested this scenario and found that the woman was not persuaded, so the distinction stands.

items.text: New contradiction: Another's ma'un does nullify get?
items.text_en: New contradiction: Another's ma'un does nullify get?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new contradiction from a baraita: if a woman refused a second husband and then received a get from a third, she is permitted to return to the second only if the third marriage ended by death or divorce, implying that ma'un from the third nullifies the second's get. But another baraita contradicts this, saying that another's ma'un does not nullify the get.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new contradiction between two baraitot: one baraita implies that another man's ma'un (refusal) nullifies the first husband's get, while the other baraita states that another's ma'un does not nullify the get.
The Gemara cites the second baraita that explicitly states that another's ma'un does not nullify the get, creating a contradiction with the first baraita.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar and Ulla: Resolving the contradiction
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Ulla: Resolving the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar again attributes the conflicting baraitot to different Tannaim. Ulla offers a different resolution: the case where ma'un nullifies the get is when the woman has been 'thrice-documented' with gittin, making her appear like an adult, so her ma'un is effective.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction by attributing the conflicting baraitot to different Tannaim.
Ulla offers a different resolution: the case where ma'un nullifies the get is when the woman has been 'thrice-documented' with gittin, making her appear like an adult, so her ma'un is effective.

items.text: Historical inquiry: The case of get then ma'un
items.text_en: Historical inquiry: The case of get then ma'un
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a historical episode during a time of danger when the question was asked: if a woman left the first husband by get and the second by ma'un, may she return to the first? Sages were hired to ask Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, who both forbade it. Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosi comments that this ruling was unnecessary, as if she is permitted to a forbidden relative (a karet prohibition), certainly she is permitted to a less severe prohibition (a lav).

sub.text: Gemara's inquiry: who is the Tanna?
sub.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: who is the Tanna?
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the ruling about a woman who left her first husband with a get and the second with ma'un, and Rav Yehuda quoting Rav introduces a verse as an opening.

The Gemara recounts that during a time of danger, this halachic question arose: if a woman left her first husband with a get and the second with ma'un, may she return to the first? Sages hired a man to ask Rabbi Akiva in prison and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in Netzivin, and both forbade it.
