Rava concluded that famine is worse than war: in war she is believed if she says he died in bed, but in famine she must say she buried him.

items.text: Other disasters: collapse, snakebite, plague
items.text_en: Other disasters: collapse, snakebite, plague
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that a building collapse and snake/scorpion bites are like war because she might think he died. Regarding plague, there is a dispute: some say it is like war because she might think he died, others say it is not because people say plague lasts seven years and a person does not die before his time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that a building collapse and snake/scorpion bites are like war because she might think he died.
One opinion holds that plague is like war because she might think he died.
Another opinion holds that plague is not like war because people say plague lasts seven years and a person does not die before his time.

items.text: Question: if she initiated the war
items.text_en: Question: if she initiated the war
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if the woman herself started the war, what is the law? Do we say she has no reason to lie?

sub.desc_en: A question is raised: if the woman herself started the war, what is the law? Do we say she has no reason to lie?

items.text: Gemara's inquiry: Does the woman's claim of peace undermine her credibility?
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: Does the woman's claim of peace undermine her credibility?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a woman who says 'peace in the world' after a catastrophe is believed, or whether her established presumption of being a widow prevents her from lying, as she would not risk undermining her status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a woman who could claim 'peace in the world' is believed, or whether her established presumption (חזקה) prevents her from lying, as she would not risk undermining her status.

items.text: First attempted proof: Case of 'a house fell on us'
items.text_en: First attempted proof: Case of 'a house fell on us'
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a case where a woman says 'a house fell on us, he died and I was saved' and she is not believed. It distinguishes this case because the husband could have also been saved by a miracle, so her claim is not reliable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where a woman says 'a house fell on us, he died and I was saved' and she is not believed, as an attempted proof for the previous question.
The Gemara distinguishes the case: since the husband could have also been saved by a miracle, her claim is not reliable, so the proof is rejected.

items.text: Second attempted proof: Case of 'gentiles fell on us'
items.text_en: Second attempted proof: Case of 'gentiles fell on us'
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a case where a woman says 'gentiles fell on us, he died and I was saved' and she is believed. It explains this follows Rav Idi's principle that a woman is armed (with her wits) and thus can save herself, but her husband may not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where a woman who says 'gentiles fell on us, he died and I was saved' is believed, as a proof for the current sugya.
The Gemara explains that this case follows Rav Idi's principle: a woman is armed with her wits and can save herself, but her husband may not, so she is believed.

items.text: Story of the groom in the fire and Rava's distinction
items.text_en: Story of the groom in the fire and Rava's distinction
items.desc_en: A story is told of a groom whose wedding canopy caught fire; his wife called people to see her husband, and they found a charred body and a hand. Rav Chiyya bar Avin thought this was like the 'house fell on us' case, but Rava distinguished because the wife did not claim a miracle, and the evidence suggested another person died. Rav Chiyya bar Avin offered alternative explanations for the charred body and hand.

sub.desc_en: A story is told of a groom whose wedding canopy caught fire; his wife called people to see her husband, and they found a charred body and a hand.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Avin's initial position
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin's initial position
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin thought this case is like the 'house fell on us' case, where the wife is not believed.
Rava objects: the cases are not comparable, because here the wife called people to see her husband, and the evidence of a charred body and a hand suggests another person died.
Rav Chiyya bar Avin offers alternative explanations: the charred body was a rescuer who died, and the hand was a burn-induced deformity that caused the groom to flee in shame.

items.text: New inquiry: Is a single witness in wartime believed?
items.text_en: New inquiry: Is a single witness in wartime believed?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new question: whether a single witness in a war is believed. The doubt is whether the reason a single witness is believed is because he would not lie about something that will become known, or because the woman investigates carefully before remarrying, but in war she might hate her husband and not investigate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new inquiry: is a single witness in a war believed? The doubt is whether the reason a single witness is believed is because he would not lie about something that will become known, or because the woman investigates carefully before remarrying, but in war she might hate her husband and not investigate.

items.text: Proof from Nehemiah's testimony and Rava's reinterpretation
items.text_en: Proof from Nehemiah's testimony and Rava's reinterpretation
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama brings a proof from Rabbi Akiva's story where Nehemiah said that Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava allowed remarrying based on one witness even in a land disturbed by troops. Rava initially objects that the text should say 'every place with troops', then reinterprets that Nehemiah was excusing himself from coming to the rabbis because of the troops, and the ruling applies everywhere.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama brings a proof from Rabbi Akiva's story where Nehemiah reports that Rabban Gamliel the Elder allowed remarrying based on one witness even in a land disturbed by troops.
The Gemara asks what is the significance of the phrase 'this country is riddled with troops' and concludes that it implies one witness is deemed credible even in war.
Rava objects that if the proof were valid, Nehemiah should have said 'every place where there are troops' rather than specifying 'this country'.
Rava reinterprets that Nehemiah was excusing himself from coming to the rabbis because of the troops, and the ruling applies everywhere, not just in wartime.

items.text: Proof from the story of Abba Yosef and the drowning students
items.text_en: Proof from the story of Abba Yosef and the drowning students
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story where two Torah scholars drowned and Rabbi married their widows based on women's testimony. Since water is like war, and women are like a single witness, this proves a single witness is believed in war. The Gemara then notes that this case involved waters without end, where the wife is forbidden, so it must be that the witnesses said they saw them brought up.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi allowed the wives of two drowned Torah scholars to remarry based on women's testimony, arguing that water is like war and women are like a single witness, thus proving a single witness is believed in war.

The Gemara objects that the case involved waters without end, where the wife is forbidden, so it must be that the witnesses said they saw the bodies brought up, making it irrelevant to the war question.

items.text: Opening principle: reliance on signs
items.text_en: Opening principle: reliance on signs
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that we do not rely on the witnesses themselves but on the signs they provide to identify a person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that we rely on the signs (סימנים) provided by witnesses, not on the witnesses themselves.

items.text: Case of deposited sesame seeds and Rav Chisda's ruling
items.text_en: Case of deposited sesame seeds and Rav Chisda's ruling
items.desc_en: A man deposited sesame seeds with a friend. The friend claimed he took them and that the current seeds are different, but he gave a count. Rav Chisda thought this is like two Torah scholars (where signs suffice), but Rava objected: sesame seeds have no identifying signs, and the count could be coincidental.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a man deposited sesame seeds with a friend, who claimed he took them and that the current seeds are different, but gave a count.
Rav Chisda thought this case is like two Torah scholars (where signs suffice), so we do not say the original seeds are gone and these are different.
Rava objected: sesame seeds have no identifying signs, and the count could be coincidental, so the case is not analogous to two Torah scholars.

items.text: Mar Kashisha's objection: concern for emptying (פינן)
items.text_en: Mar Kashisha's objection: concern for emptying (פינן)
items.desc_en: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda asks Rava: Do we not worry that a container might have been emptied? He cites a mishna where during danger, they wrote abbreviations on vessels, implying we assume the contents match the label.

sub.text: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda asks Rav Ashi whether we are concerned that a container might have been emptied (פינן), citing a mishna where during danger they wrote abbreviations on vessels, implying we assume the contents match the label.

items.text: Ravina's objection: Rabbi Yosei's ruling
items.text_en: Ravina's objection: Rabbi Yosei's ruling
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: Do we not worry about emptying? He cites Rabbi Yosei who says that even if a barrel is marked 'terumah', it is considered hullin because we assume it was originally full of terumah and then emptied.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether we do not worry about the possibility that a container was emptied, citing Rabbi Yosei's ruling that a barrel marked 'terumah' is considered hullin because we assume it was originally full of terumah and then emptied.

items.text: Resolution: dispute about whether the bailee would deny
items.text_en: Resolution: dispute about whether the bailee would deny
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that everyone agrees we worry about emptying, but they dispute whether the bailee would have denied the deposit if he had emptied it. One side says he would have denied outright; the other says he might have forgotten or left it for others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute by stating that everyone agrees we worry about emptying (פינוי), but they argue whether the bailee would have denied the deposit if he had emptied it: one side says he would have denied outright, the other says he might have forgotten or left it for others.

items.text: Case of Yitzchak the Exilarch: concern for two people with same name
items.text_en: Case of Yitzchak the Exilarch: concern for two people with same name
items.desc_en: Yitzchak the Exilarch died while traveling. A message was sent about his death. The question is whether we worry there might be another Yitzchak with the same description. Abaye says yes, Rava says no.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents the case: Yitzchak the Exilarch died while traveling from Kurdistan to Aspamia.
The gemara asks whether we must be concerned about the existence of another Yitzchak with the same description.
Abaye rules that we are concerned (חיישינן) for the possibility of two people with the same name.
Rava rules that we are not concerned (לא חיישינן) for the possibility of two people with the same name.

items.text: Abaye's proof from a get found in Nehardea
items.text_en: Abaye's proof from a get found in Nehardea
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a get found in Nehardea where the husband wrote his location. The father of Shmuel sent it to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, who ordered that all of Nehardea be checked. Rava counters that if there were a real concern, they would have checked the whole world; the order was only due to respect for Shmuel's father.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a get found in Nehardea, written with the husband's location, as evidence that we do not suspect another person of the same name.
The father of Shmuel sent the get to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, who ordered that all of Nehardea be checked for another man of the same name.
Rava objects that if there were a real concern about identity, they would have ordered the whole world checked, not just Nehardea.
Rava resolves that the order to check Nehardea was only due to respect for Shmuel's father, not because of a genuine halachic concern.

items.text: Rava's proof from two documents in Machoza
items.text_en: Rava's proof from two documents in Machoza
items.desc_en: Rava cites two documents in Machoza with similar names (Chavai bar Nannai and Nannai bar Chavai), and Rava bar Avuh collected money based on them, even though such names were common. The Gemara asks: And Abaye? (implying Abaye would disagree).

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces a proof from two documents in Machoza bearing the names Chavai bar Nannai and Nannai bar Chavai, from which Rava bar Avuh collected money, despite such names being common there.
The Gemara asks: And Abaye? (implying Abaye would disagree with Rava's proof).

items.text: Gemara's initial reasoning: why no concern for a get found in a place where the husband is not known
items.text_en: Gemara's initial reasoning: why no concern for a get found in a place where the husband is not known
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why there is no concern for the get being invalid: if the concern is that the husband might have fallen and died, he is careful; if the concern is that he entrusted the get to someone else, since the names match, he would not entrust it to him. If you say he might have given it via delivery (מסירה), documents are acquired by delivery, so it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what concern could invalidate the get, and answers that if the concern is the husband fell and died, he is careful, and if the concern is he entrusted it to someone else, since the names match he would not entrust it to him.
The Gemara considers the possibility that the husband gave the get via delivery (מסירה), and concludes that since documents are acquired by delivery, the get is valid.

items.text: The case of the get found in Sura with witnesses that the husband was in Nehardea
items.text_en: The case of the get found in Sura with witnesses that the husband was in Nehardea
items.desc_en: A get was found in Sura, written by Anan bar Chiyya from Nehardea, divorcing his wife. The Sages checked from Sura to Nehardea and found no other Anan bar Chiyya except a cripple named Anan bar Chiyya who was in Nehardea. Witnesses testified that on the day the get was written, the cripple was with them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where a get was found in Sura, written by Anan bar Chiyya from Nehardea, and after checking from Sura to Nehardea, no other Anan bar Chiyya was found except a cripple, and witnesses testified that on the day the get was written, the cripple was with them.

items.text: Abaye's ruling: no concern here
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling: no concern here
items.desc_en: Abaye says that even though he generally holds we are concerned, here we are not concerned because the witnesses say the husband was in Nehardea, so what was he doing in Sura?

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that even though he generally holds we are concerned (חיישינן), here we are not concerned because the witnesses say the husband was in Nehardea, so what was he doing in Sura?

items.text: Rava's ruling: concern here
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: concern here
items.desc_en: Rava says that even though he generally is not concerned, here he is concerned, because perhaps he went by a flying camel or by jumping, or he gave the get via delivery of words (מסירת מילי).

sub.desc_en: Rava states that although he generally is not concerned about such possibilities, here he is concerned because the husband might have traveled by a flying camel, by jumping, or by delivering the get through words (מסירת מילי).

items.text: Rav and Rav Huna's instruction to scribes about writing the place of writing
items.text_en: Rav and Rav Huna's instruction to scribes about writing the place of writing
items.desc_en: Rav and Rav Huna instructed scribes: when you are in Shilei, write Shilei, even if the words (of the get) are delivered in Hinei; and when you are in Hinei, write Hinei, even if the words are delivered in Shilei. This supports the possibility of delivery of words (מסירת מילי).

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites Rav and Rav Huna's instruction to scribes about writing the place of writing in a get (גט), supporting the possibility of delivery of words (מסירת מילי).

items.text: The dispute about the case of the sesame seeds (שומשמי) and the halakhic conclusion
items.text_en: The dispute about the case of the sesame seeds (שומשמי) and the halakhic conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what was the ruling regarding the case of the sesame seeds (a similar case of concern). Rav Yeimar said we are not concerned, Ravina said we are concerned, and the halakha is that we are concerned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what was the halakhic ruling regarding the case of the sesame seeds (שומשמי).
Rav Yeimar rules that we are not concerned about the possibility of forgery in the sesame seeds case.
Ravina rules that we are concerned about the possibility of forgery in the sesame seeds case.
The Gemara concludes that the halakha follows Ravina: we are concerned about the possibility of forgery.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah's case of a quarrel (קטטה) between husband and wife
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah's case of a quarrel (קטטה) between husband and wife
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes a quarrel between them. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: when she says to her husband 'Divorce me.' But all cases are like that! Rather, when she says 'You divorced me.' The Gemara asks: let her be believed based on Rav Hamnuna's principle that a woman is not brazen-faced before her husband. The answer is that she says 'You divorced me in front of so-and-so and so-and-so,' and when we ask them, they say it never happened.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes a quarrel (קטטה) between husband and wife in the Mishnah's case.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that the quarrel is when she says to her husband 'Divorce me.'
The Gemara objects that all women say this to their husbands, so it cannot define a quarrel.
The Gemara revises the answer: the quarrel is when she says to her husband 'You divorced me.'
The Gemara asks why she should not be believed based on Rav Hamnuna's principle.
Rav Hamnuna's principle is cited: a woman who says 'You divorced me' is believed, because a woman is not brazen-faced before her husband.
The Gemara resolves that she says 'You divorced me in front of so-and-so and so-and-so,' and when we ask them, they say it never happened, so she is not believed.

items.text: The reason for the quarrel: two opinions
items.text_en: The reason for the quarrel: two opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the reason for the quarrel (that she is not believed)? Rav Chanina said: because she is lying. Rav Shimi bar Ashi said: because she says based on what seems plausible. What is the difference between them?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the reason for the quarrel (that she is not believed)?
Rav Chanina answers: because she is lying (משום דמשקרא).
Rav Shimi bar Ashi answers: because she says based on what seems plausible (משום דאמרה בדדמי).
The Gemara asks: what is the practical difference between these two reasons?

items.text: The unresolved query about a single witness in a quarrelsome marriage
items.text_en: The unresolved query about a single witness in a quarrelsome marriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if the husband was quarrelsome, is a single witness still believed? The reason a single witness is believed is either because the matter will become known and he won't lie, or because the woman investigates carefully before remarrying. In a quarrelsome case, perhaps she does not investigate carefully. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved query: in a quarrelsome marriage, is a single witness believed because the matter will become known, or because the woman investigates carefully, which she may not do here?
The query remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding a deaf-mute woman
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding a deaf-mute woman
items.desc_en: A baraita records that the Sages challenged Rabbi Yehuda: according to your view, a deaf-mute woman who can hear (pikachat) may remarry, but a deaf-mute woman (shotah) may not? They argue that both should be permitted. The Gemara then recounts a case where Rabbi Yehuda's court instructed a woman to mourn her husband, and the Sages taught her to do so falsely to permit her remarriage.

sub.desc_en: A baraita reports that the sages objected to Rabbi Yehuda's position: if a clever woman may remarry but a foolish one may not, then both should be permitted.
A story is told of a woman who came to Rabbi Yehuda's court; the judges told her to mourn, but they actually followed the rabbis' view and intended to permit her.
The Sages conclude that both a hearing woman and a deaf-mute woman should be permitted to remarry based on their own testimony.
The Gemara recounts a case where a woman came to Rabbi Yehuda's court, and they instructed her to mourn her husband by tearing her clothes and loosening her hair.
The Gemara explains that the court, following the Sages' view, taught the woman to falsely perform mourning rituals in order to permit her remarriage.

items.text: The Mishnah: Beit Hillel's original ruling and Beit Shammai's expansion
items.text_en: The Mishnah: Beit Hillel's original ruling and Beit Shammai's expansion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Beit Hillel initially said they only heard of the ruling for a woman coming from the harvest and from that same country, as in the actual incident. Beit Shammai argued that it applies to all harvests and all locations, and that the Sages only spoke of the harvest as an example. Beit Hillel eventually retracted and ruled like Beit Shammai.

sub.desc_en: Beit Hillel states that a woman is believed only if she comes from the harvest, in the same country, and like the actual incident.
Beit Shammai objects that the rule applies to all harvests and all countries, and Beit Hillel retracted to rule like Beit Shammai.
The Mishnah concludes that Beit Hillel retracted and ruled like Beit Shammai.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's logic
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's logic
items.desc_en: A baraita records Beit Shammai's challenge to Beit Hillel: if the ruling is limited to wheat harvest, what about barley harvest? And what about other agricultural activities? Beit Hillel responds that the incident was with harvest, but the same law applies to all. Regarding location, Beit Hillel argues that in the same country people are afraid and investigate, but from one country to another they are not afraid. Beit Shammai counters that caravans are common even between distant places.

sub.text: Beit Shammai's challenge to Beit Hillel
sub.text_en: Beit Shammai's challenge to Beit Hillel
sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai challenges Beit Hillel: according to your position, if only wheat harvest is mentioned, from where do we derive barley harvest and other agricultural activities like picking olives, grapes, cutting figs, and hoeing?
Beit Hillel responds that the incident happened with harvest, but the same law applies to all agricultural activities.
Beit Hillel argues that within the same country people are present and afraid, but from one country to another they are not afraid.
Beit Shammai counters that caravans are common even between distant places, so fear exists everywhere.

items.text: The original incident involving the harvest
items.text_en: The original incident involving the harvest
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel recounts the incident: there were stacks of wheat harvest, ten men went to harvest wheat, a snake bit one and he died, and his wife came and informed the court. They sent and found her words true. At that time they ruled that a woman who says 'my husband died' may remarry or enter yibbum.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel recounts the incident: ten men went to harvest wheat, one was bitten by a snake and died, his wife informed the court, and they ruled that a woman who says 'my husband died' may remarry or undergo יבום (levirate marriage).
The incident continues: ten men went to harvest wheat, a snake bit one and he died, his wife informed the court, and they sent and found her words true.

sub.text: The court's ruling (reported by Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel)
sub.text_en: The court's ruling (reported by Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel)
sub.desc_en: At that time the court ruled that a woman who says 'my husband died' may remarry or enter ייבום (levirate marriage).

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Chananya ben Akiva and the Rabbis regarding the scope of the ruling on passing purification waters
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Chananya ben Akiva and the Rabbis regarding the scope of the ruling on passing purification waters
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Chananya ben Akiva and the Rabbis disagree based on the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. A baraita discusses restrictions on passing purification waters (mei chatat) across the Jordan in a boat, with Rabbi Chananya ben Akiva limiting the restriction to the Jordan and a boat, as in the incident. The Rabbis argue that the restriction applies to all rivers. The Gemara explains that the Rabbis can align with Beit Hillel (who limited based on fear), and Rabbi Chananya ben Akiva can align with Beit Shammai (who limited based on the incident). The incident is then recounted: a man was transporting purification waters in a boat on the Jordan, and an olive-sized piece of a corpse was found stuck to the boat's bottom, leading to the restriction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute between Rabbi Chananya ben Akiva and the Rabbis is based on the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.
A baraita is cited: one may not carry purification waters across the Jordan in a boat; Rabbi Chananya ben Akiva limits the restriction to the Jordan and a boat, as in the incident.
The Gemara infers that the Rabbis follow Beit Shammai (applying the decree to all cases) and Rabbi Chananya ben Akiva follows Beit Hillel (limiting to the exact precedent).
The Rabbis reject the inference, arguing they can align with Beit Hillel: Beit Hillel's reasoning (fear of discovery) applies only to location, but here all rivers are equally risky.

Rabbi Chananya ben Akiva rejects the inference, arguing he can align with Beit Shammai: Beit Shammai's reasoning (woman's exacting investigation) applies to all distances, but here the decree is limited to the exact incident.
The Gemara recounts the incident: a man transporting purification waters in a boat on the Jordan found an olive-sized corpse fragment stuck to the boat, leading to the restriction.

items.text: The Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on the ketubah
items.text_en: The Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on the ketubah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records that Beit Shammai says the woman may remarry and collect her ketubah, while Beit Hillel says she may remarry but not collect her ketubah. Beit Shammai argues: you permitted a severe prohibition (adultery), so why not permit light money? Beit Hillel responds: we found... (the text breaks off).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah records the positions of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding a woman who testifies that her husband died: Beit Shammai says she may remarry and collect her ketubah, while Beit Hillel says she may remarry but not collect her ketubah.
Beit Shammai objects to Beit Hillel: if you permitted a severe prohibition (adultery), why not permit the light matter of money?
Beit Hillel begins their response to Beit Shammai, but the Mishnah text breaks off here.

items.text: Mishnah: Beit Shammai's objection and Beit Hillel's retraction
items.text_en: Mishnah: Beit Shammai's objection and Beit Hillel's retraction
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that brothers do not inherit based on the wife's testimony alone. Beit Shammai objects, arguing from the ketubah clause that if she remarries she gets her ketubah, implying her testimony is trusted. Beit Hillel then retracts and rules like Beit Shammai.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that brothers do not inherit based on the wife's testimony alone.
Beit Shammai objects, arguing from the ketubah clause that if she remarries she gets her ketubah, implying her testimony is trusted.
Beit Hillel retracts and rules like Beit Shammai.

items.text: Gemara: Rav Chisda's question on the yevamah
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Chisda's question on the yevamah
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks: if the widow was a yevamah (levirate widow), her yavam inherits based on her testimony. They (Beit Hillel) derived from the ketubah, but we should derive from the Torah? The Torah says 'he shall rise up on the name of his brother'—and he has risen.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda questions why Beit Hillel derived the yavam's inheritance from the ketubah when the Torah itself says 'he shall rise up on the name of his brother'—and he has risen.
The Gemara cites the verse 'יָקוּם עַל שֵׁם אָחִיו' (he shall rise up on the name of his brother) to support Rav Chisda's point that the yavam's inheritance is Torah-based.

items.text: Rav Nachman: Distinction between requesting permission and ketubah
items.text_en: Rav Nachman: Distinction between requesting permission and ketubah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules: if a woman says 'my husband died, permit me to marry,' they permit her and give her ketubah. If she says 'give me my ketubah,' they do not even permit her to marry, because she came for the ketubah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that if a woman requests permission to remarry, the court permits her and gives her ketubah; if she asks only for her ketubah, they do not even permit her, because she came for the ketubah.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry: Combined request and order of requests
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: Combined request and order of requests
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if she says 'permit me to marry and give me my ketubah,' what is the law? Does mentioning ketubah show she came for it, or does she just say everything? And if she says 'give me my ketubah and permit me to marry,' is it clear she came for the ketubah, or because she doesn't know how to be permitted? The question stands unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if a woman says 'permit me to marry and give me my ketubah,' what is the law — does mentioning the ketubah show she came for it, or does she just say everything she has to say?
The Gemara further asks: if she says 'give me my ketubah and permit me to marry,' is it clear she came for the ketubah, or perhaps she doesn't know how to be permitted?
The question stands unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Mishnah: Who is disqualified from testifying for the widow
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who is disqualified from testifying for the widow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone is believed to testify for her (that her husband died), except for her mother-in-law, her mother-in-law's daughter, her co-wife, her yevamah (sister-in-law), and her husband's daughter. The difference between a get and death is that the document proves itself.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists who is believed to testify for the widow that her husband died, excluding five specific women.
The Mishnah distinguishes between a get (bill of divorce) and death: the document itself proves its validity.

items.text: Gemara: Inquiry about the father-in-law's daughter and the dispute with Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara: Inquiry about the father-in-law's daughter and the dispute with Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the father-in-law's daughter is also disqualified, debating the reason for disqualifying the mother-in-law's daughter. A proof is brought from the Mishnah listing only five women, but Rabbi Yehuda adds two more (the father's wife and the bride). The Sages argue these are already included, and Rabbi Yehuda explains the enmity: the bride hates her mother-in-law for revealing her secrets, and the father's wife hates the husband's daughter for revealing hers. The Sages cite the verse 'As water reflects a face'—mutual hatred. Rabbi Yehuda says that verse applies to Torah matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the daughter of the father-in-law (בת חמיה) is also disqualified, considering two possible reasons for disqualifying the mother-in-law's daughter.

The Gemara raises an alternative reason: the daughter-in-law hates the mother-in-law because she consumes her inheritance, and similarly she might hate the father-in-law's daughter for consuming the inheritance of her husband's house.
The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah listing only five disqualified women that the father-in-law's daughter is not included, as otherwise there would be six.

The Gemara rejects the proof, suggesting that the reason for disqualifying the mother-in-law's daughter applies equally to the father-in-law's daughter, so the Mishnah's count might still be consistent.
The Gemara objects that another Mishnah lists seven disqualified women, and resolves that this is the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda adds the father's wife and the bride to the list of disqualified women.
The Sages object that the father's wife is already included in the category of the husband's daughter, and the bride is already included in the category of the mother-in-law.

Rabbi Yehuda explains the enmity: the mother-in-law hates the bride for consuming her inheritance, but the bride hates the mother-in-law for revealing her secrets to her son; similarly, the husband's daughter hates the father's wife for consuming her mother's inheritance, but the father's wife hates the husband's daughter for revealing her secrets to her father.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda adds two women because the bride hates the mother-in-law for revealing her secrets, and the father's wife hates the husband's daughter for revealing her secrets.
The Sages cite the verse 'As water reflects a face, so the heart of man reflects to man' to argue that mutual hatred is natural and does not require specific reasons.
Rabbi Yehuda responds that the verse about mutual reflection applies specifically to matters of Torah, not to general enmity.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Avya: Inquiry about a later mother-in-law
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Avya: Inquiry about a later mother-in-law
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya reports a question from the West: if a woman becomes a mother-in-law after the fact (i.e., after the husband's death), is she disqualified? Does she anticipate that her son will die and the widow will fall to a yavam, causing enmity, or not?

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Avya reporting a question from the West
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Avya reporting a question from the West
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya reports a question from the West: if a woman becomes a mother-in-law after the fact (i.e., after the husband's death), is she disqualified from testifying? Does she anticipate that her son will die and the widow will fall to a yavam, causing enmity, or not?

items.text: Gemara's challenge from the Mishnah about the woman who says 'My husband died and then my father-in-law died'
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from the Mishnah about the woman who says 'My husband died and then my father-in-law died'
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah where a woman says her husband died and then her father-in-law died, allowing her to remarry and collect her ketubah, but her mother-in-law is forbidden. The Gemara asks why the mother-in-law is forbidden, suggesting it might be because we suspect the woman is lying to spite her mother-in-law, knowing she will suffer later. The Gemara deflects this by saying that case is different because the mother-in-law feels the pain immediately.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah where a woman says her husband died and then her father-in-law died, and asks why the mother-in-law is forbidden, suggesting it is because we suspect the woman is lying to spite her mother-in-law.
The Gemara deflects the challenge by explaining that the case is different because the mother-in-law feels the pain immediately, so the woman's motive to cause future suffering is not applicable.

items.text: Mishnah: Conflicting testimonies about a husband's death
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conflicting testimonies about a husband's death
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases: one witness says 'died' and one says 'did not die' – if she remarried she does not leave; one witness says 'died' and two say 'did not die' – if she remarried she must leave; two say 'died' and one says 'did not die' – even if she did not remarry she may remarry.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of conflicting testimony about a husband's death, ruling that with one witness saying 'died' and one saying 'did not die', if she already married she does not leave; with two against one, she leaves; with two saying 'died' and one 'did not die', she may marry.

items.text: Gemara's question on the first case and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the first case and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the first case distinguishes between whether she remarried or not, since Ulla said that wherever the Torah believed one witness, it is as if there are two, and the words of one witness do not stand against two. The Gemara explains that the Mishnah means: one witness said 'died' and they permitted her to remarry, then another came and said 'did not die' – she does not leave her initial permission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah distinguishes between whether she remarried or not, given Ulla's principle that wherever the Torah believed one witness, it is as if there are two, and the words of one witness do not stand against two.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah means: one witness said 'died' and they permitted her to remarry, then another came and said 'did not die' – she does not leave her initial permission.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the second case with Rabbi Nehemya's principle
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the second case with Rabbi Nehemya's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the second case is not obvious, since one witness cannot stand against two. It explains that the case involves disqualified witnesses, following Rabbi Nehemya who says that wherever the Torah believed one witness, we follow the majority of opinions, and two women are considered like two men against one man. An alternative explanation is given: if a valid witness came initially, even a hundred women are like one witness, so the case is where a woman came initially, and Rabbi Nehemya's principle is applied with two women against one woman, which is like half and half.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the case of one witness saying 'died' against two saying 'not died' is not obvious, since one witness cannot stand against two, and answers that it is needed for disqualified witnesses.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Nechemya rules that wherever the Torah believed one witness, we follow the majority of opinions, and two women against one man are treated like two men against one man.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: if a valid witness came initially, even a hundred women are like one witness, so the case is where a woman came initially.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution with Rabbi Nechemya's principle
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution with Rabbi Nechemya's principle
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the case by applying Rabbi Nechemya's principle: two women against one woman are like half and half, so the case is not obvious.

items.text: Gemara's question on the third case and its novelty
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the third case and its novelty
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the third case teaches, since it seems to be the same as the previous case with Rabbi Nechemya's principle. It answers that one might think we follow the majority only for stringency but not for leniency, so the Mishnah teaches that we do follow the majority even for leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novelty the Mishnah's third case (two say 'died', one says 'did not die') teaches, since it seems identical to the previous case that already applied Rabbi Nechemya's principle of following the majority of opinions.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that the principle of following the majority of opinions (רוב דעות) applies not only for stringency (לחומרא) but also for leniency (לקולא), which one might have thought was excluded.

items.text: Mishnah: Conflicting testimonies from women and from witnesses with different claims
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conflicting testimonies from women and from witnesses with different claims
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one woman says 'died' and another says 'did not die' – the first may remarry and collect her ketubah, the second may not. Then a case where one says 'died' and another says 'was killed' – Rabbi Meir says since they contradict each other they may not remarry, while Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon say since both agree he is not alive they may remarry. Finally, a case of one witness saying 'died' and another saying 'did not die'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the first case: one woman says 'died' and another says 'did not die' – the first may remarry and collect her ketubah, the second may not.

The Mishnah presents the second case: one says 'died' and another says 'was killed' – Rabbi Meir prohibits remarriage due to contradiction, while Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon permit it since both agree he is dead.
The Mishnah introduces the third case: one witness says 'died' and another says 'did not die' (the ruling is not stated in this excerpt).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one woman says 'he died' and another says 'he did not die', the woman may not remarry.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one woman says 'he died' and another says 'he did not die', the woman may not remarry.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'did not die', implying that silence would permit remarriage, but a co-wife cannot testify for her fellow. It answers that the case is necessary to counter the assumption that the second woman is just trying to harm her co-wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifically mentions the case where one woman says 'he did not die', implying that if she were silent, the other would be permitted, but a rival wife (צרה) is generally disqualified from testifying.

The Gemara answers that the case of 'he did not die' is necessary because one might think the woman is merely trying to ruin her rival, saying 'let me die with the Philistines' (תמות נפשי עם פלשתים), so the Mishnah teaches that she is not believed.

items.text: Dispute about the Mishnah's authorship
items.text_en: Dispute about the Mishnah's authorship
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Meir is not mentioned in the Mishnah. Rabbi Elazar says the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, while Rabbi Yochanan says even Rabbi Meir would agree that a woman's statement 'did not die' is not a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Meir's dissenting opinion is not recorded in the first clause of the Mishnah.
Rabbi Elazar answers that the Mishnah is taught according to the dispute of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, who hold that a rival wife is believed.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that even according to Rabbi Meir, in this case he agrees that a woman saying 'he did not die' is not considered a contradiction to the other woman's testimony.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah includes a case of a male witness, which contradicts Rabbi Yochanan's explanation. It concludes that this is a difficulty for Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where a male witness says 'he died' and another says 'he did not die', and a woman says 'he died' and another says 'he did not die' — the woman may not remarry; this is difficult for Rabbi Yochanan's position.
The Gemara concludes that the difficulty remains unresolved (קשיא).

items.text: Second Mishnah: Testimony of a woman and her co-wife or mother-in-law
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Testimony of a woman and her co-wife or mother-in-law
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a woman says her husband died abroad. Rabbi Tarfon permits her to remarry and eat terumah, while Rabbi Akiva prohibits both. The same dispute applies when she says her husband died and then her father-in-law died.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a woman who went overseas with her husband and returns saying he died; Rabbi Tarfon permits her to remarry and take her ketubah, while her co-wife is prohibited, and if the co-wife is an Israelite married to a priest she may eat terumah.
Rabbi Akiva disagrees, ruling that the co-wife must be prohibited from both remarrying and eating terumah to prevent transgression.

The Mishnah presents a parallel case where the woman says her husband died and then her father-in-law died; Rabbi Tarfon permits her to remarry and take her ketubah, while her mother-in-law is prohibited but may eat terumah if she is an Israelite married to a priest, and Rabbi Akiva again prohibits both remarriage and terumah for the mother-in-law.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the need for both cases
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the need for both cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary: in the first case, Rabbi Tarfon's leniency might be due to the co-wife's personal pain, but in the second case he might agree with Rabbi Akiva; conversely, Rabbi Akiva's stringency in the second case might not apply to the first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if only the first case were stated, one might think Rabbi Tarfon's leniency is specific to the co-wife due to her personal pain, but regarding the mother-in-law he might concede to Rabbi Akiva.

Conversely, if only the second case were stated, one might think Rabbi Akiva's stringency is specific to the mother-in-law, but regarding the co-wife he might concede to Rabbi Tarfon; therefore both cases are necessary.

items.text: Ruling and supporting evidence
items.text_en: Ruling and supporting evidence
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that the law follows Rabbi Tarfon. Abaye cites a baraita where a woman's testimony about her son's death is believed, but not about her husband's death, and concludes that we do not suspect her words regarding a co-wife.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Tarfon.
Abaye cites a supporting baraita: if a woman says 'I had a son abroad, my son died and then my husband died' she is believed; if she says 'my husband died and then my son died' she is not believed.

The baraita concludes that we are concerned for her words, and she performs חליצה (levirate release) but does not enter יבום (levirate marriage); this shows that we are concerned for her words but not for the words of a rival wife, supporting the ruling.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Betrothal and Robbery Cases
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Betrothal and Robbery Cases
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: a man who betroths one of five women without knowing which, and a man who robs one of five people without knowing which. Rabbi Tarfon says he may leave a ketubah or the stolen item among them and withdraw, while Rabbi Akiva requires giving a get and ketubah to each woman or paying each person.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the first case: a man who betroths one of five women without knowing which, and Rabbi Tarfon's ruling that he may leave a ketubah among them and withdraw.
Rabbi Akiva disputes Rabbi Tarfon, requiring a get and ketubah for each woman.
The Mishnah presents the second case: a man who robs one of five people without knowing which, and Rabbi Tarfon's ruling that he may leave the stolen item among them and withdraw.
Rabbi Akiva disputes Rabbi Tarfon, requiring payment to each person.

items.text: Gemara's Initial Question on Mishnah's Wording
items.text_en: Gemara's Initial Question on Mishnah's Wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah uses 'betrothed' but not 'had intercourse', and 'robbed' but not 'bought'. It asks who authored the Mishnah, suggesting it is neither the first Tanna nor Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara observes that the Mishnah uses the term 'betrothed' but not 'had intercourse', and 'robbed' but not 'bought', and questions who authored the Mishnah, concluding it is neither the first Tanna nor Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states that Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva did not dispute in the case of betrothal or purchase, but only in cases of intercourse or robbery. This clarifies the dispute's scope.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar stating that Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva did not dispute in the case of betrothal (קידושין), but only in the case of intercourse (ביאה).
The baraita continues, stating that the sages did not dispute in the case of purchase (מקח), but only in the case of robbery (גזילה).

items.text: Gemara's Analysis of the Baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's Analysis of the Baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement that the first Tanna holds they disputed in all cases. It then questions who authored the Mishnah, noting that neither the first Tanna nor Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar would have used the specific terms 'betrothed' and 'robbed'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement that the first Tanna holds they disputed in all cases, and then asks who authored the Mishnah.
The Gemara questions who authored the Mishnah, noting that neither the first Tanna nor Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar would have used the specific terms 'betrothed' and 'robbed'.

items.text: Resolution: Mishnah as Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar with Special Wording
items.text_en: Resolution: Mishnah as Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar with Special Wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is indeed Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, but 'betrothed' refers to betrothal through intercourse, and the terms are chosen to highlight the stringency of Rabbi Akiva (who penalizes even a rabbinic prohibition) and the leniency of Rabbi Tarfon (who does not penalize even a Torah prohibition).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is indeed Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and the term 'betrothed' refers to betrothal through intercourse.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah uses 'betrothed' to highlight Rabbi Akiva's stringency (penalizing even a rabbinic prohibition) and 'stole' to highlight Rabbi Tarfon's leniency (not penalizing even a Torah prohibition).

items.text: Second Mishnah: Credibility of a Woman's Testimony
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Credibility of a Woman's Testimony
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a woman who traveled with her husband and son, and reports their deaths in different orders. She is believed if she says her husband died first (making her free to marry), but not if she says her son died first (which would require levirate marriage). Similar rules apply when she reports a son born abroad or a levir. The Mishnah concludes with general principles about who is not believed regarding death.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a woman who went overseas with her husband and son, and rules on her credibility regarding the order of their deaths.
The Mishnah presents a second case: a woman who says she had a son overseas, and rules on her credibility regarding the order of the son's and husband's deaths.
The Mishnah presents a third case: a woman who says she had a yavam overseas, and rules that she is believed regarding the order of her husband's and yavam's deaths.

The Mishnah presents a fourth case: a woman who went overseas with her husband and yavam, and rules that she is not believed regarding the order of their deaths, with a general principle about who is not believed.

items.text: Rava's Question on Agency in Divorce with a Levir
items.text_en: Rava's Question on Agency in Divorce with a Levir
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman: if one delivers a get to his wife through an agent in the presence of a levir (brother-in-law), is it considered a benefit (since she hates the levir) or a detriment (since she might love him)? Rav Nachman answers from the Mishnah: 'She is suspected and performs chalitzah but does not enter yibbum,' implying it is a detriment.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether delivering a get to one's wife through an agent in the presence of a levir is considered a benefit (since she hates the levir) or a detriment (since she might love him), given the principle that one may benefit a person in their absence but not harm them.

Rav Nachman answers by citing the Mishnah's ruling that a woman who claims her husband died first is suspected and performs חליצה (removal of the shoe) but does not enter יבום (levirate marriage), implying that the get is a detriment, not a benefit.

items.text: Ravina's Question on Agency in a Quarrelsome Marriage
items.text_en: Ravina's Question on Agency in a Quarrelsome Marriage
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rava: if one delivers a get to his wife in a quarrelsome marriage, is it a benefit (since she wants to escape the conflict) or a detriment (since she prefers the stability of marriage)? Rava cites Resh Lakish's proverb that being married is better than being widowed. Abaye, Rav Pappa, and Rav Ashi add proverbs about women preferring even a difficult husband to being alone. A baraita concludes that all such women commit adultery and blame their husbands.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rava whether delivering a get to one's wife in a quarrelsome marriage is a benefit (since she wants to escape the conflict) or a detriment (since she prefers the stability of marriage).
Rava cites Resh Lakish's proverb that it is better to live as a couple than to be a widow, implying the get is a detriment.
Abaye adds a proverb: even a sesame-sized husband is better than being alone, as a woman would rather sit on a bench in the market (i.e., be married) than be isolated.
Rav Pappa adds a proverb: even a husband who is a wool-beater (a lowly trade) is preferable to being alone, as a woman would rather sit at the doorpost than be without a husband.
Rav Ashi adds a proverb: even a husband who is a pot-mender (a lowly trade) is preferable, as a woman does not need extra pot-lids (i.e., she has a husband to provide).
A baraita concludes that all such women commit adultery and blame their husbands, reinforcing that even in a quarrelsome marriage, the wife prefers the marriage to being alone.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a woman whose husband and co-wife went overseas and were told 'your husband died' may not remarry or enter levirate marriage until she knows the co-wife is not pregnant. If she has a mother-in-law, she need not worry; if the mother-in-law left pregnant, she must worry. Rabbi Yehoshua says she need not worry.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule: a woman whose husband and co-wife went overseas and were told 'your husband died' may not remarry or enter levirate marriage until she knows the co-wife is not pregnant.
The Mishnah adds: if the woman has a mother-in-law, she need not worry; but if the mother-in-law left visibly pregnant, she must worry.
Rabbi Yehoshua states that she need not worry at all.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of 'her co-wife'
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of 'her co-wife'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'her co-wife' and explains that it teaches that we worry only about this specific co-wife, not another co-wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by the phrase 'her co-wife'.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that we worry only about this specific co-wife, not another co-wife.

items.text: Question on the prohibition to remarry
items.text_en: Question on the prohibition to remarry
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah prohibits remarriage, given that most women conceive and give birth, so the co-wife is likely not pregnant. It suggests that the Mishnah might follow Rabbi Meir, who is concerned for a minority.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah prohibits remarriage, given that most women conceive and give birth, so the co-wife is likely not pregnant.

items.text: Answer: Rabbi Meir or a majority not present
items.text_en: Answer: Rabbi Meir or a majority not present
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the Mishnah is Rabbi Meir's view, but even the Rabbis would agree here because they follow a majority only when it is present (like nine stores or the Sanhedrin), not a majority that is not present.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling follows Rabbi Meir, who is concerned about a minority.
The Gemara answers that even the Rabbis would agree here, because they follow a majority only when it is present (like nine stores or the Sanhedrin), not a majority that is not present.

items.text: Objection from the case of a minor
items.text_en: Objection from the case of a minor
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the case of a minor boy and girl, where the Rabbis follow a majority that is not present, as taught in a baraita: Rabbi Meir prohibits levirate marriage for minors due to concern they might be sterile, but the Rabbis rely on the majority of minors not being sterile.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the case of a minor boy and girl, where the Rabbis follow a majority that is not present, as introduced by the baraita.
The baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir prohibits levirate marriage for minors, and the Sages question his reasoning.
Rabbi Meir answers that a minor boy might be a סריס (sterile) and a minor girl might be an אילונית (infertile), causing them to violate the prohibition of ערווה (incest).
The Sages hold that one follows the majority (רוב) of minors, and most minors are not sterile or infertile.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah must be following Rabbi Meir's opinion, since the Sages rely on a majority that is not present.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah's latter clause
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah's latter clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if the Mishnah is Rabbi Meir, the latter clause (where a mother-in-law is not a concern) would be problematic, as one should worry about the minority of miscarriages and females. The Gemara answers that since the mother-in-law is established in the marketplace, we do not worry, but the first case is established for levirate marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions that if the Mishnah is attributed to Rabbi Meir, the latter clause (where a mother-in-law is not a concern) is problematic, because one should worry about the minority of miscarriages and females.
The Gemara answers that since the mother-in-law is established in the marketplace, we do not worry, but the first case is established for levirate marriage.

items.text: Rav Nachman and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rabbah bar Avuh says the first case involves a karet prohibition, so they were stringent, while the latter case involves only a negative commandment, so they were lenient. Rava objects that both are Torah prohibitions, and offers an alternative explanation.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rabbah bar Avuh resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the first case, which involves a כרת (karet) prohibition and was treated stringently, from the latter case, which involves only a לאו (negative commandment) and was treated leniently.
Rava objects that both cases involve Torah prohibitions (דאורייתא), so the distinction between a כרת (karet) prohibition and a לאו (negative commandment) is irrelevant.
Rava begins to offer his own alternative explanation for the contradiction, though the full resolution is cut off at the end of the section.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah's first two cases regarding chazakah and rov
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah's first two cases regarding chazakah and rov
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's first case: a chazakah for yibbum and a rov for the market, where the chazakah is not as strong as the rov, but adding a minority of miscarriages creates a tie, so the woman may not marry or enter yibbum. The second case: a chazakah for the market and a rov for the market, making males a double minority, which Rabbi Meir does not worry about.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the first case of the Mishnah: a chazakah for yibbum and a rov for the market, where the chazakah is not as strong as the rov, but adding a minority of miscarriages creates a tie, so the woman may not marry or enter yibbum.
The Gemara explains the second case: a chazakah for the market and a rov for the market, making males a double minority, which Rabbi Meir does not worry about.

items.text: Discussion of the Mishnah's ruling 'she may not marry or enter yibbum' and the dispute between Ze'iri, Rabbi Chanina, and Abaye bar Avin
items.text_en: Discussion of the Mishnah's ruling 'she may not marry or enter yibbum' and the dispute between Ze'iri, Rabbi Chanina, and Abaye bar Avin
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if the Mishnah's prohibition is forever. Ze'iri says she must wait three months for herself and nine for her fellow, and she performs chalitzah in any case. Rabbi Chanina says three for herself and forever for her fellow, and she must perform chalitzah. Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin explain the decree is due to concern that the child might be viable, requiring a proclamation for the priesthood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's prohibition of marriage or יבום (levirate marriage) for the woman is permanent (forever).
Ze'iri answers that she must wait three months for herself and nine for her fellow wife, and she performs חליצה (chalitzah) in any case.
Rabbi Chanina says three months for herself and forever for her fellow, and she must perform חליצה (chalitzah).

sub.text: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin
sub.text_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin
sub.desc_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin explain that the decree is due to concern that the child might be viable, requiring a proclamation (כרוז) for the priesthood.
The Gemara objects that there might be those present at the חליצה (chalitzah) but not at the proclamation, leading to a mistaken assumption that a חלוצה (chalutzah) is permitted to a priest.

items.text: Discussion of the Mishnah's case: 'A son was given to me overseas'
items.text_en: Discussion of the Mishnah's case: 'A son was given to me overseas'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman says 'My son died and then my husband died' she is believed, but if she says 'My husband died and then my son died' she is not believed, yet she performs chalitzah. The Gemara questions why we do not worry that witnesses might come and confirm her words, requiring a proclamation. Rav Pappa answers the case is of a divorcée, and Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna says it is when she says 'I and he hid in a cave.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: a woman who says 'My son died and then my husband died' is believed, but if she says 'My husband died and then my son died' she is not believed, yet she performs חליצה (the release ceremony) and does not enter ייבום (levirate marriage).
The Gemara asks: why not worry that witnesses might come and confirm her words, requiring a proclamation (כרוז) regarding her status for the priesthood?
Rav Pappa answers that the case is of a divorcée (גרושה), who is already prohibited to a priest, so no proclamation is needed.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna answers that the case is when she says 'I and he hid in a cave,' meaning no witnesses could have seen the death, so no proclamation is needed.

items.text: Mishnah: Two yevamot each claiming their husband died
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two yevamot each claiming their husband died
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case of two yevamot, each saying 'My husband died.' Each is forbidden due to the other's husband. If one has witnesses and the other does not, the one with witnesses is forbidden, the other permitted. If one has children and the other does not, the one with children is permitted, the other forbidden. If they entered yibbum and the yevamim died, they are forbidden to marry others; Rabbi Elazar says since they were permitted to the yevamim, they are permitted to all.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of two yevamot each claiming her husband died, establishing that each is forbidden due to the other's husband.
The Mishnah states the rule: if one has witnesses she is forbidden, the other permitted; if one has children she is permitted, the other forbidden.
The Mishnah states that if they entered yibbum and the yevamim died, they are forbidden to marry others.
Rabbi Elazar argues that since they were permitted to the yevamim, they are permitted to all.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah and Rava's inquiry into Rabbi Elazar's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah and Rava's inquiry into Rabbi Elazar's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara adds a Tannaic statement: if one yevamah has witnesses and children and the other has neither, both are permitted. It then repeats the dispute about yibbum. Rava asks whether Rabbi Elazar's reasoning is that a tzarah testifies for her fellow, or that she would not harm herself. The Gemara asks what practical difference this makes.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna adds a baraita: if one yevamah has witnesses and children and the other has neither, both are permitted.
The baraita repeats the Mishnah's case of yevamot who were married and then widowed, and Rabbi Elazar's lenient ruling.
Rava asks whether Rabbi Elazar's reasoning is that a tzarah (צרה, co-wife) testifies for her fellow, or that she would not harm herself.
The Gemara asks what practical difference (נפקא מינה, practical ramification) exists between the two possible reasons.

items.text: Gemara's question about the tzara's testimony
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the tzara's testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the tzara's testimony is accepted because she is believed not to harm herself (if she remarried) or because she is considered a witness for her co-wife (even if not remarried). It cites Rabbi Elazar's statement to infer that the reason is that she would not harm herself, as she only permits the co-wife after she herself has remarried.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses a question: is the tzara's testimony accepted because she is believed as a witness for her co-wife (even if not remarried), or because she would not harm herself (only if remarried)?

The Gemara cites Rabbi Elazar's statement that once the tzara is permitted to remarry, her co-wife is also permitted, and infers that this is only when she has remarried, supporting the reason that she would not harm herself.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Elazar was speaking to the Sages according to their own reasoning: he personally holds that the co-wife is believed even without remarriage, but concedes to them that when she has remarried, she is believed because she would not harm herself, while the Sages suspect she acts like Samson's 'let my soul die with the Philistines.'

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's response to the Sages
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's response to the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar was speaking according to the Sages' reasoning: for himself, the tzara is believed even without remarrying, but for them, he concedes that only if she remarried is she believed, because she would not harm herself. The Sages, however, hold that she acts like Samson's 'let me die with the Philistines' and would harm herself to spite her co-wife.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar's statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar's statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rabbi Elazar was speaking according to the Sages' reasoning: for himself, the tzara is believed even without remarrying, but for them, he concedes that only if she remarried is she believed, because she would not harm herself, while the Sages hold that she acts like Samson's 'let me die with the Philistines' and would harm herself to spite her co-wife.

items.text: Support from a Mishnah and resolution of a concern
items.text_en: Support from a Mishnah and resolution of a concern
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah where a woman who says 'my husband died' may remarry and collect her ketubah, but her co-wife is forbidden. Rabbi Elazar permits the co-wife as well. The Gemara clarifies that this is only after the woman has remarried. It then raises a concern that she might be lying to invalidate the co-wife via a get, but resolves that the case is where she married a priest, so a get would not help.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where a woman who says 'my husband died' may remarry and collect her ketubah, but her co-wife is forbidden; Rabbi Elazar permits the co-wife as well.
The Gemara raises a concern that the woman might be lying, having come with a get, and is scheming to invalidate the co-wife.
The Gemara resolves that the concern applies only if she married an Israelite, but here the case is where she married a priest, so a get would not help.

items.text: Mishnah: Rules for identifying a corpse
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rules for identifying a corpse
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that testimony is only given based on the face with the nose, not on bodily signs or vessels, and only after death is certain. Even if the body is mutilated or eaten, one must wait three days. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava adds that not all people, places, or times are equal.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that testimony is only given based on the face with the nose, not on bodily signs or vessels, and only after death is certain, even if the body is mutilated, one must wait three days.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava adds that not all people, places, or times are equal in determining the reliability of identification.

items.text: Gemara: The requirement of forehead and face with the nose
items.text_en: Gemara: The requirement of forehead and face with the nose
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that both the forehead and the face with the nose are required. Abaye or Rav Kahana derives this from a verse: 'The recognition of their faces testifies against them.'

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that testimony requires both the forehead (פדחת) and facial features with the nose; Abaye (or Rav Kahana) cites the verse 'הכרת פניהם ענתה בם' (their facial recognition testifies against them) as a scriptural source.
Abaye or Rav Kahana derives the requirement from the verse 'The recognition of their faces testifies against them' (Isaiah 3:9).

items.text: Story of Abba bar Marta and the nose test
items.text_en: Story of Abba bar Marta and the nose test
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Abba bar Marta, who owed money to the exilarch's house, attached a piece of clay to his nose with a rag, and when he passed by them, they did not recognize him, illustrating the importance of the nose for identification.

sub.desc_en: A story is told about Abba bar Marta (also Abba bar Minyomi) who owed money to the house of the Exilarch; he disguised himself with a wax nose and passed them unrecognized, illustrating the importance of facial features.

items.text: Debate on whether simanim are de-oraita or de-rabbanan
items.text_en: Debate on whether simanim are de-oraita or de-rabbanan
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's rule that bodily signs are not sufficient for testimony implies that simanim are not de-oraita. A contradiction is raised from a case where a found object with signs is valid. Abaye resolves that the dispute is between Rabbi Eliezer ben Mahabai and the Rabbis. Rava offers two alternative explanations: either all agree simanim are de-oraita, and the dispute is about a mole common among peers, or about a mole that changes after death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's rule that bodily signs are invalid for testimony that simanim (identifying signs) are not de-oraita (of biblical authority).
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita where a found object tied in a bag or ring is valid based on simanim, suggesting simanim are de-oraita.
Abaye resolves that the Mishnah follows the Rabbis (simanim de-rabbanan) and the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Mahabai (simanim de-oraita).
Rava rejects Abaye's framing, arguing all agree simanim are de-oraita; the dispute is whether a mole (שומה) is common among a peer group (בן גילו).
Another version of Rava's view: the dispute is whether a mole changes after death (עשויה להשתנות), not about the status of simanim themselves.

items.text: Dispute over the definition of a conclusive sign
items.text_en: Dispute over the definition of a conclusive sign
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between two opinions: one holds that a distinctive sign (siman muvhak) is valid for identification, while the other holds it is not. This sets up the framework for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute between Mar and Mar concerns whether a distinctive sign (סימן מובהק) is valid for identification.

items.text: Rava's statement and the problem of borrowed items
items.text_en: Rava's statement and the problem of borrowed items
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's view that signs are Torah-law valid by citing a mishnah that accepts signs on the body and clothing. It then addresses concerns about borrowed items (sha'alah) and counterfeit rings, concluding that certain items are not lent due to superstition or risk.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's view that signs are Torah-law valid by citing a mishnah that accepts signs on the body and clothing.
The Gemara explains that signs on the body are distinctive, but signs on clothing are suspect due to borrowing (שאלה).
The Gemara asks: if we suspect borrowing, how can we return a donkey based on saddle signs?
The Gemara answers: people do not lend saddles because it causes superstition (מסקבא) for the donkey.
The Gemara asks: if an item is found tied to a purse, money-bag, or ring, how do we return it?
The Gemara answers: rings are not lent due to fear of counterfeiting; purses and money-bags are not lent due to superstition (ניחוש).
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: clothing signs refer to distinctive colors (white and red), which are not subject to borrowing.

items.text: Contradiction regarding the survival of a mutilated person
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding the survival of a mutilated person
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the mishnah says one can testify about a mutilated person (meguyad), implying he might live, but another source states that a mutilated person does not live, only does not become impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the mishnah implies a mutilated person (מגוייד) can live, but a baraita states that a mutilated person does not live, only does not become impure.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing the mishnah to the Rabbis, who allow testimony about a mutilated person, and the baraita to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who forbids it because the person might recover by cauterization.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing the mishnah to the Rabbis and the baraita to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
The baraita states that the Rabbis allow testimony about a mutilated person, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar forbids it because the person might recover by cauterization.

items.text: Challenge from the case of Asya and the exception of water
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of Asya and the exception of water
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's resolution with a case where a man was thrown into the sea and only his leg returned, and the Sages ruled based on the location of the cut. The Gemara distinguishes that water soothes the wound, allowing survival.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's resolution by citing a case from Asya where a man was thrown into the sea and only his leg returned, and the Sages ruled based on the location of the cut, implying that a severed limb can indicate death even without the body.

The Gemara distinguishes that water soothes the wound, allowing the person to survive even after being severed, so the case of Asya does not contradict the principle that a severed limb normally indicates death.

items.text: Further challenge from a Bedouin's camel and resolutions
items.text_en: Further challenge from a Bedouin's camel and resolutions
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana testifies to seeing a Bedouin cut his camel's leg, yet the camel remained vigorous. Abaye says the camel was weak, and Rava says a heated knife was used, which cauterizes the wound—consistent with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's concern.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier distinction by citing Rabba bar bar Chana's testimony that a Bedouin cut his camel's leg and the camel remained vigorous.
Abaye answers that the camel in Rabba bar bar Chana's story was weak, so the cut did not kill it.
Rava answers that the Bedouin used a heated knife that cauterized the wound, consistent with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's concern about cauterization.

items.text: Testimony about a dying person and the case of slaughter
