items.text_en: Testimony about a dying person and the case of slaughter
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that one may testify about a person whose soul is departing, and if one cut two simanim (organs) and the person fled, testimony is valid. A contradiction arises regarding writing a get, resolved by concern that the wind may have confused the signs.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that testimony about a dying person is valid only when the soul is departing, but from a place where the soul is not departing, testimony is not given.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel (second statement)
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel (second statement)
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda further reports in Shmuel's name that if one cut two simanim (shechita organs) or the majority of them and the person fled, one may testify about his death.

The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel also said that if one cut two simanim and the person gestured to write a get, they may write and give it, implying he is still alive and will eventually die.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by citing Rav Hoshaya's explanation that we are concerned the wind may have confused the simanim, or that the person himself may have confused them, so the case of writing a get is not a proof of continued life.

items.text: Gemara's question on the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava and the Sages
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava and the Sages regarding a person whose death is near. It suggests two scenarios: slaughtering in a house of marble and convulsing, or slaughtering outside without convulsing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava and the Sages regarding a person whose death is near, and suggests two scenarios: slaughtering in a marble house with convulsing, or slaughtering outside without convulsing.

items.text: Inquiry whether Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava is lenient or stringent
items.text_en: Inquiry whether Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava is lenient or stringent
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava argues leniently or stringently. It brings evidence from two incidents where men were rescued from water after several days and their wives were remarried, suggesting leniency. The Gemara distinguishes between water and other cases, noting that water causes swelling but not if there is no wound, and that immediate inspection matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava argues leniently or stringently.
The Gemara brings evidence from two incidents where men were rescued from water after several days and their wives were remarried, suggesting leniency.
The Gemara argues that if Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava is lenient, the incidents align, but if stringent, they conflict, and distinguishes water cases because water causes swelling.
The Gemara resolves that water causes swelling only if there is a wound, and immediate inspection matters, but after delay, swelling occurs.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of falling into water and other dangers
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of falling into water and other dangers
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a man fell into water, whether it has an end or not, his wife is forbidden. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei bring stories of people who fell into water or a cave and were later found alive, and the Sages rule based on the location of the recovered limb.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the ruling that if a man fell into water, whether it has a visible end or not, his wife is forbidden to remarry.
Rabbi Meir brings a story of a man who fell into the Great Well and emerged alive after three days.
Rabbi Yosei brings a story of a blind man who descended to immerse in a cave and was pulled out by his attendant, and they married off their wives after a time sufficient for death.
The Sages bring a story from Asia where only a foot was recovered, and they rule that if the limb is from the knee upward the wife may remarry, but from the knee downward she may not.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita on the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita on the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir forbids the wife in all water cases, while the Sages permit if the water has an end. Abaye defines water that has an end as that which one can see from all four sides.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Meir's position that the wife is forbidden in all water cases, and the Sages' position that she is permitted if the water has an end.
Abaye defines water that has an end as that which one can see from all four sides.

items.text: Incident with Rav Sheila and the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Incident with Rav Sheila and the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rav Sheila permitted the wife of a man who drowned in the Agma deSamkei, but Rav wanted to excommunicate him. Shmuel advised sending a query first. They asked whether such water is considered without end, and Shmuel ruled it is without end. Rav admitted his mistake, and each cited a verse about the other.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheila permitted the wife of a man who drowned in the Agma deSamkei, and Rav proposed to excommunicate him.
Shmuel advised Rav to first send a query to Rav Sheila before excommunicating him.
They sent two questions to Rav Sheila: whether water without end renders the wife forbidden, and whether the Agma deSamkei is considered water with or without end.
Rav Sheila ruled that water without end renders the wife forbidden, and that the Agma deSamkei is considered water without end.
They asked Rav Sheila why he had acted contrary to this ruling by permitting the wife.
Rav Sheila admitted his mistake: he thought the still waters of the Agma were like water with an end, but waves could have pushed the body out, so it is considered without end.
Shmuel cited a verse praising Rav for being a righteous man who was saved from error, and Rav cited a verse praising Shmuel for providing wise counsel.

items.text: Rabbi's story about a fisherman and the ruling on water with an end
items.text_en: Rabbi's story about a fisherman and the ruling on water with an end
items.desc_en: Rabbi relates a story of two fishermen, one who entered a fish cave and was thought dead, but emerged the next day. Rabbi praises the Sages' ruling that water with an end permits the wife. The Gemara questions why we don't worry about fish caves in such water, and answers that fish caves are uncommon in water that has an end.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi relates a story of a fisherman who entered a fish cave, was presumed dead, but emerged the next day, praising the Sages' ruling that water with an end permits the wife.
The Gemara questions why we don't worry about fish caves in water that has an end, given the story.
The Gemara answers that fish caves are uncommon in water that has an end, so there is no concern.

items.text: Rav Ashi's exception for a Torah scholar
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's exception for a Torah scholar
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi suggests that the ruling that water without an end forbids the wife applies only to an ordinary person, but not to a Torah scholar, because if he emerged, there would be a report. The Gemara rejects this, stating that the distinction is only between after the fact and ab initio.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi proposes that the ruling that water without an end forbids the wife applies only to an ordinary person, but not to a Torah scholar.
Rav Ashi explains that if a Torah scholar emerged, there would be a report (קָלָא), so his wife may be permitted.

The Gemara rejects Rav Ashi's distinction, stating that there is no difference between an ordinary person and a Torah scholar; the distinction is only between after the fact (בדיעבד) and ab initio (לכתחילה).

items.text: Stories of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Akiva, and a baraita on other dangers
items.text_en: Stories of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Akiva, and a baraita on other dangers
items.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel recounts seeing a ship break and later finding Rabbi Akiva alive, who survived on a plank. Rabbi Akiva tells of Rabbi Meir being saved by waves. Both praise the Sages' ruling. A baraita discusses testimony for falling into a pit of lions or a pit of snakes and scorpions, with Rabbi Yehuda ben Baira being stringent.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel recounts seeing a ship break and later finding Rabbi Akiva alive, who survived on a plank by nodding his head to each wave.
Rabban Gamliel praises the Sages' ruling that water with an end permits the wife, while water without an end forbids her.
Rabbi Akiva tells of seeing Rabbi Meir's ship wrecked and how Rabbi Meir was saved by waves tossing him to dry land.
Rabbi Akiva praises the Sages' ruling on water with and without an end.
A baraita states that one who falls into a pit of lions is not testified about, but into a pit of snakes and scorpions is; Rabbi Yehuda ben Baira is stringent even for the latter.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Tanna Kamma's view
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Tanna Kamma's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Tanna Kamma does not require a rope or ladder for a person who fell into a lime pit, suggesting that perhaps he is a colleague (חבר) who would be lifted out. The Tanna Kamma holds that the person would be injured by the lime.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Tanna Kamma does not require a rope or ladder for a person who fell into a lime pit, suggesting that perhaps he is a colleague (חבר) who would be lifted out, and explains that the Tanna Kamma holds that the person would be injured by the lime.

items.text: Baraita on falling into a furnace or cauldron
items.text_en: Baraita on falling into a furnace or cauldron
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one falls into a furnace of fire, witnesses may testify about his death. For a cauldron full of wine or oil, they may testify. Rabbi Acha says: for oil they testify because it burns, for wine they do not because it extinguishes. The Sages respond that initially it extinguishes but eventually burns.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited listing cases where one may testify about a person's death: falling into a furnace or a cauldron of wine or oil, with a dispute about whether wine extinguishes the fire initially.
The baraita adds that for a cauldron full of wine or oil, witnesses may testify.
Rabbi Acha distinguishes: for oil they testify because it burns, for wine they do not because it extinguishes.
The Sages respond that wine initially extinguishes but eventually burns, so testimony is valid.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's miracle story and its explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's miracle story and its explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir cites a story of a man who fell into a great pit and was saved by a miracle. The Sages object that one does not cite miracles. The Gemara explains the miracle: he did not sleep for three days, as per Rabbi Yochanan's statement. Rav Kahana explains that there were layers of rock, and the Rabbis say it was marble; Rabbi Meir holds it is impossible not to doze slightly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir cites a story of a man who fell into a great pit and was saved by a miracle; the Sages object that one does not cite miracles.
The Gemara asks what the miracle was, rejecting the possibility that he did not eat or drink, citing a verse where fasting is possible.
The Gemara explains that the miracle was that he did not sleep for three days, citing Rabbi Yochanan's statement that one who vows not to sleep for three days is flogged and must sleep immediately.
Rav Kahana explains that there were layers of rock, and the Rabbis say it was marble; Rabbi Meir holds it is impossible not to doze slightly, resolving the dispute.

items.text: Story of Nechunya's daughter and Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa
items.text_en: Story of Nechunya's daughter and Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa
items.desc_en: A story is told about the daughter of Nechunya the well-digger who fell into a great pit. They informed Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, who said she was safe and later that she had ascended. She said a ram and an old man led her out. When asked if he was a prophet, he said no, but that the righteous one's offspring should not stumble in his work. Rabbi Abba adds that his son still died of thirst, as God is exacting with those close to Him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts the story of Nechunya the well-digger's daughter falling into a great pit, and Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's three-hour progression from declaring her safe to announcing she had ascended.

Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa asks his daughter who rescued her, she reports a ram and an old man led her out, and he explains to the people that he is not a prophet but that the righteous one's offspring should not stumble in his work.
Rabbi Abba adds that despite the miracle, Nechunya's son died of thirst, citing the verse that God is exacting with those close to Him, and Rabbi Chanina supports this with another verse.

items.text: Mishnah: Testimony from women and children
items.text_en: Mishnah: Testimony from women and children
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that even if one hears women saying 'So-and-so died,' it is sufficient. Rabbi Yehuda says even from children saying they are going to eulogize and bury him, whether they intend or not. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava says: for a Jew, even if he intends; for a non-Jew, if he intends, his testimony is not valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that even hearing women say 'So-and-so died' is sufficient testimony.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that even hearing from children who say they are going to eulogize and bury a person suffices, whether they intend or not.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava distinguishes: for a Jew, even if he intends, it is valid; for a non-Jew, if he intends, his testimony is not valid.

items.text: Gemara's clarification on children's testimony
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification on children's testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the children might not have gone. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains they say 'We are coming from eulogizing and burying So-and-so.' Another concern is that they might be referring to a locust named after him; the Gemara answers they specify that certain rabbis and eulogizers were there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the children might not have actually gone to the eulogy and burial.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that the children say 'We are coming from eulogizing and burying So-and-so,' confirming they actually went.
The Gemara raises a concern that the children might be referring to a locust named after the deceased, not the actual person.
The Gemara answers that the children specify that certain rabbis and eulogizers were present, confirming it is the actual person.

items.text: Distinction between intent to permit and intent to testify for a non-Jew
items.text_en: Distinction between intent to permit and intent to testify for a non-Jew
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says the Mishnah's rule applies only when the non-Jew intends to permit the woman, but if he intends to testify, his testimony is valid. Rav Yosef explains how to know: if he comes to court and says 'So-and-so died, marry off his wife,' that is intent to permit; if he says 'died' simply, that is intent to testify. Reish Lakish agrees, but Rabbi Yochanan cites a case where the Sages did not agree.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel distinguishes the Mishnah's rule: it applies only when the non-Jew intends to permit the woman, but if he intends to testify, his testimony is valid.
Rav Yosef explains how to determine the non-Jew's intent: if he says 'So-and-so died, marry off his wife,' that is intent to permit; if he says 'died' simply, that is intent to testify.
Reish Lakish agrees with the same distinction between intent to permit and intent to testify.
Rabbi Yochanan objects, citing a case in Oshaya bar Rabbi where the Sages did not agree with this distinction.

items.text: Cases of non-Jewish testimony given incidentally
items.text_en: Cases of non-Jewish testimony given incidentally
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case is when the non-Jew speaks incidentally (מסיח לפי תומו). Examples include a non-Jew saying 'Who needs Chiyya? Chiyya died,' and Rav Yosef married off his wife. Another case: 'Woe to the swift horseman who died in Pumbedita,' and Rav Yosef (or Rava) married off his wife. A case of Chasa drowning: Rav Nachman said 'By God, the fish have eaten Chasa from his words,' and his wife remarried without objection. Rav Ashi deduces that for waters without end, the wife is forbidden initially but if she married, she is not removed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to find a case where a non-Jew's testimony is invalid, and answers that it is when he speaks incidentally (מסיח לפי תומו).

The Gemara brings two cases: a non-Jew saying 'Who needs Chiyya? Chiyya died,' and Rav Yosef married off his wife; and another saying 'Woe to the swift horseman who died in Pumbedita,' and Rav Yosef (or Rava) married off his wife.

The Gemara brings a case of Chasa drowning: Rav Nachman said 'By God, the fish have eaten Chasa from his words,' and his wife remarried without objection; Rav Ashi deduces that for waters without end, the wife is forbidden לכתחילה (the ideal standard) but if she married, she is not removed.

items.text: Story of a non-Jew threatening to kill a Jew
items.text_en: Story of a non-Jew threatening to kill a Jew
items.desc_en: A non-Jew told a Jew to cut grass and throw it to his animals on Shabbat, or he would kill him as he killed a certain Jew who refused to cook for him. The Jew's wife heard and came before Abaye.

sub.desc_en: A story is told of a gentile who threatened to kill a Jew unless he killed an animal on Shabbat, and the gentile mentioned killing another Jew who refused to cook for him on Shabbat; the wife heard and came before Abaye.

items.text: Gentile's report of a death
items.text_en: Gentile's report of a death
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava sends a woman to Rav Yosef, who cites a mishnah about a gentile selling produce and claiming it is orlah—his words are disregarded as self-serving. Then three stories are brought where a gentile reported the death of Jews, and the courts permitted their wives to remarry based on that report.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava sends a woman to Rav Yosef, describing him as sharp as a knife.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's citation of a mishnah
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's citation of a mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a mishnah where a gentile's self-serving claim about produce being ערלה (orlah) is disregarded, implying a gentile's report about a death is similarly unreliable unless disinterested.
Abba Yudan of Tzaydan reports a case where a gentile's report of a Jew's death led the court to permit the wife to remarry.
Two more cases are cited where a gentile's report of multiple deaths led to the wives being permitted to remarry.

items.text: Mishnah: Testimony by lamp light and bat kol
items.text_en: Mishnah: Testimony by lamp light and bat kol
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that testimony may be given by lamp or moonlight, and a woman may remarry based on a bat kol. Two stories illustrate this: a man on a mountain declared a death, and another man bitten by a snake declared his own impending death, and in both cases the wives were permitted to remarry.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that testimony may be given by lamp or moonlight, and a woman may remarry based on a bat kol (heavenly echo).
The mishnah relates a story of a man on a mountain who declared another's death, and when no one was found there, the wife was permitted to remarry.
The mishnah relates another story of a man in Tzalmón who declared his own impending death from a snake bite, and the wife was permitted to remarry.

items.text: Gemara: Bat kol and concern for demons
items.text_en: Gemara: Bat kol and concern for demons
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Shmuel teaches that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether a woman may remarry based on a bat kol. The Gemara questions whether the speaker might have been a demon. Rav Yehuda says they saw his shadow; but demons also have shadows. Rabbi Chanina reports from Yonatan the demon that demons have a shadow but not a double shadow.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Shmuel cites a baraita where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether a woman may remarry based on a bat kol, and the Gemara clarifies that the anonymous mishnah ruling 'no remarrying' follows Beit Shammai.

The Gemara questions whether the speaker might have been a demon, and Rav Yehuda in Rav's name answers that they saw his shadow, but the Gemara objects that demons also have shadows, so they saw a double shadow.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanina citing Yonatan the demon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina citing Yonatan the demon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina reports from Yonatan the demon that demons have a shadow but not a double shadow, resolving the concern that the speaker might have been a demon.

items.text: Concern for a rival wife and the ruling of Beit Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Concern for a rival wife and the ruling of Beit Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that the woman might be a rival wife (tzarah) who is not believed. The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael rules that in a time of danger, a woman may write and give a get even without identification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that the woman might be a rival wife (צרה) who is not believed to testify about her husband's death.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael rules that in a time of danger, a woman may write and give a גט (bill of divorce) even without identification, resolving the concern.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's report and the dispute about a single witness
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva's report and the dispute about a single witness
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva recounts that Nechemya of Beit Dli told him that only Yehuda ben Bava permitted remarrying based on one witness in Eretz Yisrael. Rabbi Akiva confirmed this and later reported to Rabban Gamliel, who was pleased. Rabban Gamliel then recalled that he had permitted the wives of those killed at Tel Arza to remarry based on one witness, and the practice was established to accept testimony from a witness who heard from another, from a slave, a woman, or a maidservant. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree, and Rabbi Akiva adds that a woman, slave, maidservant, or relative is not believed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva recounts that Nechemya of Beit Dli told him that only Yehuda ben Bava permitted remarrying based on one witness in Eretz Yisrael, and that he confirmed this and was asked to convey a tradition from Rabban Gamliel the Elder permitting it.

sub.text: Mishnah (Rabbi Akiva's report to Rabban Gamliel)
sub.text_en: Mishnah (Rabbi Akiva's report to Rabban Gamliel)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva reports the matter to Rabban Gamliel, who is pleased and says they have found a colleague for Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava.

sub.text: Mishnah (Rabban Gamliel's recollection and the established practice)
sub.text_en: Mishnah (Rabban Gamliel's recollection and the established practice)
sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel recalls permitting the wives of those killed at Tel Arza to remarry based on one witness, establishing the practice of accepting testimony from a witness who heard from another, a slave, a woman, or a maidservant; Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree, and Rabbi Akiva adds that a woman, slave, maidservant, or relative is not believed.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction in Rabbi Akiva's position on a woman's testimony
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction in Rabbi Akiva's position on a woman's testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Akiva's ruling that a woman is not believed, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says in Rabbi Akiva's name that a woman is believed to bring her get a fortiori. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: before the practice was established, women were not believed; after it was established, they are believed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Akiva can rule that a woman is not believed to testify about her husband's death, given a contradictory baraita.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reports in Rabbi Akiva's name that a woman is believed to bring her get (גט) a fortiori (קל וחומר).
The Gemara distinguishes: the baraita refers to women in general, who are believed, while Rabbi Akiva's ruling refers to the specific women whom the Sages declared unreliable.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: before the practice of relying on a woman's testimony was established (החזיקו), women were not believed; after it was established, they are believed.

items.text: Mishnah: The innkeeper's testimony and the response
items.text_en: Mishnah: The innkeeper's testimony and the response
items.desc_en: The mishnah recounts that the Sages told Rabbi Akiva about a case where Levi's sons left a sick companion at an inn, and the innkeeper said he died and she buried him, and the court permitted his wife to remarry. They argued that a priest's wife should be believed like the innkeeper. Rabbi Akiva responded that when she is like the innkeeper—who produced the man's staff, bag, and Torah scroll—she is believed.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the Sages telling Rabbi Akiva about a case where Levi's sons left a sick companion at an inn, and the innkeeper said he died and she buried him, and the court permitted his wife to remarry.
The Sages argue that a priest's wife should be believed like the innkeeper, using a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument.
Rabbi Akiva responds that when the priest's wife is like the innkeeper—who produced the man's staff, bag, and Torah scroll—she is believed.

items.text: Explanation of the innkeeper's testimony
items.text_en: Explanation of the innkeeper's testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the innkeeper's testimony was considered valid. Rav Kahana explains she was a gentile who spoke unsolicited, identifying the man's stick, bag, and grave. The Gemara addresses the apparent contradiction that the witnesses asked her 'Where is our friend?' and explains she cried upon seeing them, so they asked and she replied.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the innkeeper's testimony was considered valid despite her being a gentile.
Rav Kahana explains that the innkeeper was a gentile who spoke unsolicited (מסיחה לפי תומה), identifying the man's stick, bag, and grave.
A baraita taught by Abba brei d'Rav Minyomi bar Chiyya supports Rav Kahana's explanation.
The Gemara objects that the witnesses asked her 'Where is our friend?', which seems to contradict her unsolicited testimony.
The Gemara resolves that she cried upon seeing them, so they asked and she replied, preserving the unsolicited nature.

items.text: First story of Rabbi Tarfon accepting testimony
items.text_en: First story of Rabbi Tarfon accepting testimony
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts a man who testified before Rabbi Tarfon about a woman's husband. The witness described how they were traveling, a troop pursued them, the man hung from an olive branch and repelled the troop. The witness called him 'Aryeh' and the man explained his name was Yochanan ben Yehonatan, called Aryeh of Kfar Shichya. Later he died, and Rabbi Tarfon permitted the wife to remarry.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a story of a man who came to testify before Rabbi Tarfon about a woman's husband, describing how they traveled together, were pursued by a troop, and the husband climbed an olive branch and repelled them.

The witness recounts calling the man 'Aryeh', the man explaining his name is Yochanan ben Yehonatan called Aryeh of Kfar Shichya, and that he later died, after which Rabbi Tarfon permitted the wife to remarry.

items.text: Second story and Rabbi Tarfon's cross-examination
items.text_en: Second story and Rabbi Tarfon's cross-examination
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Tarfon did not require interrogation in the first story, citing another baraita where he did cross-examine a witness. In that story, the witness described a fig branch, and Rabbi Tarfon repeatedly questioned him about the name, confirming it was Yochanan ben Yehonatan Aryeh of Kfar Shichya, then permitted the wife to remarry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Tarfon did not require interrogation in the first story, citing a baraita where he did cross-examine a witness about a fig branch.

The baraita recounts the witness's testimony: he and the deceased were attacked, the deceased defended them, and the witness called him 'Aryeh,' leading to the identification as Yochanan ben Yonatan Aryeh of Kfar Shichya.
Rabbi Tarfon repeatedly questioned the witness about the exact name, confirming it was Yochanan ben Yonatan Aryeh of Kfar Shichya, and then permitted the wife to remarry.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about interrogation in marriage cases
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about interrogation in marriage cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the two stories to a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Akiva holds that witnesses for marriage cases are not interrogated, while Rabbi Tarfon holds they are. They argue over Rabbi Chanina's principle that Torah law requires interrogation for both monetary and capital cases, but monetary cases were exempted to avoid discouraging lenders. The dispute is whether marriage cases are like monetary cases (due to the ketubah) or like capital cases (due to permitting a married woman).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the two stories to a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Akiva holds that witnesses for marriage cases are not interrogated, while Rabbi Tarfon holds they are.

The Gemara explains that the dispute is based on Rabbi Chanina's principle that Torah law requires interrogation for both monetary and capital cases, citing the verse 'מִשְׁפַּט אֶחָד יִהְיֶה לָכֶם' (one law shall be for you).
The Gemara explains that monetary cases were exempted from interrogation to avoid discouraging lenders (שֶׁלֹּא תִּנְעוֹל דֶּלֶת בִּפְנֵי לֹוִין).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the dispute's basis
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the dispute's basis
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: one opinion (Rabbi Akiva) holds that marriage cases are like monetary cases because of the ketubah (כְּתוּבָּה), while the other (Rabbi Tarfon) holds they are like capital cases because they permit a married woman (שָׁרֵינַן אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ).

items.text: Concluding statement on Torah scholars increasing peace
items.text_en: Concluding statement on Torah scholars increasing peace
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Chanina states that Torah scholars increase peace in the world, citing the verse 'And all your children shall be taught of the Lord, and great shall be the peace of your children.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina concludes that Torah scholars increase peace in the world, citing the verse 'And all your children shall be taught of the Lord, and great shall be the peace of your children.'
